column2:
To die down; to lessen in force or intensity.
To decrease in force or intensity — and, transitively, to reduce something to a lower level (abate a nuisance, abate the rent).

What abates is a pressure, not a quantity: storms, pain, fever, noise, panic, criticism, enthusiasm. You wouldn't say a crowd abated, but the crowd's fury would. It also carries a sense of relief — the thing was pressing on you and has eased off. Register is a notch above plain speech: a newsreader says the floodwaters abated; your friend says the rain let up. Watch for unabated, which is the form you'll meet most often on the test — "the shelling continued unabated" = no let-up at all.
⚠️ abate ≠ abet.
- abate = die down, lessen
- abet = help someone do wrong (as in aid and abet)

One letter, opposite worlds: a storm abates; an accomplice abets.
Wait with bated breath — bated is just abated with its head cut off: breath beaten down to nothing.
Bated breath isn't less breath, it's breath held under pressure — exactly the kind of force-easing that abate describes.
1. Only when the monsoon abated did the villagers venture back to inspect what the water had taken.
2. Give the ibuprofen twenty minutes — the throbbing should abate enough for you to sleep.
Tax abatement is everyday property-market vocabulary: a city knocks down your property tax for a few years to lure you into building there. Same word, same idea — the burden beaten down.
Old French abattre = "to beat down" (Latin battuere, to beat). The storm is literally beaten flat.

That root is a GRE goldmine: battle, batter, combat, debate (beat an argument about), rebate (a beating-back of the price), and abattoir — the slaughterhouse, where things are beaten down.

Deviating abnormally from the normal or expected course.
Departing from the normal, expected, or proper course — abnormal, deviant, off-pattern.

The word wears a lab coat. Unusual is neutral, weird is casual, but aberrant measures you against a standard and reports that you failed it: aberrant cells, aberrant data, aberrant behaviour. It's the vocabulary of doctors, statisticians and disciplinary reports, so it carries a faint chill — the thing isn't just different, it's wrong in a way that needs explaining.
⚠️ aberrant ≠ abhorrent.
- aberrant = deviating from the norm (clinical)
- abhorrent = repugnant, morally disgusting (emotional)

Aberrant conduct puzzles you; abhorrent conduct sickens you.
ab-ERR-ant — the word literally has err in the middle: it has erred away from the norm.
Stress the err when you say it and you've said the definition out loud.
1. The audit flagged a handful of aberrant transactions, each one a small departure from a decade of predictable ledgers.
2. One aberrant night out doesn't make you a party animal, mate.
Photographers fight chromatic aberration — the purple-green fringing you get when a lens lets colours wander off to slightly different focal points. Same root, visible on your screen.
Latin ab- (away) + errāre (to wander) — literally wandering off.

That root is a GRE goldmine: err, error, erratic, errant, erroneous, knight-errant (a knight who wanders looking for adventures), and arrant nonsense.

To help or encourage someone in doing wrong.
To help or encourage someone in doing something wrong — supplying the means, the cover, or the push.

The word is welded to wrongdoing: you can assist a rescue, but you cannot abet one. And it isn't passive help — abetting leans toward egging on, the encouragement that makes the deed happen, which is why it sits one notch guiltier than "helped." In practice it rarely travels alone; the phrase is aid and abet, where aid covers the hands and abet covers the mouth.
⚠️ abet ≠ abate.
- abet = egg someone on into wrongdoing
- abate = die down, lessen (the storm abated)
A-bet: you don't commit the crime — you bet on the guy who does.
The abettor stays one step back, funding or urging or driving the getaway car, which is exactly why the law needs a word other than commit.
1. The bank's compliance officer was accused of abetting the fraud by waving through transfers he knew were fictitious.
2. I'm on a diet, so don't abet me — hide the biscuits.
"Aiding and abetting" is the charge read out in every courtroom scene and police procedural — the standard formula for people who didn't pull the trigger but made sure it got pulled.
Old French abeter = "to hound on, incite" — literally to bait, as in setting a dog on something. Same root as English bait and bite: the abettor is the one snapping at your heels until you go through with it.

Temporary suspension; paused pending something, not cancelled.
A state of temporary suspension — something real and still-existing whose operation has been parked, pending a decision, an event, or an heir.

Cancelled kills a thing; dormant is just natural quiet. Abeyance is deliberate and conditional: someone with authority pressed pause, and something specific is expected to restart it. The word is stiffly formal — law, parliaments, boardrooms, HR letters — and lives almost entirely inside the frozen phrases "in abeyance" and "held in abeyance." You rarely meet it in the wild as a bare noun.
⚠️ abeyance ≠ obeisance (oh-BAY-sunss) — a deep bow or gesture of submission. Nearly identical sound, unrelated sense: one pauses a matter, the other bends the knee.
Held in a-BAY-ance = held at bay — not driven off, just kept waiting at a distance.
The sound hook carries the nuance: nothing has been resolved or destroyed, it's simply been stopped where it stands until someone lets it come forward.
1. The peerage fell into abeyance in 1712, there being two equal claimants and no way to choose between them.
2. They're keeping the whole rebrand in abeyance until we see what the lawyers say.
Standard courtroom and HR wording: a ruling held in abeyance pending appeal, a disciplinary case held in abeyance pending investigation — if you ever see the word at work, it will be in that exact phrase.
Old French abeance, "a gaping, an expectation," from baer = to gape, to stand open. A medieval estate in abeyance was thought of as sitting open-mouthed, waiting for its rightful owner to appear.

Same baer gives English bay in bay window — an opening in a wall.

To hate with a shudder of moral disgust.
To hate something so deeply that it disgusts you — to recoil from it.

This is the top of the hatred scale, and it's moral, not personal. You dislike a colleague, you hate Mondays, but you abhor cruelty, torture, hypocrisy — practices and principles rather than people. It's formal, a little lofty, and it says as much about the speaker's values as about the thing: whoever abhors something is announcing where their line is.
⚠️ abhorrent ≠ aberrant. Abhorrent = loathsome, disgusting. Aberrant = straying from the normal type. An aberrant result is just odd; an abhorrent one is repellent.
ab-HOR — you back away (ab-) in horror.
The word literally has horror sitting inside it, which is exactly the intensity it carries — not mild distaste but a physical flinch.
1. The treaty's framers abhorred the very idea of a standing army, seeing in it the seed of tyranny.
2. I abhor group projects — three people vanish and one of us does the whole thing at 2am.
"Nature abhors a vacuum." The old Aristotelian maxim you've heard used about everything from politics to office gossip — nature doesn't merely dislike empty space, it rushes in to destroy it.
Latin ab- (away from) + horrēre (to bristle, to shudder) — the hair standing up on your arms. Same root gives you horror, horrid, horrendous, horrific, and abhorrent.

To tolerate, to stick to, or to remain and endure.
Three live senses, all descended from one idea — to stay put:
1. To tolerate / put up with — I can't abide his whining.
2. abide by — to stick to a rule, ruling, or promise.
3. To remain, endure, dwell (archaic/biblical) — a faith that abides.

Sense 1 almost never appears un-negated. Nobody says "I abide his whining"; they say can't abide, and it lands harder and more personally than can't stand — it suggests a settled, temperamental refusal rather than a flash of irritation. Sense 3 carries a King-James solemnity: what abides is what outlasts. And abide by is the one form fully at home in a contract or a courtroom.
You abide in an abode — so what you can't abide, you can't live with.
Same root, same idea of staying put: an abode is where you remain, and to abide something is to let it remain near you.
1. The treaty held for a century, its terms abided by even during open hostilities.
2. She can't abide people who reply with 'per my last email'.
"The Dude abides." — the closing line of The Big Lebowski, and a perfect gloss on sense 3: he doesn't win anything, he just endures.
Old English ābīdan = "to wait, remain" — from bīdan, "to bide," which still survives in bide your time. The same root gives abode: the place where you remain.

That's why the senses hang together — tolerating something is letting it stay, and abiding by a rule is standing by it.

column2:
Degraded to the lowest point; wretched or grovelling.
1. Sunk to the lowest possible state — utterly wretched, hopeless, degraded: abject poverty, abject misery, abject failure.
2. Of a person's behaviour: grovelling, self-abasing, without a shred of dignity: an abject apology, abject surrender.

Abject isn't just a strong "very bad." It marks a loss of dignity — the thing or person has been brought so low that there's nothing left to salvage. Extreme poverty is a measurement; abject poverty is degrading. And when it describes behaviour it turns faintly contemptuous: an abject apology is one that crawls, and the speaker rather despises the crawling.
Abject only ever marries misery — abject poverty, abject terror, abject failure, abject apology. There is no abject joy.
It's not a general intensifier you can bolt onto anything, but a word that says this has hit the bottom and lost its dignity there.
1. The report described families living in abject squalor, without water, power, or any prospect of relief.
2. He sent an abject three-page apology, which somehow made everyone think less of him.
"Abject poverty" is near-fixed in news and charity-appeal language — the UN, Oxfam, and every foreign-desk report reach for it. If you've heard the word at all, that's the phrase it came in.
Latin ab- (away, down) + jacere (to throw) → abjectus, "thrown down." The abject person has been cast to the floor.

That root is a GRE goldmine: eject (throw out), reject (throw back), project (throw forward), inject, dejected (thrown down in spirit), conjecture (throw ideas together), trajectory (the path of a throw).

column2:
To renounce something solemnly, usually under oath.
To renounce, repudiate, or give up something formally and solemnly — a belief, a claim, a loyalty, a habit — usually on the record and under oath.

You can quit a habit privately. To abjure it is to disown it out loud, in a way that binds you: a heretic abjures his heresy, a new citizen abjures foreign allegiance, a reformed man abjures drink. The word carries the weight of ceremony, and often a whiff of pressure — someone made you say it. Compare renounce (neutral, can be quiet) and recant (specifically taking back something you said); abjure covers what you believed in or were bound to.
⚠️ abjure ≠ adjure.
- abjure = swear away — you reject it
- adjure = swear at someone — you earnestly urge or command them

She abjured her old party; then she adjured her friends to leave it too.
Ab- (away, as in absent, abduct) + -jure (swear, as in perjure) — you don't just drop it, you swear it away, out loud.
The -jure is what makes it public and binding: abjuring is a ceremony, not a quiet change of heart.
1. The treaty obliged every signatory to abjure the use of force in settling territorial claims.
2. He's abjured caffeine about four times now, and the announcements are getting less convincing.
Galileo, hauled before the Inquisition in 1633, was forced to abjure his belief that the Earth moves around the Sun — kneeling, reading the renunciation aloud, in the classic textbook scene.
Latin ab- (away) + jūrāre (to swear), from jūs, jūris = law, oath.

That root is a GRE goldmine: perjure (swear falsely), jury (sworn panel), jurisdiction (where your law speaks), jurisprudence, conjure (originally: swear together), and abjure's twin adjure.

column2:
To exist in great numbers; to be plentiful, even overflowing.
To exist in great numbers or great quantity — to be plentiful to the point of overflow. Two shapes: opportunities abound (the things abound), or the river abounds in fish (the place abounds in/with them).

It is stronger than "there are many." Abound implies the supply is past counting — teeming, everywhere you look. It's also strictly intransitive: things abound, but you can never abound something. The word itself is neutral and slightly bookish, so it takes its colour from its subject: wildflowers abound is lush, errors abound is damning, and rumours abound is the journalist's polite way of saying nobody has checked.
abound ≈ "all around" — not just present, but present all around you.
The near-rhyme carries the nuance: abundance plus everywhere-ness, not a mere count.
1. Theories about the collapse abound, though hard evidence remains scarce.
2. Don't stress about lunch — cheap noodle places abound round here.
"Rumours abound" is a newsroom reflex — you'll meet it in headlines and match reports far more often than in conversation.
Latin abundāre = "to overflow" — ab- (off, away) + unda (wave). The wave breaks past its banks: too much, spilling over.

That unda pays out across the exam: abundant, inundate (flood in), undulate (move in waves), redundant (literally "overflowing" — surplus to need).

🚫 Nothing to do with bound. No leaping, no boundary.

Harsh and grating in manner; literally, surface-scraping.
Literally: capable of scraping or wearing down a surface — sandpaper, grit, steel wool. As a noun, the scratchy substance itself.
Of a person or manner: harsh, rough-edged, irritating to deal with.

The metaphor does the work: an abrasive person doesn't wound you, they wear on you. The fault is texture, not malice — blunt, tactless, no social cushioning. Which is why it's the standard HR euphemism for someone effective and unpleasant: "brilliant, but abrasive." Compare caustic (burns, and means to) or vicious (aims to hurt); abrasive is friction, often unintentional and usually chronic.
abrasive ≈ a-BRACE-ive — you brace yourself before the meeting.
Not because they'll destroy you, but because half an hour of that scraping leaves you raw.
1. His feedback was accurate in every particular and abrasive in every syllable; the junior staff stopped submitting drafts.
2. Don't take it personally — she's like that with everyone, just a bit abrasive before her second coffee.
Read the back of a bathroom cleaner or a whitening toothpaste: "non-abrasive" — i.e. it won't scratch the enamel. That's the whole word in one label, and abrasive people scratch the same way.
Latin ab- ("away") + rādere ("to scrape") — to scrape away.

Rādere is a quiet workhorse: erase (scrape out), razor (the scraper), raze (scrape a building to the ground), abrade, rash. Learn the root once, get five words.

Side by side; or level with something that keeps moving.
Literally: side by side and facing the same way, in a single line — three abreast, marching abreast.

Figuratively (with of): level with something that keeps moving — keep abreast of the research, of the law, of your rivals.

The figurative sense is not simply "informed." It carries the sense of a race you can lose: the subject moves on, and you have to keep pulling level with it. Saying you're abreast of developments quietly claims ongoing effort, which is why it belongs to briefings, journalism and annual reviews rather than casual talk — nobody says they're abreast of their friend's gossip.
If you're abreast of it, it's moving — the news, the field, the rivals.
The word takes of only for things that keep advancing, which is exactly why it means "not falling behind" rather than merely "knowing."
1. Compliance officers are expected to keep abreast of amendments to the statute as they are gazetted.
2. Walk single file here — you can't go three abreast on a path this narrow.
Cyclists "riding two abreast" — the phrase every driver, road sign and highway-code argument uses for bikes side by side in one lane.
a- ("on, in") + breast — chests in one line, nobody's ahead. That a- prefix is a whole GRE family: afoot, aloft, ashore, askew, awry.

To repeal or abolish formally, by official authority.
To formally abolish or repeal something that was officially in force — a law, a treaty, a constitutional provision, a right.

This is cancellation from above, on the record. You can't abrogate a habit or a friendship; the object has to be something that was enacted, and the subject has to be a body with the authority to unenact it — a parliament, a court, a state. Where revoke is everyday and annul says "it was never valid," abrogate says "it was valid, and we have struck it off." The word carries the weight of the instrument being destroyed, which is why it so often shows up when someone is angry about it.
⚠️ abrogate ≠ arrogate.
- abrogate = ab- away → you cancel a law
- arrogate = ad- toward → you grab a power that isn't yours (he arrogated to himself the right to decide)

One letter, opposite direction of travel.
ABrogate = ABolish. Same two letters, same act, and both need someone in power to do it.
If the sentence's subject couldn't plausibly abolish the thing by decree, the word is wrong.
1. The incoming government moved to abrogate the trade treaty its predecessor had signed only eighteen months earlier.
2. You can't just abrogate the tenancy agreement because you found a better tenant.
India's abrogation of Article 370 in August 2019 — the word was in every headline, every debate, for months. Note what it attached to: a constitutional provision, struck off by the state. Textbook usage.
Latin ab- (away) + rogāre (to ask, to propose a law). In Rome, to propose a bill was rogāre lēgem; to repeal it was abrogāre — to ask it away.

Rogāre is a workhorse root: interrogate (question between), derogatory (asking down, belittling), prerogative (asked first — the privilege claimed ahead of others), surrogate, arrogate.

To flee secretly, usually with stolen money.
To leave secretly and in a hurry — typically to dodge arrest, and typically with money or property that isn't yours.

This isn't plain fleeing. Flee can be innocent (people flee fires); abscond presumes guilt. The word carries a whiff of the courtroom and the ledger: bail is skipped, a treasurer vanishes, a trustee disappears with the fund. It also usually takes with — you abscond with something. Someone who merely runs away has escaped; someone who absconds has escaped and taken the cash.
ABSent + CON — the con man goes absent, and so does the money.
The two syllables hand you both halves of the meaning: the disappearance and the crime behind it.
1. The firm's treasurer absconded to a jurisdiction with no extradition treaty, taking eleven years of client deposits with him.
2. My flatmate absconded with the deposit and left me to explain it to the landlord.
It's live legal vocabulary, not just exam vocabulary: parole boards and bail courts formally class someone who skips supervision as an absconder, and that's the word that shows up in the news when a fraudster boards a flight.
Latin abscondere = ab- (away) + condere (to stow, to hide) — literally to stash yourself away.

Same condere gives recondite, "hidden away, obscure" — the knowledge equivalent of absconding.

Deliberately hold back from something, or decline to vote.
To deliberately hold back from doing something you could perfectly well do — drinking, eating, speaking, voting.

The key is that it's chosen and usually sustained. You don't abstain because you can't; you abstain because you've decided not to, often on principle, health, or religious grounds. Refrain is a single moment of restraint ("he refrained from replying"); abstain is a standing policy ("she abstained for a year"). It also has a precise institutional sense: to formally decline to vote either way — present, counted, but neither yes nor no.
Ab-STAIN — you stay away so it can't stain you. The stain was available; you declined it.
The hidden word "stain" locks in the flavour of self-denial by choice, not by inability.
1. Three members voted in favour, two against, and the chairman abstained, unwilling to commit the board either way.
2. He's abstaining this month — no beer, no wine, nothing, and he's insufferable about it.
Any committee, parliament, or UN vote has three buttons: Yes, No, and Abstain — the official way to be present and still refuse to pick a side.
Latin abs- (away) + tenēre (to hold) — literally to hold yourself away from.

That tenēre is a workhorse root: contain, retain, detain, sustain, tenacious, tenet, tenure, tenable, abstinence. Anything that grips or holds.

column2:
Existing as an idea, not a thing; also, a summary.
Adj.: existing as an idea rather than a physical thing; general and theoretical rather than tied to particular cases.
Noun: a summary — the condensed version at the head of a paper.
Verb (ab-STRAKT): to draw out, extract, or reduce something to its essentials.

All three senses are one motion: pulling the idea off the object. Note that abstract is not vague — mathematics is maximally abstract and perfectly exact; vagueness is imprecision, abstraction is distance from the concrete. Neutral in itself, but in an argument "that's too abstract" is a complaint: the point has floated free of any real case.
abstract ≠ abstruse. Abstract = removed from the concrete (an abstract principle). Abstruse = obscure, hard to follow (an abstruse proof). An abstract idea can be crystal clear; an abstruse one, by definition, isn't.
Stress it like a verb and it moves: to ab-STRACT is to pull something out — leave it AB-stract and it just sits there as an idea.
Front-stress gives you the pulled-away result (the summary, the theory), end-stress gives you the act of pulling.
1. Rawls's principle stays abstract until someone applies it to an actual tax code.
2. Can you stop being so abstract for a second and just tell me what I'm doing on Monday?
Every paper you open on arXiv starts with the Abstract — the whole argument dragged out and set down in one paragraph.
Latin abs- (away) + trahere, tractus (to drag, pull) — literally "pulled away."

That root is a GRE goldmine: extract, retract, distract, subtract, protract, contract, attract, traction, tractor. All of them are something being pulled — out, back, apart, or along.

Deep and hard to grasp without specialist knowledge.
Hard to understand because the subject matter is deep, technical, or specialised — the kind of thing you can't follow without the right training.

Obscure just means little-known; abstruse means the difficulty is in the content itself. A footnote on medieval tax law is obscure; a proof in category theory is abstruse. It nearly always carries a faint complaint — the speaker suspects the difficulty could have been avoided, that the writer went abstruse when plain would have done.
abstruse ≠ obtuse. Abstruse describes the material (too deep to follow); obtuse describes the person (too dull to follow it). "An abstruse lecture" is a compliment to the topic; "an obtuse student" is an insult.
Abstruse = a recluse of an idea — it lives shut away where only specialists visit.
The rhyme fixes both the sound (-STROOS / -CLOOS) and the nuance: the meaning isn't lost, it's holed up behind jargon.
1. His later papers grew so abstruse that even colleagues in the field read them with a pencil in hand.
2. Skip chapter four — it gets abstruse fast and you don't need any of it for the exam.
Latin abs- (away) + trūdere (to thrust, push) — literally pushed out of sight, hidden away.

That verb is quietly everywhere: intrude (thrust in), protrude (thrust forward), extrude (thrust out), obtrude (thrust in someone's face) — and unobtrusive, which doesn't push itself on you at all.

column2:
To make an existing feature stand out more sharply.
To make something already present stand out more — to heighten, sharpen, throw into relief.

The key limit: you can only accentuate what's already there. A belt accentuates a waist that exists; a recession accentuates inequality that existed. Compare emphasise, which is about what a speaker chooses to stress, and exaggerate, which inflates past the truth — accentuate stays honest, it just turns the contrast up. It works on features (a cheekbone, a curve), on effects (a flaw, a divide, a colour), and it cuts both ways: what gets accentuated can be a virtue or a defect.
⚠️ accentuate ≠ attenuate. Two syllables apart, exact opposites: accentuate turns it up; attenuate thins it down (an attenuated signal, an attenuated virus).
accentuate = put an accent on it. The accent mark adds no letter — it just makes one syllable louder.
That's the whole nuance: nothing new is created, something existing is just made to stand out.
1. The low evening light accentuated every crack in the plaster.
2. That jacket really accentuates your shoulders — wear it.
The 1944 standard "Ac-Cent-Tchu-Ate the Positive" — "You've got to accentuate the positive, eliminate the negative" — still the phrase most people have heard the word in.
Latin ad- (to) + cantus (song) → accentus, literally "song added to speech" — the rise and fall that marks a stressed syllable. The Romans heard stress as singing.

That cantare root is a GRE goldmine: chant, enchant (sing a spell onto someone), incantation, recant (sing it back), cantata, descant.

Easy to reach, obtain, approach, or understand.
Able to be reached, entered, obtained, or understood — the barrier is low.

Three shades the GRE plays with. Physical: a road, a summit, a building. Available: records, funding, evidence accessible to researchers. And the one that actually gets tested — intelligible to a non-specialist: an accessible history of the Reformation is one a beginner can follow.

Applied to a person it means approachable — the professor who keeps real office hours, the boss who answers his own email. Praise, usually. But in criticism it can turn faintly dismissive: accessible poetry, accessible pop, meaning it asks nothing of you. The word never describes the seeker's effort, only the thing's openness.
-ible sits on the thing: a book is accessible, a reader never is.
The suffix marks what can be got at, so the word always measures how open the object is, not how clever or determined you are.
1. Her lectures were prized for making quantum mechanics accessible without ever making it wrong.
2. He runs the whole company and he's still weirdly accessible — he'll actually reply to your email.
The Accessibility menu on your phone — bigger text, voice control, colour filters — is this word as a product feature: removing the barrier rather than blaming the user. Same idea as the ♿ symbol on a ramp.
Latin ad- (to) + cedere (to go, to yield) → accedere, "to approach."

cedere is a GRE workhorse: recede (go back), secede (go apart), precede (go before), concede and cede (yield), accede (go along with), exceed (go beyond).

Loud, public, collective praise.
Noun: enthusiastic public praise. Verb: to praise loudly and publicly — or to declare someone something by shouted approval (he was acclaimed king).

Praise from one person is a compliment; acclaim is praise from a crowd, a press, a field. It's collective, audible, and usually attaches to work rather than to character — a novel, a film, a performance. It also implies the verdict has settled: "widely acclaimed" means the argument is over.
⚠️ acclamation ≠ acclimation.
- acclamation = election or approval by shout (carried by acclamation — no ballot needed)
- acclimation = getting used to a climate or conditions

One is a roar of yes; the other is your body adjusting to altitude.
Nobody claims their own acclaim — the crowd claims it for you, out loud.
The hidden word claim is the giveaway that this praise is asserted publicly by others, never awarded to yourself.
1. Her second symphony met with an acclaim that the first, performed to an empty hall, had never come close to earning.
2. The film flopped at the box office but got so much critical acclaim that everyone pretends they saw it.
"Critically acclaimed" — the badge on Netflix rows, movie posters, and book jackets. It's the industry's way of saying the critics loved this even if you haven't heard of it.
Latin ad- (toward) + clāmāre (to shout) — literally to shout toward.

That root is a GRE goldmine: exclaim (shout out), proclaim (shout forth), declaim (shout formally, orate), clamour (a crowd's noise), clamorous. Every one of them is somebody making noise.

Formal agreement or harmony; to grant, or be consistent with.
Noun: a formal agreement between parties — especially nations; more loosely, a state of harmony.
Verb: to grant something (a right, a status, a courtesy) formally, or to be consistent with ("her story accords with the evidence").

Agreement is the everyday word; accord is the one that gets signed in a room with flags — treaty register, diplomatic weight. The verb is equally elevated: you don't accord someone a sandwich, you accord them recognition, honours, a hearing — it's bestowal from a position that has the standing to bestow. Learn the frozen phrase too: of one's own accord = unprompted, from nobody's urging but your own.
A chord is notes agreeing; an accord is parties agreeing — and both are harmony you can hear from across the room.
The sound hook also carries the register: a chord is deliberate and structured, and so is an accord — never a casual understanding but a composed, formal one.
1. The 1998 accord held for a decade before either side seriously tested it.
2. Nobody made her apologise — she did it of her own accord.
The Honda Accord was named for exactly this: harmony between the car, its driver, and society. A word you've read on a boot lid a thousand times.
Latin ad- (to) + cor, cordis (heart) — literally bringing hearts together. That's why "of one's own accord" means from your own heart.

One root, a whole GRE family: concord (hearts together — peace), discord (hearts apart — strife), cordial (warm, heartfelt), courage (heart), and record (originally to call back to the heart — to memorise).

A devoted follower or assistant; originally a priest's helper.
Literally, an assistant who helps a priest at the altar — the one carrying the candle. Figuratively, a devoted follower or attendant of a leader, thinker, or movement.

Outside church, it usually carries a curl of the lip. A disciple learns; a supporter agrees; an acolyte serves — junior, hovering, devoted past the point of independent judgement. Journalists reach for it when they want to say "entourage" without saying "entourage." Calling someone a founder's acolyte is never quite a compliment to the acolyte.
⚠️ acolyte ≠ neophyte. An acolyte is defined by whom he serves; a neophyte is defined by how little he knows. A twenty-year acolyte is still an acolyte; a twenty-year neophyte is a contradiction.
The acolyte carries the light — and walks behind the man holding it.
The candle-bearer image locks in both halves of the word: real devotion, permanently second in line.
1. Surrounded by acolytes who transcribed his every aside, the professor lost the habit of being contradicted.
2. He's not an advisor, he's an acolyte — he'd agree with the boss twice on the same sentence.
Star Wars: The Acolyte (2024) — the title means exactly this: not a Sith lord, but the devoted servant trailing one.
Greek akolouthos = "follower, one who walks the same path" (keleuthos = path). The meaning hasn't moved in two thousand years — someone walking behind you.

To give in quietly, without protest.
To accept or go along with something without protest — to give in quietly.

The word carries the objection you swallowed. Someone who agrees is on board; someone who acquiesces had reservations and simply stopped fighting. It's consent measured by silence rather than enthusiasm, and it usually implies a power gap — you acquiesce to a boss, a government, a stubborn spouse. Faintly disapproving: it hints at weakness, or at least at surrender.

Note the grammar the GRE likes: you acquiesce in or to a decision — never "acquiesce a decision."
AcQUIEsce — you go quiet, and the silence counts as a yes.
The word has quie(t) sitting in the middle of it, which is exactly the kind of agreement it describes — you stop objecting rather than actually consent.
1. The board acquiesced in the chairman's proposal, though several members later admitted they had never believed in it.
2. I didn't want pineapple on it, but everyone else did, so I acquiesced.
Oasis — "Acquiesce" (1995), the Liam-and-Noel duet B-side that became one of their biggest live songs. The chorus — because we need each other, we believe in one another — is two brothers who fight constantly agreeing to stop fighting, which is precisely what the word means.
Latin quiēs / quiēscere = "rest, be still", plus ad- ("to"). To acquiesce is literally to come to rest about something — to stop struggling.

That root pays out across the GRE: quiescent (dormant, inactive), quiet, tranquil, and requiem (a mass for the rest of the dead).

column2:
Eager to get and keep more — money, things, possessions.
Keen to get and keep more — possessions, property, wealth, sometimes knowledge.

Where greedy is appetite and grasping is ugly, acquisitive is cold and settled: a standing disposition to accumulate rather than a flash of hunger. It's the word for the collector, the empire-builder, the person who converts every impulse into a purchase. Mildly disapproving of people; entirely neutral in business ("an acquisitive conglomerate") and even complimentary of a mind ("an acquisitive intellect" soaks things up).
⚠️ acquisitive ≠ inquisitive. Acquisitive wants to own it; inquisitive wants to know it. One letter apart on the page, opposite appetites.
Acquire is sitting whole inside it — and acquire is a cold, transactional verb. Nobody "acquires" a sandwich.
That chill in acquire is exactly what separates acquisitive from plain greedy: accumulation as policy, not as hunger.
1. Gilded Age fortunes were built by acquisitive men who bought the railway, then the town the railway ran through.
2. Three years at that firm and he's gone properly acquisitive — everything's an "investment" now, even the watch.
M&A — mergers and acquisitions, the department whose entire job is buying other companies. Any financial paper describing a firm as "highly acquisitive" means exactly that: it grows by swallowing rivals.
Latin quaerere = "to seek, to ask," plus ad- ("toward") → acquirere, to seek out and get.

That root is a GRE goldmine: inquire, require, query, quest, conquest, request, perquisite (your "perks"), exquisite (sought out — hence choice).

Bitter and hostile — said of quarrels, splits, and negotiations.
Bitter, sharp-tongued and hostile — used of quarrels, debates, negotiations and breakups.

The word almost never describes a person; it describes the atmosphere between two sides, usually sides that were once allies. A stranger insulting you is rude, not acrimonious. A business partnership, a marriage, a band — those dissolve acrimoniously, because the bitterness is earned. It's a journalist's word: cool, formal, faintly disapproving of everyone involved.
ACRI- like acrid smoke, -MONIOUS like matri*mony* — acrimonious is matrimony gone acrid.
The word's single most common companion is divorce, and both halves of it point there.
1. The merger talks collapsed after an acrimonious final session in which each delegation accused the other of bad faith.
2. They're still fighting over the dog — it got pretty acrimonious.
The 2009 Oasis split is the textbook example — every account of the Gallagher brothers' backstage fight in Paris reaches for the same adjective.
Latin acer, acris = "sharp, keen, bitter." Literally, bitterness of temper.

The root is worth a lot elsewhere: acrid (sharp smell), acerbic (sharp wit), acute (sharp angle), exacerbate (make sharper), even eager and vinegar (vin aigre, "sour wine").

Sharp practical judgment within a particular field.
Keen, quick judgment in a practical arena — the ability to size up a situation and make the shrewd call.

This isn't raw brainpower or book learning. Acumen is intelligence that pays off. A professor can be brilliant and have no business acumen; a shop owner with no degree can have plenty. It's admiring and slightly worldly — you earn acumen through experience, not study — and it almost always comes attached to a domain: business, political, financial, tactical, legal acumen.
⚠️ acumen ≠ acuity.
- acumen = sharpness of judgment (business acumen)
- acuity = sharpness of perception (visual acuity, mental acuity)

Your eyes have acuity. Your dealmaking has acumen.
Acumen needs a job title. Nobody "has acumen" — they have business acumen, political acumen.
The word arrives married to a field, which is exactly the nuance: it's applied shrewdness, never abstract cleverness.
1. Her financial acumen turned a failing regional bank into the most profitable arm of the group within three years.
2. He can't cook, but he's got real acumen for spotting which restaurants will still be open in five years.
Scroll any job listing on LinkedIn and you'll hit "strong business acumen" in the requirements — it's HR boilerplate for knows how money actually works here.
Latin acumen = literally "a sharp point", from acuere, "to sharpen" (from acus, a needle). A person with acumen has a mind that comes to a point.

Same needle-sharp root runs through acute (a sharp angle, a sharp pain), acuity, and acupuncture — literally puncturing with needles.

Made for this one case only; improvised, unsystematic.
Made or done for this one specific purpose, with no thought to any wider plan — and therefore improvised, temporary, unsystematic.

Two flavours pull in opposite directions. Neutral-administrative: an ad hoc committee is simply one convened for a single question and dissolved afterwards — nobody is being insulted. Mildly damning: an ad hoc solution, policy, or hypothesis is a patch, cobbled together to handle the case in front of you, with no principle behind it that would survive the next case. In science and philosophy the label is close to an accusation: an ad hoc assumption is one bolted onto a theory purely to stop it being refuted.
ad hoc is one letter from a hack — and that's exactly what an ad hoc fix is.
It works for this case and nothing else, which is why the word so often carries a faint whiff of "we made it up on the spot."
1. The board appointed an ad hoc subcommittee to review the single disputed clause, with a mandate to disband once it reported.
2. There's no process — we just fix things ad hoc whenever someone complains loudly enough.
Every analytics tool sells "ad hoc queries" or "ad hoc reporting" — meaning one-off questions you ask on the spot, as opposed to the scheduled dashboards.
Latin ad hoc = "to this." Straight to this case, no further.

Worth banking the whole ad- phrasebook, since the GRE likes them: ad hominem (to the man — attack the person, not the argument), ad nauseam (to sickness), ad infinitum (to infinity), ad lib ← ad libitum (at pleasure).

Highly skilled at something, through practice not luck.
Adj.: highly skilled, expert — usually adept at or adept in something. Noun: a person who has mastered a difficult art.

The skill is earned, not innate. Apt and gifted point to raw talent; adept points to practice that has hardened into fluency, and it carries a whiff of the specialist — someone who has been initiated into the craft. It's warmer and more admiring than proficient (which merely clears the bar) and less lofty than masterful; adroit is its close cousin but leans physical or social — quick hands, quick footwork — where adept is about command of a skill.
⚠️ adept ≠ adapt. Adept (uh-DEPT) = skilled. Adapt (uh-DAPT) = adjust to new conditions. One letter, one vowel sound, two unrelated words — and adopt is lurking a third of the way behind.
You're born apt; you become adept.
The extra syllable is the extra work — adept is the skill you attained, not the talent you started with.
1. A decade in the archives had made her unusually adept at reading water-damaged handwriting.
2. He's weirdly adept at parallel parking — three seconds, one go, every time.
Every block of placeholder text you've ever seen — \"Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit\" — carries the same Latin verb, adipisci, \"to attain.\"
Latin adeptus, "having attained" (from ad- "to" + apisci "reach, obtain"). It reached English through alchemy: an adept was one who had attained the great secret of transmuting metal into gold.

That's why the word still implies attainment rather than gift — and why the noun sense sounds faintly like a member of a guild.

column2:
To stick fast — to a surface, or to a rule.
Literally: to stick fast to a surface (glue, tape, barnacles). Figuratively — the GRE sense: to follow a rule, standard, plan or belief faithfully and continuously.

The figurative use is a compliance word: you adhere to a protocol, a schedule, a treaty, a diet. Obey is about authority in the moment; adhere is about staying attached over time, usually by your own choice — which is why a believer is an adherent, not an obeyer. It's slightly formal and faintly bureaucratic; nobody says "I adhered to the recipe" over dinner, but every compliance memo says it.
⚠️ adhere ≠ cohere.
- adhere = stick to something else (tape to a wall, a party to its manifesto)
- cohere = stick together, internally (an argument whose parts hold as one)

An adhesive bonds two things; a coherent essay holds itself.
ad-HERE — you stay here, and keep staying here.
The buried word here gives you both halves at once: attachment to a fixed point, sustained rather than one-off.
1. The signatory states pledged to adhere to the terms of the accord for a further decade.
2. If you'd just adhered to the instructions, the shelf wouldn't be leaning like that.
Every workplace email that ends "please adhere to the guidelines" — the word lives in policy documents, dress codes, and safety notices.
Latin haerēre = "to stick." Add ad- ("to") and you get sticking to something.

The root pays out widely: cohere/coherent (stick together), inherent (sticking in — built into the thing), adhesive, and — the surprise — hesitate, from haesitāre, "to be stuck," which is exactly what hesitation is.

To scold mildly, or warn earnestly, with advice attached.
To reprove someone firmly but mildly — and, by extension, to urge or warn them earnestly about what to do next (he admonished them to keep silent).

The force is corrective, not punitive. A boss who castigates you wants you to feel it; a boss who admonishes you wants you to fix it — there's a note of counsel, even care, and usually a moral or authority relationship behind it (parent, judge, teacher, scripture). It's the scolding that comes with advice attached.
Ad-MON-ish — the monitor speaks: a warning meant to correct you, not crush you.
Same mon- as monitor and premonition, so an admonishment is essentially a heads-up delivered with a frown.
1. The bishop admonished his congregation to temper their zeal with charity.
2. Mum admonished me for skipping breakfast again — not angry, just disappointed and full of advice.
Courtroom boilerplate: the judge admonishes the jury not to discuss the case or read the news. Not a punishment — a warning with instructions, which is the word exactly.
Latin ad- (to) + monēre (to warn, remind). That root is a GRE goldmine: monitor (one who warns), premonition (a warning beforehand), monument (a thing that reminds you), summon, monitory.

Skilfully quick, especially at handling tricky people or moments.
Skilful and quick — especially quick in a tricky spot.

Dexterous and deft are about the hands; adroit has largely migrated to the mind. It's the word for the diplomat who defuses the question, the negotiator who reframes the deal, the witness who never quite gets cornered. Praise, but cool praise: it admires the manoeuvre more than the person, and pushed a little further it shades into slick.
adroit ≠ adept. Adept = deeply skilled through practice (an adept surgeon). Adroit = nimble in the moment (an adroit reply). You become adept over years; you are adroit in seconds.
Adroit rhymes with avoid — the adroit answer avoids the trap without ever looking like a dodge.
The rhyme carries the nuance: adroitness is escaping a difficulty with such ease that nobody sees the effort.
1. An adroit shift of the agenda buried the motion before anyone noticed it had been raised.
2. She's scarily adroit at getting out of plans she never wanted to make.
Weezer's 2002 album Maladroit — literally "clumsy," the negative of this word. If maladroit is the guy tripping over the cable, adroit is everyone else.
French à droit = "to the right." Being right-handed was skill; being left-handed was not — and English quietly imported the whole prejudice.

- adroit = to the right → skilful
- maladroit = badly to the right → clumsy
- gauche = French "left" → socially awkward
- dexterous (Latin dexter, right) vs sinister (Latin sinister, left)

One bias, six GRE words.

column2:
To make impure by mixing in an inferior substance.
To make something impure or inferior by mixing in a foreign, cheaper substance — watering the milk, cutting the olive oil with sunflower oil, padding the drugs with baking soda.

Dilute is neutral and often deliberate housekeeping; adulterate is an accusation. It implies secrecy, profit, and degradation — someone sold you the pure thing and handed you the cut thing. It stretches beyond food, too: a text, a doctrine, a bloodline can be adulterated. And you'll meet the negative twice as often as the verb: unadulterated = pure, nothing mixed in ("pure, unadulterated joy").
⚠️ adulterate ≠ adulate. Adulate (AJ-uh-layt) is to praise someone fawningly — flattery, not fraud. One debases a product, the other inflates a person.
Adultery adds an outsider to a marriage; adulterate adds an outsider to the product.
Same Latin root, same idea — something pure is corrupted by letting in what doesn't belong, and both words carry the smell of betrayal.
1. Inspectors found the honey had been adulterated with corn syrup and sold at a premium.
2. Don't adulterate a good whisky with Coke, mate.
You've heard the negative form a hundred times without noticing the verb: commentators shouting about "pure, unadulterated joy" when a last-minute goal goes in — unadulterated means nothing has been mixed in to weaken it.
Latin adulterare = "to corrupt," from ad- (to) + alter (other) — literally to make other than it was.

That alter is a workhorse: alter, alternative, alter ego, altercation, alternate, even altruism (living for the other).

Unfavourable; working against your interests.
Acting against your interests; unfavourable, harmful, hostile in effect.

It isn't a synonym for bad. Adverse is bad in opposition to something — a headwind, a ruling, a drug, a market all pushing against a specific interest. And it describes conditions, forces and outcomes, not feelings: weather, effects, publicity, a court decision. The register is formal and institutional; you meet it in medical inserts, legal judgments and risk reports far more than in speech.
⚠️ adverse ≠ averse.
- adverse = unfavourable, describing a thing — adverse weather, adverse effects
- averse = unwilling, describing a person — she is averse to flying

Test: if you can put "to" after it and a person in front, you want averse.
Adverse never tells you how anyone feels — only what's being done to them: adverse weather, adverse effects, adverse ruling.
Every natural collocation of adverse is an external force, which is exactly why a person can never be "adverse to" anything.
1. The tribunal reached an adverse finding against the bank, and the share price fell before close.
2. We'd have finished the hike, but the weather turned adverse and we bailed at the ridge.
The leaflet inside every box of medicine lists adverse effects (or adverse reactions) — the drug turning against the patient it's meant to help.
Latin ad- (toward) + vertere (to turn) = "turned against you."

Vertere is a workhorse root: adversary (one turned against you), adversity, avert (turn away), divert, convert, revert, versatile, and anniversary (the year turning round again).

To publicly argue for something; one who pleads a cause.
Verb: to publicly plead for, argue in favour of, recommend a cause or course of action.
Noun: the person doing the pleading — a champion, a supporter who speaks up (and in Scots and much European usage, literally a courtroom lawyer).

The word is louder than support. You can support something silently, in a poll or in your heart; to advocate it you have to open your mouth and take a public side. It also carries the flavour of speaking on behalf of someone else — the patient, the refugee, the defendant — which is why "advocate" attaches so naturally to the powerless. Note the preposition: you advocate for a person, but you simply advocate a policy (no "for" needed in careful prose).
Hidden inside is vocate — voice. An advocate lends you theirs.
Support is silent; advocacy is audible, which is the whole difference between agreeing with a cause and advocating one.
1. The commission's report advocated a phased withdrawal of the subsidy, over the objections of three of its own members.
2. She's been a fierce advocate for her brother ever since the school tried to quietly drop him from the programme.
Playing devil's advocate. It's a real Vatican job — the advocatus diaboli was the official appointed to argue against a proposed saint, hunting for reasons the candidate didn't deserve canonisation. Someone paid to plead the opposing side.
Latin ad- (to) + vocāre (to call) — an advocate was someone called to your side in court.

That vocāre root is a GRE goldmine: vocation (a calling), evoke (call forth), revoke (call back), provoke (call forth anger), invoke, convoke, and equivocate (call it two ways at once).

Concerned with beauty and how things look, not how they work.
Adj.: having to do with beauty and the perception of it. Noun: a coherent set of principles or a look — the minimalist aesthetic.

The word marks a domain, not a compliment. "Aesthetic considerations" means how it looks — as opposed to moral, practical, or financial considerations. So on the GRE it usually appears as one half of a contrast: the bridge was rebuilt for aesthetic rather than structural reasons. Calling a choice aesthetic can quietly mean it does nothing useful. Only in casual speech ("very aesthetic") has it drifted into meaning pretty.
⚠️ aesthetic ≠ ascetic (uh-SET-ik).
- aesthetic = concerned with beauty
- ascetic = severely self-denying — no comfort, no pleasure

An aesthete fills the room with beautiful things; an ascetic empties it.
An-aesthetic = no feeling. Knock off the an- and feeling comes back — starting with the eye's kind.
The word is about perceiving and taking pleasure in how a thing looks, never about whether it works.
1. The renovation was condemned as purely aesthetic: the façade gleamed, while the wiring behind it remained a hazard.
2. Her flat has a whole aesthetic going on — everything beige, everything matching, nothing you're allowed to touch.
Pinterest and TikTok turned it into a noun you scroll past daily — cottagecore aesthetic, clean girl aesthetic. Each one is exactly what the word means: a consistent set of rules about how things should look.
Greek aisthesthai = "to perceive, to feel." Perception first, beauty second.

That root hands you a family: anaesthetic (an- = without → no feeling), aesthete (one who feels beauty keenly), synaesthesia (senses crossing — hearing colour), kinaesthetic (feeling your own movement).

🚫 Not ascetic. That's Greek askein, "to train, to exercise" — the same idea behind an athlete's discipline, redirected at the soul.

A put-on manner adopted to impress others.
A bit of behaviour, speech, or dress that is put on rather than natural — adopted to impress or to seem a certain kind of person.

Calling something an affectation is always a verdict, not a description: you are saying the pose is fake and that you can see through it. A mannerism is just a personal quirk, morally neutral; an affectation is a quirk someone chose, and the choice is the crime. Note the scale, too — it's usually small and specific (a drawled vowel, a cigarette holder, spelling theatre the British way), not a whole false life. That smallness is what makes it faintly ridiculous rather than sinister.
⚠️ affectation ≠ affection.
- affectation = a manner you fake
- affection = fondness you feel

One letter-cluster apart, opposite in sincerity.
To affect an accent is to fake one — an affectation is the fake itself.
The verb affect has a sneaky GRE sense — "to feign" (he affected a limp) — and the noun is simply that feigning made into a thing.
1. His habit of quoting Latin at dinner was less scholarship than affectation, and the table had long since stopped pretending to be impressed.
2. She's been back from London a week and she's already saying "cheers" — total affectation.
Madonna's British accent after she moved to London — years of press mockery, and the word used almost every time.
Latin affectāre = "to strive after, aspire to" — and, by an easy slide, "to pretend to." An affectation is a quality you reach for because you don't actually have it.

Same family: affect (to feign), affected (mannered), disaffected (no longer attached).

A natural liking for, or inherent kinship with, something.
1. A natural liking or attraction toward something. 2. A resemblance or kinship between two things — languages, species, ideas, substances.

The word claims the pull is built in, not chosen. You can like jazz after deciding to; an affinity for jazz says something in you already matched it. That's why it works equally well for chemistry (elements with an affinity for oxygen) and linguistics (the affinity between Sanskrit and Latin) — no feeling required, just an inherent fit.

Watch the preposition: an affinity for something is liking; an affinity with or between things is resemblance.
Infinity has no boundary; affinity is boundaries that touch.
Both hide Latin finis (boundary) — one negates it, the other brings two borders up against each other, which is exactly what a natural kinship is.
1. Nineteenth-century scholars detected a deep affinity between Sanskrit and Latin long before anyone could explain how it had arisen.
2. I've got zero affinity for spreadsheets — numbers just slide straight off me.
Corporate affinity groups — employee networks built around a shared background or interest — and affinity credit cards, co-branded with a team or charity you already feel attached to. Both use the word in its exact sense: a pre-existing pull, which the company merely organises.
Latin affinis = "bordering on" — literally ad- (to) + finis (boundary, end). In Roman law it meant related by marriage: your family's borders now touch mine.

Finis is a workhorse root: finite, infinite, define, confine, final, finish, finance (settling up = ending it).

Comfortably, settled-ly wealthy — money that flows in steadily.
Wealthy, well-off, prosperous.

But affluent isn't rich and it certainly isn't loaded. It describes settled, comfortable, ongoing money — the kind you were probably born into or have had for years. Nobody becomes affluent overnight. It's also the sociologist's and marketer's word: it attaches naturally to groups and places — an affluent suburb, affluent households, affluent shoppers — far more readily than to one person. Neutral on the surface, but in journalism it often carries a faint sniff: affluent is how you describe privilege you're not entirely sympathetic to.
⚠️ affluent ≠ effluent. Same root, opposite plumbing: affluent = wealth flowing in; effluent (EF-loo-uhnt) = liquid waste flowing out of a factory or sewer. One is a nice postcode, the other is what the water company gets fined for.
Affluent = money that flows — like fluent speech, it's steady and effortless, never a sudden jackpot.
The -flu- in the middle is the same flow as in fluent, which is exactly the nuance: affluence is a continuous stream, not a windfall.
1. The council's report noted that the new library had been sited, predictably, in the most affluent ward in the borough.
2. They're not just doing okay — that's a seriously affluent part of town, have you seen the driveways?
"Affluenza" — the coinage that went global during the 2013 Texas case where a teenager's defence argued his wealthy upbringing left him unable to grasp consequences. Affluence treated as a disease.
Latin ad- (toward) + fluere (to flow) — wealth flowing toward you.

Fluere is a workhorse root: fluent (words flow), influence (originally a flowing-in from the stars), confluence (rivers meeting), flux, fluid, superfluous (over-flowing, hence excess), and effluent (flowing out).

An open insult to someone's dignity, delivered to their face.
Noun: an open insult — a deliberate act of disrespect aimed at someone's dignity.
Verb: to insult someone openly, to their face.

Scale and formality separate this from insult. An insult can be petty and private; an affront is public and treated as an offence against standing — your honour, your office, your rights. It's also the word English reaches for when the injured party isn't a person at all: an affront to democracy, to decency, to human dignity. And note the grammar the GRE loves: an affront is always to something.
Af-front = delivered up front, to your face, in front of everyone.
The word literally has front in it, which is exactly what makes an affront worse than a private insult — it's done openly, where the humiliation lands.
1. The ambassador walked out, calling the remark an affront to his country and to the treaty that bound them.
2. Don't put ketchup on that — the chef would take it as a personal affront.
Open any newspaper: "an affront to democracy," "an affront to human dignity." It's the standard register for outrage in print — which is why the to is welded on.
Latin ad frontem = "to the forehead" — via Old French afronter, to strike someone in the face. The insult is aimed at the front of your head.

Same root gives you front, confront, frontier, frontispiece — and, best of all, effrontery: shameless nerve, from ex- + frons, "without a face" — no blush left to give you away.

To make greater in power, wealth, or apparent importance.
To increase someone's power, wealth, or standing — or, more often, to make them appear greater than they are.

The word rarely comes out neutral. When a general aggrandizes his territory, it's expansion at someone's expense; when a colleague aggrandizes himself in a meeting, it's puffery. Compare enhance, which improves the thing itself: aggrandizing usually inflates the reputation while the substance stays put. The most common form on the GRE is self-aggrandizing — the man who tells the story so that he ends up the hero of it.
GRAND is sitting right there in the middle — to a-GRAND-ize is to make someone grand, usually grander than the facts allow.
The hidden word gives you the meaning, and the gap between "grand" and "actually grand" gives you the sneer.
1. Every reform he proposed had the convenient effect of aggrandizing the office he happened to hold.
2. It was a team effort, but you'd never know it from his self-aggrandizing LinkedIn post.
Self-aggrandizing is a staple of political journalism — it's the standard polite way a columnist calls a politician's grand gesture an exercise in self-promotion.
Latin grandis = "great, large," with ad- ("toward") — literally to make greater, via French agrandir.

One root, a useful cluster: grand, grandeur, grandiose (impressively big, or absurdly pretending to be), grandiloquent (speaking in swollen language).

Struck speechless with shock and horror.
Struck motionless by shock and horror — the frozen, open-mouthed reaction to something appalling.

Surprise is neutral, shock is clinical, but aghast always carries revulsion: you are horrified at something, usually something morally or physically ghastly. It also describes the face and the moment — a held expression, not a lasting mood. Grammatically it almost never sits before a noun: people are aghast at the news, but you don't meet "an aghast man."
aghast ≠ agog. Both are a- + one syllable, both describe a wide-eyed stare. Aghast = horrified. Agog = thrilled with eager anticipation. The crowd was agog for the verdict; the family was aghast at it.
agHASt hides GHOST — you look like you've just seen one.
That face — frozen, drained, mouth open — is exactly what aghast names, and it explains the useless silent h in the spelling.
1. The committee sat aghast as the auditor read out, line by line, where the money had gone.
2. I was aghast — he microwaved the fish. In the open-plan office.
Old English gāstan, "to terrify" — same root as gāst, spirit, which gives us ghost and ghastly. The silent h was smuggled in later purely by imitation of ghost.

The Germanic cousin Geist extends the family: poltergeist (noisy ghost), zeitgeist (spirit of the age).

To stir up — liquid, nerves, or public opinion.
To stir something up so it can't settle — three related uses:

1. Physical: shake or churn. Agitate the solution before decanting.
2. Emotional: disturb, unsettle. An agitated person is jittery, unable to sit still — visibly rattled, not calmly angry.
3. Political: campaign loudly and persistently. Always with for or against — agitate for reform.

The third sense is the GRE's favourite and the one people miss. It carries no insult on its own, but the noun agitator almost always does: those in power call you an agitator, you call yourself an activist. Note the difference in force from provoke — provoking is a single jab that gets a reaction; agitating is sustained churn that denies anyone the quiet of the status quo.
⚠️ agitate ≠ aggravate. Agitate = stir up, set in motion. Aggravate = make an already-bad thing worse (aggravate an injury). Running aggravated her knee; the diagnosis left her agitated.
The agitator in a washing machine is the spindle that never lets the water sit still.
Same word, same job in every sense — the thing that keeps water, nerves, or a nation from settling.
1. For four decades she agitated for prison reform, outliving three governments that ignored her.
2. He was agitated all morning — checking his phone, pacing, snapping at people for nothing.
Frederick Douglass's advice to a young man asking what to do with his life: "Agitate, agitate, agitate." A century later, segregationists dismissed civil-rights organisers as outside agitators — the exact word, weaponised.
Latin agere = "to drive, to do" → agitāre, its frequentative: to drive again and again, keep in motion.

That root is everywhere on the GRE: agent (one who does), agenda (things to be done), agile, act, exigent, navigate, prodigal. The frequentative -it- is the reusable bit — it means repeatedly.

Cheerful, brisk eagerness to get on with something.
Brisk, cheerful eagerness — moving fast because you're glad to.

Speed alone isn't alacrity. A prisoner marched to work moves quickly; a volunteer who jumps up before you finish asking moves with alacrity. The word carries visible willingness — the promptness is evidence of the enthusiasm. It's warm, faintly formal, and lives almost entirely in one phrase: with alacrity. Watch for dry irony too — "he accepted the free upgrade with alacrity" gently mocks how fast the hand went up.
⚠️ alacrity ≠ celerity. Celerity is bare speed (same root as accelerate) — a missile has celerity. Alacrity is speed plus gladness. Swap them and you've stripped out the cheerfulness the GRE is testing.
a-LACK-rity — yet it means there's no lack of willingness.
The sound plants "lack" in the middle of a word that means the exact opposite: zero hesitation, zero reluctance.
1. The junior clerks, sensing that promotion hung on it, took up the thankless assignment with surprising alacrity.
2. Ask him to review your code and he'll stall for a week — mention free pizza and he's there with real alacrity.
Shakespeare's Richard III, the night before Bosworth: "I have not that alacrity of spirit, / Nor cheer of mind, that I was wont to have." Richard defines the word for you in the next line — alacrity = cheer of mind.
Latin alacer / alacris = "brisk, lively, cheerful" — briskness and good cheer bundled into one adjective from the start.

Same root, travelling through Italian: allegro, the musical direction meaning not merely fast but fast and merry. If you know what allegro sounds like, you know what alacrity feels like.

Push people away until they feel like outsiders.
To make someone feel distant, unwelcome, or hostile — to lose their sympathy or support. (Legal sense: to transfer property or rights to another owner.)

Compare the neighbours: antagonize is deliberate provocation, offend is a single moment's damage. Alienate is cumulative and usually unintended — the alienator is often just being themselves, and one by one the allies drift off. It also scales up in a way the others don't: you alienate a friend, but also a fanbase, a voter bloc, an entire region. And the damage is measured in distance, not anger: the alienated don't fight you, they stop showing up.
Alien is sitting right inside it — and it's your behaviour that deports them.
To alienate is to turn your own people into aliens — outsiders looking in — usually without meaning to.
1. The new levy on smallholders alienated precisely the rural constituency the party had spent a decade courting.
2. He didn't get fired, he just alienated everyone on the team until nobody invited him to anything.
The US Declaration of Independence: "certain unalienable Rights." That's the legal sense — rights that cannot be signed away or transferred to anyone else, no matter who asks.
Latin alius = "other" → alienus, "belonging to another." To alienate is literally to make someone other.

Same root, free words: alias (otherwise called), alibi (elsewhere), alien, inalienable.

Covering absolutely everything; nothing left outside.
Covering everything within its scope — leaving nothing and nobody out.

It attaches to abstractions rather than objects: a theory, a vision, a definition, a grief, a love. Comprehensive is the auditor's word — thorough, box-ticked. All-encompassing is bigger and vaguer, and carries a hint of awe: the thing has no edges. Usually admiring, but turn it on a feeling and it becomes claustrophobic — an all-encompassing obsession has room for nothing else.
all-encompassing ≠ all-consuming. All-encompassing = includes everything. All-consuming = devours you, crowding out everything else. A framework is all-encompassing; a jealousy is all-consuming.
There's a compass in it — draw one big circle, and everything's inside.
The word literally encircles its subject, which is why it suits boundless things — visions, theories, obsessions — rather than tidy checklists.
1. Hegel's ambition was an all-encompassing system in which every art, religion and state found its allotted place.
2. She's got this all-encompassing spreadsheet for the wedding — seating, playlist, who's not speaking to whom.
Old French compasser = "to measure by pacing around" — from Latin com- (together) + passus (a step). To encompass something is to walk a ring around it.

Same root steps into compass, pass, passage, pace and surpass.

column2:
Using characters and events as a coded stand-in for bigger ideas.
Describing a story, painting or film whose surface content systematically stands for something else — a moral, a political argument, a religious scheme.

The word implies machinery, not decoration. A symbol can be a single glinting detail; an allegory is a full parallel structure, where each character and event has an assigned counterpart in the real subject. Because of that, "allegorical" often carries a faint chill in criticism — it hints that the story is a delivery vehicle for a message, and that once you've decoded it there's nothing left to discover.
If you can swap every character for an idea and the story still runs, it's allegorical.
Symbolism only decorates a story, but allegory is the story, so the substitution has to hold all the way through.
1. Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress is relentlessly allegorical: the hero is Christian, the swamp is Despond, and the road is salvation itself.
2. Everyone said the film was just a heist movie, but it's obviously allegorical — the bank is the government and the crew is us.
Orwell's Animal Farm is the standard example: every pig, horse and dog maps onto a figure in the Russian Revolution, which is why it gets taught as allegory rather than as a story about farming.
Greek allos = "other" + agoreuein = "to speak in the agora," the public marketplace. So: to speak in public but mean something other than what you say.

Both halves pay off elsewhere: allos gives allergy (the body reacting otherly), allonym, allele; the agora gives agoraphobia (fear of the open square) and even category (kata- + agoreuein, originally "to accuse publicly").

To ease pain or hardship — lessen it, not cure it.
To make pain, suffering, or a problem less severe — to take the edge off.

The word is honest about its limits: you alleviate a symptom, not the disease. Cure, eliminate and resolve claim the problem is gone; alleviate only claims the weight is lighter. That's why doctors, aid agencies and policy papers reach for it — it promises relief without promising a fix. Its objects are almost always unpleasant: pain, grief, hunger, poverty, congestion, boredom. You never alleviate a good thing.
al-LEVI-ate — same levi as levitate: it lifts weight off you, it doesn't take the load away.
Lightening ≠ removing, which is exactly the difference between alleviate and cure.
1. Morphine alleviated the worst of his pain, though the fracture itself went untreated for two more days.
2. A fan in the window alleviated the heat a bit, but honestly, it was still unbearable.
Poverty alleviation is the standard phrase in World Bank and NGO reports — chosen precisely because nobody is willing to say poverty elimination.
Latin levis = "light (in weight)" → levāre, "to lift, lighten"; ad- + levāre = to lighten toward you.

One root, a whole GRE cluster: elevate (lift up), levitate (float), levity (lightness of mood), relieve/relief (lift the burden again), lever and leverage (lifting device), even leaven (what lifts the dough).

To refer to something indirectly, without naming it.
To refer to something indirectly — to hint at it, gesture toward it, mention it without naming it.

The indirectness is the whole point. You mention a thing; you allude to it. Alluding means the listener has to do a little work: you name the affair as "recent difficulties," you name the rival's book as "a certain bestseller." So it's the verb of tact, of insinuation, and of literature — a poet alludes to Homer, a diplomat alludes to a scandal, a colleague alludes to your unread emails. Note it takes to: you allude to something, never allude something.
⚠️ allude ≠ elude.
- allude to = hint at it
- elude = escape or slip away from it (the thief eluded capture; the word eludes me)

Same Latin root, opposite directions: toward vs away.
Never said aloud — only alluded to.
The near-homophone flips the meaning: what's alluded to is precisely what nobody says out loud.
1. In his resignation letter he alluded to "differences of judgement" with the board, and named no one.
2. She kept alluding to some big announcement and then refused to tell us what it was.
Every English class you've sat in: a literary allusion is a line that nods at another text without quoting it — Eliot glancing at Dante, a film title lifted from Shakespeare.
Latin ad- ("toward") + ludere ("to play") — literally to play toward, to touch on a thing in passing.

That root pays off across a whole family: elude (play away — escape), delude (play someone false), collude (play together, secretly), prelude / interlude (play before / between), ludicrous (fit only for play).

Full of indirect references; hinting rather than stating outright.
Full of indirect references — to books, myths, events, people — made in passing rather than spelled out.

The key is deliberateness. Allusive writing isn't unclear because the writer fumbled; it's indirect on purpose, and it assumes you already know the thing being pointed at. That makes it a compliment among literary types (dense, layered, sophisticated) and a complaint everywhere else (show-offy, impenetrable to outsiders). It describes style, not people: a poem, an essay, a remark can be allusive — a person is usually evasive instead.
⚠️ allusive ≠ elusive.
- allusive = refers indirectly (from allude)
- elusive = escapes you — hard to catch, pin down, or define (from elude)

E for Escape. An allusive clue points at something; an elusive answer runs away from you.
Allusive drops the reference and leaves you to catch it — all hint, no footnote.
The hint only works if you already know the source, which is exactly why allusive style flatters some readers and locks out the rest.
1. Her prose is so allusive that a single paragraph nods at Ovid, the Book of Job, and a Motown B-side.
2. He made some allusive comment about "what happened in Lisbon" and then just changed the subject.
T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land is the textbook case of allusive writing — it packs in so many buried quotations that Eliot bolted footnotes onto the end of the poem to explain his own references.
Latin ad- ("toward") + lūdere ("to play") → allūdere, "to play at, touch on lightly, joke toward."

That lūdere root is a GRE workhorse: elude (play away → escape), delude (play someone false), collude (play together, in secret), illusion, prelude, interlude, ludicrous. Spot -lud-/-lus- and you're looking at play.

Distant and uninvolved; deliberately keeping apart from others
Keeping at a distance — physically apart, or emotionally uninvolved, declining to mingle or engage.

The distance is chosen, calm, and unexplained, which is why people read superiority into it. Shy is fear of others; reserved is a quiet temperament; standoffish is actively rude. Someone aloof simply doesn't come closer, and lets you wonder why. It's usually said by the excluded party, so it carries a faint sting — the aloof person is never the one using the word.

Common frames: hold oneself aloof from the quarrel, remain aloof from politics.
Aloof = "a roof." Up on the roof, above the party, watching it — not fighting anyone, just not coming down.
The sound hook fixes the key nuance: aloofness is elevation and distance, not hostility.
1. The ambassador remained aloof from the factional squabbling, receiving all parties and committing to none.
2. He's not unfriendly, he's just aloof — three years in the flat and I still don't know his surname.
The stock description of cats: dogs mob you at the door, cats stay aloof — present in the room, declining to participate.
Sailors' talk. Dutch loef = the windward side of a ship (English luff). The order "a-loof!" meant steer into the wind — away from the dangerous lee shore.

So aloof is literally keeping well clear of the rocks: deliberate distance from something you'd rather not be dashed against.
