column2:
Selfless — acting for others' benefit at your own cost.
Acting for the good of others at a cost to yourself, with no expectation of return.

Generous and kind describe what you did; altruistic describes why — it's a claim about motive, and an absolute one: zero self-interest. That absoluteness is what makes it a favourite of philosophers, economists and biologists (in evolutionary biology, altruism is the puzzle of why an animal would ever pay a cost for another's benefit). It's also why the word so often arrives pre-loaded with doubt: "purely altruistic motives" is a phrase people usually write in order to question it.
Altruistic — hit alt and you get the other option. Altruism is choosing the other person's option, and paying for it.
The buried alt- is the same alter = "other" you already know from alternative, and the cost to yourself is what separates altruistic from merely nice.
1. Her decision to donate the kidney to a stranger was altruistic in the strictest sense: she declined to learn the recipient's name.
2. He'll tell you he took the night shift for altruistic reasons, but he also really wanted the parking spot.
Effective Altruism — the movement that told donors to maximise lives saved per dollar, then became a byword for good intentions gone strange after the FTX collapse. The word's built-in tension between selflessness and suspicion, playing out in public.
Latin alter = "the other." French philosopher Auguste Comte coined altruisme in the 1830s as the exact opposite of egoism — living for the other rather than the self.

That root is everywhere once you see it: alter (make other), alternative (the other choice), alter ego (your other self), altercation (a quarrel — you and the other guy).

To merge separate things into a single unified whole.
To combine separate things into one unified whole — companies, departments, traditions, populations.

Weight matters here. Mix leaves the ingredients recognisable; amalgamate implies the parts genuinely fuse and stop being distinguishable — two banks amalgamate and there is now one bank, with one name and one balance sheet. It's a formal, institutional word: boards, regulators and historians amalgamate things, nobody amalgamates a salad. It also carries a faint sense of scale and officialdom that merge doesn't — which is why press releases love it.
A MALL is hiding in a-mal-gamate — a hundred separate shops pulled under one roof, trading as one address.
The point isn't that the shops sit near each other, it's that they've become a single entity with one name — which is exactly the fusion amalgamate demands.
1. The three parish schools were amalgamated into a single academy in 1974, and the old names survive only on the war memorials.
2. They amalgamated both teams into one after the layoffs — same work, half the people, new org chart.
The silver filling in a back tooth is called an amalgam — mercury dissolved into silver and tin until you can't tell which is which. Same word, same idea: not a mixture, a fusion.
Medieval Latin amalgama, "an alloy of mercury with another metal" (probably via Arabic al-malgham). Mercury is the key: it doesn't sit alongside another metal, it swallows it into one soft mass.

Family: amalgam (the alloy, and by extension any true blend), amalgamation (the corporate merger sense you meet in every business headline).

Pulled two opposite ways at once; torn, not indifferent.
Having two opposing feelings about the same thing at the same time — attraction and repulsion, wanting and dreading.

The word is routinely misused to mean meh, don't care. It means the opposite of that: an ambivalent person cares twice, in contradictory directions, and is stuck. Someone indifferent feels nothing about the job offer; someone ambivalent desperately wants it and desperately doesn't. Zero versus a tug-of-war. Register is educated and slightly clinical — it comes out of psychiatry — so it suggests a mind examining its own divided state rather than a shrug.
⚠️ ambivalent ≠ ambiguous.
- ambivalent = the person is torn between two feelings
- ambiguous = the thing can be read two ways

His reply was ambiguous; his feelings were ambivalent.
Ambi-VALENT-ine's Day — two hearts pulling at once, not a heart that's switched off.
The buried valentine keeps feeling in the word, blocking the standard error of using it for apathy.
1. The committee remained ambivalent about the merger, alive to its savings and equally alive to what it would cost the town.
2. I'm pretty ambivalent about going — I'd love to see everyone, and I'd love to be in bed by nine.
Facebook's old "It's complicated" relationship status is ambivalence in two words — not no feelings, but too many, pointing opposite ways.
Latin ambi- = "both" + valēre = "to be strong, to be worth." Both sides are strong — that's the whole word, and the reason it can't mean indifference.

ambi- gives you ambidextrous (skilled with both hands), ambiguous (drivable both ways), ambit.
valēre gives you valid, value, valiant, prevail, convalesce — all about strength or worth.

To make a bad situation less bad.
To make something bad less bad — to improve conditions that were painful, harsh, or deficient.

The word carries a precondition: nothing gets ameliorated unless it was already in a poor state. You improve a recipe, a serve, a profit margin; you ameliorate suffering, overcrowding, soil, working conditions. And it promises only partial repair — a policy that ameliorates poverty has softened it, not ended it. Register is formal and institutional: it belongs to policy papers, court judgments and NGO reports, and sounds faintly pompous in a kitchen.
a-MEAL-iorate — a hot meal doesn't cure poverty, it just makes it less bad.
The buried "meal" gives you both halves of the word: the situation was already grim, and the fix is real but partial.
1. Drainage works did something to ameliorate the flooding, though the worst-hit streets flooded again that winter.
2. A decent night's sleep won't fix the project, but it might ameliorate your mood about it.
Standard equipment in policy and legal prose — aid reports and judgments constantly promise "measures to ameliorate the effects of" a drought, a recession, a lockdown. Spot it there and you'll notice it never says the problem was solved.
Latin melior = "better" (as in meliorism, the belief the world can be made better).

Worth pairing with its opposite: pejor = "worse", which gives you pejorative — a word chosen to make something sound worse. Melior up, pejor down.

Willing to comply; open to a given method or treatment.
1. Willing to go along with a suggestion; open to persuasion, easy to work with.
2. (of a thing) Susceptible to a given treatment or method — amenable to analysis, surgery, compromise.

Almost always followed by to. Sense 1 describes low resistance, not enthusiasm: someone amenable doesn't push back, which is a step below eager and a step above grudging. It says nothing about whether they're warm — a cold, formal colleague can be perfectly amenable. Sense 2 is the workhorse of academic and medical prose, where it's coldly neutral: a problem amenable to modelling is simply one the method can get a grip on.
⚠️ amenable ≠ amiable. Amiable = friendly, likeable by nature (a disposition). Amenable = willing to comply, or open to a method (a response). A charming host is amiable; a colleague who accepts your timeline without a fight is amenable — and one can easily be either without being the other.
Amen-able — they say amen to your plan.
Amen means "so be it" — quiet assent rather than applause, which is exactly the temperature of the word.
1. The tribunal found the minister amenable to reason once the political cost of refusal was made plain.
2. Ask him — he's usually amenable to swapping shifts if you give him a day's notice.
Standard in clinical language: a tumour is described as amenable to resection, meaning surgery can actually get at it. Same word you'd use for a cooperative patient — one sense about people, one about problems.
Old French amener = "to lead to" (à + mener, to lead). Amenable is literally able to be led — which covers both senses: a person you can lead to your view, a problem you can lead to a solution. Same mener gives demeanour (how you conduct — lead — yourself) and promenade (a leading-forward, a stroll).

🚫 No connection to amare, "to love." That root gives amiable, amicable, amorous — the sound-alikes that cost marks.

column2:
to alter formally so as to correct or improve
To alter something formally in order to correct or improve it — a law, a motion, a contract, a statement, a tax return. Also of conduct: to amend your ways.

The key is that the original survives. Amending is patching, not scrapping: a bill that is amended is still that bill; a bill that is repealed is dead. Compare revise (neutral, any scale of change) and rewrite (start again) — amend is narrow, procedural, and usually official. It also carries a faint whiff of prior fault: you amend something because something in it was wrong.

Separately, the fossilised noun phrase make amends = to compensate someone for a wrong done.
⚠️ amend ≠ emend.
- amend = change a document or your behaviour, usually to improve it
- emend = correct actual errors in a text — a scholar's word for fixing a corrupt manuscript

You amend a constitution. You emend a typo in Chaucer.
A-MEND — the word has mend sitting inside it: you mend the flaw, you don't bin the thing.
Amending keeps the original intact and repairs a fault in it, which is exactly what mending means.
1. The committee voted to amend the clause rather than strike it, softening the penalty from dismissal to suspension.
2. Fine, I'll amend my statement — the food wasn't terrible, it was just cold.
The First Amendment, the Fifth, the Nineteenth — the US Constitution has never been rewritten, only patched. Every amendment is a fix bolted onto a document that still stands.
Latin ēmendāre = "to remove a fault" — from ex- (out) + menda (a fault, a blemish).

That root gives you emend and emendation, and — worn down through French — plain mend itself. All three are the same idea: take the flaw out.

🚫 Not related to amenity. That's Latin amoenus, "pleasant."

Friendly and without hostility, especially where conflict was expected.
Characterised by goodwill; conducted without hostility.

The word almost always shows up where a fight was expected and didn't happen. An amicable divorce, an amicable settlement, an amicable parting of ways — it describes the tone of a dealing between parties, not affection. Two people can end things amicably and never speak again. It's the absence of rancour, not the presence of warmth, and it carries a slightly formal, almost legal air.
amicable ≠ amiable.
- amicable describes a relationship or dealing — an amicable settlement
- amiable describes a person's disposition — an amiable colleague

Two amiable people can still have a bitter split; two cold people can split amicably.
You never hear "an amicable friendship" — only an amicable divorce, split, or settlement.
The word attaches itself to situations that could have turned ugly, which is exactly why it means peaceable rather than affectionate.
1. The border dispute was resolved amicably, both delegations signing before the deadline.
2. They split up last year but it was pretty amicable — he still crashes on her couch when he's in town.
Every celebrity breakup statement runs the same line: "The couple have decided to separate amicably and ask for privacy at this time." If a PR team wrote it, the word is in there.
Latin amicus = "friend" (from amare, to love). That root is worth banking: amity (friendly relations), amiable, amigo, enamoured.

Best of all, negate it: in- + amicus → inimical (hostile, harmful) and plain old enemy — literally not-a-friend.

column2:
Shapeless; lacking clear form, structure or definition.
Without a definite shape — and, by extension, without definite structure: a blob, a fog, a committee with no chain of command, a draft with no argument.

In science it's purely descriptive: an amorphous solid (glass, plastic) is one whose atoms sit in no crystal lattice. Outside the lab it usually carries quiet criticism, but of a cool, diagnostic kind. Vague and wishy-washy complain about how something was expressed; amorphous says the thing itself has no edges yet — nobody has drawn the outline. It describes the object, not the speaker's irritation, which is exactly why it sounds clinical rather than cross.
⚠️ amorphous ≠ amorous. Amorous is Latin amor, "love" — full of desire. One letter-cluster apart, opposite worlds: an amorous glance, an amorphous plan.
a-MORPH-ous — nothing to morph, because there's no shape there to begin with.
Note where the word actually turns up: less often on clouds and jellyfish than on strategies, movements and first drafts whose outlines nobody has bothered to draw.
1. The protest remained amorphous — no leaders, no demands, no obvious way for the government to negotiate with it.
2. Right now the plan's pretty amorphous; give me a week and I'll turn it into actual dates.
Morpheus in The Matrix is the same root — Greek morphē, "form," the god who takes any shape in dreams. He's the one who tells Neo none of the shapes around him are real.
Greek a- (without) + morphē (form). One root, a lot of GRE mileage: metamorphosis (change of form), morpheme (smallest unit of meaning-form), anthropomorphic (given human form), polymorphous (many forms), and morphine — named for Morpheus, the shape-shifting god of dreams.

To make louder, stronger, or fuller; to expand on.
To make something bigger, louder, or stronger — sound, a signal, an effect, a message.

The key is that amplify never creates; it takes something already there and turns the dial up. That's what separates it from exaggerate (which distorts) and embellish (which adds invented detail) — amplify stays neutral about whether the thing is true. Second sense, common on the GRE: to expand on a statement — "could you amplify that point?" means say more, not say it louder. Modern professional usage ("amplify underrepresented voices") is warmly positive, but the word itself carries no judgement — panic, tension, and rumours get amplified too.
Amplify hides an amp and ample — turn up what's already playing, until there's plenty of it.
The guitar amp boosts a string that's already vibrating, which is exactly why you amplify a rumour but fabricate a lie.
1. Social media did not create the outrage so much as amplify it, feeding a local grievance to a global audience within hours.
2. "You said the schedule was 'unrealistic' — care to amplify that a bit before we sign the contract?"
Every electric guitar runs through an amp — short for amplifier. The pickup produces a signal far too faint to hear; the amp does nothing but make that existing signal enormous. That's the whole word in one box.
Latin amplus = "large, spacious" + -ficāre (facere, "to make"). Literally make it large.

Same root gives you ample (plenty), amplitude (the size of a wave's swing), and amplification. And -fy / -ficāre is a free GRE bonus: clarify, ratify, mollify, vilify — all "make it X."

Belonging to the wrong era; a survival from an earlier time.
Belonging to a different time period than the one it appears in — chronologically misplaced.

It cuts two ways. Neutrally, it's a factual error: a wristwatch on a gladiator, a character in 1850 mentioning a telephone. Judgementally, it's a verdict on something that has outlived its era — a rule, an institution, a job title that should have died decades ago. That second use is where the GRE lives, and it carries a dry contempt: calling a law anachronistic says it isn't just old, it's absurd that it survived. Note the direction — anachronistic things are almost always relics dragged forward, not things arriving too early.
⚠️ anachronistic ≠ anarchistic. Anachronistic = out of time (chronos). Anarchistic = against rule (archos). One letter's difference on the page, two unrelated roots.
CHRON sits right in the middle — a clock stuck in the wrong century.
Spot chron (as in chronological) inside the word and you've got the whole meaning: the timeline is off.
1. The committee dismissed the dress code as an anachronistic relic of a workplace no one under fifty remembered.
2. Fax machines in a 2026 office? Completely anachronistic.
The Starbucks cup left on the table in Game of Thrones — a paper coffee cup in medieval Westeros, the most-screenshotted anachronism in television history.
Greek ana- (back) + chronos (time) — literally "back-timed."

Chronos is a workhorse root: chronic (lasting over time), chronology, chronicle, synchronise (same-time), chronometer.

column2:
Comparable in function or relation, though otherwise different.
Corresponding in function or relation to something else, in a way that makes a comparison legitimate — even though the two things are otherwise unalike.

The word is a claim, not an observation. Similar notes a resemblance and stops; analogous asserts that the parallel runs deep enough to reason from — if it holds for X, expect it to hold for Y. That's why it lives in argument, science and law rather than casual description. And it never means identical: the things being compared are understood to differ in substance, matching only in the shape of the relationship. Always paired with to (or with).
⚠️ analogous ≠ anomalous.
- analogous (uh-NAL-uh-guhs) = parallel, comparable
- anomalous (uh-NOM-uh-luhs) = abnormal, deviating from the pattern

One says it fits the pattern; the other says it breaks it. The GRE loves this pair.
ANA-LOG-ous — same logic, different thing.
What matches is the underlying logic or ratio, not the appearance — which is exactly why an insect's wing is analogous to a bird's.
1. The court held that a text message was analogous to a sealed letter, and extended the same protections to it.
2. Running a startup is analogous to juggling — drop one thing and you can usually recover; drop two and it's over.
Analogue audio: the groove on a vinyl record is a physical wiggle whose shape corresponds, point for point, to the sound wave. Nothing about it looks like music — it's analogous to it. That's the whole idea in one object.
Greek ana- ("according to") + logos ("ratio, proportion") → analogon, "in proportion." That's why an analogy is written as a ratio: A is to B as C is to D.

logos is a monster root — it means both word and reason/ratio: logic, dialogue, prologue, catalogue, eulogy, and every -ology.

Open, active hostility; deep-seated ill will.
Strong, active hostility toward someone — ill will with heat behind it.

Dislike is a preference; animosity is a charge. It's usually personal and usually has a history — a feud, a snub, a rivalry that never healed — and it leaks out in tone, in refusals to cooperate, in the way two people avoid each other's name. It stops short of hatred (which is total) and it isn't the cool, refined distaste of antipathy; animosity is the bad blood you can feel in the room.
Animosity is animated dislike — hostility with a pulse.
The same anim- that makes cartoons move makes this dislike live — it acts, it simmers, it isn't the passive kind.
1. Decades after the partition, the animosity between the two families had hardened into a silence neither side would break.
2. There's still real animosity there — he hasn't spoken to his old boss in six years.
Standard sports-commentary vocabulary: derby matches and title fights are always sold on "the animosity between these two" — the grudge, not the skill, is the story.
Latin animus = spirit, mind, passion. Animosity first meant spiritedness, boldness — high spirits that soured into hostile ones.

The root is a GRE workhorse: unanimous (one spirit), magnanimous (great spirit — generous), pusillanimous (tiny spirit — cowardly), equanimity (even spirit — calm), plus animate and animal (things with breath in them).

Deep-seated hostility that drives action against someone.
Ill will — a settled hostility toward someone that drives how you act toward them.

Anger is hot and passing; animus is cold and standing. It isn't the flare-up, it's the grudge underneath that explains the behaviour, which is why lawyers and journalists reach for it: you allege that a policy, a firing, or a prosecution was motivated by animus. It implies a motive, not just a mood — and it points at the hostile party, never the target.

(A second, unrelated sense belongs to Jung: the animus is the masculine element of the female psyche, paired with the anima. Context makes it obvious which is meant.)
Animus is what animates the grudge — the spirit that moves you against someone.
Same anim- as animation: animus isn't a passing temper but the driving force behind hostile action.
1. The court found that the ordinance served no purpose but to express animus toward a disfavoured group.
2. I've got no animus against the guy — I just don't want him running the meeting.
A courtroom and newsroom staple: "racial animus," "religious animus," "motivated by personal animus." When a headline says a law was struck down for animus, it means the judges decided the only thing behind it was dislike.
Latin animus = mind, spirit, passion (sibling of anima, breath/soul). The root pays for itself across the GRE: unanimous (of one mind), magnanimous (great-souled, generous), pusillanimous (tiny-spirited, cowardly), equanimity (even mind), animosity, animate.

Note the drift: the neutral Latin "spirit" narrowed in English to hostile spirit specifically.

To consecrate with oil; to designate as the chosen successor.
Literally: to smear or rub with oil as part of a sacred rite — a king at his coronation, a body before burial, a sick person receiving last rites.

Figuratively: to single someone out as the chosen one, especially a successor.

The figurative sense keeps the incense in it. To appoint a deputy is paperwork; to anoint a successor is to bless them, to hand over the aura along with the job — the choice feels ordained rather than decided. Journalists lean on it precisely for that whiff of dynasty ("the anointed heir"), and self-anointed is pure sneer: you consecrated yourself and nobody else was consulted.
⚠️ anoint ≠ appoint.
- appoint = assign to a post — administrative, revocable
- anoint = consecrate as chosen — ceremonial, quasi-sacred

A board appoints a CEO. The retiring founder anoints one.
an-OINT hides ointment — you can't anoint anyone without the oil, and that oil is what turns a mere choice into a blessing.
The word carries its own grease: ointment is right there in the spelling, and the oil is exactly what separates anointing from ordinary appointing.
1. The archbishop anointed the young queen with chrism before the crown ever touched her head.
2. Everyone knew he'd been anointed the moment the boss started bringing him to the investor calls.
Christ isn't a surname — Greek khristos means "the anointed one", a direct translation of Hebrew mashiach, Messiah. Two of the most familiar words in English are both just "anointed."
Latin in- + unguere = "to smear on." That root oils a whole family: unguent (a salve), ointment, and — best of all for the GRE — unctuous, literally "greasy," now meaning oily in the flattering, insincere way.

Not fitting the expected pattern; irregular, off-model.
Departing from what is standard, expected, or predicted by the pattern — irregular, off-model.

This is the lab-coat word for odd. Weird is a reaction, aberrant hints that something has gone morally or biologically wrong, but anomalous passes no judgement at all: it simply says this case does not fit the model. It also quietly assumes the model is sound and the case is the outlier — which is why a scientist calls a reading anomalous before deciding whether it's an error, a fluke, or a discovery.
⚠️ anomalous ≠ analogous.
- anomalous = doesn't fit the pattern
- analogous = parallel to something else, comparable

An anomalous result breaks the trend; an analogous case matches a different one.
a-NOM-alous — hear the stressed NOM as norm with the r rubbed out: the thing that won't sit on the norm.
It's a pure sound hook rather than the true root, but it locks in the key idea — the word labels something as off-pattern without calling it wrong.
1. The committee flagged an anomalous spike in third-quarter revenue: no launch, no campaign, just a number that refused to fit the curve.
2. Look, one good week is anomalous — don't rebuild the whole strategy around it.
In The Matrix Reloaded, the Architect calls Neo \"the anomaly\" — the one variable the system's model can't account for. That's the word exactly: not evil, just unpredicted.
Greek an- (not) + homalos (even, level), from homos = "same." Literally not level with the rest.

That root gives you homogeneous, homonym, homologous — all "same-ness" words.

🚫 Not from nomos (law), despite the look of autonomous and economy. Anomalous breaks a pattern, not a rule.

To provoke into hostility; to make an enemy of someone.
To provoke someone into active hostility — to behave so that a person turns against you. Also, in science: to act against, counteract, or block (one drug antagonizes another; one muscle antagonizes its partner).

The difference from annoy or irritate is what gets damaged. Annoying someone changes their mood; antagonizing them changes the relationship — you have converted a neutral party into an opponent. That's why it usually arrives as strategic advice about someone who can hurt you: don't antagonize the landlord, the regulator, the judge. It's often deliberate and always costly.
Antagonize = hand someone the role of antagonist in your story.
You're not merely irritating them — you're casting them as the villain who now works against you for the rest of the plot.
1. The proposed tariffs antagonized trading partners whose cooperation the treaty still required.
2. Just apologise — there's no point antagonizing the one guy who can approve your leave.
In pharmacology the word is literal and everyday: naloxone (Narcan) is an opioid antagonist — it blocks the receptor, working directly against the drug. Same idea as antagonizing a person: not annoying it, opposing it.
Greek agōn = "a contest, a struggle" (the games, the arena) + anti- = "against". An antagonist is the one struggling against you.

That root pays out across the list: agony (the struggle itself), agonize (to writhe in it), protagonist (prōtos, first — the one who struggles first, i.e. the lead), antagonism.

To come before in time; or mark with an earlier date.
1. To come before something else in time — to be older than it.
2. To mark a document with a date earlier than the real one (i.e. backdate it).

Sense 1 is neutral and bookish: it's what you use for gaps measured in centuries, not last Tuesday. Predate means the same thing and is the plainer, far commoner word — antedate is the stiffer, more scholarly register, and it's the only one of the pair that also carries sense 2. That second sense is where the word turns shady: nobody antedates a contract by accident, and in legal or audit contexts the word is a near-synonym for fraud.
Ante-date = put the date out front — either it genuinely stood first, or someone quietly moved it there.
One prefix covers both senses: real priority in time, or manufactured priority on paper.
1. The cave paintings at Chauvet antedate those at Lascaux by some twenty thousand years.
2. He antedated the cheque by a week so it wouldn't look like he'd missed the deadline.
Poker: the ante is the chip you put in before the cards are dealt — which is why "up the ante" means raising the stakes up front, before anyone's committed.
Latin ante = "before." It's everywhere once you see it: antecedent (going before), antebellum (pre-war), anterior (front), antechamber (the room you wait in before the real one), anticipate (take beforehand).

🚫 Not anti-. That's Greek for "against" — antidote, antiseptic, antipathy. Same sound, opposite job: ante = earlier, anti = opposed.

A deep, settled dislike — instinctive aversion, not passing anger.
A deep, settled dislike or aversion — for a person, a group, an idea, a food.

Antipathy is cold, not hot. Hatred burns and wants something to happen; antipathy just wants distance. It's also often unaccountable — you feel it before you can justify it, which is why the word suits instinctive recoil ("a lifelong antipathy to crowds") as much as considered opposition. And it's standing, not momentary: a flash of irritation is never antipathy. Formal register — journalists write of public antipathy toward a policy where speech would just say people hate it.
⚠️ antipathy ≠ apathy.
- apathy = no feeling — you don't care
- antipathy = feeling against — you care, and you're against it

The apathetic voter stays home shrugging; the antipathetic one stays home in disgust.
Anti-path — you'd take a different path to avoid them.
That captures the coldness: antipathy doesn't attack, it steers clear.
1. Her antipathy toward the new director was never spoken aloud, but it shaped every appointment she made.
2. I've got a serious antipathy to group chats — nothing personal, I just can't.
Greek anti- (against) + pathos (feeling, suffering) — literally feeling-against.

That second root is a GRE workhorse: sympathy (feeling with), empathy (feeling into), apathy (without feeling), pathos, pathetic, pathology (the study of what a body suffers).

The exact opposite; a deliberately contrasting counter-idea.
1. The direct and complete opposite of something. 2. In rhetoric, a figure that sets two contrary ideas in balanced, parallel phrasing.

Opposite is a flat statement of fact; antithesis is a verdict. Calling someone the antithesis of professionalism doesn't just place them at the other end of a scale — it says they stand against the thing, that they define it by negation. The word carries debate-club formality, so it lands hardest in argument, criticism and manifesto, and it nearly always arrives in the frame "the antithesis of ___."
Anti-thesis — not merely unlike your thesis, but the counter-claim planted directly opposite it.
The word wears its meaning openly: a thesis with an enemy bolted to the front, which is why it implies opposition rather than mere difference.
1. The committee's cautious, consensus-bound report was the antithesis of the bold reform its authors had promised.
2. Silent, minimalist, no logo anywhere — the place is the antithesis of a sports bar.
Armstrong's line from the Moon — "one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind" — is textbook antithesis: small against giant, man against mankind, in matched phrasing.
Greek anti- (against) + thesis (a placing, from tithenai, "to put"). Literally a setting-against.

That tithenai root is a GRE workhorse: thesis (a position put forward), hypothesis (placed under as a supposition), synthesis (placed together), parenthesis (placed beside), epithet (a name placed on).

Complete lack of interest or feeling; an uncaring shrug.
A total absence of interest, emotion, or concern — you don't care, and you can't be roused to.

The key is that apathy is empty, not hostile. Someone who hates a policy is engaged with it; someone apathetic won't look up from their phone. It's a flat, deadened state rather than a hot one, which is why it attaches so naturally to voters, students, and burnt-out employees. The word almost always carries a note of reproach — writers use it to accuse a public of not caring about something it should care about.
⚠️ apathy ≠ antipathy.
- apathy = a- (without) feeling — the shrug
- antipathy = anti- (against) feeling — the strong dislike

Apathy toward a candidate keeps you home; antipathy toward one gets you to the polls.
Apathy is a shrug, not a scowl.
The apathetic person hasn't taken a side — there's simply nothing there to push against.
1. Widespread apathy among younger voters, more than any organised opposition, doomed the referendum.
2. I asked what he wanted for dinner and got a shrug — total apathy, as usual.
"Voter apathy" is the phrase every news anchor reaches for the morning after a low-turnout election — nobody was angry, they just stayed home.
Greek a- (without) + pathos (feeling, suffering) = literally feeling-less.

That pathos unlocks a whole shelf: sympathy (feeling with), empathy (feeling into), antipathy (feeling against), pathetic (stirring feeling), pathology (the study of what you suffer from).

A short, crafted sentence stating a general truth.
A short, polished statement of a general truth — one sentence that compresses an observation about life into its smallest hard form. "Less is more." "The unexamined life is not worth living."

What marks it off from its neighbours is authorship and craft. A proverb is folk property, worn smooth by centuries of anonymous use; an aphorism has a writer behind it and shows the tooling — balance, surprise, often a twist of wit. A maxim tells you what to do; an aphorism tells you what is. And calling something an aphorism is mildly admiring: it means the line earned its brevity. The insult version is platitude or cliché.
Aphorism shares its root with horizon: one clean line that fences a whole truth off from everything else.
Both come from Greek horizein, "to draw a boundary" — the aphorism's whole trick is where it decides to stop.
1. Nietzsche wrote in aphorisms rather than arguments, trusting a single detonating sentence to do the work of a chapter.
2. My gran had an aphorism for everything, and annoyingly she was usually right.
Oscar Wilde is the patron saint of the form — "I can resist everything except temptation." That's the shape: short, balanced, and it turns on you at the end.
Greek aphorismos, from apo- (off, away) + horizein (to bound, to define) — literally a marking-off, a definition. Hippocrates' medical Aphorisms opened with "Life is short, art is long."

Same horizein gives you horizon — the line that bounds what you can see. Same apo- gives apogee, apostasy, apostrophe.

Visible poise — pulling off a hard thing with easy confidence.
Complete self-possession — poise, steadiness, and confidence, especially in a situation that would fluster most people.

Composure is holding yourself together; aplomb is making the hard thing look effortless. It's the outward style of the calm, not just the calm itself — a surgeon, a comic handling a heckler, a diplomat answering a hostile question. The word is admiring almost by default: you can't have aplomb doing something easy, and you can't have it while visibly straining.
Nobody ever has aplomb — they do things with aplomb.
The word lives almost entirely inside that one phrase, which is the clue that it describes how a difficult act is carried off, not a mood you sit in.
1. Handed a question she had not been briefed on, the ambassador fielded it with aplomb and moved the room along.
2. He burnt the starter, swapped in takeaway, and served it with such aplomb that nobody asked.
In classical ballet, aplomb is an actual technical term: the dancer's perfect vertical balance over the supporting leg — the body hanging dead straight, like a plumb line.
French à plomb = "to the plumb line" — i.e. hanging perfectly upright. From Latin plumbum, "lead" (the weight on a builder's string).

That root also gives you plumb (vertical; or to sound the depths), plumber (originally a worker in lead pipe), and plummet — which was the lead weight before it meant to drop like one. Someone with aplomb doesn't wobble off vertical.

column2:
The highest or farthest point of a rise.
Literally, the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth. Figuratively, the highest point something reaches — of a career, an empire, a style, a reputation.

What sets it apart from peak or height is the arc. An apogee is the top of a trajectory: something climbed to get there, and gravity is already pulling it back. Say a band's 1997 album was their apogee and you've implied the decline without stating it. Register is formal and slightly grand — it belongs in essays and obituaries, not in conversation about your Tuesday.
⚠️ apogee ≠ perigee. Apogee = farthest out; perigee = closest in. A "supermoon" is a perigee moon — near, so it looks huge.
Apogee sounds like apex — but an apex is the top of a shape, an apogee the top of a flight.
The sound gets you to "highest point"; the difference reminds you that an apogee is reached by travelling, and travel continues downward.
1. The Mughal empire reached its apogee under Akbar; every reign after it was a slow subtraction.
2. He peaked in the second year — that promotion was the apogee, and he knows it.
Watch any rocket launch stream — SpaceX, Blue Origin, ISRO — and the commentators call out apogee as the moment the vehicle stops climbing and starts coming back down.
Greek apo- = "away from" + gaia / gē = "earth." Literally "away from the earth."

Both halves pay rent: apo- gives you apostasy (standing away from the faith), apostrophe, apathy; gē gives you geology, geography, geometry — and perigee, peri- = "near, around," as in perimeter.

One who defends the indefensible; not one who says sorry.
Someone who argues in defence of a doctrine, regime, institution, or practice — especially one most people find indefensible.

The word almost never describes the person themselves; it's what other people call them. Labelling someone "an apologist for the junta" isn't reporting that they defend it — it's saying they're doing dishonest work on its behalf, dressing up the ugly parts as reasonable. Neutral defenders get called advocates or proponents; you reach for apologist when you want the defence to look like a cover-up. The one clean, non-pejorative use is theological: Christian apologists are professional defenders of the faith, and wear the title proudly.
⚠️ apologist ≠ apologetic.
- apologetic = sorry, sheepish, backing down
- apologist = sorry for nothing — standing there defending the thing

Same root, opposite posture.
An apologist never apologises.
He isn't saying "my side was wrong" — he's saying "my side was right, and here's why," which is exactly why the label stings.
1. Later historians dismissed him as an apologist for empire, forever finding civilising motives behind the gunboats.
2. Don't get me wrong, I'm no apologist for the guy — I just think the timeline doesn't add up.
It's a standard weapon in political journalism and comment threads — "a Kremlin apologist", "an apologist for Big Tobacco". Notice it's always aimed at someone, never claimed.
Greek apologia = "a speech in your own defence" (apo- "away" + logos "speech") — courtroom language, not contrition. Plato's Apology is Socrates on trial defending himself and conceding nothing.

The "sorry" sense is the late arrival; apologist simply kept the original job. Same logos family: monologue, eulogy, prologue, dialogue.

Calm someone by giving in to their demands.
To calm or pacify someone by giving them what they want — concessions, apologies, tribute. Also, in a milder sense, to satisfy an appetite: appease hunger, appease curiosity.

Placate and mollify just describe soothing someone. Appease almost always tells you the price: you bought the quiet, and you bought it by yielding. That's why the noun appeasement is close to an accusation — it says the peacemaker was weak, and that the bully will be back for more.
app-EASE — you put them at ease by giving up something of yours.
It never means winning someone over by argument; it means purchasing calm with concessions, which is why the word carries a whiff of cowardice.
1. The board appeased the striking staff with a one-off bonus, hoping the structural grievances would quietly go away.
2. I made him a sandwich just to appease him for ten minutes.
Appeasement is the word history pinned on Neville Chamberlain — handing Hitler the Sudetenland at Munich in 1938 and flying home promising "peace for our time." A year later, war. Ever since, calling a policy "appeasement" means calling it a surrender.
Old French apaisier = "to bring to peace," from Latin pax, pacis (peace).

That root pays off widely: pacify, pacifist, pacific (calm — Magellan named the Pacific Ocean for its flat water), pact (a settled agreement), and even pay — Latin pacare meant to pacify a creditor by settling up. Which is exactly what appeasing is: paying someone off so they'll calm down.

Strikingly well-suited to the occasion; exactly to the point.
Strikingly well-chosen for the occasion — apt, pertinent, exactly to the point.

It almost always describes things said: a quotation, an example, an analogy, a comparison. You don't call a jacket or a candidate apposite. And it praises aim rather than mere suitability — appropriate means nothing offends propriety, whereas apposite means the remark landed on the precise nerve of the matter. Bookish and evaluative; the word of a critic or a judge, not of casual speech.
apposite ≠ opposite. One letter apart, near-reverses in effect: apposite = perfectly on point; opposite = facing the other way. Latin ad- (toward) vs ob- (against).
Apposite is apt — same first two letters, same idea; the O in opposite points the other way.
Let the ap- tie it to apt so the stray o is the only thing you have to watch for.
1. Her closing remark — that a bridge is judged by the weight it bears, not its ornament — was the most apposite thing said all evening.
2. Nice story, but is it apposite? We're talking about budgets, not hiring.
Legal writing runs on it: judges dismiss a cited case with "counsel's reliance on Smith is inapposite" — beside the point. If you read court opinions or law reporting, the negative form shows up constantly.
Latin ad- (to, toward) + ponere / positus (to place) — "placed right next to." The idea is a remark set alongside the matter and matching it exactly.

That root is a GRE workhorse: position, deposit, composite, juxtapose, expose, apposition (in grammar, two nouns laid side by side: my brother the doctor).

column2:
Uneasy dread of what's coming; also an arrest, or understanding.
1. (usual sense) uneasy anticipation — dread about something that hasn't happened yet.
2. (legal/police) the arrest or seizure of someone.
3. (formal, older) understanding; a mental grasp of something ("beyond human apprehension").

Sense 1 is forward-facing and restrained. Fear is here and now; terror is overwhelming; anxiety is often free-floating and clinical. Apprehension attaches to a specific coming event — the scan results, the audit, the flight — and stays civil enough for a board meeting. Someone who is apprehensive still shows up; they just show up with a knot in the stomach.

On the GRE, senses 2 and 3 are the ones being tested. If "apprehension" appears in a passage and dread makes no sense, try arrest or comprehension.
Ap-PRE-hension — the fear turns up pre-, before the thing does.
The stressed middle syllable marks it as anticipatory dread, not fear of what's already in the room.
1. The delegates awaited the verdict with visible apprehension, conversation dwindling to nothing as the clock passed midnight.
2. I had this weird apprehension about the flight all week, and then it was the smoothest one I've ever taken.
Every police report and crime drama: "the suspect was apprehended near the border." That's sense 2 — the seizing — sitting in plain sight in language you hear constantly.
Latin prehendere = "to seize, to grasp", with ad- (toward). All three senses are one act of grabbing: you grab a criminal, you grab an idea, and a coming misfortune grabs you.

The root pays out widely: comprehend (grasp fully), prehensile (a tail that grips), reprehensible (fit to be seized back — i.e. blamed), apprentice (one who lays hold of a trade), prison and surprise (over-taken).

column2:
To formally inform someone of something they needed to know.
To inform someone — to formally tell them a fact they needed to know.

Register is what marks it. Tell is neutral, notify is administrative, but apprise carries a whiff of duty: the information was owed, and someone discharged the obligation. It almost always takes of ("apprised of the risks") and lives happily in the passive — lawyers, officers, doctors and boards apprise people. Nobody apprises you of the football score.
⚠️ apprise ≠ appraise.
- apprise = inform someone (uh-PRYZE)
- appraise = assess the value of something (uh-PRAYZE)

The extra a is the giveaway: appraise hides praise — you're putting a worth on it.
Apprise rhymes with advise — and both are things a lawyer does to a client, in writing.
The rhyme locks the sound (PRYZE, not PRAYZE) and advise carries the same formal, duty-bound tone.
1. The surgeon apprised the family of the risks before asking anyone to sign.
2. Keep me apprised — if the client so much as sneezes, I want an email.
"Keep me apprised." — the standard bark of every boss, detective and commanding officer in workplace and procedural drama, and of plenty of real managers too.
Via French appris, past participle of apprendre "to learn / to teach," from Latin apprehendere = "to grasp."

Same root gives you apprentice (one being taught), apprehend (to grasp — a fact, or a suspect), comprehend (grasp fully) and prehensile (able to grip). To apprise someone is to hand them something to grasp.

Formal, official praise or approval from someone whose word counts.
Formal or official approval; praise given from a position to bestow it — a nod that counts.

Approval is what a friend gives you; approbation is what an institution, a critic, or a superior gives you. It carries weight and audience: it's the word for a board's blessing, a public's acclaim, a mentor's endorsement. Slightly stiff-collared and old-fashioned — nobody says it about a sandwich.
⚠️ approbation ≠ opprobrium. Same prob- root, opposite poles: approbation = public praise; opprobrium = public disgrace.
Approbation = approval + ovation.
It's approval delivered publicly and formally, with something of an audience clapping behind it.
1. The proposal was adopted only after it won the approbation of the standing committee.
2. He kept glancing at his dad after the recital, fishing for a bit of approbation.
Jane Austen's characters live on this word — in Pride and Prejudice people are forever seeking or withholding one another's approbation, which tells you the register exactly: drawing-room, formal, socially official approval.
Latin probare = "to test, to prove good" (from probus, "upright, honest"), plus ad- "toward" — so approve after testing.

That root pays out across the exam: probity (proven integrity), probation (a testing period), probe, probable, reprobate (tested and found bad), opprobrium.

To take for one's own use, usually without permission.
Adjective: fitting, suitable for the occasion — the everyday sense.
Verb (the one the GRE tests): to take something for your own use, typically without the owner's permission; or, in official language, to set aside money for a designated purpose.

The verb sits on a moral sliding scale. When a legislature appropriates $4bn for flood defence, it is bloodless accounting. When a novelist appropriates a colleague's plot, or a settler appropriates land, the word carries quiet theft — cooler and more respectable than steal, which is exactly what makes it damning. It implies the taker had the power to simply help themselves and did.
⚠️ appropriate ≠ expropriate.
- appropriate = I take it for myself
- expropriate = an authority takes it away from an owner (compulsory purchase, nationalisation)

The ex- is the giveaway: it takes something out of someone else's hands.
The adjective mumbles its ending; the verb ATE it — and what it ate was proper to somebody else.
Hearing the hard -AYT tells you it's the verb, and the "ate" tells you something has been swallowed up that wasn't yours.
1. The committee appropriated funds for the restoration, then quietly appropriated the credit for it as well.
2. He appropriated my charger, my desk and my lunch, all before ten in the morning.
Cultural appropriation — the phrase that made this verb a headline word. It works precisely because appropriate means taking what was proper to another group and wearing it as your own.
Latin ad- (to) + proprius (one's own) — literally to make one's own.

That root is a workhorse: proper, property, proprietor, propriety, proprietary, expropriate. Note the pun buried in the pair: what is proper (fitting) and what is property (owned) come from the same word — which is why appropriate means both "suitable" and "taken".

Fitting and well-timed; or "with regard to."
Adj.: fitting, apt, well-timed — suited to what is happening right now.
Prep. (always apropos of): with regard to, concerning.

Relevant is a logical judgement; apt praises the accuracy of the fit. Apropos praises the timing — the remark landed at exactly the right moment in the conversation. It's an urbane, drawing-room word, imported whole from French and still wearing its accent, so it sounds cultivated in speech and slightly mannered in writing.
⚠️ apropos ≠ apposite. Apposite (AP-uh-zit) = strikingly well-chosen in content — an apposite quotation. Apropos = well-chosen for the occasion. An apposite line can still be raised at a terrible moment.
The word's home phrase is "apropos of nothing" — an apology issued precisely because it isn't.
People flag the exception because the default sense is arising naturally from the moment, so the idiom hands you the meaning and the usage together.
1. The chairman's remark on succession was apropos, coming days before the founder's resignation.
2. Apropos of dinner — are we still doing Thursday, or has that quietly died?
Woody Allen titled his 2020 memoir Apropos of Nothing — a book-length shrug at the idea that any of it was relevant.
French à propos = "to the purpose," from Latin prōpositum, from pro- (forward) + pōnere (to place).

That root places things forward everywhere: propose, proposition, purpose, exponent, component, opponent, postpone.

column2:
Fitting; or inclined to; or quick to learn.
1. Fitting, exactly suited to the occasion — an apt comparison.
2. Inclined or likely to — apt to overreact.
3. Quick to learn — an apt pupil.

All three run off one idea: a good fit. Sense 2 is where the GRE plays. Apt to reports a tendency that follows from what someone is actually like, and it is neutral — she's apt to work straight through the night. Liable to and prone to both tilt toward the unwelcome; apt to carries no such verdict. Sense 1 is faintly formal, the word of a critic praising a well-chosen phrase.
⚠️ apt ≠ adept. Apt = well-suited, or quick to learn (potential). Adept = already highly skilled (achievement). An apt pupil may still botch the operation; an adept surgeon won't.
Adapt = make it fit. Apt = it already fits.
An apt remark fits the moment, an apt pupil fits the task of learning, and someone apt to be late has a tendency that fits their character.
1. The eulogy closed with an apt line from Auden, so well chosen that the poem might have been written for him.
2. Don't put him on the early shift — he's apt to sleep straight through the alarm.
Stephen King's novella Apt Pupil (filmed in 1998 with Ian McKellen) — the title is sense 3: a schoolboy who turns out to be a disturbingly fast learner.
Latin aptus = "fastened, fitted" (from apere, to fasten). The family is worth banking: aptitude (a natural fit for a task), adapt (make it fit), inept (in- + aptus = not fitted → hopeless at it), and attitude, which reached English via Italian attitudine from the same aptitudo — originally the posture a body was fitted into.

🚫 Not adept. That's Latin adipisci, "to attain" — an adeptus was an alchemist who had already attained the secret. Similar sound, different root, different claim.

column2:
Decided by whim or unchecked power, not by reason or rule.
Decided by personal whim or preference rather than by reason, rule, or system — and, at full strength, power used without check or accountability.

Two settings, and the GRE tests both. In maths or logic it's neutral bookkeeping: let n be an arbitrary integer just means "any one, chosen without constraint." Everywhere else it's an accusation: to call a rule, a fine, or a deadline arbitrary is to say nobody can point to the principle behind it. Push it further and it turns political — arbitrary rule, arbitrary arrest — where the complaint is not randomness but unchecked authority, a ruler answerable only to his own say-so. That second sense is the one students miss when they file the word under "random."
Arbitrary hides the arbiter — the referee's call stands, whether or not there's a rule behind it.
An arbitrary decision is one backed by nothing but the decider's authority, which is why the word slides so easily from "random" to "tyrannical."
1. The court struck down the regulation as arbitrary and capricious, finding no evidence the agency had weighed any evidence at all.
2. Why is the cutoff 500 words? Feels totally arbitrary.
Article 9 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: "No one shall be subjected to arbitrary arrest, detention or exile." Not random arrests — arrests nobody has to justify.
Latin arbiter = "judge, one called in to decide." An arbitrary ruling is one resting on the arbiter's personal judgment alone — no rulebook above him.

That root pays out across the GRE: arbiter (the decider), arbitrate / arbitration (settle a dispute outside court), arbitrary (deciding by nothing but one's own will).

Understood by very few; obscure, secret, specialist
Known or understood by very few — obscure, mysterious, the property of specialists or initiates.

The word carries a whiff of restricted access: arcane material isn't merely hard, it's walled off, whether by secrecy (rites, spells) or by sheer impenetrable specialism (the arcane provisions of the tax code). Two flavours, then — solemn and magical, or dry and faintly exasperated. When a journalist calls a rule arcane, they mean needlessly obscure, and someone should have simplified it years ago.
⚠️ arcane ≠ archaic.
- arcane = hidden — few people understand it
- archaic = old — nobody uses it any more

A medieval spelling is archaic. A working rule nobody can decipher is arcane.
Arcane keeps its secrets in an ark — sealed, and only the initiated hold the key.
The point isn't difficulty but access: arcane knowledge is shut away, and you're on the outside of the box.
1. Behind the tapestry lay a chamber of arcane symbols, meaningless to anyone outside the order.
2. Getting reimbursed involves some arcane three-form process only Priya in accounts actually understands.
Netflix's Arcane (the League of Legends series) — the title is doing real work: the plot turns on hextech, a hidden magic only a handful of people can wield or comprehend.
Latin arca = "chest, strongbox" → arcānus = "shut in a box, secret." Same arca gives English ark — Noah's, and the Ark of the Covenant, which only priests could approach.

Behind it sits arcēre, "to shut in, keep away" — which also yields coerce (co- + arcēre, shut someone in) and exercise (ex- + arcēre, drive out).

So outdated it has fallen out of use; a relic.
Belonging to a much earlier age; so old-fashioned it has dropped out of active use.

The key isn't age, it's disuse. A cathedral is ancient, not archaic; the word thou is archaic. Something archaic has been superseded and now survives as a leftover — a law nobody repealed, a fax machine, a form of address nobody uses.

Tone flips with the target. Applied to a language or a historical period ("Archaic Greek"), it's a neutral technical label. Applied to an institution, a rule, or someone's opinions, it's a put-down: not just dated, but embarrassingly overdue for replacement.
⚠️ archaic ≠ arcane.
- archaic = outdated, no longer used
- arcane = obscure, understood by only a few

Arcane knowledge is hidden; archaic knowledge is just expired. A ritual can be both.
Archaic = archaeology minus the -ology — if you'd need a dig to find it in use, it's archaic.
The word points at something buried and out of circulation, not merely old and still standing.
1. The committee spent a year sweeping archaic provisions from the statute book, including a ban on driving cattle through the town at noon.
2. Their expenses system still runs on paper forms — it's completely archaic.
Open any dictionary entry for thou, whence, or betwixt and you'll see the usage label archaic — that tag is the word doing its day job.
Greek arkhaios = "ancient," from arkhē = "beginning."

That root spreads wide: archaeology (study of beginnings), archetype (the original pattern), archive (where the first records go) — and via arkhein, "to rule/lead," also monarch, anarchy, hierarchy.

column2:
The original pattern every later version is modelled on.
The original model or pattern from which all later versions are copied — and, by extension, the perfect, defining example of a type ("she's the archetype of the self-made founder").

It carries weight and depth. An archetype isn't just an early version; it's the deep template a whole category keeps re-enacting, which is why Jung used it for the recurring figures in myth and dream — the Hero, the Mother, the Trickster. Calling something an archetype dignifies it: you're saying it reached the bottom of the pattern, not that it's generic.
⚠️ archetype ≠ stereotype. An archetype is the deep original pattern others grow from — respectful. A stereotype is a flattened cliché imposed from outside — dismissive. The Wise Old Mentor is an archetype; "all mentors are bearded" is a stereotype.
Hidden inside is arch- as in arch-enemy and archbishop: the chief one, the one above all the others.
An archetype is the chief type — the boss version every lesser copy answers to.
1. Campbell argued that the wandering exile who returns transformed is an archetype common to Greek epic, Norse saga, and Hollywood alike.
2. That diner with the cracked vinyl booths and bottomless coffee is the archetypal American greasy spoon.
Luke Skywalker is the textbook case: George Lucas built Star Wars on Joseph Campbell's hero archetype — orphan, call to adventure, mentor, return — which is why the plot feels familiar the first time you see it.
Greek arkhē = "beginning, first, chief" + typos = "stamp, mark, model." Literally the first stamp — the die that every later impression is struck from.

Both halves pay rent across the GRE:
- arkhē → archaic, archaeology, monarch, anarchy, architect, archangel
- typos → type, typical, prototype, stereotype, typography

Burning with enthusiasm or devotion.
Burning with feeling — intensely enthusiastic, devoted, or in love. An ardent fan, an ardent supporter, an ardent admirer.

Compare the neighbours: passionate is the plain everyday word; zealous hints the person has gone too far; fervent leans religious or pleading. Ardent is warmer and more flattering than any of them — it's the word a profile-writer uses when the devotion is admirable. Note the shape of the heat: it points toward something you're committed to, never at someone in anger. You can be an ardent opponent of a policy, but you cannot be ardent with rage.
⚠️ ardent ≠ arduous. Ardent = burning with passion (Latin ardere, to burn). Arduous = steep, gruelling, exhausting (Latin arduus, high and hard). An ardent climber attempts an arduous route.
Ardent burns for, never at.
The heat is always devotion to something — a cause, a person, a team — so the word flatters the ardent one rather than accusing them.
1. Her ardent defence of the department's funding won over even the trustees who had arrived intending to cut it.
2. He's an ardent Arsenal fan — he'll drive four hours for a match he could watch at home.
Darcy's disastrous first proposal in Pride and Prejudice: \"You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.\" — the line the 2005 film hangs its whole rain scene on.
Latin ardēre = "to burn." It gives you ardour (burning enthusiasm), arson (burning property), and, at the cooler end, ardent spirits — the old name for strong liquor, because it burns.

Hard in a way that demands long, tiring effort.
Demanding severe, sustained effort; laborious and wearying.

Difficult is about complexity — a hard puzzle is difficult in an instant. Arduous is about exertion stretched over time: the climb, the training, the three-year lawsuit. It describes tasks, journeys and processes, never people, and it carries a faint note of respect — an arduous thing is worth finishing, which is why it pairs so naturally with journey, task, negotiations, ascent.
arduous ≠ ardent. Arduous = exhausting to do (Latin arduus, steep). Ardent = burning with passion (Latin ardēre, to burn). An ardent fan endures an arduous queue.
Put an H on the front: (h)arduous — hard + drags on continuously.
The hidden hard gives you the difficulty and the -uous tail gives you the part that matters — it goes on and on.
1. The restoration of the fresco proved an arduous undertaking, occupying two conservators for the better part of a decade.
2. Four buses and a ferry to get there — honestly, the trip was more arduous than the wedding.
News writing has practically welded the phrase together: refugees, expedition teams and hostages all make "an arduous journey." If you've read a headline, you've met the word.
Latin arduus = "steep, high." The original arduous thing was a hillside — hard because it's uphill, and uphill all the way. That steepness is still doing the work in the modern sense.

So striking it stops you in your tracks.
So striking that it stops you — a face, an image, a sentence, a performance that halts you mid-scroll.

The word is admiring but cool-headed. Beautiful praises the thing; arresting reports what the thing did to you — it seized your attention before you consented. That's why critics reach for it when something is compelling without being conventionally pretty: an arresting face may be odd, severe, asymmetric. Strength is high (much stronger than noticeable or striking), but the tone stays composed and slightly analytical — it's a reviewer's word, not a gushing one.
An arresting image doesn't ask for your attention — it detains it.
It's literally arrest + -ing: your eye is stopped and held, with no say in the matter.
1. Among the gallery's polite landscapes hung one arresting portrait, and the room emptied around it.
2. She's got this arresting voice — you hear two seconds of it on the radio and you stop chopping onions.
Film-review blurbs live on this word — "an arresting debut", "an arresting performance" — precisely because it flatters a film without promising it's enjoyable.
Latin restāre = "to stop, stand still," with ad- ("to") → Old French arester. To arrest a criminal is just to stop him; to arrest the spread of a disease is to halt it.

Same root, one useful oddity: restive. It once meant a horse that refused to move — and now means the opposite-looking fidgety, restless, impatient. Both senses are a creature that won't do what it's told.
