column2:
Cunning; skilled in a sly, manipulative way.
Clever and skilful — but on the GRE, almost always skill bent toward getting one over on you: cunning, wily, sly.

Two live senses, and the sly one dominates. An artful dodge, an artful question, an artful change of subject: the person is good at it, and that's exactly the problem. Compare cunning (colder, more predatory) and devious (flatly disapproving) — artful keeps a note of grudging admiration, because the craft really is impressive. The tamer sense survives in phrases about arrangement — an artful display of flowers — where it just means tastefully contrived.
⚠️ artless is not the opposite you expect. Artless doesn't mean clumsy — it means guileless, naively sincere. The opposite of artful's cunning, not of its skill.
Con artist. The art is in the con, not on the canvas.
An artful person has genuine skill, and is using it to work you.
1. His resignation letter was an artful piece of work: three paragraphs of praise that left everyone certain he had been pushed.
2. She gave an artful little shrug and somehow I ended up paying for dinner.
The Artful Dodger in Oliver Twist — Dickens's teenage pickpocket, all charm and sleight of hand. The nickname is the definition.
Latin ars, artis = "skill, craft" — which gives you artisan, artifice, artifact, artificial, and even inert (in- + ars = "without skill," hence sluggish, doing nothing).

Note the slide: English craft did the same thing, going from skill to crafty. Skill words drift toward trickery, because a trickster is only dangerous if he's good.

Clear-speaking; to put a vague thought into distinct words.
Adj.: fluent and clear in speech — able to say exactly what you mean.
Verb: to put something into clear words, especially something that was previously vague; also, literally, to join by a hinge.

The idea underneath is jointedness, not eloquence. To articulate a fear is to break a shapeless dread into named parts; an articulate speaker isn't just smooth, they deliver thought in distinct, well-hinged pieces you can follow. That's why bones and lorries articulate too — they're jointed so they can bend.

One register warning: as praise for a person, it can land as a backhanded compliment when the speaker is implying they didn't expect fluency.
An articulated lorry is one long thing split at a joint — an articulate speaker splits one long thought the same way.
Both senses are the same act: putting joints into something so it can move and be followed.
1. The witness proved unexpectedly articulate, laying out a decade of grievance in three clean paragraphs.
2. I couldn't articulate why the flat felt wrong — it just did.
The articulated lorry (and the bendy bus) — the bit in the middle that hinges is the articulation. Same word, visible joint.
Latin articulus = "little joint" (from artus, joint). Hence article — originally a distinct joint or clause of a text, which is why treaties have articles. Greek cousin arthron gives you arthritis, the disease of the joints.

Guileless and unaffected; sometimes simply unskilled.
Without guile — natural, unaffected, saying exactly what you mean because it never occurred to you to do otherwise. A secondary sense: unskilled, crude (a genuinely artless drawing).

The GRE almost always wants the first sense, and the trick is that the art being denied is artifice — cunning, calculation, technique — not painting. So an artless remark isn't clumsy, it's uncalculated. Tone is usually warm but faintly condescending: you'd call a child's honesty artless, and a diplomat's too, but only to say she'd never survive the job. Compare naive, which says the person is wrong about the world; artless only says they aren't working an angle.
⚠️ artless ≠ the opposite of artistic. artful ≠ artistic either.
- artless = guileless, no cunning
- artful = crafty, full of cunning

Neither word is about art galleries.
Artless: less art, more heart.
The art being subtracted is artifice — scheming, angling, technique — so what's left is unguarded sincerity.
1. Her testimony was so artless that the jury believed her before the lawyers had finished objecting.
2. He asked, with artless curiosity, how much everyone at the table earned.
The Artful Dodger in Oliver Twist is a pickpocket, not a painter — proof that this art means cunning. Artless is exactly what the Dodger is not.
Latin ars, artis = "skill, craft" — which slid easily into "trickery." That gives artifice, artificial, artisan, and — via in- + ars — inert, literally "without skill," now "doing nothing at all."

To find out for certain by checking or investigating.
To find out for certain — to establish a fact by checking, asking, measuring or investigating.

Find out is casual and can be accidental; you find out by overhearing. Ascertain is deliberate and ends in confidence: you went looking, and now you know. It's the register of officials, investigators and auditors — police ascertain the cause of a fire, a court ascertains a person's intent. Using it about trivia sounds comically stiff ("I shall ascertain whether we have milk"), and that stiffness is exactly what the GRE is testing you to hear.
ascertain = a- + certain: you dig until you are certain.
The word wears its answer on its face — the digging is the verb, and certainty is where it has to end up.
1. The auditors were unable to ascertain how the missing funds had left the account.
2. Give me ten minutes to ascertain whether he's actually on the flight before we panic.
Standard newsroom and police-briefing language: "Officers are still trying to ascertain the cause of the crash." Whenever an official won't yet commit to a story, this is the verb they reach for.

Severely self-denying, by choice; a person living so.
Adj.: severely self-denying — no luxury, no comfort, no indulgence. Noun: a person who lives that way, usually for religious or moral discipline.

The defining thing is that it's chosen. A poor man is deprived; an ascetic has refused. That's why the word carries either quiet admiration (monk, saint, serious artist) or a faint charge of extremism, depending on who's using it — and why "he lives an ascetic life" says something about his will, not his bank balance.

It stretches to style, too: an ascetic room, an ascetic prose style — stripped bare on purpose.
⚠️ ascetic ≠ aesthetic. Ascetic (uh-SET-ik) = stripped of pleasure. Aesthetic (es-THET-ik) = concerned with beauty. One letter, opposite instincts — and the GRE knows it.
Asc-etic rhymes with athl-etic — both are in training; the ascetic just trains at going without.
It locks in the key nuance: this is disciplined self-denial by choice, not poverty by accident.
1. The philosopher retreated to an ascetic cell furnished with a cot, a lamp, and nothing else.
2. Since January he's been on this ascetic kick — no sugar, no drinking, up at five.
Before he became the Buddha, Siddhartha spent six years as an ascetic — starving himself down to the ribs — then rejected it for the Middle Way. The whole story turns on the word.
Greek askēsis = "training, exercise" — the word for an athlete's regimen. Early Christian monks borrowed it for spiritual training, and the gym-work sense hardened into fasting and self-denial. So an ascetic is literally someone in training.

To attribute something to a particular cause, source, or author.
To assign something — a cause, a quality, an authorship — to a particular source. Almost always in the frame ascribe X to Y.

It is the bookish, judgement-neutral word: you can ascribe a triumph or a disaster, a virtue or a vice, where credit and blame each pick a side. And it usually marks an inference rather than a proven fact — scholars ascribe a play to Marlowe because the style fits, not because they watched him write it. That hedge is why the word lives in history, criticism and law: it says this is where I'm putting the responsibility, not this is settled.
⚠️ ascribe to ≠ subscribe to. You ascribe a belief to someone else (you say it's theirs); you subscribe to a belief yourself (you hold it). "I don't subscribe to that theory" — not ascribe.
A scribe is sitting inside the word, writing your name next to the deed.
The scribe records who gets charged with it — good or bad — and he's going on the evidence, not a confession.
1. Nineteenth-century editors ascribed the anonymous elegy to Coleridge on the strength of a single borrowed image.
2. Don't ascribe motives to me — I said the meeting was long, not that it was pointless.
Sociology's "ascribed status" vs achieved status: ascribed traits are the ones stamped on you at birth — caste, race, family name — assigned rather than earned. If you've seen the pair in a textbook or a policy piece, the sense is already locked.
Latin ad- ("to") + scrībere ("to write") — literally to write it onto someone's account.

Scrībere is a GRE workhorse: describe (write down), prescribe (write in advance — a doctor's order), proscribe (write someone's name on the banned list — outlaw them), inscribe, subscribe, scripture, manuscript.

A damaging insinuation about someone's character or integrity.
A damaging insinuation — a remark meant to sully someone's reputation or integrity.

It almost never travels alone or in the singular: you cast aspersions on someone. And the word is usually deployed defensively, by the person denying it — "I cast no aspersions on my colleague's honesty" — which is precisely how the doubt gets planted. An accusation is out in the open and can be answered; an aspersion is a smear, sprinkled sideways, too vague to rebut. Formal, faintly legal, and always hostile.
⚠️ aspersion ≠ asperity.
- aspersion = a slur on someone's character
- asperity = harshness of tone or manner

He answered with asperity; he answered by casting aspersions. Unrelated roots, one letter apart at a glance.
a-sper-shun — sprinkle enough dirt and people start to shun him.
The buried "shun" carries the point: no single remark accuses him of anything, but the accumulated sprinkling is what makes people back away.
1. The defence objected that counsel was casting aspersions on a witness who had not yet been heard.
2. Look, I'm not casting aspersions on your cooking — I just noticed the smoke alarm going off.
Live in courtroom and parliamentary speech, where "I cast no aspersions on the honourable member" is the standard way to insult someone while technically staying polite.
Latin aspergere = "to sprinkle on" (ad- "on" + spargere "to scatter"). The original English sense was literal — the priest's aspersion of holy water. The mud-slinging sense is the same gesture with worse contents.

spargere also gives you sparse (thinly scattered), disperse, and intersperse.

To attack repeatedly — with blows, words, or doubts.
To attack violently and repeatedly — with fists, with weapons, or (more often on the GRE) with words: critics assailed the proposal.

The force of it is in the repetition. You attack once; you assail over and over, blow after blow, question after question. It's also the standard verb for being overwhelmed from the inside: assailed by doubts, by nausea, by memories — the feeling behaves like a mob, and you are outnumbered.

Register is that of a newspaper or a battlefield, never a shrug. Note the useful offspring unassailable — an argument or a lead so strong no amount of battering dents it.
Assail = "a hail" — a hail of blows, of questions, of doubts, and it doesn't stop at one.
Hail comes down in volleys, which is exactly what separates assail from a single attack.
1. Opposition members assailed the minister for three hours, each rising in turn to demand her resignation.
2. He'd been fine all week, then at 3 a.m. he was assailed by the certainty that he'd sent the email to the wrong person.
Every news report of a mugging calls the attacker an assailant — never an "assaulter." If you can hear a police bulletin saying "the victim did not recognise her assailant," you already own the verb.
Latin ad- (at) + salīre (to leap) → assilīre, "to leap upon." An assailant literally springs at you.

Salīre is a GRE goldmine: salient (leaping out at the eye), resilient (leaping back), assault, insult (leaping on someone), exult, somersault, and the sally an army makes out of a fort.

Confidently direct about your claims, firm but not hostile.
Confident and direct in stating your views, needs, or claims — and not backing down from them.

Think of a three-point scale: passive (says nothing), assertive (says it plainly), aggressive (says it at your expense). Assertive is the approved middle — firm without hostility, which is why HR departments and therapists love the word. But it isn't purely a compliment: an assertive tone in a debate can mean the person is stating things as fact and daring you to disagree. The force is real; only the aggression is absent.
Assert + -ive — not one loud moment, but the standing habit of asserting.
The -ive suffix turns an act into a permanent trait (talk → talkative, create → creative), so an assertive person doesn't just assert once — that's simply how they operate.
1. The junior counsel was unexpectedly assertive, pressing her objection until the judge conceded the point.
2. You need to be more assertive — just tell them the deadline doesn't work instead of quietly redoing your weekend.
Assertiveness training is a standard corporate and therapeutic offering — whole workshops built on teaching people to say "no" without apologising for it. The word's everyday home is the performance review.
Latin ad- (to) + serere (to join, to bind) — to lay claim to something by putting your hand on it.

That serere root is worth banking: series (things joined in a row), insert (join something in), exert (put force out), desert (unjoin, abandon).

To ease a painful feeling — lessen it, not remove it.
To make a painful feeling less intense — grief, guilt, fear, anger, hunger, thirst.

The object is almost always an emotion, not a person: you assuage someone's fears, but you mollify the angry man. And it's partial relief, not a cure — assuaged guilt is quieter guilt, still there. The register is formal and slightly consoling, the language of eulogies, diplomacy and financial press.
Assuage near-rhymes with a stage — grief drops down a stage, it doesn't leave the stage.
The word promises reduction, never removal.
1. Nothing the priest said could assuage her grief; it only made the silence afterwards easier to bear.
2. He bought her flowers to assuage his guilt about forgetting the anniversary.
Business-page boilerplate: "The central bank moved to assuage investor fears." Whenever an institution is doing damage control, this is the verb the headline reaches for — always with fears, concerns, or doubts.
Latin ad- (to) + suavis (sweet) — literally to sweeten something bitter. That root gives you suave (smooth, sweet-mannered) and, via the cousin verb suadēre "to urge sweetly," persuade, dissuade and suasion. English sweet is the same ancient root.

Puckeringly sharp; bracingly severe in tone.
Literally: causing tissue to contract — drying, puckering, tightening. A tart, mouth-puckering taste (strong tea, unripe fruit, tannic red wine) is astringent; so is the toner that tightens your pores.

Figuratively: sharp, severe, unsparing — usually of criticism, humour, or prose.

The figurative sense keeps the physical one alive: astringent commentary is dry and tightening, not hot. Caustic burns, vitriolic attacks, acerbic is sour wit — astringent is bracing. There's a hint of the medicinal about it: it stings, but it's doing you good. Applied to a writer's style, it's often praise.
⚠️ astringent ≠ stringent. Same root, different jobs: stringent describes rules — tight, strict, hard to satisfy (stringent safety standards). astringent describes a taste, a substance, or a tone. Stringent rules; astringent wit.
a-STRING-ent — a string pulled tight: it puckers your mouth, and it tightens rather than burns.
The hidden string is the actual root, and "draws tight" is exactly the difference between astringent criticism and the scalding kind.
1. Her reviews were astringent but never cruel — she cut a novel down in three sentences and left the author grateful.
2. That tea's been brewing for twenty minutes; it's gone all astringent and it's drying out my mouth.
Walk down any skincare aisle: bottles of witch hazel labelled astringent, sold on the promise of tightening pores. That's the literal sense sitting on a shelf.
Latin ad- (to) + stringere (to draw tight, bind) — literally "binding up."

Stringere is a workhorse root: stringent, strict, constrict, restrict, constrain, and the boa constrictor. All of them squeeze.

Shrewd — quick to read a situation and spot the advantage.
Sharp in judgement — quick to see what's really going on and how to turn it to advantage.

This is praise, and it's practical praise. Intelligent is about horsepower; astute is about reading a situation — people, markets, motives — and acting on it before anyone else does. It lives in business and politics ("an astute negotiator", "politically astute"). There's a faint whiff of self-interest, of the person who noticed the angle, but the word stays complimentary: call someone cunning and you've insulted them, call them astute and you've praised them for the same skill.
astute ≠ acute. Acute is sharpness of sense or severity — acute hearing, acute pain. Astute is sharpness of judgement, and only ever describes a person or their decisions. An acute observer hears everything; an astute one knows what it means.
Astute minds are sharp; obtuse ones are blunt — geometry already taught you which angle is the dull one.
The two near-rhymes are opposites, so the obtuse angle you drew in school anchors astute at the sharp end of the scale.
1. The committee's most astute member said nothing for an hour, then asked the one question that collapsed the proposal.
2. She made one astute move — bought the flat before the new station was announced — and never had to work again.
It's the standard compliment in financial journalism: every profile of a successful investor calls them an astute reader of the market — never a clever or smart one.
Latin astūtus, from astus = "craft, cunning." The word started out meaning sly and was gradually promoted into a compliment — which is exactly why a trace of calculation still clings to it.

To weaken or thin out — reduce in force, not remove.
To weaken — to reduce something in force, intensity, quantity, or value. Literally, to make thin or slender.

This is the cool, technical word for weakening. Engineers attenuate signals, virologists attenuate viruses, lawyers say a fact attenuates a claim. Two things are built in: the reduction is gradual, along a scale, and the thing survives — what's attenuated is still there, just fainter. Undermine hints at sabotage, diminish is plain and general; attenuate is measured, usually deliberate, and sounds like it came off a lab report.
⚠️ attenuate ≠ accentuate. Two letters apart, near-opposite meanings: attenuate turns the volume down, accentuate turns it up (to emphasise). Getting them backwards flips the whole sentence.
atTENUate hides tenu- = thin: it thins a thing out, it never cuts it off.
An attenuated signal is still a signal — stretched thin, not severed.
1. Distance and two concrete walls attenuated the transmission until the broadcast was nothing but hiss.
2. Coffee and a big breakfast attenuated the hangover, but only just.
The MMR and yellow-fever shots are live-attenuated vaccines: the virus isn't killed, it's weakened until it's survivable — the definition of the word doing its job on a label you've actually read.
Latin ad- ("to") + tenuāre ("make thin"), from tenuis = "thin."

Same root gives you tenuous (a thin, barely-holding argument) and extenuate — literally to thin out the blame, which is exactly what extenuating circumstances do. English thin is a distant cousin of the same ancient root.

column2:
Credit something to a source; or an essential quality.
Verb: to assign something to its source — a cause, an author, an owner. The painting is attributed to Caravaggio. She attributed the delay to weather.
Noun: a quality that belongs to something as part of what it is. Patience is his best attribute.

The verb is a claim about origin, and it quietly admits uncertainty: you attribute a painting when you can't prove who painted it. It's neutral about praise or blame — you can attribute a triumph or a disaster. The noun is stronger than "trait": an attribute is felt to be essential, not incidental — a mercy attributed to God, strength as an attribute of a character in a game.
⚠️ attribute ≠ impute. Both assign something to a person, but impute almost always assigns something discreditable, and usually unfairly — they imputed dishonest motives to her. Attribute is even-handed; impute points a finger.
A-truh-byoot is a thing — nouns take the stress up front (REcord, CONduct, PROtest); push the stress back and it becomes a verb.
English shifts stress leftward to make a noun and rightward to make a verb, and attribute obeys the rule exactly.
1. Scholars now attribute the anonymous treatise to a minor clerk in the royal chancery, though the ascription remains contested.
2. Don't attribute it to bad luck — you didn't start studying until Sunday night.
The internet's favourite joke about misattribution: a serene photo captioned "Don't believe everything you read on the internet just because there's a picture with a quote next to it." — Abraham Lincoln. That's the verb in a nutshell — a quote assigned to a source that can't have said it.
Latin ad- ("to") + tribuere ("to allot, assign"), from tribus, tribe — originally to divide something out among the tribes.

That root pays out widely: tribute (what you pay over), contribute (give along with), distribute (deal out), retribution (paying back), tributary (a river paying into a larger one).

Daring past all limits — admirably or shamelessly.
Daring far beyond what caution allows — either boldly original (an audacious plan, an audacious heist) or shamelessly cheeky (an audacious lie, an audacious request).

Which one you get depends entirely on whether the speaker admires the risk. Brave praises; impudent condemns; audacious sits on the fence and takes its charge from the sentence around it. Either way the person has ignored a limit everyone else respected — the only question is whether the room applauds or gasps. Note the strength: audacious is never mild, and never accidental.
au-DAY-shus — the noun is audacity, and you've heard it snarled: "the audacity!"
That snarl is the cheeky half of the word, so remember the adjective as the same nerve viewed from a friendlier angle.
1. The firm made an audacious bid for a rival three times its size, and the market did not stop talking about it for a week.
2. He had the audacious cheek to ask for a raise seven days after writing off the company van.
Obama's bestseller _The Audacity of Hope_ — the title works precisely because it's a boast and a confession at once: hoping that hard is nerve.
Latin audēre = "to dare" → audāx, audācis (bold) → audacity.

🚫 Not audīre, "to hear." That's the other family entirely: audio, audience, audible, audition, auditor. Same first three letters, no relation.

column2:
to make bigger by adding to what already exists
To make something greater by adding to it — in size, amount, strength, or value.

The key restriction: there must already be something there. You create from nothing, but you augment a base that already stands — a salary, a force, a collection, a signal. Increase is the plain all-purpose word; augment is its formal cousin and usually implies a deliberate addition brought in from outside. It also differs from supplement, which quietly implies the original was deficient; augmenting carries no such insult — you can augment something already perfectly good.
Nobody augments from zero — an augmented thing is a thing that was already there.
That base requirement is the whole line between augment and create: you add to, never start.
1. The bequest augmented an endowment that was already the largest in the country.
2. He drives weekends to augment his paycheck.
Augmented reality — Pokémon GO, Snapchat filters. The camera keeps your actual room and lays extra things on top of it; that's exactly the word.
Latin augēre = "to increase, to make grow." It pays out across the exam: auction (bidding drives the price up), auxiliary (extra troops added to the main force), august / Augustus (grand, magnified), and author (Latin auctor, the one who makes a thing grow).

column2:
Majestic and dignified enough to command reverence.
Majestic and dignified in a way that commands reverence — impressive because of age, rank, or moral weight.

Not just grand. Grand can be a hotel lobby; august needs standing. It attaches to people and institutions that have earned deference — an august jurist, an august assembly, the august halls of a university — and it carries a whiff of the old and established. Because it's so formal, it turns easily ironic: call a rowdy committee "this august body" and everyone hears the sneer.
aw-GUST begins with awe — and that's exactly what it asks of you.
The month is flat AW-guhst, but push the stress off the front and the leftover "aw" is the awe an august figure inspires.
1. The verdict was delivered by an august bench of nine judges, none under seventy.
2. Three of us in a rented office — hardly the august institution the website promises.
Augustus Caesar wasn't born with that name — the Senate awarded it to Octavian as a title meaning "the venerable one," and he then renamed a month after himself. The emperor, the month, and the adjective are the same word.
Latin augustus = "consecrated, venerable," from augere = "to increase." The august person is the one who has been magnified — raised above ordinary rank.

That root pays out widely: augment (increase), auction (bidding goes up), auxiliary (added forces), author (one who makes grow).

Showing signs of future success; of good omen.
Showing signs that something will go well — favourable, promising, of good omen.

The word describes the omen, not the result. A day, a start, a debut, a set of conditions can be auspicious; the success itself cannot. That's what separates it from fortunate or successful, which report what already happened. It also sits high in register — faintly ceremonial, the language of weddings, launches, and inaugurations — and it works hardest in the negative: "not an auspicious beginning" is a dry, polite way of saying it went badly from the first minute.
Auspicious always attaches to a start: an auspicious debut, day, omen, occasion — never an auspicious ending.
If you can't put the word in front of something that hasn't happened yet, it isn't the right word.
1. The treaty was signed on an auspicious morning of clear skies and full attendance — which fooled everyone about the decade to come.
2. Losing your laptop on day one isn't the most auspicious start to a new job.
Indian weddings run on this word: families consult the calendar for an auspicious date and muhurat before anything is booked — the whole idea of a moment being pre-approved by the signs is the definition, live.
Latin auspex = "bird-watcher" — from avis (bird) + specere (to look). Roman officials read the flight of birds before battles and elections; good birds, good omen.

Both halves pay off elsewhere: avis → aviary, aviation; specere → inspect, spectacle, conspicuous, perspective.

Same root gives auspices — "under the auspices of the UN" = under its watchful sponsorship.

Stern, or stripped bare of comfort and ornament.
1. Severe or stern in manner and appearance. 2. Plain to the point of bareness — no ornament, no comfort, no indulgence.

The word describes a stripping away, not a cruelty. An austere man isn't vicious, he's unsmiling and unbending; an austere room isn't ugly, it's empty of anything you'd want. Crucially, it can cut either way: austerity is a discipline, so the word carries a faint respect that grim, bleak, or harsh never do — a monastery, a Bauhaus chair, and a budget with the perks cut out are all austere. Say it of a person and it chills; say it of a design and it can be praise.
Austere rhymes with severe — and it means the bare, stripped kind of severe.
Lock the rhyme, then add the one thing severe lacks: what's austere has had everything soft removed.
1. His prose is austere — no adjectives, no flourishes, nothing but what the sentence needs to stand.
2. The flat was clean but weirdly austere: one chair, one lamp, and not a single photo on the wall.
Austerity — the word every finance minister reaches for when the budget is being cut to the bone. Same word, wearing a suit.
Greek austērós = "drying, harsh to the tongue" — first said of wine and unripe fruit that puckers your mouth. That's the whole flavour of the word: something with all the sweetness taken out.

column2:
Giving backup support; secondary, held in reserve.
Adj.: giving supplementary support; secondary, held in reserve. Noun: the helper itself — a reserve force, a supporting organisation, or (in grammar) a helping verb.

An auxiliary thing is subordinate in rank, not in quality: it's fully capable, just not the main event — the second engine, the backup generator, the volunteer battalion. That's what separates it from ancillary, which is peripheral, off to the side, doing the menial support work. Auxiliary power can run the ship; ancillary staff mop the deck. The word is institutional and faintly technical — you meet it in engineering, the military, and grammar rather than in conversation.
AUX is sitting right at the front of it — the aux input, the spare way in when the main source can't do the job.
Nobody plugs into aux first, but it's there, wired up and ready — exactly the standing-by-in-support sense of the word.
1. When the grid failed, the hospital's auxiliary generators carried the surgical wing through the night.
2. The fire service runs on an auxiliary crew of volunteers who show up when the sirens go.
Grammar hands you the word daily: be, do, have, will are the auxiliary verbs — they carry almost no meaning themselves, they just let the main verb work ("she has finished", "I do know").
Latin auxilium = "help, aid", from augēre = "to increase" — an auxiliary force is one that adds to your strength.

That root pays off elsewhere: augment (increase), auction (bids going up), author and authority (from auctor, one who makes things grow), august (grand, enlarged in dignity).

Greedy for money; grasping and never satisfied.
Greedy for money and possessions — grasping, hoarding, never satisfied.

Not general greed: this word is specifically about wealth. A glutton isn't avaricious; a landlord raising rent on a dying tenant is. It's also a heavy, moralising word — greedy is what you call a child reaching for a third biscuit, avaricious is what a judge or a novelist calls a man whose whole character has been eaten by money. Using it is passing sentence.
⚠️ avaricious ≠ voracious.
- avaricious = hungry for money
- voracious = hungry, full stop — huge appetite for food, or for books

A voracious reader is a compliment. An avaricious one would be stealing the library.
av-a-RICH-us — the stressed syllable is literally RICH.
Say it aloud and the word tells you what it wants: riches, not food, not power.
1. The estate passed to an avaricious cousin who sold the orchards within the month.
2. He's not ambitious, he's avaricious — he'd bill his own mother for the taxi.
Avarice is the formal name of one of the seven deadly sins — the one everyone else just calls Greed.
Latin avēre = "to crave" → avarus, "greedy."

Same craving root gives you avid — an avid golfer craves the game, an avaricious one craves the prize money.

To state firmly as fact; to assert with confidence.
To state firmly as a fact — to assert something confidently, often in the face of doubt or contradiction. In law, to allege as a fact in a pleading.

Claim leaves room for scepticism, allege actively flags the thing as unproven, but aver puts the speaker's own credibility behind the statement: they are vouching, flatly, without hedging. It is formal and slightly stiff — you meet it in courtrooms, reportage and 19th-century novels, almost always followed by that. Nobody avers a guess.
⚠️ aver ≠ avert. One letter apart, opposite worlds: aver = declare it true; avert = turn away / prevent (avert your eyes, avert disaster).
a-VER = assert + verify: you don't just say it, you vouch for it.
The ver at its heart is the true of verdict and verify, which is why an averment is offered as fact rather than opinion.
1. The witness averred, without qualification, that she had seen the defendant leave the building shortly after midnight.
2. He still avers he never touched the last slice, crumbs on his shirt notwithstanding.
Open almost any American legal complaint and every numbered paragraph begins the same way: "Plaintiff avers that…" — the word is a lawyer's default verb for putting a fact on the record.
Latin vērus = "true", via ad- + vērāre → Old French averer, "to prove true."

That root is a GRE goldmine: verify, veracity, veritable, verdict (vere dictum, "truly said"), verisimilitude, and plain old very (originally "truly").

A strong dislike; the wish to stay away from something.
A strong, settled dislike of something — and the wish to stay away from it.

Hatred wants to destroy; aversion just wants distance. It is a recoil, not an attack, and it is usually aimed at a thing or activity rather than a person: an aversion to conflict, to paperwork, to cold water. Cool and slightly clinical in tone — it's the word a psychologist or an economist reaches for (aversion therapy, risk aversion), which is why it can describe a gut-level revulsion without the speaker sounding heated. Note the fixed preposition: an aversion to, never of.
⚠️ averse ≠ adverse.
- averse (to) = a person unwilling, disliking — she's averse to flying
- adverse = conditions that are harmful or unfavourable — adverse weather, adverse effects

People have averse feelings; circumstances turn adverse.
Aversion hides avert — you avert your eyes, you don't raise your fists.
The word is about turning away from something, not going to war with it.
1. He had a lifelong aversion to publicity, refusing every interview the prize brought him.
2. I don't hate the gym, I've just got a serious aversion to anyone watching me lift.
Every hiring manager and investor says "risk-averse" — the person who turns away from the risky option rather than fighting it. Behavioural economics adds loss aversion: we feel a £100 loss more sharply than a £100 gain.
Latin ab- (away) + vertere (to turn) = "a turning away."

Vertere is a GRE workhorse: avert (turn away), divert (turn aside), invert, revert, convert, subvert, controversy (turned against each other), even vertigo (the spinning world).

And it explains the trap: adverse is ad- (toward) + vertere — conditions turned against you.

To turn away, or to ward off an approaching disaster.
Two senses, one gesture.
1. To turn away — usually the eyes or the face: she averted her gaze.
2. To ward off something bad that was already coming: the pilot averted a collision.

Sense 2 is where the GRE lives, and it is narrower than prevent. You prevent anything — rust, boredom, a goal. You avert only a looming harm, and the word carries the sense of a last-minute deflection: the disaster was on its way and got turned aside. Forestall means you acted early; avoid means you personally sidestepped it; avert means the danger was real, close, and pushed off course. Sense 1 keeps the same flinch — averting your eyes is admitting there's something you can't look at.
⚠️ avert ≠ aver. Aver (uh-VUR) means to state firmly as fact — "he averred his innocence." One letter, opposite energy: avert turns away from something, aver plants a flag on it.
You only ever avert two things: your eyes, and a disaster. Both get turned away at the last second.
Lock the collocation and you get the nuance free — the object is always something bad you refuse to meet head-on.
1. Only a hastily brokered ceasefire averted a wider war.
2. He averted his eyes when she mentioned the money he still owed.
\"Crisis averted.\" — the stock phrase every news anchor and every group chat reaches for when a near-miss ends well.
Latin ab- (away) + vertere (to turn) — literally turn away.

Vertere is one of the highest-yield roots on the exam: divert (turn aside), invert (turn upside down), convert (turn together, change), subvert (turn from beneath), revert (turn back), vertigo (the room turning), versatile (turns to any task), adverse (turned against you).

Keenly enthusiastic; hungrily eager for something.
Keenly enthusiastic; devoted to a pursuit to the point of appetite. Older, sharper sense: greedy for something — avid for power.

Two settings, and the GRE tests both. Followed by a noun, it's warm and almost domestic — an avid reader, an avid golfer, someone whose hobby is a habit. Followed by for or of, it turns hungry: avid for praise, avid for revenge — that's craving, not fondness. Eager is a burst of feeling before one event; avid is a standing appetite.
Avid and avarice are the same craving — avarice wants your money, avid wants one more chapter.
Both come from Latin avēre, "to crave," so avid is greed with the appetite pointed at something harmless.
1. Two decades in opposition had left him avid for office, and the caution of his younger self was gone.
2. She's an avid baker — there hasn't been a weekend without flour on the counter since March.
The stock phrase of every CV hobbies line and dating-app bio: avid reader, avid hiker, avid traveller. Nobody writes "avid" any other way — which is exactly the collocation the GRE expects you to know.
Latin avēre = "to crave, to long for" → avidus, "greedy, eager." The same root gives avarice and avaricious — the money-hungry cousins. Knowing they're relatives is what preserves the hungry edge of avid for.

Self-evident; assumed true without needing proof.
Self-evident; true on its face, so taken as a starting point rather than argued for. Also, literally: of or based on axioms.

Obvious is casual and can be a bit rude ("that's obvious"). Axiomatic is cool and formal — it doesn't say you should have known, it says this is where the argument begins. Watch how it actually gets used: "it is axiomatic that…" is usually a move, a way of ruling something out of debate before anyone can dispute it. And it isn't dogmatic — a dogma is imposed from outside; an axiom is granted because no one sees a reason to withhold it.
⚠️ axiomatic ≠ idiomatic.
- axiomatic = needs no proof
- idiomatic = phrased the way a native speaker would actually say it
Axio*matic* ≈ auto*matic* — accepted automatically, no proof required.
The claim goes through on its own, without anyone stopping to justify it.
1. The judgment rests on a principle the court treated as axiomatic: that no one may profit from his own wrongdoing.
2. Round here it's axiomatic that you don't touch the thermostat.
School geometry: Euclid's axioms — a straight line can be drawn between any two points, etc. — are the handful of statements you're allowed to assume so that everything else can be proved.
Greek axios = "worthy" → axiōma, "something thought worthy of acceptance." An axiom is a claim worthy enough to be let in without a ticket.

Same root: axiom, axiology (the study of value), and the chemists' axial? — no, that one's unrelated (Latin axis).

So unoriginal and overused it has gone flat.
So ordinary, so predictable, so often repeated that it has gone flat — a remark, plot, compliment or design with no originality left in it.

Banal is a verdict, not a description. Common and ordinary just report frequency; banal adds contempt and boredom — the thing is stale and the speaker is tired of it. It attaches most naturally to things that were supposed to be interesting: art, conversation, writing, ideas. A bus timetable can't be banal; a poem, a wedding speech, or a corporate slogan very much can.
Banal ideas should be banned — you've heard them a thousand times.
The hidden word ban is also the actual root, and the exasperation in "ban it already" is exactly the contempt the word carries.
1. The gallery's much-hyped centrepiece proved banal — a slogan in neon, a gesture exhausted decades ago.
2. His best man's speech was so banal I could have written it myself: she's the lucky one, he's punching above his weight, to the happy couple.
Hannah Arendt's phrase "the banality of evil" — her report on the Eichmann trial, arguing the worst crimes were carried out by a dull functionary doing paperwork, not a monster.
From Old French banal, "shared by all the lord's tenants," from ban — a feudal lord's proclamation summoning everyone. The village mill and oven were banal: everybody had to use them. Compulsory for all → used by all → utterly common → dreary.

Same ban root: banish, banns (of marriage, proclaimed publicly), abandon, contraband, bandit (a man proclaimed an outlaw).

column2:
To expel someone from a place by official decree.
To force someone to leave a place — permanently, by order of an authority. By extension: to drive away something unwanted (a thought, a fear, a smell).

The word carries a decree behind it. You are expelled and forbidden to return, and someone with power said so. Compare the neighbours: exile names the resulting condition and can be self-chosen; expel is institutional and bureaucratic (school, party, club); ostracize is a group quietly freezing you out with no legal force at all. Banishment is the formal sentence — old, absolute, slightly biblical in flavour, which is why the figurative use ("banish the thought") sounds a touch grand even when it's casual.
ban + vanish — a ban that makes you vanish.
The rhyme with vanish gives you the disappearance, and the hidden ban gives you the missing half — that it was ordered, not chosen.
1. The duke banished the poet from the city, on pain of death should he ever return.
2. One coffee and the hangover was banished.
Romeo, told he is banished from Verona rather than executed, howls "Ha, banishment! Be merciful, say 'death'" — the whole tragedy turns on that one sentence being handed down.
Frankish bannan = "to proclaim, to command under threat of penalty." A ban was a public proclamation; to banish was to proclaim someone out.

That root pays off across the exam: ban, abandon (put under someone else's bann, i.e. give up control), bandit (Italian bandito, a man publicly proclaimed an outlaw), contraband, and — surprisingly — banal: things open to all the lord's tenants by proclamation became things ordinary, and then things dull.

Ornate to the point of excess; the curling 1600s style.
Capital B: the European style of art, architecture and music from roughly 1600–1750 — curling, gilded, dramatic, packed with detail.
Lowercase: so elaborately ornamented that the ornament has taken over.

Used of the period, it's a neutral technical label. Used of anything else — prose, software, a plot, an excuse — it's a jab: the thing is fussily complex, decorated past the point of usefulness. Note the flavour: baroque complexity is decorative, almost showy, not merely difficult. A tax code is byzantine (tangled, bureaucratic); a sentence with six subordinate clauses and three metaphors is baroque.
baroque = "broke" — the clean plain line, broken up with curlicues until it's buried.
The word sounds like broke, and that's the charge against it: simplicity broken into ornament for ornament's sake.
1. The palace's baroque façade — cherubs, scrolls, gold leaf on every surface — left no square inch at rest.
2. His excuse got so baroque that by the third subplot I stopped believing any of it.
Vivaldi's Four Seasons and Bach's organ works are Baroque music — and you can hear the definition in them: trills, runs and curlicues stacked on top of a simple tune.
Portuguese barroco = an irregular, misshapen pearl — valuable, but lumpy and asymmetrical rather than clean. Jewellers' slang became art critics' insult, then the name of a whole era. The pearl is the meaning in miniature: ornate, showy, not smooth.
column3: g13 register::formal connotation::depends antonym::stripped-bare-vs-gilded antonym::tangled-vs-plain-simple intensity::decoration-to-excess meaning::overdecorated-style

column2:
A sustained, overwhelming bombardment — of shells, or of words.
Noun: a heavy, continuous outpouring aimed at a target — originally artillery fire, now equally questions, criticism, texts, complaints.
Verb: to hit someone with exactly that.

Volume alone isn't a barrage; the word carries direction and sustained pressure. A torrent is shapeless, a volley is one burst — a barrage is aimed, relentless, and leaves the receiver pinned down with no chance to answer. That's why it pairs so naturally with criticism, questions, abuse: things fired at a person who can't fire back.
BARrage — a bar of fire laid across your path: you can't get through, and you can't get a word in.
The hidden bar is the literal root, and it captures the nuance — a barrage doesn't just arrive, it blocks you.
1. Behind a creeping barrage of shellfire, the infantry moved up to the ridge.
2. He'd been home ten seconds before his mum barraged him with questions about the car.
Newsroom boilerplate: a minister always "faced a barrage of criticism" — never a trickle, never a helping. If you can hear that headline phrase, you've got the word.
French barre = "bar" → barrer, "to block off." A barrage in French is a dam — a barrier across a river (Britain still uses it that way: the Cardiff Bay Barrage). In WWI, tir de barrage meant "barrier fire": a curtain of shells dropped to seal off a stretch of ground. The military sense walked into English from there, then spread to words.

Same barr- family: bar, barrier, barricade, debar, embargo.

Producing nothing — infertile land, or fruitless effort.
Producing nothing: land too poor to grow crops, a woman or animal unable to bear young, or an effort/period that yields no result — barren negotiations, a barren decade for the club.

The word isn't a synonym for empty. A cupboard is empty; a field is barren — the failure is one of yield, of something that ought to produce and can't. That's why it stings when aimed at a person: barren is the old, cold, blaming word for infertility, and modern writing prefers infertile for exactly that reason. Keep it for landscapes and fruitless efforts.
A barren baron leaves no heir — the bloodline, like the soil, yields nothing.
Same sound, and the image locks in the key idea: not merely bare, but incapable of producing.
1. Nothing grew on that barren hillside but gorse and wind-bent thorn.
2. Three meetings in and we've got nothing — completely barren.
In The Handmaid's Tale, Gilead's law holds that sterile men don't exist — there are only women who are fruitful and women who are barren. The novel's whole horror runs on that one word.

column2:
Morally low; contemptible, driven by ignoble motives.
Morally low — contemptible, dishonourable, unworthy of a decent person. Base motives, base instincts, base flattery.

Forget the noun (bottom, foundation) — the GRE wants the adjective, and it is a judgement of character. Vile and disgusting react to the deed; base measures the person against a standard of honour and finds them beneath it. It attaches most naturally to motives and impulses rather than acts: greed, cowardice, spite, betrayal for money. The word carries a whiff of the pulpit and the nineteenth-century novel — nobody says it in a bar, which is exactly why it reads as withering on the page.
⚠️ base ≠ baseless.
- base accusation = a contemptible one, made from a filthy motive
- baseless accusation = a groundless one, with no evidence behind it

Different words entirely — baseless belongs to the other "base," the foundation.
Base is bass — the low note. A base man is a low man.
They sound identical because they are the same word, and "low" is the whole idea: low pitch, low character.
1. He refused the bribe, calling it an appeal to the basest part of a public servant.
2. Selling your friend's secrets for a promotion? That's just base.
Commodity markets and chemistry still split metals into precious and base — gold and platinum on one side, copper, lead and zinc on the other. The cheap ones were literally the low, ignoble metals; alchemists spent centuries trying to raise them.
Late Latin bassus = "low, short" → French bas. Same root gives bass (the low voice), abase and debase (to bring low), and the basset hound — a low-slung dog.

🚫 Not the other base. Foundation, baseball, basis, baseless all come from Greek basis, "a step, a footing." Identical spelling, unrelated word.

Rude about sex in a funny, cheerful way.
Indecent about sex — but comically so. Bawdy humour is coarse, loud, and openly rude about bodies and appetites.

The key is that it's funny, not filthy. Obscene offends, lewd leers, pornographic arouses — bawdy wants a laugh, and usually gets one from a whole room. It's the register of tavern songs, limericks, and Shakespeare's puns, so the word carries a whiff of indulgent amusement even when the speaker pretends to disapprove.
A bawdy joke is a body joke — told for a laugh, not a leer.
Near-rhyme with body fixes both the subject matter and the cheerful, unserious tone that separates bawdy from obscene.
1. The tavern scenes are frankly bawdy, and the Victorian editors quietly cut every one of them.
2. Grandma had three drinks and started telling bawdy stories about the war.
Any school edition of Shakespeare — the footnotes forever explaining that some innocent-looking line is a bawdy pun. It's the standard word critics use for his dirty jokes.
From bawd — a brothel-keeper or procuress (a bawdy house was legal-speak for a brothel). So bawdy is literally "of the bawd": the talk you'd hear in that establishment.

Muddled and foggy-headed; gently, often comically confused.
Thoroughly confused — unable to think clearly, muddled in the head.

Where bewildered is wide-eyed and slightly dramatic, and perplexed is the polite, intellectual version, befuddled is soft and faintly comic. It suggests a fogged, slow-witted confusion rather than shock: the person isn't reeling, they're just not tracking. It's the word for the professor who has mislaid his glasses, the grandparent facing a self-checkout machine, the jury that the lawyer has deliberately muddled. Note also that it's usually done to someone — a question, a rulebook, or a drink befuddles you.
Befuddled rhymes with muddled — the brain is stirred, not stunned.
The rhyme keeps you on the gentle, foggy end of confusion rather than the shocked end where bewildered and dumbfounded live.
1. The committee's report left even its own authors befuddled, so densely was it hedged with qualifications.
2. I gave him the Wi-Fi password three times and he still just stood there looking befuddled.
From fuddle (1580s), "to get drunk, to muddle with drink" — plus the intensifier be- (as in bedazzle, bewitch, besmirch, all meaning "to thoroughly do X to someone"). So befuddled literally means drunk-confused, which is exactly the flavour it kept: hazy, slow, harmless.

That be- prefix is worth banking on its own — it turns a verb outward onto a victim, and it shows up all over the GRE (beguile, belabour, bemoan, bereft).

Charm someone in a disarming way, often to deceive them.
To charm or enchant someone — usually in a way that lowers their guard, and often in order to trick them. A secondary sense: to while away time pleasantly (they beguiled the afternoon with cards).

Charm is harmless; deceive is hostile. Beguile sits in between and refuses to choose. The charm is doing work on you — it's disarming you while you enjoy it. That's why the word can describe a lovely view, a clever swindler, or a person who is both. On the GRE, expect it where a passage wants pleasure and manipulation in the same breath: you are beguiled into things, rarely by accident.
Beguile hides guile behind a smile.
The cunning (guile) is literally inside the word, but it arrives wrapped in charm — which is exactly why it works.
1. The prospectus beguiled hundreds of small investors with projections that no one had audited.
2. He's so charming that you don't notice you've been beguiled into paying for dinner again.
Sofia Coppola's film The Beguiled (2017) — a wounded soldier taken in by a girls' boarding school, charmed, fussed over, and quietly destroyed. The title is the definition: seduction with a knife in it.
be- (thoroughly) + guile (cunning, trickery) — so literally "to work guile on someone."

That root is still a live English word, and it gives you guileless (innocent, no cunning at all — a common GRE answer choice) and wily / wile, its close cousin.

Owing someone a favour; under obligation to them.
Owing someone for a favour, gift, or support — under obligation to them. Almost always followed by to: beholden to donors, to her uncle, to no one.

Gratitude is a warm feeling; being beholden is a debt that limits you. It says someone has leverage — that you can't fully criticise, refuse, or walk away. That's why the word appears so often in the negative: "I'm beholden to no one" is a boast of independence, and "beholden to lobbyists" is an accusation. Rarely a comfortable word about a relationship you enjoy.
Beholden = someone has a hold on you.
The word wears hold in the middle: the debt isn't felt, it's a grip — which is exactly why people insist they're beholden to nobody.
1. Having financed the campaign himself, he could claim to be beholden to no party machine.
2. She paid for her own flight — she didn't want to be beholden to her in-laws all week.
Standard political-press vocabulary: candidates promise they won't be beholden to donors or special interests, and reporters use it as shorthand for bought influence.
A fossil: it's the old past participle of behold, from Old English behealdan — "to hold, keep, be bound to."

🚫 Nothing to do with seeing. Modern behold means "look upon," but beholden kept the original hold sense and never picked up the eyes. Same hold family as uphold, withhold, household.

To disguise the truth about; to contradict or disprove.
Two senses, one idea:
1. To give a false impression of — the surface misrepresents what's underneath. Her steady voice belied her panic.
2. To show something to be false — evidence contradicts a claim. The sales figures belie his optimism.

The direction is what gets tested. The subject of belie is the liar: the calm face, the young skin, the cheerful forecast. Whatever follows the verb is the truth being covered up or knocked down. So belie never means "reveal" — though the sentence usually leaves you knowing the hidden truth anyway, which is exactly why people flip it.

Register is written and formal — reviews, obituaries, analysis. Said aloud it sounds bookish.
⚠️ belie ≠ betray. They fit the identical sentence frame and point opposite ways:
- His grin belied his nerves = the grin hid them.
- His grin betrayed his nerves = the grin gave them away.

One conceals, one leaks.
Be-lie — the appearance be a lie.
The thing doing the belying is the one telling the lie, so whatever comes after it is the truth being denied.
1. The manor's peeling shutters belied the fortune still sitting in the family trust.
2. Don't let the tiny shopfront fool you — it belies how much money they move.
A stock line in sports and music writing: "her slight frame belies the power in her serve," "his boyish face belies twenty years on the road." Same shape every time — small surface, big hidden truth.
Old English belēogan = "to deceive by lying" — be- ("about, over") + lēogan, "to tell a lie." The word is literally to lie about something.

🚫 Not the lie that means recline (Old English licgan), and no relation to believe, despite the look.

column2:
To make someone or something seem unimportant or small.
To talk about someone or something as smaller, lesser, or less impressive than it really is — to make light of an achievement, a fear, a person.

The weapon here is dismissal, not abuse. Where insult is loud and vilify is vicious, belittling is usually calm, even smiling: "it's not really that hard," "she got lucky." It needs a height gap — the belittler speaks from above, and the damage is cumulative rather than explosive. You can belittle someone's work while being perfectly polite about it, which is exactly why the word is so often used of bosses, parents, and rivals.
A belittler doesn't shout at you — he shrinks you.
The word literally holds little: the aim isn't to wound but to make you, or your achievement, seem small.
1. Critics belittled the discovery as a lucky accident, and it took a decade for her name to be restored to it.
2. Don't belittle it — you finished a marathon, that's not "just jogging".
Open almost any workplace anti-bullying policy and you'll find "belittling" listed alongside intimidation and exclusion — HR's word for harm done in a reasonable tone of voice.
Coined by Thomas Jefferson (1780s), who built it as be- + little = "to make little of." British reviewers were outraged by the vulgar new Americanism; it outlived them.

That be- prefix is a quiet GRE workhorse meaning make/treat as: bemoan, bedevil, befriend, becalm.

column2:
Aggressively hostile; actively waging or picking a fight.
Adj.: aggressively hostile — actively looking for or carrying on a fight.
Noun: a nation or party engaged in a war ("the belligerents met in Geneva").

Angry is a feeling; belligerent is a posture. The belligerent person isn't sulking or seething — they're leaning in, raising their voice, daring you to answer. It's the standard word in two very different registers: diplomats use it neutrally for combatant states, and police reports and bar stories use it for the man who won't leave quietly. Both keep the same core: hostility that has already moved into action.
Belligerent — he's already rung the bell for round one.
The fight is underway, not merely brewing — that's what separates belligerent from plain irritable.
1. Both belligerents claimed the ceasefire had been broken by the other side.
2. Three drinks in, he got belligerent and started shouting at the bartender.
It's the fixed phrase in incident reports and news copy: "the passenger became belligerent and was removed from the flight." Nobody writes "became angry" — belligerent signals it escalated.
Latin bellum (war) + gerere (to wage, to carry on) — literally war-waging.

bellum unlocks a cluster: antebellum (before the war), bellicose (itching for a fight), rebel (re- + bellum, to wage war back), casus belli (the trigger for war).

🚫 Not bene- (good). Benevolent, benefit, benign are a different root entirely — one letter apart, opposite worlds.

column2:
A fixed standard that other things are measured against.
Noun: a fixed standard or reference point against which other things are measured, compared, or judged.
Verb: to test something by measuring it against that standard.

The word is cold and quantitative — a benchmark is a line, not an ideal. A paragon is perfection you admire; a benchmark is simply the agreed measuring stick, and it can be mediocre (a fund can beat its benchmark and still lose money). It also implies comparability: the same test, run the same way, on everything. That's why it belongs to reviewers, analysts, and engineers rather than to praise.
⚠️ benchmark ≠ hallmark.
- benchmark = the standard you measure against
- hallmark = a distinguishing feature that identifies something ("obsessive detail is the hallmark of his work")
A benchmark is a mark, not a medal — you measure against it, you don't win it.
Clearing a benchmark only means you crossed the reference line, which is why a chip, a fund, or a student can be "above benchmark" and still be unremarkable.
1. The 1962 recording remains the benchmark against which every later performance of the concerto is quietly judged.
2. Don't benchmark yourself against people who got a ten-year head start.
Every phone and laptop review runs benchmark scores — apps like Geekbench and 3DMark exist for nothing else: run the identical test on every device so the numbers can be lined up side by side.
Literally a bench + a mark. Victorian surveyors chiselled a mark into a wall or stone at a precisely known height, then rested the bracket ("bench") of their levelling rod in it — every other elevation in the district was measured from that one immovable cut.

So the whole modern meaning is already in the object: a fixed physical reference point that everything else is measured from. Same -mark family, different jobs: landmark (you navigate by it), hallmark (it identifies), earmark (it reserves).

Actively doing good — generous in deed, not merely in intent.
Doing good; generous and kindly in action — actually conferring benefits on people.

The word points at deeds, not feelings. A beneficent donor has already funded the ward; a benevolent one is fond of the idea. It also carries a slight tilt of power: the beneficent party is usually the one with means — a patron, a monarch, a foundation — bestowing good downward. That makes it warm but a touch grand, and easy to turn ironic ("our beneficent landlord").

Keep it apart from beneficial too: beneficial describes things that do good (exercise, rainfall); beneficent describes agents who do good.
⚠️ beneficent ≠ benevolent.
- beneficent = does good — `bene` + fic (facere, to do)
- benevolent = wishes good — `bene` + vol (velle, to wish)

A benevolent billionaire smiles at the hospital appeal. A beneficent one pays for it.
Beneficent hides benefit — someone actually got one.
If no benefit has changed hands, the word you want is benevolent.
1. The college owes its library, its observatory and half its endowment to a single beneficent industrialist who never once visited.
2. My aunt had a beneficent phase where she'd turn up unannounced with groceries and pay off your phone bill.
Disney's Maleficent is this word's exact evil twin: male- (ill) + -fic- (doing) = ill-doing, built on the same frame as bene- + -fic- = good-doing. Swap the first syllable and you flip the fairy.
Latin bene (well) + facere (to do, to make).

bene- gives you benefit, benefactor, benediction (well-speaking), benign, benevolent. -fic-/facere gives you factory, manufacture, efficient, artifice — and malefactor, the beneficent man's opposite number.

column2:
Kindly disposed; wishing others well, usually from above.
Well-meaning and kindly; disposed to do good, and usually in a position to.

The word points at disposition, not action — a benevolent person wishes you well; whether they write the cheque is another matter. It carries a faint air of altitude: the benevolent party is the one with the power, the money, or the age. That's why it sits so naturally in benevolent fund, benevolent society, benevolent dictator — and why, applied to a boss or an empire, it can turn quietly sardonic. Kind is warm and equal; benevolent is gracious and slightly above you.
⚠️ benevolent ≠ beneficent.
- benevolent = wishes good (the intention)
- beneficent = does good (the deed)

A benevolent millionaire means well; a beneficent one has funded the hospital.
Bene-VOLENT wills you well; MAL-evolent wills you ill.
The shared `-volent` is wishing, so both words are about what someone intends toward you, and only the prefix decides which way.
1. The foundation's benevolent intentions were never in doubt; its accounting was another matter entirely.
2. My landlord's in a benevolent mood this week — he actually fixed the boiler.
In software, the person who founded a project and still has final say is the BDFL — Benevolent Dictator For Life, the title Python's community gave Guido van Rossum. Total control, exercised kindly: the word doing exactly the work it always does.
Latin bene (well) + volens, from velle (to wish, to will).

bene- pays out everywhere: benefit, benefactor, benediction (well-speaking), benign, benevolent. And velle gives you volition, voluntary, volunteer — all about the will.

Flip the prefix to mal- (badly) and you get the exact mirror: malevolent, malediction, malign, malefactor.

column2:
Harmless or kindly; in medicine, not cancerous.
Gentle and kindly in manner; harmless in effect; medically, not cancerous; of weather or conditions, mild and favourable.

Most of its force is negative — it says what isn't there. A benign tumour isn't a healthy one, just one that won't kill you; a benign smile is pleasant but tells you nothing. Compare benevolent, which is active goodwill (someone doing good), and benign, which is mostly the absence of threat. That's why GRE passages use it for things that look dangerous and turn out not to be: a benign policy, a benign amendment, benign neglect.
⚠️ benign ≠ benighted. Benighted (bih-NYE-tid) means ignorant, unenlightened — from night, morally in the dark. Nothing to do with kindness: a benighted era is a backward one.
benign rhymes with fine — and "it's fine" is exactly how much reassurance it gives.
Fine isn't good, it's just not bad — which is the whole register of the word.
1. The tribunal dismissed the clause as benign, a formality with no power to compel anyone.
2. The dog looks terrifying but he's completely benign — he'll just drool on you.
The word you wait for after a biopsy. "The results came back benign" is the good-news line in every hospital scene — and note what it actually promises: not cured, just not cancer.
Latin bene = "well" (+ gignere, "to be born" — literally well-born, hence well-natured).

bene is one of the best roots on the GRE: benefit, benefactor, benevolent, benediction, beneficiary. Its twin is male- = badly: malign, malevolent, malediction, malefactor. Learn the pair and you get twenty words — benign and malign are exact opposites, built the same way.

to scold someone harshly and at length
To scold someone harshly and at length — angry, loud, usually in front of other people.

Length and heat are what make it berate rather than anything milder. A rebuke can be one cold sentence; censure is formal and written down; admonish is almost gentle, a warning with care in it. Berating is a tirade — and the word quietly indicts the berater too. Nobody berates with dignity; the verb implies someone who has lost their temper and is enjoying the volume.
Be-RATE — he's giving you a rating, out loud, at length, and it's one star.
The hidden word rate keeps the idea of a verdict being pronounced over you, and "at length" is the part that separates berating from a quick telling-off.
1. The tribunal noted that the officer had berated the recruits for a full hour, well past any disciplinary purpose.
2. She berated the delivery guy for ten minutes before realising she'd typed the wrong address herself.
Standard sports-desk vocabulary: a manager gets sent off for berating the referee — the exact word headlines reach for when someone won't stop shouting.
be- (thoroughly, all over) + rate, an old English verb meaning to chide — so, literally, "to scold all over."

That be- prefix is worth owning; it means thoroughly across a whole family: belabour (beat a point to death), besiege, bewilder, bemoan, bespatter. It's the prefix of overdoing it.
column3: g24 register::neutral connotation::negative antonym::tongue-lashings-vs-praise-that-counts connotation::scolding-at-full-volume intensity::scolding-mild-to-savage meaning::scolding:-heat-rank-and-hurt

column2:
Stripped of something you once had; left desolate.
Deprived of something — stripped of a quality, comfort, or possession you once had (bereft of hope, bereft of charm). Used alone, it means left desolate, hollowed out by loss.

The word carries a history that lacking does not: to be bereft, you must have had the thing and had it taken. A room can lack windows; only a person bereft of friends has lost them. The register is elevated and literary — in speech it lands as either genuine grief or dry hyperbole ("the menu was bereft of anything edible").
bereft vs. bereaved. Bereaved is narrow — you have lost a person, to death. Bereft is wide — you can be bereft of money, ideas, or dignity, as well as of a person.
bereft = "be left" — left behind, without the thing you used to have.
The sound carries the whole nuance: not merely missing something, but left holding nothing after it was taken away.
1. Stripped of her titles and her income, she returned to the village bereft of everything but her name.
2. He came out of that meeting completely bereft — three years of work, binned in ten minutes.
Monty Python's Dead Parrot sketch: "'E's bereft of life, 'e rests in peace!" — one of the shopkeeper's euphemisms for dead, which is exactly the kind of loss the word implies.
From bereave = be- (thoroughly) + reave, an old verb meaning to rob, to plunder (a Viking reaver was a raider). Bereft is simply its old past participle — literally "robbed of."

That root hands you the nuance for free: nothing is bereft that wasn't first taken.

To hand over disloyally; to reveal what was meant to stay hidden.
1. To hand over or be disloyal to someone who trusted you — a friend, a country, a cause, a confidence.
2. To reveal unintentionally something you were trying to keep hidden.

Sense 2 is the one the GRE cares about, and it turns on involuntariness. You don't betray a feeling on purpose — the subject is usually a small traitorous detail (a tremor, a flush, a pause) that leaks the truth its owner was working to conceal. "His smile showed his nerves" is odd; "his smile betrayed his nerves" is exact, because it implies the nerves were meant to stay private. Even in this quiet sense the word keeps a whiff of treachery: something has gone over to the other side.
⚠️ betray ≠ belie. In the same sentence frame they point opposite ways:
- Her calm face betrayed her panic → the panic got out.
- Her calm face belied her panic → the panic stayed hidden; the face lied about it.
Be-TRAY — you serve your friend up to the enemy on a tray, and if your hands shake, the tray hands over your secret too.
Both senses are one act — something gets handed over against someone's interest, whether it's a person or a piece of the truth.
1. A faint tremor in his voice betrayed the confidence his words were claiming.
2. I told her I didn't mind, but my face betrayed me instantly.
Poker's whole vocabulary runs on this sense: a tell is any twitch or hesitation that betrays your hand — you never mean to show it, which is exactly the point.
Latin tradere = trans ("across") + dare ("give") — to hand over.

The same root splits into opposite moralities: tradition (knowledge handed down to you) and treason / traitor / betray (a person handed over to the enemy). Also extradite — handed across a border.
column3: g03 register::neutral connotation::negative antonym::letting-it-out-vs-keeping-it-in connotation::broken-faith intensity::broken-word-to-treachery lookalike::belie-belittle-betray meaning::made-known:-disclosed-let-slip-or-duly-t second-meaning::saying-it-without-saying-it

column2:
Ruined or withered by a creeping, spreading affliction.
Ruined, withered, spoiled — struck by something that eats away at what was once healthy or promising.

The word starts in agriculture: a blight is a plant disease that shrivels a crop in the field. Everything else is that image applied elsewhere. So blighted carries three things a plain word like ruined doesn't: the damage crept in from outside, it spread, and the thing was flourishing or full of promise beforehand. A blighted career had prospects. A blighted neighbourhood had life in it. Blighted hopes were real hopes. Nothing is blighted if it was never going anywhere.
⚠️ blight ≠ plight. A blight is the affliction that ruins something; a plight is the bad situation a person is stuck in. The famine was a blight; the farmers' plight was starvation.
b-LIGHT-ed — the light has gone out of it.
Something blighted was once lit up with promise and has been slowly dimmed by an outside affliction.
1. Decades of factory closures left the town blighted — half its shopfronts boarded, its young people gone.
2. One bad tackle and his whole season was blighted.
Potato blight caused the Irish Famine — a fungus that crept through the fields and turned a healthy staple crop black in the ground. That's the literal picture behind every figurative use.

Cheerfully carefree — usually carelessly, culpably so.
Cheerful and carefree — and, in most modern use, carefree about something you should have taken seriously.

The old sense is pure sunshine: light-hearted, unclouded, happy. The GRE sense has an edge on it. Look at the company it keeps — blithe disregard, blithe indifference, blithe assumption, blithely ignored. That pairing tells you the whole story: the cheerfulness is real, but it's cheerfulness made possible by not looking. Careless is just sloppy; blithe is sloppy while smiling, which is what makes it damning. The word rarely accuses someone of malice — it accuses them of a lightness that costs other people something.
Blithe hides lithe — it glides lightly over everything, including the thing it should have stopped for.
The lightness is the point: a blithe person doesn't push through the problem, they skim right past it without noticing it was there.
1. The inquiry condemned the ministry's blithe assumption that the flood defences would hold for another decade.
2. He blithely told me the flights were "basically sorted" — three days before we were meant to leave.
Noël Coward's comedy Blithe Spirit — a man haunted by the ghost of his first wife, who is cheerfully, maddeningly unbothered by the chaos she causes. Coward lifted the title from Shelley's skylark: "Hail to thee, blithe Spirit!"
Old English blīþe = "joyous, gentle, kind" — the same root that gives you bliss. Blithe is bliss worn on the outside: bliss is the feeling, blithe is the manner. The disapproving edge is a modern addition; the root itself is entirely sunny.

column2:
Fake — a claim that collapses the moment you check it.
Fake, counterfeit, not genuine — especially something presented as real evidence: bogus credentials, bogus statistics, a bogus invoice, a bogus charity.

Two things set it apart from its neighbours. First, what it attacks: bogus goes after claims and documents — things that assert something and then collapse under checking — where phony goes after people and sincerity. Second, the register: spurious and counterfeit are what the report says; bogus is what you say out loud, with contempt, and it doubles in casual speech as simply "unfair, rubbish" (that fine is totally bogus). It's the one word in this family that comes with an eye-roll built in.
Hocus-pocus is fake magic; bogus is fake everything else — and both get said with a sneer.
The shared -ocus sound carries the shared attitude: not just false, but cheaply, insultingly false.
1. The journal retracted the study after an audit revealed that half the trial data were bogus.
2. They slapped a £40 "processing fee" on the ticket — completely bogus.
Bill & Ted's Bogus Journey (1991) — in their slang, bogus is the opposite of excellent, which is exactly the dismissive, informal flavour of the word.

Noisily energetic and rowdy, but cheerfully so.
Noisily energetic and unruly — loud, physical, full of high spirits. Also, of wind or sea: rough, wild, turbulent.

The warmth is what sets it apart. Rowdy hints at trouble brewing; raucous is about the harshness of the sound itself; boisterous keeps its good humour — the noise comes from people enjoying themselves too much, not from malice. You'd call a family dinner or a pub full of fans boisterous, and only half be complaining.
Boisterous starts with boys — a houseful of them: deafening, exhausting, harmless.
The "boys" buried in the spelling carries the exact tone — chaos you tolerate rather than chaos you call the police about.
1. Three days of boisterous seas kept the fleet at anchor.
2. The party got boisterous around midnight — someone was singing, badly, standing on a chair.
It's the standard euphemism on a child's school report: "boisterous" is what a teacher writes when she means this child never stops shouting but wants to sound fond about it.

column2:
Prop up or strengthen something that's flagging.
Verb: to prop up, strengthen, or reinforce — usually something abstract: morale, confidence, an argument, a claim, an economy, a defence.
Noun: a long firm cushion used as a support.

The word carries an implication about the object: whatever you bolster was sagging, thin, or under pressure. You don't bolster a case that's already airtight — you bolster the shaky one. Compare reinforce (flat, neutral, just adds strength) and corroborate (strictly evidence confirming evidence): bolster is propping-up work, and it quietly admits the thing needed propping.
⚠️ bolster ≠ bluster. One letter apart, opposite jobs: bolster = quietly prop something up; bluster = loud, empty, threatening talk. The blusterer makes noise; the bolsterer adds support.
A bolster is the long pillow you shove behind whatever's sagging.
The noun is the whole verb: you only reach for the cushion when something is drooping — a sinking back, a weak argument, a falling currency.
1. The defence produced three new witnesses to bolster an alibi the jury had plainly begun to doubt.
2. One good week won't fix it, but it did bolster the team's confidence a bit.
Headline English lives on this verb — measures to bolster the economy, reinforcements sent to bolster the front line. If you read business or war reporting, you've met it a hundred times, always attached to something in trouble.
Old English bolster = "a long pillow, cushion." The noun never left: a bolster is still that firm cylindrical pillow, and in carpentry it's the block that takes the load. The verb is just that made literal — to shore up with a cushion.

Puffed-up, pompous language with nothing behind it.
Of speech or writing: inflated, pompous, high-sounding — and empty. Grand words doing the work that substance should be doing.

The charge is against the style, not the argument. A bombastic speaker isn't lying and isn't stupid; he's padding — swelling small thoughts with big vocabulary and thunderous delivery. It's always an insult, and it carries a whiff of the ridiculous: the listener can hear the gap between the volume and the content. Compare eloquent (grand and earned), verbose (merely too many words), grandiloquent (the close cousin — same puffery, slightly more polished-sounding).
Bombastic sounds like bomb blast — all bang, no shrapnel.
The sound hook gives you the loudness; "no shrapnel" gives you the emptiness that makes it an insult.
1. The general's bombastic address promised total victory in a war his own staff privately expected to lose.
2. Skip his TED talk — it's forty bombastic minutes to say "work hard."
Shaggy's 1995 hit "Boombastic" — a deliberate pun on bombastic, and the song is four minutes of the narrator boasting about himself in enormous language. The word means exactly what he's doing.
Bombast was literally cotton stuffing — the padding tailors packed into Elizabethan doublets to make a man's chest look bigger (Latin bombax, "cotton"). Bombastic speech is padded the same way: bulked out to look impressive.

🚫 Nothing to do with bomb. The explosive is unrelated (Greek bombos, "booming noise") — the resemblance is what makes the mnemonic work, not what makes the word mean this.
