column2:
A timely benefit or blessing, often granted from outside.
A thing that helps a lot, arriving at just the right moment — a benefit, a blessing, a windfall.

Two things distinguish it. First, a boon comes from outside: luck, weather, a policy, a patron. You don't grind for a boon, you receive one — which is why "a boon to farmers" sounds right and "a boon I earned" sounds wrong. Second, it's slightly elevated and headline-ish — journalists and speechwriters reach for it far more than people do in conversation. Its natural opposite is bane, and the pair is often set against each other deliberately.

There's an older, still-live sense too: a favour asked for and granted — "grant me a boon." That's the original, and it explains the rest.
Boom → boon: shift one letter and it's still sudden good news you didn't have to work for.
A boom and a boon both drop into your lap from the outside — that unearned, from-elsewhere quality is the whole word.
1. The late monsoon proved a boon to a district that had written off the season's harvest.
2. Free coffee in the office kitchen is a genuine boon when you're running on four hours' sleep.
In every English retelling of Hindu mythology, the gods grant a boon — Ravana asks Brahma for one and gets invulnerability. That's the word's oldest sense sitting in plain sight: a favour requested and given by a higher power.
Old Norse bón = "a prayer, a request." A boon was first the thing you asked for; only later did it become the good thing that simply arrives.

🚫 Not French bon ("good") — despite the look. The one exception is the fossilised phrase boon companion (a jolly drinking friend), which really does come from bon. Different word, same spelling.

Crudely ill-mannered — coarse and oblivious rather than deliberately cruel.
Rude and coarse in a clumsy, unrefined way — loud, tactless, no social polish.

The insult is about breeding, not malice. A cruel person knows exactly which nerve they're standing on; a boorish one doesn't notice there's a nerve there at all. It's the word for the man who talks with his mouth full, interrupts the toast, and asks what your flat cost — offensive by coarseness rather than intent. There's a whiff of class snobbery baked in: calling someone boorish says as much about the speaker's sense of refinement as the target's manners.
⚠️ A boor ≠ a bore.
- boor = coarse, ill-mannered — you want him to behave
- bore = tedious — you want him to stop talking
A boor eats like a boar — grunting, snuffling, elbows out, and entirely unbothered.
The near-homophone carries the exact nuance: an animal at the table isn't being malicious, it simply has no manners.
1. His boorish conduct at the reception — the interruptions, the unasked-for opinions on his hosts' wine — ensured he was never invited again.
2. Don't be boorish, put your phone away, her parents are right there.
Gaston in Disney's Beauty and the Beast is the walking definition — Belle recoils at the thought of being "the wife of that boorish, brainless…" He's not evil yet, just loud, vain, and chewing with his mouth open.
Dutch boer = "farmer, peasant" — the same word as the South African Boer. A boor was originally just a countryman; the contempt was added by townspeople, and it stuck so hard that the farming sense died out entirely.

That's why the word means unpolished rather than nasty: it started as a sneer at people who had never learned drawing-room manners. Same Germanic root as neighbour (Old English gebūr, "dweller nearby").

A showy display of courage that covers real fear.
A swaggering show of courage — bold talk, strutting, defiance staged for an audience.

The word quietly calls the bluff. Bravery is a fact; bravado is a performance, and using the word implies the performer is covering fear, doubt, or weakness. Nobody praises you for bravado — it's what onlookers call your courage when they don't believe it. Often paired with softeners that admit the hollowness: empty bravado, false bravado, a touch of bravado.
⚠️ bravado ≠ bravura.
- bravado = hollow display of boldness — negative
- bravura = dazzling display of technical skill (a pianist's bravura passage) — a compliment
Bravado = bravery + ado — much ado about nothing.
The extra syllables are the fuss and the noise, and there's nothing underneath them.
1. The general's talk of marching on the capital by Friday was pure bravado; his supply lines had collapsed a week earlier.
2. He kept saying the interview went great, but you could hear the bravado in it — he was terrified.
A boxing weigh-in: two fighters nose to nose, snarling promises for the cameras. That's the standard word for it — all bravado until the bell.
Spanish bravada / Italian bravata, from bravo = bold, wild, swaggering.

Same root family: brave, bravo! (shouted at a bold performance), bravura, and desperado — the -ado ending is Spanish swagger, and it's doing the same work in both outlaw words.

Shamelessly bold — openly wrong and not embarrassed about it.
Adj.: boldly and openly wrong — doing the improper thing in full view, with no shame and no attempt to hide it.
Verb (usually brazen it out): to face down an accusation by refusing to look embarrassed.

Bold is admiring, audacious can be admiring, brazen almost never is. The scandal isn't the act, it's the openness — a brazen lie is one told to your face by someone who knows you know. It carries a hint of contempt for the audience: the person isn't sneaking, because sneaking would concede that the rule mattered.
⚠️ brazen ≠ blazon.
- brazen = shameless (from brass)
- blazon = to display or proclaim publicly, as on a coat of arms — hence emblazoned across a banner.

Both are about being seen; only brazen is about not caring.
Brazen has brass in it — and brass doesn't blush.
The metal face is the whole point: the person can't redden, so the boldness reads as shamelessness rather than courage.
1. The minister offered a brazen denial, contradicting a recording that had been broadcast an hour earlier.
2. He just walked out with the office monitor under his arm — you have to admire the brazen cheek of it.
Newsrooms have a fixed collocation for it: a brazen daylight robbery. The word is doing real work there — not that the thieves were skilled, but that they didn't bother with the dark.
Old English bræsen = "made of brass." The metaphor jumped from the metal to the face: hard, unblushing, unmoveable. That's why you can brazen it out — put on a brass front and refuse to concede that you've been caught.

column2:
Shortness — usually the virtue of saying it in few words.
Shortness — either of expression (few words) or of duration (a short span of time).

Applied to speech or writing, it's almost always praise: brevity is a skill, the discipline of cutting to the point. That's what separates it from terseness (short to the point of rudeness) and curtness (short because annoyed). Conciseness is its closest neighbour, but conciseness stresses density of content, brevity simply stresses shortness — a one-word answer has brevity even if it says little.

The time sense runs the other way emotionally: the brevity of life, of a friendship, of summer — there it's wistful, a complaint that the good thing ended.
⚠️ brevity ≠ levity. One letter apart, both GRE staples: brevity = shortness; levity = lightness, not-taking-it-seriously (Latin levis, "light" — same root as alleviate).
brev + -ity — the -ity turns "brief" into a quality you possess, like clarity or purity.
That suffix is why brevity reads as a virtue rather than a measurement: a memo isn't just short, it has brevity.
1. The judge thanked counsel for her brevity, noting that the afternoon's argument had run to four hours on the same point.
2. Keep it short — brevity is your friend when nobody reads past the first line of an email.
Polonius in Hamlet: "Brevity is the soul of wit" — a line he delivers in the middle of a long, rambling speech, which is the joke.
Latin brevis = "short." It's hiding in a big family: brief, abbreviate, abridge, breviary (the shortened prayer book), and the musical breve.

column2:
Restrain or curb; also to recoil in wounded pride.
Noun: the headgear — straps, bit and reins — by which a rider steers and checks a horse.
Verb (transitive): to restrain, curb, keep something powerful under control.
Verb (intransitive, usually bridle at): to react to an insult with visible wounded pride — chin up, head drawn back.

To bridle something is not to crush it. The horse still runs; you're just holding the reins. So bridle your tongue, bridle his ambition implies real force being steered, not extinguished — which is why the word carries a whiff of discipline and self-command rather than suppression. The bridle at sense is narrower than "get angry": it's offence taken on behalf of one's dignity, and it shows on the body before it reaches the mouth.
⚠️ bridle ≠ bridal. Same sound, no relation. Bridal = of a bride (bridal gown, bridal suite). Bridle = the horse's reins, and restraint. The GRE won't test the wedding word — but it will punish you for reading one as the other.
A bridle yanks a horse's head back — bridle at an insult and your own head snaps back.
One gesture covers both senses: the check applied to something powerful, whether that's a horse, your temper, or your pride rearing up.
1. The treaty was designed less to disarm the republic than to bridle it — its army intact, its ambitions leashed.
2. Call him "kid" one more time and watch him bridle.
You almost certainly know the negative first: unbridled ambition, unbridled enthusiasm, unbridled capitalism — power with nothing holding the reins. Strip the un- and you have the word.
Old English brīdel, from bregdan = "to pull, jerk, weave." That yank gives you braid (pulling strands together) and upbraid (jerking a fault up in someone's face — to scold).

🚫 Nothing to do with bride. That's a separate Germanic word; the identical sound is coincidence.

A soothing, worn-out remark; or the dull person who makes it.
A trite, comforting remark offered as if it were wisdom — "everything happens for a reason," "time heals all wounds." By extension, a tediously conventional person who deals in such remarks.

What separates it from cliché or platitude is the sedative effect. A cliché is merely worn out; a bromide is worn out and deployed to soothe — to smooth over grief, conflict, or hard questions so nobody has to think. Calling something a bromide accuses the speaker of dodging, not just of being unoriginal. The word itself is bookish; it shows up in criticism, obituaries of speeches, and political columns far more than in speech.
A bromide is what your bro says when he has nothing useful: "it is what it is, mate."
The hidden bro flags the key nuance — it's meant kindly and lands as comfortingly empty, not merely stale.
1. The minister's statement offered nothing but bromides about resilience and lessons learned, and not one word about who had signed off on the contract.
2. Don't give me the "everything happens for a reason" bromide — I just want someone to admit it went wrong.
The modern specimen everyone recognises: "thoughts and prayers" after a disaster — soothing, automatic, and criticised precisely because it substitutes for action. That is a bromide in one phrase.
Greek brōmos = "stench." It named bromine, a foul-smelling element — and potassium bromide was the standard Victorian sedative, dosed out for nerves, insomnia and hysteria.

So a bromide is literally a tranquilliser in verbal form: a phrase administered to calm you down. Once you see the drug, the meaning never slips.

column2:
To tolerate — almost always as "brook no."
Verb: to tolerate, to put up with — to allow something to stand.

Two things make it strange. First, it lives almost entirely in the negative: brook no dissent, brook no delay, brook no interference. You will rarely see anyone brook anything. Second, it belongs to authority — a general, a headmistress, a chairman. Tolerate is what an equal does; brook no is what someone with power announces, and it closes the conversation rather than opening it.

Noun: a small stream. Same spelling, completely different word.
Nobody ever brooks a thing — they brook no thing.
Lock the word to its collocation: if "no" isn't sitting right after it, you're probably looking at the stream.
1. The colonel's orders would brook no discussion; the column moved at dawn.
2. Fine, come along — but I'm brooking no whining about the hill.
Tennyson's much-anthologised poem "The Brook" — "men may come and men may go, but I go on for ever" — is the other brook, the stream. Useful as a marker for which sense is which.
Old English brūcan = "to use, to enjoy" — so "brook no X" originally meant "get no enjoyment out of X," which softened into "won't stand for it." It's a cousin of Latin fruī (to enjoy), the root behind fruit, frugal, and usufruct.

🚫 The stream brook is Old English brōc, a separate word entirely. No connection beyond spelling.

Charmingly rural — the countryside as a pretty picture.
Of the countryside, and charmingly so: green fields, grazing animals, unhurried quiet.

The word never describes farm work as work. Agrarian is economic, rustic is rough and a bit unpolished, rural is just a census category — bucolic is the countryside seen from outside and admired. It carries a faint whiff of the picturesque: someone calling a village bucolic is enjoying the view, not mucking out the barn. Occasionally used drily, exactly because that gap between the pretty picture and the actual mud is easy to poke at.
Bucolic, bovine — same cow. Bucolic is cow-country as scenery.
The bou- is Greek for ox, so the word literally means cowherd-ish — and cows in a field are the postcard, not the labour.
1. The novel opens on a bucolic valley of hedgerows and slow rivers, all of which the railway will have swallowed by chapter nine.
2. Two days of bucolic bliss and then the Wi-Fi died and we drove straight back to the city.
Estate agents and travel brochures live on this word — "bucolic charm", "bucolic setting" is standard copy for any cottage with a field near it. If you've read a countryside listing, you've read bucolic.
Greek boûs = ox, cow → boukolos = cowherd. The same bou- pays off elsewhere: bovine (cow-like), bulimia (bous + limos, "ox-hunger"), and butter (bou-tyron, cow-cheese).

Able to float; irrepressibly cheerful, hard to keep down.
Three linked senses: able to float (or to keep other things afloat); cheerful and light-hearted; and, of markets or demand, rising, healthy, doing well.

The emotional sense isn't loud joy — it's unsinkable joy. Ebullient bubbles over at you; buoyant simply refuses to go down. It implies pressure that should have sunk the person and didn't, so it carries a quiet compliment about resilience rather than volume. A buoyant mood survives bad news; a buoyant economy survives a bad quarter.
There's a buoy sitting inside buoyant — shove one underwater and it pops straight back up.
That pop-back-up is the whole word: not merely happy, but impossible to hold down.
1. Despite the verdict, his spirits remained oddly buoyant, as though the worst news had failed to reach him.
2. She came out of the interview buoyant — practically skipping to the car.
Financial news lives on this word: "buoyant demand," "a buoyant housing market" — the sense of an economy bobbing up rather than sinking.

column2:
To sprout and then grow or expand rapidly.
To sprout, bud, and then grow or expand rapidly and healthily.

It carries two things ordinary grow doesn't: an organic, living flavour, and a sense of promising beginnings — something small getting visibly bigger, fast. A tumour doesn't burgeon; a career, a city, a music scene does. That's why the word is almost always positive, and why you meet it mostly as the adjective burgeoning in front of a noun: a burgeoning demand, a burgeoning talent, a burgeoning middle class. Note also that it needs no object — things burgeon on their own; you don't burgeon them.
b-URGE-ON — growth being urged on.
The hidden word gives you the nuance exactly: not steady growth, but growth with momentum behind it.
1. By the 1890s the port had burgeoned into the busiest on the coast, its warehouses spilling out past the old walls.
2. Her side hustle burgeoned into an actual business before she'd even quit her day job.
Business and tech journalism runs on it — "a burgeoning startup scene", "burgeoning demand for chips". If you've read a market report, you've read this word.
Old French burjon = "a bud, a shoot." The literal sense is a plant putting out buds — which is why the word still smells of springtime and early promise rather than mere increase.

🚫 Not related to bourgeois. That's from Germanic burg, "town" — borough, burgher, Edinburgh. Similar look, unrelated root.
column3: g03 register::formal connotation::positive antonym::fertile-vs-barren antonym::lying-dormant-vs-breaking-out antonym::swelling-vs-dying-down intensity::growth-out-of-control meaning::multiply-fast

column2:
To polish to a shine; to enhance a reputation.
Literally: to polish metal by rubbing until it gleams. Figuratively — and this is how the GRE uses it — to improve the lustre of something abstract: a reputation, an image, credentials, a legacy.

The key limit is that you can only burnish what already exists. Build a reputation, burnish an existing one — it's buffing a surface, not manufacturing substance. That's why the figurative use carries a faint whiff of PR: when a newspaper says a politician is burnishing his image, the implication is cosmetic work on the shine rather than change underneath.
⚠️ burnish vs. tarnish — near-rhymes, exact opposites.
- burnish = rub bright
- tarnish = go dull, stain

A scandal tarnishes the record the memoir was written to burnish.
Tar blackens; burn brightens.
The rhyme locks the pair as opposites, and the "rubbing" idea reminds you that burnishing works on a surface that's already there — it polishes a reputation, it doesn't build one.
1. Rather than answer the allegations, the firm spent a fortune on advertising designed to burnish an image it had spent a decade dulling.
2. He's only doing the charity 5K to burnish his UCAS form, and everyone knows it.
Political journalism runs on this verb — "burnishing his foreign-policy credentials," "a trip meant to burnish her legacy" are newsroom boilerplate before any election.
Old French burnir / brunir = "to make brown, to make bright", from Germanic brūn (brown) — the colour of polished bronze catching the light. Same root gives you brown and brunette.

To prop up or strengthen an argument or structure from outside.
Noun: a stone or brick support built against the outside of a wall to stop it collapsing outward.
Verb: to strengthen or prop something up — usually an argument, a claim, a case, a regime.

On the GRE it is almost always the verb, and almost always figurative: you buttress a claim with evidence. The word carries its architecture with it — the support comes from outside, is added deliberately, and quietly implies the thing couldn't stand on its own. Bolster can just boost morale; buttress is structural and load-bearing. And note the collocation: you buttress a position, not a person.
A buttress butts up against the wall — pushing back from outside so the wall doesn't fall.
The hidden butt (to shove against) tells you the support is external pressure applied to something already leaning.
1. The dissertation buttressed its central claim with three decades of census data.
2. Don't walk in with a hunch — buttress it with numbers or they'll tear it apart.
Notre-Dame de Paris. When it burned in 2019, every news report went straight to the flying buttresses — the stone arms bracing the walls from outside, the only reason the shell stayed standing.
Old French bouter = "to thrust, to push against." That single root pushes through a useful family: abut (to push up against — adjoining land), rebut (to push back against a claim), butt (heads), even button (thrust through a hole).

So buttress, abut, rebut are all one idea — force applied against something.
column3: g24 register::formal connotation::neutral antonym::propping-up-vs-undermining intensity::propping-up-fighting-for:-bolster-buttre meaning::backing-a-claim-with-evidence meaning::prop-up-add-to-turn-up second-meaning::siege-engineering-inside-an-argument

column2:
Maddeningly complicated, tangled with rules and hidden scheming.
Excessively complicated and convoluted — a system of rules, procedures or plots so tangled that no outsider can follow it.

Complex is neutral and can be admiring; byzantine is always a complaint. It carries two charges at once: the thing is impossibly intricate, and the intricacy shields insiders — hidden channels, backroom deals, rules nobody will explain. A byzantine tax code isn't just hard; it's suspiciously hard.
BIZantine — a biz so knotted with rules and back channels that only insiders know how it really works.
The "biz" at the front pins both halves of the word: bureaucratic tangle plus insider scheming.
1. The committee's byzantine approval process required eleven signatures, three of them from officials whose roles no one could define.
2. Getting a refund from them is byzantine — I've been transferred four times and I still don't know who's in charge.
Computer science has the Byzantine Generals Problem — and its offspring, Byzantine fault tolerance, the property blockchains brag about. The name was chosen precisely because it means generals sending contradictory, possibly treacherous messages that no one can untangle.
From Byzantium — the Greek city Constantine rebuilt as Constantinople, capital of the Eastern Roman Empire (now Istanbul). Its court was legendary in the West for layered officialdom, elaborate ceremony and palace intrigue, so by the 1800s the empire's name became the adjective for that whole condition.

This is one of the rare words where the history is the definition: the Byzantine bureaucracy was byzantine.
column3: g13 register::formal connotation::negative antonym::crystal-clear-vs-impenetrable antonym::tangled-vs-plain-simple connotation::obscurity-blamed-on-the-writer intensity::elaborate-convoluted-tortuous-byzantine: meaning::twisted-past-following second-meaning::proper-nouns-that-became-verdicts

column2:
Harsh and jarring; a clashing mess of noise.
Harsh, jarring, discordant — a mixture of sounds that clash instead of blending.

Loudness alone isn't enough. A jet engine is deafening but not cacophonous; it's one sound. Cacophony needs many sounds fighting each other — horns, shouting, drills, a dozen conversations. And it's a verdict, not a measurement: the speaker is telling you the noise is ugly. It transfers easily to non-sound clashes too — a cacophonous colour scheme, a cacophonous chorus of opinions on a policy — always with that sense of too many things at once, none of them agreeing.
Caca-phonous — it sounds like caca.
The nursery word for filth is hiding in plain sight at the front, and it's no accident — that caco- really does mean "bad", so cacophonous is literally bad-sounding, not merely loud.
1. The square at dusk was cacophonous — vendors bellowing, mopeds, and the call to prayer all colliding over one another.
2. Six people on the call unmuted at once and it turned into a cacophonous mess.
The orchestra tuning up before the conductor walks on — thirty instruments sawing away in different keys. That two-minute racket is the textbook cacophony, and the silence that follows it is the point.
Greek kakos = "bad" + phōnē = "sound, voice." Bad-sound.

Both halves pay off elsewhere. Phōnē gives you symphony (sounds together), euphony (good sound — the exact antonym), phonetics, telephone. And kakos gives you kakistocracy, government by the worst people — a word worth knowing on its own.

To coax someone into doing something through persistent flattery.
To get someone to do something by sustained sweet-talk — flattery, coaxing, small promises, wearing down resistance with charm rather than argument or force.

Two things are always implied: the target didn't want to do it, and the persuader kept at it. You can't cajole someone in one sentence, and you can't cajole a willing person. Next to persuade (neutral, reason-based) and browbeat (force), cajoling sits in between — soft pressure applied repeatedly. The word carries a faint smirk: it credits the cajoler's skill while hinting the tactics were slightly beneath honest argument. It's affectionate when a parent does it to a toddler, faintly cynical when a lobbyist does it to a senator.
ca-JOLE = ca-JOLLY — you jolly them along until they say yes.
The stressed syllable is literally the sound of jolly, which is the tactic: keep things light and flattering until the reluctant person gives in.
1. Only after weeks of dinners and quiet promises did the ambassador manage to cajole the smaller states into signing.
2. I had to cajole him into coming out — three texts, a free drink, and a lift home.
It's a fixture of political reporting: a party whip spends the night before a vote cajoling holdouts — the standard pairing is "cajoling and arm-twisting," which tells you exactly where the word sits on the scale (the soft half).

Disastrous; causing ruin on a large, irreversible scale.
Causing or amounting to disaster — ruin on a scale that can't be walked back.

Unfortunate is a shrug, disastrous is the everyday workhorse, calamitous is the heavy, formal one — the word historians and editorial writers use for the decision that wrecked a bank, a campaign, a fleet. It points at consequences, not feelings: a thing is calamitous because of the wreckage it left, not because it felt bad at the time. It also carries a faint note of judgement — someone usually caused the calamity.
⚠️ calamitous ≠ calumnious.
- calamitous = disastrous
- calumnious = slanderous (from calumny, a false, malicious accusation)

One ruins your life; the other ruins your name.
There is no such thing as mildly calamitous.
The word has only one setting — total ruin — which is why it never takes a softening adverb the way bad, unfortunate, or even disastrous will.
1. The decision to fortify the northern passes proved calamitous, costing the empire both its army and its grain supply.
2. Buying at the top of the market was, in hindsight, absolutely calamitous.
Calamity Jane — the Wild West markswoman, and Doris Day's 1953 musical. The nickname was the point: trouble arrived with her.

Hardened to others' suffering; unfeeling.
Hardened against other people's suffering; showing no feeling or concern where feeling is owed.

A cruel person wants you to hurt; a callous person simply doesn't register that you're hurting. That's the whole charge — not malice but a missing reaction, the shrug where sympathy should have been. It's also a word about becoming: people are described as callous after long exposure has worn the softness off them — surgeons, landlords, war reporters. Strong enough to be an accusation, and it usually lands on an act or a remark ("a callous joke") as readily as on a person.
⚠️ callous ≠ callow. Callous = hardened, unfeeling (too much experience). Callow = green, immature, inexperienced (too little). A callow youth becomes a callous veteran.
A callus is skin too thick to feel. A callous person is thickened somewhere else.
The word hides callus whole, and that's exactly the metaphor — not sharpness, just numbness where sensitivity used to be.
1. Years in the claims department had made him callous to grief, which he processed at a rate of forty files a day.
2. Texting "k" after she told you her dog died is a bit callous, mate.
"Callous disregard" is a set phrase in courtrooms and newspapers — the standard wording for indifference so total it counts as wrongdoing. If you've read a verdict summary, you've read this word.
Latin callum / callus = "hard skin." A callus is what forms where the skin is rubbed over and over until it stops feeling anything — and that is the entire meaning of callous, transplanted to the heart. Same root gives callus, calloused, callosity.

column2:
Young and inexperienced; unformed, not yet seasoned by life.
Young and inexperienced — immature not through stupidity but through never having been tested by life.

The word is a put-down delivered from above: an older, wiser speaker looking down at someone who talks confidently about things he hasn't lived through. Milder than naive (which implies you'll be conned) and softer than green (which is about job skills) — callow is about character not yet formed. It clings to the noun youth almost as a fixed phrase: a callow youth.
⚠️ callow ≠ callous. They are near-opposites.
- callow = unhardened — soft, raw, unformed
- callous = hardened — unfeeling, indifferent to others' pain

A callow recruit flinches at the sight of blood; a callous one doesn't.
Callow rhymes with fallow — a field nothing has grown in yet.
Neither the field nor the boy has produced anything yet, and both are judged on that emptiness.
1. His maiden speech in the House betrayed a callow confidence that the older members listened to in amused silence.
2. I was twenty-two and completely callow — I thought quitting a job by text was a power move.
Old English calu = "bald, featherless." A callow bird is a chick that hasn't grown its flight feathers — it physically cannot leave the nest yet. That's the whole picture the word still carries: not ready, not fledged.

🚫 Not callous. That's Latin callum, "hard skin" — same root as callus, the thickened patch on a guitarist's fingertip. Unrelated word, opposite idea.

column2:
A deliberate lie told to destroy someone's reputation.
A false statement made deliberately to destroy someone's reputation — or the practice of making them.

Slander is the courtroom word; calumny is the moral one. It carries the speaker's disgust with it: you don't call something calumny unless you think the victim is innocent and the accuser is vile. And unlike rumour or gossip, which can drift into being by accident, calumny is aimed — someone chose the lie and chose the target. Formal, faintly biblical, and best deployed when you want the accusation itself to sound shameful.
calumny ≠ calamity. Calumny is a slander; a calamity is a disaster. Similar rhythm, unrelated words — a calumny can cause a calamity, which is exactly why the exam likes the pair.
Calumny = a poisonous column — a lie set in print to ruin a name.
The sound hook holds the nuance: a column is written, published and deliberate, never an accidental slip of gossip.
1. The biography rescues her from two centuries of calumny, showing that the letters used to condemn her were forged.
2. He didn't just disagree with me — he went around the office spreading outright calumny about my expenses.
Hamlet to Ophelia: "Be thou as chaste as ice, as pure as snow, thou shalt not escape calumny." — i.e. innocence is no defence against a determined liar.
Latin calumnia = "a false accusation, a trick," from calvī, "to deceive."

The surprise: challenge is the same word. Calumnia → Old French chalenge, which originally meant an accusation or false claim, before softening into "a dare." So a challenge and a calumny are etymological twins — one kept the fight, the other kept the lie.

Openly honest, especially about the uncomfortable.
Honest and open, especially about something awkward, unflattering, or usually kept quiet. Second sense: unposed — a candid photo is one taken before anyone arranged their face.

Where blunt and brutal imply the speaker enjoyed it, and frank is merely direct, candid carries a whiff of disclosure — the speaker had a reason to hide this and chose not to. That's why it's almost always approving: you're candid about your own failures, doubts, or finances. A CEO who is candid about a bad quarter earns credit; one who is blunt about it just upset the room.
Candid is a candle — it lights up the part of the room you'd rather leave dim.
Same root, and it captures the nuance exactly: candour isn't just saying things, it's illuminating what was conveniently in shadow.
1. In a candid memoir, the former minister admits he knew the figures were wrong and signed off anyway.
2. Can I be candid? That shirt is not doing what you think it's doing.
Candid Camera, the hidden-camera show that ran for decades — the whole premise is catching people unposed, before they've had time to arrange themselves.
Latin candidus = "shining white", from candēre, "to glow" — the same root as candle and incandescent.

The bonus: a Roman seeking office wore a bleached white toga to advertise his purity — hence candidate. So candid, candle, incandescent, candidate all come from one glow.

Shrewd and careful, especially about money.
Shrewd and careful — quick to spot an advantage and hard to cheat, especially in money, bargaining, or judging people.

Cunning and crafty hint that someone is working an angle on you; canny hands out credit. It's the praise you give a person who never overpays, never signs the bad contract, and knows exactly when to walk away. Note the scale, too: canny is quiet, practical competence, not dazzling brilliance — a canny investor is careful, not a genius.
canny ≠ the opposite of uncanny. Uncanny means eerie, unsettlingly strange (an uncanny resemblance) — it is not "unshrewd." The pair split centuries ago; treat them as separate words.
Canny is just can + -y — he can see what you're up to.
The hidden can is literal: the word grew out of the old sense of can meaning "to know how," so a canny person is the one who knows how.
1. The negotiators were canny enough to let the other side name a figure first.
2. Buying that flat before the line opened was a canny move — it's worth double now.
Sports and business journalism run on it: a transfer window bargain is always "a canny bit of business," a veteran manager "a canny operator."
Scots and northern English, from can in its old sense "to know, to know how" — the same root as ken (Scots for "know"), cunning (originally just "knowledgeable"), and know itself.

That root also explains uncouth: un- + couth, "not known" → unfamiliar → boorish. And uncanny started as "not safely known" — beyond ordinary knowledge — which is how it drifted to eerie while canny stayed with worldly know-how.

column2:
Declare a saint; enshrine as official and beyond question.
1. For the Church to formally declare a dead person a saint. 2. More broadly, to enshrine something as officially great, authoritative, beyond questioning — admit a book, film or figure into "the canon."

This is always an act of institutional power, not personal enthusiasm. You can adore a novel; only the syllabus, the academy, the Church can canonize it. And the effect is permanence — canonization freezes a reputation, puts it past debate. Because of that finality, the word turns dryly ironic the moment the thing being enshrined doesn't deserve it: a mediocre album canonized by critics who were there at the time.
⚠️ canon ≠ cannon. A canon is a rule or an official list (one n); a cannon fires cannonballs (two ns). Nothing is ever "cannonized."
Canonize = put on the CANON — the official list you're no longer allowed to argue with.
The word is hiding in plain sight: canonizing isn't praising something, it's filing it somewhere permanent by authority.
1. Pope Francis canonized her in 2016, nineteen years after her death and two verified miracles later.
2. Give it ten years and they'll have canonized that show — you won't be allowed to say it was boring.
Every fandom argument about what "counts" — is the Star Wars Expanded Universe canon? — is a fight over what's been canonized. Same word, same idea: an authority decides what's officially real and what gets thrown out.
Greek kanōn = a straight measuring rod — hence a rule, a standard. What measures up gets on the list.

That rod runs through canon (the approved body of scripture or works), canonical (authoritative, standard), canon law, and canonize itself.

To stop resisting and accept the other side's terms.
To stop resisting and accept the other side's terms — to surrender, usually on agreed conditions.

The word presupposes a fight. You cannot capitulate to something you never opposed: there was a siege, a standoff, a months-long argument, and then it broke. Acquiesce means you went along quietly from the start; concede can be gracious, even sporting; capitulate is the white flag going up after the resistance has been ground down. It usually casts the surrenderer as the weaker party, so it stings when applied to a person — "the board capitulated to shareholder pressure" is not a compliment.
⚠️ capitulate ≠ recapitulate.
- capitulate = give in
- recapitulate (recap) = summarise, run back over the main points

Same root, opposite exam answers.
Cap it. You finally put a lid on the fight — but only because you'd been fighting.
The "cap it" in the first syllables marks the moment resistance gets sealed off, which is the part surrender alone doesn't tell you.
1. After eleven weeks of siege the garrison capitulated, marching out under terms that spared the town.
2. I held out on the puppy for a year, then capitulated the second she started crying at dinner.
Traders talk about capitulation — the point in a crash where the last stubborn holders finally give up and dump everything. It's the word doing exactly its job: they resisted the whole way down, then broke.
Latin caput, capitis = "head" → capitulum, "little head", i.e. a chapter heading. To capitulate was originally to draw up terms under headings — the surrender document was written in numbered articles.

That head-root is everywhere: capital, captain, chapter, decapitate, per capita, and recapitulate (go back over the headings).

Prone to sudden, unreasoned changes of mood or decision.
Given to sudden, unaccountable changes of mood, opinion or behaviour — acting on whim rather than reason.

Fickle is intimate and emotional (a fickle lover, a fickle fanbase). Capricious is bigger and colder: it attaches to whoever holds the power — a capricious king, a capricious examiner, capricious weather, capricious fate. The sting isn't that they change, it's that the change obeys no logic you can predict or appeal to. And note the tonal split from whimsical: whimsy is charming, caprice is unnerving, because you have to live under it.
Capricious = Capri-CORN, the goat — it bolts up the cliff the instant the mood takes it, and nobody gets a reason.
Goats don't wander, they lurch — which is the word exactly: not gradual change but abrupt, unexplained swerves.
1. The emperor's justice was capricious: two men committed the same offence, and one was pardoned before lunch, the other exiled by evening.
2. Don't bother planning the barbecue — April weather here is capricious as hell.
In US law, courts throw out a government agency's decision for being "arbitrary and capricious" — the standard phrase for a ruling made on no rational basis. If you ever read a news story about a policy being struck down, this is the wording.
Italian capriccio = "a whim, a sudden start" — and Italians linked it to capra, "goat", for the animal's abrupt leaping.

The goat runs through the family: Capricorn (the goat-horned sign), caper (to skip about), capriole (a horse's leap), caprice (the whim itself). In music a capriccio is a piece that changes direction on impulse — same idea, scored.

column2:
Fault-finding over trifles; objecting for the pleasure of it.
Given to finding fault over trivialities — raising petty objections, seizing on small errors, quibbling for the sake of it.

A critical reader wants the work to be better. A captious one wants you to be wrong. The word passes judgement on the objector, not the object: it says the complaints are small, the motive is point-scoring, and the pleasure is in the catching. It also describes a disposition, not a single remark — you can be captious all afternoon. Formal, faintly withering; it's the word for the committee member who spends forty minutes on a footnote.
captious ≠ capricious. Both open with cap-, both are exam regulars. Captious = nitpicking, out to catch you. Capricious = whimsical, changing on a impulse. A captious boss objects to everything; a capricious boss objects to a different thing each day.
Captious — he's out to capture you in a slip.
Not a review, a gotcha: the captious critic hunts the trivial error so he can hold it up.
1. The referee's report was captious throughout, disputing the spelling of place names while ignoring the argument entirely.
2. Don't be so captious — I know I said "less" instead of "fewer," and no, it doesn't change the point.
Latin captiōsus = "designed to entrap" — a captious question was originally a trick one, a snare dressed as an enquiry. From capere, "to take, to seize."

That root is a workhorse: capture, captive, caption, captivate, susceptible, recuperate. Keep the seizing sense and the word stays honest — the captious man is grabbing at your mistakes.
column3: g25 register::formal connotation::negative antonym::above-pettiness-vs-mired-in-it connotation::care-for-detail-curdled-into-a-fault connotation::complaint-as-a-temperament meaning::fault-finding-over-trifles

column2:
An exaggerated portrait or description that mocks by amplifying real traits.
Noun: a portrait or description that exaggerates distinctive features for comic or satirical effect. Verb: to depict someone that way.

The key is that a caricature never invents — it amplifies. The nose was always big; the cartoonist just gave it three more inches. That's why it stings: you can't fully deny it.

Used figuratively, it's an accusation. "That's a caricature of my position" means: you took something real, blew one part out of proportion, and attacked the result. Compare parody, which mimics a style, and satire, which has a target and a moral point — caricature is narrower and more personal, aimed at a face, a manner, a person.
A caricature can't make it up — it can only turn it up.
Every feature in a caricature is genuinely there; only the volume is dishonest.
1. The paper's cartoonist caricatured the chancellor as a stooped clerk buried under his own ledgers.
2. Come on — that's a caricature of what I said, and you know it.
The seaside-pier or theme-park artist who'll draw you in ten minutes with a giant head, tiny body and one enormous grin — that's the trade name for exactly this: a caricature.
Italian caricare = "to load, to pile on" (from Latin carrus, a wagon). A caricature is a face with too much freight on it.

Same root, quietly everywhere: cargo, charge, carriage, car, chariot, discharge, surcharge — all about loading and hauling. A surcharge is an extra load of money; a caricature is an extra load of nose.

To rebuke severely, usually in public and on the record.
To rebuke or criticise severely — a punishing telling-off, usually delivered publicly and from a position of moral authority.

Where criticise is neutral and scold is domestic, castigate is the register of editorials, inquiry reports and judgements: the speaker is not just disagreeing, they are pronouncing you at fault. It implies the target deserved it, and it implies an audience — you castigate someone for a specific failing, on the record. Almost never used of a quiet word in private.
⚠️ castigate ≠ instigate.
- castigate = lash someone for what they did
- instigate = start the thing off

The rioters were instigated by one man; the judge later castigated them all.
You castigate in print; you yell in person.
If there's no audience and no moral high ground, it isn't castigation — it's just shouting.
1. The commission's final report castigated the regulator for a decade of wilful inattention.
2. My editor castigated me for missing the deadline — three paragraphs of email, all of it deserved.
It's a newsroom workhorse: whenever a headline says an inquiry, a court or an opposition leader "castigated" someone, that's the word doing its one job — official blame, said out loud.
Latin castigāre = castus ("pure, chaste") + agere ("to drive") — literally to drive someone back into purity. Punishment as moral correction, not revenge.

That root pays out widely: chaste, chasten, chastise (the same word worn down through French), caste (a "pure" bloodline), and incest — in- + castus, "not chaste."
column3: g02 register::formal connotation::negative antonym::praising-to-the-skies-vs-tearing-down connotation::scolding-at-full-volume intensity::scolding-mild-to-savage meaning::savage-public-criticism

column2:
Violently destructive on a world-changing scale.
Violently destructive on an enormous scale — a disaster that overturns and remakes whatever it hits.

The word carries scale plus transformation. Catastrophic names a bad outcome; cataclysmic says the old order is gone and the landscape afterwards is unrecognisable — an asteroid strike, a flood, the collapse of an empire. That's why it also works for non-disasters: a cataclysmic shift in the industry means everything realigned, not that anyone died. Formal, high-intensity, and easily hyperbolic — reach for it and you've committed to world-altering, so a delayed train doesn't qualify.
Cataclysm ≈ chasm — it doesn't just damage things, it rips a gap between before and after.
The near-rhyme fixes the key idea: a cataclysm is a rupture in history, not merely heavy damage.
1. The eruption of Thera was cataclysmic, ending a civilisation and reshaping the Aegean coastline in a single season.
2. Losing one client isn't cataclysmic — calm down, we'll survive the quarter.
World of Warcraft: Cataclysm earned its name literally — the expansion tore up and permanently redrew the game's existing world map, which is exactly what the word promises.
Greek kataklysmos = "a flood, a washing away" — kata- (down) + klyzein (to wash). The original cataclysm was the Deluge.

kata- pays off across the GRE: catastrophe (a turning down), cataract (water dashing down — and the film that comes down over the eye), catapult (hurling down), catalyst (loosening down).

Disastrous on a total, sudden, no-recovery scale.
Disastrous in the fullest sense — sudden, total, and beyond repair.

Disastrous stretches to cover a ruined dinner party; catastrophic does not. It implies the thing didn't merely go badly, it stopped existing in working form: a bank, a bridge, a harvest, an ecosystem. Engineers use it precisely — catastrophic failure means a part gave way all at once rather than wearing down gracefully — and that technical sense colours the ordinary one. Casual speech does inflate it ("my hair looks catastrophic"), but the joke only works because the real word is so absolute.
There is no such thing as slightly catastrophic.
The word sits pinned at the top of the damage scale, so unlike bad, costly or damaging it refuses to be dialled down — if it can be softened, it isn't catastrophic.
1. The 2008 collapse was catastrophic not because losses were large but because the mechanism of lending itself ceased to function.
2. One wrong keystroke and the whole database was gone — genuinely catastrophic, and I'd skipped the backup.
Therapists talk about catastrophizing — spiralling from "he hasn't texted back" to "my life is over." The habit is named after the word precisely because the leap is always to total ruin, never to mild inconvenience.
Greek kata- (down) + strephein (to turn) = katastrophē, "the overturning." In Greek drama it was a neutral technical term: the sudden final turn of the plot — the scene after which nothing can be undone.

That strephein shows up again in apostrophe (a turning away — to address someone absent) and strophe (the turn a chorus made across the stage). The cata- "down" half runs through catapult, cataract, catalyst.

Giving relief by purging pent-up emotion.
Adj.: providing release from strong or bottled-up emotion, so that you feel purged and lightened afterwards. Noun (medical, older): a purgative — a drug that empties the bowels.

The relief is on the far side of something intense: you sob, you scream into a pillow, you finally say the thing at the funeral. Soothing calms you down, therapeutic helps you heal over time; cathartic discharges a build-up in one go, and the experience itself is often unpleasant. That's why grief, rage, and horror films can all be cathartic, and a warm bath usually isn't.
Before it cleaned out feelings, a cathartic cleaned out bowels.
The medical sense is the literal one — a purge — so remember cathartic as emptying out, not cheering up.
1. The confession was cathartic for her, though it cost her every friendship she had left.
2. Honestly, deleting that group chat was weirdly cathartic.
Aristotle's Poetics is where the idea lives: tragedy exists to give the audience catharsis — a purging of pity and fear. Every \"I watched a sad film and cried and felt better\" is that theory in action.
Greek katharos = "pure, clean" → katharsis, a cleansing. The medieval Cathars took the same root as their name: "the pure ones."

Burning; bitingly sarcastic in a way meant to wound.
Literally: able to burn or eat away flesh and material by chemical action — lye, acid, drain cleaner.
Figuratively: bitingly sarcastic; scathing.

A caustic remark is corrosive, not merely clever. Sarcasm can be affectionate and sarcasm can be dumb; caustic is neither — it's sharp, controlled, and aimed to strip something off the person it hits. There's usually bitterness behind it, which is why caustic describes critics, exes and burnt-out colleagues far more often than comedians.
Caustic soda strips paint. Caustic wit strips skin.
The chemical meaning is the literal one, so the figurative sense keeps the damage — a caustic line is meant to leave a mark, not get a laugh.
1. His caustic review of the production was quoted for years, chiefly by people who had not seen it.
2. Don't ask her for feedback before coffee — she goes full caustic.
The caustic soda on the drain-cleaner bottle under your sink — the skull-and-crossbones warning is the whole meaning of the word in one label.
Greek kaiein = "to burn" → kaustikos, "burning."

Same root gives you cauterize (seal a wound by burning it) and holocaust (holos "whole" + kaustos "burnt" — burnt whole). Once you hear the burn in it, the sarcastic sense stops being a separate definition to memorise.

Airily dismissive about something that deserves seriousness.
Adjective: offhand and dismissive about something that deserves care or seriousness.
Noun (historical): a horseman or gallant — specifically a Royalist supporter of Charles I.

The insult isn't laziness or cruelty; it's airy unconcern from above. A careless doctor made a mistake. A cavalier doctor waved the risk away as beneath discussing — the fault is the attitude, not the error. It implies the speaker thinks you're too grand, or too breezy, to take the stakes seriously, and it's a word you use about people with some power to be casual with.
Cavalier almost always comes with about — and whatever follows about is something that deserved better: safety, facts, other people's money.
Nobody is ever cavalier about something trivial, so the word convicts the person the moment it's used.
1. The report condemned the firm's cavalier disregard for basic safety procedure.
2. Don't be so cavalier about the deadline — that thing is due Friday and you've written nothing.
The Cleveland Cavaliers — sword-and-horseman logo, named for exactly the swaggering mounted gentlemen the word came from.
Latin caballus = "horse" → Italian cavaliere, "horseman, knight." A cavalier was a gentleman on horseback, looking down — literally — on everyone on foot. That lofty ease curdled into the modern insult.

Same horse gives you cavalry, cavalcade, and (via French cheval) chivalry and chevalier.

Note the split: chivalrous kept the horseman's honour, cavalier kept his arrogance.
column3: g12 register::neutral connotation::negative antonym::on-guard-vs-asleep-at-the-wheel intensity::unbothered-to-unfeeling meaning::airily-unconcerned

column2:
To stop or come to an end — formal register.
To come to an end, or to bring something to an end.

Stop is the everyday word and works on anything, including a single motion — stop the car. Cease is its formal cousin, and it wants something ongoing: fire, trading, operations, breathing, rain, publication. It carries the tone of an announcement or an order — treaties, legal notices, official statements. "Cease immediately" is what an authority writes; "cut it out" is what a person says. It also leans final: things that cease tend not to resume.

Note the fixed phrase never ceases to — he never ceases to amaze me — one of the few places the word sounds casual.
⚠️ cease ≠ seize. Cease (SEES) is to stop; seize (SEEZ) is to grab. Near-opposites, one letter apart — and the spelling breaks the "i before e" rule in seize, which is why people mix them up on the page.
The de-CEASED has ceased. And in-cessant noise never does.
Both cousins point the same way: deceased is the formal word for stopped-for-good, and incessant is literally "not ceasing" — the register stays official in every one of them.
1. Trading on the exchange ceased at noon and did not resume for three days.
2. He never ceases to amaze me — third time this month he's locked himself out.
A cease and desist letter — the lawyer's opening move, telling you to stop doing the thing and never start again. And every news ceasefire: the fire ceases, the war doesn't necessarily end.
Latin cedere = "to go, to yield, to give way" → cessare, "to leave off." Yielding ground is the common thread across a big GRE family: cede (hand over), concede, recede, precede, secede, cessation, incessant, deceased.

To suppress or cut objectionable material; the official who does it.
Verb: to inspect material and cut out or suppress whatever an authority finds objectionable — obscene, seditious, or secret.
Noun: the official who does the cutting.

Censoring is suppression by power — a state, a studio, a school board, an army. It isn't editing for quality; it's removal for control. The content is made to disappear.
⚠️ censor ≠ censure.
- censor = delete the message
- censure = formally condemn the person for it

A senator can be censured. A senator's speech can be censored.
Cens*or* is an agent, like edit*or* — a man who cuts. Cens*ure* is like in*jure* — it wounds a reputation.
The censor deletes what you said; the censure is the public scolding for having said it.
1. Wartime officials censored the soldiers' letters, cutting place names out of the page before the mail went home.
2. She censored herself mid-sentence, remembering that her boss was standing right behind her.
Every time Spotify offers you the "Clean" version next to the Explicit one, you're looking at a censored track — the same song with words surgically removed.
Latin censēre = "to assess, to judge." The Roman censor was a magistrate with two jobs: take the census, and police public morals — he could strike your name off the rolls for bad conduct.

That one root gives you a family: census (counting), censor (suppressing), censure (condemning), censorious (fault-finding).

🚫 Not sensor. That's Latin sentīre, "to feel" — sense, sentiment, sentient, consent. Identical sound, unrelated word.

Formal public condemnation by an official body.
Verb: to condemn someone formally and publicly for misconduct. Noun: that condemnation itself.

Censure is criticism with institutional standing behind it — a vote, a ruling, a signed statement from a body entitled to pass judgement. Your friend can criticise you; only a board, a court, a legislature or a professional association can censure you. And it stops at words: a censured official keeps the job and the salary but wears the mark permanently. That's the scale — heavier than rebuke, more public than reprimand, one step short of expel.
⚠️ censure ≠ censor.
- censure = condemn the person
- censor = delete the message

A senator can be censured. A senator's speech can be censored.
You get censured by a body, never by a person — it takes a vote.
If nobody had to raise a hand for it, it's just criticism.
1. The committee voted to censure the judge for accepting undisclosed gifts, though it stopped short of demanding his resignation.
2. He got off with a censure — a strongly worded letter in his file and absolutely nothing else.
The word surfaces in the news almost only in one setting: the US Congress voting to censure one of its own — a formal slap on the record that carries no fine, no removal, just the permanent black mark.
Latin censēre = "to assess, to judge." One root, four GRE words: census (counting), censor (suppressing), censure (condemning), censorious (habitually fault-finding).

Intellectual rather than emotional; brainy, sometimes coldly so.
Literally of the brain; figuratively, driven by intellect rather than emotion or instinct — analytical, cool-headed, demanding thought.

Applied to a person or a work, it's admiration with a slight chill in it. A cerebral film makes you think; it doesn't make you cry. Calling a footballer cerebral means he reads the game rather than outrunning people. And it tips easily into criticism — too cerebral means bloodless, over-clever, all head and no pulse.
Visceral hits you in the guts; cerebral hits you in the brain.
Same grammar, opposite organ — and the organ tells you the temperature, since guts are hot and immediate while brains are cool and slow.
1. His novels are admired more than they are loved: cerebral, exact, and reluctant to raise their voice.
2. It's a fun match but a cerebral one — nobody's charging around, they're just picking each other apart.
Cerebral palsy — the everyday medical term that pins the root down: a condition originating in the brain, not the muscles.

Annoyed embarrassment at being humiliated or proved wrong.
The sting of wounded pride — embarrassment, annoyance and disappointment mixed together, felt when you've failed, been outdone, or been proved wrong.

Not guilt and not shame: those concern wrongdoing, while chagrin concerns dignity. Losing an argument to a junior colleague is chagrin; lying about it is shame. It's a civilised, restrained word — you rarely howl with chagrin, you swallow it — and it lives above all in the frozen phrase "much to my chagrin," where it's often faintly self-mocking.
cha-GRIN — the tight little grin you put on when you've just been shown up.
The word hides grin because chagrin is the feeling you have to smile politely through, which is exactly its restrained, pride-bruised register.
1. To the ambassador's evident chagrin, the treaty he had spent four years negotiating was rewritten in a single afternoon.
2. Much to my chagrin, the six-year-old solved the puzzle in about nine seconds.
French chagrin = grief, vexation — the same word as French chagrin, a rough granular leather (English shagreen) once used as a rasp for smoothing wood. Something that chafes: chagrin is the constant fine abrasion of a bruised ego, not a clean wound.

To publicly fight for a cause; a defender or winner.
Verb (the GRE sense): to fight publicly on behalf of a cause, person, or idea — to defend and promote it.
Noun: a winner; or a defender who fights for someone else's cause.

The verb is the one that gets tested, and the everyday "winner" sense hides it. To champion something is stronger than to support it and more active than to endorse it: you attach your name and take the hits. A senator can quietly support a bill, but the senator who champions it is the one on the floor arguing for it week after week. Always positive about the causes' defender — though the GRE cheerfully has people champion terrible causes too.
A champ fights. To champion a cause is to fight for it — not just to clap for it.
The "champ" sitting inside the word keeps the verb combative, which is exactly what separates championing from mere approving.
1. Throughout her tenure on the bench she championed the rights of defendants too poor to afford counsel.
2. He's been championing that scruffy little café for years — half the street eats there because of him.
Corporate and NGO language runs on this verb — \"we champion diversity,\" \"championing open source.\" Every time an organisation wants to sound like it's fighting for something rather than merely permitting it, it reaches for champion.
Latin campus = "field" → Late Latin campiō, "a fighter in the field." In medieval trial by combat, if you were too old, too ill, or too female to fight, you hired a champion to fight in your place — which is precisely why the verb still means to fight on someone else's behalf.

Same root: camp, campaign (originally an army taking the field), campus.

Cautious and sparing, especially about giving something up
Cautious, hesitant, unwilling to risk it — and, crucially, sparing: a chary person doesn't just watch their step, they hold something back.

The word almost always takes of or about: chary of praise, chary about commitments, chary of lending money. That construction is the tell. Where cautious describes how you move, chary describes how little you hand over — approval, information, cash, trust. It's a quiet, bookish word, and it carries a faint suggestion of stinginess that plain caution doesn't: being chary with compliments makes the compliment worth more, but also makes you look tight-fisted.
chary ≠ wary. Wary is watching for danger — eyes up, threat outside. Chary is holding back from giving — hands closed, the thing withheld. You are wary of a stranger; you are chary of trusting him with your keys.
Chary hides care — too much care to let go of it.
It's care worn as an adjective: the chary man cares so much about the praise, or the money, that he keeps it.
1. The committee was notably chary of endorsing any figure it could not independently verify.
2. He's chary with compliments — one "not bad" from him is worth a standing ovation from anyone else.
Old English cearig = "full of care, anxious" — the same caru that gives you care and careworn. Chary is simply care turned into an adjective and left to age for a thousand years, drifting from "sorrowful" to "cautious" to "sparing."

🚫 Nothing to do with charity, charisma, or cherish — those are Latin/Greek imports (carus "dear", charis "grace"). Chary is homegrown Germanic.

To scold or punish severely, from a position of authority.
To rebuke severely — and, in older or biblical use, to punish physically for a fault.

Where criticise judges the work and rebuke just checks the behaviour, chastise comes with a moral high horse. The chastiser is above you and says so: a parent, a coach, a bishop, an editorial page. It's a telling-off delivered as correction — for your own good — and the older sense of a beating still hangs faintly on it, which is why the word feels heavier than a mere scolding.
⚠️ chastise ≠ chasten.
- chastise = deliver the scolding (active, someone does it to you)
- chasten = humble someone, usually the after-effect — "a chastened manager faced the press"

You chastise a player; the player walks off chastened.
Chastise hides chaste — the punisher thinks he's purifying you, so it always comes down from above.
You chastise a child, a subordinate, or a government you disapprove of — never your boss.
1. The editorial chastised the council for approving the development without a single public hearing.
2. Mum chastised me for twenty solid minutes about the state of my room.
A newsroom staple: "chastised" is what headlines use when one powerful body publicly tells off another — "IMF chastises government over spending." If you see it, someone is being scolded from a height.
Latin castus = "pure" → castigāre, "to make pure, to correct" — punishment as purification.

Same root gives you castigate (to rip into someone verbally), chasten, chaste, chastity — and incest, literally in-castus, "not chaste."

Blindly convinced your own group beats everyone else's.
Displaying blind, boastful conviction that your own group is superior — your country, your sex, your race, your team — usually with contempt for everyone outside it.

Two flavours live in the word. The original is fanatical patriotism; the everyday modern one is male chauvinism, the assumption that men are the better sex. Either way it is not mere loyalty — a patriot loves his country, a chauvinist needs yours to be worse. The word is always an accusation, and it paints the person as smug and slightly ridiculous rather than dangerous.
SHOW-vin-istic — he shows off that his side always wins.
The showing-off is the point: chauvinism is superiority worn loudly, not quiet allegiance.
1. The editorial's chauvinistic insistence that no foreign scientist had contributed anything of note drew ridicule from every university in the country.
2. He made some chauvinistic crack about her parking, and the whole table went quiet.
"Male chauvinist pig" — the 1970s feminist insult that made the word household English. If you've heard the phrase, you already know the tone: mocking, not fearful.
From a man: Nicolas Chauvin, a soldier of Napoleon's army so grotesquely devoted to the Emperor that French vaudeville turned him into a stock comic idiot. His name became the word.

That's why the tone is absurd rather than sinister — it was born as a punchline.

column2:
To restrain or halt the progress of something.
Verb: to stop or slow the progress of something; to hold it within limits.
Noun: whatever does the restraining — a curb, a brake, a counterweight.

The GRE will not test the "examine it" or "tick the box" sense you use daily. It tests this one: she checked her anger, a check on executive power, the advance was checked at the river.

The force of the word is partial containment. Halt stops a thing dead, suppress crushes it, abolish removes it — but a checked thing is still there, still pushing, merely held. It's the word for a counterweight rather than a kill switch, which is why power is checked and impulses are kept in check rather than destroyed.
A king in check isn't captured — just cornered. That's the whole word.
Check restrains and confines; it never eliminates.
1. The treaty was designed to check Prussian ambition, not to dismantle it.
2. He wanted to snap back, but he checked himself — her father was in the room.
Checks and balances — the phrase for the whole American constitutional design. No branch is abolished; each is merely held in place by the others. That's check in its exact sense.
Persian shāh = "king", borrowed through Arabic and Old French eschec — the warning cry when a king was under threat.

One root, a surprising family: chess, checkmate (shāh māt, "the king is helpless"), exchequer (the treasury, named for the chequered counting-cloth), chequered, and cheque (a written order that checks fraud by leaving a counterfoil).

To hold dear and protect, with lasting tenderness.
To hold something dear and care for it tenderly — over time, not in a flash.

Sitting between like and love, it adds two things neither has: protectiveness and duration. You treasure a watch; you cherish the grandmother who gave it to you. It also takes abstractions — you can cherish a hope, a memory, a belief — and there the word turns faintly wistful, sometimes ironic: to cherish an illusion is to keep hugging something you should have let go of.
Look at what it takes as an object: memories, moments, people, hopes — never things you could simply buy again.
The collocations give away the nuance — cherishing is reserved for the irreplaceable, which is why it always carries a trace of fear of loss.
1. He cherished the letters long after the hand that wrote them had stilled, rereading them each winter.
2. Look, just cherish this — you'll never all be in the same room again.
The wedding vow: "to have and to hold… to love and to cherish, till death do us part." Note that it's the slow verb in the line — not passion, but a promise of ongoing care.
Old French cher = "dear" (as in ma chérie), from Latin cārus, "dear, costly."

Same root: charity (cāritas, dearness → love for others) and caress. If something is cher, it is both beloved and expensive — the word never quite forgets the price of losing it.

Sly trickery — winning by loopholes and quibbles, not force.
Trickery — specifically the clever, fiddly, technically-legal kind: deception through loopholes, quibbles, procedural sleight-of-hand and fine print.

Scale matters. A mugging isn't chicanery; a contract clause buried on page 40 is. It implies cunning rather than force, and usually a professional setting where the rules themselves are the weapon — lawyers, politicians, accountants, election officials. The word carries a dry, faintly amused contempt: you say it about someone who won, but disgracefully.
Chicanery starts like chic — it's trickery in a good suit.
Nothing crude or violent about it: the chicaner wins by being slick, technical and hard to pin down.
1. The judge dismissed the filing as procedural chicanery designed to run out the clock rather than to argue the case.
2. Three hidden fees and an auto-renewal? That's not a deal, that's chicanery.
In Formula 1, a chicane is that tight artificial S-bend bolted onto a straight to stop cars going flat out — same word, and it's literally a swerve to get around something. Chicanery is a chicane through the rules.
French chicaner = "to quibble, to wrangle over legal niceties." The legal flavour never washed out — that's why chicanery still smells of courtrooms and small print rather than street crime.

column2:
Gallant and honourable, in the old knightly way.
Courteous, gallant and honourable — behaving with the courage, generosity and protectiveness of an ideal knight, especially toward someone weaker or toward women.

Polite is about manners; chivalrous is about a code. It carries self-sacrifice — giving up the seat, the coat, the advantage — and it always looks slightly backdated, which is why it's so often used with a wink ("very chivalrous of you"). Praise, but praise with a period costume on.
⚠️ chivalrous ≠ cavalier. Both grew out of the word for horse, and they ended up opposites: chivalrous = gallant and considerate; cavalier = airily dismissive, treating serious things as trifles. The knight on the horse became a gentleman in one word and a snob in the other.
It starts with shiv — a chivalrous man would take the shiv for you.
The sound hook fixes the key part of the meaning: not mere politeness, but taking the hit on someone else's behalf.
1. Their surrender was met with chivalrous treatment: the officers kept their swords, and the wounded were carried out first.
2. He walked her to her car at 2am, which was chivalrous, though mostly he just wanted to keep talking.
The stock complaint "chivalry is dead" — muttered whenever nobody holds a door or gives up a seat — is this word's everyday afterlife.
French cheval = horse → chevalier, a horseman, i.e. a knight → chivalry, the knight's code. Only rich men had horses, so the horse-word became the class-word became the manners-word.

Same root, whole family: cavalry (horse soldiers), cavalier, chevalier, Spanish caballero.

Rude and ungracious, especially in the face of kindness.
Rude, surly and ungracious — especially in response to someone else's kindness or generosity.

Churlish isn't loud rudeness or aggression; it's meanness of spirit on a small scale — the grudging thanks, the sulky refusal, the petty complaint about a free gift. Where rude describes an act and surly describes a mood, churlish passes judgement on your character: you were given something and you couldn't rise to it. Note also where it lives — the word is most at home in the negative, conceding a point: it would be churlish not to admit she was right.
Churlish is a churl's answer to a kindness — small, sour and ungrateful, never grand.
Listen for its favourite frame, "it would be churlish to refuse" — the word exists to name bad grace in the face of generosity, not open hostility.
1. Given how much the committee had conceded already, it would be churlish to press them further.
2. He mumbled a churlish thanks and shoved the present under the sofa without opening it.
Shakespeare, As You Like It — the exiled Duke endures "the icy fang / And churlish chiding of the winter's wind." The wind isn't violent, just meanly ungenerous; that's the exact temperature of the word.
Old English ceorl = a churl, the lowest rank of free peasant. The aristocracy did this constantly: take a class label, turn it into a character flaw. Villain ← villein (a farm serf), boor ← a farmer, vulgar ← the common crowd, ignoble ← not of noble birth. Learn the pattern and four GRE words come free.

Same Germanic root as Karl / Charles, which simply meant "free man."

To restrict within firm, externally set limits.
To draw a boundary around something and thereby restrict it — to fix the limits of a power, a role, a freedom, a life.

Where limit is plain and restrict is practical, circumscribe is the formal, almost legal word for limits imposed from outside and in advance: a constitution circumscribes a president's powers; poverty circumscribes a childhood. It doesn't claim the limits are unfair — only that they are firm, external, and define the whole permitted space. In geometry it keeps its literal job: to draw a figure around another so it just touches.
⚠️ circumscribe ≠ circumvent.
- circumscribe = draw the boundary — this far and no further
- circumvent = get around the boundary — slip past the rule

A law circumscribes what you may do. A loophole lets you circumvent it.
The circle is drawn around you — you don't get to draw it.
Circumscribed powers, roles and lives are hemmed in by something external — a charter, a class, a disease — not by the person's own choosing.
1. The treaty sharply circumscribed the monarch's authority, leaving him a crown and very little else.
2. After the injury her world got circumscribed to one room and a flight of stairs she couldn't manage.
School geometry: the circumscribed circle drawn around a triangle so it touches all three corners — the outer limit of the shape, made visible.
Latin circum (around) + scrībere (to write, to draw) — literally to draw a line around.

Scrībere is a GRE workhorse: describe (write down), inscribe (write into), prescribe (write beforehand — the doctor's order), proscribe (write off — outlaw), transcribe, subscribe, scripture.

column2:
Cautious and watchful; weighing consequences before acting.
Cautious and watchful; unwilling to act or speak until the risks and consequences have been weighed.

The caution is calculated, not nervous. Timid and wary suggest fear; circumspect suggests judgement — the person has surveyed the situation and is deliberately holding back. It's a compliment in the mouth of a lawyer, banker or diplomat, and only mildly a criticism elsewhere (too circumspect = too slow to commit). Register is formal; you write it, you rarely shout it.
Circumspect people look all the way round the corner before they turn it — held back by calculation, not by nerves.
The circle is the full sweep of consequences they check first, which is why the word praises judgement rather than diagnosing fear.
1. The board was circumspect in its statement, conceding the loss without naming a single executive responsible for it.
2. Be a bit more circumspect about what you post — that account isn't as private as you think.
Cricket commentary lives on this word: a batter playing a circumspect innings is leaving deliveries and refusing the big shot — not scared, just pricing the risk of each ball.
Latin circum (around) + specere (to look) — literally looking around you before you move.

Both halves pay off across the GRE: circum- gives circumference, circumvent, circumscribe, circumlocution; -spect gives inspect, prospect, retrospect, conspicuous, perspicacious.

column2:
Indirect — inferred from surrounding facts, not directly proven.
Depending on circumstances rather than on direct proof — and so, of evidence, indirect: it points to a conclusion by inference instead of demonstrating it.

A second, quieter sense: incidental, not essential (circumstantial details of a plan). A third, older one runs the opposite way — a circumstantial account means one crammed with particulars.

The word almost always carries a downgrade. Calling a case circumstantial concedes that nobody saw it happen; the facts sit around the crime, fitting it neatly, without ever touching it. Note the strange tension the word holds: circumstantial evidence can be abundant, minute and utterly convincing — and still, by definition, unwitnessed.
Substantial evidence stands under the claim and holds it up; circumstantial evidence only stands around it.
Both words are built on Latin stare, "to stand" — the prefix decides whether the facts support the conclusion or merely surround it.
1. The prosecution's case was wholly circumstantial: a receipt, a tyre track, and a man who could not say where he had been.
2. Look, they saw his car outside — that's circumstantial, it doesn't prove he did anything.
The stock line of every courtroom drama and true-crime podcast: "It's all circumstantial." Said by a defence lawyer, it means you can't prove it; said by a juror, it usually means but we all know.
Latin circum (around) + stare (to stand) → circumstantia, "the things standing around" — the surroundings of an act.

Both halves pay off elsewhere: circum- gives circumvent, circumscribe, circumspect, circumference; stare gives substantial, status, stance, stationary.

Loudly, insistently noisy — a crowd demanding something.
Loud and noisy — specifically the noise of many voices making a demand: protest, complaint, insistence.

The demand is what separates it from its neighbours. Raucous is rowdy for fun; strident is one harsh voice; vociferous is loud and forceful but can be a single person; clamorous is a mass of noise pressing for something — a crowd at the gates, the press outside a courthouse, a room of hands in the air. Mildly disapproving: the speaker usually finds the din excessive, even when the cause is fair. It extends to non-human noise (clamorous gulls, clamorous bells) and to metaphor (clamorous demands for reform).
clamorous ≠ calamitous. Clamorous = deafeningly noisy. Calamitous = disastrous. A clamorous meeting is merely loud; a calamitous one ends careers.
Clamorous ≈ claim-orous — a crowd that isn't just loud, it's claiming something.
Same Latin root as claim, and it pins the nuance: clamorous noise always has a demand inside it.
1. The gallery grew clamorous as the verdict was read, and the judge threatened to clear the room.
2. Ten minutes into the outage the support channel was clamorous — everyone shouting the same question at once.
British news writes it constantly in noun form: "a growing clamour for the minister's resignation." Nobody ever clamours quietly — the word only comes out when a crowd wants something.
Latin clāmāre = "to shout." It hands you a whole shelf of words: claim (shout that it's yours), exclaim, proclaim (shout forth), acclaim (shout for), declaim, reclaim — and clamour itself, the shouting of many.

🚫 Not glamorous. That's Scots glamour, a corruption of grammar (once meaning occult learning). One letter apart, no relation.
