column2:
Secret and organised — hidden because it isn't allowed.
Kept secret, hidden, concealed — especially something organised and deliberately hidden because it isn't allowed.

The word almost always carries a whiff of illegitimacy: clandestine meetings, affairs, labs, cells, operations. It describes a planned activity, not a personality — which is what separates it from furtive, which describes manner (a furtive glance, shifty and nervous). Covert is the neutral, official term an agency would use about itself; clandestine is what the newspaper calls it afterwards. Nobody runs a clandestine bake sale.
CLANdestine — a clan meeting after dark, doors bolted, nobody told.
The hidden word gives you the key nuance: this is group secrecy, planned and conspiratorial, not one person looking shifty.
1. The pamphlets were printed at a clandestine press in the cellar of a bookshop, three streets from the censor's office.
2. They'd been dating for months — very clandestine, separate cars, separate entrances, the whole thing.
The CIA's spy branch was literally called the National Clandestine Service — the officers who run deniable operations abroad, as opposed to the analysts at desks.
Latin clam = "secretly", kin to celāre, "to hide" — the same root under conceal and (via cella, a hidden room) cell and cellar.
column3: g11 register::formal connotation::negative antonym::hidden-vs-out-in-the-open connotation::secrecy-that-implies-guilt intensity::degrees-of-concealment meaning::hidden-from-view:-the-act-the-manner-the

column2:
A loud, harsh, ringing din of metal on metal.
A loud, harsh, ringing noise — metal striking metal, and going on for a while: bells, hammers, alarms, armour, machinery.

Din and racket are generic; clangor is specifically resonant and metallic, a sound with a ring in its tail. It's also a literary word — nobody complains about the clangor of their neighbours, they complain about the noise. Writers reach for it when they want the reader to hear the sound, and it usually carries a hint of the industrial or the martial.
⚠️ clangor ≠ clamor. Clangor is metal ringing; clamor is voices shouting. A crowd clamors; the bells above it clangor.
Clang + -or: a clang that keeps going.
The word wears its own sound effect on the front, and the suffix stretches one strike into a sustained metallic din.
1. The retreat was sounded, and the valley filled with the clangor of bells from every church still standing.
2. I woke at six to the clangor of someone unloading the dishwasher like it owed them money.
Poe's The Bells stacks both words in a single line — "In the clamor and the clangor of the bells!" — the alarm-bell stanza, all iron and panic.
Latin clangere = "to resound", used of trumpets and clashing metal — imitative, the Romans heard the same noise you do.

The useful part is what it is not: clamor comes from clamare, "to cry out" — the root behind claim, exclaim, proclaim, claimant. Metal clangs; mouths claim.
column3: g05 register::literary connotation::negative antonym::kinds-of-loud-kinds-of-quiet intensity::soft-to-deafening meaning::harsh-clashing-sound

column2:
To hide or disguise something by covering it over.
Noun: a loose sleeveless outer garment that hangs from the shoulders.
Verb (the GRE sense): to cover, hide, or disguise — to wrap something so it passes unseen.

To cloak is concealment by covering, never by destruction: the thing is still there, just draped. That's the difference from erase or suppress. It also carries a whiff of motive — you cloak greed in the language of duty, cloak a takeover as a merger — so it usually points at a gap between the surface and what's underneath. Slightly literary in tone; a report will say concealed, a novelist will say cloaked.
Cloak rhymes with smoke — and smoke hides what's behind it without removing a thing.
Cloaking is a screen laid over something that still exists, which is why the word so often implies a truth waiting to be uncovered.
1. The regime cloaked its purges in the vocabulary of reform, calling each arrest a "procedural review."
2. He tried to cloak the fact that he'd forgotten her birthday by acting mysterious about a "surprise."
Harry Potter's Invisibility Cloak — the garment whose entire job is to hide what's still standing right in front of you.
From Medieval Latin clocca = "bell" — the early travelling cloak hung in a wide bell shape from the shoulders.

Same bell root gives you clock (which began as a bell that struck the hour) and the cloche — the bell-shaped hat, and the glass dome over a dessert.

sweet or sentimental to the point of sickening
So sweet, rich, or sentimental that it becomes sickening — pleasure that curdles from too much of itself.

The word is only ever an insult, and it carries a physical aftertaste: the third slice of cake, perfume that fills the lift, a film that keeps telling you to cry. Sweetness alone isn't cloying — excess without a break is. Note the built-in time signature: something becomes cloying, usually after it was briefly pleasant.
Cloying rhymes with annoying — sweetness that stays until it annoys.
The rhyme carries the whole nuance: the problem isn't the sugar, it's the not stopping.
1. The novel's final chapter dissolves into cloying sentiment, as though the author distrusted his readers to feel anything unprompted.
2. Her Christmas playlist is fine for a day, but by the fourth of January it's just cloying.
It's a staple of film criticism — the standard word reviewers reach for when a movie's emotional score, voiceover, and slow-motion hugs are all working on you at once.
From cloy, older sense "to clog, to block up" — via Old French encloer, from Latin clavus = "nail." To cloy a gun was to nail its touch-hole shut.

That's the useful image: cloying sweetness clogs. Same clavus gives you clove — the spice literally named for looking like a little nail.

column2:
A bunch of similar things packed close together.
Noun: a number of similar things bunched close together — grapes, stars, houses, cases of a disease.
Verb: to gather or grow in such a bunch (fans clustered around the exit).

What the word insists on is proximity, not organisation. A group can be defined by anything (interests, membership); a cluster is defined by things sitting near each other in space, time, or data. That makes it the scientist's word of choice — a cluster of infections, cluster analysis, a globular cluster — because it reports a concentration without claiming a cause. On the GRE it usually turns up as the neutral verb for "crowd together tightly."
⚠️ cluster ≠ clutter. A cluster is things packed together (a cluster of berries); clutter is things strewn about in a mess (a cluttered desk). Concentration versus disorder.
A cluster is a clot — stuff stuck in one lump, by nearness, not by plan.
Cluster and clot really are cousins, and "clot" captures the key idea: a dense lump that formed by things simply ending up next to each other.
1. Epidemiologists identified a cluster of infections within three streets of the water pump.
2. Everyone clustered round the one guy with a phone charger.
In tech it's a job-title-level word: a Kubernetes / Azure cluster is a heap of machines wired close enough to behave like one — proximity doing the work, exactly as the word says.
Old English clyster, a bunch — kin to clot. Both mean a lump of things stuck together, which is the whole word in one image.

To merge gradually into a single unified whole.
To come together and merge into one whole — droplets, factions, ideas, a plan.

The key is that the parts stop being separate. A crowd gathers and stays a crowd of individuals; things that coalesce fuse, and you can no longer pick out what went in. It's also gradual and usually unforced — nobody coalesces things, they coalesce. That's why it fits mercury beads, rival factions, and half-formed thoughts equally well, and why "the committee coalesced the reports" sounds wrong: use merged or combined when there's an agent doing the joining.
⚠️ coalesce ≠ convalesce.
- coalesce = separate things grow together
- convalesce = a sick person gets better (recuperate)

Factions coalesce; patients convalesce.
-esce = gradually becoming: adol*esce*nt, conval*esce*, coal*esce*. Never a snap — always a process.
That Latin -esc- ending marks a slow becoming, which is exactly the nuance: coalescing is drift and fusion over time, not an instant merger.
1. Over three decades the scattered guilds coalesced into a single national union.
2. Give me a day — the idea's still bits and pieces, it hasn't coalesced yet.
Election-night newsreading: when a primary field thins, commentators say the party is coalescing around a frontrunner — the rivals' support pooling into one bloc.
Latin com- ("together") + alescere ("to grow up"), from alere, "to nourish."

Same root: coalition (groups grown together), adolescent (still growing up), alimony (money to nourish), aliment. Coalition is the giveaway — a coalition is literally what coalescing produces.

To over-protect someone into softness.
To treat someone with exaggerated tenderness — shielding them from difficulty, effort, or consequences. (Literal sense, still in use: to cook an egg in water kept deliberately just below the boil.)

Pamper is about luxuries; coddle is about protection. You coddle by removing the hard thing — and the word carries the built-in accusation that the removal has made the person soft. It's a judgement, almost always spoken by someone who disapproves: no parent describes their own parenting as coddling. Typical objects are children, star players, and employees.
A coddled egg never meets a rolling boil — and neither does a coddled person.
The cooking sense is the whole word: heat kept low on purpose, so nothing ever toughens.
1. The report argued that the regulator had coddled the banks for a decade, treating every warning sign as a matter for private conversation rather than penalty.
2. Stop coddling him — he's twenty-six, he can call the landlord himself.
The Coddling of the American Mind — Lukianoff and Haidt's much-argued-about 2018 book on over-protected students. The title is the definition: protect people from every discomfort and you leave them less able to handle any.

Forcing someone by threat or pressure rather than persuasion.
Making someone act against their will by threat, pressure, or intimidation — force applied to the decision, not necessarily to the body.

The key is that the victim still "chooses" — they sign, they confess, they hand over the money — but the choice was hollowed out beforehand. That makes coercion colder and more procedural than bullying and far more formal than arm-twisting; it is a word with legal teeth (a contract signed under coercion is void). In political theory it can be neutral, even technical — "the state's monopoly on coercion" — but in ordinary use it is an accusation.
Coerce rhymes with worse — "do it, or things get worse."
Coercion is the threat hanging over the choice, not the blow itself.
1. The tribunal ruled that the testimony had been obtained by coercion and struck it from the record.
2. They didn't fire him — they just made it clear he'd never get another shift, which is coercion with better manners.
Every courtroom scene where a confession gets thrown out: nobody was beaten, the suspect was simply worn down and threatened until signing was the only way out — that's coercion, and it's why the evidence dies.
Latin co- (together) + arcēre (to fence in, shut off) — to hem someone in until only one option is left. That's the meaning exactly: coercion narrows the fence, it doesn't throw the punch.

Same root arcēre gives exercise (ex-arcēre, to drive out, keep at work) and arcane (shut away, hidden).

Clear and logically forceful — an argument that compels agreement.
Of an argument, case, or explanation: clear, logical, and forceful enough to compel agreement.

The praise lands on the reasoning, not the speaker. Eloquent is about style, persuasive is about effect — a con man can be both. Cogent says the logic itself holds: tight, well-evidenced, hard to answer. It's cool, formal praise, the kind a judge, examiner, or peer reviewer gives — and its negative is quietly brutal, because "no cogent explanation was offered" means the reasoning was not merely unconvincing but structurally empty.
A cogent argument has cogs — it's a machine that drives you to the conclusion.
The gears mesh: each step turns the next, so you're moved along by the mechanism rather than talked into it.
1. The dissent was the more cogent opinion: fifteen pages, no rhetoric, every claim carrying its own evidence.
2. He talked for ten minutes and never made one cogent point.
Standard courtroom and peer-review currency — judgments regularly say a party \"advanced no cogent reason,\" which is a polite way of saying the argument had nothing under it.
Latin cogere = "to drive together, to compel" (co- together + agere to drive). A cogent argument literally forces you along — the same agere behind agent, agenda, agile, act, exact, agitate.

🚫 Nothing to do with cognition. That's cognoscere, "to know" — recognise, cognizant, incognito. Cogent isn't about being knowledgeable; it's about being irresistible.

column2:
To think something over long and hard.
To think hard about something; to turn a matter over in the mind, deliberately and at length.

Plain thinking is what everyone does; cogitating is thinking with the effort showing. The word is heavy, Latinate, and faintly pompous — which is why it's so often used tongue-in-cheek, about someone staring at the ceiling doing nothing visible. Used straight, it suggests slow, sustained deliberation rather than a flash of insight; you cogitate on a problem for a week, you don't cogitate for a second.
Cogitate — the cogs are visibly turning.
It's not quick thought but grinding, laborious machinery of thought — which is exactly why the word so easily turns comic.
1. The committee cogitated for three months and produced a report recommending further cogitation.
2. He's been cogitating over which laptop to buy since March — just pick one.
Descartes' _cogito ergo sum_ — "I think, therefore I am." Cogito is literally this verb in the first person.
Latin cogitāre = "to think", from co- (together) + agitāre (to drive, to turn over) — thoughts churned around in the head.

That agitāre gives you agitate, agitator, and (via agere, to drive) agent, agenda, exigent.

Hanging together; logically consistent; intelligible.
Hanging together — the parts fit, so the whole makes sense. Of an argument, plan or story: logically consistent, no gaps or contradictions. Of a person: able to speak intelligibly.

Watch the two very different bars it sets. Applied to thinking, coherent is usually the floor, not the ceiling — "a coherent strategy" quietly implies the rival strategy is a mess, and "coherent" alone is faint praise for an essay that is organised but says nothing. Applied to a speaker, it drops lower still: "she was barely coherent" means drunk, concussed, or half-asleep. It's about the parts holding together, never about whether the thing is true — a conspiracy theory can be perfectly coherent.
⚠️ coherent ≠ cohesive.
- coherent = makes logical sense (an argument, a sentence)
- cohesive = sticks together as a unit (a team, a mixture, a paragraph's flow)

A cohesive team can still produce an incoherent plan.
Co-HERE — every part stayed here, together; nothing wandered off on its own.
Incoherence is bits of thought scattering in different directions, so coherence is simply all of them holding one position.
1. The dissertation was elegantly written but never assembled itself into a coherent argument.
2. He'd been awake for thirty hours and couldn't string together a coherent sentence.
A laser is just coherent light — ordinary bulbs throw waves out every which way, a laser gets them all in step, which is why the beam holds a straight line across a room instead of scattering.
Latin cohaerēre = "to stick together" (com- "together" + haerēre "to stick, to cling").

That haerēre is worth banking: adhere / adhesive (stick to), inherent (sticking inside, inseparable), cohesion, and — the one nobody expects — hesitate, literally to be stuck fast, unable to move on.

To invent a word or phrase that catches on.
Verb (the sense the GRE tests): to invent a word, phrase or name and put it into circulation. Noun: a stamped piece of metal money.

The verb is narrow in a way invent and devise are not: you coin language, not machines or plans. It also carries a quiet claim of authorship — saying Freud coined "id" credits him with the term and implies the term caught on. Nobody coins a word that nobody else ever uses; a failed one is just a made-up word.

The literal metal sense survives in coinage, which does double duty: money, and a newly minted word.
Coin a word the way a mint coins money: stamp it fresh, then let it circulate.
Both senses hang on one idea — something new is struck into existence and then passes from hand to hand.
1. Orwell coined "doublethink" in 1949, and the term has outlived the novel that carried it.
2. My sister coined "hangry" for our family years before the internet got hold of it.
People say "to coin a phrase" right before uttering a cliché — a joke about pretending to have just invented something everyone has said a thousand times.
Latin cuneus = "wedge" — the wedge-shaped die that stamped the metal. The die's name became the money's name, and the money's name became the verb.

Same root: cuneiform (wedge-shaped writing), quoin / coign (a cornerstone, a wedge).

Work jointly with someone — or with the enemy.
To work jointly with others on a shared piece of work — a paper, an album, a project.

The second sense is the one the GRE cares about: to cooperate traitorously with an enemy occupying your country. Same word, no separate spelling. The mayor collaborated in peacetime is praise; the mayor collaborated under occupation is an accusation of treason — and collaborator carries that stain even more strongly than the verb. Context alone decides which sense you're reading, so watch for war, occupation, or resistance nearby.
⚠️ collaborate ≠ corroborate.
- collaborate = work with someone
- corroborate = confirm someone's account with evidence

A witness who corroborates your alibi supports it; a witness who collaborates with you helped commit the crime.
Co-labour. Every collaborator labours alongside someone — the only question is whose side.
The word itself is morally blank, which is exactly why it can mean both a co-author and a traitor.
1. Historians still argue over how many officials actively collaborated with the occupying regime, and how many merely complied.
2. We collaborated on the deck for about three hours and honestly she did most of it.
Every "feat." credit on Spotify is a collab — the shortening is so ordinary that the war sense catches people completely off guard on the exam.
Latin com- (together) + laborare (to work), from labor (toil).

That root spreads wide: labour, laboratory (a workroom), elaborate (worked out in detail), belabour (to keep working at something past the point of use).

To secretly cooperate with someone for a dishonest purpose.
To cooperate secretly with someone for a dishonest, fraudulent, or illegal purpose.

You cannot collude alone: the word requires two or more insiders and a victim outside the arrangement. Where conspire suggests a plot with a target and a plan, collude suggests a quiet understanding — often between parties who are supposed to be rivals or independent: two bidders on the same contract, an auditor and the firm he audits, a landlord and the "independent" surveyor. It's the vocabulary of regulators and courts rather than thrillers, which is why it sounds coldly damning: no smoke-filled room needed, just a nod.
co- needs a partner, -lude means they're playing — collusion is a game two people play on a third.
The prefix tells you it takes at least two, and the lud- tells you someone outside the deal is being played.
1. The commission found that the three suppliers had colluded for a decade, carving the market into territories and never underbidding one another.
2. You two colluded on this, didn't you? Nobody books the same terrible restaurant twice by accident.
"No collusion" — Trump's endlessly repeated line through the Russia investigation put the noun into every news bulletin for two straight years.
Latin com- (together) + lūdere (to play) → collūdere, "to play along together."

That lud-/lus- root is a GRE goldmine, and every member keeps the sense of play: prelude and interlude (played before/between), ludicrous (fit only for play), delude (play someone false), elude (play your way out), allude (play toward a thing without naming it), illusion (a trick of play).

Formal courtesy and mutual respect between rival states or institutions.
Courteous, respectful conduct between parties who are under no obligation to be nice to each other — states, courts, chambers of a legislature. In law, comity of nations is one jurisdiction voluntarily honouring another's laws or rulings out of mutual respect rather than legal duty.

This is procedural politeness, not warmth. Comity is what stops rivals from wrecking each other's business: restraint, deference, the observed form. It's a structural virtue — it belongs to institutions and their dealings, so you praise the comity of the Senate, never the comity of your flatmate.
⚠️ comity ≠ amity.
- amity = actual friendship, genuine goodwill
- comity = the courtesies exchanged, whether or not the goodwill is there

Two nations can maintain perfect comity while sharing no amity at all.
Comity is what keeps a committee from becoming a brawl.
The sound hook carries the nuance too — it's the formal courtesy of bodies and institutions, not private affection.
1. Out of comity, the French court enforced the American judgment though no treaty compelled it.
2. There's no comity left on that board — they cut each other's mics now.
Political commentary reaches for it constantly: every piece mourning "the collapse of comity in the Senate" means the handshake norms are gone — not the friendships.
Latin comis = "courteous, obliging" → comitas, courtesy.

🚫 Nothing to do with comedy (Greek kōmōidia, "revel-song") or committee (from commit). Three unrelated words that happen to look alike.

To begin — formally, officially, or ceremonially.
To begin — but with an air of formality, procedure, or ceremony.

Begin and start are neutral workhorses; commence wears a suit. It belongs to proceedings, hostilities, trials, terms, and rituals — things with an official starting point that someone declares. Use it of a hearing or a countdown and it sounds right; use it of eating your sandwich and you sound pompous (which is exactly why it's often used as a joke). It also implies a first beginning, not a resumption.
Commence is begin in a gown — which is why graduation is called commencement.
The word only ever shows up where there's a podium, a robe, or a rulebook.
1. Proceedings will commence at nine sharp, and latecomers will not be admitted to the chamber.
2. Right, everyone's here — let the chaos commence.
American universities call graduation commencement — not the end of your degree, but the official beginning of everything after it. The whole ceremony is the word's definition acted out.
Latin com- (intensive) + initiare = "to initiate, begin" — the same initiare behind initial, initiate, initiative. So commence is literally "to initiate," which is why it never quite loses its ceremonial edge.

Proportionate — matched in scale, size, or degree to something else.
In proportion to something else — matching it in size, degree, or quality. Almost always followed by with (or sometimes to).

It isn't a synonym for equal. Equal things are the same amount; commensurate things are on the same scale — the punishment fits the crime, the pay fits the experience, the effort fits the reward. So the word carries a quiet judgement of fairness: saying a sentence was not commensurate with the offence is an accusation. It's formal, faintly bureaucratic, and lives in contracts, job ads, and sentencing remarks rather than in conversation.
commensurate ≠ commiserate. Commensurate = proportionate (measure). Commiserate = to share someone's misery, to sympathise (misery). Your bonus is commensurate with your sales; your friend commiserates when it turns out to be nothing.
com-MENSUR-ate = co-measured — the two things read the same on the same ruler.
The word has measure hiding in the middle of it, and the co- insists there must be two things being measured against each other — which is why it never stands alone but drags a "with" behind it.
1. The court held that a decade in prison was in no way commensurate with the theft of a bicycle.
2. They want ten years' experience and offer an intern's wage — the salary is hardly commensurate with the job.
Every job ad that ends \"salary commensurate with experience\" — HR code for we'll decide once we've seen you.
Latin com- ("together") + mensura ("a measuring"), from metiri, "to measure."

That root pays out widely: measure, dimension, mensuration, immense (literally un-measurable — too big to measure), and menstrual (a monthly measure).

To share in someone's misery, sympathising as a fellow sufferer.
To express sympathy or sorrow with someone over their misfortune — to share in their bad luck out loud.

The word is horizontal, not vertical. You console someone from a position of strength and you pity them from above, but you commiserate as a fellow sufferer — same layoff, same lost match, same terrible manager. It also carries a faint social warmth: commiserating usually means talking, often over a drink, and it fixes nothing by design. Note the grammar, which encodes the meaning: you commiserate with a person, over or about the disaster.
⚠️ commiserate ≠ commensurate.
- commiserate (kuh-MIZ-uh-rayt) = share in someone's misery
- commensurate (kuh-MEN-suh-rit) = proportionate, in measure with — "a salary commensurate with experience"

Same prefix, different second half: miser (wretched) vs mensura (measure).
Co-miser-ate — there's a miser in the middle, and the two of you are equally poor in luck.
The co- is load-bearing: you climb down into the misery beside them rather than dispensing comfort from above, which is why the word almost always takes with.
1. After the verdict, the defence team retired to a back room to commiserate over eighteen months of wasted work.
2. We spent the entire train ride home commiserating about our boss.
British sport and quiz shows run on the pairing "congratulations or commiserations" — the winner gets one, the loser gets the other. That stock phrase is the whole meaning in a word: what you say to the person who just lost.
Latin com- (with) + miser (wretched, pitiable) — literally to be wretched together.

That root pays out widely: misery, miserable, miserly (a miser is, etymologically, a wretch), and the Miserere psalm — "have mercy."

So convincing or gripping you can't resist it.
Adj.: so convincing, or so gripping, that you can't resist it — either an argument you can't refute or a story you can't put down.

Two lanes, same force. Compelling evidence leaves no room to disagree; a compelling film leaves no room to look away. Either way the word implies pressure: a merely persuasive argument invites you to agree, a compelling one gives you no honest alternative. Strong praise, and slightly more objective-sounding than fascinating — it says the power is in the thing, not in your taste.

There is also a plainer legal/formal use — a compelling reason = one that genuinely forces the decision (as in "compelling state interest").
⚠️ compelling ≠ compulsive.
- compelling = irresistible to others (a compelling case)
- compulsive = driven by an urge within (a compulsive liar)

A compulsive liar can't stop; a compelling liar can't be doubted.
Compelling has compel sitting inside it — it doesn't ask you, it drives you.
If you can shrug it off, it wasn't compelling.
1. The prosecution assembled a compelling case: three witnesses, a dated receipt, and CCTV footage timed to the minute.
2. I meant to watch one episode, but it was so compelling I lost the whole night.
It's the default word on every book jacket and streaming blurb — "a compelling read," "compelling television." Critics reach for it precisely because it praises the grip, not just the quality.
Latin com- (intensive) + pellere = "to drive, to push." Literally to drive someone into it.

That root drives a whole GRE family: propel (drive forward), expel (drive out), repel (drive back), dispel (drive apart — dispel a rumour), impel (drive on), compulsion, pulse.

Adequately skilled — good enough, rarely more than that.
Having the skill or qualification to do something properly — able to meet the standard required.

Watch the ceiling built into it. Competent certifies that nothing went wrong; it never says anything went well. Call a surgeon skilled and you're praising her; call her competent and you've only confirmed she shouldn't be struck off. Reviewers weaponise this — "a competent thriller" means dull but functional.

It also has a hard legal sense with no faint praise in it at all: legally fit or authorised. A defendant competent to stand trial, a witness competent to testify, a court of competent jurisdiction — there it means qualified, full stop.
Competent = fit to compete — in the race, but not winning it.
The word literally hides compete, which is exactly the level it grants you: qualified to be on the field, never described as the best on it.
1. The tribunal ruled that she was competent to manage her own financial affairs.
2. The food was competent — nothing was wrong with it, and nothing was worth ordering twice.
Anyone who's had a performance review knows this one: "competent" in the box means meets expectations — the polite ceiling right below "strong" and just above trouble.
Latin competere = "to come together, be suitable" — com- (together) + petere (to seek, aim at, rush toward).

petere is a GRE workhorse: petition (seek formally), appetite (seek toward), impetus (rush into), perpetual (seeking on and on), centripetal (seeking the centre) — and compete, the same word as competent, which drifted from "coincide, be fit" to "rival."

Smugly satisfied — pleased enough to stop trying.
Smugly satisfied with how things are — so pleased with yourself or your situation that you stop checking, stop improving, stop worrying.

The word always carries a warning inside it: the danger you've stopped noticing is still there. Content is a compliment and satisfied is neutral, but complacent is a rebuke — it says your comfort is unearned, or at least unwise. Note the two flavours: complacent about a threat (the ignored risk) and complacent in success (the champion who stops training).
⚠️ complacent ≠ complaisant.
- complacent = pleased with yourself
- complaisant (kuhm-PLAY-zuhnt) = eager to please others; obliging to a fault

A complacent host thinks the party is going brilliantly; a complaisant host will fetch you anything you ask for.
Com-PLEASE-ant — so pleased with yourself you've gone placid.
The middle of the word is pleased, and its cousin placid supplies the rest of the meaning: pleased into stillness, which is exactly when things go wrong.
1. Two decades of unchallenged dominance had made the firm complacent, and it never saw the smaller rival coming.
2. We were 3–0 up at half time and got complacent — ended up drawing.
Corporate and sporting cliché you've heard a hundred times: "there's no room for complacency." Nobody ever says it about a team that's losing — it's the thing you warn winners about.
Latin complacēre = "to please greatly" (com- intensive + placēre, "to please").

That root is worth banking: placid (calm), placate and implacable (impossible to soothe), placebo (literally "I shall please"), complaisant, and plain please.

Completing each other; each part supplies what the other lacks.
Serving to complete something; combining so that each part supplies what the other lacks.

Two complementary things are not alike — they're interlocking. Compatible people merely get along; complementary people cover each other's gaps, and neither is whole alone. That's why it's the standard word for a good partnership ("complementary skills") and for exact technical pairings: complementary angles sum to 90°, complementary colours sit opposite on the wheel, complementary DNA strands pair base for base.
⚠️ complementary ≠ complimentary.
- compl*e*mentary = completes the other thing
- compl*i*mentary = praising, or free of charge

The hotel gives you a complimentary breakfast. The eggs and the coffee are complementary.
Compl-E-mentary hides complete; compl-I-mentary hides I like it.
The E-word fills a gap, the I-word pays a compliment — one spelling letter decides which.
1. The two ministers brought complementary strengths to the negotiation: one commanded the detail, the other the room.
2. They're a weirdly complementary pair — he can't cook, she can't drive, so it works.
Every action-film poster is orange-and-teal — the two complementary colours on the wheel, chosen because skin tones pop hardest against their opposite.
Latin complēre = "to fill up." Fill something up and it is complete; the thing that does the filling is the complement.

Same root gives replete (filled again, stuffed), deplete (un-filled), plenty, plenary.

To do what a rule, order, or demand requires.
To act as a rule, order, or request demands — to do the thing you've been told to do.

The word is cool and impersonal. Obey is personal and can sound childlike or servile; comply is what you do with a regulation, a subpoena, a safety standard, a police instruction. It says nothing about whether you agree — plenty of compliance is grudging, and the noun compliance often carries a faint whiff of box-ticking. It also implies the demand came from somewhere with power: you never comply with a suggestion from an equal.
⚠️ compliant ≠ complacent.
- compliant = yielding, doing as told
- complacent = smugly pleased with yourself, dangerously unworried

A compliant employee follows the rules; a complacent one stops checking whether they still work.
You obey a person; you comply with a rule.
Comply almost never takes a person as its object — the "with" pulls in an impersonal authority, which is exactly why the word feels bureaucratic rather than submissive.
1. The firm was fined heavily after failing to comply with disclosure rules for three consecutive quarters.
2. Just comply for now — argue about the policy after we're out of the building.
The mandatory annual compliance training every office makes you click through — anti-bribery, data handling, harassment. Nobody's persuaded by it; everyone complies.
Latin complēre = "to fill up, fulfil" (com- + plēre, "to fill") — you comply by filling the requirement someone set.

Same root, big family: complete, complement (what fills the gap), replete, supply, plenty, implement.

Odd cousin: compliment is the same word — it reached English via Spanish cumplir, "to fulfil the courtesies." Comply fills an obligation; compliment fills a social one.

To worsen something bad by adding to it
Verb: literally, to put together from parts — but the sense the GRE wants is to make an already bad thing worse by adding to it.
Noun: a mixture of combined elements (chemistry); also a walled-off group of buildings.
Adjective: made of more than one part — a compound fracture, a compound sentence.

Aggravate and worsen just say the trouble grew. Compound says a second, separate act was piled onto the first — lying about the crash compounds the crash. That's why it lands as quiet blame: the original problem may have been bad luck, but compounding it was a choice. It also carries the maths of compound interest — the damage feeds on itself and accelerates.
⚠️ compound ≠ confound. To compound a problem is to worsen it; to confound someone is to baffle them (or to refute an expectation — the results confounded the sceptics).
Compound interest — the money grows on top of itself. Compound a mistake and the mistake starts earning interest.
The word never means a single loss; it means a loss that keeps generating more loss.
1. The airline's refusal to explain the delay only compounded the passengers' anger.
2. Don't compound it by texting him at 2am — you've done enough damage for one night.
News coverage keeps the odd noun sense alive: a raid on a compound in Abbottabad, the Kennedy compound at Hyannis Port — a walled cluster of buildings, not a chemical.
Latin compōnere = "to put together" (com- together + pōnere to place). One root, a whole shelf of words: compose, component, composite, deposit, postpone, exponent, position.

🚫 The walled-enclosure compound is a different word entirely — Malay kampung, "village", brought back by traders and reshaped to look like the Latin one.

Settle by mutual concession; or damage, weaken, expose to danger.
Sense 1 (the everyday one): a settlement where each side gives something up — or to reach one.
Sense 2 (the one the GRE tests): to damage, weaken, or expose to danger — a reputation, an immune system, a password, a principle.

The two senses split cleanly by grammar. The noun is respectable: a compromise is what reasonable adults arrive at. The participle is never respectable: something compromised is tainted, breached, no longer trustworthy. And to compromise oneself means to have surrendered a principle in a way you can't take back — the word carries the faint smell of a deal made in private.
⚠️ compromise ≠ comprise.
- compromise = settle by concession, or endanger
- comprise = consist of (the committee comprises nine members)
Hiding inside it is promise — a co-promise. Both sides promise away a piece; when you promise away a piece of yourself, you're compromised.
The same act — giving part of something up — is a virtue between two parties and a defect within one.
1. Chemotherapy compromises the immune system, leaving patients vulnerable to infections a healthy body would shrug off.
2. We compromised: he got the aisle seat, I got the armrest.
Every breach notification you've ever received — \"your credentials may have been compromised\" — is sense 2 doing its job: not negotiated, but broken into and no longer safe.
Latin com- (together) + promittere (to promise) → a compromissum, the mutual promise two disputing parties made to accept an arbiter's ruling.

promittere = pro- (forth) + mittere (to send), and mittere is a workhorse root: mission, transmit, permit, dismiss, emit, remit, submit.

Meant to soothe hostility and win the other side over.
Intended to soothe someone's anger and win them back — to end hostility rather than win the argument.

It describes the manner, not the surrender. A conciliatory remark concedes nothing; it just lowers the temperature. Note the distance from its neighbours: apologetic admits fault, obsequious grovels, placatory hints the other side is being humoured — conciliatory stays dignified, the register of diplomats, negotiators and HR. Its faint downside is only ever the suspicion of weakness: someone too conciliatory is caving.
Conciliatory is re*concil*e with the re- stripped off — the opening move, not the finished peace.
A conciliatory gesture is what you offer before reconciliation, which is why it can be made and still refused.
1. After a week of trading insults, the minister struck an unexpectedly conciliatory note, conceding that both sides had grievances worth hearing.
2. He didn't apologise exactly, but he brought coffee and used his most conciliatory voice, which was close enough.
Political journalism runs on one collocation: "struck a conciliatory tone." Any time a leader softens after a row, that is the sentence the news writes.
Latin concilium = "an assembly, a calling-together" (com- "together" + calāre "to call"). To conciliate is literally to call the two sides back into the same room.

Same root: council (the assembly itself) and reconcile (call them together again).

Decisive; settling the matter beyond further doubt.
Settling a question beyond any further argument — proof or evidence so decisive that the matter is closed.

It's an on/off word, not a dial. Compelling, persuasive, strong all describe evidence that moves you while leaving room to doubt; conclusive leaves no room at all. That's why it lives mostly in the negative — no conclusive evidence, the tests were inconclusive — and why claiming something is conclusive is a big claim. Courtroom, lab report, and inquiry register.
⚠️ conclusive ≠ concluding.
- concluding = last in sequence — the concluding chapter, the concluding remarks
- conclusive = settles it — conclusive proof

A concluding argument can be entirely unconvincing.
Con-CLUS-ive — the clus is close: it closes the case.
Anything less than conclusive leaves the case still open.
1. The committee found the accounts irregular, but nothing conclusive enough to justify a referral to the prosecutor.
2. Two grainy photos aren't conclusive — get me something that actually proves he was there.
The stock phrase every news bulletin and inquiry report reaches for: "there is no conclusive evidence that..." — the polite way of saying we suspect it but can't prove it.
Latin claudere = "to shut, to close", via concludere ("to shut up, close off").

One root, a whole GRE family: conclude, preclude (shut out in advance), exclude, seclude, recluse (one shut away), closure. Wherever you see -clude / -clus-, think shut.

To overlook or tacitly accept something you know is wrong.
To accept or overlook something wrong — to let an offence pass without protest or punishment.

You can only condone what you already consider bad; condoning a kindness is nonsense. And it stops short of approval: to condone is to not object, to look away, to tolerate. That's why it lives overwhelmingly in the negative — "I do not condone this" — where the speaker is drawing a line between themselves and someone else's conduct. Silence from someone with the power to act is the classic way of condoning.
⚠️ condone ≠ condemn. Near-identical openings, opposite verdicts: condone = let it slide; condemn = denounce it. If a sentence sounds harsh, the word is condemn.
con-DONE — you treat the wrongdoing as done, over with, not worth raising.
The hidden word done carries the nuance exactly: not "well done," just done — let it pass.
1. The tribunal held that a government which fails to prosecute such abuses effectively condones them.
2. Look, I'm not saying I condone what he did — I just don't think he should lose his job over it.
The boilerplate of every corporate statement and celebrity apology: "We do not condone this behaviour." It's the phrase institutions reach for when they need to be seen not-looking-away.
Latin condōnāre = "to give away, remit, forgive" — con- (thoroughly) + dōnāre (to give). You forgive a debt by giving it up.

Same dōnāre gives donate, donor, donation, and pardon (per- + dōnāre, "to give thoroughly").

🚫 Condemn is unrelated: con- + damnāre, "to inflict loss on" — the root of damn, damnation, indemnity.

Creating the conditions that let something good happen.
Tending to make something happen; creating the conditions in which a desired outcome can develop.

It describes a setting, not a cause. A quiet room doesn't produce concentration — it's conducive to it, meaning it clears the way. That's the difference from causes or produces: conducive is enabling, indirect, background. It's also grammatically clingy — the word barely exists without to after it, and what follows to is almost always something wanted (learning, sleep, recovery, growth). Register is formal-to-managerial: it lives in policy documents, school prospectuses, and doctors' advice rather than in heated speech.
⚠️ conducive ≠ conductive.
- conducive = helps bring about (an atmosphere conducive to trust)
- conductive = carries heat or electricity (copper is conductive)

One shapes outcomes, the other carries current.
Nothing is just conducive — it's conducive to something. The word points forward, like an arrow.
If you can't finish the sentence with "…to what?", you've used the wrong word.
1. The committee concluded that overcrowded wards were not conducive to recovery.
2. Three flatmates, one bathroom, and a broken heater — hardly conducive to revision.
Sleep-hygiene advice everywhere: "make your bedroom conducive to sleep" — cool, dark, no screens. The word does nothing but set up conditions, which is exactly what it means.
Latin con- (together) + dūcere (to lead) — literally leading toward. Conditions lead you to the result.

That root is a GRE workhorse: conduct, induce, deduce, seduce, produce, abduct, aqueduct, ductile — all leading, drawing, or channelling something somewhere.

A huge, destructive fire; by extension, a large-scale conflict.
A large, destructive fire — one that spreads and takes out buildings, blocks, forests. By extension, a war or conflict on that scale.

Size is the whole point. A fire can be any size; a blaze is what the news calls a house fire; a conflagration is the kind that gets a name and a date — the Great Fire of London, Chicago 1871. It's formal and slightly historical in tone, and it carries the sense that control was lost: nobody puts a conflagration out quickly. Used figuratively — a political conflagration, a family conflagration — it keeps that shape: something local that spread until it had consumed everything near it.
Hear flagrant sitting inside it — same blaze, different scale: a flagrant lie burns in plain sight, a conflagration burns the whole street.
Both words come from the same "burning" root, so if you can hear flagrant you can hear the fire — and the con- ("all together") tells you it's everything alight at once, not one candle.
1. By dawn the conflagration had taken four blocks, and the brigade had abandoned everything east of the river.
2. One offhand comment in the group chat and the whole thing was a conflagration by lunchtime.
Wildfire coverage reaches for it the moment a fire stops being one fire: reporters say blaze while it's in the hills and switch to conflagration once it jumps into neighbourhoods.
Latin flagrāre = "to burn, blaze", with con- here meaning thoroughly — burning all over.

Same root gives you flagrant (an offence so blatant it's blazing) and the legal phrase in flagrante delicto, literally "while the crime is still blazing" — caught in the act.

To baffle utterly — or to defeat what everyone expected.
Three linked senses, all on the exam:
1. to bewilder someone completely — confusion so total it stops thought.
2. to defeat or frustrate something expected — the result confounded the polls.
3. to mix up two things that should be kept apart — don't confound correlation with cause.

Confuse is ordinary and personal; confound is grander and usually has a winner. When something confounds you, it hasn't merely muddled you — it has outmatched you. That's why sense 2 works so cleanly: predictions, critics, and doctors get confounded, and the thing doing the confounding comes out on top.
⚠️ confound ≠ compound. To compound a problem is to add to it, make it worse. To confound it is to baffle or defeat it. One letter, opposite direction.
Con-FOUND: the con artist FOUND a way — you're not just puzzled, you're beaten.
The hidden found keeps the winner in the picture, which is what separates confound from plain confuse.
1. The novel's ending confounded every critic who had confidently predicted a tidy reconciliation.
2. He was supposed to lose in straight sets, and he confounded the lot of us.
Any paper you read has a confounding variable — the lurking third factor that pours cause and effect together so you can't tell which is which. Sense 3, doing daily work in statistics.
Latin con- (together) + fundere (to pour) — literally to pour together until nothing can be told apart.

That root is a goldmine: confuse (the same word, worn smooth), fuse, infuse, diffuse, profuse, effusive, transfusion, refund (pour back).

Pleasantly agreeable; suited to your temperament or your needs.
1. (of people) pleasant, friendly, easy to get along with — because their temperament suits yours. 2. (of places, work, conditions) agreeable, well-suited to your needs or tastes.

The key is fit, not virtue. Kind and generous describe a person in isolation; congenial is relational — it says this person or place agrees with you. A dour recluse can be congenial company for another dour recluse. It's a mild, civilised, slightly bookish compliment: warm but unexcited, the word for a good dinner guest rather than a beloved friend.
⚠️ congenial ≠ congenital.
- congenial = agreeable, well-suited — a congenial host
- congenital = present from birth — a congenital heart defect

One letter apart, and only one of them is a compliment.
Congenial = genial with (con-) you — the "con" makes it a match, not just a mood.
Genial describes someone's warmth on its own; the con- adds the second party, which is why congenial always implies suitability to somebody or something.
1. The delegates found the Geneva sessions unexpectedly congenial, the disputes conducted over coffee rather than through lawyers.
2. Rainy Sunday, nobody talking, cat on the radiator — honestly the most congenial afternoon I've had all year.
Job ads and hotel listings run on this word — "a congenial working environment," "a congenial atmosphere." It's the register of polite advertising: promising you'll fit in without promising anything specific.
Latin con- (together) + genialis, from genius — your guardian spirit, from gignere "to beget." So: sharing a spirit with.

That root is a GRE goldmine: genius, genial, genuine, genus, generate, gene, progeny — and congenital, literally "born together with you," which is exactly why it means "from birth" and not "friendly."

Based on guesswork or inference, not on evidence.
Based on guesswork or inference rather than evidence — plausible, but unproven.

The word doesn't say wrong; it says unsupported. Where "speculative" hints at wishful reaching and "baseless" is an insult, conjectural is the cool academic label a historian or scientist attaches to a reconstruction they can't document: reasonable, honestly flagged, still air. Call someone's argument conjectural and you haven't refuted it — you've quietly demoted it from finding to hunch.
Con-JECT-ural — a guess in a tweed JACKet.
The formal dress is the whole point: it's still a guess, just one wearing scholarly clothes.
1. The dating of the manuscript remains conjectural; no colophon survives, and the scribe's hand matches nothing else in the archive.
2. Everything after "he probably left around midnight" is conjectural — you're making it up as you go.
Goldbach's Conjecture, the Poincaré Conjecture — in mathematics a conjecture is precisely a statement everyone believes and nobody has proved. Goldbach's has stood unproven since 1742.
Latin conicere = "to throw together" (com- together + jacere to throw) — you fling scraps of evidence into a pile and see what shape they make.

jacere is a GRE workhorse: project (throw forward), eject, inject, reject (throw back), trajectory, dejected (thrown down), adjacent (thrown near).

An expert judge of quality in matters of taste.
An expert judge of quality in something where quality is a matter of taste — art, wine, food, music, cigars.

The key isn't how much you know, it's how finely you can discriminate. An expert on wine knows the regions; a connoisseur can tell you the vintage from the glass. Against its neighbours: an aficionado or buff brings enthusiasm, a dilettante brings dabbling, a connoisseur brings a trained palate and a verdict. The word flatters — which is why it curdles easily into self-regard, and why "he fancies himself a connoisseur" is an insult.
Amateur loves it (Latin amare); connoisseur knows it — same French -eur, rival claims.
The suffix marks the person, and the stem tells you what qualifies them: feeling versus knowledge.
1. The museum's new curator is a connoisseur of early Flemish painting, able to date a panel from its craquelure alone.
2. He's a full-on crisp connoisseur — one bite and he'll tell you the batch was fried too long.
Luxury packaging runs on this word: whisky, chocolate and coffee sold as "for the true connoisseur." The pitch is pure flattery — buy this and you're the one with the discerning palate.
Old French conoisseor, from Latin cognoscere = "to get to know." That root is a GRE goldmine: recognize, cognition, cognizant, incognito, reconnaissance, cognoscenti (the in-the-know set).

The modern French spelling is connaisseur — English kept the older -oi-, which is why the word looks misspelled even when it isn't.

General agreement across a group, short of unanimity.
General agreement within a group — the settled collective position on a question.

Crucially, it is not unanimity. A consensus is the sense of the room: most people agree, the holdouts stop objecting, and the group moves on without ever taking a formal tally. That's why committees, scientific bodies and newsrooms love the word — it claims collective authority ("the scientific consensus") without promising that every single person signed off. Slightly institutional in register; you reach, build, or break a consensus, and "consensus of opinion" is redundant padding.
⚠️ consensus ≠ census.
- consensus = agreement felt in common
- census = an official head*count*

The overlap is why people misspell it "concensus" — there is no c in the middle.
Consensus has sense in it, not census — it's a shared sense, not a headcount.
Nobody counts votes to reach a consensus; the group simply senses together that the matter is settled.
1. After three days of negotiation the delegates arrived at a fragile consensus on emissions targets.
2. There's no consensus in this house about where we're going for dinner, and there never will be.
Every climate report and vaccine story leans on the phrase "the scientific consensus" — a claim that the field has broadly settled, deliberately not a claim that every scientist agrees.
Latin com- (together) + sentīre (to feel) — literally feeling together.

That root is a GRE goldmine: sense, sentiment, sentient, consent, assent, dissent, resent, sentinel.

🚫 Not census. That's Latin censēre, "to assess" — the same root as censor and censure. Similar look, unrelated word.

Standing out plainly; impossible not to notice.
Easy to see or notice; standing out so plainly that it attracts attention.

Obvious is about the mind — the point lands. Conspicuous is about the eye — the thing sticks out of its surroundings. And it usually carries a faint discomfort: the conspicuous person is the one everybody clocks, the conspicuous spending is the kind meant to be seen. Turn it up and you get vulgarity (conspicuous consumption); invert it and you get the sly idiom conspicuous by his absence — so expected that the gap itself is loud.
⚠️ conspicuous ≠ perspicuous.
- conspicuous = easily seen — it stands out
- perspicuous = clearly expressed — a perspicuous explanation leaves no confusion

(And perspicacious = sharp-sighted, shrewd, said of a person.)
Conspicuous hides spic — the same spec- as specs: you don't need your glasses to spot it.
Conspicuous isn't merely visible — it's visible to someone who wasn't even looking.
1. Her red coat made her conspicuous in a hall of grey suits — which was, of course, the point.
2. Don't be so conspicuous, mate — you're the only one in the library wearing sunglasses.
Conspicuous consumption — Thorstein Veblen's phrase for buying things purely so other people see you can afford them. It's the standard label for the flex: the logo bag, the supercar in a city with a 20 mph limit.
Latin specere = "to look", with con- as an intensifier: fully in view.

That root is a GRE goldmine: spectacle, inspect, prospect, suspicion, specimen, perspicacious — all of them about looking.

column2:
To plot secretly together, usually toward harm.
To plot secretly with others toward an end that is usually illegal, treacherous, or harmful.

The word is built for two or more. You can plot alone and you can scheme alone, but conspiring takes accomplices — which is why the law treats conspiracy as its own crime, separate from the act itself. It also implies concealment: colleagues who openly agree to undercut a rival are colluding; the same people meeting in a car park at midnight are conspiring.

There's a second, softer use where the subject isn't people at all: events conspired to ruin the trip. Here it's half-joking fatalism — the world behaving as if it had organised itself against you.
There is no such thing as a solo conspiracy — con- means you need someone to whisper with.
The con- ("together") is the whole nuance: secrecy plus a partner, not one person's private scheming.
1. Three junior officers were accused of having conspired to depose the general while he was abroad.
2. Roadworks, a dead phone and a train strike all conspired to make me forty minutes late.
Paulo Coelho's most-quoted line from The Alchemist — "when you want something, all the universe conspires in helping you to achieve it" — is the rare benign use, and it's plastered over half the internet's motivational posters.
Latin con- (together) + spīrāre (to breathe) — literally to breathe together, close enough to share air while whispering.

That root pays off across the exam: inspire (breathe in), expire (breathe out — then, stop breathing), aspire (breathe toward), perspire, respiration, and spirit itself.

To interpret ambiguous words or acts as meaning something particular.
To assign a particular meaning to words or actions — to take them as meaning something.

Where interpret is broad and neutral (you interpret a poem, a dream, a dataset), construe shows up precisely where a reading is contested or could go the other way. It carries a whiff of the courtroom: someone is deciding which of two possible meanings a sentence or a gesture will officially bear. That's why it so often appears defensively — "don't construe my silence as consent", "this shall not be construed as an admission". If nothing is ambiguous, nobody needs to construe it.
con-S-TRUE — out of an ambiguous phrase, you pick which reading is true.
The word literally hides true in it, and construing is the act of settling which meaning counts as the true one.
1. The court construed the clause narrowly, holding that it covered damage to the building but not to its contents.
2. He asked if I was busy this weekend, and I stupidly construed that as an invitation.
Buried in almost every contract and terms-of-service you've ever scrolled past: "This Agreement shall be construed in accordance with the laws of..." — lawyers use the word constantly, because their whole job is fixing which reading wins.
Latin construere = con- ("together") + struere ("to build") — literally to build up. You build a meaning out of the parts of a sentence.

Same struere gives you construct, structure, instruct (build knowledge into someone), obstruct, destroy. Add mis- and you get misconstrue: you built the meaning wrong.

To think about something long, deeply and unhurriedly.
To think about something long, deeply and unhurriedly — or to look at it that way. Second, everyday sense: to consider doing something serious (contemplating a career change).

Consider is practical and can take five seconds; contemplate takes an afternoon. It carries weight and stillness — you contemplate mortality, a painting, a divorce, not which sandwich to order. Using it for something trivial sounds either pompous or deliberately ironic, and that irony is half its everyday use ("I'm contemplating a second biscuit").
con-TEMPLE-ate — thinking done at temple pace: slow, quiet, and about something that matters.
The hidden word temple is not a coincidence but a real root, and it gives you the tone as well as the meaning — reverent, sustained, never hurried.
1. Sitting with the letter unopened, she contemplated the life it would end and the one it would begin.
2. He's been contemplating quitting for about three years now, so I wouldn't hold your breath.
Latin contemplārī, from com- + templum. A templum was originally the patch of sky an augur marked off with his staff and then watched, for hours, for the flight of birds — only later did it become the building. To contemplate is to stare into your marked-off patch and wait for meaning to arrive.

Same root: temple, contemplative.

Of the same era as; or belonging to the present day.
Adj.: (1) belonging to the same time as something else; (2) belonging to the present — modern, current.
Noun: a person living at the same time as another — Leibniz was a contemporary of Newton.

Sense (1) is the one the GRE tests, and it's relational: contemporary with or of something. So "contemporary accounts of the battle" means written by people who were there — not written by modern historians. When the word stands alone with no comparison point ("contemporary art", "contemporary dance"), the era it matches is ours. Same word, two clocks: it always means "of that time," and context decides which time.
⚠️ contemporary ≠ contemporaneous. Contemporaneous only ever means "happening at the same time," usually of events or documents (contemporaneous notes) — it can never mean "modern." Anything described as contemporaneous is being dated, not praised as current.
Contemporary hides tempo — two things keeping the same tempo are running on the same clock.
The buried tempo pulls you to the "same era as" sense rather than the lazy "modern" reading.
1. Scholars prize the diary because it is contemporary with the siege itself, not a reconstruction written forty years later.
2. My gran and Elvis were contemporaries, which she brings up roughly once a week.
A Museum of Contemporary Art shows work by artists who are alive now — the label is a date range, not a style.
Latin con- (together) + tempus, temporis (time) — literally "sharing a time."

That root pays off everywhere: temporary (lasting a short time), temporal (of time, or of the worldly world as opposed to the eternal), tempo, extempore (out of the moment, unprepared), temporize (stall for time).

Scorn for someone judged worthless or beneath you.
The feeling that a person or thing is worthless, beneath serious consideration — scorn delivered as a verdict.

Anger says you wronged me; contempt says you are beneath me. That's the register difference: hatred grants the enemy status, contempt withholds it. It runs cold and looks downward, which is why it reads as arrogance in the person feeling it. Note the fixed phrases: to hold someone in contempt, and beneath contempt — so worthless it doesn't even merit the sneer.

Second, legal sense: contempt of court is open defiance or disrespect of a court's authority, and it will get you jailed.
⚠️ contemptuous ≠ contemptible.
- contemptuous = feeling it — the sneering one
- contemptible = deserving it — the despicable one

A contemptuous critic; a contemptible excuse.
-uous feels it, -ible earns it: a contemptuous judge holds a contemptible man in contempt.
The same suffix split runs through pitiable / pitying and despicable / disdainful — -ible always points at the target, not the sneerer.
1. He treated the committee's findings with undisguised contempt, not troubling to read past the first page.
2. She didn't even argue with him — just a little laugh, pure contempt, and walked off.
Every courtroom drama's "I'll hold you in contempt!" — the judge's threat when someone won't stop talking back. Real procedure, and the one place the word gets shouted.
Latin contemnere = "to scorn, to think nothing of" (con- intensive + temnere, "to despise").

🚫 Nothing to do with tempt. That's Latin temptare, "to test, to try" — attempt, temptation. The shared spelling is an accident.

To argue a disputed point; to struggle or compete.
Two senses, both about strain against opposition:

1. To assert in the face of disagreement. Not merely to say — to maintain a position that someone else is pushing back on. This is why academic and journalistic prose reaches for it: "critics contend that the study was underpowered" flags the claim as contested and quietly distances the writer from it. Swap in "argue" and you lose the hint of a live dispute; swap in "claim" and you add a sneer that contend doesn't have.

2. To struggle or compete. Contend with a problem = grapple with it, difficulty implied but not defeat. Contend for a prize = be a serious rival for it, not a hopeful bystander.
contend that = argue · contend with = struggle · contend for = compete.
The preposition, not the verb, tells you which of the three senses is running.
1. Several economists contend that the shortage was engineered, not accidental.
2. Between the strike and the rain, we had enough to contend with before the van broke down.
Marlon Brando in On the Waterfront: "I coulda been a contender." A contender is one who contends for the title — a real threat, not a filler on the card.
Latin contendere = con- ("together") + tendere ("to stretch") — to strain against. That's the through-line: an argument, a rival, and a hardship are all things you pull taut against.

tendere is a GRE workhorse: tension, tendon, extend, intend, pretend, portend, distend — and contentious, which is just contend turned into a personality.

Quietly satisfied; wanting nothing beyond what you already have.
Adj.: satisfied with what you have; not wanting more. Verb: content oneself with = to accept something lesser without complaint.

This is a low-temperature word. Happy and delighted point upward; content points at an absence — no craving, no restlessness, nothing missing. You can be content and completely unexcited. That's why "he was content to stay in the junior role" reads faintly of settling: contentment is peace, but on the GRE it often shades into undemanding acquiescence.
⚠️ content ≠ contentious. Content = at peace, wanting nothing. Contentious = quarrelsome, or hotly disputed. Near-identical spelling, opposite temperament — and unrelated roots (hold vs strive).
conTENT = your wanting is con-tained.
The satisfied sense and the container sense are the same word: desires held in, lid on, nothing spilling out toward more.
1. Having renounced the estate, he professed himself content with a scholar's stipend and a room facing the garden.
2. Honestly? Give me a sofa and bad TV and I'm content.
Philippians 4:11 — "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" — the verse that fixed the word's meaning in English as acceptance, not joy.
Latin continēre = "to hold together, hold in" (con- together + tenēre to hold) → contentus, "restrained, satisfied."

The whole family is about holding: contain, container, continent (as an adjective, self-restrained), incontinent (unable to hold it in), countenance (your bearing — how you hold yourself). And tenēre alone gives tenacious, tenant, retain, detain, tenable.

Likely to cause argument; or itching to start one.
Two linked senses:
Of a thing: likely to cause argument — disputed, fought over. A contentious clause, a contentious border, a contentious appointment.
Of a person: eager to argue — quarrelsome, always ready to pick a fight.

Controversial just reports that people disagree; contentious puts you in the room while they do it — it carries the friction, the raised voices, the fact that this thing generates fights rather than merely attracting them. Applied to a topic it's neutral-to-wary; applied to a person it's a straight criticism, and a slightly formal one — you'd write it in a performance review, not shout it across a table.
⚠️ contentious ≠ contented. Contented = quietly satisfied (Latin continēre, "to hold in"). Contentious = fighting (Latin contendere, "to strain against"). Opposite moods, unrelated roots — the shared "content" is a coincidence.
con-TEN-tious = con + TENSION. A contentious issue is one loaded with tension.
The sound hook is also the true root — tension and contentious both come from Latin tendere, "to stretch tight."
1. The land reform bill's most contentious provision — retroactive compensation — consumed three days of debate on its own.
2. Don't sit him next to my uncle; he gets contentious after two drinks and argues about everything.
Law firms split their entire practice this way: contentious work means litigation — suing, defending, disputes — while non-contentious work is contracts and deals where nobody is fighting. Same for "contentious probate": the will someone is challenging.
Latin contendere = "to strain, to strive against" (con- "with/against" + tendere "to stretch").

Tendere is a workhorse root: tension, tendon, extend, intense, portend, tent (stretched canvas) — and its contendere branch gives contend, contention, contest. A contentious person is permanently straining against someone.
