column2:
To break or act against a law, rule, or treaty.
To act in violation of a law, rule, treaty or regulation. In a second, more abstract sense: to conflict with or contradict a principle, claim or finding.

This is the vocabulary of compliance, and it wants a written object. You break a promise and you betray a friend, but you contravene Article 5. The tone is cool and procedural — no anger in it — because the offence is against the text, and what follows is a penalty, not a scolding.
⚠️ contravene ≠ circumvent.
- contravene = break the rule head-on
- circumvent = get around the rule without technically breaking it

The bank that lends to a sanctioned firm contravenes the sanctions; the bank that routes the money through a shell company circumvents them.
Contravene needs a contract — you can only contravene something someone wrote down.
If the thing being broken isn't a clause, code, statute or treaty, the word is wrong.
1. The tribunal held that the deportations contravened the state's obligations under the refugee convention.
2. Pretty sure hanging a TV on that wall contravenes about four clauses of my lease.
A newsroom stock phrase: "contravenes the Geneva Conventions." When a broadcaster reaches for contravene instead of breaks, it's signalling that a formal legal instrument — not a moral one — has been violated.
Latin contra (against) + venīre (to come) — literally "to come against."

venīre is a high-yield GRE root: intervene (come between), convene (come together), prevent (come before), circumvent (come around), advent (a coming), venue (the place you come to).

A minor mishap or petty quarrel at the worst possible moment.
An inconvenient mishap — or a small, awkward dispute — that arrives at exactly the wrong moment.

Size is the whole point: a contretemps is beneath the level of a crisis. A cancelled flight, a seating-plan row, two ministers snapping at each other in a corridor. Calling something a contretemps is a way of shrinking it — the French word puts a napkin over the mess and implies the speaker is far too composed to be rattled by it. Used about a real catastrophe, it reads as sarcasm or as damage control.
Contre + temps = counter-tempo. You're off the beat — a stumble, not a collision.
The mishap is defined by bad timing rather than by scale, which is why the word stays small and faintly amused.
1. A minor contretemps over precedence at the state dinner was smoothed over before the first course arrived.
2. We had a bit of a contretemps with the neighbours about the bins, and now nobody says hello.
Diplomatic journalism runs on this word: when two governments have a public spat too petty to call an incident, the papers call it a contretemps — the word itself is the de-escalation.
French contre-temps = "against the time / off the beat." It began as a fencing term: a thrust made on the wrong count, at the wrong instant.

Both halves pay rent elsewhere: contra- gives contradict, contrary, counter, contraband; temps ← Latin tempus gives tempo, temporal, contemporary, extempore, temporary.

Deeply, humbly sorry; crushed by guilt for a wrong done.
Feeling and showing deep, humbled regret for something you did wrong.

Sorry is the minimum; apologetic is the performance; contrite is the state of being genuinely crushed by your own guilt — head down, defences gone, no excuses offered. It presumes real fault, not a mishap, and it carries a moral, almost confessional weight. Note how often it attaches to appearance: someone looks contrite, sounds contrite — which is exactly why "suitably contrite" is so often said with a raised eyebrow.
Contrite has trite in it — and trite means worn out. A contrite person has been worn down by guilt.
Both words come from the same idea of rubbing something away, so the contrite one isn't just apologising — they've been ground flat.
1. The minister issued a contrite statement, accepting full responsibility and declining to name anyone else.
2. He turned up the next morning looking thoroughly contrite, holding two coffees and not saying much.
The Act of Contrition — the prayer said in Catholic confession, and the one every dying gangster gasps out in a mob film. Same word, same idea: you're not just apologising, you're broken up about it.
Latin conterere = "to grind down, wear away" (com- intensive + terere, "to rub"). To be contrite is to be ground to pieces by remorse.

That root pays out across the GRE: trite (a phrase rubbed smooth by overuse), attrition (wearing an enemy or a workforce down), detritus (what's rubbed off — debris), detriment (damage by wearing away).

A baffling problem or puzzle with no clean answer.
A problem that baffles you — a hard question with no clean answer. Older, narrower sense: a riddle whose answer is a pun.

Tone is the giveaway: a conundrum is puzzling rather than agonising. A dilemma forces you to pick between two bad options; a conundrum leaves you stuck one step earlier, unable to work out what's even going on. It carries a faint intellectual relish — the speaker is half-enjoying the difficulty — so it fits "the pricing conundrum" but sits badly on genuine tragedy.
A conundrum cons you, then leaves your head drumming.
Both halves are hiding in plain sight: it tricks you rather than wounds you, which is why the word stays playful even when the problem is serious.
1. The committee faced the familiar conundrum of a policy that was popular, affordable, and unworkable — but never all three at once.
2. So I've got a conundrum: two job offers, same salary, and I can't stand either boss.
Headline writers live on it — "the productivity conundrum", "the China conundrum". Spot the pattern and you've got the register: a problem serious enough to write about, puzzling enough that nobody has the answer.

Recovering from illness — stronger each day, not yet well.
Adjective: recovering from illness or injury — gradually regaining strength. Noun: the person doing the recovering.

The word marks a middle state, and that's its whole point: a convalescent is no longer sick and not yet well. Recovering is the plain everyday word; convalescent is clinical and slightly genteel — it carries the smell of a nursing home, a sanatorium, a long slow armchair-and-blanket stretch rather than a Tuesday off work with the flu. It implies time. Nobody is convalescent for an afternoon.

It also travels figuratively: a convalescent economy is one that has stopped collapsing but is still weak.
-escent = becoming. An adolescent is becoming an adult; a convalescent is becoming well.
That suffix always means mid-process, never arrived — which is exactly why a convalescent is still in bed.
1. After the surgery he spent six weeks convalescent at his sister's house on the coast, walking a little further each morning.
2. She's out of hospital but still convalescing — don't invite her to a five-a-side game just yet.
Convalescent plasma — blood plasma taken from recovered patients — was headline news through 2020 as an experimental COVID treatment. Recovered donors, literally the convalescent.
Latin valēre = "to be strong, to be well" + con- (intensifier) + -escere (begin to). To convalesce is to start growing strong again.

That root is a goldmine: valid (strong enough to hold), invalid (not strong — both the argument and the wheelchair sense), prevail, valiant, valour, value, and the Roman farewell vale ("be well").

Following accepted custom; standard, and often unoriginal for it.
Following accepted custom, standard practice, or the ordinary way of doing things — and, by extension, unoriginal.

Two temperatures live in one word. Applied to a method it's flatly descriptive: conventional surgery, conventional financing, conventional weapons (i.e. not nuclear). Applied to a person or a work of art it turns into a quiet insult — conventional taste, a conventional novel, a depressingly conventional wedding. The put-down is never loud; that's what makes it sting. Note the difference from traditional, which honours the past on purpose — conventional just does what the room already does, without asking why.
Convention = what the crowd came together and agreed on. Conventional = you never thought to ask who agreed, or when.
The word carries convention whole inside it, so the sneer is built in: you're not choosing the standard, you're defaulting to it.
1. Her thesis was flawlessly argued but thoroughly conventional, restating the field's consensus without once disturbing it.
2. Nice guy, great job, conventional as a beige sofa.
In every news report on war, "conventional weapons" means the ordinary kind — as opposed to nuclear, chemical, or biological. Nothing mild about them; they're just the standard-issue ones.
Latin convenīre = "to come together" (con- together + venīre to come). A convention is literally a coming-together — of delegates, or of everyone's unspoken agreement about how things are done.

That venīre root is a GRE workhorse: convene, intervene, advent, venue, souvenir, revenue, prevent.

A firmly held belief; also a court's verdict of guilt.
1. A belief held so firmly it's part of who you are. 2. A formal verdict of guilt in court — and the criminal record it leaves.

A conviction outranks an opinion and outweighs a belief: it has moral stake in it, and abandoning it costs you something. You have opinions about films; you have convictions about right and wrong. Hence the courage of one's convictions — the assumption is that they may cost you.

There's a third, everyday use: conviction as force of delivery. "He said it without conviction" doesn't mean he was lying — it means nothing behind the words was pushing. On the GRE, the tell is context: a deeply held conviction is the belief; a prior conviction is the rap sheet.
There's a convict hiding inside conviction — and a jury only convicts once it's convinced.
Both senses are the same event, one legal and one internal: the case has been argued, the verdict is in, and the matter is no longer open to debate.
1. Her pacifism was not a pose but a conviction, held through two wars and the loss of most of her friends.
2. He apologised, but you could tell his heart wasn't in it — no conviction behind a word of it.
Yeats, The Second Coming: "The best lack all conviction, while the worst are full of passionate intensity." Half the internet quotes it during elections, and it hangs entirely on the belief sense.
Latin convincere = con- (thoroughly) + vincere (to conquer) — literally "to defeat utterly," then "to defeat in argument, prove guilty."

vincere is a workhorse root: victory, victor, invincible, evict, evince, vanquish, convince. A conviction is a belief that beat all the others.

Cheerfully sociable, in the way of good food and company.
Cheerful, sociable and warm — specifically in the way of people gathered around food and drink.

Friendly describes a disposition; convivial describes an occasion. It carries the table with it: a shared meal, a loosened tie, wine going round, everybody talking at once. You can be friendly to a stranger in a lift, but you cannot be convivial alone — the word needs company, and usually needs a host. It's a compliment with a faint glow of indulgence: a convivial evening was long, and nobody was in a hurry to leave.
⚠️ convivial ≠ congenial.
- congenial = agreeable, well-suited to you — a congenial colleague, a congenial climate
- convivial = festive, good company — a convivial dinner

A congenial person suits your temperament; a convivial person pours you a drink.
con + VIV = living it up, together — same viv as vivid, revive, survive.
The viv supplies the life and the con supplies the crowd, which is why a solitary cheerful person is genial but never convivial.
1. The negotiations, frosty all week, ended in a surprisingly convivial dinner at which both delegations sang.
2. He's a nightmare in meetings but properly convivial the moment someone lights a barbecue.
Restaurant and hotel reviews live on this word — "a convivial atmosphere," "convivial shared plates." It's reviewer-speak for loud, warm, and you'll stay too long.
Latin convivium = "a banquet" — literally con- (together) + vivere (to live). A convivium was a dinner party, and the guests were convivae, "those who live together."

vivere is a workhorse root: vivid, vivacious, revive, survive, viable, vivisection — and bon vivant, the person who lives well and dines better.

Needlessly twisted and intricate; impossible to follow.
Twisted, coiled, folded in on itself — and so, of an argument, plot, sentence, or process: so intricate it can no longer be followed.

Complex can be a compliment and complicated is often just an honest fact, but convoluted blames the maker: the tangle didn't have to be there. It carries a faint whiff of suspicion too — convoluted excuses, convoluted accounting, convoluted procedures all hint that the twisting is doing work someone wants hidden. The literal sense (folded, coiled) survives mainly in anatomy: the convoluted tubules of the kidney.
No one has ever been praised for a convoluted explanation — the word is a verdict, not a description.
Reach for it only when you mean the complexity was avoidable and someone chose it.
1. The statute's convoluted drafting had spawned three decades of contradictory rulings.
2. Her explanation for the missing money got more convoluted every time she told it.
It's the standard word in film reviews for a Christopher Nolan plot — Tenet and Inception get called convoluted almost as a reflex, meaning: too many folds, and not all of them earned.
Latin volvere = "to roll", with con- = "together" — rolled up together, coiled.

That root is a GRE goldmine: revolve (roll back), evolve (roll out), involve (roll in), devolve (roll down), voluble (words that roll out easily), and volume (a rolled scroll).

Plentiful; produced or flowing in generous, ample quantity.
Present in large quantity — plentiful, abundant, more than enough.

It leans toward things that are produced, poured out, or consumed: copious notes, copious tears, copious rainfall, copious amounts of coffee. You'd rarely call a mountain range copious, because copious describes output and supply, not sheer size. Tone is mildly formal but common in speech, and the flavour is generous rather than excessive — say profuse for gushing, prodigal for wasteful. Copious just means the well kept giving.
Copious notes fill copies and copies of pages — same word underneath.
Copy and copious are literally the same Latin root, so copious means abundance that keeps being turned out, not a single big pile.
1. The witness gave copious testimony, filling three days of transcript with detail no one had asked for.
2. He took copious notes in the meeting and still had no idea what was decided.
The Cornucopia in The Hunger Games — the giant golden horn spilling out weapons and supplies at the start of the Games. Same root, and it's an image of overflow.
Latin copia = "abundance, plenty" — itself co- + ops ("wealth, resources," the root behind opulent).

The surprise: copy comes from here too. A medieval copia was an abundance of a text — make more of it, and you've made a copy. Cornucopia = cornu (horn) + copia = the horn of plenty.

Warm and friendly, but politely so — not intimate.
Adj.: warm, friendly, sincerely pleasant.
Noun: a sweet fruit syrup or liqueur (originally a heart-strengthening tonic).

The warmth here is real but kept at arm's length. Cordial is what you call relations between two countries that have stopped shouting, or the tone of a host who is genuinely glad you came but doesn't know you well. Affable is easy-going, effusive gushes, warm can be intimate — cordial is heartfelt politeness with the formality left on. That's why diplomats love it: "a cordial meeting" says friendly and says nothing.
Cordial has a cord in it — a line running from the heart, but a line all the same: a handshake, not a hug.
The warmth is genuine and comes from the heart, yet it stays at a measured distance.
1. After a decade of frozen borders, the two delegations parted on cordial terms — no treaty, but no insults either.
2. Her ex showed up at the wedding and they were perfectly cordial, which somehow felt worse than a fight.
The bottle of lime cordial or Ribena in the fridge: it was originally sold as a heart tonic — the drink and the adjective are the same word, both meaning "good for the heart."
Latin cor, cordis = "heart." A cordial welcome is heartfelt; a cordial drink was medicine to strengthen the heart.

That root runs everywhere: courage (heart to face it), accord and concord (hearts together), discord (hearts apart), record (originally to learn by heart), core.

Having a physical body; material rather than spiritual.
Having a physical body; material and touchable rather than spiritual, ghostly, or abstract.

It's the word you reach for when the existence of a body is the point in question — theology (soul vs. flesh), ghost stories (can it be touched?), law (corporeal property you can seize, as against an incorporeal right like a patent). Physical is the everyday word and carries no argument; corporeal is formal and always implies a contrast lurking nearby with something that has no body.
⚠️ corporeal ≠ corporal.
- corporeal = having a body (a corporeal being)
- corporal = inflicted on the body — corporal punishment — or an army rank

Both from corpus, but only corporeal means "made of flesh."
Corpor-eal = corpse + real. If it has a corpse, it's real — it's got a body.
The nasty little image fixes the point that corporeal is specifically about possessing flesh, not merely about being real.
1. Medieval theologians argued endlessly over whether angels take corporeal form or merely appear to.
2. He looked so pale walking in that I half-wondered if he was still corporeal.
In Harry Potter, the mark of a truly skilled wizard is a corporeal Patronus — one that takes a full animal body — as opposed to the thin silver wisp most students manage.
Latin corpus, corporis = "body." One root, a huge family: corpse, corpulent (fat), corps and corporal (military bodies), corporation (a legal "body" of people), corpuscle (a tiny body in the blood), incorporate (take into the body).

And the direct opposite is built in: incorporeal = bodiless.

To show two things vary together, without claiming cause.
Verb: to show, or to have, a mutual relationship — two things that rise and fall together. Rainfall correlates with crop yield.
Noun: either of two things so linked — fluency is a correlate of early reading.

The whole force of the word is that it stops short of cause. To say two things are related is vague; to say they correlate is a measured, almost statistical claim: they track each other, and that is all you are promising. It's the vocabulary of researchers and analysts hedging honestly — strong on pattern, silent on why.
⚠️ correlate ≠ corroborate.
- correlate = two things move together
- corroborate = evidence backs up a claim

Your alibi is corroborated by a witness, not correlated with one.
Co-relate: they relate together — side by side, neither one steering.
The cor- is just "co-", so the word means partnership between two facts, never one pushing the other.
1. Longitudinal data correlated parental income with university completion, though the authors declined to call one the cause of the other.
2. Weirdly, my worst gym days correlate with the days I skip breakfast.
"Correlation does not imply causation" — the most-quoted line in all of statistics, and the reason journalists get scolded every time a study says coffee drinkers live longer.
Latin com- ("together") + relatus ("carried back"). Before an r, com- assimilates to cor- — which is the same prefix hiding in correspond, corroborate, correct, and corrupt. Spot a cor- and you're usually looking at "together" or "thoroughly."

To back up a claim with independent supporting evidence.
To support a claim with independent evidence — a second witness, a document, a lab result that backs up what was already asserted.

It is a supporting word, not a proving word. Corroboration always arrives second: there must be a story on the table first, and the corroborating fact strengthens it without being the whole case. And it must come from elsewhere — your own repetition corroborates nothing. Register is formal: courtrooms, journalism, science. In plain speech people say back up.
⚠️ corroborate ≠ collaborate.
- corroborate = confirm someone's account
- collaborate = work together on something

Near-identical sound, opposite jobs — the GRE loves this pair.
Co-rroborate: the co- means it takes someone else — you can never corroborate your own story.
That prefix carries the whole nuance: corroboration is by definition second-hand support, so a witness repeating himself adds nothing.
1. Two independent laboratories corroborated the finding before the journal would print it.
2. Nice alibi — got anyone who can corroborate that?
Every police procedural and courtroom drama runs on the line "Can anyone corroborate your story?" — which is also exactly how lawyers and journalists use it at work: one source is a rumour, two is a fact.
Latin robur = "oak, hardwood, strength." To corroborate is literally to strengthen together — you put an oak beam under someone's claim.

Same root gives robust (oak-strong) and roborant (a strengthening tonic). 🚫 The -labor- in collaborate is a different root entirely (labor, "work") — that's why the two words mean unrelated things.

At home in many cultures; worldly and unprovincial.
Adj.: at home in many countries and cultures; free of local or national narrowness. Of a place, it means the mix — people, food, languages from everywhere. Of a person, it means the temperament: unfazed by difference.

Noun: someone who is that.

The praise is not for the passport stamps but for the absence of provincial reflex — a cosmopolitan doesn't find foreignness startling. Worldly hints at experience of vice; urbane is about polish and manners; cosmopolitan is about range. Its true opposites are parochial and provincial, and GRE passages love that axis.
⚠️ cosmopolitan ≠ metropolitan.
- metropolitan = of a big city — a matter of size (metropolitan area, metropolitan police)
- cosmopolitan = of many cultures — a matter of mix

A town can be metropolitan and still deeply parochial.
Cosmopolitan sounds like cosmo-politician — someone who can work any room, in any country.
The word rewards social ease among strangers, not miles travelled.
1. Trieste under the Habsburgs was a genuinely cosmopolitan port, where Italian, Slovene and German were all spoken on the same street.
2. She's the most cosmopolitan person I know — three languages, five cities, and she still can't work the London Tube.
Cosmopolitan the magazine, and the Cosmo cocktail Sex and the City made famous — both sell exactly one fantasy: the worldly, city-slick woman who belongs anywhere.
Greek kosmos (world, order) + politēs (citizen) — literally "citizen of the universe." Diogenes the Cynic, asked where he was from, is said to have replied kosmopolitēs.

Both halves pay off elsewhere: kosmos gives cosmos, cosmic, microcosm — and cosmetic, because kosmos also meant ordered arrangement, i.e. adornment. Polis gives politics, police, metropolis, acropolis.

A person's face or expression; or to tolerate, allow.
Noun: a person's face, especially as it shows feeling — the expression, the look. ("a grave countenance")
Verb: to tolerate, permit, or give approval to something.

The noun is literary and slightly old-fashioned; face is the plain word, countenance is the one that implies you can read something off it. The verb is where the GRE lives, and it has a habit: it appears overwhelmingly in the negative — would not countenance, refused to countenance, cannot countenance. To countenance something isn't to like it; it's to let it stand without objecting. So the person who "will not countenance dissent" is drawing a line, not stating a preference.
Can you face it? If you can't, you will not countenance it.
The noun (face) and the verb (allow) are the same act — keeping a straight face at something instead of refusing to look at it.
1. The headmaster would not countenance the slightest breach of the rules, and his countenance on the morning of the inquiry made that plain before he spoke.
2. I don't care how late it is — I'm not countenancing another round of "just one more episode."
Blake's hymn "Jerusalem" — "And did the Countenance Divine / Shine forth upon our clouded hills?" — the noun sense, a face shining down.
Latin continēre = "to hold together" → continentia, "the way you hold yourself, self-control." Your countenance is your face held in place.

Same root gives contain, container, continent (land held together), and continence (holding yourself in check).

A fake made to pass as the genuine article.
Adj.: made in exact imitation of something genuine in order to deceive. Noun: the fake item itself. Verb: to make such an imitation (or, more loosely, to feign a feeling).

Two things have to be true: there's a real original, and someone means to pass the copy off as it. A replica is honest, an imitation may be harmless, a fake is the everyday catch-all — counterfeit is the cold, legal-sounding one, the word that appears on a seizure notice. It attaches most naturally to money, passports, medicines, luxury goods: things whose whole value is that they're authentic.
Counterfeit money has to cross a counter — the fake only counts if someone takes it as real.
That built-in "counter" keeps the essential part in view: a counterfeit isn't just a copy, it's a copy made to be passed.
1. Customs officers destroyed some forty thousand counterfeit vials, each stamped with a pharmaceutical logo it had no right to bear.
2. That's a counterfeit — look at the stitching, no way that bag came out of a Prada factory.
The felt-tip pen a cashier swipes across your banknote is a counterfeit-detection pen — it darkens on ordinary wood-pulp paper, but not on the cotton stock real currency is printed on.
Old French contrefait = "made against" — Latin contra (against) + facere (to make). Something manufactured in opposition to the real thing.

That facere shows up disguised as -feit / -fit in a small family worth knowing: forfeit (something "done wrong," hence surrendered as a penalty), surfeit (over-done, an excess), benefit (well-done). Same root, undisguised, in fact, factory, manufacture, artifice.

Hidden or disguised; done without open acknowledgement.
Concealed, disguised, not openly acknowledged.

Two flavours. In the institutional sense, covert means deliberately hidden by design — a covert operation is planned, funded and deniable, and the whole point is that the sponsor's hand never shows. In the everyday sense, it means unstated rather than invisible: covert hostility, a covert glance, covert racism — the thing is perfectly perceptible, it just never gets said out loud.

Compare the neighbours: furtive is nervous and gives you away; clandestine and surreptitious carry a whiff of the illicit. Covert is the coolest of the four — controlled, professional, often sanctioned from above.

Noun: a thicket that gives game animals cover.
⚠️ covert ≠ overt. They are exact opposites and one letter apart. Covert = covered up; overt = out in the open. Exam sentences love pairing them ("not overt hostility but ___ resistance").
Covert has cover in it — and it's under cover, not in a corner.
The hidden word gives you the meaning, and "under cover, not in a corner" keeps the tone right — covert is organised concealment, not twitchy sneaking.
1. The committee concluded that the agency had run a covert campaign of influence for nearly a decade, funded through shell companies.
2. Nobody said anything, but there was a covert eye-roll going round the table every time he mentioned his promotion.
Covert ops — the standard term in intelligence and in every spy film about it. If the CIA denies it, it was covert.
Old French covert, past participle of covrir "to cover" (Latin cooperire). Covert is literally covered.

Its opposite is built the same way: overt is the past participle of Old French ovrir "to open" (Latin aperire) — literally opened. Covered vs opened, and the pair is locked.

Same family as cover and coverage; also curfew (couvre-feu, "cover the fire") and kerchief (couvre-chef, "cover the head"). From aperire on the other side: aperture, overture.

To crave something that belongs to someone else.
To want something badly — specifically something that belongs to someone else.

Plain wanting is morally blank; coveting is loaded. The word carries a whiff of sin and envy: you are eyeing your neighbour's car, your colleague's job, your friend's spouse. It also implies the desire is sustained and inward — a slow ache you nurse, not a quick impulse.

One twist worth knowing: the participle coveted flips positive. "The coveted Booker Prize" just means everybody wants it, and the prestige rubs off on the thing, not the shame onto the wanter.
⚠️ covet ≠ covert. One transposed letter, opposite worlds: covet = desire what isn't yours; covert (KOH-vert / KUV-ert) = hidden, secret — a covert operation. A spy runs covert missions; a thief covets the jewels.
Covet hides Cupid — same root, and Cupid's arrow always points at somebody else's beloved.
The Cupid link gives you both halves of the word: burning desire, aimed where it has no business being.
1. For thirty years he had coveted the corner office, and on the day he got it he found the view unremarkable.
2. Don't pretend — you've coveted that jacket since the moment she walked in wearing it.
The Tenth Commandment: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house... nor his wife." Note that the sin isn't wanting a house — it's wanting his.
Latin cupere = "to desire", via cupiditas and Old French coveitier.

Same root gives you Cupid (the god of desire), cupidity (greed for money — a favourite GRE word), and concupiscence (lust).

Playfully or evasively reticent; shyness performed, not felt.
Two linked senses:

1. Pretending to be shy or modest — usually to charm or tease. 2. Deliberately vague; unwilling to give details.

The key is that it's shyness performed, not felt. A shy person can't help it; a coy person is choosing it, and wants you to notice the withholding. That's why "coy" carries a faint eye-roll: a coy smile is inviting you to press further, and a CEO who is coy about the numbers isn't bashful — she's managing you.
Coy is hiding inside decoy — and a decoy works by pretending to be what it isn't.
Coyness is bait: the withholding is the lure.
1. The minister remained coy about the date of the election, deflecting every question with a smile.
2. Stop being coy — just tell me who you're texting.
Andrew Marvell's "To His Coy Mistress" — the most famous seduction poem in English, and the whole thing is a man arguing that her coyness (holding back, teasing him along) is a waste of the little time they have.
Old French coi = "quiet, still," from Latin quietus. English coy first meant simply "quiet, modest" — then slid into affected modesty, which is where it sits today.

Same root gives you quiet, quiescent, acquiesce, requiem — all the "at rest" words.

Cunning; clever at getting its way by sly means.
Clever at getting what you want by indirect, sly means — trickery, misdirection, a plan you didn't see forming.

The word carries a grudging compliment. Devious and duplicitous condemn; crafty half-admires. It suits small, contained cunning — a kid who talks his way out of chores, a negotiator who buries the real term in clause nine — rather than grand villainy. Note also that crafty has drifted clean away from craft meaning handiwork: a crafty person is not good with their hands, they are good at working you.
A crafty person crafts — quietly, in advance, and the thing they're building is a trap.
The skill is genuine; it's the aiming of it at you that makes it crafty.
1. Her crafty redrafting of the contract shifted every risk onto the buyer while appearing to concede on price.
2. He gave me this crafty little smile and I knew instantly he'd already sold my ticket.
Sports commentary keeps this sense alive: a crafty left-hander in baseball, or a crafty veteran midfielder — someone who has lost the pace and now wins by guile.
Old English cræft meant strength, then skill, then power — the same root as German Kraft, "force." English kept the honest branch (craft, craftsman, handicraft, aircraft) and grew a shady one: skill exercised in secret becomes cunning, as in witchcraft.

That drift is the whole word — skill quietly repurposed.

Cowardly in a way that earns contempt.
Cowardly — but contemptibly, shamefully so.

Afraid is a feeling anyone can have; timid is a temperament; craven is a verdict. It says the person had a duty to stand firm and folded anyway, usually to save their own skin. Nobody calls themselves craven — it's an accusation, and a withering, slightly old-fashioned one, at home in editorials and courtrooms rather than conversation. Its natural companions are capitulation, surrender, silence, appeasement: the cowardice of someone who gave in when it counted.
Craven = caves in.
Say it fast and "craven" collapses into "cave-in" — which is exactly what the craven person does the moment pressure is applied.
1. The committee's craven silence on the matter told the public everything it needed to know.
2. He talked a big game all week, then made some craven excuse and didn't show up.
It's the standard insult of political journalism — craven capitulation, craven refusal to condemn. If you've read a newspaper opinion page, you've met this word doing exactly that job.
Probably from Old French cravanter, "to crush, overwhelm" — the craven is the man already broken. In medieval trial by combat, a fighter who cried "craven!" formally surrendered: he kept his life and lost his honour. That's still the flavour — defeat you chose.

🚫 Nothing to do with crave. Different word entirely; a craven person wants less, not more.

column2:
Believable enough to take seriously — not the same as true.
Believable; worthy of being taken seriously. Also of a person or effort: convincing enough to be a real contender (a credible candidate, a credible attempt).

Notice what it stops short of. Credible is a bar cleared, not a verdict delivered — a credible witness may still turn out to be lying, and a credible threat is one plausible enough to act on, not one confirmed. It sits above conceivable and well below proven. Journalists, lawyers and security officials live on this word precisely because it lets them signal "worth believing" without claiming "true."
⚠️ credible ≠ credulous.
- credible = deserves to be believed (the story)
- credulous = too ready to believe (the sucker who swallows it)

A credulous audience will believe things that aren't remotely credible.
-ible means able: cred-ible is believ-able — able to be believed, which is a long way from being true.
The suffix only ever grants a capacity, so the word promises plausibility and nothing more.
1. The commission dismissed the memo for want of a credible account of where the money had gone.
2. Give me one credible reason you were three hours late and I'll drop it.
Every news bulletin that reports police found "no credible threat" — the phrase is doing exactly this job: plausible enough to take seriously, not confirmed.
Latin crēdere = "to believe, to entrust." One root, a whole GRE cluster: creed and credo (what you believe), credentials (papers that make you believable), credence, credulous (believes too easily), incredulous (refuses to believe) — and credit, which is literally someone believing you'll pay them back.

column2:
A gradual swell in loudness or intensity — the build, not the peak.
A gradual increase in loudness — and by extension, any steady swell in intensity, pressure, or noise.

The word names the climb, not the summit. Strictly, a crescendo is the eight bars of getting louder; the loud bit at the top is the climax. So "the argument rose to a crescendo" is the usage careful writers wince at — the crescendo is the rising. GRE sentence-completion loves this: a blank wanting crescendo wants building, swelling, mounting, not peak or culmination. Note also that it's neutral machinery — a crescendo of applause and a crescendo of complaints are equally idiomatic.
Crescendo is the crescent moon — swelling toward full, not the full moon itself.
Same root, same idea: both name growth in progress, which is why the peak is never the crescendo.
1. The murmur of the crowd swelled to a crescendo as the doors of the courthouse finally opened.
2. The washing machine does this awful crescendo thing right before it starts walking across the kitchen.
The Beatles' "A Day in the Life" — that vast orchestral crescendo where forty musicians climb from their lowest note to the highest over 24 bars, twice, before the final piano chord. Textbook definition, textbook execution.
Italian crescendo = "growing", from Latin crescere, "to grow" — the present participle, literally "in the act of growing."

That root pays out across the GRE: crescent (the growing moon), increase, increment, accrue, excrescence (an ugly outgrowth), and recruit (re-crescere, fresh growth for the army).

Visibly deflated after a hope is dashed.
Dejected and visibly downcast — the face-falling disappointment that follows a hope being dashed.

It is a drop, not a state: you have to have been up to be crestfallen. That's what separates it from dejected or despondent, which can be someone's baseline mood. It also implies you can see it — the shoulders, the face — so it's usually said of someone else, and said with a touch of sympathy. Mild-to-moderate: a crestfallen person got bad news, not a tragedy.
A crest is the bit that stands up — a rooster's comb, a plume on a helmet. Crestfallen is that going limp.
The word carries its own before-and-after: high hopes up top, then the droop.
1. The delegation returned crestfallen, having been received politely and refused entirely.
2. He came out of the interview crestfallen — you could tell before he said a word.
It's the standard word for the losing dugout at the final whistle — commentators reach for "crestfallen" every time the camera cuts to the bench.
Latin crista = "tuft, plume, comb" — the thing on top that stands up. A knight's crest sat on his helmet; a rooster's crest sits on his head. Both go down when he loses.

To sing or murmur softly, low, and sentimentally.
To sing or murmur in a low, soft, sentimental voice — usually to soothe someone, or to seduce them.

Volume is the whole point: you can belt, you can croon, and they are opposite ends of one dial. A croon is intimate, close-up, almost private — a mother over a cot, a singer with his lips on the microphone. It carries warmth by default, but writers also use it with a raised eyebrow, because sustained sweetness curdles into schmaltz: he crooned about her eyes for four straight verses. The verb also stretches beyond music to any soft cooing speech — you can croon reassurance at a nervous dog.
Croon rhymes with moon — and crooning is what you do about the moon, softly, at night, to someone half-asleep.
The rhyme fixes both the sound and the register: low, dark, sentimental — never loud.
1. The nurse crooned to the infant in a language no one else in the ward recognised.
2. He crooned the last chorus straight at her, and honestly it was a bit much.
Crooner is a real job description: Sinatra, Bing Crosby, Nat King Cole — and Michael Bublé is still billed as one. The whole style exists because microphones got sensitive enough that a singer could stop shouting and just murmur.
From Middle Dutch kronen, "to groan, lament" — and in Scots, crune meant the low bellow of cattle. The sentimentality is modern; the lowness of the pitch was there from the start.

Unwieldy — too bulky or clunky to handle smoothly.
Hard to handle because it's too large, heavy, or awkwardly built — and by extension, any system so clunky and over-complicated that it slows everything down.

The complaint is about friction, not pain. Something onerous imposes real hardship; something cumbersome merely makes you struggle with it — the suitcase that won't fit through the door, the eight-step approval form that eventually works. It's mild, practical, faintly exasperated: the word of someone who got there in the end, but wishes they hadn't had to.

On the GRE it usually shows up in the figurative sense — cumbersome machinery, bureaucracy, prose.
burdensome, troublesome, tiresome, cumbersome — the -some family all name a nuisance; cumbersome's nuisance is bulk.
Park it beside its rhymes and keep the distinguishing bit: the trouble is that the thing is too big or clunky to manage smoothly, not that it's painful or wrong.
1. The committee's cumbersome review procedure required four signatures before a single sentence could be published.
2. This laptop's fine, but the charger's so cumbersome I just leave it at home.
This is a workplace staple: a cumbersome approval process, a cumbersome UI, cumbersome paperwork. It's the standard polite complaint for something that technically works but makes you work for it.
From cumber, "to hinder, block up" (Old French combrer, from Late Latin cumbrus, a barrier or heap of rubble) + -some, "full of."

The useful payoff is the family: encumber (to weigh down), encumbrance (a burden — in law, a claim against property), and the GRE favourite unencumbered — free of baggage, financial or otherwise.

Clever in a sly, scheming, get-what-you-want way.
Adj.: clever at getting what you want by indirect, sly, often deceptive means.
Noun: that skill itself — he won by sheer cunning.

The cleverness is never in doubt; the honesty is. Clever is neutral, shrewd is hard-headed but respectable, cunning is foxlike — it implies scheming, self-interest, and a willingness to go around the rules rather than through them. Calling a rival's plan cunning half-admires it and half-accuses it. The one clean use is of animals and thieves in stories, where slyness is the whole charm.
⚠️ cunning ≠ canny. Both come from the same "know" root, but canny means shrewd and prudent — a canny investor is careful with her money, and nobody is being tricked. Add the deceit and you get cunning.
Cunning = CAN + winning — he knows how he can win, and he isn't fussy about how.
The word literally grew out of can ("to know how"), so the knowing is real — it's the method that's crooked.
1. The minister's resignation was a cunning manoeuvre: he left before the report could name him, and returned to the cabinet within a year.
2. She's not the smartest player at the table, but she's cunning — she'll let you win two hands and then clean you out.
Baldrick's catchphrase in Blackadder — "I have a cunning plan." The joke is that the plans are always elaborate, sneaky, and terrible, which is the word's whole flavour in four syllables.
Old English cunnan = "to know how, to be able" — the ancestor of modern can. So cunning first meant simply skilled (the King James Bible praises a "cunning workman"); the sly sense crept in later, as knowledge people used on you rather than for you.

Same root: can, canny, uncanny (literally un-knowable — hence eerie), and Scottish ken (to know).

To restrain or limit something without stopping it entirely.
Verb: to hold something in check — restrain, limit, keep within bounds.
Noun: the raised edge of a pavement; originally the chain under a horse's jaw that checks it.

Curb is moderation, not abolition. You ban a thing to end it; you curb it to keep it running at an acceptable level — and it implies the thing was already in motion and pulling hard. Governments curb inflation, spending, emissions; people curb their temper, their appetite, their tongue. It's the standard, faintly bureaucratic verb of policy prose, and it always carries the sense of a hand on the reins of something with its own momentum.
A curb doesn't stop the traffic — it keeps it in its lane.
The kerb you drive beside is the whole meaning: it constrains without halting, which is exactly what curbing inflation or curbing your temper does.
1. The central bank raised rates sharply in an attempt to curb runaway inflation.
2. Could you curb the sarcasm for ten minutes? My parents are right there.
Curb Your Enthusiasm — the title is an order to dial it down, not switch it off, which is the verb in one phrase.
Latin curvāre ("to bend") → Old French courbe. A curb was the chain under a horse's jaw: pull it and the head bends, and the horse checks itself.

Same root as curve, curvature, curvaceous — bending is the through-line: you bend a thing's course rather than break it.

A grumbling, ill-tempered old grouch — often said fondly.
A bad-tempered, grumbling person — stereotypically old, male, and unimpressed by everything modern.

Unlike misanthrope, which is cold and serious (hating humanity on principle), a curmudgeon is loud, specific, and faintly comic: he complains about the music, the prices, the neighbours' bins. That's why the word is usually said with a grin — people cheerfully call themselves curmudgeons, which nobody does with misanthrope. The implication is gruff surface, not real malice.
A cur is a snarling mongrel dog — and a curmudgeon is all bark.
The growl is real but the bite isn't, which is exactly the word's affectionate edge.
1. The old critic had settled into the role of literary curmudgeon, dismissing each new novel before he had finished the first chapter.
2. He's a bit of a curmudgeon about group chats, but he'll still drive you to the airport at 5am.
Carl Fredricksen in Pixar's Up — the growling old man who tells the kids to get off his lawn and then turns out to be the softest character in the film. That arc is the word.

Hasty and superficial; a quick pass that misses the details.
Done quickly and without attention to detail — a fast pass over the surface, skipping anything that would take time.

The word almost always carries a shrug of disapproval: it names an inspection that should have been thorough and wasn't. Brief is neutral, concise is a compliment, but cursory is a quiet accusation of laziness — a cursory apology isn't really an apology, and a cursory safety check is how people get hurt. It attaches by habit to acts of looking: a cursory glance, a cursory reading, a cursory inspection.
Cursory moves at cursor speed — it runs across the page and stops for nothing.
Same root, same image: the blinking cursor sweeps over every word and reads none of them.
1. Even a cursory examination of the accounts would have revealed the discrepancy; the auditors managed to miss it for three years.
2. He gave the contract a cursory skim, signed it, and spent the next year regretting clause 14.
Lawyers and journalists lean on one stock phrase: \"even a cursory glance at the evidence shows…\" — a polite way of saying anyone who bothered to look for five seconds would know you're wrong.
Latin currere = "to run" (via cursor, "a runner"). A cursory look literally runs past its subject.

That root is a GRE goldmine: current (water running), occur, recur, incur, concur, excursion (a run out), precursor (one who runs ahead), courier, discourse.

column2:
To cut short or reduce, usually by imposed limit.
To cut short or reduce the extent of something — a trip, a budget, a right, a freedom, a broadcast.

Two things pin it down. First, curtailing shortens; it doesn't abolish — the thing survives in a smaller form. Cancel the programme and it's gone; curtail it and it runs twenty minutes. Second, it's nearly always imposed from outside and unwelcome to someone: powers curtail liberties, illness curtails a career, a storm curtails play. You rarely curtail your own pleasures voluntarily. Register is formal-institutional — the word of policy documents and news reports, not of chat.
Curt + tail — dock the tail. The animal still walks; it's just been cut short.
The two words hiding inside give you both halves of the meaning — curt (short, clipped) and the docked tail that reminds you the thing is trimmed, not destroyed.
1. The emergency statute curtailed the right of assembly for the duration of the crisis.
2. We had to curtail the holiday by three days when his visa fell through.
The phrase you heard on loop in 2020: measures to curtail the spread of the virus — restrict and shrink it, not eliminate it.
Latin curtus = "shortened, cut off" — the same root that gives you curt (a curt reply is a clipped one).

The odd spelling comes from Old French courtault, a horse with a docked tail. English speakers heard tail in it and respelled accordingly — a false etymology that happens to be a perfect mnemonic.

So difficult or vast it saps your confidence before you start.
So large, difficult or forbidding that it drains your confidence before you begin.

The word describes an effect on the person facing the thing, not a property of the thing itself — a mountain, a reading list and a job interview can all be daunting, and none of them are dangerous. It sits well below terrifying: it's the sinking feeling at the size of the task, not fear for your safety. Note also that it's polite, faintly formal office English — "a daunting challenge" is what you call something you fully intend to do anyway.
Daunting rhymes with haunting — it looms over you before you've even started.
Both words are about something hanging over you rather than attacking you, which is exactly why daunting is intimidation, not danger.
1. The prospect of reconstructing the archive from water-damaged fragments was daunting, but she began that morning regardless.
2. Forty tabs open and a deadline tomorrow — honestly, it's a bit daunting.
In Divergent, the fearless faction is called Dauntless — literally "the un-daunt-able ones", the people nothing looms over.
Latin domāre = "to tame", via domitāre and Old French danter. To daunt someone is to tame them — break their spirit so they back down.

That gives you the high-value GRE cousin: indomitable = "un-tame-able", the person who cannot be daunted. Same root, opposite end.

To move or work far too slowly; to dilly-dally.
To move or do something far more slowly than needed, drifting along, wasting time without meaning to.

The tone is mild and often exasperated-but-fond — it's the word for children trailing behind on the walk home, not for serious obstruction. A procrastinator never starts; a loiterer hangs about one spot and looks slightly suspicious; a dawdler is genuinely on the way, just taking forever about it. There's no defiance in it, only aimlessness, which is why "stop dawdling" is a nudge rather than a rebuke.
Dawdle rhymes with waddle — you are moving, just uselessly slowly.
The rhyme locks in the key nuance: a dawdler hasn't refused the task or stopped in place, they're waddling toward it at a useless pace.
1. He dawdled over the last chapter for three months, rereading paragraphs he had already approved.
2. Don't dawdle — the film starts in ten minutes and you're still looking for socks.
column3: g18 register::neutral connotation::negative antonym::brisk-vs-dragging antonym::tireless-industry-vs-work-dodging connotation::idleness-blamed:-seven-different-accusat meaning::moving-far-too-slowly meaning::won-t-do-the-work

column2:
A shortage of something needed — scarcity, not total absence.
A scarcity of something needed or wanted — too little of it to go round.

Not zero: a dearth is a shortage, where "absence" or "void" would mean none at all. It is formal, faintly literary, and almost always followed by of + an abstract noun — a dearth of evidence, of talent, of imagination. It also carries an implied judgement: the speaker thinks there ought to be more. Lack is flat and neutral; dearth editorialises.
Dearth — when something is scarce, it becomes dear (costly).
The word is literally dear + -th, the same suffix that turns warm into warmth, so a dearth is a state of pricey scarcity, not outright nothing.
1. The commission's report cited a dearth of reliable data on long-term outcomes.
2. There's a real dearth of decent coffee round here — it's petrol-station stuff or nothing.
It's a headline-writer's staple: "a dearth of affordable housing," "a dearth of qualified nurses." If you've read an op-ed complaining that there isn't enough of something, you've met it.
Old English dēore = "costly, precious" + the suffix -th, which turns an adjective into the noun for its state: warm → warmth, long → length, true → truth, strong → strength. A dearth was originally a time when grain was dear — scarce, so expensive. The price meaning faded; the scarcity stayed.
column3: g07 register::formal connotation::negative antonym::everywhere-vs-thin-on-the-ground antonym::overflowing-supply-vs-shortage intensity::thin-supply-to-none-at-all meaning::not-enough-of-it

column2:
To lower the value, quality, or dignity of something.
To lower the value, quality, or dignity of something — usually by mixing in something inferior, cheapening it, or dragging it down morally.

The word carries a sense of corruption from within, not destruction from outside. You don't debase a thing by smashing it; you debase it by diluting it while it keeps its old name and face value. A currency is debased when the coin still says silver but is half copper; a language is debased when the words survive but mean less; a person is debased when they're made to act beneath themselves. There's always a before — something had worth, and you degraded it.
⚠️ debase ≠ abase.
- debase = cheapen the quality or worth of a thing (coinage, art, standards)
- abase = humble the status of a person, especially oneself (he abased himself before the king)

You debase the currency; you abase yourself.
De-BASE = drop it to the base metal — same face value, less gold in it.
The word wears its meaning on the outside: base metals are the cheap ones (lead, copper), so to debase is to sneak them in while the surface still looks precious.
1. Successive emperors debased the denarius until a coin of silver was a coin of copper wearing a thin silver skin.
2. He wouldn't debase himself by begging for a job he'd been doing for free all year.
"Debasing the currency" is live financial vocabulary — every argument about money-printing, inflation, or Bitcoin's fixed supply runs on it, and it means exactly what it meant to the Romans: same coin, less metal.
de- (down) + base, but not the base you stand on — this is Latin bassus, "low, short." That's the base in base metals and in the old insult "a base and cowardly act," and the bass that's a low note.

So the whole word is literally "to lower the low-ness" — to push something further down the scale of worth.

So weakening that you can no longer function.
Draining someone's strength so badly that they can no longer function normally — used of illnesses, injuries, pain, anxiety, strikes, sanctions.

The word marks a threshold, not a degree of unpleasantness. A migraine can be painful without being debilitating; it becomes debilitating the moment you can't work, drive, or stand light. Damaging means harm was done; debilitating means capacity was taken away, and usually taken away for a stretch of time rather than in one blow. It's the standard word of doctors, insurers and journalists, so it carries a clinical, matter-of-fact tone even when describing something awful.
De-BIL-itating quietly deletes your a-bil-ity.
Use it only when the thing takes function away, not when it is merely painful or inconvenient.
1. A debilitating tremor ended a surgical career that had lasted thirty years.
2. Three hours of sleep and back-to-back meetings — by Friday the tiredness was genuinely debilitating.
It's the gatekeeping word on disability and insurance paperwork: the form never asks whether your condition is bad, it asks whether it is debilitating — i.e. whether it stops you doing the job.
column3: g11 register::neutral connotation::negative antonym::full-of-life-vs-drained-of-it intensity::weakening:-from-dialed-down-to-disabled meaning::weakening-without-destroying meaning::weak-and-liable-to-break

column2:
To expose a popular claim as false or inflated.
To expose something as false, exaggerated, or fraudulent — a myth, a claim, a reputation, a theory.

You don't debunk a stray error; you debunk something that had standing. The claim was believed, promoted, maybe sold. So the word carries a puncturing quality — pretension deflated, mystique stripped off. Disprove is what a proof does, coolly and privately; debunk is public and faintly gleeful, and it puts the debunker on the side of hard sense against humbug. It also implies the exposer did work — dug up the evidence — rather than merely doubting out loud.
De-bunk = take the bunk out. Bunk is slang for nonsense, and de- strips it away.
The word is literally built to remove the rubbish from an inflated claim, which is why it always implies the claim was puffed up in the first place.
1. The biographer debunked the founder's carefully cultivated legend of self-made poverty, producing bank records that showed otherwise.
2. Took me one search to debunk that — the photo's from 2011.
MythBusters ran for fourteen years on a single verb: take a widely believed claim, test it, and stamp it BUSTED. That is debunking as a full-time job.
From bunk, short for bunkum — and bunkum is a place. In 1820 a congressman from Buncombe County, North Carolina droned on with an irrelevant speech, admitting he was only "talking for Buncombe," i.e. for the folks back home. Buncombe became American slang for empty showy talk, shortened to bunk, and in 1923 a novelist stuck de- on the front.

So the whole word means "removing the hot air from a political speech" — which is still exactly what it does.

Luxuriously self-indulgent in a way that suggests decline.
Marked by luxury and self-indulgence that signals moral or cultural decline — an empire in its late, pleasure-soaked years; art that has gone soft and ornamental; a person who lives for comfort.

The word carries an accusation inside the compliment. Luxurious praises the thing; decadent praises it while implying something is rotting underneath — that the pleasure is what people do instead of building, fighting, or believing.

That charge has been mostly drained out by advertising, where "decadent" now just means very rich and slightly naughty (chocolate, spa days). On the GRE, expect the older, harsher sense: declining, degenerate, past its peak.
⚠️ decadent ≠ decedent (dih-SEE-duhnt). A decedent is a dead person in legal language — "the decedent's estate." One is a rich dessert; the other is a corpse in a will.
Decadent desserts are decay you can taste.
Both words start from the same falling-apart idea, so even the menu version keeps a whiff of rot — pleasure on the way down.
1. Gibbon portrays a decadent Rome, its citizens numbed by spectacle while the frontiers quietly gave way.
2. Three desserts and a nap at 2pm — a decadent Sunday, and I regret nothing.
Dessert menus. "Decadent chocolate torte" is the one place marketers cheerfully advertise moral collapse — proof of how far the word has been softened.
Latin cadere = "to fall." De- + cadere = to fall away, fall off.

That root falls all through English: cascade (falling water), decay, deciduous (trees whose leaves fall), cadence (the falling of the voice), accident and coincidence (things that befall you), occident (the West, where the sun falls).

Work out the meaning of something coded or barely legible.
To work out the meaning of something that resists being read — a coded message, a dead script, a doctor's handwriting, someone's motives.

The word always implies obstruction plus effort: there is a meaning in there, and something is in the way. Decode and decrypt are technical and systematic (you have a key, a method, a machine); decipher can be pure squinting persistence, and works just as well on a scrawled note as on Linear B. Interpret assumes the text is legible and the difficulty is in the meaning; decipher assumes the difficulty is in getting at the message at all. The negative, indecipherable, is the form you'll meet most often on the exam.
De-cipher = take the cipher off it — strip the disguise, and the meaning was there all along.
The de- is subtraction, so you're not creating meaning, you're removing whatever was hiding it.
1. Scholars spent two decades attempting to decipher the tablets, whose script had no surviving bilingual key.
2. I still can't decipher what my dad wrote on this shopping list — is that "eggs" or "legs"?
The Imitation Game — Turing and the Bletchley Park team deciphering Enigma is the most famous act of deciphering in modern history, and the film is essentially two hours of the word in action.
Cipher comes from Arabic ṣifr = "zero, empty" — the same word that gave English zero. When Arabic numerals reached medieval Europe, the strange new symbols looked like secret writing, so cipher drifted from "zero" to "code."

Both senses survive: you decipher a coded message, and a person of no consequence is dismissed as "a mere cipher" — a zero, a placeholder. That second sense is the one the GRE likes.

Proper, dignified conduct that fits the occasion.
Behaviour that fits the occasion — dignified, restrained, correct by the unwritten rules of the setting. The adjective is decorous.

Note what it is not about: goodness. Decorum governs form, not morality — you can be a scoundrel and still observe perfect decorum at the funeral. It's also entirely situational: what counts as decorum in a courtroom differs from a wedding, and breaching it offends the occasion rather than any principle. The word itself is formal and faintly institutional — judges demand "order and decorum," Parliament invokes it, your friends never do.
Decorum is décor for behaviour.
Décor is what makes a room look right for its purpose; decorum is what makes your conduct look right for the room — both are about surface fittingness, not inner worth.
1. The chamber maintained a chilly decorum even as the two ministers traded accusations through gritted teeth.
2. Try to show some decorum at dinner — it's her parents, not the lads.
Wilfred Owen's Dulce et Decorum Est — Horace's line that it is "sweet and fitting to die for one's country," which Owen calls "the old Lie." The poem's whole force comes from that word meaning seemly, what the occasion demands.
Latin decēre = "to be fitting, to be seemly." The neuter of decōrus ("becoming") gave the noun.

The root pays out widely: decent (fitting, hence respectable), decorous, decorate, décor — and, negated, indecent. All circle the same idea of what suits.

To condemn something loudly and publicly.
To condemn something openly and loudly — to denounce it as wrong, harmful, or worthless.

Volume and audience are built in. You can criticise a policy quietly over coffee, but you decry it from a podium, in print, in public. It also aims at things rather than people: you decry a trend, a ruling, a shortage, a fashion — where denounce points a finger at a person. And it carries a faint moral posture; the person decrying is taking a stand, sometimes more than they're making an argument.
⚠️ decry ≠ descry. Descry (also di-SKRYE) means to catch sight of something far off — "he descried a sail on the horizon." One condemns, one merely spots.
Decry has cry in it — nobody decries anything quietly.
The word is literally "to cry down": public noise aimed at dragging something's value to zero.
1. Economists decried the tariffs as a tax on the poor dressed up as patriotism.
2. Everyone decries the group chat until they need something from it.
A headline workhorse — \"Critics decry the ruling,\" \"Residents decry cuts to bus routes.\" Journalists reach for it precisely because it means complained loudly and publicly without conceding the complaint was right.
Old French descrier = "to cry down" — de- (down) + crier (to cry, to proclaim). It was originally a money word: a king could decry a coin, publicly proclaiming it worthless so nobody would take it. That's still the shape of the modern sense — shouting a thing's value down to nothing.

To attack someone's reputation with false public statements.
To damage someone's reputation by saying or publishing false things about them.

The falsity is built in — you cannot defame someone with the truth, however brutal. That's what separates it from insult or criticise: an insult wounds the person, defamation rewrites how everyone else sees them. It's also public by nature (a private sneer defames nobody) and carries a courtroom hum — defamation is an actual tort, split into libel (written) and slander (spoken).
defame ≠ defile. Defame blackens a reputation with lies; defile dirties something sacred or pure — a temple, a river, a memory.
De-fame — you are removing the fame, i.e. stripping off the good name, and you're doing it with a lie.
The word wears its meaning on the outside: fame here means "reputation," and the de- pulls it down.
1. The pamphlet defamed the magistrate as a taker of bribes, a charge the court found to be wholly invented.
2. Say that about me in public and I'll sue you for defaming me.
The Depp v. Heard trial (2022) — streamed and memed for six weeks — was a defamation suit: the argument was never "she was mean," it was "she published something false that destroyed his name."
Latin fāma = "report, rumour, what people say about you" — so fame originally just meant reputation, good or bad.

That root pays off across the list: famous, infamous (famous for something bad), infamy, defamation.

Respectful yielding to another's judgment or authority.
Respectful yielding — letting someone else's judgment, wishes, or authority prevail over your own.

The yielding is voluntary and measured. Obedience is compelled; servility and obsequiousness are grovelling; deference is the polite half-step back you take for seniority, rank, or expertise, and it usually reflects well on you. Note the common frame "in deference to" — in deference to her grief, we cancelled the party — where it means "out of respect for," not "in submission to." Push it too far and it curdles: deferential can be a quiet insult, describing someone with no opinions of his own.
⚠️ deferential ≠ differential. Deferential = respectfully yielding. Differential = to do with a difference (a differential rate, a car's differential). One bows; the other subtracts.
Deference = defer + -ence: you defer to them — hand over the call, with a slight bow rather than a white flag.
The bow marks the respect and the "slight" marks the limit — it's courtesy, not surrender.
1. The junior barrister spoke last, in deference to counsel who had argued the case for thirty years.
2. I don't actually like sushi — I picked the place out of deference to the birthday girl.
In law, "Chevron deference" was the rule that courts should defer to a government agency's reading of a statute — the judges standing back and letting the experts' interpretation stand. The Supreme Court scrapped it in 2024, and every headline was about courts no longer deferring.
Latin dēferre = "to carry down, bring low, submit" — de- (down) + ferre (to carry). You carry your own view downward so someone else's can sit on top.

ferre is a GRE workhorse: transfer (carry across), refer (carry back), confer (carry together), infer (carry in), offer, suffer, fertile.

To turn aside; to fend off blame by redirecting it.
To turn something aside from its course — a bullet, a blow, a beam of light. Figuratively: to fend off criticism, blame, or an awkward question by steering attention elsewhere.

The key is that nothing is stopped or absorbed — it is angled away. A blocker takes the hit; a deflector lets it glance off. That's why the figurative use carries a faint whiff of evasion: you rebut a charge by answering it, you deflect it by making it someone else's problem. Compared with dodge or duck, though, deflect sounds practised and controlled — the politician who deflects is smooth, not panicking.
deflect ≠ defect — one letter apart. Deflect = bend aside. Defect (n.) = a flaw; (v., dee-FEKT) = to desert your country or side.
Reflect bends it back; deflect bends it away — either way, it never sticks to you.
Both share flect ("bend"), so the prefix does all the work: re- returns the thing to its source, de- just sends it off sideways.
1. Pressed on the missing funds, the minister deflected the question toward his predecessor and moved briskly on.
2. Every time I ask him about the wedding date he deflects — suddenly he's very interested in the dog.
Deflector shields in Star Wars and Star Trek: they don't absorb incoming fire, they bend it away from the hull — the word's literal job, in one bit of sci-fi hardware.
Latin de- (away) + flectere (to bend). That root is a GRE goldmine: flexible (bendable), reflect (bend back), inflection (a bend in a curve, or in the voice), genuflect (bend the knee), flexor (the muscle that bends a joint).

Skilful and quick, with a light, effortless touch.
Skilful and quick — handling something with neat, economical, unfussy competence.

Skilful is a general compliment; deft is about the lightness of touch. A deft move looks effortless and takes no more effort than it needs — a surgeon's stitch, a diplomat sidestepping a hostile question, a chef boning a fish in four seconds. It praises finesse rather than power or brilliance, and it's often used of small physical movements or delicate social manoeuvres. Nothing in it is negative: deft is admiring, mildly formal, and a favourite of critics ("a deft touch").
Deft is daft with one letter changed — and one is all quick skill, the other all foolishness.
They really are relatives (both from Old English gedæfte, "gentle, meek"), but the meanings split hard, so let the near-spelling remind you deft = clever hands, daft = no sense at all.
1. The negotiator's deft handling of the walkout kept both delegations at the table.
2. She deftly flipped the pancake without even looking up from her phone.
The stock film-review phrase "a deft touch" — critics reach for it whenever a director handles tricky material lightly instead of hammering it.
🚫 Not related to deaf, despite the spelling. But it is the same word as daft: Old English gedæfte meant "mild, gentle," which drifted one way into "meek → silly" (daft) and the other into "fitting, skilful" (deft).

column2:
To make a god of; to exalt beyond all criticism.
To make a god of something — literally, in the religious sense (Rome deified its dead emperors), or figuratively, to treat a person or thing as above criticism.

In modern use it's almost always the figurative one, and it usually carries a shrug of disapproval. Admire is fine, idolise is a bit much, deify says the worshipper has lost all judgment — the object can now do no wrong. Note the direction: you deify someone else. It describes the fans, the biographers, the party faithful, and quietly indicts them.
⚠️ deify ≠ edify. One letter apart, both about raising someone up — but edify = instruct, improve morally (an edifying book), while deify = worship. A sermon edifies the congregation; the congregation deifies the preacher.
-fy = make it so: simpl*ify*, pur*ify*, dei*fy* — make a deity out of a man.
The word is just deity with the factory suffix bolted on, and the promotion is always undeserved — men don't qualify.
1. Later historians deified the founder, scrubbing the massacres out of the record and leaving only the marble.
2. Stop deifying your manager — he's a guy with a spreadsheet, not an oracle.
The Roman Senate really did vote emperors into godhood after death — which is why Vespasian, dying, is said to have cracked: "Vae, puto deus fio" — "Dear me, I think I'm becoming a god."
Latin deus (god) + -ficare (to make, from facere). Literally "god-make."

Deus is a workhorse root: deity, divine, deism, deus ex machina — and adieu, which is French à Dieu, "to God."
