column2:
Harmful — quietly, cumulatively, in the clinical sense.
Harmful; causing damage, especially to health or wellbeing.

This is the lab-coat word for harm. Destructive is loud and ruinous is final, but deleterious harm is quiet and cumulative — the damage sleep debt does to your heart, the damage a policy does to a school system over a decade. It also carries an air of clinical detachment: a doctor, a scientist, or a report says "deleterious effects." A person shouting at you does not.
⚠️ deleterious ≠ delirious. Deleterious = harmful. Delirious = wildly confused or wildly excited. Similar mouthfeel, unrelated meanings — a fever can leave you delirious, and the fever itself is deleterious.
Deleterious doesn't erase you — it erodes you.
The lookalike "delete" gets you to harm, and the correction — erode, not erase — gets you to the slow, accumulating kind of harm the word actually names.
1. Prolonged exposure to low-level noise has a measurably deleterious effect on children's reading comprehension.
2. Three coffees after 8pm is a deleterious habit and I'm choosing not to think about it.
In genetics, every mutation gets sorted into one of three buckets: beneficial, neutral, or deleterious. It's the standard technical label — which is exactly why the word sounds like a paper rather than an insult.
Greek dēleisthai = "to hurt, injure" → dēlētērios, "noxious."

🚫 Nothing to do with delete. That's Latin delere, "to blot out" (deletion, indelible). The resemblance is pure coincidence — useful as a hook, false as history.

Done on purpose after weighing it; or, to weigh carefully.
Adjective, sense 1: done on purpose, with the consequences already weighed — not accidental, not impulsive.
Adjective, sense 2: unhurried and measured — "a deliberate pace," "deliberate movements."
Verb: to think or discuss something over carefully before deciding.

Intentional just means you meant it. Deliberate says you thought about it first — which is why it's the word prosecutors and critics reach for: deliberate cruelty, a deliberate snub, a deliberate falsehood. The forethought is what makes it damning. Turned the other way, the same forethought is a compliment: a deliberate craftsman, a deliberate decision. Sense 2 is the same idea applied to speed — deliberate slowness isn't sluggishness, it's someone taking the time the thing deserves.
De-LIBRA-te — the scales are sitting in the middle of the word. You weigh first, then act.
Weighing takes time, which gives you both senses at once: the slow measured pace, and the fact that whatever follows was decided, not stumbled into.
1. The committee deliberated for six hours before conceding that no version of the proposal could survive a vote.
2. That wasn't a slip of the tongue — she left his name off the list, and it was 100% deliberate.
"The jury is still deliberating" — the line every courtroom drama and news bulletin uses for the hours the verdict takes. Twelve people in a room, weighing.
Latin dē- + lībrāre = "to weigh out," from lībra, a pair of scales. Same libra as the zodiac sign Libra (the scales), as equilibrium (equal weights), and as the lb abbreviation for pound.

🚫 Not liber, "free." That's liberate, liberty, liberal — a different root that happens to look identical. Deliberating has nothing to do with freeing anything.

To mark out the exact boundaries or outline of something.
To draw the outline of something, or — far more often on the GRE — to describe it precisely, edge to edge, so its limits are unmistakable.

The word is about boundaries, not detail. You describe a landscape; you delineate a border. To delineate two theories is to show exactly where one stops and the other begins; to delineate a role is to say what falls inside it and what does not. It's a cool, technical, faintly bureaucratic verb — the language of contracts, treaties, and organisational charts, never of gossip. Its natural companion adverb is clearly, and the reason it collocates so hard is that the whole point of delineating is removing ambiguity.
de-LINE-ate — you draw a line around it.
The word wears its meaning in the middle: not "tell me about it," but "put a line where it ends."
1. The treaty delineated the frontier river by river, leaving no stretch of the border open to interpretation.
2. Before we start, can someone delineate who's actually responsible for what? I've had three people tell me it's not their job.
Read almost any job description or team charter and you'll hit "clearly delineated roles and responsibilities" — corporate boilerplate for we have drawn lines so you can't blame each other.

A false belief clung to despite all evidence.
A false belief held with full conviction and immune to evidence — and, by extension, the state of holding one.

A mistake gets corrected. An illusion dissolves the moment someone shows you the wires. A delusion survives its own refutation — that's the defining feature, and why the word indicts the believer, not the belief. There's a clinical shadow on it too (psychiatry uses delusion as a technical term for a fixed false belief), so calling someone's plan a delusion isn't saying it's wrong; it's saying they can't be reached. In everyday use — delusions of grandeur, she's delusional — the tone drops from diagnostic to mocking.
⚠️ delusion ≠ illusion.
- illusion = out in the world — a trick of light or stagecraft that fools everyone looking
- delusion = inside the head — it fools only its owner

You share an illusion with the whole audience. You hold a delusion alone.
A mistake dies when you show it the evidence; a delusion grips harder.
What makes a belief a delusion isn't that it's false — it's that contradicting it only tightens the hold.
1. The regime's last months were governed by the delusion that the army was still loyal and the borders still held.
2. If you reckon you'll pass that exam without opening the book once, that's not confidence, mate, that's a delusion.
\"Delusions of grandeur\" is the phrase you've heard a hundred times — and it tells you something: delusions tend to arrive flattering, sized to fit the person holding them.
Latin dēlūdere = "to play false, to mock" — from lūdere, "to play" (ludus = a game). A delusion is reality playing you for a fool.

That root pays out across the whole exam: ludicrous (fit to be laughed at), prelude / interlude (played before / between), allude (play toward — hint at), elude (play away from — escape), collude (play together — secretly), illusion, elusive.

To object mildly or hesitate rather than flatly refuse.
To raise an objection or hesitate before agreeing — to balk, politely.

The force is deliberately low. A person who refuses has said no; a person who demurs has only signalled reluctance — a raised eyebrow, a "well, I'm not sure that's quite right," a delay dressed as courtesy. It's the vocabulary of boardrooms, courts and diplomacy, where open refusal is rude but silence is consent. Often it's a way of not answering at all: asked to comment, he demurred.
⚠️ demur ≠ demure.
- demur (dih-MER, verb) = object mildly, hesitate
- demure (dih-MYOOR, adj.) = modest, shy, reserved in manner

One letter, different word class, different meaning. A demure guest might still demur.
demur ends in -mur, as in murmur — an objection murmured, never shouted.
That murmur captures the strength of it: audible disagreement, well short of a no.
1. Counsel demurred at the judge's characterisation of the evidence, though he declined to press the point.
2. I asked if he'd cover my shift and he demurred — didn't say no, just went very quiet about it.
Standard press-conference shorthand: when a reporter asks a politician whether she'll run and the write-up says "she demurred," it means she dodged without ever refusing.
Latin morari = "to delay" (from mora, a delay), with de-. To demur was originally to hold things up — which is exactly why it still means hesitating rather than refusing.

Same root: moratorium (an official delay), and the legal demurrer (a plea that stalls a case).

To belittle unfairly; to blacken someone's reputation.
To attack someone's reputation or belittle their worth — to run them down unfairly.

The unfairness is baked in. You can criticise a book fairly, but to denigrate it is to talk it down beyond what it deserves, and the word quietly convicts the speaker as much as the target. It also tends to be a campaign rather than an outburst: a steady drip of belittling remarks, often about a person's character, competence, or achievements. Register is formal — it's the word of editorials, HR policies and eulogies-in-reverse, not of a pub argument.
denigrate ≠ deprecate. To denigrate is to blacken someone else's name; to deprecate is to express mild disapproval — which is why self-deprecating is charming (you're gently mocking yourself) and self-denigrating would be bleak.
de-NIG-RATE — you de-rate them: knock their rating down below what it's worth.
The word ends in the sound of rate, and denigrating is exactly that — marking someone down unfairly rather than judging them accurately.
1. The memoir is generous to his rivals, refusing to denigrate even the men who engineered his downfall.
2. Stop denigrating your own work — you spent two years on that thing.
Latin de- (completely) + niger (black) → denigrare, "to blacken." You blacken a name, and the reputation is what's stained.

Same niger gives French noir — as in film noir, the genre literally named "black film."

column2:
To condemn publicly and forcefully.
To condemn something publicly and openly — to stand up and declare a person, act, or idea evil, false, or intolerable. Secondary sense: to inform against someone to the authorities ("he was denounced to the police").

Volume is built into the word. You can disapprove privately and criticise mildly, but you cannot denounce quietly — it's a public act, aimed at an audience, and it puts the speaker's own reputation behind the charge. It also outranks criticise in heat: criticism finds fault, denunciation demands that others share the outrage.
⚠️ denounce ≠ renounce.
- denounce = publicly attack someone else's wrongdoing
- renounce = formally give up something of your own (a claim, a throne, a faith)

A cardinal may denounce heresy; a king renounces the throne.
De-NOUNCE = announce, turned against someone.
Same -nounce as announce, so it's inherently a public broadcast — the de- just aims it downward at a target.
1. In a speech to the assembly, she denounced the new statute as a licence for the powerful to rob the poor.
2. He went online and denounced the whole company by name, which felt great for about a day.
Orwell's 1984 runs on the second sense — children are trained to denounce their own parents to the Thought Police, and Parsons is turned in by his seven-year-old daughter.
Latin nuntiare = "to announce" (from nuntius, a messenger), plus de- "down, against."

The root is a GRE workhorse: announce, pronounce, renounce, enunciate, nuncio (the Pope's messenger-ambassador). Note the spelling shift in the noun — denounce → denunciation, where the Latin nunti- resurfaces.

How you carry yourself — posture, bearing, and manners.
The way a person carries and conducts themselves — posture, bearing, and outward manners.

This is behaviour as graded by an onlooker. It's a schoolmaster's word, faintly old-fashioned and institutional: the thing finishing schools taught and report cards scored. Where demeanour is the air or mood you give off, deportment is the visible discipline of the body and its manners — how you stand, sit, enter a room, address your elders — measured against a standard of propriety.
⚠️ deportment ≠ deportation. Both grew out of deport, but they split: deportment = how you carry yourself; deportation = being carried out of the country. The exam likes this gap.
Port = carry, so deportment is how you carry yourself — which is exactly why its synonym is bearing.
Both words are the same idea twice: deportment carries the Latin for "carry," and bearing carries the English one.
1. The headmistress praised her deportment — spine straight, hands still, not a word out of turn.
2. Loved the interview answers, but his deportment was a mess — slouched, fidgeting, checking his phone.
The old finishing-school exercise of walking across a room with a book balanced on your head — that class was literally called deportment, and British school reports once carried a grade for it beside conduct.
Latin portāre = "to carry." One root, a large family: portable, transport, export, porter, portfolio (a case for carrying loose leaves), comport and comportment (a near-twin of deportment).

To remove a ruler from power; to take sworn testimony.
Two distinct senses, both worth knowing:

1. To remove someone from high office — a king, a dictator, a party leader — by force or by formal act.
2. (Legal) To take sworn testimony from someone out of court, or to give it yourself.

Sense 1 is the GRE one, and it's specifically about rank. You depose a ruler, not a shop assistant; the word carries the weight of a throne or a presidency. It's also colder and more formal than its neighbours: overthrow implies violence, oust is scrappy and can apply to anyone, abdicate is the ruler stepping down willingly — depose is the neutral, almost procedural statement that the office was taken away. A palace coup, a vote of no confidence, and an armed revolt can all depose a leader.

Sense 2 turns up in every legal thriller: the lawyer deposes the witness, and the transcript is the deposition.
De-pose = to un-pose: take the king down off his royal pose — or put your sworn words down on the record.
Both senses are literally "putting down": a monarch down from the throne, testimony down onto the page.
1. The generals deposed the emperor within a week, installing a nephew who could be relied upon to sign whatever they put in front of him.
2. They deposed the CEO over a WhatsApp group before he'd even landed.
In any legal drama — Suits, Better Call Saul — someone is always being deposed in a glass conference room: sworn in, recorded, no judge in sight. That's sense 2 in its natural habitat.
Latin de- (down) + ponere (to put, to place) — literally to put down.

That root is a GRE goldmine: deposit (put down money), position, compose, impose, postpone (put after), component, exponent, repository.

column2:
Deep, settled moral corruption — wickedness as character, not slip.
Deep, thoroughgoing moral corruption — wickedness that has settled into the character rather than flared up once.

The word is heavy and judgemental, with a pulpit or courtroom behind it. Immorality is a category, vice is a habit, but depravity says the rot goes all the way down: this person is not tempted, they are spoiled. It's the term reached for in cases of cruelty, perversion, and appetite indulged past any restraint — never for a small lapse. Calling someone's conduct depraved marks the speaker as morally appalled, not merely disapproving.
⚠️ depravity ≠ deprivation.
- depravity = you are morally rotten (Latin pravus, crooked)
- deprivation = you have been denied something (Latin privare, to strip)

Slum children suffer deprivation; the men who exploit them show depravity.
Depravity rhymes with gravity — a constant moral falling, not one stumble.
Gravity pulls always and everywhere, which is exactly the claim the word makes: the corruption is permanent and total, not an isolated slip.
1. The report catalogued a depravity the committee's members had not believed possible in a licensed institution.
2. He watched two hours of the show and declared the whole thing a monument to human depravity — then queued up episode three.
"Depraved indifference" — the US homicide standard you've heard every prosecutor say on Law & Order: killing not by intent but by a recklessness so total it shows contempt for human life.
Latin pravus = "crooked, bent", with de- as an intensifier: utterly bent. English morality runs on the straight/crooked metaphor — upright, rectitude, straight-laced, correct — and depravity is that line warped out of true.

To disapprove of mildly; to mark as obsolete.
To express disapproval of something — to say, in measured terms, that it is undesirable or ill-advised. In tech, the specialised sense: to mark as obsolete, still working but officially discouraged and headed for removal.

The disapproval is cool, not hot. You denounce a scandal, you condemn a crime — you deprecate a tendency, a habit, a fashion. It's the disapproval of a committee or a leading article: dry, authoritative, no raised voice. That mildness is why self-deprecating means playing yourself down with a joke rather than actually attacking yourself.
⚠️ deprecate ≠ depreciate.
- deprecate = disapprove of, discourage
- depreciate = fall in value (a car depreciates the moment you drive it off the lot)

Note the extra i — and that self-deprecating is the standard form.
Depreciate drops the price; deprecate drops the praise.
One is about worth on a balance sheet, the other about approval withheld — politely.
1. The editorial deprecated the government's habit of legislating by press release, though it stopped short of calling for resignations.
2. Careful — that function's been deprecated since version 3; it still runs, but it'll vanish next release.
Every programmer meets this word as a yellow warning: `DeprecationWarning` — your code works today, but the maintainers officially disapprove and are removing it.
Latin de- ("away") + precari ("to pray") — to pray something away, to avert it by entreaty. It started as a plea, not an attack, which is exactly why the modern word still disapproves so quietly.

Same root: imprecation (a curse — praying at someone), precarious (held only by someone else's goodwill, so liable to collapse), and plain pray.

To mock something as beneath serious consideration.
To mock or ridicule — to laugh at something as beneath serious consideration.

The contempt is what does the work. Tease is affectionate, mock can be playful, but to deride is to dismiss from above: the target isn't just funny, it's worthless. It's the verb of choice for critics and columnists — proposals, films, and beliefs get derided, usually in public and usually by someone who thinks the matter is already settled. Noun form derision carries the same sneer.
⚠️ deride ≠ decry.
- deride = laugh at it as ridiculous
- decry = denounce it as wrong or harmful

You deride a silly idea; you decry an injustice. Derision is amused; decrying is deadly serious.
deride rhymes with snide — the laugh comes with a sneer.
Both words pair humour with contempt, which is exactly what separates deriding from merely teasing.
1. Contemporary reviewers derided the novel as sentimental trash; a century later it is required reading.
2. Everyone derided his plan to drive there in one go — then he did it in eleven hours.
"Widely derided" is a standing phrase in tech and film journalism — the fixed label for a product launch or sequel the internet decided to laugh at.
Latin rīdēre = "to laugh", plus de- (down, at) — to laugh down at someone.

That root is worth banking: ridiculous (laughable), ridicule, derision, and the GRE favourite risible (RIZ-uh-buhl, laughable, absurd).

Unoriginal; drawn wholly from an earlier source.
Adj.: taken from an existing source rather than invented — and therefore unoriginal.
Noun: a thing that comes from something else (in finance, a contract whose value is drawn entirely from an underlying asset).

As criticism it is cold rather than angry. Calling a novel derivative is not calling it stolen or fake — the writer did the work, honestly. The charge is that everything worth noticing in it came from somewhere else, so there is nothing of the maker in it. Reviewers, examiners and critics reach for it precisely because it sounds measured: plagiarised is a legal accusation, hackneyed is a sneer, derivative is a diagnosis.
Derivative = derive + im*itative* — it flows from a source, so it has no source of its own.
The insult is not theft but dependence: pull out what it borrowed and nothing is left standing.
1. The jury praised her technique but found the collection derivative, a careful echo of designers who had shown a decade earlier.
2. It's not a bad album, it's just derivative — you can name the band behind every track.
A financial derivative — an option, a future — has no value of its own; every penny it is worth is drawn from the asset underneath it. That is the adjective in one object.
Latin dē- (away) + rīvus (stream) → dērīvāre, to draw water off from a channel. A derivative work is a ditch led off someone else's river.

Same root: river, derive, and — pleasingly — rival, from rivales, two people forced to share one stream.

column2:
To dry out completely; to drain of all moisture or vitality.
To dry out completely — to remove every trace of moisture, preserving the thing as a husk.

Dry is a state; desiccate is a process taken to its limit. You don't desiccate a shirt on a radiator — you desiccate fruit, soil, a corpse. The result is shrivelled and rigid, but it keeps.

The figurative use is where the GRE lives: a desiccated prose style, a desiccated old don, a desiccated marriage — technically intact, emotionally drained of all juice. It's a sneer about lifelessness, not about aridity.
⚠️ desiccate ≠ desecrate (DES-uh-krayt). Desiccate = dry to a husk; desecrate = violate something sacred. A drought desiccates a field; a vandal desecrates a grave.
Desiccate doesn't dry something off — it dries something out.
Towels dry you off; a desiccant packet dries the whole box out until nothing living is left in it.
1. Centuries in the sealed tomb had desiccated the body until the skin lay on the bone like paper.
2. Forty years of committee work had desiccated him — all procedure, no pulse.
Every shoebox, vitamin bottle and beef-jerky bag contains a little sachet marked DESICCANT — DO NOT EAT: silica gel, there to desiccate the air inside.
Latin siccus = "dry", with de- as an intensifier: dry thoroughly. That intensifying de- is why the word means total drying rather than mere dampness removed.

Ruling by absolute personal power, arbitrarily and oppressively.
Exercising absolute power arbitrarily and oppressively — the rule of one person whose will is the only law.

Authoritarian describes a system; despotic points at a person. The word carries whim as much as cruelty: a despot doesn't just oppress, he oppresses however he feels like today, with nobody able to say no. That's why it scales down so easily — a despotic manager, a despotic father, a despotic committee chair. Always an accusation, never neutral, and slightly grander and more literary than bossy or dictatorial.
des-POT-ic — the stress lands on POT, the same pot as potent and potentate: one person holds the whole pot of power.
Say it out loud and the emphasis itself tells you where the power sits — all of it in one hand.
1. The reforms were less a concession than a performance: despotic rule dressed in the vocabulary of consent.
2. He runs that kitchen on despotic lines — nobody plates a thing until he's inspected it.
History class gives you the fixed phrase "enlightened despot" — Frederick the Great, Catherine the Great — rulers who kept every scrap of absolute power and simply promised to use it well.
Greek despotēs = "master of the house" — literally house-lord. That's the nuance in miniature: a despot treats a whole country as his private household, where his word simply is the rule.

The -pot- is the power root: potent, potential, omnipotent, potentate, plenipotentiary.

Aimless, half-hearted, hopping from thing to thing.
Moving from one thing to another without plan, method, or enthusiasm — aimless and half-hearted at the same time.

Two ingredients have to be present. Random alone isn't enough: desultory carries a distinct droop of energy, the sense that nobody much cared whether the thing got finished. A desultory conversation drifts and dies; desultory revision is twenty minutes here, a different chapter there, nothing retained. It's a quietly damning word — the critic's way of saying an effort was made, technically.
desultory ≠ dilatory.
- desultory = doing it aimlessly, hopping about
- dilatory = doing it late, dragging your feet

A dilatory student hasn't started. A desultory one has started four times.
De-SULT-ory work gets no re-SULT — you leap off before anything lands.
Both words hide Latin salire, "to leap," and the hidden result is exactly what desultory effort never produces.
1. The committee's desultory inquiry sprawled over three years and concluded nothing.
2. We had a desultory chat about the weather and then both pretended our phones had buzzed.
Cricket and football writing leans on it constantly — "a desultory afternoon session," "desultory passing in midfield" — meaning the players were technically out there and not really playing.
Latin desultor — the circus trick-rider who leapt from one galloping horse to another (de- "off" + salire "to leap"). Desultory is the mind doing that: never on one horse long enough to ride it anywhere.

Salire is a high-yield GRE root: salient (leaping out at you), resilient (leaping back), exult, insult, assail, somersault.

column2:
Discourage someone from acting by making the consequences frightening.
To stop someone from doing something by making the prospect of it frightening or costly — prevention through fear of consequences.

The mechanism matters: you don't deter someone with a good argument, you deter them with a threat, a risk, a price. Dissuade works on reasons; deter works on nerve. Note also that the target is usually the action, not the person's opinion — a deterred burglar still wants your TV, he just isn't willing to pay for it. It's the standard verb of security, policing, and defence policy, and it stays cool and neutral even when what's doing the deterring is a fence, a fine, or a warhead.
⚠️ deter ≠ defer.
- deter = frighten off an action
- defer = postpone it, or yield to someone's judgment (I defer to the expert)

One letter, opposite jobs: bad weather deterred the climbers; the climbers deferred the ascent.
deTERror — hiding inside deter is terror, because that's the tool it uses.
If nobody's afraid of anything, nobody's been deterred — you've only persuaded them.
1. Steep fines have done little to deter illegal dumping along the riverbank.
2. Don't let one bad review deter you — just send the thing out again.
The Cold War ran on deterrence: neither side attacked because the retaliation would be unsurvivable. Same logic, smaller scale, on every "CCTV in operation" sign — the camera isn't there to catch you, it's there to put you off.
Latin dē- (away) + terrēre (to frighten) — literally to frighten away.

That terrēre is the big prize: terror, terrify, terrible, terrific (originally "causing terror"), and deterrent. Once you hear the terror in deter, the definition is automatic.

To take away from the value or merit of something.
To take away from the value, quality, or good impression of something — usually a small subtraction, not a demolition.

To ruin is total; to detract is a shaving-off. A cracked frame detracts from a painting — the painting is still good, just worth a little less. Note the grammar, because the GRE tests it: you detract from something, never detract something. The second, rarer sense is human — to disparage, to talk a reputation down, which is why a critic is a detractor.
detract ≠ distract. Distract pulls your attention away; detract pulls the value down. A ringing phone distracts you from the film; bad acting detracts from it.
Nothing detracts a thing — things detract from it, one notch down, never to zero.
Lock in the preposition and you've locked in the size of the damage: partial, not fatal.
1. The clumsy final chapter does not seriously detract from a novel of otherwise remarkable control.
2. Sure, the seats are ugly, but that hardly detracts from a car this cheap.
Detractors is the word sports and political coverage reaches for constantly — "his detractors say he peaked three seasons ago." Same root, and it tells you exactly what a detractor does: chips away at your standing.
Latin de- (down, away) + trahere (to pull, drag) — to drag value downward.

trahere is one of the highest-yield GRE roots: tractor (pulls), attract (pulls toward), extract (pulls out), retract (pulls back), subtract (pulls out from under), protract (drags out lengthwise), contract (pulls together), abstract (pulled away from the concrete).

Harmful or damaging, usually gradually and stated clinically.
Causing harm, loss, or damage — especially harm that shows up as a measurable effect on something.

It's the cool, official word for bad. Devastating shouts, pernicious implies something creeping and sinister, but detrimental is what a doctor, an auditor, or an HR report says: harm stated as a finding, with no anger in it. It also barely stands alone — you're almost always detrimental to something (health, morale, the environment, your case). And the harm is usually cumulative rather than a single blow: late nights are detrimental to your health; a bullet is not.
Detri-mental hides TRIM — it trims a bit off you at a time, and the tone stays clinical, never furious.
The hidden "trim" gives you both halves of the word: steady wearing-away, described in a calm official voice.
1. The committee concluded that the proposed tariffs would be detrimental to long-term growth in the region.
2. Look, three hours of doomscrolling before bed is detrimental to literally everything about you.
This is the house style of public-health and workplace copy — "detrimental to your health," "detrimental to team morale." When an institution wants to say this is hurting you without sounding alarmed or accusing anyone, this is the word it reaches for.
Latin terere = "to rub, wear away"; de- + terere → dēterere, "to rub off," giving dētrīmentum, damage caused by wearing down.

That root pays out across the GRE: attrition (wearing away by friction), trite (an idea rubbed smooth by overuse), detritus (the debris left after rubbing away), contrite (crushed, worn down by guilt).

To turn aside from a set course, plan, or standard.
To turn aside from an established course, standard, or norm — a route, a plan, a protocol, an average.

The word only works if there is a fixed path to leave; it always implies a reference line. That makes it cooler and more measurable than its neighbours: you stray aimlessly, you digress in speech, but you deviate from something specified — the flight plan, the recipe, the mean. Left alone it's neutral, even clinical (engineers and statisticians live in it). The disapproval is imported by context: deviate from procedure is an accusation, and the shadow of deviant darkens the word whenever the norm being left is a social one.
de-VIA-te — there's a via sitting in the middle: you go off the via, off the way.
Spotting via reminds you the word needs a road to leave — no established path, no deviation.
1. The pilot deviated from the filed route to skirt a line of thunderstorms.
2. Follow the recipe exactly — the one time I deviated, it came out like glue.
Standard deviation — the stats measure you've met a hundred times. It's literally the average amount your data wanders off the mean.
Latin de- (away from) + via (road, way) — "off the road."

Via is a workhorse root: devious (off-road, hence sneaky), obvious (ob-via — lying in the way, so you can't miss it), trivial (tri-via — the three-way crossroads where people swapped idle gossip), envoy, voyage, viaduct.

Sneaky and scheming; getting there by crooked, indirect means.
Getting what you want by sneaky, roundabout, underhanded means; scheming. (Literal, older sense: winding, indirect — "a devious mountain track.")

The word's eye is on the route, not the lie. Dishonest judges your morals; devious describes your method — the loops, the cover stories, the third party who "happened" to mention it. Because the method takes brains, devious carries a flicker of grudging respect that deceitful never has, and it's the one you can aim at a sibling half-fondly. Aimed at a politician or a contract, it's not fond at all.
⚠️ devious ≠ dubious. Devious = sneaky, a quality of the person or plan. Dubious = doubtful, either uncertain yourself or not to be trusted. A dubious scheme might just be badly thought out; a devious one was thought out very well.
A devious plan can earn a grudging smile — a dishonest person never does.
Devious points at the ingenuity of the crooked route, which is why it's the one accusation that can double as a compliment.
1. The report exposed a devious arrangement of shell companies, each one routing the money a further step from its owner.
2. You told Mum I was at the library so you could take the car? That's devious.
The 2021 TikTok craze of filming yourself stealing school property was called the "devious lick" — sneaky, planned, and pleased with itself, which is the word exactly.
Latin de- (off) + via (road) = "off the main road." The devious person won't travel in a straight line.

That via is a GRE workhorse: deviate (turn off the road), obvious (ob + via — lying right in your way, so you can't miss it), trivial (tri + via — where three roads meet, the street corner where the cheap gossip is), plus viaduct, convey, envoy.

column2:
Skilful and quick, especially with the hands.
Skilful and quick, above all with the hands — a surgeon, a pickpocket, a pianist. Extended sense: mentally nimble, handling a tricky situation with ease.

This is plain praise for fine motor control and speed, with no hint of trickery in it — a dexterous fraudster is skilled at the doing, not sly by definition. Next to adroit (which drifts toward social and verbal cleverness) and deft (which adds lightness and grace), dexterous stays closest to the fingers.
DEK-struhs — the card sharp who works the deck without you seeing his hands move.
The stressed syllable is "deck," which pins the word to fast, precise fingerwork rather than general cleverness.
1. A dexterous watchmaker can seat a hairspring thinner than a human hair without once resting his wrist.
2. He's weirdly dexterous with chopsticks for a guy who can't tie his own shoelaces.
Dexter's Laboratory — the boy genius named straight from Latin dexter, forever doing delicate precision work with tiny instruments.
Latin dexter = "right, right-handed" — and the right hand was the skilled, lucky one.

The pairing is the payoff: dexter (right) gave us dexterous, dexterity, ambidextrous ("right-handed on both sides"), while sinister (left) gave us sinister — the left hand was the clumsy, ill-omened one. Same prejudice built into French: adroit is literally à droit, "to the right."

column2:
A long, bitter, abusive rant against someone or something.
A long, bitter, abusive attack in words — spoken or written — against a person, group, or idea.

Two things define it: length and venom. A sharp insult isn't a diatribe; a diatribe goes on, and on, past the point where anyone is still persuaded. The word is almost always used against the speaker — calling something a diatribe concedes that it was forceful but denies that it was reasoned. A critic delivers a critique; a critic who has lost the room delivers a diatribe.
Die-a-tribe — it drags on so long the whole tribe would rather die than hear the end.
The sound hook stores the two things that matter: it's an attack, and it's punishingly long.
1. His resignation letter began as a courtesy and ended as a six-page diatribe against the board.
2. Ask him about parking and you'll get a twenty-minute diatribe about the council.
Standard press shorthand: a politician "launched into a diatribe against the media." The verb launch into is the collocation to memorise — it's how the word almost always arrives.
Greek dia- (through) + tribein (to rub, wear away) — a discourse that rubbed away the hours. In Greek it meant a learned lecture; English kept the length and dropped the learning.

Same tribein gives tribology, the science of friction and wear.

A split into two sharply opposed, either/or halves.
A division into two parts — specifically two that are treated as opposed, mutually exclusive, and between them covering everything.

Not any old split. A distinction separates two things; a dichotomy insists there are only two and you must pick one: mind/body, nature/nurture, art/commerce. Because that insistence is so often bogus, the word carries a faint whiff of suspicion — writers reach for it precisely when they're about to point out that reality is messier. Careful users also flag a second, sloppier sense you'll see in journalism ("the dichotomy between his public warmth and private cruelty"), where it just means a jarring contrast within one thing.
The word you actually meet is false dichotomy — and that companion word tells you what the noun is for.
A dichotomy is an either/or, and the interesting question is always whether the "or" is real.
1. The seminar dismantled the tidy dichotomy between high and popular art, arguing that neither category had ever held its shape.
2. Work hard or have a life — that's a total dichotomy, and honestly a fake one.
"You're either with us or against us" — the textbook example wheeled out whenever a logic or debate class teaches the false dichotomy fallacy.
Greek dikha = "in two" + temnein = "to cut." Literally a cutting in two.

That -tomy = cut is worth a lot: anatomy (cutting a body up to study it), appendectomy, lobotomy, epitome (something cut short), and atom — a-tomos, "un-cuttable," what the Greeks thought you'd hit when you ran out of cuts.

To speak for transcription; to impose terms with authority.
Verb: (1) to speak words aloud so someone else can write or type them down; (2) to lay down terms, rules or conditions with authority — to impose rather than propose.
Noun: an order or governing principle handed down (the dictates of conscience, the dictates of fashion).

The thread joining both senses is one-way flow: the person dictating supplies the words, the other party supplies only the pen. Sense (2) is the GRE sense and it carries no consultation — you negotiate terms but you dictate them, and calling someone's manner dictatorial is never a compliment. There is a third, cooler use where no person is in charge at all: budget dictates the timeline, symptoms dictate treatment — here it just means "determines, leaves no choice," and the tone is flatly neutral.
Dictate is what a dictator does — he talks, you take it down, nobody argues.
The two words are literally the same root, and the dictator image supplies the missing half of the definition: not just speaking, but speaking that cannot be answered back.
1. The victors did not negotiate at Versailles; they dictated the terms and handed Germany a pen.
2. Look, I'm not trying to dictate how you spend your weekend — I just need the car back by six.
Microsoft Word and Google Docs both put a literal Dictate button in the toolbar — tap the mic, talk, and the machine plays scribe. That's sense (1) sitting in your ribbon every day.
Latin dicere, dictum = "to say" → the frequentative dictāre, "to say over and over, to prescribe."

This root is one of the best returns on investment in the whole GRE list: verdict (truly-said), contradict (speak against), edict (spoken out by authority), predict, indict, benediction, diction, dictionary, dictum, dictator.

An authoritative pronouncement; a short saying stating a general truth.
A formal pronouncement from someone with the authority to make it — or, more loosely, a pithy saying that states a general truth.

What separates it from maxim, adage and proverb is that a dictum has a speaker behind it. Proverbs are anonymous and worn smooth by centuries of use; a dictum is attributable — a judge's, a critic's, a founder's — and it carries the weight of that person's standing. "Less is more" is Mies van der Rohe's dictum; "look before you leap" is nobody's. It also leans official: in law, obiter dicta are the judge's remarks made in passing, authoritative in tone yet not actually binding.
dictum ≠ diktat. A dictum is an authoritative saying — you may quote it or ignore it. A diktat is a harsh order imposed on someone who has no choice (originally, terms forced on a defeated nation). Same Latin root, very different pressure.
Dictum is dictated — it comes down from rank, never up from folklore.
That buried dict- ("say") is the same one in dictate, and it's the tell that a dictum always has an authority attached, unlike an anonymous proverb.
1. The court's ruling turned on a single dictum from a 1932 opinion that no one had cited in decades.
2. His whole management style boils down to one dictum: never send an email you wouldn't want screenshotted.
Any lawyer will tell you the first thing you learn reading a judgment is to separate the holding from the dicta — the part that binds from the part the judge just felt like saying.
Latin dīcere = "to say"; dictum = "the thing said."

One of the highest-yield roots on the exam: dictate, dictator, dictionary, verdict (truly said), edict, contradict, predict, indict, benediction, malediction, valedictorian.

Meant to instruct — often preachily so.
Designed to teach — especially to teach a moral lesson rather than simply entertain or inform.

The word swings on tone. Applied to a textbook, a museum label, or a fable, it's flatly descriptive: instruction is the point. Applied to a novel, a film, or a person, it's almost always a complaint — the work has stopped trusting you and started lecturing. A didactic writer wants a verdict delivered, not a story told; a didactic friend answers a question you didn't ask and adds the lesson at the end. Most GRE passages use it in this second, faintly weary sense.
⚠️ didactic ≠ pedantic.
- didactic = preachy — pushing a lesson on you
- pedantic = fussy — correcting your details

The didactic uncle tells you what the story means. The pedantic one tells you it's "fewer," not "less."
Didactic — the lesson you didn't ask for.
The sound of the first two syllables carries the sting: instruction arriving uninvited.
1. Her later novels grew increasingly didactic, each character reduced to a mouthpiece for a position the author had already settled.
2. Great film, but that last speech was so didactic — we'd got the point twenty minutes earlier.
Every Aesop fable that ends "and the moral of the story is…" is didactic literature in its purest form — the tale exists only to deliver the line.
Greek didaskein = "to teach."

Worth the detour for its cousin: autodidact — self-teacher, someone educated without schooling. That one shows up on the GRE more often than didactic does.

Lacking self-confidence; hesitant to put yourself forward.
Lacking confidence in yourself; hanging back, hesitant to speak up or push your own claim.

The word describes self-doubt made visible as reserve. Shy is a temperament around people; modest is a virtue you can choose; diffident is the suspicion that you aren't quite good enough, showing up as a half-raised hand. It's also cooler than insecure — no neediness, no drama, just someone quietly underrating themselves. The tone is formal and faintly sympathetic: the speaker usually thinks the diffidence is unwarranted.
⚠️ diffident ≠ indifferent.
- diffident = doubts himself
- indifferent = doesn't care

A diffident student cares enormously and says nothing; an indifferent one doesn't care and says nothing. Same silence, opposite cause.
Confident, diffident — same word, prefix swapped: with trust vs. trust taken away.
Both are built on Latin fides (trust), so diffident is confident's exact negative — and the trust being withheld is trust in yourself.
1. Brilliant on paper but diffident in person, she let three louder colleagues present her findings before she said a word.
2. He gave this diffident little shrug when I asked if he'd won — turns out he'd come first.
Latin dis- (apart, away) + fīdere (to trust) — trust withdrawn.

One root, a whole GRE shelf: confident (with trust), fidelity (faithfulness), fiduciary (trusted with money), infidel (without the faith), perfidy (treachery), bona fide (in good faith) — and the classic dog's name Fido, "I trust."

column2:
Spread thin and unfocused; to scatter widely.
Verb: to spread something out over a wide area until it's evenly scattered — heat, light, scent, power, tension.
Adjective: spread out, not concentrated; of writing or speech, rambling and unfocused.

The adjective is the GRE's favourite, and it's a put-down. Calling an essay diffuse doesn't mean it's empty — it means the material is all there but pooled nowhere, so no point ever lands. It's the opposite of concise, cogent, trenchant: not a lack of content, a lack of a centre.
⚠️ diffuse ≠ defuse.
- diffuse = spread it thin
- defuse = pull the fuse out — make a bomb, or a crisis, safe

You defuse tension. Writing "diffuse the tension" is one of the most common errors in English — and it's testable.
Diffuse light has no beam; diffuse prose has no point.
Either way the stuff is present and spread everywhere, which is exactly why nothing lands.
1. The committee's report was so diffuse that a third reading still failed to surrender a thesis.
2. Turn the lamp on — that overhead light's too diffuse to read by.
The reed diffuser on someone's shelf is named for its job: it spreads scent evenly through the whole room instead of concentrating it in one spot. Same with a photographer's flash diffuser — it kills the harsh beam.
Latin dis- (apart) + fundere / fūsus (to pour) — poured apart.

That pouring root runs everywhere: confuse (poured together), profuse (poured forth), effusive (gushing out), infuse, transfusion, fusion.
column3: g13 register::formal connotation::depends antonym::sharp-edged-form-vs-shapeless-mass lookalike::diffuse-profuse-profound meaning::spread-widely-outward meaning::too-many-words-on-the-page meaning::without-clear-shape root::root:-fundere-fusum-to-pour

column2:
A temporary wandering off the main subject, then back.
A temporary departure from the main subject in speech or writing — you wander off, then (usually) come back.

The word assumes there is a main road. That's why it's mild: a digression isn't an error or a failure of logic, just a detour, and it's often affectionate or self-aware — writers announce their own. Compare tangent (more casual, and you may never return), rambling (pure criticism, no structure implied), and excursus (a formal, deliberate side-essay). Calling a lecture "a series of digressions" is a gentle complaint; calling it "rambling" is not gentle at all.
⚠️ digression ≠ transgression.
- digression = you step aside from the topic
- transgression = you step across a moral or legal line

One derails a lecture; the other gets you fired.
A digression is a detour, not a wrong turn — you rejoin the road.
Both start with d and both leave the main route, but a detour is understood to be temporary — which is exactly why the word is forgiving rather than damning.
1. The essay's long digression on medieval bookbinding is charming, but it stalls the argument for six full pages.
2. Sorry, that was a total digression — where were we?
The stock phrase "But I digress" — the little apology writers and speakers drop before steering back to the point. If you've heard someone say it, you already know the word means I wandered off, and I'm coming back.
Latin digredi = "to step away" — di- (apart) + gradi (to step, to walk).

gradi is a GRE workhorse: progress (step forward), regress (step back), egress (step out), ingress (step in), gradual (step by step), grade (a step in a series), aggressive (stepping at someone).

Slow to act; delaying, often on purpose.
Slow to act; inclined to delay — and, said of an action, done in order to cause delay.

Calling someone slow describes a pace. Calling them dilatory files a complaint. The word carries an edge of blame: the delay was avoidable, and quite possibly the point. That's why it lives in formal registers — memos, court filings, school reports, letters from a solicitor. A friend who takes three weeks to reply is terrible at texting; a contractor who takes three weeks to reply is dilatory, and you're building a case.
Dilly-dally → dilatory: the same dragging of feet, in a suit and tie.
Both start dil- and both mean stalling, but dilly-dally is a parent nagging a child while dilatory is what goes in the formal complaint.
1. The tribunal found the company's disclosure dilatory, noting that documents requested in March had arrived, incomplete, in November.
2. Stop being so dilatory about the visa — the flights are in six weeks.
A live term of art in law and parliament: a judge or a Speaker can rule a motion dilatory — filed for no purpose but to burn the clock. It's the official word for stalling, which is exactly the flavour it keeps in ordinary prose.
Latin differre = "to put off" (dis- "apart" + ferre "to carry"), whose participle stem is dilat-. Delay is literally carrying the thing away from now. The same -lat- stem runs through relate, translate, collate, elate, legislate — all things carried.

🚫 Not dilate. That's dilatare, from latus meaning "wide" — pupils dilate, cervixes dilate. Identical-looking stem, unrelated root: one is carried, the other is broad.
column3: g03 register::formal connotation::negative antonym::brisk-vs-dragging antonym::tireless-industry-vs-work-dodging connotation::idleness-blamed:-seven-different-accusat lookalike::desultory-dilatory-dilettante meaning::moving-far-too-slowly meaning::won-t-do-the-work

column2:
Dabbler who plays at an art without serious commitment.
Someone who dabbles in an art or subject for pleasure and without serious commitment — enough knowledge to talk at a party, not enough to do the work.

The sting is not incompetence but pretension: an amateur simply isn't paid, and can be devoted and excellent; a dilettante performs expertise he hasn't earned. Calling someone a dilettante says they're playing at it. As an adjective — a dilettante interest in physics — it means shallow, easily dropped.
dilettante ≠ dilatory. Dilatory (DIL-uh-tor-ee) means slow, delaying, dragging your feet — a dilatory tenant hasn't paid rent. Same opening syllable, unrelated roots. The dilettante does it badly; the dilatory man hasn't got round to doing it at all.
A dilettante is a debutante of the arts — same -tante ending, same instinct: turn up for the party, leave before the work.
The rhyme carries the contempt, which is the part the definition alone misses.
1. Critics dismissed him as a dilettante — three exhibitions, four abandoned novels, and no discernible craft behind any of them.
2. Don't ask me, I'm a total dilettante — I've watched two YouTube videos on fermentation and now I own a crock.
Italian dilettante = "one who delights (in something)," from Latin delectāre, to delight. It began as a compliment — an eighteenth-century gentleman who loved painting or music without earning from it — and curdled into an insult once professional became the word of praise.

That root is still visible in delight, delectable, delectation — which is the memory key: a dilettante is in it purely for the delight, and quits the moment it stops being fun.

column2:
Very small in stature; also a smallness-signalling word form.
Adjective: extremely small; undersized.
Noun: a word-form that signals smallness or affection — piglet, kitchenette, Charlie, Annie.

Tiny is a plain measurement; diminutive is a formal, slightly appraising word, and it attaches to people far more often than to objects — a diminutive fighter, a diminutive grandmother. It carries a faint note of this is smaller than you'd expect, which is why it can read as charmed ("her diminutive frame") or as quietly patronising, depending on who's speaking. Note the shape: this is smallness of stature, not of importance — for that you'd want trivial or negligible.
dimin*utive hides minute — and minute* (my-NEWT) means tiny.
The middle of the word is the answer, and the front half (dimin-) is diminish, so the word literally reads "made smaller, to a minute size."
1. At barely five feet, the diminutive conductor still commanded ninety players without raising her voice.
2. He drives this diminutive little hatchback that looks like it should come with batteries.
Every -ie / -y nickname is a diminutive in the grammatical sense: Charlie, Annie, Katie, doggy. English shrinks a word to make it small and fond — which is exactly the flavour the adjective carries too.
Latin minuere = "to lessen" (from minus, "less"). One root, a whole GRE shelf: diminish, diminution, minute (tiny), minimum, minor, minuscule, and minister — originally the lesser one, the servant.

A slow, mournful funeral song — or anything that drags.
A slow, mournful song or chant for the dead — the music of a funeral, a lament sung over a grave.

The literal sense is ceremonial and sombre, but the word does most of its modern work as an insult about tempo and mood: any performance so slow, flat and joyless that it feels like a funeral. A lament expresses grief; a dirge is the sound of it — heavy, dragging, sung aloud. Call a ballad a dirge and you're not praising its depth, you're saying it killed the room.
A dirge drags you down to the dirt.
Dirge and dirt share the opening sound, and both belong at the graveside — which also gives you the sneering sense, since a dirge is anything that drags.
1. The procession moved to a dirge of low brass, each note held longer than seemed bearable.
2. Their new album is one dirge after another — I nearly fell asleep at the gig.
Claudius in Hamlet, listing the upside-down state of Denmark: "With mirth in funeral and with dirge in marriage." A dirge at a wedding is exactly how wrong the word feels out of place.
From Latin dīrige — "direct!" — the first word of the antiphon sung in the medieval Office of the Dead: Dirige, Domine, Deus meus, in conspectu tuo viam meam ("Direct my way in thy sight, O Lord"). The service got nicknamed after its opening word, and the nickname became the name for the music.

Same root as direct, dirigible (a steerable airship) and dirigisme (state direction of an economy) — all from dirigere, "to steer."

Faint but detectable; able to be made out with attention.
Able to be perceived, detected, or made out — visible, audible, or mentally recognisable.

Its home is the edge of perception. Something visible is simply there to see; something discernible is only just there, and you had to look or listen carefully to catch it. That's why it lives so naturally in the negative — no discernible effect, no discernible pattern — which is the careful person's way of saying "we examined it properly and found nothing," not merely "there was nothing."
⚠️ discernible ≠ discerning.
- discernible = can be detected — a property of the thing
- discerning = has sharp judgement — a property of the person (a discerning critic, a discerning palate)
No discernible difference — the phrase it's practically married to.
The word is a verdict delivered after looking hard, so it always implies faintness and effort rather than plain visibility.
1. Across twelve months of trials the drug produced no discernible improvement over the placebo.
2. Three weeks on the new keyboard and there's no discernible difference — I spent £200 on nothing.
The stock phrase of product reviews and audio forums: "no discernible difference between the lossless file and the 320kbps MP3" — i.e. we A/B'd it carefully and still couldn't hear it.
Latin cernere = "to sift, to separate" — so dis-cern is to sift one thing apart from another, which is exactly the close-attention flavour the word keeps.

Same root, big family: discern, discrete (kept separate), secret (se- apart + cernere = set apart), concern, certain.

A devoted pupil who follows and spreads a master's teaching.
A committed pupil of a particular teacher — someone who learns a doctrine directly from a master, lives by it, and passes it on.

The word is heavier than follower and more personal than adherent. You can be a follower of a trend or an adherent of a doctrine, but a disciple is bound to a person: there is a master, there is submission, and the loyalty runs deeper than agreement. In secular use it keeps a faint religious perfume, which is why journalists reach for it when a business or political figure has a circle who repeat his lines a bit too faithfully — "a disciple of Milton Friedman" can be respect or a raised eyebrow.
A follower follows a cause; a disciple follows a teacher.
The word always implies a named master standing at the other end of the devotion.
1. Freud's early disciples split into rival schools within a decade of his death, each claiming to hold the true method.
2. He's such a disciple of that fitness guy that he won't eat before noon anymore.
The Twelve Disciples — and the label is exact: as disciples they were the ones being taught, and only once sent out did the same men get called apostles (Greek apostolos, "one sent out"). Disciple = learner, apostle = messenger.
Latin discipulus = "pupil," from discere, "to learn."

That gives you discipline — originally the training given to a pupil, only later the punishment that enforces it. Its twin root docēre, "to teach," covers the other half of the classroom: docile (teachable), doctor (teacher), doctrine, document.

To unsettle or embarrass someone, defeating their composure.
To throw someone off balance — to embarrass, unsettle, or frustrate them so that their poise collapses.

It is stronger and more active than embarrass: someone does it to you, and what gives way is your composure, your argument, your plan. A witness is discomfited by a lawyer's question; a general's strategy is discomfited by bad weather. Older texts use it to mean rout in battle, and that military edge still lingers — being discomfited is a small defeat, not just a blush. Formal, faintly bookish, and almost always passive: he was visibly discomfited.
⚠️ discomfit ≠ discomfort. Discomfort is a state you're in (physical or mild, often self-caused: a stiff chair, a hard question). Discomfit is something inflicted — an agent unsettles or defeats you. The two are unrelated in origin and only overlap by accident of sound.
Hidden inside is comfit — a sugared sweet — not comfort. Different word, different job.
Spotting that the middle isn't comfort stops you from downgrading the word to "made mildly uneasy" — discomfit means someone actively undid you.
1. The minister was visibly discomfited when the reporter produced the memo he had denied ever seeing.
2. Nothing discomfits my dad like being asked to say a few words at a party.
Old French desconfire = "to undo, destroy" — des- (un-) + confire (to make, put together), from Latin conficere.

That confire root is a useful one: confection, confetti (originally sweets thrown at Italian carnivals), and comfit — the sugared almond hiding in the middle of this word.

🚫 Nothing to do with comfort. That's Latin fortis, "strong" — fortify, fortitude, effort. Same sound, unrelated family.

Unsettling; throwing you off balance or composure.
Unsettling in a way that throws you off balance — it disturbs your composure, confidence, or sense of what's normal.

Strength matters here: terrifying is fear, appalling is moral shock, but disconcerting is much cooler and smaller — you're not frightened, you're wrong-footed. It's the word for a stare held one second too long, a smile that doesn't match the news, an answer that doesn't fit the question. Educated, slightly understated register: a British reviewer or a doctor uses it precisely because it withholds panic.
There's a concert inside it — dis-concert means the orchestra fell out of tune, not that the hall caught fire.
The damage is to harmony and poise, not to safety — which is exactly why the word stays mild.
1. The witness gave her testimony with a disconcerting calm, as though describing someone else's life.
2. It's a bit disconcerting when your GPS says "turn left" and there's just a lake there.
From concert (via French concerter, from Latin conserere / concertare — "to bring into agreement"), plus the reversing prefix dis-. To concert is to get parties acting in harmony; to disconcert is to break that harmony.

Same root gives you concert, concerted (a concerted effort = agreed and coordinated, not merely strong), and concerto.

To treat as less important; to mark down in credibility.
The GRE sense is not shopping. To discount a claim, a rumour, a witness, or a theory is to treat it as less important than it appears — to knock down the weight you give it.

The force of the word is partial. You aren't calling it false; you're marking it down. A historian discounts a chronicle because the author had an axe to grind — the chronicle still gets used, just cautiously. Compare the neighbours: refute kills a claim with argument, dismiss waves it away entirely, discount quietly reduces its value. It also carries a faint suggestion that the discounter may be too quick — "he discounted her warning" almost always ends badly.
A shop discount takes money off the price; a mental discount takes credibility off the claim.
Same move either way — the thing is still there, just worth less than it was asking for.
1. Later scholars discounted his memoir, noting that every page positioned him beside a great man at a decisive hour.
2. Yeah, I'd discount anything he says about the restaurant — his brother owns it.
Finance uses the word in exactly this sense: a discounted cash flow values money arriving in ten years at less than money arriving today, and when analysts say "the market has already discounted the news," they mean it has been weighed and marked down, not ignored.
Old French desconter, from Latin dis- (away) + computare (to reckon, to count up) — literally to count away, to subtract from the reckoning.

Computare is a workhorse root: compute, computer, count, recount, account. Keep the literal image and the abstract sense falls out — discounting an argument is subtracting it from your total.

Careful not to be noticed; tactfully protective of what's private.
Careful about what you say and do, so as not to attract attention or give away something private; tactful.

It's a compliment about judgment, not a description of shyness. A secretive person seems to be hiding something; a discreet one is trusted with something. The word almost always implies a third party being protected — the client, the friend, the affair, the diagnosis. Note also the pairing with inquiry and glance: a discreet enquiry is one made so lightly that nobody realises a question was asked.
⚠️ discreet ≠ discrete.
- discreet = tactful, unobtrusive
- discrete = separate, individually distinct (discrete data, discrete units)
In discrete, the T pushes the two E's apart — separated. In discreet, the E's stay together, keeping it between them.
The spelling itself acts out the meaning: split E's for split things, huddled E's for a kept confidence.
1. The family's solicitor made discreet enquiries, and no word of the settlement ever reached the press.
2. Can you be discreet about this? I haven't told my manager I'm interviewing.
Online checkouts promising \"discreet packaging\" — a plain brown box with no branding, protecting you from the neighbours rather than from thieves. That's the word in one image: not hidden, just not announced.
Latin discernere = "to separate, to distinguish" (dis- apart + cernere to sift). Its participle discretus gave English one word that later split into two spellings — the sifting sense stayed with discrete, the sense of a person with good judgment went to discreet.

The root pays off elsewhere: discern, discernment, concern, certain, secret (se- + cernere, "set apart").

A mismatch between two things that should have agreed.
A difference between two things that were supposed to match — two figures, two accounts, two testimonies, the label and the contents.

The word is quietly accusatory without naming a culprit. A difference is just a fact; a discrepancy is a difference where agreement was expected, so it implies something has gone wrong — sloppiness, error, or a lie — while staying scrupulously neutral about which. That is why auditors, journalists and lawyers love it: it flags the problem and postpones the blame.
⚠️ discrepancy ≠ disparity.
- discrepancy = two accounts that should agree don't (the ledger vs. the receipts)
- disparity = an unequal gap between two things, no agreement ever expected (wealth disparity, a disparity in size)
There is no discrepancy without a pair that was meant to tally.
If the two things were never supposed to be identical, what you have is a difference or a disparity — the word only fires when a match was expected.
1. The auditors flagged a discrepancy of £40,000 between the reported revenue and the deposits actually received.
2. There's a discrepancy between what he told me and what he told you, and I'd like to know which of us he lied to.
It's the standard word on a stock-take or a bank reconciliation: retail and finance teams literally file a "discrepancy report" when the count on the shelf doesn't match the count in the system.
Latin dis- (apart) + crepāre (to rattle, creak, make a noise) → discrepāre, "to sound different, to be out of tune." Two accounts that don't ring the same note.

Same root gives you decrepit — creaked out, worn to rattling.

Cold contempt for what you think is beneath you.
Noun: contempt for something you regard as unworthy of you.
Verb: to treat with that contempt — or to refuse to do something because it's beneath you (he disdained to answer).

Temperature is what sets it apart. Scorn is loud and contempt is harsh, but disdain is cold — a raised eyebrow, a refusal to engage, the look you give something you've decided not to take seriously. It always implies the disdainer is standing higher up, which is why it says as much about their vanity as about the thing dismissed.
dis- + deign: you will not deign to stoop to it.
The word deign is literally sitting inside disdain, and it carries the looking-down-from-above posture that separates disdain from ordinary dislike.
1. The ambassador received the apology with visible disdain, and disdained to answer it in writing.
2. He looked at the microwaved lasagna with total disdain and ordered a pizza.
Mr Darcy at the Meryton ball in Pride and Prejudice — refusing to dance, dismissing Elizabeth as \"tolerable, but not handsome enough to tempt me.\" That's disdain in one line: not anger, just a man who won't lower himself.
Latin dignus = "worthy." Add dis- (not) and you get "to deem unworthy" — which is exactly what the word still does.

The root pays off widely: dignity, dignitary, deign (to consider something worthy of your effort), indignant (angry at being treated as unworthy), indignity, and condign (a punishment worthy of the crime).

To free something from knots, snarls, or complications.
To free something from knots, snarls, or twisted-together parts — literally (cables, hair, fishing line) or figuratively (a person from a bad marriage, the facts from the rumours).

The word carries patience. Extricate is a rescue — you get out of the trap, fast, and how you did it doesn't matter. Disentangle is the slow, careful undoing of something that got knotted over time, strand by strand, with nothing torn. It also implies the two things were genuinely intertwined, not just stuck together: you disentangle threads, loyalties, finances, arguments — things that grew into each other.
Alexander cut the Gordian knot. He did not disentangle it.
The word rules out the shortcut — disentangling is the unglamorous work of undoing every loop by hand.
1. The biographer's task is to disentangle the man from the myth that his admirers spent forty years spinning around him.
2. It took her two lawyers and a year to disentangle her finances from his.
Standard newsroom vocabulary for divorce, corporate demergers, and Brexit — "disentangling the UK from four decades of EU law" was the stock phrase, and it was chosen precisely because it meant slow and clause-by-clause, not one clean cut.

Insincere while pretending to be innocent or naive.
Insincere — pretending to know less, or to mean better, than you actually do.

It is not plain lying. A disingenuous person says something technically defensible while wearing a mask of innocence: the feigned question, the "I had no idea this would upset anyone," the argument built on a definition they know isn't the one in play. The fakery is in the guilelessness, not just the facts.

Register matters: this is the educated, deniable accusation. In a debate or a review you can call an argument disingenuous and stay civil; call it a lie and the room changes.
⚠️ ingenuous ≠ ingenious. Ingenuous = frank, artless, unguarded (the opposite of this word). Ingenious = clever, inventive. One letter, two unrelated qualities — and disingenuous is the negative of the first, never the second.
dis-in-genu-ous — "this ain't genuine", and what's fake is the innocence.
The sound of the word hands you genuine, and the dis- cancels it — with the specific fraud being an act of not-knowing.
1. The minister's claim that he had never read the report was disingenuous at best; his own annotations ran down its margins.
2. Don't be disingenuous — you knew exactly how that would sound when you sent it.
Listen to any political interview or press briefing: disingenuous is the standard weapon there precisely because parliamentary and broadcast conventions forbid calling someone a liar outright.
Latin ingenuus = "freeborn" — and a freeborn Roman was assumed to speak frankly, so the word slid into "candid, open." Add dis- and you get someone faking that openness.

Underneath sits gignere / genus (to beget, to be born), which pays for itself across the exam: genuine, genus, congenital, indigenous, progeny, genesis.

🚫 Not ingenious. That's Latin ingenium, "inborn talent" — cleverness, not candour.

Impartial; having no personal stake in the outcome.
Impartial — having no personal stake, no side to gain by, no axe to grind.

This is a compliment. A disinterested referee, auditor, trustee or judge may care deeply about the matter and still be trusted, because nothing in the outcome touches their pocket or their pride. It describes a position, not a mood: you can be riveted by a case and disinterested in it at the same time. Reach for it wherever fairness depends on the absence of a stake.
⚠️ disinterested ≠ uninterested.
- disinterested = neutral, no stake — a virtue
- uninterested = bored, no attention — a shrug

The GRE tests this pair constantly, and the "bored" reading of disinterested is the wrong answer.
A disinterested judge has no money on the game; an uninterested one has no eyes on it.
Dis- strips away the old sense of interest — a financial stake — while un- strips away attention.
1. The estate was placed in the hands of a disinterested third party, so neither brother could accuse the other of tampering.
2. Don't ask his best mate to score the argument — get someone disinterested.
Boardroom language keeps the strict sense alive: when a company approves a deal involving one of its own executives, the bylaws demand a vote of the disinterested directors — the ones with no financial stake, who must recuse-proof the decision.
Interest comes from Latin interesse, "to be between, to concern" (inter- between + esse to be) — and in English it first meant a legal or financial share in something. So disinterested = holding no share. The modern "curiosity" sense of interest came later, which is exactly why the two words drifted apart.

esse also gives you essence, essential, entity, present.
