column2:
To take apart piece by piece; to systematically undo.
To take something apart piece by piece — a machine, a stage set, a bureaucracy, an argument, a whole political system.

The word carries method, not violence. You destroy a building with a wrecking ball; you dismantle it with crews and inventory lists. That's why it's the standard verb for undoing big structures deliberately — dismantle apartheid, dismantle the tariff regime, dismantle a nuclear programme — the undoing is as organised as the building was. It also implies the thing was assembled in the first place, so calling something dismantled quietly says it was constructed, not natural.
DISassemble, not DEstroy — the dismantler brings a screwdriver, not a sledgehammer.
The force of the word is in the patience of it: part by part, in order, usually on purpose.
1. The incoming administration set about dismantling the regulatory apparatus its predecessor had spent a decade assembling.
2. Took us twenty minutes to build that shelf and an hour to dismantle it when we moved.
Headline English about disarmament: North Korea or Iran agreeing to dismantle its nuclear facilities. Nobody writes "destroy" there — the whole point is verified, bolt-by-bolt removal with inspectors watching.
Old French desmanteler = "to strip of a mantle (cloak)", from Latin mantellum. It was then used of fortresses: to dismantle a town was to tear down its walls — the walls being the cloak it wore.

Same root gives you mantle (a cloak, hence "the mantle of leadership") and mantelpiece (the hood over a fireplace).

So different in kind as to be incomparable.
Different in kind, not just in degree — so unlike that the things resist being compared or lumped together.

Two shirts of different colours are different; a shirt, a tax code and a whale are disparate. The word is usually doing one of two jobs: insisting that a comparison is illegitimate ("these are disparate cases"), or flagging that a collection is a grab-bag of mismatched parts ("disparate sources", "disparate systems"). Formal and analytical — it's the vocabulary of reports and arguments, not of conversation.
⚠️ disparate ≠ desperate. Desperate (DES-puh-ruht) is hopeless, frantic, willing to do anything. Nearly the same sound, opposite half of the dictionary — the GRE will happily exploit the eye-slip.
dis-PAR-ate = not on par. Different things you can still rank; disparate things you can't even score on the same card.
The hidden par ("equal") is the whole point: disparate items aren't merely unequal, they're not on comparable terms at all.
1. The committee's report stitched together disparate strands of evidence — census data, coroners' records, a century of parish registers — into a single argument.
2. Our team is five people from five disparate backgrounds, and somehow the standups still work.
"Disparate impact" — the standard term in employment and housing law for a neutral-looking rule that lands unequally on different groups. If you've read a hiring-policy or compliance document, you've met the word there.
Sits in the family of Latin par = "equal" — the par of parity, par for the course, peer, and disparity (from dispar, "unequal"). Lock that root in and you get several GRE words at once.

Hand out in measured portions; (with *with*) do away with.
1. To hand out in measured portions — medicine, cash, advice, justice.
2. dispense with — to do without something, to waive it as unnecessary.

Sense 1 is cool and official: pharmacists, courts, and machines dispense; friends share and hosts offer. The word implies an allotted amount, a rule behind it, and no warmth in the giving — which is why "dispensing wisdom" is faintly sarcastic, as if the advice came out of a slot.

Sense 2 is the one the GRE actually tests, and it's brisk to the point of dismissal: let's dispense with the formalities means sweep them aside, we're above that.
⚠️ dispense ≠ disperse.
- dispense = give out in portions (a pharmacy dispenses pills)
- disperse = scatter, break up (police disperse a crowd)

One distributes, one dissolves.
A dispenser never gives you the whole bottle — one measured squirt, by the rules.
That metered, impersonal quality is the whole flavour of the word — and dispense with is the opposite move: no portion at all, the thing is waived entirely.
1. The colonial magistrate was empowered to dispense justice without appeal, a licence that corrupted him within a year.
2. Let's dispense with the introductions — we've all read each other's emails.
Every ATM screen that says "Cash dispensed" — a machine handing you an exact allotted amount, never a penny more.
Latin dispendere = "to weigh out" — dis- (out) + pendere (to weigh, to hang, to pay). Weighing out is literally what a dispenser does.

pendere is a high-yield GRE root: pension (money weighed out), compensate (weigh against), ponder (weigh in the mind), pendant (hanging), expend, indispensable (can't be waived).

To scatter apart until the gathering thins away to nothing.
To scatter in every direction — a crowd, seeds, smoke, light — so that what was concentrated becomes thin and spread out.

The key is that the gathering itself dissolves. Distribute hands things out on purpose, to chosen recipients; disperse just breaks the mass apart and lets the pieces go wherever. That's why the word does double duty: physically neutral in science (pollen disperses on the wind, a prism disperses light), but faintly coercive in the news, where crowds are ordered to disperse by someone with a baton.
⚠️ disperse ≠ disburse.
- disperse = scatter — the crowd, the fog
- disburse = pay out — the funds

Disburse has a purse in it. Money comes out of a purse; everything else disperses.
Disperse leaves things sparse — same root, one letter apart.
You haven't dispersed a crowd by moving it somewhere else; you've dispersed it when it's thinned out to nothing.
1. Windborne spores disperse across hundreds of miles, which is why the blight reached the coast before anyone had named it.
2. One whiff of tear gas and the whole square dispersed in about ninety seconds.
The standard police loudhailer line at any protest — "This is an unlawful assembly. You are ordered to disperse." You've heard it in news footage and in half the riot scenes ever filmed.
Latin dis- (apart) + spargere (to scatter, sprinkle).

That root is worth banking: sparse (scattered thinly), intersperse (scatter among), and the GRE favourite aspersion — literally sprinkling onto, hence to cast aspersions, flicking dirt at someone's name.

To hide your true feelings or motives behind a false front.
To conceal your real feelings, motives or beliefs behind a false appearance — to put on a face. (Also transitive: he dissembled his fury.)

Lying is about facts; dissembling is about self-presentation. You needn't state a single falsehood to dissemble — a composed smile over contempt does it. The word is genteel and faintly literary, which is exactly why journalists and lawyers reach for it: it lets you accuse someone of deceit without saying "he lied." The dissembler is a smooth operator, not a caught-out fibber.
dissemble ≠ disassemble. Disassemble = take a machine apart. Dissemble = put a face on. One removes parts, the other adds a mask.
Hiding inside it is semble — "to seem." A dissembler works on how things seem, never on what's true.
That's the whole nuance: dissembling manages appearances rather than asserting facts, which is why it feels more like acting than lying.
1. Under cross-examination the minister dissembled for an hour, conceding nothing and denying nothing.
2. Don't dissemble — I saw your face when she walked in.
Watch any political interview write-up: when a reporter can't prove a lie but won't call the answer honest, the verdict is always "the candidate dissembled." It's the polite word for lying, and its natural habitat is the press gallery and the courtroom.
Latin dissimulāre = "to make unlike, to disguise" — from similis, "like, similar."

That root is worth banking: similar, simulate, assimilate, simultaneous, verisimilitude (the appearance of truth), and the stiffer twin dissimulate. All of them turn on likeness and seeming.

🚫 Not disassemble. That's assemble (Latin ad + simul, "together") with dis- undoing it — same distant family, entirely different job.

To spread information widely, from one source to many.
To spread something widely — information, ideas, findings, sometimes spores or disease — outward from one source to many recipients.

The shape of the word is one-to-many and deliberate. You don't disseminate to a friend; you disseminate to a field, a public, a population. Compare the neighbours: circulate passes a thing around inside a closed group, divulge lets out one secret, broadcast is the plain-English version — disseminate is the institutional register, the verb of ministries, journals, and press offices. It says nothing about whether the content is true, only that it went far.
⚠️ disseminate ≠ dissemble.
- disseminate = scatter it outward (spread widely)
- dissemble = cover it up (hide your real feelings or motives)

Opposite directions: one publishes, one conceals.
dis-SEMIN-ate — the same SEMIN as seminar and semen: seed, flung outward.
One sower, a whole field — which is why you disseminate findings to thousands rather than to one person.
1. The committee's mandate was to disseminate the trial results to clinicians before the paper cleared peer review.
2. Someone screenshotted the memo and it got disseminated across half the company by lunchtime.
Research grant applications routinely require a \"dissemination plan\" — a section spelling out how you'll push the results out to the world once the money's spent.
Latin dis- (apart) + sēmināre (to sow), from sēmen = seed. Literally: scatter the seed in all directions.

That root pays off across the exam: seminal (an idea that seeds everything after it), seminar (a seed-plot for young minds), seminary, inseminate.

English did the same metaphor twice — broadcast originally meant sowing seed by hand across a wide arc, long before radio borrowed it.

To disagree openly with an official or majority view.
Verb: to disagree openly with an official position, a majority, or an established doctrine.
Noun: that disagreement — or the people voicing it.

Dissent needs something to push against: a ruling, a consensus, a church, a party line. You can disagree with a friend over dinner; you dissent from a verdict. It's reasoned and on the record — the dissenter states grounds, usually in the very forum that overruled them. Milder in action than rebellion (no one is storming anything) but weightier in tone than objection, because dissent implies conscience rather than mere preference.
⚠️ dissent ≠ assent. One letter, opposite meanings: assent = agree, consent; dissent = refuse to. "The board assented" and "the board dissented" describe opposite meetings.
Dissent starts with diss — but it's a diss filed in writing, with reasons attached.
The "diss" gets you the disagreement; "with reasons attached" gets you the formality that separates dissent from just griping.
1. Two justices dissented, warning that the majority had quietly gutted a century of precedent.
2. Nobody dissented — everyone just nodded along and let the daft plan through.
Ruth Bader Ginsburg made the word a brand: her dissenting opinions and the black beaded "dissent collar" she wore to deliver them turned "I dissent" into T-shirt material.
Latin dis- (apart) + sentīre (to feel) — literally to feel apart from the rest.

That root is a GRE goldmine: consent (feel with), assent (feel toward), resent (feel it back), plus sentiment, sentient, consensus.

column2:
Someone who openly opposes an official or ruling power.
Noun: someone who openly opposes an official policy or ruling power. Adj.: holding and voicing such opposition.

The word carries risk. Anyone can be a critic; a dissident disagrees with a government, church, or party that can punish them for it — exile, prison, a lost career. Compare the neighbours: a rebel takes up arms, a heretic offends doctrine, a contrarian disagrees for sport. The dissident's weapon is only speech, and the price is personal. Note also who's speaking: the regime says "dissident" to mark you as a problem; the outside world says it to mean you're brave.
⚠️ dissident ≠ diffident.
- dissident = loudly opposed to authority
- diffident = shy, lacking self-confidence

Nearly the opposite temperament, one letter apart.
Dis-SID-ent — he sits apart (sedere, to sit), and in a police state an empty chair gets noticed.
The word isn't about arguing, it's about visibly refusing to sit with everyone else — which is why it's dangerous.
1. Samizdat manuscripts circulated hand to hand, keeping dissident thought alive through decades of censorship.
2. She was the one dissident voice on a board that had already decided everything over lunch.
The phrase you've read a hundred times in headlines: "Russian dissident Alexei Navalny" — poisoned, jailed, and dead in an Arctic prison. That's the whole meaning of the word in three words of news copy.
Latin dis- (apart) + sedēre (to sit) — literally "to sit apart."

That root is a GRE goldmine: reside (sit back), preside (sit in front), subside (settle down), sedentary (sitting), sediment (what sits at the bottom), assiduous (sitting at it doggedly), insidious (sitting in ambush).

To swell or bulge outward from internal pressure.
To swell or bulge outward from pressure inside — a stomach after a huge meal, a balloon, a corpse, a vein under a tourniquet.

The direction matters: things expand in any manner, but they distend because something within is pushing the walls out. It's the vocabulary of bodies and containers, and it almost always carries discomfort — a distended belly is bloated, strained, wrong. You'd never call a happy stretch distension.
Extend reaches outward; distend bulges outward — same tend (stretch), but the pressure is inside.
Both words are the root tendere, "to stretch," so the prefix does all the work: extending is voluntary reach, distending is being stretched from within.
1. Weeks of famine had distended the children's bellies — the cruel paradox of hunger that looks like fullness.
2. Two plates of biryani in, I was flat on the sofa with a distended stomach, regretting every bite.
Standard clinical shorthand: every physical exam note in a hospital records the abdomen as "soft, non-distended." Doctors write the word dozens of times a day.
Latin dis- (apart) + tendere (to stretch) — stretched apart from within.

Tendere is a high-yield GRE root: extend, tension, tendon, tent (stretched fabric), contend, portend, tendentious.

To boil something down to its pure, potent essence.
Literally: to purify a liquid by boiling it and condensing the vapour — how whisky, gin and essential oils are made.
Figuratively: to extract the essential core of something large and reduce it to concentrated form.

The key is that the result is stronger, not just smaller. To summarise is to make short; to condense is to compress the bulk; to distill is to throw away everything inessential so what remains is more potent than the original. It implies patience and judgement — you distill a decade of research into one paragraph, and the paragraph hits harder than the decade.
⚠️ distill ≠ instill.
- distill = draw the essence out of something
- instill = drip a quality into someone (instill discipline in the cadets)

Same root, opposite direction.
A still makes moonshine — what drips out is far stronger than what went in.
The word literally contains the apparatus, and distilling always yields something more concentrated than the source, never merely shorter.
1. Her final chapter distills forty years of fieldwork into a single, devastating claim about kinship.
2. Just distill it for me — I don't need the whole deck, give me the one thing that matters.
"Triple Distilled" on a bottle of Jameson — the whole boast is that running it through three times makes it purer and smoother. That's the figurative sense in miniature: more passes, less junk, stronger spirit.
Latin de- (down) + stillare (to drip), from stilla, "a drop." To distill is to let something come down drop by drop — which is why the word carries that sense of slow, patient extraction.

Same drop gives you instill (to drip in, gradually) and distillation.

column2:
To twist out of true shape, physically or in meaning.
To twist something out of its true shape — a face, a signal, an image — or to misrepresent facts, motives, or words by bending them away from the truth.

The key is that distortion works on something real. A lie invents; a distortion takes the actual quote, the actual statistic, the actual photograph, and warps it until it says something else. That's why it's the harder accusation to rebut — every piece is genuine, only the shape is wrong. Note also that the word is perfectly neutral in technical use: lens distortion, harmonic distortion, a distorted waveform. Nobody is being accused of anything.
⚠️ distort ≠ contort.
- contort = twist into a grotesque shape — a contorted face, a contortionist's body. No deception implied.
- distort = twist away from the truth or the original. Deception, or at least inaccuracy.
A distorted guitar is still playing the right note — just bent out of shape. Same with distorted facts.
Distortion never replaces the original, it deforms it — which is exactly what separates it from an outright fabrication.
1. The committee accused the newspaper of distorting its findings, quoting a single sentence and omitting the paragraph that qualified it.
2. Stop distorting what I said — I said it was expensive, not that we couldn't afford it.
The distortion pedal every rock guitarist steps on — Linkin Park's whole sound runs through it. The pedal doesn't change the notes; it drives the signal until the clean waveform is crushed out of shape. That's the word, literally.
Latin dis- (apart) + torquēre, tortus (to twist) — to twist apart.

Torquēre is a workhorse root: contort (twist together), extort (twist money out of someone), retort (a reply twisted back at you), tortuous (full of twists), torture, torque, and legal tort — a "twisted" wrong.

Suffering, strained, or damaged — a person, a company, or a fabric.
Suffering — upset, anxious, in pain or in trouble.

It sits below distraught: a distressed person is visibly struggling but still coping; a distraught one has come apart. It's also the calm, official word for someone else's crisis — a distressed passenger, a vessel in distress, fetal distress. You rarely say "I'm distressed" about yourself; it's what the report says about you.

Two specialist senses the GRE likes: in finance, distressed assets or debt belong to a company in trouble, so they sell cheap. In design, distressed leather, wood or denim has been deliberately battered to look worn — the only sense where the word is a selling point.
Stress is sitting right inside it — and dis- stretches that stress until something gives.
Whatever has been stretched past comfort is distressed: a person, a company's balance sheet, or a pair of jeans.
1. The lifeboat crew reached the distressed vessel an hour before the storm closed in.
2. She turned up distressed jeans and a distressed face, having paid extra for one of them.
Distressed denim — the rips and fading you pay a premium for. Same word, same idea: fabric put under strain until it looks like it's been through something.
Latin distringere = "to stretch apart, draw tight" (dis- apart + stringere to pull tight).

That stringere root is a GRE goldmine: stringent (tightly binding), astringent (makes tissue contract), strict, constrict, restrict — and district, originally the territory a lord could draw tight under his control.

Moving apart from a shared starting point; differing.
Moving apart from a common point; differing, branching off in another direction.

The word carries a shared origin: two things can only diverge if they started together. Opinions diverge after agreeing on the facts; species diverge from an ancestor; roads diverge from one junction. Different is a flat statement of unlikeness; divergent describes the widening gap over time. It is also cool and analytic — where deviant condemns and heretical accuses, divergent just measures the angle. Technical uses lean on the same picture: a divergent series never settles on a value, and divergent thinking is idea-generation that fans outward instead of narrowing to one answer.
Divergent paths veer apart — but they have to leave from the same verge.
The verg- in the middle is the same verge as "the verge of the road," and the sound hook to veer keeps the essential condition in view: a common starting point, then separation.
1. The two economies grew along sharply divergent paths after 1990, despite starting from near-identical output.
2. We agree on the numbers — it's what to do about them where we're divergent.
Robert Frost's "Two roads diverged in a yellow wood" — the most quoted line in American poetry, and a perfect definition: one wood, one traveller, two paths peeling apart.
Latin dis- (apart) + vergere (to bend, incline, turn). The root pays off across a family: converge = bend together, verge = the edge where a surface starts to bend away, verge on = incline toward.

column2:
Cut off from something it ought to be connected to.
Beyond the marriage sense, the one the GRE actually tests: separated from, cut off from, having no working connection with.

The word carries an accusation. Unrelated is a neutral fact; divorced implies the two things were once joined, and ought still to be — so the split is a failure. A theory divorced from the evidence isn't merely different from the evidence; it has drifted free of the thing that was supposed to anchor it. That's why it lands as criticism: the speaker is saying you've lost your tether.

Almost always passive and almost always followed by from.
On the GRE, divorced is nearly always followed by from — and never by a spouse.
The moment you see "divorced from," swap in "cut loose from what should be holding it down."
1. His grand economic model, elegant on paper, was wholly divorced from the conditions of any actual market.
2. Mate, that budget is divorced from reality — rent alone eats half of it.
"Divorced from reality" is the standard put-down in political and business commentary — a forecast, a manifesto, a boss's timeline. Hear that phrase and you're hearing this exact sense.
Latin dīvertere = "to turn aside" — di- (apart) + vertere (to turn). A divorce is literally two people turning away from each other.

vertere is one of the highest-yield GRE roots: divert, convert, invert, subvert, avert, revert, versatile, vertigo, adverse, controversy — every one of them a turning.

To reveal something private or confidential.
To reveal something that was meant to be kept private — a secret, a source, a salary, a confidence.

You can only divulge what was withheld. Announcing tomorrow's weather isn't divulging; naming your anonymous source is. The word carries a whiff of breached trust — even when the divulging is voluntary, there was a seal on the thing. It's also noticeably formal: police, lawyers and press officers divulge; your friend just tells you.
Divulge = make it vulgar — drag the private thing out to the vulgus, the common crowd.
The secret stops being yours the moment it becomes everybody's.
1. The bank is legally forbidden to divulge a client's account details to any third party.
2. Don't divulge how much you paid for it — he'll never let it go.
The stock line in every press conference and corporate email: "We're not able to divulge further details at this time." If it's a stonewall, the verb is almost always this one.
Latin dīvulgāre = "to spread among the people," from vulgus = the common crowd.

Same root gives you vulgar (of the crowd → coarse) and the Vulgate (the Bible put into the people's Latin). Divulging is the act of handing a private thing to the public.

Rigidly applying theory regardless of what reality demands.
Adj.: insisting on a theory or doctrine rigidly, without regard for practical consequences. Noun: a person who does that.

The sting isn't that the belief is wrong — it's that reality is never allowed to test it. A dogmatic person won't question their beliefs; a doctrinaire person won't adjust them to the case in front of them. Hence the standard collocation: a doctrinaire Marxist, doctrinaire free-market policy — theory arriving fully formed, evidence optional. Nobody has ever called themselves doctrinaire; it is always someone else's diagnosis.
doctrinaire ≠ doctrinal.
- doctrinal = relating to doctrine — neutral (a doctrinal dispute between two churches)
- doctrinaire = enslaved to doctrine — an insult

A doctrinal difference is a topic; a doctrinaire opponent is a problem.
Doctrin-aire — like a millionaire, he's rich in doctrine and spends none of it on reality.
The -aire suffix marks a person defined by what they're loaded with, and this one's entire fortune is theory.
1. The reforms failed less from bad intentions than from a doctrinaire refusal to let local conditions modify the plan.
2. He's not a bad teacher, just so doctrinaire about phonics that he'd rather blame the kid than the method.
A stock epithet in political commentary, almost always bolted to an ideology: a doctrinaire Marxist, doctrinaire libertarian, doctrinaire free-market economics. If you see the word, an -ism is usually the next one along.
Latin docēre = "to teach." The family is huge and free: doctrine (what's taught), doctor (originally a teacher, not a physician), document, indoctrinate, and docile — literally teachable.

Note the pair at either end of that list: docile = too easily taught; doctrinaire = taught once and never again.

column2:
Based on written records; also, a fact-based film.
Adj.: consisting of or based on written records — contracts, ledgers, letters, receipts.
Noun: a film built out of real footage and records rather than invented scenes.

The GRE almost always wants the adjective, and it lives in legal and historical prose: documentary evidence is what you can put in a folder, as opposed to testimonial evidence, which walks into court and talks. The word carries a quiet claim to reliability — a paper trail can't misremember or change its story. So calling a case "documentary" implies it rests on hard record, not on someone's account of events.
A documentary shows you the footage; documentary evidence shows you the paperwork — either way, here's the record, not my opinion.
The familiar film sense and the exam sense are the same idea: something assembled out of actual documents rather than narrated from memory.
1. The prosecution's case was almost entirely documentary — bank transfers, signed invoices, and a single incriminating email.
2. There's no documentary proof he ever worked here; we're going off what two people vaguely remember.
Lawyers split evidence into three buckets in everyday practice: documentary (the paperwork), testimonial (the witness), and physical (the object). Hear one, you've placed the word.
Latin docēre = "to teach" → a document was originally a lesson or proof.

That root pays off across the GRE: docile (teachable, easily led), doctrine (what is taught), indoctrinate (to teach until it can't be questioned), doctor (originally a teacher), docent (museum guide who teaches you the room).

Stubbornly persistent; refusing to quit despite difficulty.
Refusing to give up — grinding on through difficulty, setback, and boredom without letting go.

Stubborn is a criticism (you won't move); dogged is usually a compliment (you won't stop). It praises endurance rather than brilliance: the dogged detective isn't the clever one, he's the one still knocking on doors in month nine. Note the tone it carries — unglamorous, patient, slightly plodding. Dogged determination and dogged persistence are near-fixed phrases; if you hear either, someone is being admired for sheer refusal to quit.
A dog with a bone. It won't let go, and it isn't being clever about it.
That captures both halves of the word — total refusal to release, with no cunning involved.
1. Her dogged pursuit of the archive records, over four years and three countries, finally produced the document that broke the case.
2. He's not the smartest guy on the team, but he's dogged — he'll still be at that spreadsheet at midnight.
Sports and news writing runs on the verb form: an athlete dogged by injuries, a politician dogged by scandal — the trouble trails them like a hound that won't be shaken off. Same relentlessness, pointed at you instead of by you.
Straight from dog — specifically the hound on a scent, which is why the verb to dog means to follow and hound someone without let-up.

🚫 Nothing to do with dogma or dogmatic. That's Greek dogma, "opinion, decree" (→ dogmatic, orthodox, paradigm). A dogged person won't quit; a dogmatic person won't listen.

column2:
Asserting opinions as unquestionable fact; rigidly closed to argument.
Laying down opinions as if they were settled fact — rigidly attached to a doctrine and unwilling to hear evidence against it.

The insult isn't that the person is wrong; it's that they're closed. An opinionated person argues hard, a dogmatic one refuses to argue at all, because for them the question was decided before you spoke. It's almost always an accusation, and it carries a faint whiff of the pulpit or the party line — belief handed down rather than worked out.
DOGMA + auto*MATIC* — the belief comes out automatically, with no thinking in between.
The -matic ending is the whole point: positions asserted on reflex, never re-examined.
1. The review dismissed his monograph as dogmatic — confident assertion where the evidence demanded a question mark.
2. Don't be so dogmatic about it; you've never even tried pineapple on pizza.
Steve Jobs, Stanford 2005: "Don't be trapped by dogma — which is living with the results of other people's thinking." That line defines the noun the adjective comes from.
Greek dogma = "an opinion, a decree", from dokein = "to seem, to think."

That root pays off across the exam: orthodox (ortho- straight + doxa opinion = correct belief), heterodox (other belief), paradox (para- beyond belief), doxology.

column2:
Temporarily inactive but alive, able to wake up again.
Temporarily inactive — asleep rather than finished. A dormant volcano, seed, disease, account, or rivalry is doing nothing right now, but the capacity to act is intact and could return.

The whole force of the word is the implied comeback. Extinct and defunct close the door; dormant leaves it ajar. That's why it so often appears in warnings and reassurances alike — "a dormant infection" is not a cured one, and "dormant talent" is a compliment about what hasn't happened yet. It's a calm, slightly clinical word: no drama, just paused.
dormant — a dorm at 3pm: nobody's moving, everybody's alive.
The students in there aren't gone, they're sleeping, and they'll be up and loud by evening — which is exactly the promise dormant makes about a volcano, a seed, or a feud.
1. The bacterium can lie dormant in the lungs for decades before any symptom appears.
2. My gym membership's been dormant since January, but I keep paying for it.
Volcanoes are officially sorted into active / dormant / extinct — and the middle category exists precisely because "quiet for 300 years" is not the same as "over." Vesuvius is classed dormant, not extinct.
Latin dormīre = "to sleep." The family is unusually easy: dormitory (a sleeping room), dormer window (it sits in the roof over the bedrooms), and the dormouse — named for how much it hibernates, which is why Lewis Carroll's is permanently nodding off at the tea party.

Drab, unstylish, dull-looking — usually clothes.
Shabby, drab, and out of fashion in appearance — dull clothes, dull grooming, no style.

The insult is aimed at dullness, not dirt or poverty. Something dowdy may be perfectly clean, well-made and expensive; it is simply joyless, shapeless, and a decade behind. It also carries a faint condescension and is aimed at women far more often than men — which is exactly why the GRE likes it as a tone question. Cousins split cleanly: shabby = worn out, gaudy = too much flash, dowdy = too little.
Dowdy rhymes with cloudy — nothing is wrong with the outfit, it's just overcast.
The rhyme fixes the nuance: dowdy clothes aren't torn or filthy, they're grey, flat and lifeless.
1. Her portrait shows a woman deliberately dowdy, as though plainness were a form of moral proof.
2. I turned up in a dowdy brown cardigan and everyone else was in sequins.
The Devil Wears Prada is ninety minutes of this word: pre-makeover Andy in the lumpy blue sweater is what dowdy looks like, and the whole film is about it being fixed.

Cruelly severe — punishment far harsher than the offence deserves.
Excessively harsh and severe — used of laws, rules, penalties, and policies.

The word is an accusation of disproportion. Calling a punishment draconian doesn't say the offence was innocent; it says the response was wildly out of scale with it — a life sentence for a small theft, a school expelling a child over a dress code. It attacks rules and the people who write them, not personalities: a cruel teacher, but a draconian attendance policy. Journalistic and political in flavour, and never a compliment — nobody describes their own regime as draconian.
Draconian = dragon-ian — the rulebook breathes fire on a parking ticket.
The absurd mismatch is the point: the word condemns the size of the punishment, not the crime.
1. The tribunal struck down the statute as draconian, noting that a first-time offender faced the same term as a repeat arsonist.
2. Two weeks' pay docked for being five minutes late? That's a bit draconian.
A newsroom staple: every COVID lockdown, immigration bill, and social-media ban gets called "draconian measures" by whoever opposes it — the word is essentially a headline's way of saying too far.
A real man. Draco wrote Athens' first written law code around 621 BC, and it prescribed death for almost everything — including stealing a cabbage. Plutarch reports the crack that Draco's laws were written not in ink but in blood.

So the word carries his reputation, not a general idea of strictness: one legislator so over-the-top that his name became the adjective for punishment out of all proportion.

Amusing in a dry, odd, understated way.
Amusing in an odd, dry, understated way — funny because it's peculiar, not because it's uproarious.

Scale matters: a hilarious joke makes you laugh out loud, a droll one gets a slow half-smile and a raised eyebrow. The humour is deadpan, delivered flat, often faintly old-fashioned or whimsical — the sort of wit that never signals it's joking. Said sincerely it's a compliment (a droll storyteller is good company); said flatly to someone's face — "How droll." — it's pure sarcasm, meaning the opposite.
Droll has roll in it — but nobody's rolling on the floor laughing.
The buried word is exactly what droll humour never produces: it's the quiet smile, not the belly laugh.
1. His memoirs are droll rather than funny — a lifetime of disasters recounted in the tone of a man reading a weather report.
2. She's got this droll way of complaining where you're not sure for about three seconds whether she's serious.
It's a stock word in British film and theatre reviews — the standing critic's label for deadpan delivery, the comic who never cracks a smile at his own line.

Doubtful: either unconvinced, or quietly not to be trusted.
Doubtful — and it points both ways:

- Feeling doubt: I'm dubious about his plan. (hesitant, unconvinced)
- Causing doubt: a dubious character, dubious accounting. (fishy, not to be trusted)

The second sense is where the GRE lives, and it works by understatement. Fraudulent is a charge you'd have to prove; dubious is a raised eyebrow — it says the thing smells wrong without committing you to saying so. That deniability is why journalists and auditors love it. It also runs ironic: a dubious honour or dubious distinction is an achievement nobody wants (the dubious distinction of the highest crash rate in Europe).
Dubious = duo — of two minds, and never quite committing to either.
The word hovers between yes and no, which is exactly its tone: you don't accuse, you just decline to believe.
1. The committee accepted the figures, though several members remained dubious about how the surplus had appeared overnight.
2. He got the flat cheap, off a bloke with a dubious haircut and an even more dubious contract.
News writing runs on the fixed phrase "the dubious distinction of" — the standard polite way to report that someone leads a league table nobody wants to top.
Latin dubium = "doubt", from duo = "two" — wavering between two options.

The same du- pays out elsewhere: doubt, indubitable (not to be doubted — the classic "certainly" word), dubiety, and plain double.

To trick a gullible person; also, that person.
Verb: to trick or deceive someone into believing something false.
Noun: the person so tricked — a gull, a sucker, a mark.

The word's weight sits on the victim, not the trickster. Defraud points at a crime, swindle at money, deceive at the lie itself — but to be duped is to have been credulous, and the word quietly says so. Hence the noun: a dupe isn't just someone who was lied to, it's someone who was easy to lie to. It carries a faint condescension, which is why "I was duped" is an admission as much as a complaint.
Change one letter and a dupe is a dope — and a dope is exactly who gets duped.
The near-homophone carries the nuance: the word blames the gullible mark, not the con artist.
1. The pamphlet duped thousands of small investors into a company that owned nothing but a leased office and a logo.
2. He spent an hour on the phone before realising he'd been duped by a guy reading off a script.
The beauty-world "dupe" — a £6 lipstick sold as a dupe for a £40 one. Different sense (that one's short for duplicate), but it works the same way: something cheap passing for the real thing.
🚫 Not from duplicate. English took it straight from French dupe, "a gull, one easily fooled" — traditionally traced to de huppe, "hoopoe," a bird with a reputation for being filthy and stupid.

The look-alike overlap is a coincidence: the duplicate sense of "dupe" arrived centuries later, by a completely separate road.
column3: g06 register::neutral connotation::negative antonym::easily-fooled-vs-hard-to-fool connotation::coaxing-that-shades-into-manipulation meaning::cheat-someone-out-of-something meaning::unseasoned-and-easily-taken-in

column2:
Two-faced and deceitful; running a deliberate double game.
Deceitful in a two-faced way: saying one thing while doing or intending another, often to two audiences at once. (Noun: duplicity — not "duplicitousness.")

A liar tells one falsehood; a duplicitous person runs a sustained double game — the friendly face to you, the knife behind it. It implies system and premeditation, not a slip. The word is formal and openly damning: you don't call someone duplicitous in passing, you call them it when you've decided they're rotten.
⚠️ duplicitous ≠ duplicative.
- duplicitous = two-faced, deceitful
- duplicative = merely repetitive, redundant

A duplicative report wastes your time. A duplicitous colleague wrote it to cover his tracks.
DUPE is sitting right at the front — and it takes two faces (dupli-) to dupe you properly.
The doubling is the point: one mouth for each audience, which is what separates duplicity from an ordinary lie.
1. The memo revealed a duplicitous strategy: reassuring regulators in public while lobbying to gut the very rules in private.
2. He was all smiles at lunch and then trashed her in the meeting — completely duplicitous.
The 2009 film Duplicity — Clive Owen and Julia Roberts as corporate spies who spend the whole movie double-crossing everyone, including each other. The title is the plot.
Latin duplex, duplic- = "twofold, double." Same root gives duplex, duplicate, duplicity.

Zoom out to -plic-/-plex- (plicāre, "to fold") and you unlock a GRE family: complicated (folded together), implicate (folded in), explicit (folded out, so plain), replicate, perplex.

Threat or force that makes your consent meaningless.
Compulsion by threat, violence, or unlawful pressure — force applied to make someone act against their will.

It lives almost entirely in one phrase: under duress. And it carries a built-in excuse. Saying you acted under duress is saying the act wasn't really yours: your consent was manufactured, so it shouldn't count. That's why it's a legal term first — a contract or confession obtained under duress is voidable. Pressure is neutral and can be fair; duress means the choice was taken away. It also gets used with dry humour for trivial coercion ("I watched the sequel under duress"), and the joke works precisely because the word is so heavy.
⚠️ duress ≠ distress. Duress is pressure someone puts on you; distress is the suffering you feel. A hostage signs under duress and is in distress.
Duress is dur- as in endure and obdurate — someone gets hard with you until you say yes.
The hardness is coming from outside, which is why whatever you agreed to doesn't stick.
1. The court set aside the confession, finding it had been extracted under duress after eleven hours without counsel.
2. "I only agreed to the family photo under duress — Mum threatened to cancel Christmas."
Alarm panels and bank systems have a duress code — a second PIN you enter when someone is forcing you, which opens the door normally but silently calls the police. The word survives there in its purest sense: doing the thing, but not freely.
Latin dūrus = "hard" → dūrāre, "to harden, to last."

One root, a lot of GRE words: durable and duration (lasting), endure (stay hard under strain), obdurate (hardened against persuasion), dour (hard-faced), during. Duress is the hardness turned on a person until they give way.

Doing what's required — obedient, correct, often without real warmth.
Doing exactly what duty, custom, or family obligation requires — obedient, conscientious, reliably correct in conduct.

The word almost never describes passion. A devoted son visits because he wants to; a dutiful son visits because it's Sunday. Praise, yes — but cool praise, and in modern usage it tips easily into faint praise or quiet mockery: dutiful applause, a dutiful nod, a dutiful phone call home. The action is performed correctly and the feeling is missing. Watch the noun it attaches to: obligations (dutiful wife, dutiful heir) or hollow gestures (a dutiful laugh).
Duty-full — full of duty, empty of desire.
The word is literally duty + full, and that's the whole nuance: the obligation is fully discharged, the enthusiasm isn't there.
1. A dutiful heir, he managed the estate for thirty years without once admitting he had wanted to be a painter.
2. She gave the joke a dutiful laugh and went back to her phone.
The Prodigal Son parable: the famous brother is the one who ran off, but the dutiful one is the elder brother who stayed home, did everything right, and sulked when the party was thrown for someone else — obedience without joy, in one character.
Duty comes from Old French deü, "that which is owed," from Latin dēbēre — to owe. So dutiful means "full of what you owe," which is exactly why it sounds like a debt being paid rather than a love being felt.

That root pays out elsewhere: debt, debit, debenture, indebted — and endeavour, from en devoir, "to put oneself in duty."

Steadily shrinking, little by little, toward nothing.
Steadily shrinking, bit by bit, in a way that points toward nothing left.

Decreasing is neutral arithmetic and can stop anywhere; plummeting is fast and dramatic. Dwindling is slow, continuous, and already sad — it carries the implication that the thing will eventually run out. It also has no villain: supplies dwindle, crowds dwindle, hope dwindles, all by themselves, with nobody doing it. That's why it attaches to things you're counting anxiously — funds, numbers, reserves, time.
Dwindle is swindle with one letter changed — and both take your money slowly, a little at a time.
The rhyme fixes the gradualness: nothing is seized in one grab, it just quietly gets less and less.
1. Attendance at the village church has dwindled from three hundred to a scattered dozen in the front pews.
2. We started with a full tank and a big plan, and by Tuesday both were dwindling fast.
It's the default word of business and climate reporting: dwindling cash reserves, dwindling glaciers, dwindling subscriber numbers. If you learn one collocation, learn dwindling reserves — it's practically a fixed phrase.
Old English dwīnan = "to waste away, languish." The -le on the end is the English "keep doing it, little by little" suffix — the same one in spark-le, crumb-le, trick-le, nib-ble. So dwindle is literally to go on wasting away, in small instalments — the suffix, not the root, is what encodes the slowness.

An easing of hostility between rivals.
An easing of hostility between rivals — usually states, sometimes people — after a period of strain.

Détente is a lowering of temperature, not a friendship. Nobody has forgiven anybody; the two sides have simply stopped aiming. It's cool, diplomatic, headline vocabulary — you'd read it about superpowers, warring departments, or two relatives who have agreed not to bring up the will. Applied to a small human quarrel it lands drily, half-joking, because it dresses a squabble in the language of arms control.
⚠️ détente ≠ entente.
- détente = the tension drops between enemies
- entente = an understanding, a friendly alignment (the Triple Entente, the Entente Cordiale)

Enemies reach a détente. Friends form an entente.
Dé-tente = de-tensed. The bowstring is slackened — but the bow is still loaded.
That second half is the nuance: relaxing the pull is not the same as putting the weapon down.
1. After eighteen months of sanctions and recalled ambassadors, the summit produced a fragile détente.
2. Mum and my aunt have reached a détente — they still don't speak, but nobody's storming out of Christmas this year.
Détente is the standard name for the 1970s thaw in the Cold War — Nixon and Brezhnev, the SALT talks, the handshake photos. The missiles stayed in their silos the whole time, which is exactly what the word means.
French détente = "a slackening, a release" — originally the catch that releases a crossbow trigger. From Latin tendere, "to stretch."

That root is a GRE workhorse: tension, tense, extend, distend, intense, portend, tendon, contend. Anything stretched tight. Put dé- ("un-, away") in front and you get the stretch coming off.

Bubbling over with cheerful, unmissable, slightly excessive energy.
Overflowing with cheerfulness and energy — visibly, audibly delighted.

This is joy that leaves the body. A happy person can be quiet; an ebullient one cannot — talking fast, laughing loud, greeting strangers. The word almost always approves, but it keeps a faint edge of too much: a hint that the mood is running hotter than the occasion requires and may not last. That edge is why journalists reach for it about crowds, campaigns and stock markets as often as about people.
E-BOIL-ient — joy at a rolling boil, lid rattling, spilling down the sides of the pot.
Boiling is the whole idea: the feeling isn't just warm, it's escaping the container where everyone can see it.
1. The Prime Minister returned from the summit ebullient, promising reporters a deal by Friday.
2. He came back from the interview ebullient — bought a round for the whole office before they'd even called him.
Financial pages love "ebullient markets" — traders bubbling with optimism, prices frothing up. The root rather gives away how those stories tend to end.
Latin ebullīre = "to boil out" — ex- (out) + bullīre (to boil).

Same bullīre gives you ebullition (a sudden outburst of feeling), bouillon (broth — literally boiled stuff), and plain boil itself.

Oddly unconventional, but harmlessly — even charmingly — so.
Adj.: deviating from the conventional in a harmless, distinctive way. Noun: a person who does exactly that.

The word is tolerant. Weird and bizarre push the odd person away; eccentric keeps them, with a smile. It implies the oddity is stable and self-contained — a man who wears the same purple suit daily and keeps forty clocks is eccentric; a man who frightens strangers is not. There's also a quiet class edge to it: the rich and the tenured get called eccentric, everyone else gets called strange.
⚠️ eccentric ≠ eclectic.
- eccentric = off-centre — odd, unconventional
- eclectic = selected from many sources — a wide-ranging mix

An eclectic record collection is broad. An eccentric one is all kazoo music.
Off-centre, not off the rails.
The eccentric has merely drifted from the middle of normal — still functioning, still likeable, just not standing where everyone else is.
1. The college indulged its most eccentric don, who lectured barefoot and addressed his students exclusively in the third person.
2. My aunt's a bit eccentric — she's named all the garden gnomes after prime ministers.
The press can't resist "eccentric billionaire" — Howard Hughes, Musk, any tech founder mid-scandal. Watch what the phrase does: the money is what converts unhinged into eccentric.
Greek ek (out of) + kentron (centre) — literally out of centre. It started as astronomy: an eccentric orbit is one whose centre isn't where it ought to be.

Same centr- family: concentric (sharing a centre), egocentric (self at the centre), epicentre, centrifugal.

column2:
A rung or tier in a hierarchy — usually the upper ones.
A level or rank within a hierarchy — one tier of an organisation, and the people occupying it. (Military sense: troops or ships arranged in staggered parallel lines, each stepped back from the one ahead.)

Level is flat and neutral; echelon presumes a whole ladder of them, with power concentrated at the top. It's institutional vocabulary — governments, armies, corporations, sports leagues — and it almost always comes attached to the top of the structure: the upper echelons, the highest echelons of the party. Using it about a diner's staff would be a joke.
You almost never hear lower echelons — the word is a rung, and it gets mentioned when someone's near the top of the ladder.
Lock the collocation "upper echelons" and you've locked both halves at once: the literal rung and the whiff of power that comes with it.
1. The report was circulated only within the upper echelons of the ministry, and never reached the officials who would have to implement it.
2. He started in the mailroom and clawed his way into the top echelon in six years.
In Splinter Cell, Sam Fisher works for Third Echelon — a covert tier buried inside the NSA's hierarchy. The name is doing exactly what the word means: naming a rank-level, not a place.
French échelon = "rung of a ladder," a diminutive of échelle (ladder), from Latin scala.

That root pays off elsewhere: escalate (climb the ladder), escalator, scale (as in scale a wall), scalar. Every one of them is a ladder in disguise.

Drawn deliberately from many different sources or styles.
Drawn from a wide variety of sources, styles, or traditions rather than following one school.

The word carries approval, and the reason is deliberateness. An eclectic library isn't a jumble — someone picked each thing on its own merits, ignoring the boundaries between genres. Say a collection is random and you're calling it thoughtless; say it's eclectic and you're crediting the taste behind it. It also quietly denies originality: an eclectic thinker borrows widely instead of inventing a system.
⚠️ eclectic ≠ eccentric.
- eclectic = gathered from many sources
- eccentric = off-centre, odd, deviating from the norm

An eclectic wardrobe pulls from six decades; an eccentric one is just strange.
Hiding inside e-clect-ic is elect — you elect the best bits from everywhere.
That buried verb is the whole nuance: eclectic means chosen, never merely mixed.
1. The architect's style was frankly eclectic, marrying Gothic tracery to a steel frame without apology.
2. His playlist is so eclectic it went from Gregorian chant to drill in two songs.
A restaurant menu or a bar's music policy described as "eclectic" — the standard compliment for a lineup that refuses to sit in one genre.
Greek eklektikos, "selective" — from ek (out) + legein (to pick, gather). The ancient Eclectics were philosophers who took doctrines from every school rather than joining one.

Its Latin cousin legere (to choose, read) pays out across the exam: select, elect, elite, collect, legible, lecture.

to outshine completely; a blotting-out of light
Noun: one body passing in front of another and blotting out its light — a solar or lunar eclipse.
Verb (the GRE sense): to outshine so completely that the other thing is no longer noticed.

The eclipsed thing isn't beaten or destroyed — it's still there, just invisible while something brighter stands in front of it. That's what separates eclipse from defeat or surpass: it's about attention, not victory. It also implies a before-and-after — a predecessor, an earlier record, an older sibling — so it very often shows up in the passive: his early novels were eclipsed by the trilogy. Neutral in itself, but it usually carries a faint sadness for whatever got left in the shade.
Eclipse has clips in it — you get clipped out of the picture, not knocked out of it.
Being eclipsed means still being there and simply not being seen.
1. Her later diplomatic career so thoroughly eclipsed her time on the bench that few recall she was ever a judge.
2. Great party, but the free bar completely eclipsed the speeches — nobody remembers a word of them.
Bonnie Tyler's "Total Eclipse of the Heart" — the karaoke standard. The heart isn't gone; it's blotted out.
Greek ekleipein = "to leave out, to fail to appear" — ek- ("out") + leipein ("to leave"). The sun doesn't die during an eclipse; it fails to show up.

Same leip- root gives you ellipsis (the three dots marking words left out) and ellipse (a circle with something left out of it).

Sparing, efficient use of resources — nothing wasted.
Beyond "the nation's finances," the sense the GRE tests is sparing, efficient use of any resource — words, movement, effort, materials. An economy of gesture. Economy of style.

Used this way it's almost always praise: it means nothing is wasted, not that little is spent. A stingy person practises parsimony; a good writer practises economy — same reduction, opposite verdict. It implies skill and control, the sense that everything left in is doing work.
⚠️ economic ≠ economical.
- economic = to do with the economy (economic policy, economic growth)
- economical = thrifty, sparing (an economical little car)

An economic decision affects GDP; an economical decision saves you money.
Economy isn't less — it's no waste.
That distinction is why "economy of prose" is a compliment while "cheap prose" is an insult.
1. Vermeer's late paintings achieve their power through sheer economy: a single window, one figure, nothing else in the room.
2. Watch her cook — total economy of movement, not one wasted step between the fridge and the pan.
Economy class on a plane: the seat designed so that not one cubic inch is spent on anything you don't strictly need. Fly it once and the meaning of the word is in your knees.
Greek oikos (house) + nomos (law, management) → oikonomia, "household management" — running the home without waste. That's why the thrift sense is the original one and the national-finances sense came later.

Both halves pay off elsewhere: oikos gives ecology and ecumenical; nomos gives autonomy, astronomy, taxonomy, gastronomy — all "the rules governing X."

column2:
To improve someone morally or intellectually; to uplift.
To instruct or improve someone morally, intellectually, or spiritually — to leave them a better person, not merely a better-informed one.

Teach transfers information; edify elevates character. That's why you can be taught to weld but not edified by it. The word carries a faint pulpit echo — high-minded, slightly lofty, a touch improving-in-the-Victorian-sense — so in modern use it tilts dry and ironic. Its commonest habitat is the negative: "not an edifying spectacle," "hardly edifying," meaning the thing was squalid or degrading to watch.
EDIFy hides EDIFice — you're building someone up like a building.
Edifying doesn't just fill a person with facts, it constructs something better in them — which is why a lecture edifies and a bar brawl does not.
1. The society's evening lectures were founded to edify the working men of the parish, not merely to occupy them.
2. Three hours of grown adults screaming on live TV — not exactly edifying.
British press and sports commentary run on one stock phrase: "not an edifying spectacle." Players brawling, a party leader shouted down in the Commons — that's the sentence that follows.
Latin aedificāre = "to build" (aedes, a building or temple + facere, to make). Church Latin borrowed it for building up the soul, and that metaphor is the whole word.

Same root gives you edifice — a large, imposing building — so the pair locks together: an edifice is built of stone, edification is built in a person.

Actually works — produces the intended effect, especially a remedy.
Capable of producing the intended effect — it actually works.

Where effective is the everyday word for anything that works, efficacious is the lab-coat version, reserved almost entirely for remedies and measures: a drug, a treatment, a vaccine, a policy, a ritual. You'd call a manager effective; calling him efficacious sounds like you're prescribing him. It also carries a whiff of proven under test conditions rather than merely useful in practice — which is exactly why medicine loves it.
⚠️ efficacious ≠ efficient.
- efficacious = it produces the result
- efficient = it produces the result without waste

A treatment can be efficacious and wildly inefficient: it cures you, at ten thousand pounds a dose.
The -acious family is all about being full of something — audacious, tenacious, voracious. Efficacious = full of effect.
Once you hear the suffix as "bursting with," the word stops being a fancy synonym and becomes a claim that the thing is loaded with actual working power.
1. Trials found the compound efficacious against the resistant strain, though its side effects kept it off the market.
2. Honestly, tea and eight hours' sleep is the most efficacious thing I've tried for a hangover.
The 2020–21 vaccine headlines ran on this word's noun form — "95% efficacy in trials." That's the natural habitat: a number from a controlled study, not a vibe.
Latin efficere = "to bring about" — from ex- ("out") + facere ("to make, to do").

Facere is one of the great GRE roots: factory, manufacture, benefactor, facile, feasible, affect, effect. Anything with -fac-, -fic-, -fect- is doing or making something.

column2:
Shameless nerve; audacity that should have blushed and didn't.
Shameless, insolent boldness — nerve of a kind that ought to have produced a blush and didn't.

Audacity can be admiring; effrontery never is. It always carries the speaker's outrage at someone's gall — the offence isn't the act alone but the barefaced confidence with which it was done. Note the collocation: it lives almost entirely in "had the effrontery to —", and whatever follows that phrase is something the speaker considers indefensible. Formal, faintly indignant, the register of a judge or an affronted letter to the editor.
effrontery ≠ affront. Same root, one letter apart. An affront is the insult itself (he took it as an affront); effrontery is the shamelessness of the person delivering it. You offer an affront; you have the effrontery.
Effrontery is in-your-FRONT-ery — done to your face, without flinching.
The word wears front in the middle of it, which is exactly where the nerve is: brazen, frontal, no shame and no retreat.
1. Having lost the case, the defendant had the effrontery to demand that the court cover his legal fees.
2. He turned up two hours late and then had the effrontery to complain the food was cold.
French effronté = shameless, from Latin frons, frontis = forehead, brow — literally "without a brow," someone whose face cannot blush.

That root is a workhorse: front, frontal, confront (brow to brow), frontier (the facing edge), affront (a slap to the face), effrontery (a face that won't redden).

column2:
Believing everyone deserves equal status, rights, and rewards.
Holding — or built on — the principle that all people are equal and deserve equal rights, status, and rewards. As a noun, a person who believes that.

The word points at structures, not sentiments: pay bands, voting rights, who speaks first in a meeting, who inherits. A generous boss isn't egalitarian; a boss who abolishes the private office and flattens the pay scale is. Note also that democratic describes how decisions get made, while egalitarian describes how status and resources get distributed — a democracy can be deeply unequal.

Tone is usually approving, and slightly lofty — it belongs to political writing, sociology and manifestos rather than casual speech. Critics use it drily, for levelling they think has gone too far.
⚠️ egalitarian ≠ humanitarian. Egalitarian is about equal standing — no one above anyone else. Humanitarian is about relieving suffering — feeding, healing, rescuing. An aid convoy is humanitarian; abolishing the caste system is egalitarian.
e-GAL-itarian — every gal, every guy, the same share.
The stressed middle syllable hides the point: equal shares by arrangement, not kindness handed down.
1. The founders imagined an egalitarian republic, though they wrote its charter while owning the people who served them.
2. It's a pretty egalitarian office — the CEO queues for coffee like everyone else.
The French Revolution's motto — Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité — is this word's root standing in the middle of the most famous slogan in political history, still stamped on French coins.
French égal ← Latin aequus / aequalis = "level, even."

That root pays off across the GRE: equity (fairness), equanimity (a level mind under pressure), equivocate (giving two claims equal weight, so you say nothing), adequate (levelling up to the requirement), and iniquity — in- + aequus, literally "un-level," hence gross injustice or wickedness.

column2:
Outstandingly, conspicuously bad — bad enough to point at.
Outstandingly bad — bad in a way that stands out, conspicuous enough that people notice and name it.

Not a synonym for "very bad." Egregious is a verdict handed down: judges, editors, referees and inspectors reach for it, and it lands on the offence, not the person — an egregious error, an egregious lie, an egregious breach. It implies the fault was so plain that missing it was itself a failure. Say it about a small private mistake and you sound absurd.

Historical twist worth knowing: it once meant outstandingly good, and flipped to sarcastic use around the 1500s. That reversal is why the root looks so oddly complimentary.
Sounds like "a grievous" — and an egregious fault is a grievous one that everybody can see.
The word never covers small quiet faults — only ones bad enough to point at, which is why it pairs almost automatically with error, lie, foul, violation.
1. The auditors described the omission as an egregious breach of fiduciary duty, and the board resigned within a week.
2. Forgetting the client's name in the pitch meeting was bad; calling him by his rival's name was egregious.
It's the standard escalation word in law and sport: courts speak of "egregious misconduct" as a threshold that triggers real sanctions, and a commentator saying "that's an egregious foul" means the card is coming out.
Latin ē- (out of) + grex, gregis (flock, herd) — literally standing out from the herd. Originally a compliment: distinguished, head and shoulders above the crowd. Sarcasm dragged it downhill until only the bad kind of standing out survived.

The flock unlocks a whole set: gregarious (happy in the herd), congregate (flock together), segregate (flock apart), aggregate (herded into one mass).

Worked out in painstaking detail; or, to say more.
Adj.: worked out in great detail; made of many carefully arranged parts. Verb: to develop something in detail, or to say more about a point already made.

Complicated is a complaint — it means hard to follow. Elaborate points at the effort that went in: someone built this, part by part, usually to impress. An elaborate meal, an elaborate costume, an elaborate apology. That admiration curdles fast, though — the moment effort looks disproportionate, elaborate turns suspicious: an elaborate excuse, an elaborate hoax, an elaborate scheme. Nobody labours that hard over a story that's true.
e-LABOR-ate — the labour is sitting right there in the middle of the word.
Elaborate never means merely complex; it means somebody worked at it.
1. The cathedral's façade is elaborate to the point of vertigo — every niche filled, every surface carved.
2. "Interesting." "Care to elaborate?"
"Could you elaborate on that?" is the standard meeting-room request for more detail — the one sense of the word you'll hear spoken aloud most weeks.
Latin ex- ("out") + laborāre ("to work") = worked out. The labor root runs everywhere: laboratory (a workplace), laborious, collaborate (work with), belabour (work a point to death).

column2:
Joyfully lifted up by some particular piece of good news.
Adjective: filled with high spirits — joyful and lifted up, usually by something specific that just happened.

Elation is joy with an event attached: you're elated at the news, by the result, to hear it. Happy can be a steady state; elated is a spike, and a short one — nobody is elated for a fortnight. It sits above pleased and delighted but below euphoric, which carries a hint of something unreal or chemical. The word is warm and slightly formal, which is why journalists reach for it: winners, survivors and parents-to-be are described as elated far more often than they describe themselves that way.
⚠️ elated ≠ belated. One letter apart, no relation: belated = late, overdue (a belated birthday card). Belated congratulations may still leave someone elated.
Moods run on air pressure: elated or deflated.
Elated is the up-pole of that pair — buoyant, inflated by good news — and like deflation it's caused by something, not just a temperament.
1. Elated by the acquittal, she walked out of the courthouse into a wall of cameras.
2. He was elated — he'd checked the results page about nine times before he believed it.
The default word of sports and news reporting: "an elated Ronaldo", "elated rescuers". If someone's just won or just been saved, a headline will call them elated.
Latin efferre, "to carry out, raise up" — past participle ēlātus, "lifted".

The -lat- ("carried") chunk is worth owning, because it pays out across the exam: translate (carried across), relate (carried back), collate (carried together), prelate (carried in front → high-ranking), superlative (carried above the rest). Elated = carried upward.

column2:
Basic, introductory — the first and simplest level of something.
Concerned with the first and simplest parts of a subject — introductory, rudimentary, requiring no advanced knowledge.

Applied to material, it's flatly neutral: an elementary textbook, elementary arithmetic. Applied to a person's mistake or question, it turns barbed — "an elementary error" means one so basic you should be embarrassed to have made it. Same word, and the insult lives entirely in what you attach it to.
⚠️ elementary ≠ elemental.
- elementary = basic, beginner-level — an elementary mistake
- elemental = raw, primal, of the fundamental forces — elemental rage, elemental fury of the storm

Elementary is small and simple. Elemental is huge and primitive.
Elementary school comes before everything else — and calling a grown-up's question elementary is telling them that's where they belong.
The school sense fixes the meaning (the very first level) and the sneer fixes the tone.
1. A grasp of elementary statistics is assumed before the seminar begins.
2. Mate, you forgot to plug it in — that's an elementary mistake.
"Elementary, my dear Watson" — Holmes's catchphrase in the films (not, in fact, in Conan Doyle's stories in that exact form), and the title of the Sherlock series Elementary. The tone is the point: he means obvious to anyone paying attention, which is why it stings.
Latin elementum = a first principle, a rudiment — and, in the plural, the letters of the alphabet, the very first thing a Roman child was taught. Elementary knowledge is literally your ABCs.

To draw out a response, reaction, or information from someone.
To draw out a response, reaction, or piece of information from someone — by asking, prompting, or provoking.

The word assumes the thing was already there, latent, and needed coaxing into the open. That's what separates it from its neighbours: you provoke a reaction (aggressive), you extract a confession (force), but you elicit — skilfully, often quietly, usually by asking the right question. And it points at a person: you elicit a laugh, an answer, a confession, a groan. A chemical reaction isn't elicited.
⚠️ elicit ≠ illicit. Same sound, unrelated words.
- elicit (verb) = draw out — elicited a response
- illicit (adjective) = illegal, forbidden — illicit substances

If it's a thing you do, it's elicit. If it's a thing you'd get arrested for, it's illicit.
Elicit extracts; illicit is illegal — like illogical, illegible, immoral.
That opening il- is the standard Latin negative prefix, so illicit is a "not-allowed" adjective, while the bare e- ("out") makes elicit the verb that pulls something out of a person.
1. Under patient cross-examination, the barrister elicited an admission the witness had spent two years avoiding.
2. My joke elicited exactly one laugh in the whole room, and it was mine.
In software and product work the process of finding out what users actually need has a formal name: requirements elicitation — so called precisely because you can't just ask outright, you have to draw it out of them.
Latin ēlicere = ex- ("out") + lacere ("to lure, entice") — literally to lure it out. The persuasion is baked into the word.

That same lacere shows up, via dēlicere ("lure away"), in delight, delectable and delicious — all things that entice you.

🚫 Not the root of illicit. That's licēre, "to be permitted" — giving licit, licence, and (oddly) leisure. Identical sound, unrelated family.

Believing a chosen few are superior and should rule.
Holding — or acting on — the belief that a chosen few (by birth, money, brains, or taste) are superior and should get the power, the say, and the good seats. As a noun, the person who thinks that way.

This is a word people throw at others. Nobody describes themselves as an elitist; it's a charge of contempt for ordinary people, aimed at attitude rather than achievement. A surgeon who is genuinely the best in the country isn't elitist — she becomes elitist the moment she implies that people like her should decide things for people like you. Register is political and journalistic, and it stings: it accuses you of snobbery and of wanting that snobbery institutionalised.
⚠️ elite ≠ elitist.
- elite = the top tier — usually a compliment (elite athlete, elite unit)
- elitist = the ideology of the top tier — always an attack

Being elite is a fact about you. Being elitist is a fact about how you treat everyone else.
An elitist insists that the elite should be in charge.
The -ist is what does the damage — it upgrades a description of a group into a creed someone is accused of holding, exactly as in racist or sexist.
1. The reforms were denounced as elitist: free tuition, but only for those who had already survived a school system the poor could not afford.
2. Charging forty quid for a burger and calling it "curated" is peak elitist nonsense.
Anton Ego in Ratatouille — the gaunt food critic whose whole posture says taste belongs to people like me. The film's answer to him is its slogan: "Anyone can cook." That's the anti-elitist argument in three words.
Latin ēligere = "to pick out, choose" (ē- out + legere to gather, select). The elite are literally the chosen ones.

Same root, same idea of choosing: elect, election, eligible, select, elegant (originally "choosy about taste" — which is where the snobbery seeps in).

Fluent and graceful in speech; movingly, vividly expressive.
Speaking (or writing) fluently, gracefully, and persuasively — with language that moves people.

Articulate only means you make yourself clear; eloquent means you make people feel it. It is praise, and fairly high praise: it implies command of rhythm and phrasing, not just vocabulary. Note the second sense the GRE likes — a thing can be eloquent without words at all: an eloquent silence, an eloquent glance, statistics that are eloquent about a country's decline. There, it means vividly expressive.
eloquent ≠ loquacious. Same root, opposite compliment: eloquent = speaks well; loquacious = speaks a lot (and usually too much). The bore at the party is loquacious; the person who quiets the room is eloquent.
Eloquent is elegant with a Q — elegance, but in speech.
The near-rhyme carries the nuance exactly: eloquence is not loud or lengthy but graceful, which is why a silence can be eloquent too.
1. His eulogy was brief and eloquent; not a word of it was wasted, and half the church was in tears by the end.
2. She didn't say anything — but the look she gave him was pretty eloquent.
It's the standard word reached for about King's I Have a Dream — routinely called the most eloquent speech in American history, and a good ear-test for what eloquence actually sounds like.
Latin ex- (out) + loquī (to speak) — "speaking out."

That root is a GRE goldmine: loquacious (talkative), colloquial (speaking together — everyday talk), soliloquy (speaking alone), circumlocution (talking around the point), grandiloquent (speaking grandly, i.e. pompous), elocution, and ventriloquist — literally a belly-speaker.

To make an obscure thing clear by explaining it.
To make something clear by explaining it — to shed light on a difficult point.

The word presumes prior obscurity. You explain directions to a stranger; you elucidate a tangled clause, a contested passage, a mechanism nobody has pinned down. It's the vocabulary of the lecture hall, the courtroom and the journal abstract — a lawyer asked to "elucidate" is being told, politely, that what they just said was mud. And unlike clarify, which can be a quick fix ("let me clarify — 3pm, not 4"), elucidating implies sustained, expert unpacking.
elucidate ≠ elicit. To elucidate is to shed light on something obscure; to elicit is to draw out a response, a confession, a laugh. You elicit an answer from a witness; you elucidate the answer once you have it.
e-LUCID-ate — the word lucid is sitting inside it. You elucidate what wasn't lucid yet.
Nothing needs elucidating unless it was murky first, which is exactly why the word sounds heavier than explain.
1. The footnotes do more to elucidate the poem's central image than the twenty pages of commentary preceding them.
2. Could you elucidate that last bit? You lost me somewhere around the second slide.
It's the workhorse verb of scientific abstracts — papers exist "to elucidate the mechanism of" some protein, reaction or disease. If you've ever skimmed a PubMed abstract, you've read it a dozen times.
Latin lux, lucis = light, via lucidus = bright, clear. The e- is "out": to bring out into the light.

That root is worth a lot of GRE marks: lucid (clear-minded), translucent (light passes through), pellucid (perfectly clear — of prose or water), elucidate, and Lucifer, literally light-bringer.

Slipping out of reach just as you close on it.
Hard to catch, find, or pin down — it escapes you as you reach for it.

The word carries motion. Something rare is simply scarce; something elusive is actively slipping away — a fugitive who's always one town ahead, a memory that dissolves the moment you reach for it, a word on the tip of your tongue. It works on the physical (an elusive suspect), the abstract (an elusive concept, an elusive scent), and the desired (that elusive promotion).

Tone shifts with the target: applied to a thing you want, it's faintly frustrating; applied to a person — a boxer, a winger, a witness — it edges into admiring, because escaping is a skill.
⚠️ elusive ≠ illusive.
- elusive = it escapes you (from elude)
- illusive = it deceives you; it isn't really there (from illusion)

An elusive fortune is real but always just out of reach. An illusive one was never there.
e-LOOSE-ive — it stays loose, never in your grip.
The stressed syllable literally sounds like loose, which is the whole nuance: not absent, just never held.
1. A unified theory of the four forces has remained elusive for a century, retreating each time physicists think they have closed on it.
2. I've been chasing him for three weeks — the man is elusive, he never picks up.
Wildlife documentaries have worn this word smooth: "the elusive snow leopard" is practically a fixed phrase — the animal you film for six months and glimpse for four seconds.
Latin ēlūdere = "to escape by play" — ex- (out) + lūdere (to play). The sense of dodging is baked in: you get away by playing with your pursuer.

That lūdere root is a GRE goldmine: allude (play toward → hint), delude and illusion (play someone false), collude (play together, secretly), prelude and interlude (play before / between), ludicrous (fit only for play).

To decorate — or to dress a true story in invented details.
1. To make something prettier by adding decorative detail — beads on a dress, gold leaf on a manuscript, a flourish on a melody.
2. To make a story more interesting by adding details that aren't true.

Sense 2 is the GRE one, and its charge is mild. Fabricate invents the whole thing; embellish starts from something real and dresses it up. That's why it's the word people use when they're half-forgiving someone — a storyteller embellishes, a fraudster lies. Say a witness embellished her account and you've cast doubt without calling her a liar.
em-BELL-ish — you put a belle on it: prettier, not truer.
The word hides belle, "beautiful woman," and that's exactly what embellishing does — improves the surface while leaving the truth underneath untouched.
1. The monks embellished the margins with gilt vines and small, improbable beasts.
2. He tells the story every Christmas and embellishes it a bit more each year — there were two robbers last time, now there are four.
Shop for a party dress online and half the listings say "embellished" — retail code for sequins, beading, or appliqué stitched onto a plain base.
Old French embellir, from bel / beau = "beautiful" — the same root behind belle, beau, beauty, belladonna, and Italian bellissimo.

🚫 Not Latin bellum, "war." Identical-looking root, opposite world: bellicose, belligerent, antebellum, rebel. One makes things pretty, the other starts fights.
