column2:
Able to feel what another person feels, from inside.
Able to enter another person's feelings — to register what they're experiencing from the inside, rather than merely noting it.

It's warm and approving, and it implies skill, not just goodwill: an empathetic doctor, manager, or listener is credited with an ability. That's why it has become the favourite compliment of HR decks and leadership profiles — which also means it can sound faintly corporate if you overuse it. Note too that it says nothing about acting: you can be empathetic and do nothing. Compassionate adds the impulse to help.
⚠️ empathetic ≠ sympathetic.
- empathetic = feeling with you — I share the emotion
- sympathetic = feeling for you — I'm sorry it happened, from where I stand

A sympathetic nod at a funeral; an empathetic friend who has buried a parent too.
em-PATH-etic — you get in their PATH and walk it.
The hidden word path is the whole distinction: empathy walks the other person's road, while sympathy calls out to them from your own.
1. The novel's power lies in its empathetic rendering of a mind unlike the reader's own.
2. She's the one you call when things go wrong — she's just weirdly empathetic, like she already knows.
Atticus Finch in To Kill a Mockingbird: "You never really understand a person until you climb into his skin and walk around in it." That sentence is the definition of empathetic, and it's built on the same image as the trick.
Greek en- (in) + pathos (feeling, suffering) — literally feeling-into.

One root, a whole GRE cluster: sympathy (feeling with), antipathy (feeling against), apathy (no feeling), pathos, pathetic, telepathy, and medical pathology (the study of suffering).

Based on observation and experiment, not on theory.
Based on observation, measurement, or experiment rather than on theory, doctrine, or pure reasoning.

The word labels the source of a claim, not its truth. "Empirical" doesn't mean correct — it means this came from going and looking. Its opposite is theoretical or a priori, never false. In academic and professional writing it carries quiet prestige: empirical evidence is data you collected, as against a hunch, a model, or an anecdote. But the older flavour still surfaces on the GRE — an empiric was once a physician who worked by trial and error with no theory at all, so the word can shade toward crude, atheoretical rule-of-thumb.
Empirical hides a pirate — and it's the same root. Pirates don't theorise; they go out and try it.
Both words come from Greek peira, "a trial, an attempt" — empirical knowledge is what you get by attempting the thing, not by reasoning about it in a chair.
1. The elegance of the model was never in doubt; what it lacked was empirical support.
2. Stop arguing about which headline is better — just run the test and get some empirical data.
Every A/B test at work is empiricism in miniature: nobody's opinion about the button colour wins, the click data does.
Greek empeiria = "experience," from peira = "a trial, an attempt."

That root pays out widely: experience and experiment (things you try), expert (someone who has tried it often), peril (a trial that might kill you) — and pirate, from peiratēs, "one who makes attempts on" ships.

Imitate someone in order to match or outdo them.
To imitate someone in order to match or surpass them — copying with ambition behind it.

The word carries admiration and rivalry at once. Imitate is neutral and can be mindless; mimic and ape are faintly insulting, suggesting a copy with nothing behind it. Emulate always points upward: you emulate a mentor, a champion, a predecessor — someone whose level you want to reach. Praise the copier, not mock him.

(Computing has borrowed it flatly: one machine emulating another just means reproducing its behaviour, no ambition involved.)
⚠️ emulate ≠ simulate.
- emulate = actually do what the model does, to match it
- simulate = fake it, or model it for study

A flight simulator pretends to be a plane. An emulator genuinely runs the other machine's software.
Emulate rhymes with elevate — you copy someone to rise to their level.
The rhyme locks in the direction of the word: emulation is imitation aimed upward, at someone better than you.
1. Successive Mughal emperors sought to emulate Akbar, and each fell short in a different way.
2. He started waking at five and reading two books a week, trying to emulate his older sister.
Playing old Nintendo or PlayStation games on a laptop means running an emulator — software pretending to be the original console, well enough to run its actual cartridges.
Latin aemulus = "rival." Not "copier" — rival. Emulation was born competitive: you match your rival's feat in order to beat it. That buried rivalry is exactly what separates emulate from imitate on the exam.

To bewitch — or to delight as if by magic.
To put under a magic spell — and, in everyday use, to delight someone so completely that they seem spellbound.

Both senses run at once, which is the whole point. Please and charm leave you in control; enchant takes the control away — the enchanted person is held, absorbed, not quite responsible for themselves. It's warmer and more helpless than impress, and softer and more sustained than dazzle, which flashes and fades. Slightly old-fashioned, faintly romantic: a landscape, a voice, a child, or a first meeting enchants you; a spreadsheet does not.
CHANT is sitting in the middle of it — somebody sang, and you never got a vote.
Enchantment is something done to you, which is why the word implies surrender rather than mere approval.
1. The old harbour town enchanted her: she had meant to stay two nights and stayed eleven.
2. Don't let him enchant you with that accent — he still hasn't paid rent.
Taylor Swift's "Enchanted" — "I was enchanted to meet you" — is the delight sense exactly: one meeting, and she's spellbound for the rest of the song.
Latin incantāre = "to sing a spell upon" — in- (on) + cantāre (to sing). Magic was chanted, so the singing verb became the bewitching one.

cantāre pays out widely: chant, incantation, canticle, descant, accent, and recant — literally to sing back, i.e. to take back what you said.

To intrude gradually on someone else's space, rights, or time.
To intrude little by little on what belongs to someone else — their land, rights, authority, or time.

An invasion is announced; an encroachment is noticed late. The word carries gradualness and creep: a hedge that grows six inches a year, a department quietly absorbing another's work, the sea taking the coast. Because the advance is incremental, no single step looks outrageous — which is exactly why the word implies a slow theft that should have been stopped earlier. Almost always used by the side being pushed back, and almost always with resentment.

Standard collocation: you encroach on (or upon) something.
Hidden inside encroach is roach — a roach never bursts in, it just gets a little further in each night.
Encroaching is pest-like advance: unauthorised, incremental, and noticed only once it is well inside.
1. The court held that the boundary wall encroached upon a metre of the adjoining plot and ordered it demolished.
2. Work's started encroaching on my weekends and I'm putting a stop to it.
Municipal anti-encroachment drives — the bulldozers that clear illegal structures and stalls off public land — are a permanent fixture of local news headlines.
Old French encrochier = "to hook in, seize", from croc, a hook. You don't march in — you hook a bit of the neighbour's land and drag it your way.

Same hook gives you crochet (a little hook), crook (a hooked staff — and the man who hooks what isn't his), and croquet (hooked mallet).

Covering a whole subject exhaustively, in encyclopedia-like detail.
Covering a huge range of a subject, in exhaustive detail — the way an encyclopedia does.

Nearly always it lands on someone's knowledge or memory, and it's a compliment with a whiff of hyperbole: encyclopedic knowledge of 1970s soul, an encyclopedic memory for faces. It praises breadth plus retrievable detail — not depth of insight. A scholar can be encyclopedic and still say nothing original.

Turn it on a book, a film or a writing style and the warmth drains out: encyclopedic there means comprehensive to the point of being flat, catalogue-like, no argument, just everything.
⚠️ encyclopedic ≠ encyclical. An encyclical is a letter from the Pope circulated to the whole Church — same circle root, completely different word. Nothing encyclopedic about it.
En-CYCL-o-pedic — the cycle is the giveaway: it goes all the way round a subject, leaving no arc uncovered.
The praise is for full coverage of the circle, not for how deep any one point is drilled.
1. His notes on the campaign were encyclopedic — every rally, every donor, every misquote — yet he never ventured a single conclusion.
2. She's got encyclopedic knowledge of the Marvel films; don't start an argument with her about timelines.
Wikipedia editors slap articles with a maintenance tag for not being written in an "encyclopedic tone" — meaning: neutral, comprehensive, no opinions, no jokes. That tag is the second sense of the word.
Greek enkyklios paideia = "education in the circle" — the full round of general learning every free citizen was supposed to have.

- kyklos = circle → cycle, bicycle, cyclone, encyclical
- paideia = the rearing of children, from pais/paidos = child → pediatric, pedagogue, pedant

🚫 The ped- here is child, not foot. Pedal, pedestrian, pedestal come from Latin pes/pedis — unrelated.

column2:
Permanently present in a particular place or group.
1. (of a disease or condition) constantly present in a particular place or group. 2. (of a plant or animal) native to and found only in one region — lemurs are endemic to Madagascar.

The key idea is permanent residence, not arrival. An epidemic surges and passes; something endemic has settled in and become part of the furniture. That's why the figurative use bites so hard: say corruption is endemic to the ministry and you're not reporting an outbreak, you're saying it's structural, baked in, and nobody expects it to leave. Biology's use is the neutral one; applied to human institutions, it's close to an indictment.
⚠️ endemic ≠ epidemic.
- endemic = en- (in) — always in the population, steady background level
- epidemic = epi- (upon) — sweeping onto the population, a sudden spike

Malaria is endemic to the tropics; cholera broke out as an epidemic.
Endemic things never end — they're the resident, not the visitor.
The false syllable end is a lie about the etymology but a perfect grip on the meaning: an endemic problem is the one that's always been there and shows no sign of stopping.
1. Chronic underfunding is endemic to the region's public hospitals, less a crisis than a permanent condition.
2. Honestly, missed deadlines are just endemic here — nobody even flinches anymore.
The whole 2022 debate over whether COVID had "gone endemic" — meaning not gone, but downgraded from emergency to permanent background resident.
Greek dēmos = "the people." En-dēmos = "in the people."

One root, a whole cluster: democracy (rule by the people), demographic (measuring the people), demagogue (one who leads — and inflames — the people), epidemic (upon the people), pandemic (all the people).

To give a permanent fund to, or gift with a natural quality.
Two linked senses:

1. To give a large sum of money or property to an institution, so that it produces income permanently — to endow a hospital, a scholarship, a professorship.
2. To furnish someone with a quality or ability from birth — endowed with perfect pitch.

Both senses are grand and one-directional. You give someone a fiver; you endow a university — the word implies size, permanence, and a giver with means. In sense 2 the gift comes from nature, God, or luck, never from effort: being endowed with a talent is the opposite of having earned it, which is why the word so often shades into "born lucky."
An endowment is built never to end — you live off the interest and never touch the gift.
The "end" sitting inside the word flags the key nuance: this isn't a donation that gets spent, it's a permanent capital gift.
1. The alumna endowed a chair in medieval history, stipulating that the post could never be abolished.
2. He's endowed with the kind of memory that makes revision look easy — the rest of us have to work.
The US Declaration of Independence: "...that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights." Sense 2 exactly — gifts you're born holding, not ones you're granted.
Old French endouer, from Latin dos, dotis = "dowry" — the property that came with a bride. That root gives you dowry, dower, and dowager (the widow living on her dower). Hear the dow in en-dow and the money is right there in the word.

To drain of strength and vitality; to leave limp.
To drain of energy, vitality or force; to leave someone weak and listless.

This isn't ordinary tiredness. Tire is what a run does to you; enervate is what a swampy climate, a long illness, or years of soft living do to you — a slow sapping that leaves you limp and without will. It carries a hint of moral softening as well as physical weakness, and it's a formal, written word: heat, luxury, and bureaucracy enervate; a gym session just tires you out.
⚠️ enervate ≠ innervate.
- enervate = take the nerve out → weaken
- innervate = supply nerves in → stimulate, activate

One letter, opposite directions. (And despite the look of it, enervate is the opposite of energize, not a synonym.)
Enervate wears energize's face — but that E is for empty.
The word looks like a boost and delivers the reverse: a slow draining that leaves you limp rather than merely tired.
1. Months of tropical damp had enervated the whole garrison; by August the men could barely shoulder their rifles.
2. That three-hour status meeting enervated me — I got home and just stared at the wall.
Latin ē- (out) + nervus (sinew, tendon, nerve) — literally "to cut the sinews out." A hamstrung animal is the picture: still alive, no strength left.

Same root: nerve, nervous, unnerve, innervate — and note that nervus first meant sinew, which is why "he has some nerve" means gall, not neurons.

column2:
To give rise to — usually a feeling or a condition.
To give rise to, bring about, cause something to come into being.

The object is almost always abstract — trust, resentment, loyalty, debate, a sense of unease. You engender conditions and feelings, not objects: a policy can engender confidence, but nothing engenders a bridge. Register is formal and slightly bookish; it belongs to editorials, court judgments and academic prose, where cause would sound blunt and create too deliberate. It also implies a side-effect rather than an aim — the thing arises from the situation, often without anyone intending it.
engender ≠ endanger. Same eight letters, nearly the same order — but engender brings something into existence, endanger puts something at risk. Secrecy may engender distrust; it may also endanger the deal.
You can engender trust, loyalty, or hatred — you cannot engender a chair.
The gen- buried in the middle means birth (as in genesis, generate), and what this verb gives birth to is always a feeling or a state of affairs, never a physical thing.
1. Decades of unexplained delays had engendered a deep public scepticism that no press release could dispel.
2. Turning up unannounced with a lawyer doesn't exactly engender goodwill.
Latin gignere / genus = "to beget, to be born", reaching English through Old French engendrer, "to father a child."

That root is one of the best investments on the GRE: genesis, generate, genre, genus, gene, congenital, progeny, indigenous, genuine, primogeniture. Whenever you see gen-, think birth or kind.

Mysterious in an intriguing, riddle-like way.
Mysterious and hard to interpret — puzzling in the way a riddle is puzzling.

The flavour is alluring, not alarming. An enigmatic person or remark holds something back and makes you lean in; you feel there's a solution behind it. Compare cryptic, which is deliberately obscure and usually irritating, and inscrutable, which gives you nothing to work with at all. Applied to a person, enigmatic is often quietly flattering — it grants them depth.
e-NIGMA-tic ends like magnetic — the mystery pulls you in rather than pushing you away.
That's the whole difference from cryptic: an enigmatic silence is fascinating, a cryptic one is annoying.
1. His late poems remain enigmatic, offering the reader a door without a key.
2. She gave me this enigmatic little smile and left, and I spent the whole train ride trying to decode it.
The German Enigma machine of WWII — the cipher device Turing's team broke at Bletchley Park, dramatised in The Imitation Game. It was named for the Greek word for riddle, which is exactly what enigmatic means: riddle-like.

Deep, lasting mutual hostility; the state of being enemies.
Deep, settled hostility between people or groups — the condition of being enemies.

Animosity flares up and dies down; enmity just sits there. It names a standing relationship rather than a feeling of the moment, and it doesn't have to be actively expressed — two families can be at enmity for eighty years without a word exchanged. It's usually mutual, often inherited, and the register is formal and slightly grand: clans, nations, houses, and factions have enmity; your annoying coworker gets animosity.
⚠️ enmity ≠ amity. Amity = friendly relations (the Treaty of Amity and Commerce). Same root, opposite sign — the en- is a buried "not."
Enmity = enemy + -ity — the state of being enemies, not a flash of temper.
-ity builds lasting conditions (purity, sanity, gravity), so enmity is hostility that has hardened into a permanent arrangement.
1. Centuries of enmity between the two houses had outlived every person who could remember how it began.
2. There's no enmity there — we just haven't spoken since the wedding.
Genesis 3:15, King James Bible — God to the serpent: "And I will put enmity between thee and the woman." Not a quarrel; a permanent state of war written into the world.
Latin amīcus = "friend" (from amāre, to love). Add the negating in- and you get inimīcus, "not-friend" → Old French enemi → enemy, and its abstract noun enmity.

One root, both poles: amicable, amiable, amity on the friendly side; enemy, enmity, inimical on the hostile side. Inimical ("harmful, hostile to") is the GRE's favourite member of that family.

Weary boredom from a life that no longer interests you.
A listless, settled boredom — dissatisfaction born of having nothing that interests you, and suspecting nothing ever will.

Plain boredom is situational and short: a delayed flight, a dull meeting. Ennui is a climate, not a weather event — chronic, faintly philosophical, and worn almost as a credential. It belongs to people with the leisure to be bored: aristocrats, poets, disaffected teenagers in black. Calling it ennui rather than boredom is itself a small act of self-flattery, and good writers use it knowing that.
Ennui is boredom that has been to Paris.
Same emptiness, but slower, grander, and quietly pleased with itself for feeling it.
1. A summer of country weekends left her in a state of ennui no invitation could cure.
2. Three months into the job it wasn't stress, it was ennui — I just stopped caring what the emails said.
Wes Anderson's The French Dispatch is set in a town called Ennui-sur-Blasé — "Boredom-on-Jaded." The joke only lands if you know the word, and knowing the joke locks the word in.
Latin in odiō — "in hatred," as in mihi in odio est, "it is loathsome to me." Through Old French enuier this became two English words from one source: ennui, and its plainer twin annoy.

That's the whole scale in one root: what merely irritates you is an annoyance; what deadens you is ennui. Related through odium: odious, odium.

column2:
To follow as a result of what came before.
To follow as a consequence — to happen next, and happen because of what just happened.

Two things pin it down. First, it never takes an object: things ensue, you can't ensue anything. Second, it's a narrator's word — the register of reports, minutes, and news copy ("a scuffle ensued"), not of conversation. Follow is plain sequence; ensue insists on causal link and adds a faint formality, as if someone is writing the incident up afterwards.
⚠️ ensue ≠ ensure. Ensue = to follow as a result (no object). Ensure = to make certain of (always takes an object). Ensure the doors are locked, or chaos will ensue.
Look at what actually ensues: chaos, panic, silence, a lengthy legal battle. Nothing good ever ensues.
The word's stock companions are all aftermath, so remember it as the verb for what spills out after the trouble starts.
1. When the treaty collapsed, three decades of intermittent border war ensued.
2. He knocked over the candle, and you can guess what ensued.
"Hilarity ensues" — the stock phrase in film blurbs and Netflix synopses for the chaos that follows the setup. It's so overused it's become a joke, which is exactly why it sticks.
Latin sequī = "to follow" (via Old French ensivre, "to follow upon"). That root is a GRE goldmine: sequence, consequence, sequel, subsequent, pursue, prosecute, obsequious (following your boss around), non sequitur (a statement that doesn't follow).

To grip someone's attention so totally they can't look away.
To hold someone's attention so completely that they lose all awareness of anything else — to captivate, spellbind, charm into helplessness.

Interest and fascinate leave you in charge of yourself; enthral takes that away. The enthralled person isn't choosing to keep watching — they can't stop. It's surrender, and it's almost always pleasurable surrender, which is what separates it from transfix (shock-frozen) or obsess (uncomfortable, self-generated). Usually passive: you are enthralled by something, and the something has the power.
En-THRALL = put into thrall — and a thrall is a slave.
The enthralled audience isn't merely watching the performer — it belongs to them.
1. The soprano's final aria enthralled a hall of two thousand into total silence.
2. I meant to watch one episode and it enthralled me straight through till 3 a.m.
"Enthralling" is the standard blurb word on book jackets and Netflix descriptions — an enthralling thriller. Critics reach for it precisely when they mean you will not be able to put this down.
en- (put into) + thrall, from Old Norse þræll = "slave." A Viking thrall was literally chattel — the bottom of Norse society.

The old sense survives intact in "in thrall to": in thrall to her addiction means enslaved by it, not delighted by it. Same root, no metaphor softening.

column2:
Having a rightful claim — or arrogantly assuming one.
1. Having a rightful claim to something: entitled to a refund, to three weeks' leave, to a fair hearing.
2. Of a person: assuming privileges and deference they haven't earned — "an entitled brat."
3. Given a title: a novel entitled Middlemarch.

The grammar tells you which one you're getting. Entitled to something is cold and bureaucratic — contracts, statutes, HR handbooks; no judgement at all. Entitled standing alone in front of a person is a moral verdict, and a sharp one: it says the claim is imaginary and the claimant is insufferable. Sense 1 is what the law grants you; sense 2 is what you grant yourself.
En-TITLE-d — he thinks he holds a title, like a duke, and the world should curtsy.
The insult sense is exactly that: someone behaving as though rank entitles them to service they never earned.
1. Under the terms of the settlement, every claimant is entitled to compensation regardless of when the injury occurred.
2. He's so entitled he sent the coffee back twice and then asked for the manager's manager.
In US politics, Social Security and Medicare are called entitlement programs — benefits you have a legal right to, not favours. Half the country's arguments about them come from hearing the other sense of the word.
Latin titulus = "title, inscription, label." To entitle is literally to put a title on something — hence a book entitled X, and hence a person who acts as if he'd been handed a rank.

Same root: title, subtitle, entitlement, and the GRE favourite titular — holding the title but not the power (the titular head of state).

To beg earnestly but courteously; to plead.
To ask someone earnestly and humbly for something — to plead, to beg with feeling.

The word is dignified begging. Beg can be abject and implore is nearly frantic, but entreat keeps its manners: it's the plea of someone who has no power in the situation but has not lost their composure — a petitioner, a wife, a subject addressing a king. It carries urgency without hysteria, and it usually rides on affection or respect rather than desperation. Faintly archaic now, so in modern prose it sounds deliberately elevated.
Entreat = beg so politely you're practically asking to be treated kindly.
The word treat sits right inside it, and that's the tone — pleading with courtesy, not grovelling.
1. The ambassador entreated the council to delay the vote until the survivors could be heard.
2. She entreated me not to tell her mother, and honestly, I wasn't going to anyway.
One of the most quoted lines in the King James Bible, Ruth to Naomi: "Entreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee." Still read at weddings and funerals.
Old French entraitier = "to deal with, negotiate" — from Latin tractare, "to handle," and behind it trahere, "to drag, draw."

To entreat was originally to treat with someone — to negotiate — and only later narrowed to the pleading half of a negotiation. That root pays off everywhere: treat, treaty, treatise, tract, traction, extract, retract, protract.

Dug in so firmly that change is nearly impossible.
Firmly established and very hard to dislodge — a position, habit, interest or attitude that has settled in so deep that ordinary pressure won't shift it.

The word says nothing about whether the thing is good, popular or true — only that it is immovable. That's the whole point of it. So it tends to arrive with a sigh: entrenched poverty, entrenched corruption, entrenched attitudes — the speaker is usually describing an obstacle, not a virtue. The one clean exception is law and constitutions, where entrenching a right is deliberate protective armour: made deliberately difficult to amend.

Note the verb too: an army entrenches itself, and so does a bureaucrat who has made himself impossible to fire.
Hidden in the middle: trench. An entrenched belief isn't merely held — it's dug in.
Which is why you can't argue it out; you'd have to dig it out, and why the word almost always attaches to something the speaker wishes would move.
1. Decades of subsidy had so entrenched the industry that no minister would risk touching it.
2. Don't bother arguing with him about it — his views are entrenched, you'd need a shovel.
Standard newsroom furniture: entrenched interests, deeply entrenched inequality. If you've read a page of political or policy journalism, you've met this word doing exactly this job.
Old French trenchier = "to cut." A trench is a cut in the ground; to entrench is to put yourself into one and defend it. WWI is the picture the word never lost — both armies so entrenched that the front line barely moved in four years.

Same root, two more GRE words: trenchant (cutting, incisive — a trenchant critique) and retrench (cut back, especially spending).

column2:
Lasting a very short time; fleeting, often beautifully so.
Lasting a very short time; here and then gone.

Compare the neighbours: temporary is administrative (a temporary badge), transient is clinical or technical (a transient fault), fleeting is emotional (a fleeting glance). Ephemeral is the literary one, and it usually carries a hint of admiration — the shortness is part of what makes the thing lovely. Cherry blossom, a sunset, a mood, internet fame. It also has a hard technical life in engineering (ephemeral storage, ephemeral keys, ephemeral containers), where it means short-lived by design, don't rely on it.
⚠️ ephemeral ≠ ethereal.
- ephemeral = short-lived (about time)
- ethereal = delicate, airy, otherworldly (about texture)

A voice can be ethereal for three hours. That performance was ethereal, not ephemeral.
Ephemeral doesn't complain about the brevity — it admires it.
You call a rival's fame ephemeral to belittle it, but you call blossom ephemeral to praise it — the word leans wistful, not dismissive.
1. The exhibition collected the ephemeral matter of a city — tickets, handbills, receipts — none of it meant to survive the week it was printed.
2. Don't get attached to that job title, mate, it's ephemeral — they reorg every six months.
Instagram and Snapchat Stories vanish after 24 hours — the tech press literally calls it ephemeral content, and the Greek root means "lasting a day." The product and the etymology agree to the hour.
Greek epi (for) + hēmera (day) = ephēmeros, "lasting one day."

Same root elsewhere: ephemera (tickets, flyers — printed matter never meant to be kept) and ephemeris (the day-by-day table of where the planets will be). And the mayfly's order is Ephemeroptera — the insect that famously gets one day of adult life.

column2:
Calm, level composure held under pressure or provocation.
Calmness and evenness of mind, especially under pressure — composure that holds when things go wrong.

The word carries the strain with it. Nobody praises your equanimity on a quiet Sunday; it's invoked when there was provocation, bad news, or humiliation and the person did not wobble. It also isn't numbness — an equanimous person feels the blow and stays level anyway, which is why it reads as a virtue rather than a temperament. Register is formal and admiring; "she took the verdict with equanimity" is a compliment paid at a slight distance.
⚠️ equanimity ≠ magnanimity. Both end in -animity ("-mindedness"), but equanimity is an even mind (calm under fire) and magnanimity is a great mind (generous, forgiving to a rival). You keep your equanimity; you show magnanimity to someone else.
Equ-animity = an equal mind: the level stays the same however hard the ground shakes.
"Level" only means anything when something is trying to tip you, which is why the word needs a crisis to appear in.
1. He received the news of his dismissal with an equanimity that unsettled the board more than anger would have.
2. Three flights cancelled and she just shrugged — I've never seen anyone handle an airport with that much equanimity.
It's the standard English rendering of the Buddhist upekkhā, so it's everywhere in meditation apps like Headspace and Calm — sessions literally titled "equanimity," meaning: notice the discomfort, don't get dragged by it.
Latin aequus ("even, equal") + animus ("mind, spirit") = even-mindedness.

The animus half is the profitable one — it gives you a free GRE cluster: unanimous (one mind), magnanimous (great spirit), pusillanimous (pusillus, tiny — a tiny spirit, i.e. cowardly), animosity (spirit turned hostile).

column2:
Fair and just — calibrated to circumstance, not identical shares.
Fair and impartial — dealing with everyone justly, giving each party what they are properly due. In law, it also means relating to equity: the branch of justice that softens rigid rules to reach a fair result.

The word most people reach for instead is fair, but equitable is the courtroom-and-boardroom register: it implies a considered judgement about who deserves what, not a warm feeling. And it is not a synonym for equal. Equal means identical shares regardless of circumstance; equitable means shares calibrated to circumstance — which is often deliberately unequal. A settlement can be perfectly equal and grossly inequitable.
⚠️ equitable ≠ equable.
- equitable = fair, just (EK-wi-tuh-buhl)
- equable = even, unvarying — an equable temper, an equable climate (EK-wuh-buhl)

A judge is equitable. A judge who never loses her temper is equable.
Equal cuts the cake into identical slices; equitable cuts it so everyone leaves fed.
The whole exam value of the word lives in that gap — equitable answers to fairness, not to sameness.
1. The tribunal's task was to devise an equitable division of the estate, weighing each heir's contribution rather than simply counting heads.
2. Splitting the bill down the middle isn't equitable when I had a salad and you had three cocktails.
The "E" in DEI — diversity, equity, inclusion. Organisations swapped "equality" for "equity" precisely to make this distinction: not the same treatment for everyone, but fair treatment given where each person starts.
Latin aequus = "level, even." From it: equal, equity, adequate, equanimity (a level mind), equilibrium, equinox (day level with night).

The high-value one is the negative: in- + aequus → iniquity, literally un-levelness — which is why "iniquity" means wickedness rather than mere inequality.

🚫 Nothing to do with equestrian or equine — those are equus, "horse."

column2:
To speak ambiguously on purpose, dodging commitment without quite lying.
To speak deliberately ambiguously in order to avoid committing yourself, conceal the truth, or leave yourself an escape hatch.

The key is that it isn't a lie. A liar says something false; an equivocator says something technically defensible that he knows you will read the wrong way. That's why the charge stings — it accuses you of both cowardice and calculation at once. The word is almost always hostile: nobody describes their own answer as equivocating.
⚠️ equivocate ≠ vacillate.
- equivocate = waver in your words — say something slippery on purpose
- vacillate = waver in your mind — genuinely can't decide

A vacillator is indecisive. An equivocator has decided — to say nothing pinned down.
You already know unequivocal — "no room for doubt." Equivocate is what's left when you take the un- off: the room for doubt, left in on purpose.
Everyone offers unequivocal support; the moment the support gets hedged, qualified and re-worded, you're watching someone equivocate.
1. Pressed on whether he had authorised the payment, the minister equivocated for twenty minutes and conceded nothing.
2. Don't equivocate — are you coming to the wedding or not?
Macbeth runs on this word — the drunk Porter jokes about "an equivocator, that could swear in both the scales against either scale," and Macbeth dies realising the witches' promises were exactly that: true in a sense he never meant.
Latin aequus (equal) + vox, vocis (voice) — a statement with two equal voices, pointing both ways at once.

That voc- root is a GRE workhorse: vocal, vociferous, vocation (a calling), evoke, revoke, provoke, unequivocal.

column2:
Wipe out completely, root and all — usually something harmful.
To destroy something completely and permanently — to pull it out root and all so it cannot come back.

The word carries totality. Reduce and curb admit a remainder; eradicate claims there is none left to regrow. It also comes loaded with a target: you eradicate diseases, poverty, corruption, pests — almost never something good. And it has a faintly institutional ring, the language of campaigns and five-year plans rather than of one person tidying up.
A radish is a root — er*adic*ate is yanking the root out, so nothing grows back.
Cutting the weed off at ground level is removal; taking the root is eradication, which is why the word implies permanence and not just absence.
1. The commission was charged with eradicating the corruption that had grown into every level of the ministry.
2. You can't just spray the kitchen — you've got to eradicate the nest or they're back next week.
Smallpox is the standard example: the WHO declared it eradicated in 1980 — not merely controlled, but gone from the planet. Polio campaigns still use the same word, deliberately.
Latin rādīx, rādīcis = "root." E- (out) + rādīc- = "root it out."

Same root gives radical (going to the root of things), radish (the root you eat), and radix in maths.

Irregular and unpredictable; inconsistent with no discernible pattern.
Irregular and unpredictable — moving, behaving, or performing with no consistent pattern.

The complaint isn't that something is bad, it's that you can't rely on it. An erratic student aces one paper and fails the next; an erratic pulse skips and races. The word implies a baseline that should be steady, and isn't — so it carries a faint suggestion of instability, even mental instability, when applied to a person ("erratic behaviour" is what witnesses report before something goes wrong).
erratic ≠ erroneous. Both come from errare, but erratic = inconsistent (wandering), erroneous = wrong (mistaken). An erratic calculator sometimes gives you the right answer; an erroneous one never does.
Er-RAT-ic — watch a rat cross a room: darting, doubling back, no straight line anywhere.
The stressed syllable hands you the image, and a rat's path is the exact quality of the word — not wrong, just impossible to predict.
1. The composer's late works are erratic — a masterpiece and a shapeless fragment written in the same month.
2. His sleep schedule's been so erratic lately that he's basically living in a different time zone every day.
"Driving erratically" is the standard phrase in police reports and news bulletins — swerving, speeding up, braking for nothing. It's the everyday use that fixes the meaning: not necessarily illegal, just unpredictable enough to alarm everyone nearby.
Latin errāre = "to wander." Not "to be wrong" originally — the wrongness came later, from the idea of straying off the path.

That root fans out usefully: err, error, erroneous (strayed into wrongness), errant / knight-errant (literally a wandering knight), aberrant (wandered away from the norm).

Geologists still use the old sense: an erratic is a boulder a glacier carried miles from its home rock and abandoned in a field where it doesn't belong.

column2:
Former; the one-time ally, rival, or star — no longer.
Former, one-time, previous — the thing or person someone used to be. Archaically also an adverb meaning formerly.

Former is flat reporting; erstwhile comes with a faint backward glance, and often a raised eyebrow. It's the word for relationships that ended and changed status: an erstwhile ally, an erstwhile rival, an erstwhile heartthrob. The implication is that was then, sometimes with quiet amusement at how far things have moved.

Grammar point worth banking: it sits in front of the noun. "Her erstwhile business partner" — never "her partner is erstwhile."
Erst = first with the f knocked off. Your erstwhile partner came first — and is now firmly in the past.
Erst really is the old superlative "earliest," so an erstwhile anything belongs to the first chapter, not this one.
1. The treaty was signed by two erstwhile enemies who had spent a decade shelling each other's capitals.
2. He's now working for his erstwhile boss's biggest competitor, which must make Christmas awkward.
Newspaper and obituary English runs on it — "his erstwhile ally," "the band's erstwhile frontman." If you read business or football coverage, you've absorbed this word without ever looking it up.
Old English ǣrest = "earliest," the superlative of ǣr = "before" — which also gives you ere ("ere long") and early. German kept it plain: erst still means "first."

So erstwhile is literally "at the earliest while" — back in the day.

Deeply learned from books; scholarly rather than merely clever.
Deeply learned — possessing knowledge got from long reading and study.

The praise is specifically for accumulated book learning, not brainpower. A quick-witted person is clever; a person who has read everything and can cite it is erudite. It's a formal compliment, usually paid to scholars, critics, and their writing — an erudite footnote, an erudite lecture. The faint shadow it carries is dustiness: erudition is deep but bookish, and can be miles from practical sense.
e-RUDE-ite — the rude (raw, unpolished) has been taken out of you by books.
That hidden rude is the actual root, and it tells you erudition is polish acquired by study, not intelligence you were born with.
1. His commentary on the manuscripts is erudite to the point of intimidation — four languages cited on the first page.
2. She's erudite about jazz in a way that makes you realise you've just been listening to it.
In Divergent, the Erudite are the faction that prizes knowledge above all — blue-clad, bookish, and led by Jeanine, who has read her way into ruling everyone.
Latin ērudīre = "to polish, to instruct" — literally ex- (out of) + rudis (raw, rough, untrained). To educate someone was to take the rawness out of them.

That rudis gives you rude (unrefined), rudimentary (still at the raw stage), and rudiments (the first rough basics).

To intensify step by step, usually for the worse.
To increase by stages in intensity, scale, or seriousness — or to push a matter up to a higher authority.

Two flavours, one shape. A quarrel escalates into a brawl, a border skirmish into a war, a repair bill into a mortgage: each step provokes the next, and reversing is far harder than climbing. That step-by-step, self-feeding quality is what separates it from increase (flat, quantitative) and soar (fast and often welcome). Escalation is rarely good news.

The office sense is bureaucratic rather than violent — "I'll escalate this to my manager" means moving the problem up a rung, not making it worse. Same ladder, calmer building.
An escalator has no jump button — it lifts you one step at a time, and you can't easily get off.
Escalate is stepwise, self-continuing intensification — not a sudden leap, and not something you can simply step back down from.
1. Both governments insisted they sought peace, even as troop movements escalated the crisis week by week.
2. It was a joke about parking, and somehow it escalated into three people not speaking at Christmas.
The escalator at any mall is the word made literal — and its corporate cousin, "let me escalate this to my supervisor," is what you hear ten minutes into a support call.
Backwards from what you'd guess: escalator came first (a 1900 trademark, from escalade — scaling a wall with ladders), and escalate was cut out of it decades later, hitting its stride in the Cold War: escalation, de-escalate, escalatory.

Underneath is Latin scala = "ladder, stairs" — which also gives scale (to climb), escalade, and echelon (a rung of the hierarchy).

column2:
To deliberately avoid something, usually on principle.
To deliberately avoid or abstain from something — to keep away from it by choice.

Avoid is neutral: you avoid a pothole. Eschew carries a reason, usually a principle, a taste, or a discipline — you had access to the thing and turned it down. It's formal, slightly bookish, and almost always takes an abstract or category object: eschew violence, eschew luxury, eschew jargon, eschew meat. You can't eschew something that was never on offer.
⚠️ eschew ≠ askew. Eschew (es-CHOO) is a verb — to shun. Askew (uh-SKYOO) is an adjective/adverb — crooked, off-centre. A hat sits askew; a monk eschews wine.
es-CHEW — you won't even chew it. The plate is pushed away on principle.
The hidden word chew fixes the refusal-of-something-offered sense: the food was right there and you declined it.
1. The order eschews all property, holding even a spare pair of shoes to be an indulgence.
2. He eschews group chats entirely — says he'd rather be unreachable than be in nine of them.
"Eschew obfuscation" — the standing joke among editors and style guides, a rule against unclear writing that breaks its own rule. If you remember the gag, you remember the word.
Old French eschiver, from a Germanic root meaning "to shy away, to shun" — the same root that gives English shy (and German scheuen). A shy creature avoids; so does someone who eschews. The related skew / askew branch drifted off to mean slanting away.

column2:
Understood only by a small circle of initiates; obscure.
Understood by, or intended for, only a small circle of initiates — the inner few with the special knowledge.

The key isn't difficulty, it's access. Quantum field theory is hard; an esoteric joke is one that four people in the room are equipped to get. So the word always implies an in-group and an out-group, and the speaker is usually standing outside — "esoteric debates," "esoteric jargon" carry a faint sigh of why does this exist. Used of mystical or occult traditions, though, it turns straight-faced and even reverent.
⚠️ esoteric ≠ exoteric.
- esoteric = for the inner circle
- exoteric = for the outside world, i.e. the public, popularised version

A guru's exoteric teachings go in the paperback; the esoteric ones stay with the disciples.
Esoteric — for the e-so-few.
The material needn't be difficult; what makes it esoteric is that the audience is tiny and on the inside.
1. The society preserved a body of esoteric doctrine that was never committed to print and never spoken outside the order.
2. Half his references were so esoteric that the rest of us just nodded and hoped he'd move on.
Walk into any large bookshop and you'll find a shelf labelled Esoterica — tarot, alchemy, secret orders. Same word, used exactly as the Greeks meant it: knowledge for the initiated.
Greek esō = "within." Aristotle reportedly gave two kinds of lecture: the esoteric ones inside the school for enrolled students, and the exoteric ones outside it for the general public.

That prefix pair pays off everywhere: eso- (within) vs exo- — exit, exodus, exoskeleton, exotic.

Worthy of respect; deserving esteem, formally granted.
Worthy of respect; deserving to be held in high regard.

It's cool-blooded praise. Admirable has warmth, beloved has affection, but estimable is the respect you grant someone on their merits — solid, creditable, worth taking seriously. Because it's formal and a touch old-fashioned, it very often arrives with a raised eyebrow: "my estimable colleague" in a debate almost always means the speaker is about to disagree with him. Praise held at arm's length.
estimable ≠ inestimable — they are not opposites.
- estimable = worthy of respect
- inestimable = too great to be measured (inestimable value, inestimable loss)

The in- negates the "can be counted" sense, not the "worthy" one — so inestimable is the bigger compliment, not the insult.
Estim-able = esteem-able. Able to be esteemed — but esteem is measured out, never gushed.
The -able suffix tells you it's a rating someone has earned, which is why the word sounds like a formal appraisal rather than genuine affection.
1. The committee was chaired by an estimable jurist whose opinions no one dared summarise carelessly.
2. He's an estimable guy — I'd trust him with the accounts, I just wouldn't want to be stuck at dinner with him.
Courtroom and parliamentary boilerplate: "my estimable colleague" — a phrase that has never once been followed by agreement.
Latin aestimāre = "to value, to put a price on." The whole family is one act of appraisal: estimate (put a number on it), esteem (put a value on a person), estimable (worth valuing), inestimable (off the scale).

No longer close to someone you once were; alienated.
No longer close or affectionate with someone you once were; alienated. Of spouses, it also means living apart but not yet divorced.

The word depends entirely on a prior bond — you can be estranged from a father, a brother, a best friend, but never from someone you never knew. It describes cold distance rather than open warfare: not a screaming match but years of unreturned calls. Register is restrained and slightly formal, which is why journalists reach for it — "his estranged sister" reports a rupture without taking sides or naming the cause.
Estranged = made STRANGE again — the person who knew you best is now a stranger.
The whole word is strange with a prefix, and that's exactly the tragedy in it: intimacy converted back into strangerhood.
1. After the will was read, the brothers remained estranged for the better part of two decades, communicating only through solicitors.
2. She hasn't spoken to her dad since the wedding — they're basically estranged now.
Celebrity news runs on this word: the moment a marriage collapses, every headline switches from "his wife" to "his estranged wife" — the polite press code for they're done, but the paperwork isn't.
Latin extraneus = "outside, foreign" → Old French estrangier. To estrange someone is literally to make them an outsider.

Same root, three useful words: strange, stranger, and the GRE favourite extraneous (= irrelevant, from outside the matter at hand).

A soft word swapped in for a blunt or ugly one.
A mild, vague or roundabout word used in place of a blunt, harsh or taboo one — passed away for died, let go for fired, between jobs for unemployed.

Two flavours, and the GRE cares which one you hear. At the kind end it's tact: you say passed away to spare a grieving person. At the other end it's laundering — collateral damage, enhanced interrogation, rightsizing — words chosen so nobody pictures what actually happened. Because of that second flavour, calling something "a euphemism" is usually a mild accusation: you're pointing out that the speaker picked the soft word deliberately. The opposite move has its own name — a dysphemism (croaked, bean-counter).
Eu- is the good prefix — euphoria, eulogy, euphemism. A eulogy says only nice things about the dead; a euphemism says only nice things about the ugly.
Both words work by leaving the unflattering part out.
1. The report never used the word torture, retreating instead into the euphemism "enhanced interrogation."
2. "Restructuring" is just a euphemism for firing half the floor and hoping nobody says so.
Every flight safety briefing: "in the unlikely event of a water landing." Nobody lands on water — that's a crash, wrapped in a soft word so 200 people stay calm.
Greek eu- (good, well) + phēmē (speech, saying) = "speaking well of."

Both halves pay off. eu- gives you euphoria (good feeling), eulogy (good words), euphony (good sound), euthanasia (good death). phēmē gives you blasphemy — blas- (evil) + phēmē, the exact mirror image: speaking ill of the sacred.

Intensely elated — a soaring high that won't last.
Feeling intense, soaring elation — happiness dialled far past ordinary happiness.

Scale matters: pleased < delighted < elated < euphoric. This is the top of the ladder, and it's a state, not a temperament — nobody is euphoric by nature, only for an hour. The word also carries a faint clinical shadow: doctors use it for the high of morphine or mania, and journalists use it for the mood of a market right before it crashes. So calling someone euphoric can gently suggest the feeling is chemical, disproportionate, or about to end.
⚠️ euphoric ≠ euphonic.
- euphoric = feeling wonderful
- euphonic = sounding wonderful (pleasing to the ear — euphony)

A euphoric crowd; a euphonic choir.
-phor is the carry ending — a meta·phor carries meaning across, eu·phor·ia carries you off the ground.
Anything carried has to be set down again, which is exactly why euphoria is a high that comes with a landing.
1. The delegates emerged euphoric, convinced that a treaty two decades in the making had finally been secured.
2. I was euphoric for about ten minutes after the results came out, then remembered I still had to move house.
HBO's Euphoria (Zendaya) — a series named for exactly this sense of the word: highs that are chemical, enormous, and never last.
Greek eu = "good" + pherein = "to carry, to bear" — literally "carrying well."

Both halves pay off across the GRE. eu-: eulogy (good words), euphemism (good speech), euphony (good sound), euthanasia (good death). -phor/-pher: metaphor (carry across), periphery (carried around), phosphorus (light-bearer).

To dodge or escape something by cleverness rather than facing it.
To get away from something — a pursuer, a duty, a question — by dodging, trickery or sheer slipperiness rather than meeting it head-on.

Avoid is neutral: you avoid the motorway at rush hour. Evade carries a charge of bad faith — it assumes something had a claim on you (the police, the tax office, the interviewer) and you wriggled out. That's why evasive is never a compliment: an evasive answer isn't a refusal, it's an answer shaped to look like one while telling you nothing.
⚠️ evade vs. elude. You evade actively — dodging, ducking, taking evasive action. Something eludes you passively, by slipping away: the fox eluded the hounds, the word eludes me, sleep eluded her. You can evade a question; a question can't evade you.
Evade rhymes with fade — the evader doesn't refuse, he fades sideways out of the frame.
That sideways slip is the whole flavour of the word: no confrontation, no honest "no", just a smooth exit that leaves you holding nothing.
1. For six years the fugitive evaded capture, drifting between border towns under a series of borrowed names.
2. Every time I ask what he actually does for a living, he evades the question and starts on about the weather.
Al Capone — bootlegging, racketeering, a body count — was finally jailed for tax evasion. Note the distinction lawyers live by: tax avoidance (arranging your affairs legally) is fine; tax evasion (hiding the money) is a crime. The same gap in tone, written into the law.
Latin ē- (out) + vādere (to go) — literally to go out of it.

vādere is a workhorse root: invade (go in), pervade (go through everything), evade (go out). Even English wade is a cousin — going through with effort.

Fading away; vanishing almost as you notice it.
Fading out of existence almost as soon as it appears — mist, a scent, a chord, a mood.

Where ephemeral is about lifespan (a mayfly, a fad — it lasts a day and then it's over), evanescent is about the vanishing itself: the thing is thinning, dissolving, already half-gone while you're still looking at it. It's the softest word in this family — no tragedy, no waste, just delicate disappearance — and it's almost always used of something lovely and insubstantial rather than something merely short.
-escent means in the process of becoming — adolescent, convalescent, luminescent. Evan-escent = in the process of vanishing.
The suffix supplies the key idea that this isn't gone yet — it's going, right now, in front of you.
1. The evanescent glow on the water lasted the length of a held breath, then the cloud closed over the sun.
2. Her enthusiasm for the gym proved evanescent — three weeks, tops.
The band Evanescence — the noun form, straight up. "Bring Me to Life" is one long fade-into-nothing, and the name was chosen for exactly that meaning.
Latin ex- ("out") + vanescere ("to vanish"), from vanus = "empty."

That root gives you vanish, vain (empty of substance), vanity, evanescent — all built on the idea of nothing being there.

column2:
Dodging a direct answer or a direct hit.
Avoiding a direct answer or a direct hit — dodging the question, the commitment, or the pursuer.

Two lives. Of speech: deliberately non-committal, and almost always a soft accusation — calling someone evasive implies they have something to hide but stops short of saying they lied. It's the word journalists, lawyers and interviewers reach for because it's damning yet legally safe. Of movement: neutral and technical — evasive action, evasive manoeuvres, what a pilot or a driver does to avoid a collision. No guilt in that sense at all.
⚠️ evasive ≠ elusive.
- evasive = actively dodging you — an evasive witness
- elusive = hard to catch or pin down, no intent required — an elusive scent, an elusive cure

An evasive suspect knows you're asking. An elusive memory isn't hiding on purpose.
Evasive people evade; elusive things elude — only one of them knows you're looking.
Evasive points at a choice being made, which is why it lands as a quiet accusation, while elusive is just a property of the thing itself.
1. Pressed three times on what he had known and when, the minister grew evasive, retreating into the passive voice.
2. Every time I ask what he does for work he gets weirdly evasive and changes the subject.
"Evasive manoeuvres" — the standing order on the bridge in Star Trek, and the same phrase used in real aviation and driving for a hard swerve away from a collision. That's the innocent, physical sense of the word doing its day job.
Latin vadere = "to go", plus ex- = "out" → evade, "to go out of the way."

One root, a whole GRE family: evade (go out of), invade (go into), pervade (go through — a smell that pervades the house). Fix vadere = go and all three unlock.

to call up a feeling, memory, or image indirectly
To call up a feeling, memory, image or atmosphere — usually indirectly, by suggestion rather than by force.

What's evoked was already latent in the person; the trigger only stirs it. A smell evokes a childhood kitchen, a chord evokes dread, a photograph evokes a decade. Compare its siblings: provoke pushes a reaction out of someone (anger, a fight), elicit extracts a specific response in a transaction (an answer, a confession), and evoke simply summons something that was sleeping. It is also the standard verb of criticism — reviewers say a novel or a painting evokes something, meaning it succeeds at conjuring a mood without stating it.
⚠️ evoke ≠ invoke.
- evoke = call a feeling up, often unintentionally — the tune evoked her grandmother
- invoke = deliberately call on an authority, rule or power — he invoked the Fifth Amendment

You evoke nostalgia; you invoke a clause.
Evoke rhymes with awoke — it wakes something that was already asleep in you.
That rhyme carries the nuance: the feeling was yours all along, and the smell, song or line merely woke it.
1. The memorial's bare stone evokes absence more powerfully than any statue could.
2. One bar of that song and boom — instantly evokes every school bus ride I ever took.
Land Rover named a car the Evoque — a deliberate respelling of evoke, because the whole pitch was that the thing should stir a feeling rather than list its specs.
Latin ē- (out) + vocāre (to call), from vōx, voice — literally "to call out."

That root is a GRE goldmine: invoke (call on), revoke (call back), provoke (call forth, aggressively), convoke (call together), plus vocation (a calling), advocate, vocal, equivocate.

column2:
To make an already bad situation worse.
To make an already bad thing worse — more severe, more painful, more inflamed.

The word carries a precondition: there must already be a problem. You can worsen anything, but you can only exacerbate a deficit, a drought, a shortage, tensions, an injury, an illness. And it takes an impersonal subject — a policy, a comment, a heatwave exacerbates; people generally don't. Register is formal: it's the verb of medical charts, editorials, and policy reports, where worsen would sound too plain and aggravate too casual.
⚠️ exacerbate ≠ exasperate.
- exacerbate = make a bad situation worse
- exasperate = make a person furious

The strike exacerbated the shortage; the shortage exasperated the shoppers.
Hidden inside is acerb — bitter. To exacerbate is to add bitterness to something already sour.
Nothing sweet can be exacerbated — the sourness has to be there first.
1. Rather than calming the crowd, the mayor's remarks exacerbated a resentment that had been building for years.
2. Don't text him at 2 a.m. — you'll just exacerbate things.
Standard hospital language: an "acute exacerbation of COPD" is a flare-up of a disease the patient already has — exactly the word's precondition, printed on charts every day.
Latin ex- (thoroughly) + acerbus = "bitter, harsh", from acer = "sharp."

That root cuts across the vocabulary list: acerbic (sharp-tongued), acrid (sharp smell), acrimonious (sharp-tempered dispute), acute (sharp angle, sharp pain) — and even eager, which once meant "keen, sharp," and vinegar, French vin aigre, "sour wine."

Demanding great care, effort and skill; hard to satisfy.
Making severe demands on your care, effort, or skill — either of a person (hard to satisfy) or of a task (requiring precision and stamina).

Unlike picky, fussy or nitpicking, exacting grants the demander legitimacy: the standard is high because the work genuinely requires it, not because someone is being difficult. An exacting editor is respected and exhausting at once. And the word costs you something — exacting work drains you, which demanding only half implies.
⚠️ exacting ≠ exact. Exact = precise, correct. Exacting = demanding. An exacting standard isn't a precisely-specified one; it's one that's hard to meet.
Hear the verb exact — "to exact a toll." An exacting job exacts a toll from you.
The buried word isn't the adjective exact (precise) but the verb exact (to demand and extract), which is exactly what such a boss or task does to you.
1. Restoring the fresco was exacting work: a square inch a day, under magnification, with solvents mixed fresh each morning.
2. She's exacting, sure — but nothing she asks for is unreasonable, and the final cut is always better for it.
"Built to exacting standards" is the fixed phrase of premium advertising — Swiss watches, single malts, hi-fi speakers. If a product page brags about tolerances, this word is nearby.
Latin exigere = "to drive out, demand, require" (ex- out + agere to drive). The demanding sense is the original; "precise" came later, from the idea of a payment weighed out to the last coin.

Same root: exact (v., to demand and take), exigent (pressing, urgent), exigency (an urgent demand), and via agere — agent, agenda, agile, act.

Worn past patience by repeated irritation; frustrated to the sighing point.
Pushed past the end of your patience — intensely irritated and worn down, usually by something that has happened again.

The word carries repetition and fatigue. You get angry in one moment; you become exasperated after the fifth time you've explained it, the third failed attempt, the child who has asked "why?" eleven times. It's also fairly powerless: the exasperated person has tried the reasonable options and run out. That's why it collocates almost automatically with sigh, groan, eye-roll — never with punch.
⚠️ exasperate ≠ exacerbate.
- exasperate = irritate a person past their patience
- exacerbate = make a problem worse

Your excuses exasperate me; they exacerbate the situation.
Exasperated ends in a sigh, not a shout.
It's the deflated, worn-thin end of patience after one repetition too many — not a sudden explosion of rage.
1. After three hours of circular debate, the chairwoman gave an exasperated wave of the hand and adjourned the meeting.
2. I'm getting exasperated — that's the fourth time I've sent you the same link.
Latin asper = "rough", with ex- as an intensifier: to thoroughly roughen someone — rub them raw.

Same root gives you asperity (harshness of tone or manner) — a GRE word in its own right. Keep the pair: asperity is the rough edge; exasperated is what being scraped by it repeatedly leaves you.

To criticise savagely in public; literally, to strip off skin.
To denounce someone ferociously and publicly. (Older, literal sense: to strip the skin off.)

This is criticism as flaying — sustained, itemised, and delivered by someone with standing to deliver it. Judges excoriate counsel; editorials excoriate ministers; inquiries excoriate agencies. Set it beside its neighbours: berate is loud and personal in the moment, rebuke is short and almost polite, excoriate is the long articulate demolition that leaves nothing of the target intact. It also quietly flatters the critic — you have to be somebody before your attack counts as an excoriation.
⚠️ excoriate ≠ exonerate. Same shape, opposite verdicts: excoriate = flay them in public; exonerate = clear them of blame. "The inquiry ___ the chief constable" reverses completely depending on which one you pick.
Ex-CORE-iate — peel the hide off until only the core is left.
The "core" you hear in the middle is the point: it isn't a jab, it's stripping someone down layer by layer in front of an audience.
1. The inquiry's final chapter excoriated the regulator for a decade of deliberate blindness.
2. Don't post that draft tonight — the replies are going to excoriate you.
Still literal in medicine: DSM-5 lists excoriation disorder (compulsive skin-picking), and dermatologists write "excoriations" for scratch marks on a chart — the skin sense never left the word.
Latin ex- ("off") + corium ("hide, skin") — to take the hide off. Corium also gives cuirass, the leather breastplate.

🚫 Not excruciate. That's Latin crux, "cross" — pain on a cross, not pain from a flaying. Different root, different torture.

column2:
To clear someone of blame, usually by evidence.
To clear someone of blame or guilt — to show they weren't at fault.

This is a word of evidence, not of mercy. Forgive leaves the guilt in place and waives the punishment; exculpate removes the guilt itself, usually because a document, an alibi, or a witness proves the person didn't do it. It stops short of praise: to be exculpated is to be shown not-blameworthy, whereas to be vindicated is to be shown right. Register is formal and heavily legal — lawyers, inquiries, board reports. Its exact opposite, inculpate, is the word for evidence that points the finger back at you.
⚠️ exculpate ≠ expurgate. Exculpate frees a person from blame; expurgate strips the dirty bits out of a text. Same ex- opening, entirely different object.
Exculpate takes the blame exit; inculpate lets it in.
The prefix does all the work — the shared middle culp is the blame, and ex- / in- simply point it out of you or into you.
1. The inquiry exculpated the engineers entirely, laying the failure at the door of the contractor who had signed off on the welds.
2. Don't try to exculpate yourself — I saw you eat the last slice.
"Exculpatory evidence" is the phrase every courtroom drama and true-crime podcast runs on: in the US, prosecutors are legally obliged to hand the defence anything exculpatory — evidence that clears the accused.
Latin ex- (out of) + culpa (fault, blame).

Culpa is a high-yield root: culpable (deserving blame), culprit, inculpate, exculpatory, and the confession mea culpa — literally "my fault."

Detailed, systematic interpretation of a text, especially scripture.
A detailed, systematic interpretation of a text — classically scripture, but also law, poetry, or philosophy.

This isn't a "reading" or a "take." Exegesis is excavation: line by line, with tools — original language, historical context, what the word meant then. The governing assumption is that the meaning is already in the text and must be drawn out, not supplied by you. Heavily academic; the word signals a seminary, a law review, or a graduate seminar. It also turns dry and faintly mocking when aimed at something small — a 4,000-word exegesis of a two-line lyric.
⚠️ exegesis ≠ exigency.
- exegesis = painstaking interpretation of a text
- exigency = an urgent demand or pressing need

Both are GRE regulars and both start ex-g. One is slow scholarship; the other is an emergency.
Exe-JEE-sis has Jesus buried in the middle — scripture is its home turf, and the job is to lead the meaning ex (out) of the verse, never to read yours in.
The hidden name fixes the register — sermons and scholarship, not casual opinion — and the ex- fixes the direction of travel: meaning comes out of the text, not into it.
1. His exegesis of the passage turned on a single Greek particle that three centuries of translators had quietly ignored.
2. It's four paragraphs of small talk, mate — you don't need a full exegesis of what she meant by "sure."
Any sermon that takes one verse and unpacks it for twenty minutes is exegesis in its natural habitat — it's the core skill divinity schools train, and the same move constitutional lawyers make on a single clause.
Greek exēgeisthai = "to lead out" — ex- (out) + hēgeisthai (to lead, to guide). The exegete is a guide walking you out of the text with its meaning in hand.

That second half is the payoff: hēgeisthai also gives you hegemony — leadership, one state guiding (dominating) the rest. Two GRE words, one root about leading.

Complete to the last case; nothing left out.
Covering every single case, leaving nothing out.

Put it on a scale: careful < thorough < exhaustive. Thorough means you did the job properly; exhaustive means there is literally nothing left to check — every file opened, every name on the list, every possibility eliminated. It describes coverage, not effort, and it is almost always praise: an exhaustive study, an exhaustive search, an exhaustive account. The faint shadow it can cast is excess — an exhaustive answer to a simple question is more than anyone wanted.
⚠️ exhaustive ≠ exhausting.
- exhaustive = nothing was left out
- exhausting = it wore you out

An exhaustive review may well be exhausting, but the words are making completely different claims.
An exhaustive list is one nobody can add to.
The test isn't how hard you worked — it's whether anything is left over.
1. The commission's exhaustive inquiry ran to nine volumes and interviewed every surviving witness.
2. I did an exhaustive search of the flat and the keys are just gone.
Almost every job description ends with the same line: \"This list of responsibilities is not exhaustive.\" — HR code for and anything else we think of later.
Latin ex- (out) + haurīre (to draw water) — to bail a well until it's dry. That's the whole word: an exhaustive search drains the subject dry; an exhausted person has been drained the same way; something inexhaustible can't be emptied no matter how much you take.
