column2:
Thrilling in a way that leaves you elated and energised.
Thrilling in a way that leaves you elated and physically charged up — heart going, grinning, more alive than before.

Exciting is broad and can shade into anxiety; thrilling leans on danger and suspense. Exhilarating is the joyful end of that family: the rush plus the lift. It describes cold air, first descents, standing ovations, winning arguments — the things that leave you energised, not drained. It's an unambiguously happy word, so it never carries dread the way "a thrilling near-miss" can.
Hidden inside it: ex-HILAR-ating — the same hilar as hilarious.
Both words mean "made high-spirited," but hilarious lifts your laugh and exhilarating lifts your pulse.
1. The first unaided flight was, by every account in the diary, an exhilarating three minutes that no later triumph quite matched.
2. Cycling downhill in the rain with no brakes — terrifying, but honestly kind of exhilarating.
It's the default adjective of car advertising — every sports-saloon ad promises "an exhilarating drive," never merely an exciting one, because exhilarating sells the feeling you're left with rather than the risk.
Latin hilaris = cheerful (via Greek hilaros), with ex- as an intensifier: "to gladden thoroughly." Same root gives hilarious and hilarity — and the name Hilary, which simply meant "cheerful."

To urge someone earnestly and passionately toward action.
To urge someone earnestly to do something — by appeal, encouragement, and moral heat rather than by command.

The word carries fervour and zero authority. A general orders; a coach, a preacher, a campaigner exhorts — all passion, no power to compel. That's why exhortation so often shades into futility: newspapers exhort the government to act, and the government carries on regardless. It's urging that can only hope to be obeyed.
⚠️ exhort ≠ extort.
- exhort = urge you to do it (words only)
- extort = force it out of you by threat

The preacher exhorts the congregation; the gangster extorts the shopkeeper.
ex-HORT = ex-HOARSE — the half-time speech that leaves the coach shouting himself raw.
All that hoarse effort and still nobody has to listen — which is exactly the flavour of exhorting.
1. The bishop's letter exhorted the faithful to charity in a season of plenty, though he could compel nothing.
2. Mum spent the whole drive exhorting us to be polite to Gran, and we ignored every word of it.
Henry V's "Once more unto the breach, dear friends" is the textbook exhortation — a leader with a broken army and nothing but words, roaring men back at a wall.
Latin ex- (thoroughly) + hortārī (to urge, encourage) — literally to urge hard. Same root gives hortatory and hortative, both meaning "urging" and both fair GRE game.

🚫 Nothing to do with horticulture. That's hortus, "garden."

Urgently pressing; demanding immediate action or high standards.
1. (of a situation) urgent; requiring immediate action. 2. (of a person or task) demanding, exacting, hard to satisfy.

Urgent just says the clock is running. Exigent says the situation is actively making demands on you — it presses, it exacts, it leaves you no slack. That's why the two senses live in one word: an exigent crisis and an exigent boss both want something from you now, and neither will take "later" for an answer. It's a formal word — you'll meet it in law, journalism and boardrooms, not in conversation.
⚠️ exigent ≠ exiguous.
- exigent = demanding, pressing
- exiguous = scanty, meagre, too small

An exigent deadline on an exiguous budget: huge pressure, tiny resources.
Exigent = "exact" with a different ending — an exigent situation exacts something from you.
Same Latin verb, same idea of extracting payment under pressure, which is exactly why the word means demanding as well as urgent.
1. The board deferred the strategy review, judging the liquidity crisis the more exigent matter.
2. Sorry, can't chat — something exigent just landed in my inbox and it's on fire.
"Exigent circumstances" — the legal doctrine every cop show leans on: police may enter without a warrant when someone's in danger or evidence is about to be destroyed. If you've heard a TV detective justify kicking a door in, you've heard this word.
Latin exigere = "to drive out, demand, require" — from ex- (out) + agere (to drive, to do).

That root pays out widely: exact (both "precise" and "to exact a toll"), exigency, and from agere alone — agent, agenda, act, agile, agitate. Anything that drives.

To officially clear someone of blame or accusation.
To officially clear someone of blame for something they were accused of.

The force of it is affirmative: an acquittal only says guilt wasn't proved, but an exoneration says the person didn't do it. It's the strong word — courts, inquiries, internal investigations, DNA labs. And it's about blame, not sin: a priest absolves you, an investigation exonerates you.
Nobody exonerates themselves. A court, a report, or a lab test does it for you.
That's why the word lives in the passive — "was fully exonerated" — and why protesting your innocence never counts as exoneration.
1. The tribunal's final report exonerated the two officers, attributing the failure to a defect in the equipment itself.
2. Turns out the cat knocked the vase over, so I'm exonerated — you owe me an apology.
The Innocence Project headlines you see every few months — "man exonerated after 27 years by DNA evidence" — are the word's natural habitat, and they show the full sense: not released on a technicality, but proven innocent.
Latin ex- (off) + onus, oneris (burden) — literally to take the load off. The blame was weight on your shoulders; exoneration lifts it.

Same root gives you onerous (burdensome, heavy going) and onus (the burden of proof) — both GRE regulars.

Wildly excessive — usually a price far beyond fair.
Far beyond what is reasonable or customary — grossly excessive.

In practice it attaches to prices, fees, rents, salaries, demands, claims — things measured in money or scale. Expensive is a fact; exorbitant is a verdict, and an indignant one: it says the amount has left the range any fair person would accept. Slightly formal, common in journalism and complaint letters, and almost always spoken by the person being charged, never the person charging.
Ex-ORBIT-ant — the price has left orbit.
Orbit is sitting right there in the middle of the word, and that's literally the metaphor: a normal price stays in its track, an exorbitant one flies off it.
1. The tribunal found the landlord's demands exorbitant, some four times the prevailing rent for comparable flats.
2. Forty quid for a burger and a Coke? That's exorbitant, mate.
The word the internet reaches for every time Ticketmaster's checkout page adds its exorbitant service fees — a near-fixed collocation with "fees."
Latin ex- (out of) + orbita (a wheel-track, a rut) — literally "off the track." Originally a legal term for a case that fell outside the ordinary course of law; the sense narrowed to prices that fall outside the ordinary range.

Same orbita/orbis (circle, wheel) gives you orbit, orbital, and orb.

Drive out an evil spirit — or a haunting memory.
To drive out an evil spirit by ritual, prayer or command — and, far more often on the GRE, to rid yourself of something that haunts you: a memory, a guilt, a reputation, an old influence that still has a grip.

The figurative sense carries the ghost with it. You don't exorcise clutter or spare furniture; you exorcise what clings — something unwanted, faintly shameful, and hard to shake. It also implies effort and something like ceremony: writing the book, burning the letters, winning the rematch. Compare plain remove (mechanical) or dispel (an illusion simply evaporates) — exorcising is a struggle against a thing that resists leaving.
⚠️ exorcise ≠ exercise. One letter apart, opposite worlds: exorcise (with an o) casts out demons; exercise works the body or uses a right ("exercise caution", "exercise the option").
Look inside: exORCise — you're kicking the orcs out of the house.
The hidden ORC is only in the demon-word, never in exercise, and it captures the sense of expelling something monstrous that won't leave on its own.
1. The memoir was less a confession than an attempt to exorcise a childhood she had never been able to speak of aloud.
2. Beating them in the final finally exorcised thirty years of losing to that lot.
The Exorcist (1973) — the priest is there to exorcise the demon, which is exactly the job description.
Greek ex- ("out") + horkos ("oath") → exorkizein, literally "to bind by oath" — the exorcist expels the spirit by swearing an oath at it ("I command you, in the name of…"). That's why the word implies a formula, not just a shove.

From far away — foreign, and strikingly so.
Originating in a distant foreign country; by extension, strikingly unusual or glamorous because it comes from somewhere else.

The word only exists from the outsider's angle — nothing is exotic to itself. A mango is exotic in Oslo and breakfast in Mumbai. That built-in viewpoint is why exotic turns sour when applied to people: it flatters and distances in the same breath, treating a person as scenery. Applied to fruit, birds, or holidays it's warm and inviting; applied to a woman's face it now reads as condescending.

Technical uses strip the glamour out entirely and keep only "non-native / non-standard": an exotic species is an invasive weed, and an exotic option is just a derivative that isn't plain vanilla.
⚠️ exotic ≠ esoteric.
- exotic = strange because it's from outside (Greek exō)
- esoteric = obscure because it's known only to those inside (Greek esō, "within")

Tantric chanting is exotic to a tourist; the meaning of the chant is esoteric even to most locals.
EXotic things EXited somewhere else to get here — which is why nothing is exotic at home.
The ex- fixes the word's whole logic: it labels the traveller, not the thing, so the label says where you are standing.
1. The conservatory housed a collection of exotic orchids, coaxed into flower under glass a thousand miles from the forests that bred them.
2. He came back from three weeks in Lisbon acting like he'd been somewhere exotic.
Joe Exotic of Tiger King — a man who named himself after the exotic animals (foreign, non-native, kept where they don't belong) that filled his zoo.
Greek exō = "outside" → exōtikos, "from abroad." The same root is stamped on a big, easy family: exit, exodus, exterior, exoskeleton (skeleton on the outside), exogenous (arising from outside), exoplanet (a planet outside our solar system).

To speak or write at great length on a subject.
To speak or write at length and in detail on a subject — usually with on or upon: he expatiated upon the virtues of the metric system.

The word is bookish and faintly amused. Elaborate is neutral and often invited ("could you elaborate?"); ramble is openly rude; expatiate sits between them — it grants that the speaker has plenty to say while hinting they said rather more of it than anyone needed. You expatiate at an audience, not with them, and the verb almost always has a slight tilt of the eyebrow. It rarely appears in speech at all; when it does, it's the writer's word for a lecture nobody asked for.
⚠️ expatiate ≠ expatriate.
- expatiate = go on at length (spatium, space)
- expatriate = leave your native country (patria, fatherland)

An expat living in Lisbon may expatiate on Portuguese tax law, but the words share nothing but a look.
ex-SPACE-iate — you take up a lot of space.
The word has space buried in the middle of it, and that is exactly what an expatiating speaker consumes — pages of it, minutes of it.
1. The preface expatiates upon the author's methods for some thirty pages before a single argument appears.
2. Don't ask him about his sourdough starter — he'll expatiate for an hour.
Latin exspatiari = "to wander off, to spread out" — from ex- (out) + spatium (space, room, a racecourse). Originally you expatiated by roaming physically; now you roam verbally.

spatium is a useful root to own: space, spacious, spatial, and the sense of stretching out in all of them.

🚫 Not patria. That's expatriate, patriot, patriarch, repatriate — fatherland words, no relation.

Practical and convenient — often at the cost of principle.
Adjective: convenient and effective for getting a result right now — whether or not it is fair, honest, or wise.
Noun: a makeshift means to an end (a temporary expedient).

The word almost always leaves a stain. Calling a decision prudent praises the judgement behind it; calling it expedient quietly says the person did what worked for them and left principle out of it. Note the giveaway collocations — politically expedient, merely expedient, it was expedient to — each one setting up a reason someone should have known better. In the neutral noun sense it just means a stopgap, but even there it admits the fix is second-best.
⚠️ expedient ≠ expeditious.
- expedient = convenient, self-serving — a judgement on the ethics
- expeditious = prompt and efficient — a judgement on the speed

An expeditious refund is fast. An expedient refund is the one they issued to stop you talking to a journalist.
An expedient gets your feet out of the trap; it never promises your hands stay clean.
The buried ped- ("foot") makes it an escape route, and an escape route is judged by whether it works, not by whether it was honourable.
1. The minister abandoned the pledge the moment it ceased to be expedient, and dressed the retreat up as sober realism.
2. We propped the shelf up with a phone book — an ugly expedient, but it held.
"Politically expedient" is a newsreader's stock phrase, and it is never a compliment — it means the move polls well and costs the country something.
Latin expedīre = "to free the feet" (ex- "out" + pēs, pedis "foot") — to get someone unstuck.

Its opposite is built the same way: impede = in- + pedis, to shackle the feet. One root, two directions: expedite, expedient, impede, impediment, plus pedestrian, pedal, pedigree.

To speed something up by clearing away the delays.
To make a process happen sooner by clearing away whatever is slowing it down — paperwork, queues, approvals, red tape.

Hasten and accelerate describe raw speed; expedite describes speeding up a system. There's an implied bureaucracy, an implied backlog, and usually implied authority — someone with the power to move your file to the top of the pile. You expedite a shipment, a visa, a claim, an investigation. You don't expedite a walk, a song, or a friendship. It's a boardroom-and-back-office word, and it quietly flatters the speaker: I know how to get things unstuck.
⚠️ expedite ≠ expedient. Same Latin root, different jobs.
- expedite (verb) = hurry it along
- expedient (adj.) = convenient rather than principled — the fast option, taken because it's easy, often with a whiff of moral shortcut

Expediting the report is admirable. Firing the whistleblower was merely expedient.
Nobody expedites a sunset. You expedite a request.
The word only attaches to things stuck in a process, which is why it always carries the smell of queues, forms and someone with the clout to skip them.
1. The tribunal agreed to expedite the hearing, citing the claimant's deteriorating health.
2. Can you call them and expedite it? We've been waiting three weeks for a signature.
Every checkout page and passport office sells you the same thing: expedited shipping, expedited processing. You pay extra not to make the truck drive faster — but to jump the queue. That fee is the definition.
Latin expedīre = "to free the feet" — ex- (out) + pes, pedis (foot). To unshackle someone so they can finally move.

Its exact opposite is built the same way: impede = feet in the shackles. Same root gives pedestrian, pedal, pedigree, impediment, and expedition (a party freed to set out).

🚫 Not the ped- in pedagogy or pedant — that's Greek paid-, "child."

Able to be explained; there's a reason behind it
Capable of being explained or accounted for.

The word is quieter than it looks. Explicable doesn't mean obvious or clear — a thing can be baffling on the surface and still be explicable, because the claim is only that a satisfying account exists once you dig. It carries a faint tone of deflation: people reach for it to take the mystery out of something ("her behaviour was entirely explicable, given the pressure she was under"). Note also that the negative twin, inexplicable, is far commoner in speech; when the bare positive turns up, it's usually formal, argumentative, and defending a plain explanation against a dramatic one.
You almost never meet it alone — it comes in as "perfectly explicable", mopping up someone else's mystery.
Lock the collocation and you lock the tone: the word's job is to say calm down, there's a reason.
1. The discrepancy in the accounts, alarming at first sight, proved explicable as a rounding error carried forward across three quarters.
2. Sure, he stormed out — which is pretty explicable when you've been in that meeting for four hours.
Standard move in science and audit writing: a result is dismissed as "explicable by chance alone" — the polite way of saying nothing to see here.
Latin ex- (out) + plicāre (to fold) — to unfold something, spread the pleats flat so it can be read.

That fold-root is a GRE goldmine: complicate (fold together), implicate (fold someone in), replicate (fold back again), pliable (foldable), plus deploy, display, employ — all folding and unfolding in disguise.

Using people unfairly for your own profit.
Treating people (or a resource) as something to be used up for your own profit, unfairly and usually by someone with the power to get away with it.

Note the split in the family: exploit the verb is often neutral — you exploit an opportunity, a weakness in the market, a gap in the defence — and exploit the noun is downright admiring, a daring feat. Exploitative never is. It is a verdict: the speaker has already decided the arrangement is unjust. It carries a whiff of the boardroom and the op-ed page — landlords, sweatshops, gig apps, unpaid internships — and implies an imbalance of power, not merely a bad bargain. Two equals striking a greedy deal are grasping; a company squeezing people who have no other option is exploitative.
exploit = ex-PLOY — an exploitative boss has a ploy for using you.
The sound hook keeps the blame in the word: it isn't just using something, it's a scheme run at someone else's expense.
1. The report condemned the plantation's exploitative contracts, which bound labourers to debts they could never repay.
2. That internship is straight-up exploitative — sixty hours a week and they pay you in "exposure."
It's the standard phrase in labour journalism: every gig-economy or fast-fashion exposé you've scrolled past runs on "exploitative working conditions."
Latin plicāre = "to fold"; explicāre = "to unfold, unroll" — which became Old French esploit, "an achievement, a profit," hence exploit.

That fold-root is a workhorse: explicit (unfolded, spelled out), explicate, complicated (folded together), implicate, pliable, deploy and employ (both literally "unfold").

Still existing; surviving when most of its kind hasn't.
Still in existence; not lost, not destroyed, not extinct.

The word almost always looks backwards in time. You don't call your phone extant — you call it that when something has survived a process that destroyed the rest: three of the letters are extant, the oldest extant copy of the manuscript, the last extant colony of a species. It carries the quiet implication that most of the set is gone. Register is scholarly — archivists, historians, biologists, lawyers — and it's coolly neutral: no relief, no celebration, just the surviving inventory.
⚠️ extant ≠ extinct. One letter, opposite verdicts — extant = still here; extinct = wiped out. An extant species is alive today; the dodo is extinct.
Ex-STANT — it's still standing. Ex-TINCT — it's been extinguished.
The -stant is literally stare, "to stand," while -tinct is the same root as extinguish, so one word is upright and the other is snuffed out.
1. Of the twelve original panels, only four are extant; the rest burned with the abbey in 1643.
2. There's exactly one extant photo of my grandad as a kid, and my mum won't let anyone touch it.
Open almost any Wikipedia species page and the taxobox reads "Extant" or "Extinct" right under the fossil-range bar — the two words are the standing labels for alive-today versus gone.
Latin ex- (out) + stāre (to stand) — "standing out, still standing there."

stāre is a workhorse root worth banking: status, stable, stance, constant, stationary, obstacle (something standing in the way), circumstance (what stands around you), substance (what stands underneath).

🚫 Not related to extent — that's tendere, "to stretch" (extend, tension, tendency). Same first five letters, unrelated word.

column2:
To speak or perform on the spot, without preparation.
To speak, perform, or compose on the spot, without preparation — no notes, no script, no rehearsal.

Unlike wing it (which admits you're bluffing) or improvise (broad — you improvise a meal, a splint, a plan), extemporize is formal and almost always about performance in front of people: a speech, a sermon, a solo. And it quietly flatters. Someone who extemporizes is holding the room without a net; the word grants them poise rather than exposing them as unprepared.
⚠️ extemporize ≠ temporize.
- extemporize = improvise — speak with no preparation
- temporize = stall — draw things out to buy time and avoid committing

The minister who extemporized gave a speech. The minister who temporized gave no answer.
TEMPO is sitting inside it — the extemporizer keeps the tempo with no score in front of him.
The image is a musician, not a panicking student: unprepared but perfectly in time, which is exactly the competence the word implies.
1. When the teleprompter failed, she abandoned the prepared text and extemporized for eleven minutes without a stumble.
2. He forgot his cue cards, so he just extemporized the toast — honestly it was better than the written one.
School and college competitions still run an Extempore event — you're handed a slip of paper with a topic and get sixty seconds before you speak. That's the word in its native habitat.
Latin ex tempore = "out of the time" — i.e. straight out of the moment, with none set aside to prepare.

From tempus, temporis (time), which pays out widely: tempo, temporary, temporal, contemporary, extemporaneous.

Partly excusing: making an offence seem less serious, not innocent.
Making an offence seem less serious by supplying a partial excuse — context that reduces the blame without removing it.

Watch the size of the claim: an extenuating fact does not say she didn't do it or she did nothing wrong. It says she did it, and here is why you should judge her less harshly. Guilt stands; the punishment shrinks. That's why it lives in courtrooms, HR meetings and disciplinary hearings — it's the language of a plea, not a defence. Compare exonerate (clears you completely) and mitigate (its plain-English twin, used for punishments and risks as well as for blame).
⚠️ extenuate ≠ attenuate. Both come from Latin tenuis, "thin", and both mean "make thinner" — but attenuate thins anything (a signal, a virus, a bond), while extenuate thins only blame.
ex-TENU-ating has tenuous buried in it — it makes the case against you thin, not nonexistent.
A thinned case is still a case, which is exactly why extenuating circumstances reduce a sentence instead of cancelling it.
1. The judge accepted that his age and coercion were extenuating circumstances, and reduced the sentence accordingly.
2. Look, being tired is not an extenuating circumstance — everyone else made the meeting.
Universities run on this word: the "extenuating circumstances" form you file to get a deadline extended or a failed exam discounted. You admit the work was late — you're arguing the lateness should count for less.
Latin tenuis = "thin" → extenuare, "to make thin, whittle down."

The root pays out across the GRE: tenuous (a thin argument, barely holding), attenuate (weaken, thin out), tenuity. Extenuating facts whittle the blame down to something thinner.

To praise highly, loudly and in public.
To praise highly and enthusiastically — usually out loud, at length, and in public.

Praise is the plain word; extol turns the volume up and adds a podium. You commend an employee in a review, but you extol a hero at a ceremony. The register is elevated, almost sermon-like, which is why it carries a faint risk of overdoing it: when a politician extols the virtues of hard work, the word is doing half the eye-rolling for you. Note that collocation — extol the virtues/merits/benefits of is where this verb lives about 80% of the time.
⚠️ extol ≠ exhort. To extol is to praise someone; to exhort is to urge them to act. A coach exhorts the team at half-time and extols them afterwards.
Ex-TOLL — you ring the bells for them.
Bells are loud, public and celebratory, which is exactly how extolling differs from quietly praising.
1. The obituary extolled her four decades of service without once mentioning the scandal that ended them.
2. Dad won't shut up about that air fryer — he's been extolling it to strangers in the queue.
Psalm 145 opens "I will extol thee, my God, O king" — the King James phrasing that fixed this word in its worshipful, ceremonial register.
Latin ex- ("up") + tollere ("to lift, raise") — to extol is literally to raise someone up, onto the pedestal.

Same lifting root gives you elate (spirits raised) and the -lation words built on tollere's partner form lātus: relate, translate, prelate, superlative.

Irrelevant; coming from outside and not belonging.
Coming from outside and therefore not belonging — irrelevant to the matter at hand.

Extra means there's more than you need; extraneous means it was never part of the job. A fourth paragraph restating your argument is superfluous; a paragraph about your childhood is extraneous. The word is a quiet dismissal — it says this doesn't bear on the question, which is colder than saying it's wrong. Register is formal and faintly clinical: editors, lawyers and scientists strip out extraneous detail, extraneous evidence, extraneous noise.
extraneous ≠ erroneous. Erroneous = mistaken (it's wrong). Extraneous = irrelevant (it may be perfectly true, it just doesn't belong here).
extra + strange — not merely spare, but a stranger: it came in from outside.
That's the whole nuance — extraneous material isn't excess of the right stuff, it's foreign matter that wandered in.
1. The judge ruled the letters extraneous to the charge and refused to admit them.
2. Just answer the question — I don't need all the extraneous backstory about your flatmate.
Any lab report or psych study: you control for extraneous variables — the outside factors that sneak in and muddy your result.
Latin extrāneus = "external, foreign," from extra = "outside."

Same root, unrecognisably worn down through French: strange and stranger — literally the outside one. Also estranged (pushed outside) and extraordinary (outside the ordinary).

column2:
Extend a known trend past the data into unknown territory.
To take what you know — a trend, a sample, a few data points — and project it outward into territory you have no data for. Also, loosely: to infer a general conclusion from a narrow piece of evidence.

The word always carries a whiff of risk. A calculation is certain; an extrapolation is a bet that the pattern holds where you can't see. In technical writing it's neutral bookkeeping ("extrapolate the curve to t=0"); in argument it's often a quiet accusation — "you're extrapolating from a sample of one." Assume, guess, and extrapolate all leap beyond the evidence, but only extrapolate claims a method for the leap.
⚠️ extrapolate ≠ interpolate.
- interpolate = estimate between two known points (inside the data)
- extrapolate = estimate beyond the known points (outside the data)

You interpolate Tuesday's temperature from Monday's and Wednesday's. You extrapolate next August's.
Extra — you're drawing extra line past where the dots stop.
The data ends, the pencil keeps going — which is exactly why an extrapolation can be confidently, elegantly wrong.
1. From three fragmentary inscriptions the historian extrapolated an entire system of provincial taxation — persuasive, but resting on almost nothing.
2. Don't extrapolate from one good week and start telling people we've turned the business around.
Election night: with 8% of votes counted, the networks "project" a winner. That projection is pure extrapolation — and the famous misfires are what happens when the sample doesn't behave like the rest.
A modern coinage (1870s), built on extra- = "outside, beyond" — the same prefix in extraordinary (beyond the ordinary), extraneous, extracurricular, extraterrestrial.

The -polate half was simply borrowed from interpolate to make a matching opposite, so the prefix carries the whole meaning: inter- = between the data, extra- = beyond it.

Excessive — beyond what the occasion or the evidence warrants.
Going beyond what is reasonable — in spending, in scale, or in claims. An extravagant gift costs more than the occasion warrants; an extravagant promise claims more than the facts support.

The judgement is always about proportion, not amount. Lavish admires the abundance; opulent just describes the richness; profligate condemns the waste as a moral failing. Extravagant sits between them — it says the thing overshot its occasion, and the speaker may be scandalised, amused, or quietly impressed.

Half its GRE life has nothing to do with money: extravagant claims, extravagant praise, extravagant theories. If you only remember the yacht, you'll misread the sentence.
Extra-vagant: it's gone extra far and wandered past the line — past what's warranted, not just past what's affordable.
The hidden "extra" keeps the excess, and "wandered off" keeps the point that it can be a claim straying past the evidence, not only a budget.
1. The biographer dismissed these extravagant claims of royal descent as the family's favourite fiction.
2. Forty quid on a birthday cake for a dog is a bit extravagant, mate.
Advertising regulators exist mostly to police extravagant claims — \"clinically proven,\" \"melts fat overnight.\" That's the non-money sense in daily use.
Latin extra (beyond) + vagari (to wander) — literally wandering outside the bounds.

That vagari root is a GRE goldmine: vagrant (wanders with no home), vagabond, vagary (a wandering whim), and vague (a meaning that won't stay put).

column2:
To manufacture — or to invent a falsehood in convincing detail.
1. To manufacture or construct something, especially from prepared parts — fabricate a steel beam.
2. To invent something false and pass it off as real — a story, an alibi, evidence, a quotation.

The second sense is the GRE one, and it's harsher than lie. To lie is to say one false thing; to fabricate is to build a falsehood — assemble it, give it details, make it hold together under inspection. That's why it attaches to nouns like evidence, testimony, sources, records: things that took work to fake. Forge is its exact twin in this double life — you forge metal, and you forge a signature.
Fabricate hides fabric — you weave cloth from thread, or you weave a story from nothing.
Both senses are workmanship: one produces an object, the other produces a lie with all its seams sewn shut.
1. The tribunal found that the officer had fabricated his contemporaneous notes some weeks after the arrest.
2. He didn't just forget my birthday — he fabricated an entire flight delay, with a gate number.
Prefab housing — pre-fabricated, built in parts off-site — is the same word doing its honest day job, and a useful reminder that sense 1 is the literal one.
Latin faber = "craftsman, smith", giving fabrica, "workshop, a thing made."

That one root branches twice into English: fabric (the woven thing) and fabricate (the making). And fabrica went through French to become forge — which is why forge carries the identical build-it/fake-it split.

Joking flippantly when the moment demanded a serious answer.
Treating a serious matter with deliberately inappropriate humour — joking when the moment called for a straight answer.

It is not a compliment. Witty praises the joke; facetious criticises the timing. The word usually arrives as a rebuke ("don't be facetious") or as a pre-emptive defence ("I was only being facetious"), which tells you what it implies about the speaker: a smart-alec dodging the actual question. The joke may even be funny — the charge is that it was flippant, not that it fell flat.
⚠️ facetious ≠ fatuous. Facetious is joking on purpose; fatuous (FACH-oo-uhs) is stupid without knowing it — a smug, empty remark from someone who thinks it's profound. The facetious man is being clever; the fatuous man only thinks he is.
f-a-c-E-t-I-O-U-s — all five vowels, in order. The word is showing off, and so is the person.
It's the classic spelling curiosity, and it doubles as the meaning: facetiousness is cleverness performed at the wrong moment.
1. Asked to explain the missing funds, he offered a facetious remark about the office coffee budget, and the committee's patience ran out.
2. "Sorry, I was being facetious — I do actually think you should take the job."
The everyday habitat of this word is damage control: the "/s" tag online, or someone backtracking with "I was being facetious" after a joke lands in a serious thread.
Latin facētus = "witty, elegant" — originally pure praise. English kept the wit but soured the timing: what was once a compliment for a polished conversationalist is now a mild telling-off for cracking jokes in the wrong room.

🚫 Nothing to do with face or facet (those are Latin faciēs).

Effortless, fluent skill at doing something.
1. An effortless ability to do something well — a facility with numbers, a facility for languages.
2. (everyday) A building or service set up for a purpose — a medical facility.

The GRE tests sense 1. Facility isn't raw talent or deep genius; it's smoothness in execution — the thing looks easy when you do it. Aptitude is potential, facility is potential already fluent. And it's faintly double-edged: praising someone's facility for excuses, or for turning a phrase, can hint that the ease came cheaply.
⚠️ facility ≠ facile. Same root, opposite verdict. Facility = admirable ease (a facility with words). Facile = ease that shows the work wasn't done (a facile argument is shallow, not skilled).
A facility is a building that makes a job easy — the trait is the same easiness, installed in a person.
The boring sense you already know and the GRE sense are one idea: facility is whatever makes the doing effortless.
1. Her facility with cross-examination was such that witnesses often conceded points before realising they had been led there.
2. He's got this weird facility for remembering everyone's coffee order after meeting them once.
Every sign you walk past — sports facility, correctional facility, medical facility — is naming a place built to make one activity easy. Same word, same idea, just poured into concrete.
Latin facilis = "easy," from facere = "to do, to make." That root is everywhere: facilitate (make easy), faculty (an ability — or the people who have it), factory, manufacture, benefactor, affect. If a GRE word has fac- or fic- in it, it's usually about doing or making.

column2:
Splitting a group into rival, self-interested camps.
Given to forming factions — creating, or arising from, dissension inside a group that is supposed to be one body: a party, a cabinet, a church, a committee.

The word is always spoken from the standpoint of the whole. Calling a bloc factious is a charge that they've put their sub-group ahead of the organisation, and usually that the quarrel is self-interested rather than principled — it's the vocabulary of political science and of people who think unity was the point. Note the scope: it describes splits between groups, never a single person's bad temper.
⚠️ factious ≠ fractious.
- factious = splitting into rival camps (a factious senate)
- fractious = irritable, unruly (a fractious toddler, a fractious horse)

Fractious has the fract of fracture and fractious tempers snap. Factious has faction.
FACTIOUS = FACTION + -OUS. The word literally has the answer inside it.
If a group is full of factions, it is factious — the split is between camps, not inside one cranky person.
1. The republic's collapse owed less to foreign armies than to the factious nobility, each house pursuing its own advantage.
2. Two months in, the book club had gone factious — the literary-fiction crowd wasn't speaking to the thriller people.
Madison's Federalist No. 10 is the most famous warning about faction ever written — the whole essay is about how a republic can survive citizens splitting into rival interest groups.
Latin facere = "to do, to make." A factio was a group that acts together — originally a chariot-racing team at the Roman circus, later a political bloc.

That root is everywhere: factory, manufacture, benefactor, artifact, facile, affect.

column2:
Based on broken reasoning, and so misleading.
Based on faulty reasoning; containing a logical error, and therefore misleading.

The charge is against the argument, not the arguer's honesty — you can be entirely sincere and still fallacious. That's what separates it from false: "false" means the claim is untrue; "fallacious" means the path to the claim is broken, so the conclusion is unearned even in the odd case where it happens to be true. It's a cool, academic word — the language of debate judges, philosophers and editorials, not of shouting matches.
⚠️ fallacious ≠ fallible.
- fallacious = this reasoning is wrong
- fallible = this person could be wrong

Every expert is fallible; only some of their arguments are fallacious.
Fallacious hides FALL — a hole in the logic you fall into, and an argument that falls apart.
The flaw is structural, so the whole thing collapses under weight rather than simply being untrue.
1. The court dismissed as fallacious the notion that a signature obtained under duress constitutes consent.
2. His whole plan rests on the fallacious idea that if it worked once, it'll work forever.
Any internet argument where someone replies \"that's a logical fallacy\" — straw man, slippery slope, ad hominem. Those are the catalogued species of fallacious reasoning.
Latin fallere = "to deceive, to trip up." One root, a big family: fallacy, fallible, infallible, false, fail, fault, default. Notice the through-line — every one of them is about something giving way underfoot.

Capable of making mistakes; liable to err.
Capable of making mistakes; liable to be wrong.

Note the capable of — fallible describes a standing capacity for error, not an error actually made. Calling a witness fallible doesn't say she lied; it says her memory is human equipment and human equipment slips. That's why the word usually arrives as a graceful concession — "I'm fallible," "juries are fallible," "the test is fallible" — a humane admission rather than an attack. Its real work is often done by its opposite: things are declared infallible, and fallible is what everything else quietly is.
⚠️ fallible ≠ fallacious.
- fallible = the thinker can err (a person, a memory, a method)
- fallacious = the argument does err (it contains a logical flaw)

A fallible scientist may still reason soundly; a fallacious proof is already broken.
Fallible = able to fall — not fallen, just never guaranteed to stay standing.
The hidden fall plus -ible ("able to be") gives you the exact force of the word: potential for error, not proof of it.
1. Every constitution assumes that rulers are fallible, and builds the machinery to correct them.
2. Look, I'm fallible — I thought the meeting was Thursday.
Papal infallibility — the Catholic doctrine that the Pope cannot err when defining doctrine ex cathedra. It's the most famous claim of exemption from being fallible, which is precisely why the word sticks to it.
Latin fallere = "to deceive, to trip up." One root, a large family: fallacy (a deceiving argument), false, fail, default, fault, and infallible.

Useful shade: the Latin is about being deceived, not merely being careless — a fallible mind is one that can be fooled.

Left unplanted to recover; idle for now, not barren.
Of farmland: ploughed but deliberately left unsown for a season so the soil can recover. Figuratively: a stretch of time that produces nothing — a career, a mind, a talent lying idle.

The word insists the ground is still good. Barren means nothing will grow; fallow means nothing is growing yet, by choice or by pause, and the harvest is expected back. So calling a writer's decade fallow is gentler than calling it wasted — it grants that something may be replenishing underneath.
⚠️ fallow ≠ callow. Fallow = resting, unproductive for now. Callow = young and inexperienced (a callow recruit). One letter, two unrelated ideas — and the GRE knows it.
f-ALLOW — the field is allowed to rest; it isn't dead, it's off duty.
The hidden allow carries the whole nuance: the idleness is permitted and temporary, not a verdict of infertility.
1. Half the estate lay fallow that year, the soil left to gather back what three seasons of wheat had stripped from it.
2. He calls it a fallow stretch; his bandmates call it four years of not writing anything.
Standard in arts and sports writing — a band's "fallow period" between albums, a striker's "fallow spell" in front of goal. Always implies the form is expected to return.

column2:
To lose strength or steadiness part-way through.
To lose strength, steadiness or momentum part-way through something — to stumble in step, waver in resolve, or break and tremble in voice. As a noun, that break itself: a falter in her voice.

The key is that it's involuntary and mid-motion. You hesitate because you're weighing something; you waver because two options are pulling at you; you falter because the thing keeping you going — legs, nerve, funding, breath — is giving out. It also implies something was already underway and moving: an economy, a march, a speech, a career. And it's a wobble, not a stop — the faltering runner may still finish.
Falter = one letter from fault and one sound from fall — the step that faults, the voice about to fall apart.
Nobody chooses to falter; something structural gives way underneath you.
1. Halfway through the eulogy his voice faltered, and he gripped the lectern until he could go on.
2. She didn't falter for a second — walked straight in and asked for double.
Business and sports headlines run on this word: talks faltered, the recovery faltered, United faltered in the second half. It's the standard verb for something that was going well and started losing steam.

Dreamed up rather than reasoned out; imaginatively unrealistic.
1. Existing only in the imagination; not grounded in fact or reason — a fanciful explanation. 2. Elaborately, playfully inventive in design — a fanciful hat, fanciful curlicues.

Sense 1 is a soft put-down. Calling a theory fanciful doesn't accuse anyone of lying — it says the idea is charming, ingenious, and completely untethered from evidence. It's gentler than absurd, more indulgent than baseless, and milder than fantastical (which implies something wild and outlandish). The speaker sounds patient rather than angry.

Sense 2 is straightforwardly warm: applied to a building, a dress, or a cake, fanciful is a compliment about imaginative excess.
Fanci-ful = full of fancy, empty of fact.
The -ful suffix tells you what's inside the idea — imagination, and nothing else holding it up.
1. The committee dismissed his fanciful account of the missing funds, noting that no bank in the country worked that way.
2. She had this fanciful plan to quit her job and open a bakery in Lisbon by September.
Trademark law calls invented brand names — Kodak, Xerox, Exxon — fanciful marks: words conjured out of pure imagination, attached to nothing real, which is exactly why they get the strongest legal protection.
Fancy is a worn-down contraction of fantasy, from Greek phantasia = "appearance, image in the mind", from phainein, "to show."

That root shows up everywhere: fantasy, phantom, phantasm, phase, phenomenon, diaphanous, emphasis. All of them are about something appearing — which is the point of fanciful: it appears real to the mind, and nowhere else.

Exacting about detail, to the point of fussiness.
Attentive to detail to an extreme degree — and, by extension, hard to please, easily put off by mess, sloppiness, or dirt.

Two shades, and the GRE uses both. Of a worker: exacting, nothing left unchecked. Of a person: fussy, faintly squeamish, offended by the imperfect.

Where meticulous is pure praise, fastidious praises and needles in the same breath — it says the care is real but has passed the point of comfort. Call an editor fastidious and you mean she catches everything; call a dinner guest fastidious and you mean he sent the plate back.
fas-TIDI-ous — tidy, stressed so hard it becomes a personality.
The stressed syllable literally hides tidi, and that's the word: tidiness pushed past virtue into fuss.
1. The manuscript bears the marks of a fastidious editor: not a comma out of place, not a source unverified.
2. He's so fastidious about his kitchen that you feel bad putting a mug down.
Agatha Christie's Hercule Poirot is the type made flesh — the symmetrical breakfast eggs, the waxed moustache, the "order and method." Fastidious in both senses at once: nothing escapes him, and nothing crooked is tolerated.
Latin fastīdium = "loathing, disgust" — from fastus (arrogance) + taedium (weariness). So the original fastidious person wasn't careful; he was disdainful, sick of the shabbiness around him. That disgust still sits under the modern word, which is why it never reads as flat praise.

Same taedium gives you tedium and tedious — the bored half of the compound.

🚫 Nothing to do with fast. The fasti- is disgust, not speed.

column2:
To understand fully; also a six-foot unit of depth.
Verb: to understand something fully after real effort — to get to the bottom of it.
Noun: a nautical unit of depth, six feet.

The verb keeps the sounding-line inside it: what you fathom is deep, murky, hard to reach. You understand a bus timetable; you fathom a motive, a grief, a decision that makes no sense. And it lives mostly in the negative — I can't fathom why she said it — so the word usually reports failure at the bottom of something, not success. Neutral in register, but faintly weary; the speaker has already tried.
Fathom = depth. So can't fathom it = can't touch the bottom.
Both senses are one idea — a fathom measures how deep the water is, and to fathom something is to reach the bottom of it, which is why the word shows up most often when you can't.
1. The commission never fathomed how the order had been approved, only that no one would admit to signing it.
2. I still can't fathom why he drove four hours to a party he left after ten minutes.
The Little Mermaid opens with the sailors' shanty "Fathoms Below" — a song about how deep the ocean goes, which is exactly the literal sense the verb is built on.
Old English fæthm = the span of a man's outstretched arms, about six feet. Sailors measured depth by hauling up the sounding rope and counting it off in arm-spans — so a fathom became a unit of depth, and to fathom became to find the bottom.

To flatter and grovel with cringing, servile eagerness.
To flatter and fuss over someone in a cringing, servile way — praise, attention and physical eagerness all aimed at a person with power over you.

The word carries the observer's contempt built in. Flatter describes what you say; fawn describes the whole grovelling posture — hovering, agreeing, laughing too hard. Nobody ever says it of themselves: you fawn over a boss, a celebrity, a rich uncle, and the person watching finds it slightly disgusting. Praise is neutral, flattery is calculated, fawning is undignified.
Fawn is fond with the volume broken.
Same warm sound, but the affection is pitched loud enough that everyone can see who outranks whom.
1. The courtiers fawned on the new favourite, discovering in him virtues they had failed to notice a week earlier.
2. Everyone at the table went quiet and started fawning the second the investor walked in.
The trauma-response list that's everywhere online — fight, flight, freeze, fawn. "Fawn" is the fourth one: you survive the threat by appeasing it. That's the word exactly.
Old English fagnian = "to rejoice, welcome gladly" — used above all of a dog wagging its tail at its master. That image is the whole word: delight performed at the feet of someone above you. Same root as fain ("gladly" — I would fain go).

🚫 Not the baby deer. That fawn came a different way entirely, from Latin fetus ("offspring") via French faon. Two unrelated words that collided in spelling.

Able to be done with the means available.
Capable of being done — a plan that can actually be carried out with the time, money, and materials available.

The word judges execution, never merit. A feasible scheme may still be pointless, unethical, or doomed; all feasible certifies is that the mechanics work out. It's the vocabulary of engineers, planners, and budget committees — cool, measured, faintly grudging. "That's feasible" is not enthusiasm; it's a green light on the arithmetic.
⚠️ feasible ≠ plausible.
- feasible = it can be done (plans, projects, routes)
- plausible = it can be believed (excuses, theories, alibis)

A plausible explanation, a feasible plan — swap them and the sentence breaks.
Feasible answers "can we?" — never "should we?"
A feasibility study asks whether the bridge can be built, not whether anyone wants it there.
1. The committee concluded that a tunnel was technically feasible but ruinously expensive.
2. Sure, we could rewrite the whole thing by Friday — it's feasible, just miserable.
Feasibility study — the standard first phase of any construction, software, or startup project. If you've ever sat through a meeting about whether something can be built before anyone argues about whether it should be, you've met the word in its natural habitat.
Old French faisable, "doable," from faire ← Latin facere = "to do, to make."

That root is a GRE goldmine: facile (easily done), factotum (does everything), efficacious (gets it done), artifice, benefactor, deficient, feat.

column2:
Useless and irresponsible; incapable of getting anything done.
Lacking the competence, energy, or responsibility to get anything done — useless and unreliable in one word.

The contempt is dismissive rather than angry. A villain is never called feckless; a wastrel is. It brands a whole character, not a single failure: the person who means well, promises much, and year after year delivers nothing. Its natural targets are layabouts, absentee fathers and idle heirs, and it carries a faint Scots–British sneer.
⚠️ feckless ≠ reckless.
- reckless = acts too much, without care for consequences
- feckless = never gets round to acting at all

The reckless one totals the car; the feckless one never got round to buying one.
Feck is effect with the front bitten off — so feckless is literally effect-less.
He isn't harmful, he's just a person whose efforts never produce any effect.
1. A feckless heir, he spent thirty years and most of the estate discovering that he had no talent for anything.
2. Don't put him on the rota — he's feckless; he'll say yes and then just not show up.
British tabloids and welfare debates run on the phrase \"feckless fathers\" — men who won't work and won't pay. If you've seen the word in print, it was probably in that collocation.

Richly fruitful; teeming with offspring or ideas.
Fruitful — able to produce abundant offspring, crops, or ideas. Literal of soil, wombs and orchards; figurative of minds, decades, and artistic movements.

Set it against its neighbours: prolific counts the output (a prolific novelist — twenty books), fertile is the plain agricultural word, but fecund describes generative power itself, and carries a lushness bordering on excess — teeming, overflowing, almost too much life. It's a literary word; a soil scientist says fertile, a critic says fecund.
Fecund rhymes with second — a fecund mind never stops at the first idea.
The rhyme carries the key nuance: not one good yield but an endless supply of them.
1. The Nile's annual flood left a fecund black silt along its banks, and an empire grew out of it.
2. Three albums in two years — the guy's having a stupidly fecund decade.
Demographers keep the two words apart deliberately: fecundity is the biological capacity to bear children, fertility is how many are actually born. Capacity versus tally — exactly the distinction the word carries everywhere else.
Latin fēcundus = "fruitful," from a root meaning to suckle, to produce. Same family: fetus (the thing produced), feminine (fēmina, she who suckles), and felicity (fēlix originally meant fruitful, and only later happy — a fruitful harvest being the original good luck).

Weak enough to invite pity — or contempt.
Lacking strength — physically frail (a feeble old man, a feeble pulse), or lacking force and effect (a feeble excuse, a feeble protest).

Weak just reports a fact; feeble passes judgement. Applied to a body it asks for pity; applied to an effort — an argument, a joke, an apology — it drips contempt: the attempt was made, and it was pathetic. Note the built-in insufficiency, too. A feeble light isn't merely dim, it's too dim to see by.
A feeble handshake, a feeble excuse, a feeble joke — everything feeble attaches to is something you'd be embarrassed by.
The word's stock collocations all carry a sneer, so remember it as "weak and not worth respecting" rather than plain weak.
1. By his last winter the composer was too feeble to hold a pen, and dictated the final bars to his daughter.
2. "Traffic" is a pretty feeble excuse when you live ten minutes away.
Latin flēbilis = "to be wept over," from flēre, "to weep." The pity is baked into the word: something feeble is, literally, something you'd cry about.

To fake a feeling or condition convincingly.
To put on a false appearance of a feeling, state, or condition — to pretend convincingly that you feel or have something you don't.

Notice what it takes as an object: you feign surprise, ignorance, illness, indifference, sleep, enthusiasm. It's almost always an inner state being performed outward. Fake is blunt and covers objects too (fake Rolex, fake passport); feign is bookish, and the deceit is usually social rather than criminal — the polite lie of looking interested, the schoolboy stomach ache. It implies control and composure: someone feigning is managing their face well.
feign ≠ feint. Feign is the verb for faking a feeling; a feint (n.) is a fake attack — a boxer's jab meant to draw a guard, an army's diversionary move. Same root, different jobs: you feign boredom, you throw a feint.
The classic thing to feign is a FAINT — and the words sound nearly identical.
A staged swoon is the perfect feign: a whole bodily state performed for an audience, with nothing actually wrong.
1. Summoned before the committee, he feigned an ignorance of the accounts that no one in the room believed.
2. She feigned sleep until her flatmate stopped asking about the dishes.
Every football match where a player rolls around clutching a shin that was never touched — commentators call it exactly that: feigning injury.
Latin fingere = "to shape, mould, invent." The idea is sculpting something that wasn't there — which is why the same root gives you fiction, figment, figure, and effigy (a shaped likeness). Feigning is moulding an expression the way a potter moulds clay.

A fake move made to draw the defence the wrong way.
Noun: a mock attack or deceptive movement made to draw an opponent's guard away from where you'll actually strike.
Verb: to make such a move.

A feint is deception designed to be seen — it fails if the other side doesn't take the bait. That makes it tactical rather than dishonest: boxers, fencers, generals and negotiators all feint, and nobody calls it lying. Compare a ruse (any trick) or a bluff (pretending to hold strength you lack) — a feint is narrower and more physical: a committed-looking movement in the wrong direction, made so the right one lands.
⚠️ feint ≠ faint. Identical sound.
- feint = a fake move to mislead
- faint = to pass out (or: barely perceptible — a faint smell)

You feint to the left; you faint on the floor.
feint = feign + t — you feign the punch to the head so the real one lands on the ribs.
The extra t is the only thing separating the word from feign, and the whole point of a feint is that it must look real enough to pull a reaction.
1. Napoleon's feint toward the enemy's left drew the reserves out of position, and the true assault fell on a hollowed-out centre.
2. He feinted like he was going to pass, then just walked it straight past the keeper.
Any football stepover — Ronaldo's shimmy, Neymar's shoulder drop — is a textbook feint: the body says left so the ball can go right.
French feindre = "to pretend," from Latin fingere = "to shape, mould, invent."

That root is worth banking: feign, fiction, figment, effigy, fictitious — all things moulded up rather than found.

Aptly chosen and pleasing; a happy, well-judged choice.
Well-chosen and pleasing — especially of words, phrasing, or timing. Secondarily: happy, fortunate (a felicitous outcome).

Apt means it fits. Felicitous means it fits and delights — the reader or listener feels a small click of pleasure at how right it is. It's a praise word, and a fairly bookish one: critics, eulogists and reviewers reach for it about a metaphor, a title, a turn of phrase. Its negative, infelicitous, is the polite way to call a remark clumsy or badly timed.
⚠️ felicitous ≠ fortuitous.
- felicitous = aptly, pleasingly chosen (credit to the chooser)
- fortuitous = happening by chance (nobody chose it)

A felicitous phrase was crafted; a fortuitous meeting just happened.
Hiding inside is Felicity — the phrase isn't merely correct, it's a happy find.
If a word choice only works, it's apt; if it makes you happy it was chosen, it's felicitous.
1. Her review singled out one felicitous line — a city described as "a clock with no hands" — and dismissed the remaining four hundred pages.
2. Naming the group chat "Damage Control" turned out to be a felicitous choice, given how the holiday went.
Felix Felicis, the Liquid Luck potion in Harry Potter — Rowling built the name straight from the root: felix = lucky, happy. Drink it and everything you choose turns out to be exactly the right choice.
Latin felix, felicis = "happy, lucky, fruitful." It gives you felicity (bliss), felicitate (to congratulate), infelicitous (badly put), and the name Felix.

Note the shift: Latin felix leans on luck; English felicitous has moved toward aptness — happiness in the choosing, not in the chance.

Burning with sincere, wholehearted feeling.
Burning with feeling — intensely sincere, wholehearted, unembarrassed by its own heat.

The word almost always approves. A fervent believer, a fervent hope, a fervent supporter: the emotion is deep and genuine, and the speaker respects it. That's what separates it from zealous (which hints at excess) or fanatical (which condemns outright). Fervent heat is warmth, not danger — you'd happily call your own convictions fervent, which you'd never do with rabid. It also pairs habitually with the quiet, inward emotions: hope, prayer, wish, belief, admiration.
fervent vs. fervid. Same root, different temperature. Fervent = warmly sincere (approving). Fervid = overheated, feverish, slightly too much (often disapproving). A fervent plea moves you; a fervid one makes you back away.
FER-vent = a fever with a vent — real heat, but let out safely.
Fervent feeling runs hot yet stays sincere and controlled, which is why the word praises rather than warns.
1. Her fervent defence of the accused clerk lasted an hour, and the committee, though unmoved, did not interrupt.
2. He's a fervent Arsenal fan — he's cried at more matches than at weddings.
Lincoln, Second Inaugural Address: "Fondly do we hope, fervently do we pray, that this mighty scourge of war may speedily pass away." Hope and prayer — the word's two natural companions, in one line.
Latin fervēre = "to boil, to glow." The heat is literal at the root and metaphorical in every descendant: fervour (boiling passion), fervid (overheated), effervescent (ef- out + boil — bubbling over), ferment (what boiling yeast does to sugar, and what unrest does to a country).

Passionate to the point of boiling over.
Burning with feeling — passionate, ardent, intensely emotional.

The heat is literal in the root and audible in the word. Fervent admiration is warm and sincere and you'd be glad to receive it; fervid admiration runs a degree hotter, and a writer who picks it is often hinting the feeling has boiled past good sense — a fervid nationalist, a fervid fan, a fervid denunciation. It's a literary, slightly disapproving word: intensity observed from the outside, usually by someone cooler than the person being described.
fervid vs. fervent. Same root, different temperature. Fervent = sincerely, warmly passionate (approving). Fervid = feverishly passionate (often too much). A fervent prayer; a fervid mob.
FER-vid = fever + vivid — feeling hot enough to be a symptom.
Fervent is body-warm; fervid is running a temperature.
1. His pamphlets were fervid to the point of incoherence, each page hotter and less persuasive than the last.
2. She's a fervid Arsenal fan — don't bring up the referee unless you've got an hour.
Latin fervēre = "to boil, to seethe." Literal boiling, then metaphorical.

One root, a free family: fervent (glowing), fervour (passion), ferment (bubbling — in a vat or in a country), and effervescent — boiling out, which is exactly what fizzy water and bubbly people do.

Burning intensity of feeling, usually for a cause or faith.
Intense, burning warmth of feeling — passion at boiling point, usually about a cause, a faith, or a leader.

Set it against its neighbours: passion is generic and often private; zeal is passion converted into action (the zealot is out doing things); fervor is the heat itself, the emotional temperature of a person or a crowd. It's a slightly elevated, writerly word, and it travels in a small set of company — religious, patriotic, revolutionary, nationalistic fervor. That company is why it cuts both ways: a writer can use it to admire sincerity, or to hint that a crowd has stopped thinking and started burning.
fervor ≠ furor. Fervor is heat inside people who believe; furor (FYUUR-or) is a public uproar or scandal — the outrage a thing causes. A tweet sparks a furor; the believers who defend it act with fervor.
Fervor has a fever in it — a temperature you run, not a job you do.
Fever fixes both the heat and the key distinction from zeal: fervor is felt, zeal is done.
1. The pamphlet was written in the fervor of the first revolutionary summer, and every line reads like a man shouting.
2. He talks about his five-a-side team with a fervor most people save for religion.
Latin fervēre = "to boil, to glow." The heat is literal and still audible in the family: fervent, fervid (hotter, often too hot), ferment (bubbling away — also political ferment), and effervescent — ex- + fervēre, "boiling out," which is exactly what fizzy water does.

To rot or worsen from being ignored.
Literally: of a wound or sore — to become infected, to suppurate, to rot instead of healing.
Figuratively: of a grievance, rumour, or problem — to grow worse and more poisonous because it was left alone.

The whole force of the word is neglect over time. Something merely bad doesn't fester; something ignored does. A festering resentment is one nobody addressed, and the implication is always that it was fixable earlier and isn't now. Compare simmer (contained heat, might still be released harmlessly) and smoulder (hidden but not yet corrupt) — fester adds pus, decay, and blame for the delay.
⚠️ fester ≠ foster. Foster = nurture something so it grows well (foster care, foster talent). Fester = leave something alone so it goes bad. One letter, opposite outcomes: you foster a child, you let a grudge fester.
Fester rhymes with pester — and both get worse the longer you leave them.
The rhyme carries the key idea: festering isn't just being bad, it's steadily worsening through neglect.
1. Unaddressed by either government, the border dispute was left to fester for a generation.
2. Just tell her she annoyed you — don't let it fester for six months and then explode.
Uncle Fester in The Addams Family — the pallid, ghoulish uncle whose name is the word itself, and who looks exactly like something left in a cellar too long.
From Latin fistula = "pipe, tube" — and, in medicine, an ulcer that tunnels through flesh. Via Old French festre into English. Same root as the modern medical fistula: an abnormal channel that won't close and won't heal.

Changeable in loyalty or affection; won and lost on a whim.
Changing your mind, loyalty, or affection constantly and for no good reason — devoted today, indifferent tomorrow.

Changeable is a neutral description; fickle is a mild accusation. It carries a whiff of shallowness: the fickle person isn't reasoning their way to a new position, they're just following whatever they happen to feel this week. That's why it attaches so naturally to lovers, fans, voters, markets, and fate — anything whose favour you can't count on. Note the direction of blame: calling someone fickle means you were let down by them.
⚠️ fickle ≠ finicky. Fickle = changes what it wants. Finicky = knows exactly what it wants and rejects everything else. A fickle eater orders something different every visit; a finicky eater sends it back.
Fickle rhymes with tickle — they go with whatever tickles them today.
The rhyme carries the nuance: it's whim, not judgement, that moves them.
1. Public taste is fickle, and the studio that reads it correctly one year is bankrupt the next.
2. She's so fickle — best friends in September, doesn't text her back by October.
Juliet, waving Romeo off into exile: "O Fortune, Fortune! all men call thee fickle." She's actually hoping Fortune lives up to the word — if it's that changeable, it might change back and send him home.
Old English ficol = "deceitful, treacherous" (kin to befician, "to deceive"). The original sense was outright dishonesty, and that's why the modern word still stings — a fickle person hasn't merely changed, they've broken faith.

column2:
Metaphorical, not literal; in art, representational.
1. Not literal — using metaphor, simile, or image to mean something other than the plain words. "Drowning in paperwork" is figurative; you are dry.
2. In art: representational — depicting recognisable people and things, as opposed to abstract.

The word is the workhorse antonym of literal, and it's descriptive rather than approving: calling language figurative just classifies it, it doesn't praise it. Note the split personality — in a grammar context it means "not to be taken at face value," but in a gallery it means almost the opposite, "actually shows a real thing." GRE passages use both senses, so let the surrounding subject decide which one is live.
Figurative = full of figures — figures of speech, or figures on a canvas.
The whole word is just figure + -ative, and which kind of figure you mean — a turn of phrase or a human form — is exactly what splits the two senses.
1. The manifesto's talk of "cleansing fire" was figurative, though its critics chose to read it otherwise.
2. When I said I'd kill for a coffee, that was figurative, obviously.
Gallery and auction labels lean on sense 2 constantly — Lucian Freud and Francis Bacon are filed as figurative painters, meaning you can see a body in the paint, unlike a Rothko.
Latin fingere = "to shape, mould, form" → figura, "a shape." A figure is a shape given to a thing — a body, a number, a phrase.

Same root, wide family: figment (something moulded in the mind), fiction, effigy, feign (to shape a false face).

Fussy over trifles; or, of a device, temperamental.
Of a person: fussy and hard to please over small details. Of a thing or task: temperamental, demanding fiddly attention to work at all — a finicky carburettor, a finicky recipe.

Where fastidious can be a compliment and punctilious sounds dignified, finicky never flatters — but it's mild, more eye-roll than insult. It's the word for someone who sends the salad back because the dressing is on it, and the tone is domestic and slightly comic rather than scornful. Note the second sense: things can be finicky too, which is the one the GRE likes.
Finicky ends in -icky — to a finicky eater, everything is icky.
The childish sound of "icky" carries the nuance exactly: the objections are petty and small, so we find them faintly ridiculous rather than offensive.
1. The curator was finicky about humidity, rejecting three galleries before consenting to lend the panel.
2. Don't bother making him dinner — he's so finicky he won't eat anything the sauce has touched.
Recipe writers use it constantly as a warning label: hollandaise, macarons and soufflés are all described as finicky — meaning the technique will punish you for the smallest slip.
From older finical, built on fine — someone who insists on excessively fine distinctions. Same root branch as refine, finesse, finery.

column2:
Irregular and restless; starting and stopping without rhythm.
Happening in short, irregular bursts with pauses between — stop-start, unsteady, never settling into a rhythm.

Intermittent is a neutral clock word: the light blinks, the signal drops. Fitful carries restlessness and frustration with it — the starting and stopping is unsatisfying, and usually the thing never properly gets going. Hence its favourite companions: fitful sleep, a fitful breeze, fitful progress, a fitful recovery. If a nation's economy grows fitfully, the writer is telling you the growth doesn't hold.
Fitful = "in fits and starts" — the fit is a spasm, not a good fit.
The everyday phrase by fits and starts already means exactly this, and fitful is just that phrase compressed into an adjective.
1. Her recovery was fitful — weeks of steady improvement undone by a single bad night.
2. I got maybe three hours of fitful sleep, half of it waiting for the alarm to go off.
Macbeth on the murdered Duncan: "After life's fitful fever he sleeps well." Life as a bout of restless, feverish twitching — and death as the first real rest.
From the noun fit in its old sense of a sudden seizure or paroxysm — an epileptic fit, a coughing fit, a fit of rage. Something fitful comes in those little attacks.

🚫 Not the fit that means "suitable" or "in shape." Unrelated word entirely — a fitful jacket is not a well-tailored one.

Shockingly obvious wrongdoing, too brazen to overlook.
Of an offence: so obvious and so outrageous that it can't be excused or ignored. A flagrant violation isn't just visible — it's shameless.

Compare blatant: blatant is about loudness and can be almost neutral (a blatant lie, a blatant plug). Flagrant carries moral heat — it's reserved for breaches of law, duty, or decency, and it implies the offender didn't even bother to hide. That's why it lives with a fixed set of nouns: flagrant violation, abuse, breach, disregard, misconduct. The word condemns the act, not the person.
⚠️ flagrant ≠ fragrant. One letter apart, opposite worlds: flagrant = scandalously obvious wrongdoing; fragrant = sweet-smelling. A flagrant garden is a crime scene; a fragrant one is roses.
There is no such thing as flagrant kindness — flagrant only ever modifies a wrong.
If the noun after it isn't a violation, abuse, breach, or disregard, you've picked the wrong word.
1. The tribunal found a flagrant disregard for the safety rules: the alarms had been disconnected months before the fire.
2. Parking across two disabled bays outside the hospital — that's just flagrant.
The NBA grades its worst fouls as Flagrant 1 and Flagrant 2 — not the sneaky trips, the unnecessary-and-excessive contact everyone in the arena saw.
Latin flagrāre = "to blaze, to burn." A flagrant offence is one still burning in plain sight.

Same fire gives you conflagration (a huge blaze) and the legal phrase in flagrante delicto — literally "while the crime is blazing," i.e. caught red-handed.

column2:
Showy and colourful in a stylish, attention-grabbing way.
Showy, colourful, theatrical — dressing, speaking, or behaving in a way designed to be noticed.

Tone is what to watch. Ostentatious sneers at vulgar wealth; garish means it hurts to look at; flamboyant is usually half-admiring — the person has flair and knows it, and the display is more fun than offensive. Applied to people it points at style and personality (a flamboyant conductor, a flamboyant winger); applied to things it means bold colour and swagger (a flamboyant waistcoat, a flamboyant signature). It only turns critical when the context makes the showiness inappropriate — a flamboyant eulogy.
flam-BOY-ant = FLAME + buoyant — it burns bright and floats up where everyone can see it.
The flame is the colour and heat of the display, and the buoyancy is the lightness that keeps it charming rather than crass.
1. His flamboyant courtroom manner — the pauses, the sweeping gestures — won juries that the evidence alone might not have.
2. She turned up to a beach wedding in a flamboyant purple suit and completely got away with it.
Freddie Mercury is the word's default illustration — practically no profile of him is written without "flamboyant" in the first paragraph, and it's always meant as a compliment.
French flamboyer = "to blaze, to flame", from Latin flamma. Late Gothic architecture is literally called Flamboyant for its flame-shaped window tracery.

Same fire: flame, inflame, flambé, flammable — and flamingo, the flame-coloured bird.

Just out of the nest — inexperienced, but with promise.
Noun: a young bird that has just grown its flight feathers and left the nest; by extension, a beginner.
Adj.: new, inexperienced, only just up and running — a fledgling democracy, a fledgling airline.

Where novice is flatly factual and amateur edges toward incompetent, fledgling is sympathetic: it says untested and fragile, but airborne. The word grants potential. Calling a company fledgling means it might make it; calling it amateurish means it won't. Note that it's applied to ventures and institutions far more often than to people.
fledge (grow flight feathers) + -ling (the little-one suffix: duck*ling*, sap*ling*, year*ling*).
A little thing that has just got its wings — which is why the word sounds hopeful rather than insulting.
1. The treaty was signed by a fledgling republic that had held exactly one election.
2. He's a fledgling cook — everything's edible, nothing's on time.
Business and foreign-desk journalism runs on it: fledgling startup, fledgling democracy, fledgling industry — all meaning too young to judge yet.
From Old English flycge, "feathered, fit to fly" — same family as fly and flight. That's also why full-fledged means fully feathered, i.e. ready for anything; a fledgling is the stage just before.

column2:
Overdecorated in style; or red and flushed in the face.
1. Excessively ornate — of prose, speech, music, or decoration: overloaded with flourishes.
2. Of a face or complexion: red, flushed, ruddy.

Calling a style florid is never a compliment. Ornate can be admiring, elaborate is neutral, but florid says the decoration has crowded out the sense — too many flowers, not enough stem. Applied to a face, it's the flush of heat, drink, or high blood pressure, not the glow of health; doctors also use it for a symptom that has bloomed into full, unmistakable view (florid psychosis).
⚠️ florid ≠ fervid.
- florid = overdecorated (or red-faced)
- fervid = burning with passion

A florid speech is fussy. A fervid one is on fire. A politician can manage both at once.
FLOR = floral. Florid prose is flowery prose; a florid face has bloomed.
Both senses are the same picture — something has flowered too much, on the page or on the cheeks.
1. His florid dedication ran three paragraphs before it managed to name the person it was thanking.
2. Uncle Ray came in from the garden florid and sweating, complaining about the heat.
Florida — Ponce de León landed at Easter and named it Pascua Florida, "flowery Easter." Same root, and the state is genuinely lush. Florid = Florida = full of flowers.
Latin flos, floris = "flower." The family is large and free: floral, flora, floret, flourish (to bloom, to thrive), efflorescence, and flourish in the musical sense — a decorative curl of notes, which is exactly what florid writing is made of.
