column2:
To break a rule openly and with contempt.
To openly disregard a rule, law, or convention — and to make no secret of it.

Breaking a rule and flouting one are different acts. You can break a rule quietly, by accident, in shame. Flouting is defiance on display: the rule is known, the breach is deliberate, and the contempt is part of the point. It takes rules as its object — flout the law, flout convention, flout the ban — never people. Journalists live on this word, so it carries a faint tone of official disapproval, as though a clipboard is being filled in nearby.
flout ≠ flaunt.
- flout = defy a rule openly
- flaunt = show off something you have

You flaunt your wealth; you flout the tax code. Mixing them up is one of the most common errors in edited English — and the GRE knows it.
Flout rhymes with shout — and hides out: you break the rule out in the open, loudly.
A secret violation is never a flout; the whole word depends on being seen.
1. The company flouted environmental regulations for a decade, treating the fines as a routine cost of doing business.
2. He flouted the dress code so hard he showed up to the wedding in flip-flops.
Pandemic headlines ran on this verb — "partygoers flouting lockdown rules" was in the news almost daily in 2020, always with that tut-tutting official tone.

Utterly baffled — visibly, comically stumped.
Completely baffled — so confused you have no idea what to do next.

The word is light on its feet. Bewildered has a hint of distress, perplexed is cool and intellectual, but flummoxed is faintly comic: you're stumped, and everyone can see it on your face. It's the confusion of a man staring at flat-pack instructions, not of a man facing tragedy. Informal and slightly jokey, so it takes the sting out — people say "I'm utterly flummoxed" about themselves far more readily than they'd admit to being lost.
⚠️ flummoxed ≠ flustered. Flummoxed = you can't understand; flustered = you can't cope — rattled, flapping, but perfectly clear on what's going on.
Flumm-OX — you stand there blinking like an ox.
The ox hiding at the end catches the flavour of the word: not quiet inner puzzlement but big, dumb, visible bafflement.
1. The committee was flummoxed by a clause that appeared to forbid the very thing the statute was written to permit.
2. Ask him anything about football and he'll talk for an hour — ask him to work the dishwasher and he's completely flummoxed.

Rattled and muddled; briefly losing your composure.
Rattled — agitated and muddled to the point where you fumble your words or lose your thread.

It is a small, brief loss of composure, usually from surprise, embarrassment, or being put on the spot. Panic implies real danger; flustered implies only that someone caught you off guard and you went pink and started over. It is a gentle, almost affectionate word — you can be flustered by a compliment. Note the pressure comes from outside: things fluster you, and the flustered person is trying (and visibly failing) to stay smooth.
⚠️ flustered ≠ blustered. One letter, opposite postures: the flustered person is quietly rattled and losing control; the blustering person is loudly bullying and pretending to have it.
Fluster = flutter + fussed.
Both hidden words are right there in the sound, and both are small, flappy, harmless agitations — not real distress.
1. Cross-examined on a detail she had not anticipated, the witness grew visibly flustered and contradicted her earlier account.
2. Don't get flustered — they're just asking where the file is.
Hugh Grant built an entire career on it — the stammering, apologising, permanently flustered Englishman of Four Weddings and a Funeral and Notting Hill.

To thwart a scheme; or a contrast that makes another shine.
Verb: to stop a plan, plot, or attempt from succeeding.
Noun: a person or thing whose contrast makes another's qualities stand out (Watson is a foil to Holmes).

The verb wants an attempt already in motion — you foil a robbery, an escape, a coup, not someone's vague ambitions. It's the headline word for last-minute frustration of a scheme ("Police foil plot"), and it carries a faint whiff of the adventure story: the foiler is the good guy, the foiled a bit ridiculous. Compare thwart (heavier, more deliberate obstruction) and frustrate (drier, often about systems rather than schemes).

The noun sense has nothing to do with blocking. A foil doesn't compete with the hero — it flatters by comparison, throwing the other's traits into relief.
Kitchen foil does both jobs: wrap a scheme and it suffocates; slip it under a diamond and the diamond blazes.
One word, two functions — smother the plot, or sit behind something and make it shine.
1. Customs officers foiled the smuggling operation hours before the shipment was due to leave the port.
2. Ravi's whole weekend plan was foiled by one email from his boss.
\"Curses, foiled again!\" — the stock cartoon-villain line (Snidely Whiplash and every moustache-twirler since). That's the verb's exact flavour: a scheme blocked at the last second, and the schemer left looking silly.
Two different words that collided in spelling.

The verb is Old French fouler, "to trample" — you tread a plan underfoot.

The noun is Latin folium, "leaf" — a leaf of thin metal. Jewellers set a bright foil behind a gem so it caught more light, and that literal trick gave us the literary meaning: the character placed behind the hero to make him sparkle. Same root: foliage, portfolio, folio, exfoliate, trefoil.

To deliberately stir up trouble and keep it simmering.
To stir up trouble — unrest, rebellion, discord, resentment — and keep it going.

Incite is a spark: one speech, one moment, and the crowd moves. Foment is slow heat applied over time, usually from off-stage — the agitator working the room for months, the foreign power funding both sides. It carries blame: nobody foments by accident, and the object is always something bad. You can foment a mutiny, a strike, a panic; you cannot foment goodwill.
⚠️ foment ≠ ferment.
- foment (verb) = deliberately stir up trouble — someone is doing it
- ferment = to brew/bubble; as a noun, a state of agitation ("the country was in a ferment") — no agent required

Writing "ferment a rebellion" is a classic slip; the rebellion ferments on its own, but a person foments it.
Foment rhymes with torment — and keeps the same bad company.
Both are second-syllable verbs for inflicting something unpleasant on purpose, so if the object isn't ugly, the word is wrong.
1. Colonial administrators accused the pamphleteers of fomenting sedition among the garrison troops.
2. He wasn't in the argument — he just sat there fomenting it, feeding each side quotes from the other.
Standard diplomatic-accusation vocabulary: governments and news wires routinely charge rival states with "fomenting unrest" or "fomenting instability" — a phrase you'll meet in almost any foreign-affairs report.
Latin fovēre = "to warm." A fomentum was a warm compress laid on the skin — and fomentation is still the medical term for one. That's the whole image: you don't light the fire, you hold warmth against the spot until it inflames.

column2:
Bold in a way that ignores obvious danger.
Bold in a way that ignores the danger — daring without judgment.

The daring is real; that's what separates it from plain stupidity. A foolhardy person genuinely has nerve, they just have no brakes. Reckless is careless about consequences generally; audacious admires the nerve; foolhardy grants the courage and then condemns it as wasted. It's the word you use for the climber who went up without ropes — half admiration, mostly disapproval, and a strong hint that it will end badly.
fool + hardy — the hardy half is real toughness; the fool half is the missing brain.
Both words are sitting right there in plain sight: courage present, sense absent.
1. The general's foolhardy advance across open ground cost him half a division before noon.
2. Swimming out there at night was foolhardy and you know it — brave, sure, but you could've drowned.
Alexander Pope's line "fools rush in where angels fear to tread" — later the Elvis/Ricky Nelson standard Fools Rush In — is foolhardiness in one sentence: charging in exactly where the wiser party won't.
hardy here doesn't mean tough-plant hardy — it's Old French hardi, "bold, daring." So the word is literally "foolishly bold." Same root gives hardihood (audacity) and the older sense of foolhardiness.

To patiently hold back from doing what you could justly do.
To hold back from doing something — to refrain, endure, be patient.

It isn't plain abstain. Abstaining is self-denial (you skip the wine, you skip the vote); forbearing is restraint aimed at someone else — you could strike back, foreclose, correct, complain, and you choose not to. The word carries the provocation inside it, so it always implies patience and a touch of mercy on the part of whoever forbears. Register is elevated, faintly biblical: "forbear to judge," "he forbore comment."

Note the irregular past: forbore / forborne, exactly like bore / borne.
⚠️ forbear ≠ forebear.
- forbear (for-BAIR) = hold back
- forebear (FOR-bair) = an ancestor — someone who came before

Your forebears died; you forbear from mentioning it.
To forbear is to bear it — you take the provocation instead of hitting back.
The word literally has bear (endure) in it, and that's the whole nuance: not avoidance, but absorbing something you'd be entitled to answer.
1. The court urged the creditors to forbear a further six months rather than force the family from the house.
2. I forbore from saying "I told you so," which honestly took everything I had.
Mortgage and student-loan forbearance — the lender is legally entitled to demand payment and formally agrees to hold off. Exactly the word's meaning, on a real document.
Old English forberan = for- + beran (to bear, carry).

The prefix for- here means away, abstain from, refuse — and it unlocks a family: forgo (go without), forbid (bid against), forsake, forswear, forfeit. Whenever you see this for-, expect a negative.

column2:
To be an omen of something bad; to sense coming evil.
To be an omen of something bad; or, of a person, to feel in advance that something bad is coming.

The word runs one way only. Predict and portend are directionally neutral — you can portend a golden age. Nothing ever forebodes good luck: the verb carries the dread built in, so it needs no adjective to darken it. Note also that the bare verb is now rare and faintly literary; the living forms are the noun foreboding ("a sense of foreboding") and the adjective ("a foreboding silence"), and those are what the GRE will usually put in front of you.
⚠️ foreboding ≠ forbidding.
- foreboding = signalling doom to come — a foreboding hush before the verdict
- forbidding = harsh, unwelcoming to look at — a forbidding grey fortress

A forbidding cliff is merely ugly and steep; a foreboding cliff is about to have someone fall off it.
Bode takes well or ill — forebode only ever takes ill.
Test it by collocation: if you can't slot in disaster, doom or ruin after it, you want portend or predict instead.
1. The stillness of the birds, the fishermen said, foreboded a storm none of the instruments had yet registered.
2. I don't know why, but I had this foreboding all morning that he was going to quit.
The two low strings under a horror-film trailer, before anything has happened on screen — that's a foreboding score, telling you the bad thing is coming while the character is still fine.
fore- (before) + Old English bodian (to announce), from boda = "a messenger." A forebode is literally a messenger who arrives ahead of the event — and this one only ever brings bad news.

Same Germanic root sits in bid in its old sense of announce, command — which is where forbid comes from.

Able to be predicted or expected in advance.
Able to be predicted, anticipated, or reasonably expected before it happens.

The word is less about what will happen than about what a sensible person could have known was likely — which is why it quietly assigns responsibility. A foreseeable consequence is one you don't get to be surprised by. And in the foreseeable future, it marks the stretch of time you can actually plan for: deliberately vague, usually shorter than it sounds, and a polite way of saying "don't ask me for a date."
Foreseeable keeps two homes: the foreseeable future and reasonably foreseeable harm — one is a hazy horizon, the other is a verdict.
Which home you're in sets the tone — planning talk is loose and hedged, liability talk means somebody should have seen it coming.
1. The collapse was not a freak event but the foreseeable result of a decade of deferred maintenance.
2. Rent's going up and the trains still don't run, so I'm stuck at my parents' place for the foreseeable future.
In negligence law, entire cases turn on the phrase "reasonably foreseeable" — you're liable for the harm an ordinary person would have seen coming, and not for the freak accident nobody could. Insurers, engineers and safety reports all live on that one adjective.

Head something off by acting before it can happen.
To head something off by acting first — to prevent an anticipated event by taking steps in advance.

The word carries foreknowledge and timing. Prevent just reports the outcome; forestall says you saw it coming and moved early enough to block it. It's also quieter than preempt — preempting is a seizure, striking first to take what the other side wanted; forestalling is defensive, a door bolted before the knock. What you forestall is almost always unwelcome: a crisis, a lawsuit, an objection, a rival's next move.
fore + stall — you put a stall in its path before it arrives.
The stall only works if you set it up ahead of time, which is exactly the foreknowledge the word insists on.
1. To forestall any challenge to the succession, the regent had the rival claimants married off before the old king was buried.
2. I texted him first to forestall the whole "you never call me" speech.
Standard central-bank and headline language: rates are raised to forestall inflation, bailouts arranged to forestall a run on the bank. If you learn one collocation, learn forestall a crisis.
Old English foresteall = an ambush — literally a "standing (steall) in front of" someone on the road. Medieval English law used forestalling for buying up goods before they reached the market, cornering the supply before anyone else could bid.

fore- is a whole free family: forecast, foresee, forewarn, foreboding — all of them "before."

To choose to go without something you could have had.
To go without something — to deliberately give up or abstain from a thing you could perfectly well have had.

The key is that it's a choice, not a loss. You don't forgo a wallet you dropped; you forgo the dessert, the bonus, the second drink. It's cooler and more restrained than sacrifice (which advertises the pain) and far milder than renounce (which is a public, near-permanent break). Forgo is the quiet, sensible word — you weighed it up, and you passed.
⚠️ forgo ≠ forego.
- forgo = go without it
- forego = go before it (hence foregoing, "the foregoing paragraph," and a foregone conclusion)

The E in forego is the E in "earlier."
Forgo = for + go: you let it go.
The whole word is sitting there in plain sight — the thing was yours to take and you let it go by.
1. Rather than compromise the study's independence, she forwent the industry funding entirely.
2. I'll forgo the airport lounge if it means we get an extra hour in bed.
Straight out of Economics 101: opportunity cost is defined as the value of the next best alternative forgone. Every textbook uses this exact word — and every textbook spells it without the E.
Old English forgān — the prefix for- meaning away, off, past + gān, "to go." Literally to go past a thing.

That for- prefix (nothing to do with fore- = before) is a small GRE family, and it always carries a whiff of away / against / undoing: forsake (abandon), forbid, forbear (hold off), forswear (renounce under oath), forlorn (utterly lost).

column2:
To abandon someone or something you owed loyalty to.
To abandon, desert, or renounce — a person, a faith, a habit, a home.

The word only works where a bond or claim existed. You can abandon a car; you can only forsake something that had a hold on you. Abandon is neutral and physical, desert is a breach of duty, but forsake is the vow-word: elevated, biblical, faintly reproachful, and often used of someone walking out on love or loyalty. It also runs the other way — forsaking drink or ambition is renunciation rather than betrayal, and there the tone turns almost noble.
forsake vs. forswear. Forsake = walk away from something you were bound to. Forswear = renounce it by oath (or, in its second sense, to perjure yourself). You forsake your friends; you forswear cigarettes.
for-SAKE: you leave them for your own sake.
The hidden word flags the sting the synonyms lack — forsaking is abandonment that puts your interest above the tie you owed.
1. He forsook a partnership at the firm for a monastery in the hills, and never once said he regretted it.
2. She swore she'd never forsake her friends for a bloke — three weeks later nobody had heard from her.
The traditional wedding vow: "forsaking all others, keep thee only unto her, so long as ye both shall live." The one place the word still gets said out loud — and it's about loyalty, not luggage.
The prefix for- here isn't "for" — it's the Old English negator meaning away, utterly, wrongly. Once you spot it, a whole set opens up: forbid (order away), forgo (go without), forswear (swear off), forlorn (utterly lost), forget (fail to grasp).

column2:
Quiet courage to endure hardship over the long haul.
Courage of the enduring kind — strength of mind that lets you bear pain, hardship, or fear over time without collapsing.

Bravery charges; fortitude holds. It's the virtue of the cancer ward, the long trial, the grinding setback — not the burning building. It implies quiet dignity rather than heroics, and it always suggests duration: nobody shows fortitude for ten seconds. Formal and warmly approving, the word a eulogy reaches for.
Fortitude: a fort doesn't attack — it withstands the siege.
The fort hidden in the word is defensive, which is exactly the flavour of courage meant — absorbing punishment, not delivering it.
1. Through eighteen months of treatment she bore the illness with a fortitude that silenced everyone who had pitied her.
2. Sitting through four hours of his holiday photos took real fortitude.
The two marble lions outside the New York Public Library are named Patience and Fortitude — christened by Mayor La Guardia in the Depression for the qualities he said New Yorkers would need to get through it.
Latin fortis = "strong." The root is everywhere: fort, fortress, fortify, force, effort — and comfort, literally "to strengthen (someone) thoroughly."

column2:
Happening by chance, not by design.
Happening by chance, without design or planning — accidental, unforeseen.

Strictly, the word reports causation, not quality: a fortuitous event simply wasn't arranged by anyone, and it can be a windfall or a disaster. Popular usage has dragged it toward "happily accidental," and most writers now use it that way, but the GRE tests the older, neutral sense — chance, full stop. On an exam, read it as unplanned and let context decide whether the outcome was good.
⚠️ fortuitous ≠ fortunate.
- fortuitous = by chance (says nothing about the outcome)
- fortunate = by good luck (says nothing about the cause)

A fortunate heir planned nothing and gained much; a fortuitous collision was nobody's plan and helped no one.
Fortuitous rhymes with circuitous and gratuitous — the -itous family all describe how a thing came about (by a winding route, without cause, by chance), never how good it was.
Tie the rhyme to "manner of arrival" and the luck drops out of the definition, which is exactly where the exam sets its trap.
1. The discovery of penicillin was fortuitous: a contaminated dish that Fleming had every reason to throw away.
2. We ran into each other at the airport — totally fortuitous, neither of us knew the other was flying.
Sports commentary leans on it constantly — "a fortuitous deflection off the defender's shin" means the goal came from chance, not skill, and often carries a faint sting.
Latin forte = "by chance" (ablative of fors, chance) → fortuitus. Same root as fortune and misfortune — note that fortune itself was originally neutral, the goddess who dealt out good and bad alike.

🚫 Not from fortis, "strong." That's the other family: fort, fortify, fortitude, effort. A fortuitous rescue is a lucky one, not a sturdy one.

Irritable and quarrelsome; unruly, liable to break into squabbling.
Irritable and quarrelsome; unruly, hard to keep in line.

Two habitats. Of a person — usually a child, a patient, a passenger — it means cranky and difficult, complaining and resisting. Of a group — a coalition, a union, a parliament, a family — it means the members squabble among themselves and could split apart at any moment.

Milder and more detached than belligerent or truculent: a fractious person is a nuisance, not a threat. It's a word an observer uses about someone else's bad temper, often with a faint weariness — the tone of a nanny or a political correspondent, not of someone spoiling for a fight.
⚠️ fractious ≠ factious.
- fractious = bad-tempered, unruly
- factious = creating factions, stirring up dissent

A fractious toddler is merely difficult; a factious minister is deliberately splitting the party.
Fractious = one fracture away from falling apart.
The word is visibly fracture plus an adjective ending, which catches both senses at once — the temper that snaps and the alliance that cracks.
1. The armistice was administered by a fractious committee whose members agreed on nothing but their contempt for one another.
2. He'd been stuck on a delayed flight for six hours with two fractious kids and no snacks left.
Political journalism runs on this word — "a fractious coalition," "fractious talks," "the party's fractious right wing." If you read any election coverage, you've met it a dozen times.
Latin frangere / fractus = "to break." English fraction once meant not a number but a breaking apart — discord, dissension; fractious is the adjective from that lost sense.

Same root, huge family: fracture, fragment, fraction, fragile, frail, infringe, refract.

column2:
Weakness of body or character; breakability that invites sympathy.
1. Physical weakness — the delicacy of the very old, the ill, the underfed.
2. A moral weak spot — a small, habitual failing in an otherwise decent person.

The word asks for sympathy rather than blame. Weakness can be a verdict on you; frailty treats the flaw as built in, part of the material you're made of, not a choice you made. Hence "human frailty" — the plural frailties almost always means the little vices we forgive: vanity, gossip, a weakness for gambling. Calling someone frail is tender; calling them weak is a judgement.
Frail is fail with an r — frailty is the weakness that makes you fail, not the wickedness that makes you guilty.
The word points at breakability, so the tone is pity, not accusation.
1. Her mind stayed razor-sharp long after the frailty of her body confined her to the chair.
2. Look, he's a good boss — buying a boat he can't afford is just one of his frailties.
Hamlet's bitter line about his mother's hasty remarriage: "Frailty, thy name is woman!" — one of the most quoted half-lines in Shakespeare, and it's the moral sense, not the physical one.
Latin fragilis = "breakable," from frangere = "to break." The same Latin word entered English twice: fragile straight from the Latin, and frail worn down through Old French frele.

That root breaks open a whole shelf: fragment, fraction, refract (light broken at an angle), infringe (break in on a right), frangible.

Openly honest, especially about something awkward.
Open and direct in speech — saying the true thing plainly, without softening or evasion.

Three near-neighbours, three different temperatures. Honest just means not lying. Blunt means you didn't bother with tact and probably bruised someone. Frank sits between: the subject is delicate — money, failure, someone's chances — and you deal with it head-on anyway. That's why it so often comes pre-announced ("to be frank," "let me be frank with you"): the speaker is flagging that comfort is about to be traded for truth. Being called frank is usually a compliment; being called blunt usually isn't.
Frank rhymes with blank — a frank answer is point-blank.
Point-blank gives you both halves at once: aimed straight at the awkward thing, and fired with no cushion in between.
1. The report is unusually frank about the trial's failures, naming the two sites where the data was simply never collected.
2. I'll be frank — you're not getting that promotion this cycle, so let's talk about next year.
"Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn." — Rhett Butler's exit line in Gone with the Wind, routinely voted the most famous line in film history. It's the word doing exactly its job: he's about to say something brutal, so he warns you first.
From the Franks, the Germanic tribe that conquered Gaul. Under Frankish rule only Franks held full liberty — so frank came to mean free, then free-speaking.

That root is worth owning: France (land of the Franks), franchise and enfranchise (to grant a freedom or a vote), lingua franca (a free-trade common tongue), and to frank a letter — stamp it to travel free of postage.

Loaded with trouble; tense and strained.
Two uses, and the GRE wants both.

1. fraught with X = loaded with, full of — and X is essentially always something bad: danger, peril, difficulty, risk, contradiction. You will not see "fraught with joy."

2. fraught, standing alone = tense, strained, anxious. A fraught silence. A fraught relationship. Things got fraught.

What links them is latent trouble, not present disaster. A fraught situation hasn't gone wrong yet — it is carrying the makings of going wrong. "Dangerous" states the threat outright; fraught says the threat is packed inside, waiting. And the standalone sense adds a human edge: people in a fraught room are stressed, wary, walking on eggshells.
fraught rhymes with taut — the situation is pulled tight and one tug from snapping.
Fraught isn't broken yet; it's under tension, which is exactly why the word implies trouble stored up rather than trouble arrived.
1. Any attempt to redraw the border would be fraught with consequences the treaty's authors never anticipated.
2. We can invite both of them, but I'm telling you now, that table is going to be fraught.
Newsrooms run on it: "a process fraught with difficulty," "a fraught relationship between the two leaders." If you learn one collocation, learn fraught with peril — that pairing is half the word's exam life.
Fraught is freight. Middle Dutch vracht = cargo; Middle English fraught meant a ship laden with goods. The literal cargo sense died and the metaphor took over — so fraught with danger is, word for word, carrying a hold full of danger.

Wildly fast, hectic, energetic to the point of chaos.
Wildly fast and energetic; hectic to the point of looking out of control.

The word describes pace and motion, not feeling. A trading floor, a drum solo, a toddler's birthday party, a newsroom on election night — all frenetic. It can be said with admiration (frenetic energy on stage) or exhaustion (a frenetic schedule), but either way the picture is the same: too much happening, too fast, with no visible governor on it.
⚠️ frenetic ≠ frantic.
- frenetic = wild speed and activity — a frenetic pace
- frantic = wild with fear or urgency — a frantic search for a missing child

A dance can be frenetic. A parent is frantic.
frenetic = frenzy + kinetic — a frenzy in motion.
The blend keeps the two halves of the meaning together: kinetic is the movement, frenzy is the lack of control, and neither half is about fear.
1. The final act unfolds at a frenetic tempo, the strings sawing away as though the orchestra were fleeing the hall.
2. Two coffees in, he was typing at this frenetic pace and answering three Slack threads at once.
Live sports commentary runs on this word — "a frenetic first ten minutes" is standard football-pundit English for a game that opens at breakneck speed.
Greek phrēn = "mind" → phrenitis, "inflammation of the brain," i.e. delirium. The word literally meant brain-fevered.

That root is worth banking: frantic and frenzy are the same word arriving by different routes, and schizophrenia (split mind) and phrenology (mind-reading by skull bumps) come from the same phrēn.

to worry constantly over small things; to wear away
Verb: to worry in a small, continuous, unproductive way — and, in its physical sense, to wear something away by constant rubbing (a rope frets against rock).
Noun: a state of low-grade agitation ("in a fret about the exam").

Scale matters: you don't fret over a car crash, you fret over whether you locked the car. It's chronic, petty, and visibly fidgety rather than sudden or profound — and because it's mild, telling someone "don't fret" is half comfort, half dismissal. The two senses are the same idea: something small, repeated, quietly eroding what it touches.
Fret rhymes with sweat — not a scream, just a small, constant damp anxiety that wears you down.
Both senses are in the rhyme: low-level and repetitive, and the wearing-down is literal in the "rubbed away" meaning.
1. He spent the week fretting over a single line in the contract, long after the lawyers had stopped caring.
2. Mum, stop fretting — the flight lands at eight, it's fine.
Macbeth's most quoted speech: life is "a poor player, that struts and frets his hour upon the stage" — all that fussing and agitation, signifying nothing.
Old English fretan = "to devour, eat up" — the same root as German fressen, the verb used for animals gorging rather than people dining.

That's the whole word in one image: worry eats at you, and rust or rope eats away at what it rubs.

The outer edge; outside the mainstream, often suspect.
Noun: the outer edge or margin of something — of a forest, a city, a crowd, a movement. (Also the literal decorative border of hanging threads on a rug or shawl, and in British English the hair cut across the forehead — bangs.)
Adjective: on the margins; outside the accepted mainstream.

The useful GRE sense is positional and then judgemental. A fringe group isn't just small — it sits outside the centre of legitimacy, and the word quietly says the centre is where the sensible people are: fringe theories, the lunatic fringe, fringe candidate. But the same outsider position flips positive when the centre is the establishment: fringe theatre means daring and unofficial, not crackpot. Note also fringe benefits — perks at the edge of your salary, not part of the main pay.
F-RING-e — a ring sits around the middle, never in it.
The hidden ring puts you on the outer band: close enough to touch the thing, never part of its centre.
1. Her proposals, dismissed as fringe eccentricities for a decade, are now written into party policy.
2. He's a bit fringe — swears the moon landings were filmed in a shed.
The Edinburgh Festival Fringe got its name literally: in 1947 eight uninvited companies turned up and performed on the edge of the official festival. It's now bigger than the thing it was excluded from — which is the word's whole ambiguity in one story.

Not worth serious attention; silly, pointless, without merit.
Not worth serious attention; lacking weight, purpose, or merit. Of a person: silly, given to trifles, unwilling to be serious.

The word is a verdict, not a description. Trivial just says a thing is small; frivolous says it had no business taking up the time it took — there is always an implied "when you should have been doing something that mattered." It also splits cleanly by target: a frivolous thing (a purchase, a lawsuit, a complaint) is baseless or pointless; a frivolous person is flighty and can't be trusted with anything grave. Faintly disapproving in a well-mannered way — the reproach of someone too polite to say "stupid."
Frivolous = frills — pure decoration, nothing load-bearing.
Both start fri-, and a frill is the part of a garment you could cut off and lose nothing — which is exactly the charge the word makes.
1. The court dismissed the suit as frivolous and ordered the plaintiff to pay costs.
2. We blew the whole afternoon on something completely frivolous and I regret nothing.
"Frivolous lawsuit" is the phrase you've heard on every legal drama and news segment — a case with no legal merit at all, which a judge can throw out and fine the lawyer for filing. That collocation carries the full meaning: not merely weak, but undeserving of the court's time.
Latin frivolus = "worthless, trifling" — tied to friāre, "to crumble." A frivolous argument crumbles the moment you lean on it.

Same crumbling root gives GRE-worthy friable (easily crumbled — friable soil, friable rock).

Producing real results; worth the time spent.
Producing good results — productive of something worth having.

The word judges the outcome, not the effort. A gruelling day of work that produced nothing is not fruitful; a ten-minute conversation that solved everything is. Its opposite, fruitless, is the standard GRE pairing, and the contrast is exactly that: effort spent versus something to show for it.

Mildly warm and slightly formal — it lives in business and diplomatic speak (a fruitful exchange of views, a fruitful collaboration), where it can quietly mean "nobody stormed out." The literal sense (soil, trees, bearing fruit) still exists but is now mostly poetic.
You can only call it fruitful if you can name the fruit you walked away with.
The test isn't how hard the work was — it's whether you're carrying something when you leave.
1. Three years of correspondence between the two laboratories proved unexpectedly fruitful, yielding a vaccine neither could have developed alone.
2. Long meeting, but actually fruitful for once — we came out with a decision.
"Be fruitful, and multiply" — Genesis 1:28, one of the most quoted lines in English, and the original literal sense: bear fruit, produce offspring.

column2:
The pivot point a lever turns on; the decisive thing.
The fixed point on which a lever pivots — and, figuratively, the thing on which a whole situation turns.

Size is the point. A fulcrum isn't the biggest or strongest part of the system; it's the small, still part that makes enormous force possible. So calling someone the fulcrum of a negotiation says more than "important" — it says the whole weight rests on them, and shift them an inch and the outcome changes. Compare linchpin (holds things together, stops collapse) and crux (the hard central problem): a fulcrum is about leverage, not cohesion or difficulty.
Fulcrum = full + crumb — a crumb-sized point bearing the full weight.
The fulcrum is tiny and never moves, yet everything the lever manages to lift depends on it.
1. A handful of undecided senators became the fulcrum of the entire bill: small in number, decisive in effect.
2. My gran is the fulcrum of that family — take her out and the whole thing tips over.
The bolt in the middle of a seesaw is a fulcrum — which is why shuffling toward the centre kills your leverage and the heavier kid pins you in the air.
Latin fulcrum = "bedpost, support," from fulcīre, "to prop up." The word has barely changed job in two thousand years: it is still the thing propping everything else up.

Interchangeable — any one unit substitutes perfectly for another.
Interchangeable: each unit is perfectly substitutable for another of the same kind, so which particular one you get makes no difference. A dollar, a barrel of crude, a share of stock, a bushel of wheat.

The word is stronger than similar or replaceable — fungible things aren't merely alike, they're indistinguishable for the purpose at hand. It comes out of law and finance and still carries that clipped, contractual tone. Applied to things it's neutral bookkeeping; applied to people it turns cold fast: calling workers fungible says they're units, not individuals.
Nobody's wedding ring is fungible. Their cash is.
The test is whether swapping in an identical unit would bother you at all — if yes, it isn't fungible.
1. Under the terms of the warehouse receipt the grain was fungible: any ton in the silo discharged the obligation.
2. Management talks like engineers are fungible — swap one out, ship the same code.
NFT = non-fungible token. The whole point of the name: every other crypto coin is fungible (your Bitcoin = my Bitcoin), but an NFT is one specific, non-swappable item.
Latin fungī = "to perform, discharge a duty" — from the phrase fungī vice, "to serve in place of." That root also gives you function, perfunctory (going through the motions), and defunct (done performing).

🚫 Nothing to do with fungus. Different Latin word, and the g is soft.

Sneaky in a way that shows — secretive and visibly guilty.
Done quietly and quickly to avoid being noticed — sly, stealthy, hole-and-corner.

The word almost always carries guilt. Covert describes an operation and is neutral; furtive describes a manner, and the manner betrays the person: the darted glance, the hand sliding into a pocket, the tab closed too fast. A truly secret act is one nobody sees. A furtive act is one you can see — you just can't see what's behind it. That's why "furtive" in a sentence usually means the sneaking failed.
Furtive hides a thief — Latin furtum, "theft" — and what gives him away is the glance, not the goods.
Covert means nobody notices; furtive means somebody did, which is why the word always sounds like an accusation.
1. Between courses he stole a furtive look at his watch, hoping the hostess would not see it.
2. Why are you being so furtive about the phone? Just show me the message.
Police stop-and-frisk reports are full of the phrase "furtive movements" — the officer's standard written justification for a search, and the exact reason civil-liberties lawyers attack it: a nervous glance isn't evidence of anything.
Latin fur = thief, furtum = theft. A furtive person moves the way a thief moves.

Same root, unexpectedly: ferret — Latin furittus, "little thief," for the animal that slinks into burrows. Which is why you ferret out a secret.

Doomed to achieve nothing; pointless no matter how hard you try.
Incapable of producing any useful result — doomed before it starts, not merely unlucky.

Unsuccessful reports an outcome; futile passes judgement on the whole attempt. Calling an effort futile says the failure was structural — the thing could never have worked — which is why it usually comes with an implied so stop. It carries a weary, slightly superior tone: the speaker can see the pointlessness that the person still trying cannot. Reserve it for effort. A futile gesture is one that changes nothing; a trivial one is small; a fruitless one merely came back empty this time.
F + utile — the f kills the utility before the effort even begins.
That "before" is the whole nuance: a futile attempt isn't one that failed, it's one that was never going to work.
1. Further negotiation proved futile; each delegation had arrived bearing terms the other had already refused twice.
2. Arguing with him about referees is futile — save your breath.
"Resistance is futile." The Borg's line in Star Trek — the perfect use of the word, because they don't mean you'll probably lose, they mean your losing is already decided.
Latin futilis = "leaky, that pours out easily" — said of a vessel that cannot hold what you put in it. From fundere, "to pour." Pour all you like into a cracked jug; you end up with nothing.

Same root, easy family: fusion, infuse, profuse, effusive, refund, transfusion.

column2:
An embarrassing public slip of the tongue.
An embarrassing blunder — almost always something said, in public, in front of exactly the people who shouldn't have heard it.

Scale is the whole point. A blunder can lose a battle; a gaffe loses you a news cycle. The tone is wince, not condemnation — journalists reach for the word when they're half-enjoying the spectacle. And it's usually a slip of tact, not of manners: a faux pas means you breached etiquette, a gaffe means you let something tactless or inconveniently true escape your mouth.
Gaffe rhymes with laugh — the room laughs, nobody dies.
That rhyme fixes the scale of the word: a gaffe costs you dignity, never the outcome.
1. The ambassador's gaffe — congratulating the minister on a promotion he had not yet received — was replayed on every evening bulletin.
2. I called his wife by his ex's name. Total gaffe. I'm never going to a dinner party again.
Journalist Michael Kinsley's famous line, now a standard bit of political shorthand: "A gaffe is when a politician accidentally tells the truth."

To contradict or deny — nearly always used in the negative.
To deny, contradict, or dispute something — to declare that a statement or claim is not true.

It is a stiff, bookish word, and it keeps strange company: in modern English it lives almost entirely inside a negative. You will read "no one can gainsay her achievement" or "there is no gainsaying the numbers" far more often than a plain "he gainsaid me." That habit carries the nuance — the word usually appears precisely to say that the thing is beyond dispute. Where contradict is a neutral everyday act, gainsay implies challenging the validity or truth of an assertion, often with a whiff of futility.
Nobody ever gainsays — things are only "beyond gainsaying."
Lock the word to its negative frame and you get both the meaning (to say against) and the way it is actually used — to declare something undeniable.
1. Whatever one thinks of his methods, there is no gainsaying the scale of what he built.
2. Sure, the food's overpriced — but I'm not going to gainsay anyone who says it's the best in town.
The King James Bible, Luke 21:15: "I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist." That biblical weight is exactly why the word still sounds so formal.
Pure Old English, and transparent once split: gēan ("against") + say. It's the same gēan buried in again and against — so gainsay is literally say-against.

🚫 Nothing to do with gain (profit). That's from French gaaignier; the resemblance is an accident of spelling.

To shock a person or group into sudden, decisive action.
To shock someone into sudden action — to jolt a person, crowd, or movement out of apathy and into doing something.

The force is a jolt, not a coaxing. You encourage a team over weeks; you galvanize them in a moment, usually with a speech, a crisis, or an outrage. It also implies the target was inert beforehand — you can't galvanize people who were already busy. And it's warm: the galvanizer is admired, whereas an incite-r is blamed. Politics, activism and business love it — galvanize support, galvanize the base, galvanized into action.
Nobody is ever galvanized and then just sits there. The word is almost always followed by the doing: galvanized into action, galvanized the crowd to march.
Galvanize never describes a mood — only a trigger, so if nothing visibly happens next, it isn't the right word.
1. The verdict galvanized a protest movement that had been dormant for a decade.
2. One furious email from the client galvanized the whole team — we shipped the fix by lunch.
Galvanized steel — buckets, nails, roofing sheets — is iron given a zinc coat by an electrical process named after the same man. The metal in your hardware store and the crowd in the speech share a root.
From Luigi Galvani, the 18th-century Italian anatomist who made a dead frog's leg kick by touching it with metal — proof that electricity moves flesh. That twitch is the word: something lifeless, a current, sudden movement.

Same man gives you galvanic and the galvanometer.

Talking far too much, ramblingly, about trivia.
Excessively talkative — especially in a rambling, aimless way, about things that don't matter.

The judgement is built in. Talkative is neutral, loquacious is a compliment in a suit (fluent, articulate), voluble is speech that flows fast and easily — but garrulous is the listener's complaint. It implies you can't get away: the trivia, the digressions, the story about the neighbour's fence. Classically attached to old men on porches and strangers on long train journeys.
⚠️ garrulous ≠ querulous.
- garrulous = talks too much
- querulous = complains too much (whining, peevish)

Same -ulous ending, opposite failing: one is a chatterbox, the other is a grumbler.
Garrulous starts like gargle — a noise from the throat that just keeps going.
Gargling isn't speech and it isn't content, which is exactly the accusation: sound where conversation should be.
1. The memoir is charming for eighty pages and then turns garrulous, every anecdote spawning three more.
2. Our cab driver was so garrulous I learned his entire divorce before we hit the motorway.
Latin garrīre = "to chatter" — an imitative word, the babble of birds. The Eurasian jay, a bird that will not shut up, is still classed as Garrulus today.

Socially clumsy in a way that suggests poor breeding.
Socially clumsy — lacking the tact, polish, or ease that a situation calls for. Said of people, remarks, and gestures: a gauche question, a gauche gift.

Note who's speaking. Awkward is sympathetic and usually inward — you feel awkward. Gauche is a verdict delivered from above: the speaker is claiming to know the rules and pronouncing that you don't. It implies the blunder came from not being brought up right, not from nerves. So the word says as much about the person using it as the person described — there's a whiff of the snob in anyone who reaches for it.
Gauche near-rhymes with posh — it's what posh people call everyone else.
The rhyme fixes the sound (GOHSH) and the sneer built into the word at the same time.
1. Asking a novelist how much money she makes is considered gauche, however sincerely one means it.
2. He gave the bride a gift receipt with the present — a bit gauche, but at least she could swap it.
French gauche = simply "left" — as in the left hand, the clumsy one. Left-handedness has been slandered in half of Europe's vocabulary, and it gives you a matched set worth memorising together:

- gauche ← French left = clumsy
- sinister ← Latin sinister, left = ominous, evil
- adroit ← French à droit, to the right = skilful, deft
- dexterous ← Latin dexter, right = nimble

Learn one, get four. (In French politics la gauche is still just the left wing — no insult intended there.)

column2:
Awkwardly tall and ungainly, the way teenagers are.
Awkward and ungainly in the body — especially tall, thin, and badly coordinated, with limbs that seem to have arrived before the control over them did.

This is a word about the body, not the personality: a gawky person may be perfectly charming, they just knock over the glass. And it's rarely cruel — gawky is the mild, half-fond word we reserve for adolescence, carrying the assumption that they'll grow out of it. Call an adult gawky and you're being gentler than if you'd said clumsy or oafish.
gawky vs. gauche. Gawky is clumsy in the limbs — you trip on the step. Gauche (GOHSH) is clumsy in the manners — you ask the widow what the house sold for.
Gawky is one letter off lanky, and it's exactly lanky plus gawk: too much limb, and everyone's staring.
Hear the -anky/-awky pair and you get the build; hear gawk inside it and you get the stares that the build attracts.
1. At fifteen he was all wrists and knees, a gawky boy folded uncomfortably into a school blazer two sizes too small.
2. Don't laugh — I was so gawky at that age I could trip over a flat floor.

Genuinely relevant to the matter under discussion.
Relevant to the matter at hand — genuinely bearing on the point under discussion.

Relevant is the flat, everyday word; germane is what you reach for when relevance itself is the argument. It lives in debate, committee rooms and courtrooms, and it turns up negated more often than not: "That's not germane." It also claims more than mere topical overlap — a fact can be about the same subject and still not be germane, because germane means it actually attaches to this question. In parliamentary procedure there is literally a germaneness rule: an amendment must relate to the bill it's amending, or it's thrown out.
Germane points grow from the same germ as the argument; everything else is a weed.
The word hides germ — a seed — and a germane remark sprouts from the very question being asked, not from the soil next door.
1. The judge ruled the defendant's charitable donations were not germane to the question of whether he had signed the contract.
2. Great story, but is any of this germane to why the server went down?
Shakespeare put it in Hamlet, mocking a courtier's overblown talk of duelling: "The phrase would be more germane to the matter if we could carry cannon by our sides."
Latin germanus = "of the same parents" — a full brother or sister. So a germane point is kin to the topic, not a stranger wandering in. That's also the old phrase cousin-german, meaning a first cousin.

Behind it sits germen, "sprout, bud" — which gives you germ, germinate, germinal.

🚫 Nothing to do with Germany. That name has a separate, murky origin; the resemblance is an accident.

Smooth, easy talk that's too slick to be sincere.
Speaking (or spoken) with easy, ready fluency — but a fluency that betrays shallowness or insincerity. A glib answer comes out too fast, too polished, and clearly cost the speaker no thought.

The word is never a compliment. Fluency itself is admired; glib is what you call fluency when it has replaced substance — the salesman, the politician with a soundbite for every hard question, the friend who says "everything happens for a reason" at a funeral. Calling someone glib accuses them of trading depth for smoothness.
glib rhymes with fib and with ad-lib — talk that's made up on the spot and slides out too easily.
Both rhymes carry the accusation: no preparation behind it, and probably not true.
1. His glib assurances about the safety record collapsed the moment anyone asked for figures.
2. Don't give me the glib version — I actually want to know what went wrong.
Tom Cruise on the Today show in 2005, jabbing a finger at the host over psychiatry: "Matt, Matt, Matt — you're glib." The clip has been replayed and parodied for twenty years, and it's exactly the right use: you're answering too easily about something you haven't thought about.
From Low German/Dutch glibberig = "slippery." The original English sense was literally smooth and slick; it slid straight onto speech. Keep the physical image and the word defines itself — glib words are slippery: they go down easily and you can't get a grip on them.

To relish your win or their loss, openly and smugly.
To dwell on your own triumph — or someone else's misfortune — with obvious, self-satisfied pleasure, usually in front of them.

Gloating is pride with a victim. You can be proud alone in a room; you can only really gloat at someone. Note also the asymmetry of who uses the word: it is an accusation levelled at other people, never a neutral description of yourself. And it needn't involve winning at all — watching a rival fail is enough (gloat over is the standard collocation: gloat over her downfall).
Gloat = glow: satisfaction you can see on the face — and they can see it too.
Private pleasure isn't gloating; it only counts once it's on display for the loser.
1. Rather than gloat over his opponent's collapse, the champion praised him at length in the press conference.
2. He didn't just win the bet — he had to gloat about it for a solid week.
Nobody ever admits to it in the present tense. The word's natural habitat is the phrase \"I don't mean to gloat, but…\" — said, always, by someone about to gloat.

Quietly downcast; wearing a low, mildly sulky mood.
Visibly downcast — low-spirited, sullen, and usually quiet about it.

Scale matters: despondent and morose are heavy words for real despair, while glum is everyday, mild, and often temporary — the mood of someone whose team lost, whose plans got cancelled, whose Monday is going badly. It's also the most readable of the sad words: you can be secretly miserable, but glum shows on the face and flattens the room. Slightly sulky at the edges, so it can carry a faint note of "cheer up."
glum ≠ grim. Glum is sad and deflated; grim is harsh, forbidding, severe. A glum face wants comforting; a grim face wants obeying.
Glum rhymes with mum — the glum one has gone quiet.
The rhyme carries the nuance: glumness is silent, sulky low spirits, not loud grief.
1. The delegates filed out glum and silent, the treaty unsigned for a third straight year.
2. He sat glum on the sofa with the takeaway menu, still sulking about the cancelled trip.
From Middle English gloumen, "to look sullen, to frown." Same root-cluster as gloom, gloomy, glower (to scowl), and gloaming (twilight) — the gl- words for darkening skies and darkening faces.

Provoke someone into action by persistent needling.
Verb: to provoke or drive someone into doing something, typically by persistent needling.
Noun: a spiked stick used to drive cattle — and by extension, anything that spurs you on.

Urge appeals to your reason, spur pushes a willing horse; goad works by irritation. The goaded person acts to make the jabbing stop, which is why they so often act badly — the standard collocation is goaded into a fight, a mistake, an unguarded remark. Sympathy usually sits with the goaded, blame with the goader.
go + ad — an ad that nags you until you finally go.
A goad doesn't persuade you, it pesters you into moving.
1. The columnist's jibes were calculated to goad the minister into an unguarded reply.
2. Don't let him goad you — he just wants you to swing first.
The biblical line "it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks" (Acts 9:5) is rendered in modern translations as "kick against the goads" — the ox that lashes back at the driver's stick only hurts itself.
Old English gād = a spear-point / pointed stick for driving oxen. The literal object survives inside the metaphor: someone goading you is jabbing you along like livestock.

To please by giving someone exactly what they wanted.
To please someone by giving them what they wanted; to indulge a desire, whim, or appetite.

Satisfy answers a need — hunger, a requirement, a condition. Gratify answers a wish. That's why the objects it takes are so often appetites: you gratify a craving, a whim, someone's vanity, your own curiosity. When the object is a person ("I was gratified to hear..."), it turns quietly formal and dignified — a pleasure you'd admit to at a podium. When the object is a desire, a faint smell of self-indulgence comes with it.
Gratify = make grateful — and the fastest way to make someone grateful is to hand them the thing they were craving.
The -fy ("make") plus grat- ("pleased, thankful") gives you the whole word, and "craving" keeps the indulgent edge attached.
1. The committee was gratified to learn that the endowment had survived the crash intact.
2. He gratifies every craving the second it shows up — three food deliveries before noon.
Instant gratification — the phrase every app, casino and social feed is engineered around, and the thing the famous marshmallow test asks children to delay. Same word, and the "give the craving what it wants, now" sense is exactly right.
Latin grātus = "pleasing, thankful." One root, a big family: grateful, gratitude, congratulate, ingratiate (worm your way into someone's favour), gratuity (thank-you money), grace.

⚠️ Watch the drift in gratuitous: grātis = "free of charge" → "unearned" → today's meaning, uncalled-for (gratuitous violence). Same root as gratify, opposite mood.

Uncalled for and unjustified; also, given free of charge.
Done or given without cause, need, or justification — nobody asked for it and nothing warranted it. A secondary, older sense survives in formal and legal use: free of charge, given without expectation of return.

The everyday sense is almost always an accusation. Unnecessary is a neutral measurement; gratuitous says the excess was gleeful — the insult was thrown in for sport, the gore lingered because someone enjoyed filming it. It carries a whiff of bad taste and self-indulgence on the part of whoever did it. Note the collocations that do the heavy lifting on the GRE: gratuitous violence, cruelty, insult, swipe.
⚠️ gratuitous ≠ fortuitous. Same ending, opposite worlds: gratuitous = uncalled for (and unwelcome); fortuitous = happening by chance (and usually lucky).
A gratuity is money nobody made you give — so anything gratuitous is thrown in unasked.
The tip is the harmless version of the same idea; swap the money for an insult or a bloodbath and you have the modern meaning.
1. The judge dismissed the passage as a gratuitous attack on a witness whose credibility was never in question.
2. Great film, but did we really need that gratuitous ten-minute torture scene?
It's the standard phrase of every film critic and ratings board: a movie flagged for "gratuitous violence" isn't being called violent, it's being called violent for no reason.
Latin grātis ("for free"), from grātia = "favour, grace, thanks." Free-of-charge came first; "unearned" slid into "unjustified."

The root is a GRE goldmine: gratis, gratuity, gratitude, grateful, ingratiate, congratulate, grace.

🚫 Not related to fortuitous — that's Latin fors, "chance" (also fortune, fortunate).

Sociable by nature; happiest among people.
Fond of company; sociable by nature — happiest in a crowd. In biology, it also means living in flocks or herds (gregarious geese, gregarious ants).

This describes appetite, not manners. Affable means pleasant when approached; gregarious means going out to do the approaching — the person who takes an empty evening as a problem to be solved. It's a temperament word, warm and faintly bookish, and it says nothing about whether someone is charming, only that people are what recharges them.
⚠️ gregarious ≠ egregious. Same flock-root, opposite lives: e-gregious is out of the flock (e- = out), and now means conspicuously, shockingly bad — an egregious error. Gregarious is squarely in the flock, and is a compliment.
Gregarious = gathers-various — various people, gathered, on purpose.
The gregarious one doesn't merely tolerate the crowd, they go and assemble it.
1. Beneath the diplomat's gregarious manner lay a professional's instinct for who in the room was worth knowing.
2. He's so gregarious he'll come back from a five-minute coffee run with two new friends.
Nature documentaries run on this word — flamingos, starlings and wildebeest are all described as gregarious species, meaning they simply don't live alone.
Latin grex, gregis = "flock, herd." The flock root pays for itself across the exam: congregate (flock together), segregate (flock apart, se- = aside), aggregate (add to the flock), egregious (out of the flock).

A wrong you feel entitled to complain about, often formally.
A real or imagined wrong that gives you grounds to complain — and, by extension, the formal complaint itself.

Not the same as an annoyance or a gripe. A grievance carries a claim of injustice: someone did something to me, and I am owed redress. That's why it lives in institutional language — grievance procedure, file a grievance, union grievance — where a complaint gets a case number.

It also has a slow-burning political sense: grievances are nursed, harboured, aired. A gripe evaporates; a grievance is kept.
A grievance is grief with paperwork.
The word literally hides grieve — but the -ance turns private hurt into a filed, formal claim against somebody.
1. The petition set out the colonists' grievances against the Crown, item by numbered item.
2. He's still got a grievance about being passed over in 2019 — brings it up every single time.
Seinfeld's Festivus has a fixed order of ceremony: the Feats of Strength, and before them the Airing of Grievances — where Frank Costanza tells everyone at the table exactly how they've disappointed him that year.
Latin gravis = "heavy." A grievance is a wrong that weighs on you.

That root is a GRE goldmine: grave (serious), grievous (seriously bad), grief, aggravate (literally make heavier), gravity, gravitas.

To abase yourself — beg or apologise with all dignity gone.
To lie or crawl face-down before someone; figuratively, to beg, flatter, or apologise in a way that throws away your dignity.

The word carries the observer's contempt. Apologising is neutral, pleading can be dignified — grovelling is what you call an apology that has gone too far, performed upwards at someone with power over you. Nobody describes their own behaviour as grovelling except as a joke ("I grovelled, and he gave me the extension"). It implies self-abasement bought cheaply, and it makes the reader think less of the one doing it.
Grovel = gro(und) level — nose in the dirt, looking up at the boss.
The word puts you physically below the person you're addressing, which is exactly the loss of standing that separates grovelling from merely apologising.
1. Courtiers grovelled before the emperor, foreheads pressed to the flagstones until he deigned to speak.
2. I had to grovel to the landlord for about ten minutes before he agreed to fix the boiler.
Its natural habitat is the apology email — "so sorry to chase, entirely my fault, whenever you get a moment" — the grovelling register everyone recognises at work.
From Middle English grovelling = "face downward" (Old Norse á grúfu, "on one's face"). That was an adverb, but people heard the -ing as a verb and invented grovel to fit — so the word literally means lying flat on the ground, and the figurative sense never lost that posture.

column2:
To complain in a low, muttering, half-hearted way.
Verb: to complain in a low, muttering, half-audible way. Noun: that kind of complaint — or a low rumbling sound (thunder, an empty stomach).

Volume is the whole point. A protest is aimed at someone; a grumble is aimed at nobody in particular and is meant to be overheard rather than heard. It implies grudging compliance — the grumbler does the thing anyway, muttering the entire time. That makes it mild and faintly comic: you can grumble about the weather, the queue, your knees. Nobody grumbles about an atrocity.
G + rumble. A grumble is a complaint that rumbles — low, continuous, never quite a bang.
The word literally contains rumble, which fixes both senses at once: the muttered griping and the belly noise.
1. The backbenchers grumbled about the new tax but filed obediently through the voting lobby.
2. Stop grumbling and pass me the spanner.
Your stomach grumbling before lunch — same word, same low rolling noise, which is exactly why the complaining sense feels the way it does.

Easily fooled; swallows whatever you tell them.
Easily tricked or deceived — believing whatever you're told, with no instinct to check it.

The word carries a faint sneer. Calling someone gullible isn't observing that they were misled once; it labels them a standing easy mark, someone con artists find. Naive blames inexperience and can be almost tender; credulous is the cool, formal version, used of beliefs and audiences ("a credulous public"). Gullible is the playground-blunt one, and it's always at the believer's expense.
Gullible has your gullet in it — it goes straight down, no chewing.
The gullible person swallows the story whole rather than biting into it first.
1. The scheme relied on a steady supply of gullible investors, each persuaded that the returns were merely unusual rather than impossible.
2. He's so gullible he'll believe you if you tell him the WiFi is stronger near the window.
The oldest prank in the schoolyard: "You know 'gullible' isn't in the dictionary?" — and someone always goes to check.
From gull, an old English word for a dupe — and, as a verb, to cheat someone. It survives in that verb: to be gulled is to be taken in. So a gullible person is, literally, gullable — able to be gulled.

column2:
Worn out and stale from being repeated too often.
Worn out and drained of force by overuse — stale from being repeated too often.

It is aimed almost exclusively at language and ideas: phrases, plots, metaphors, opening lines, plot twists. You don't call a chair hackneyed. And the charge is laziness, not falsity — a hackneyed line is usually one that was good, which is precisely why it got used to death. Where cliché names the offending thing, hackneyed is the verdict passed on it, and it carries a faint sniff of the literary critic: mildly contemptuous, never neutral.
A hack writer writes hackneyed prose.
The word wears its insult on its sleeve — hack is the writer-for-hire churning out the same tired phrases, and hackneyed is what comes out.
1. The screenplay's dialogue was so hackneyed that reviewers could finish each line before the actors did.
2. Please don't end the toast with "last but not least" — it's so hackneyed everyone's already cringing.
London's black cabs are still licensed, in law, as hackney carriages — the same word, one step back: a horse for hire.
From Hackney, the London district where horses were bred and hired out. A hackney was a rented nag — ridden by everyone, worn down by everyone, and never anyone's prized mount.

That gives you the whole family in one image: hack (a writer for hire, grinding out routine copy), hackney carriage (a cab for hire), and hackneyed (an idea so hired-out it's exhausted).

column2:
To hold back or slow down; also, a large basket.
Verb: to hold back, slow down, or make difficult. Noun: a large lidded basket (laundry, picnic).

The verb is about drag, not blockage. Thwart defeats a plan outright; impede puts something in the way; hamper weighs you down so you can still move, just badly — clumsily, slowly, at half strength. Rain doesn't stop the rescue, it hampers it. Note the standard collocation: things are almost always hampered by something — bad weather, budget cuts, a torn hamstring, missing data. Neutral register, common in news and academic prose alike.
⚠️ hamper ≠ tamper. Both mean interfering with how something works, one letter apart. Hamper = slow it down from outside; tamper (with) = meddle inside it, usually to alter or sabotage. Rain hampered the investigation; someone had tampered with the evidence.
Strap a picnic hamper to your back and you're hampered — still walking, just slower.
The basket sense gives you the verb's exact flavour: a burden that encumbers rather than a wall that stops.
1. Chronic underfunding hampered the department's research for a decade, though it never quite halted it.
2. Don't wear those boots on the hike — they'll just hamper you.
The laundry hamper in the corner of your room is the same word — a basket so bulky it slows you down carrying it.

Done with no plan or care; thrown together at random.
Done with no plan, order, or care — thrown together and left to chance.

Random is neutral and often technical: a random sample is a good thing. Haphazard always carries a shrug of disapproval — it says a human being should have organised this and didn't. Compare arbitrary, where someone did choose, just for no good reason; haphazard means nobody was really choosing at all. It's the standard polite word for criticising process: haphazard record-keeping, a haphazard search, books stacked haphazardly.
⚠️ haphazard ≠ hazardous. Hazardous = dangerous. Haphazard = disorganised. Haphazard wiring may well end up hazardous, but the word itself says nothing about risk — only about sloppiness.
hap + hazard — per-haps stacked on top of a dice game. Two words for luck, zero for planning.
Both halves mean "chance," so the word is doubly unplanned — which is exactly the complaint it makes.
1. The commission found record-keeping at the ministry to be haphazard at best, with entire years of correspondence unaccounted for.
2. He packed in a haphazard rush and arrived in Oslo with three chargers and no coat.
Old Norse happ = "luck, chance" — and it pays out across the language: happen (what luck brings), happy (originally lucky), hapless (luck-less), mishap, perhaps.

Hazard came from Arabic az-zahr, "the dice," via Old French as the name of a dice game — chance again, and only later "danger."

Unlucky in a pitiable, faintly comic, helpless-bystander way.
Unlucky — dogged by misfortune, and unable to do much about it.

The tone is pity from a safe distance, usually with a faint smile in it. A hapless person isn't doomed or tragic; they're the one who gets rained on, blamed, tripped up — misfortune keeps landing on them while they stand there taking it. That passivity is baked in: hapless people have things done to them. It's also almost always said about someone else — a narrator's word, a journalist's word — and it quietly makes the subject slightly ridiculous. Hence the stock pairings: hapless victim, hapless bureaucrat, the hapless defending champions.
⚠️ hapless ≠ helpless.
- hapless = unlucky — bad things keep happening to you
- helpless = powerless — you can't act at all

A strong swimmer can be hapless (three cancelled flights); a hapless swimmer isn't necessarily helpless in the water.
You are never hapless in your own story — only in someone else's.
Nobody calls themselves hapless, because the word carries an onlooker's amused pity, which is exactly the nuance that separates it from plain unlucky.
1. The novel follows a hapless clerk whose every attempt at romance collapses into farce.
2. Some hapless intern got blamed for taking the whole site down.
Sports commentary runs on this word — the bottom-of-the-table side is always "the hapless Bears," never merely the losing one. Pundits reach for it to make defeat sound faintly comic.
Old Norse happ = "luck, chance" → English hap, luck. Add -less: without luck.

That tiny root is hiding in a lot of everyday words: happen (what befalls you by chance), happy (originally lucky, not cheerful), perhaps (by chance), mishap, haphazard — all built on luck, not on feeling.

A long, loud, scolding speech at a captive audience.
Noun: a long, loud, hectoring speech — scolding or ranting dressed up as address.
Verb: to subject someone to one.

Three things have to be true before it's a harangue: it goes on too long, it comes at people rather than to them, and it's moralising or angry. A lecture can be boring but well-meant; a tirade is a hot burst of rage; a harangue is the sustained version — the speaker has the floor and the audience can't escape. It's always the listener's word, never the speaker's: no one has ever described their own remarks as a harangue.
ha-RANG — it still rang in your ears an hour after he stopped.
The buried rang catches the two things that define the word: loud, and far longer than anyone wanted.
1. The general's farewell address turned into a forty-minute harangue on the moral decay of the younger officers.
2. Ask him one question about crypto and he'll harangue you until your food goes cold.
Through French from Old Italian aringa, "a public speech" — from aringo, the assembly ground, and behind that a Germanic word for ring: the ring of people standing round the speaker. Baked into the word is the crowd that has to stand there and take it.

column2:
A sign or person that something — usually bad — is coming.
A person or thing that goes ahead and signals what is coming — a forerunner, an advance sign.

A harbinger is never the event itself, only its announcement: the first robin is a harbinger of spring, not spring. And though the dictionary is neutral, usage leans dark — the word's default company is doom, disaster, decline, recession. Say something is a harbinger and people brace. Next to it, omen is superstitious (the universe is warning you), herald is grander and happily positive, and precursor is flat and technical. Harbinger is the literary, headline-writing choice — elevated enough that you write it far more often than you say it.
Harbinger = herald — both start with "h-er/har-", both arrive first, and neither one is the news.
Lock the pair together and you keep the essential point: a harbinger only announces the thing, which is why it works as a warning rather than a fact.
1. The collapse of two regional banks was, in hindsight, a harbinger of the crisis that swallowed the decade.
2. Three grey hairs in one week — a harbinger of thirty, apparently.
Financial and political journalism runs on it: any week the markets wobble, some headline calls it a harbinger of recession. That collocation — harbinger of + something bad — is how you'll actually meet the word.
Old French herberge = "lodging, shelter." A medieval harbinger was the officer sent ahead of an army or a royal progress to book the lodgings — the man who arrived first so the king could arrive next.

Same root as harbour/harbor, the shelter a ship runs to. Once you see the advance man riding ahead, the modern sense is automatic.

Acutely distressing; leaves you shaken long after.
Acutely distressing — an experience or account so painful it leaves you shaken afterwards.

Scale matters: unpleasant is a bad afternoon, harrowing is the thing you still can't talk about. It attaches to the ordeal or the telling of it — a harrowing escape, a harrowing testimony, harrowing footage — almost never to a person. And the pain is mental: a harrowing story doesn't hurt your body, it wrings you out.
⚠️ harrowing ≠ harried. Harried = hassled, pestered, rushed off your feet (a harried waiter). Harrowing = soul-wrenching. A harried morning is annoying; a harrowing one is traumatic.
h-ARROW-ing — an arrow through you, not a scratch on you.
The hidden word marks the intensity: harrowing things pierce and stay lodged, which is why the word belongs to ordeals rather than mere inconveniences.
1. The commission's report contained harrowing testimony from survivors of the siege, much of it read aloud in silence.
2. I finally watched that documentary about the cave rescue — absolutely harrowing, I couldn't sleep after.
Hamlet's Ghost, on what he could tell his son: "I could a tale unfold whose lightest word / Would harrow up thy soul." Even the lightest word of it would tear him open — that's the register the adjective still carries.
A harrow is a farm implement: a heavy spiked frame dragged across ploughed ground to rip the clods apart. To harrow someone is to drag that over their mind.

The literal tool is still in the language — and the metaphor is why the word means lacerating, not merely sad.

Arrogant in bearing — visibly looking down on everyone.
Arrogant in a visible, chin-up way — treating other people as beneath you and letting it show in your manner.

Arrogant is about the claims you make; haughty is about the bearing you carry — the cool stare, the clipped reply, the refusal to be impressed. It's the aristocrat's vice, and it's always an outsider's verdict: nobody describes themselves as haughty. Slightly literary, faintly old-world, and never a compliment.
Haughty is haute with a -y: haute couture is high fashion, and a haughty person keeps her chin at exactly that altitude.
The word is literally "high-y," which is why it names a posture rather than an opinion.
1. The duchess received her guests with a haughty civility that made everyone feel dismissed and inspected at once.
2. He gave me one haughty look over his glasses and went back to his laptop.
Proverbs 16:18, King James Bible: "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall." — the word's home turf, and a reminder that it always precedes a comeuppance.
Old French haut = "high" (from Latin altus), so haughty = high-and-mighty, literally.

Same root pays out across the exam: altitude, alto, exalt, hauteur (the noun for this exact manner), and haute cuisine.

Willfully set on your own course; refuses to be steered.
Determined to have your own way; bent on your own course and deaf to advice, warning, or authority.

Compare the neighbours: obstinate and stubborn are about refusing to move — you dig in. Headstrong is the opposite kind of failure: plenty of movement, no steering. The headstrong person charges ahead on their own judgement while everyone shouts from behind. It's most often aimed at the young and spirited — a headstrong daughter, a headstrong young officer — and it carries a flicker of grudging admiration that pigheaded never does.
⚠️ headstrong ≠ headlong.
- headstrong = self-willed — you won't be told
- headlong = reckless haste — you rush in without looking

A headstrong man ignores the advice; a headlong one never waits to hear it.
Not a wall — a runaway horse. A stubborn horse won't move; a headstrong one won't be steered.
The word is about ungovernable forward motion, not immovability — which is why the natural verbs around it are rein in, curb, and break.
1. Against the counsel of every adviser in the room, the headstrong young king marched his army north before the thaw.
2. She's headstrong — tell her not to do something and that's basically a dare.
Shakespeare, The Taming of the Shrew — Petruchio on Katherina: "thus I'll curb her mad and headstrong humour." Note the verb he reaches for: curb, which is literally a strap on a horse's bridle.
