column2:
Leaning toward something; disposed but not committed.
Having a tendency, leaning, or willingness toward something (inclined to agree); also, literally sloping (an inclined plane).

On the GRE it's almost always the mental sense — and it is a hedge. Saying "I'm inclined to think so" commits you to a lean, not a position; the exit door stays open, which is why it's the language of committees and diplomats. Set it against its neighbours: determined or bent on is locked in, prone and apt describe a statistical tendency usually toward something bad (prone to error). Inclined is mild, neutral, and voluntary — a preference, not a flaw and not a decision.
An incline is a slope, not a cliff — being inclined is a tilt of the mind, not a fall into commitment.
The word keeps its physical sense intact: you're tipped in one direction, but nothing has been settled.
1. The board is inclined to approve the merger, though it has asked for one further round of figures.
2. I'm inclined to say yes, but let me sleep on it.
Everyday English already uses the exact GRE sense in "musically inclined," "mathematically inclined" — someone whose natural bent tips that way, without any claim that they've trained for it.
Latin inclinare = "to lean toward" (in- + clinare, to bend or lean).

That root pays off across the exam: recline (lean back), decline (lean away, or downward), proclivity (a leaning-forward — a natural tendency), declivity / acclivity (a downward / upward slope), and even climate (Greek klima, the "slope" of the earth toward the sun).

Out of place; jarringly mismatched with its surroundings.
Out of place; clashing with what surrounds it. A thing is incongruous when it doesn't match its setting, its company, or the rest of itself.

The word describes a mismatch, not a fault. Inappropriate accuses; incongruous just registers the clash — a tuxedo at a beach barbecue, a nursery rhyme sung at a funeral. Very often the effect is faintly comic, and writers use it exactly for that: the detail that refuses to blend in. Note it needs a context to clash with — nothing is incongruous on its own.
incongruous vs. incongruent. Incongruous = doesn't fit the surroundings (the everyday, literary word). Incongruent = doesn't correspond or align, used technically — congruent triangles, incongruent data sets. If you're describing a scene, you want incongruous.
in-GROUP-ous — it isn't in the group.
The middle of the word sounds like group, and that's precisely the complaint: the thing sits there without belonging to the set around it.
1. A glass tower rose behind the abbey, incongruous among four centuries of grey stone.
2. He turned up to the funeral in neon trainers — a bit incongruous, but nobody said anything.
Latin congruere = "to come together, to agree." Add in- ("not") and you get things that refuse to come together. Same root gives congruent (shapes that agree exactly) and congruity — so incongruous is literally not-agreeing-with.

Impossible to argue against; proven beyond any dispute.
So firmly established that it cannot be argued against — the case against it simply has nowhere to stand.

This is the top of the certainty scale, and it is a claim about evidence, not about feelings. Undeniable can describe a mood or a charm; incontrovertible wants facts, data, documents, DNA. It's also heavy, formal machinery — courtroom, editorial, scientific paper — so in casual speech it lands as either very serious or slightly pompous. Note too that it grades the proof, not the importance: a fact can be incontrovertible and utterly trivial.
⚠️ incontrovertible ≠ uncontroversial.
- incontrovertible = the evidence is so strong that argument is impossible
- uncontroversial = nobody happens to be arguing about it

A dull, uncontroversial claim may rest on nothing at all; an incontrovertible one can still start a fight.
incontrovertible ______ — the blank is nearly always evidence, proof, or fact. Never opinion.
The word rates how checkable something is, so it only attaches to things that could, in principle, be checked.
1. The tribunal found the documentary record incontrovertible: the orders had been signed a full week before the raid.
2. Look, the timestamps are right there — that's incontrovertible, mate, stop arguing.
Courtroom staple: the closing-argument line "the evidence is incontrovertible" is the prosecutor's move in roughly every legal drama — and in real filings too.
Latin contrā (against) + vertere (to turn) → controvert, "to turn an argument against." Slap in- on the front and nothing can be turned against it.

vertere is one of the best roots to own for the GRE: convert, divert, invert, avert, subvert, revert, versatile, adverse, controversy.

Unable to believe it — visible, open disbelief.
Unwilling or unable to believe something — and showing it.

This word lives on a face, not on a fact. An incredible story provokes an incredulous listener: raised eyebrows, flat "you're joking," the pause before the laugh. It's stronger than skeptical (which is a considered stance, often habitual) and lighter than dismissive — the incredulous person hasn't decided you're lying, they just can't get the claim to go down. Note the tell: things are almost never incredulous; people, looks, tones and stares are.
⚠️ incredulous ≠ credulous.
- credulous = believes too easily — gullible, a soft touch
- incredulous = won't believe at all — the raised eyebrow

The conman needs a credulous mark; he fears an incredulous one.
The story is incredible; the face is incredulous.
-ible endings describe the thing being judged, while -ulous joins jealous, zealous, querulous as a word for how a person is reacting.
1. The witness's account was met with incredulous silence from the bench.
2. He gave me this incredulous look, like — you drove four hours for a sandwich?
Caravaggio's famous painting "The Incredulity of Saint Thomas" — Doubting Thomas, refusing to believe until he can put his finger in the wound. That's the word in one image: not deceit, just a man who cannot accept what he's being told.
Latin crēdere = "to believe" + in- (not). One of the highest-yield roots on the exam: credible (believable), credence (belief granted), credentials (things that make you believable), creed and credo (what one believes), credit (belief in your ability to pay), credulous (believing too readily).

Improper — a breach of good manners, not of morals.
Not in keeping with good taste or propriety; socially improper, unbecoming, in breach of decorum.

The offence is against manners, not morals. An indecorous remark at a funeral is one that was too jolly, too loud, too familiar — nobody was harmed, the occasion was. The word also carries a whiff of the speaker's own primness: it's the vocabulary of etiquette columns, obituaries and disapproving aunts, so it often sounds gently arch rather than genuinely outraged.
indecorous ≠ indecent.
- indecorous = bad manners — wrong for the occasion
- indecent = bad morals — obscene, offensive

Dancing on the table at a wake is indecorous. Doing it without trousers is indecent.
In-DECOR-ous — your behaviour doesn't match the decor.
The word literally has decor sitting inside it: the room, the occasion, the dress code all set a tone, and you clashed with it.
1. The ambassador's laughter during the minute's silence was widely reported as indecorous, though no one dared call it worse.
2. Texting your ex from the wedding reception is a bit indecorous, mate.
Latin decorus = "seemly, fitting", from decēre, "to be becoming." One root, a whole cluster: decorum (the standard you breached), decor (what suits a room), decorate, decorous — and decent, which started life meaning "appropriate" before it drifted toward morality. That drift is exactly why indecorous and indecent now part company.

Tireless; impossible to wear down over long effort.
Incapable of being tired out — able to keep going at something long after everyone else has flagged.

This is a compliment, and a fairly grand one. Tireless is plain description; indefatigable is admiration, usually for sustained effort over months or years rather than one long night — an indefatigable campaigner, researcher, advocate, fundraiser. Note what it isn't: not strength, not speed, not talent. It's stamina of will. It also carries a faint edge of "this person will not let the matter drop," so it can be used dryly about someone whose persistence you find exhausting.
in-de-FATIGUE-able — the word fatigue is sitting right there in the middle, wearing a hat and a tail.
Strip the in- and the -able and you're left with fatigue: not-able-to-be-fatigued.
1. For forty years she was the indefatigable advocate of a cause almost no one else thought worth defending.
2. He's indefatigable — three flights, two time zones, and he still turned up to the 9am asking questions.
The Royal Navy has kept an HMS Indefatigable on the books since 1784 — Britain names warships for the quality it wants them to have (Indomitable, Invincible, Dreadnought): the ship that cannot be worn down.
Latin fatigāre = "to tire out." Add in- ("not") and -able: not tire-out-able.

Same root gives you fatigue (tiredness — and metal fatigue, where the metal itself gets worn out) and army fatigues, originally the clothes worn for tiring menial work.

Having no fixed end, limit, or precise form.
Not fixed or limited — with no stated end, boundary, or precise form. Two flavours: of time ("an indefinite postponement" — no return date given), and of outline ("an indefinite shape on the horizon" — blurry, unspecified).

The word doesn't claim endlessness; it claims the limit was never set. A contract suspended indefinitely may resume next week — nobody has said. That's why it carries a faint chill in official language: "detained indefinitely," "on indefinite leave." The speaker isn't promising forever, they're refusing to promise anything.
⚠️ indefinite ≠ infinite.
- indefinite = the limit is undeclared
- infinite = there is no limit

An indefinite delay might end on Tuesday. An infinite one never ends.
in + DEFINE + it — nobody has defined it.
Hearing "define" inside the word keeps you on unspecified rather than unending — the boundary exists, it just hasn't been drawn.
1. The tribunal adjourned for an indefinite period, offering the families no date to hold on to.
2. They said the shop's shut indefinitely, which probably means it's shut for good.
Grammar class: a and an are the indefinite articles — "a dog" doesn't specify which dog, while the (definite) pins it down. Same logic, every sentence you speak.
Latin finis = "end, boundary." To define something is to set bounds around it; add in- ("not") and you get the unbounded, unpinned thing.

That root pays out across the exam: finite, infinite, finish, final, confine, definitive.

A formal criminal charge; or damning evidence of failure.
Legal: a formal written charge accusing someone of a serious crime, handed down by a grand jury.
General: a fact, result, or statement that stands as damning evidence against something — "the report is an indictment of the whole system."

An indictment is an accusation, not a conviction: it opens the case, it doesn't close it. The general sense keeps that courtroom weight — calling something an indictment doesn't merely criticise it, it presents it as proof of guilt. So criticism is an opinion offered; an indictment is a charge that the evidence itself makes. Almost always preceded by damning, stinging, or searing.
Indictment opens the trial; verdict closes it — same dict, opposite ends.
Both are things spoken (dict) by the court, but the indictment is only the charge going in, while the verdict is the truth (ver) coming out.
1. A grand jury returned a twelve-count indictment against the former treasurer, though he was later acquitted on every charge.
2. That the hospital ran out of beds in week one is a pretty damning indictment of the planning, isn't it?
Journalism runs on the phrase "a damning indictment of..." — you'll see it in a news headline or op-ed most weeks, always about a failing system rather than a person in the dock.
Latin dicere / dictāre = "to say, to proclaim"; in-dictāre = to proclaim against. The silent c was stuffed back in by medieval scribes to make the word look properly Latin — same vanity that gave debt its silent b.

That root is a GRE workhorse: verdict (truth-said), edict, dictate, contradict, jurisdiction, benediction, malediction, dictum.

column2:
Angry at being wronged; offended in your dignity.
Angry — but specifically angry at something you consider unjust, unfair, or insulting to you. Noun: indignation.

Furious is about heat; indignant is about standing on your rights. The indignant person isn't just upset, they're claiming the moral high ground: how dare you. It carries a whiff of wounded dignity, which is why it works both ways — sympathetic when the grievance is real, faintly comic when it isn't (the indignant customer who was in fact in the wrong queue).
⚠️ indignant ≠ indigent.
- indignant = offended, morally angry
- indigent = desperately poor

One letter, two unrelated words. An indigent man may well be indignant, but they are not the same claim.
in-DIGN-ant — someone stepped on your DIGNITY.
The word wears its own explanation: this is anger on behalf of your worth, not just bad temper.
1. The minister was indignant at the suggestion that the report had been altered before publication.
2. She sent back an indignant three-line email: she had paid, and she had the receipt.
Latin in- (not) + dignus (worthy) → unworthy — an indignity is treatment beneath you, and indignation is the reaction to it.

Dignus is a generous root: dignity, dignify, deign (condescend to think someone worthy), disdain (think them un-worthy), indignity.

🚫 Not indigent — that's Latin indigere, "to lack." Different root entirely.

Making no distinctions; hitting or taking everything alike.
Making no distinctions — choosing at random, or not choosing at all; sweeping up the innocent with the guilty, the good with the junk.

The word carries blame. Random is neutral, even mathematical; indiscriminate implies someone who should have sorted and didn't. That failure is the whole accusation — an indiscriminate reader devours anything with pages, indiscriminate praise is worthless because it's handed to everyone, and indiscriminate shelling is a war crime precisely because it doesn't ask who's standing there. Strongest in contexts of harm, but usable lightly for anyone with no filter.
indiscriminate ≠ indiscreet. Indiscriminate = makes no distinctions (takes everything). Indiscreet = keeps no secrets (says everything). Both are lapses of judgement, but one is a bad filter on intake, the other a bad filter on output.
A discriminating palate picks; an indiscriminate one eats whatever's on the table.
Strip the in- and you get the connoisseur who sorts carefully — so indiscriminate is the refusal, or inability, to sort at all.
1. The tribunal condemned the indiscriminate shelling of the district, which spared neither hospital nor school.
2. He's an indiscriminate swiper — right on everyone, then acts surprised when the dates go badly.
The standing phrase in war reporting and UN statements: "indiscriminate attacks on civilians." It's the technical charge — the weapon couldn't distinguish a soldier from a child, and was fired anyway.
Latin cernere = "to sift, to separate" — the grain from the chaff. Add dis- (apart) and you get discernere: to tell one thing from another.

That sieve runs through a whole family: discern (tell apart), discrete (separate, distinct), secret (se-cernere, sifted aside), concern, certain. So indiscriminate is literally unsifted — everything left in the pile together.

Absolutely necessary — remove it and the whole thing stops.
Absolutely necessary — something (or someone) you cannot do without.

The test is subtraction, not praise: essential describes what belongs to a thing's nature, vital is dramatic and life-or-death, but indispensable means take it away and the whole operation stops working. It's also an absolute — things aren't "quite" indispensable — which is why applying it to a person is the highest possible compliment, and why it's so often said sarcastically about people who think they are.

Note the spelling: -able, never -ible.
Strip the in- and you get dispense — what you can hand out and be rid of.
A pharmacy dispenses pills across the counter and lets them go; the indispensable is the one thing that never leaves the building.
1. Clean water and a functioning postal service were, in the committee's view, indispensable to any plan for the region.
2. She's the only one who knows how the billing system actually works — she's basically indispensable.
The line attributed to Charles de Gaulle: "The graveyards are full of indispensable men." — the standard deflation of anyone who thinks the place can't run without them.
From Latin dispensare, "to weigh out, pay out" — built on pendere, "to weigh, to hang." A church dispensation was originally a weighing-up that released you from an obligation; something dispensable can likewise be let go.

That root pays out widely: pending, pendulum, ponder (weigh in the mind), compensate, stipend, pensive.

Habitually lazy; averse to any exertion.
Habitually averse to exertion — lazy as a settled disposition rather than a single lapse.

Lazy is a blunt everyday accusation; indolent is the drawing-room version — cooler, more formal, and it describes a temperament, not a bad afternoon. It also carries a whiff of comfort and ease: the indolent man isn't struggling against sloth, he's perfectly content. Writers use it half-admiringly of heat, luxury and long summers (an indolent stretch by the pool), which slothful — with its sin-and-sermon weight — never allows.

Medicine keeps a second sense: an indolent tumour or ulcer is slow-growing and causing little pain.
⚠️ indolent ≠ insolent.
- indolent = won't get up
- insolent = mouths off when he does

One syllable apart, opposite vices: indolence is doing nothing, insolence is disrespect.
In-dolent = no pain — he won't take pains, and he feels none about it.
The Latin dolor ("pain") sits inside the word, which is why indolence is lazy without guilt — and why a doctor's "indolent" growth is the painless, slow one.
1. Two generations of indolent heirs had spent the fortune without once adding to it.
2. He's not tired, he's just indolent — the man has never voluntarily stood up.
Oncologists say it every day: indolent lymphoma — the slow, quiet kind you monitor rather than attack. Same idea as the lazy heir, just applied to cells.
Latin in- (not) + dolēre (to feel pain, to grieve) → indolens, "feeling no pain." Originally medical; the "lazy" sense came from not taking pains.

That root pays out elsewhere: condolence (grieving with you), doleful, dolorous, and the name Dolores (Our Lady of Sorrows).

To lead someone into doing something; to bring about.
1. To lead someone into doing something — usually by offering them something. 2. To bring about or cause a state or process (induce sleep, induce vomiting, induce labour). 3. In logic: to infer a general rule from particular cases.

Force compels and orders command; induce works sideways. The person still walks in on their own feet — but the path was laid for them. That's why the noun is inducement: money, a discount, a promise, a threat sanded down into an offer.

In the causing sense it carries a whiff of the artificial. A drug induces sleep; a doctor induces labour. The outcome wouldn't have come on its own — or not yet.
induce ≠ deduce. Both are ducere, but they run opposite ways: induce reasons up from particular cases to a general rule (every swan I've seen is white → swans are white); deduce reasons down from the rule to the case. Induction can be wrong; valid deduction can't.
You can't induce anyone without an induce-ment — the carrot is built into the word.
Nobody is forced by an inducement; they're offered one, and then they choose exactly what you wanted.
1. The treaty's tax concessions were designed to induce foreign manufacturers to build their plants inland rather than at the ports.
2. No amount of free pizza could induce me to sit through another three-hour all-hands.
Induced labour — when a birth won't start on its own, the hospital starts it. Everyday proof that induce means "make it happen that wouldn't have, or not yet."
Latin in- ("in") + dūcere ("to lead") — literally lead in.

-duc- is one of the highest-yield roots on the GRE: conduct (lead together), produce (lead forth), reduce (lead back), seduce (lead astray), abduct (lead away), educate (lead out), aqueduct (leads water). Spot -duc- and you're looking at leading.

Hardworking and steadily productive.
Hardworking in a steady, energetic, productive way — someone who is always at it and has the output to show for it.

Compare the neighbours: diligent stresses care and attention to detail, assiduous stresses stubborn persistence, industrious stresses sheer productive activity — work getting done, visibly and continuously. It is always praise, but praise for effort rather than brilliance, which is why it can land as a consolation prize: the industrious student is the one who grinds, not the one who dazzles.
⚠️ industrious ≠ industrial.
- industrious = a person who works hard
- industrial = of factories, manufacturing, heavy production

An industrious worker; an industrial estate. Never the reverse.
An industrious person is a one-man industry — always something in production.
The word literally has industry inside it, and the point is output: not just trying hard, but steadily turning out work.
1. Over three industrious decades she built a modest practice into the largest firm in the county.
2. He's not the cleverest on the team, but he's dead industrious — first one in, last one out.
It's the classic school-report word: "a quiet, industrious pupil" — teacher code for works hard, isn't a star. That double edge is the whole flavour of the word.
Latin industria = "diligence, purposeful activity."

The useful bit: industry originally meant hard work, not factories — that older sense survives fossilised in industrious. Learn it that way and industrious vs industrial stops being confusing.

Impossible to escape, no matter how hard you struggle.
Impossible to escape or avoid; certain to happen however hard you fight it.

Inevitable is the everyday word and can be cheerful — an inevitable promotion, an inevitable sequel. Ineluctable is the high-literary cousin, and it carries the sense of a struggle already lost: the thing is closing in, you've tried, it's coming anyway. Death, decay, consequences, fate. Use it about tax deadlines and you sound like you're being funny — which is one way people do use it.
⚠️ ineluctable ≠ ineffable. Same shape, different word: ineffable = too great to be put into words (ineffable joy). Ineluctable = impossible to escape (ineluctable decline).
in-e-LUCK-table — no amount of luck gets you off this table.
The stressed syllable literally sounds like luck, and luck is exactly what won't save you.
1. The report traced the ineluctable decline of the empire from its first unpaid legion to its last.
2. Stay up till 3 a.m. and the ineluctable result is a wasted Tuesday.
Joyce opens the Proteus chapter of Ulysses with "Ineluctable modality of the visible" — Stephen shutting his eyes on the beach and finding the world still there. It's the most quoted appearance the word has.
Latin luctārī = "to wrestle." Ē-luctārī is to wrestle your way out of something; put in- on the front and you can't.

That root pays off elsewhere: reluctant is re- + luctārī — someone wrestling back against being made to do it. Not shy, not lazy: resisting.

Clumsily incompetent — bad at it in an embarrassing way.
Lacking skill or competence — and bungling it visibly.

Unskilled is a neutral fact about training; inept is a verdict. It says the person handled the thing badly, awkwardly, and slightly embarrassingly — the botched handshake, the fumbled negotiation, the sentence that lands wrong. It carries a wince, and often a whiff of contempt from the speaker. Incompetent accuses someone of being unfit for the job; inept accuses them of being clumsy at it, which stings in a smaller, more personal way.
inept ≠ inapt.
- inept = the person is clumsy, unskilled
- inapt = the thing is unsuitable, badly chosen

An inept speaker gives an inapt analogy.
in-ept is apt that has already fumbled its own spelling — a-p-t trips and comes up e-p-t.
The word doesn't just mean "not apt," it enacts the clumsiness, which is exactly the flavour inept adds over plain "unskilled."
1. The commission's report was a monument to inept administration: three years of meetings, and not one decision anybody could act on.
2. He's a good guy, but he's completely inept in a kitchen — he set fire to pasta.
The phrase you've heard a hundred times is "socially inept" — the standard collocation, used of someone who is fine on paper and a disaster in a room. If you can only remember one pairing, remember that one.
Latin aptus = "fitted, suited" → ineptus, "not fitted."

One root, a free set of words: apt (fitting), aptitude (natural fit for something), adapt (make it fit), and — via French — attitude (originally a figure's fitting posture).

column2:
An awkward or ill-chosen phrase; a polite word for a blunder.
An awkward, ill-chosen or inappropriate expression — a phrase that lands badly. More broadly, any small unfortunate feature of a thing, or (older, rarer) plain unhappiness.

Register does the work: this is the reviewer's and the diplomat's word. Calling a sentence clumsy is an insult; calling it an infelicity is a courtesy — you concede the writer meant well and simply picked the wrong words. It's mild, countable ("a few infelicities of style"), and almost always about phrasing rather than fact: an infelicity isn't an error, it's a tactless or graceless way of putting a thing.
⚠️ infelicity ≠ infidelity. One is a badly chosen phrase; the other is a badly chosen partner. Read the middle syllables — -lic- (Latin felix, happy) vs -del- (fides, faith).
An infelicity is a blunder in a bow tie.
Same mistake, dressed politely — which is exactly why critics and diplomats reach for the word.
1. The translation is accurate enough, but a scattering of infelicities — "he ambulated to the door" — betrays a tin ear.
2. The apology was fine apart from one infelicity: he called her "the complainant" three times.
Felix Felicis, the liquid-luck potion in Harry Potter, is the root doubled up — felix = lucky, happy. Put in- on the front and you have the opposite: the unlucky, unhappy choice of words.
Latin felix, felicis = "happy, lucky, fruitful" + the negating in-.

The whole family is cheerful except this one: felicity (bliss), felicitous (aptly, happily phrased), felicitations (congratulations), and the name Felix — "the lucky one."

Note that felicitous already means well-put, not merely happy — so infelicitous is the natural adjective for a phrase that misses.

To tell — or, on the GRE, to pervade and shape.
Everyday sense: to tell someone something — pass on facts.

The sense the GRE actually tests: to pervade and give shape to something from the inside. A conviction, an experience, a tradition informs a body of work — it isn't mentioned in it, it's the thing quietly determining its form.

The difference is direction. Information is handed over, external and detachable; when grief informs a painter's late canvases, it's soaked in, inseparable, visible in every choice. So "a deep suspicion of authority informs his journalism" is not saying anyone told him anything. Note the third sense too — inform on/against someone is to snitch, and that one is squarely negative.
FORM is sitting right there in the middle of it — to in-form is to put form into a thing.
Whatever informs a work is the invisible mould it was shaped in, not a message delivered to it.
1. A stubborn empiricism informs every argument in the book, even where the author never names it.
2. Three years of waiting tables informs how much I tip, honestly.
Corporate and design-speak leans on exactly this sense all day: "the user research informs the redesign," "these findings will inform our strategy." Nobody was told anything — it means shaped the outcome.
Latin informāre = "to give form to, to shape" — in- (into) + forma (form). The "tell someone" meaning is the later, watered-down one; shaping came first.

Same root, free of charge: form, conform (shape yourself to fit), reform (shape again), deform, formation, formula, format.

Cleverly inventive; strikingly smart in design or contrivance.
Strikingly clever and inventive — said of a solution, device, plan, or of the mind that devises them.

The praise is for contrivance, not wisdom or depth. Brilliant admires raw intellectual power; creative admires originality; ingenious admires the neat trick — the unexpected workaround, the elegant bit of engineering that makes you say how did you think of that? It attaches happily to things as well as people (an ingenious hinge, an ingenious loophole), and it survives moral doubt: an excuse, a scam, or a forgery can all be ingenious, and calling it so is still a compliment to the craft.
ingenious ≠ ingenuous.
- ingenious = cleverly inventive
- ingenuous = innocent, frank, unguarded

An ingenious child builds a trap out of coat hangers; an ingenuous child tells you exactly where it is.
Ingenious has an ENGINE in it — same word, same root; an ingenious mind is an idea engine.
Engines are contraptions, and ingenious is precisely the praise you give a clever contraption or the person who rigged it.
1. The dam's fish ladder is an ingenious piece of design, coaxing salmon upstream by exploiting the very current that blocks them.
2. She found an ingenious way to fit a month's clothes into a carry-on — vacuum bags and a lot of nerve.
Cervantes' novel is El ingenioso hidalgo Don Quijote — "The Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote". The title is doing sly work: his ingenuity is real, and it is aimed entirely at windmills.
Latin ingenium = "inborn talent, natural capacity" (in- "in" + gignere "to beget") — the same root behind genius, ingenuity, congenital.

It also gives engine: a medieval engin was any ingenious contrivance, usually a siege machine. Engine and ingenious are the same word wearing different clothes.

🚫 Not the root of ingenuous. That's Latin ingenuus, "free-born" — hence frank, unspoilt, the manner of someone with nothing to hide.

Innocently open and frank, from inexperience rather than courage.
Innocently frank; open and trusting because you have never learned to be otherwise.

An ingenuous person says the true thing without calculating what it costs them. Candid is a choice; ingenuous is a condition — it comes from inexperience, not courage. That's why the word runs warm but slightly condescending: the speaker is charmed and also faintly aware that this person will be eaten alive. Push it further and you're at naive; pull it back toward polish and you lose it entirely.
ingenuous ≠ ingenious. One letter, opposite compliments: ingenuous = guilelessly open; ingenious = cleverly inventive. Calling a con artist's scheme "ingenuous" says he's a sweet innocent, which is precisely what he isn't.
Hidden inside in-genu-ous is genuine — no filter, no angle.
And the sneaky cousin disingenuous is someone faking that openness, which fixes both words at once.
1. Her ingenuous account of the meeting, offered without a trace of self-protection, damaged her far more than a lie would have.
2. He asked what her salary was — not rude, just ingenuous enough to think it was a normal question.
The ingénue — the stock innocent-young-woman role in theatre and film (Audrey Hepburn built a career on it). Same root, same quality: wide-eyed and unguarded.
Latin ingenuus = "native-born, freeborn" — from in- (in) + gignere (to beget). A freeborn Roman had no need to flatter or dissemble, so "freeborn" slid into "frank, unguarded."

The gen- root is everywhere: genuine, genus, generate, congenital, indigenous — and yes, ingenious too (Latin ingenium, inborn talent). Same family, diverged completely: one inherits honesty, the other inherits brains.

Fixed so deep by long habit it can't be removed.
Fixed so deeply — into a habit, belief, or surface — that it can't be scrubbed out. Used of prejudices, customs, reflexes, and literal dirt.

The word carries time and repetition: nothing is ingrained overnight. A belief you merely hold is a belief; one you've held so long it moves your hands before your mind catches up is ingrained. It also carries resistance — you say "ingrained" precisely when you're conceding how hard the thing will be to shift, which is why it so often turns up next to prejudice, habit, corruption, and grime.
⚠️ ingrained ≠ innate.
- innate = there from birth, in the genes
- ingrained = worked in later, by years of repetition

An ingrained habit was learned. That's the whole distinction the GRE is testing.
In the grain — not on the surface.
Dirt on the surface wipes off; dirt down in the grain of the wood is part of the wood now, and so is an ingrained habit.
1. Reform failed because the corruption was ingrained in the ministry's every procedure, not confined to a few officials.
2. Forty years in the army and he still can't slouch — the posture's ingrained.
Cleaning-product advertising runs on this word: every bathroom spray and washing powder promises to lift ingrained dirt and grime — the stuff that's got into the surface, not sitting on it.
From "dyed in grain" — cloth coloured right through the fibre with kermes dye instead of tinted on the outside. The dye was in the grain, so it never washed out.

Behind it is Latin granum = "grain, seed," which pays out elsewhere: granule, granary, garner, and — via pomegranate, the seed-packed fruit — grenade, a bomb named for looking like one.

column2:
Hold back, restrain, or dampen — not outright forbid.
To hold back, restrain, or slow down — a person's impulse, a chemical reaction, a plant's growth, your own tongue.

The key is that inhibiting is a drag, not a wall. It dampens and restrains; the thing still happens, just less or later. Cold weather inhibits growth — it doesn't abolish it. And the restraint is often internal: the inhibited person isn't forbidden from speaking, they just can't get the words out. That's why the noun inhibitions means shyness and self-restraint, not rules imposed from above.
⚠️ inhibit ≠ prohibit.
- inhibit = hinder, dampen — no authority required, no total stop
- prohibit = forbid by rule — an authority, and an absolute ban

Fear inhibited her from applying; the rules prohibited her from applying.
Inhibited people hold it in; prohibited things are kept out.
Inhibition is a brake applied from inside, while prohibition is a barrier put up from outside.
1. Low soil temperatures inhibit germination, delaying the crop by several weeks.
2. Two drinks in, whatever was inhibiting him wore off and he wouldn't stop talking.
The everyday phrase "alcohol lowers your inhibitions" — nobody means it removes a ban; it means it releases the internal brake.
Latin habēre = "to have, to hold" + in- (in): to hold in.

The whole family is built on holding: exhibit (hold out for viewing), prohibit (hold away — forbid), habit (what holds you), habitat (where something holds itself), ability (having the hold on a skill).

🚫 Not inhabit. That's Latin habitāre, "to dwell" — one letter apart, opposite job.

Harmful to; working against something's survival or success.
Harmful to; working against. Also, more rarely, openly hostile (an inimical stare).

On the GRE it almost always arrives in the first sense and almost always with to: conditions inimical to growth, a climate inimical to free speech. That matters, because the harm is usually structural, not personal — a policy, a temperature, a bureaucracy. Nothing is angry at you; the conditions simply make thriving impossible. Compare hostile, which needs a hater, and detrimental, which is bloodlessly neutral about damage. Inimical sits between: no hater, but a real sense of opposition — the environment is set against the thing.
⚠️ inimical ≠ inimitable.
- inimical = harmful to — an insult to whatever it touches
- inimitable (ih-NIM-ih-tuh-buhl) = impossible to copy — high praise

One syllable apart, opposite verdicts: his inimitable style is a compliment; a style inimical to clarity is not.
Strip the in- and you're left with amical — friendly. Inimical = un-friendly conditions, not an unfriendly person.
The prefix flips amicable into its opposite, and the "conditions" half is what keeps you from mixing it up with plain personal hostility.
1. The committee found the merger inimical to competition in every market it examined.
2. Open-plan offices are pretty inimical to getting any actual thinking done.
A regulator's stock phrase: US securities and insurance statutes repeatedly bar conduct "inimical to the public interest." If you ever read a licence revocation, you'll meet the word in its natural habitat.
Latin inimīcus = in- ("not") + amīcus ("friend") — literally "un-friend."

That one root pays out across the exam: enemy (same word, worn down through French), amicable, amity, amiable. Spot amic- and think friend; spot in-amic- and think the opposite of friend.

column2:
Harmless — often suspiciously so, or blandly so.
Harmless — incapable of causing injury or offence.

Harmless is plain description; innocuous almost always arrives with suspicion attached. You reach for it when harm was possible, expected, or later discovered: an innocuous-looking package, an innocuous remark that started the whole fight. It is the word for things that pass inspection.

Its second life is dismissive. Call a novel, a pop album, or a policy proposal innocuous and you mean it is so inoffensive it is boring — nothing in it could hurt you, and nothing in it could move you either.
in-NOC-uous — it can't knock you.
The stressed middle syllable sounds like knock, and the in- cancels it: no knock, no damage — but note that you only say it about something that could have landed a blow.
1. The compound proved innocuous in every trial, though the committee kept testing it for another two years.
2. It was an innocuous question — I genuinely didn't know it would set him off.
Standard vocabulary in security briefings: phishing training warns you about the innocuous-looking attachment or the innocuous-looking link — harmless on the surface, which is the entire point.
Latin in- (not) + nocēre (to harm) — literally "not harming."

Nocēre is worth banking: it gives noxious (harmful), obnoxious (originally exposed to harm, now the harm itself), nuisance, and innocent — someone who has done no harm.

Curious out loud — the kind that asks questions.
Curious — specifically, curious in a way that asks. Where curious is a state of mind, inquisitive is a behaviour: the questions actually come out of your mouth, one after another.

That's what tips it. A child, a scientist and a nosy neighbour can all be inquisitive, and the word leans warm or cold depending on whether the questions are welcome. Praise on a CV ("an inquisitive mind"), mild complaint at a dinner party ("she was rather inquisitive about my salary"). It never reaches the flat rudeness of nosy, but it's the polite word you reach for when nosy is what you mean.
inquisitive ≠ inquisitorial. Inquisitive asks out of interest; inquisitorial interrogates out of suspicion — the tone of the Inquisition, harsh and accusing. A toddler is inquisitive; a hostile cross-examination is inquisitorial.
inQUIZitive — there's a quiz hiding in it, and you're the one being quizzed.
The buried quiz captures the whole nuance: not silent wondering but out-loud questioning, which is delightful for about four questions and then starts to feel like a test.
1. Darwin's genius was less raw brilliance than an inquisitive patience — he would worry at a single earthworm for years.
2. Sorry, I don't mean to be inquisitive, but how much did you actually pay for it?
Job ads and appraisals run on it — "we're looking for an inquisitive mind" is corporate for asks good questions and won't just do what they're told.
Latin quaerere = "to seek, to ask." It pays for itself many times over: query, quest, question, inquire, require, acquire, conquer, exquisite (literally "sought out"), and the GRE favourite perquisite/prerequisite.

Spot quir / quisit / quer / ques in a word and the idea underneath is almost always seeking.

Impossible to read; giving nothing away.
Impossible to read or interpret; giving away nothing under examination.

The word is about resistance to being read, not difficulty in itself. Something obscure is murky; something complex is tangled; something inscrutable presents a perfectly clear surface and still tells you nothing — a blank face, a poker-flat tone, the motives of a god or a market. It's almost always applied to the outside of a mind: expressions, smiles, silences, decisions. Faintly unnerving, and often faintly admiring — the inscrutable person is holding cards you can't see.
in-SCRUT-able — the thing you cannot scrutinise.
The whole word scrutiny is sitting inside it with a not bolted on the front: you may stare as hard as you like and come away with nothing.
1. The chairman listened to the whole proposal with an inscrutable expression, and left without indicating whether he was pleased or appalled.
2. He gave me one of those inscrutable looks — no idea if I was about to be promoted or fired.
The stock adjective for the Mona Lisa's smile — five centuries of critics staring at one face and still not agreeing what it means.
Latin scrutari = "to search through, rummage, examine" — originally what rag-pickers did, sifting through scruta, "junk." Add in- (not) and -able: not able to be rummaged through. Same root gives you scrutiny, scrutinise, scrutineer.

🚫 Not related to scruples. That's Latin scrupulus, "a small sharp stone in your shoe" — a nagging moral qualm. Unscrupulous is about conscience; inscrutable is about visibility.

Harming slowly and secretly; noticed only after the damage.
Doing harm gradually and secretly — the damage advances while it looks harmless, or while nobody is looking at all.

Two things make a thing insidious: it's slow, and it's camouflaged. A mugging isn't insidious; a debt that quietly compounds is. Compare sinister, which advertises menace, and pernicious, which is simply very destructive whether or not it hides. Insidious is the one where the alarm comes too late — you discover it by finding the wreckage. That's why it attaches so naturally to diseases, addictions, propaganda, and slow-rotting workplace cultures.
⚠️ insidious ≠ invidious.
- insidious = harming stealthily
- invidious = provoking resentment or envy (an invidious comparison, an invidious distinction)

Ranking your friends by attractiveness is invidious. Slipping something into their drink is insidious.
Insidious — it's already inside you before you notice it.
The hidden word gets both halves of the meaning: concealment plus the fact that it has already got in and started working.
1. The most insidious propaganda never argues with you; it simply repeats a premise until you stop hearing it as a claim.
2. Sitting all day is insidious — you feel fine for years, then your back gives out at thirty-five.
Insidious (2010), James Wan's horror franchise — the whole premise is a presence that has quietly got inside the house and the child long before anyone realises anything is wrong. The title is doing exactly what the word means.
Latin insidiae = "an ambush" — literally in- (in) + sedēre (to sit). Troops sitting in wait by the roadside. Every part of the modern sense is in that picture: hidden, patient, lethal on contact.

sedēre is a workhorse root: sedentary (sitting), reside, preside, sediment, session, and the GRE favourite assiduous (sitting at a task).

Bland to the point of dullness; flavourless, in food or people.
Without flavour; by extension, without interest, character, or spark.

The word is a sneer. Mild and plain are neutral descriptions; insipid is a verdict — it says the thing should have had flavour and failed to deliver any. It works on soup, on prose, on a melody, on a person, and in every case it implies the critic tasted carefully and found nothing there. Slightly more literary and more withering than boring: you call a lecture boring, you call a novel insipid.
⚠️ insipid ≠ insidious. Both open in-si-, and there the resemblance ends: insipid = flavourless, dull; insidious = creeping and treacherous, harmful by stealth. An insipid remark bores you; an insidious one damages you quietly.
in-SIP-id — take a sip, taste nothing, and say so with a curl of the lip.
The hidden sip fixes the tasting metaphor, and the curled lip fixes the contempt that separates insipid from a neutral word like mild.
1. Reviewers dismissed the novel as an insipid imitation of far braver books.
2. The tea was insipid — basically hot water with ambitions.
Standard wine- and food-critic vocabulary: an insipid wine is one with no acid, no fruit, nothing to say — the polite word for "watery."
Latin in- (not) + sapidus (tasty), from sapere = "to taste" — and, because taste and judgement were one idea to the Romans, also "to be wise."

That double sense pays out across the exam: sapid (full of flavour), savour, savoury, sage, sapient, Homo sapiens — the "wise" ape, literally the one with taste.

Boldly disrespectful, especially toward someone above you.
Openly disrespectful in a bold, contemptuous way — rude with an attitude of superiority behind it.

Rudeness aimed upward. Insolence needs a hierarchy to offend: a servant to a master, a student to a teacher, a private to an officer, a teenager to a parent. The offence isn't the words alone but the refusal to defer — the shrug, the smirk, the tone. And the word is usually chosen by the person being disrespected, which makes it faintly pompous: calling someone insolent announces that you expected deference and didn't get it.
⚠️ insolent ≠ indolent. One letter apart, both GRE regulars: insolent = disrespectful; indolent = lazy. The insolent employee talks back; the indolent one never gets up.
Insolent begins like insult — an insult delivered upward, with a shrug.
Any insult is rude, but the insolent one is aimed at someone who outranks you and expected better.
1. The magistrate found his insolent silence more offensive than any answer he might have given.
2. One more insolent remark like that and you're off the team.
In The Phantom of the Opera, the Phantom's furious line at Raoul — "Insolent boy! This slave of fashion, basking in your glory!" — is the word in its natural habitat: a self-styled superior enraged that an inferior didn't bow.
Latin insolens = in- ("not") + solere ("to be accustomed") — literally not behaving as one is accustomed to. The insolent person breaks the customary deference.

Same root, unexpectedly: obsolete (ob- + solere) — something that has fallen out of the accustomed use.

column2:
Cut off and narrow-minded, like life on a small island.
Literally of an island; on the GRE, almost always the figurative sense: cut off from outside influence, and narrow because of it — interested only in one's own circle, incurious about anything beyond it.

The word attacks range, not intelligence. A brilliant scholar can be insular. It also carries a hint of complacency — the insular don't feel deprived by their isolation; they think their small world is the whole world. Cooler and more clinical than bigoted or provincial: it diagnoses a condition rather than throwing an insult, which is why it survives in serious writing about communities, academic fields and countries.
Insular minds are insulated — nothing from outside gets in.
Insulation isn't hostile, it's just sealed — which is exactly the temperature of the word: not aggression, but a closed system that never lets a foreign idea through.
1. The department had grown insular, citing only its own faculty and dismissing work published anywhere else.
2. Her hometown is lovely but pretty insular — three generations of the same families, and everyone else is a tourist.
Latin insula = "island." An island is land with the world held at arm's length — that's the whole word.

One root, a useful family: isle and isolate (to make into an island), insulate (wrap it off from its surroundings), peninsula (paene "almost" + insula = almost an island), and even insulin — named for the islets of Langerhans, little islands of cells in the pancreas.

column2:
Able to be understood — the meaning gets through.
Able to be understood; comprehensible.

It's a low bar, not a compliment. Lucid praises writing as clear and elegant; intelligible only certifies that the meaning got through at all. That's why it lives mostly in the negative or the grudging — barely intelligible, scarcely intelligible, unintelligible mumbling. Applied to someone's speech, it usually implies a listener was straining.

In philosophy it hardens into a technical sense: the intelligible world is what's grasped by intellect alone, as opposed to the sensible world of what you can see and touch.
⚠️ intelligible ≠ legible.
- legible = the marks on the page can be made out
- intelligible = the meaning can be got

A note can be perfectly legible and still unintelligible — every letter crisp, the sentence nonsense.
Intelligible — you can get the intel out of it.
The information reaches you, which says nothing about whether it was delivered well.
1. His prose becomes intelligible only on a second reading, once the terminology has settled.
2. She was crying so hard that maybe one word in five was intelligible.
Transcripts and closed captions stamp [unintelligible] into the text wherever the audio defeats the transcriber — a court record, a leaked call, a YouTube auto-caption. The tag marks exactly this: sound arrived, meaning didn't.
Latin inter (between) + legere (to pick out, read) → intellegere, "to read between, to discern."

legere is a GRE workhorse: legible, lecture, legend (things to be read), elect and select (pick out), collect, and intellect itself.

Swappable one for the other with no difference in effect.
Able to be swapped one for the other with no loss — either one does the job equally well.

The claim is about function, not identity: two things can differ in look, brand, or wording and still be interchangeable, so long as substituting one changes nothing that matters. Two words are interchangeable when the sentence means the same either way; two bolts are interchangeable when either holds.

Point it at people or creative work and it turns cold: interchangeable candidates, interchangeable pop songs. There it means nothing distinguishes them — and therefore nothing is lost when one replaces another.
The stock phrase is interchangeable parts — so call a person interchangeable and you've just called them a part.
The word's home turf is machinery, which is exactly why aiming it at people carries the sting of "mass-produced, replaceable, no one would notice."
1. In careful usage the two terms are not interchangeable: every forgery is a fake, but not every fake is a forgery.
2. Honestly, half these streaming thrillers are interchangeable — same plot, different actors.
Interchangeable parts is the phrase every history class hangs on the birth of mass production — Eli Whitney's muskets, then Ford's assembly line. The whole industrial revolution rests on parts you don't have to hand-fit.

A go-between standing between two parties.
Noun: a go-between — a person, firm, or thing that stands between two parties and passes something along (messages, money, goods, negotiations).
Adjective: occupying the middle position; intervening.

An intermediary is defined by position, not power. A mediator actively works to settle a dispute; an arbitrator decides it; an intermediary may do nothing more than carry the message across. The word is neutral in law and business — banks, brokers, and agents are intermediaries by trade — but it turns faintly sour whenever the implication is that the middle party is taking a cut for adding nothing, which is why "cut out the intermediary" is a selling point.
⚠️ intermediary ≠ intermediate.
- intermediary = the party in the middle (a broker)
- intermediate = the position in the middle (an intermediate stage, intermediate French)

A broker is an intermediary at an intermediate stage of the deal.
Inter-MEDIA-ry — the media sit in the middle, carrying the message between two sides without being either one.
The word literally has media buried in it, and like the media an intermediary transmits rather than decides.
1. The treaty was negotiated through a Swiss intermediary, since neither government would be seen speaking to the other.
2. Just send it straight to her — I'm not being your intermediary every time you two fall out.
In economics a bank is textbook-labelled a financial intermediary: it doesn't own your money or the borrower's loan, it just sits between savers and borrowers and clips a margin. Every "no middleman" ad is selling disintermediation.
Latin inter (between) + medius (middle) — literally "in the middle of."

Medius is a workhorse root: medium, median, mediate, medieval (the Middle Ages), Mediterranean (the sea in the middle of the earth), and mediocre — literally "halfway up the mountain," i.e. middling.

Endless — so long that it becomes unbearable.
Endless — or rather, so long that it feels endless.

This is a word of complaint, not measurement. Nothing is literally interminable; calling a speech interminable tells you about the listener's suffering, not the clock. Lengthy is neutral, protracted is faintly clinical, but interminable is exasperated — the speaker has been trapped and wants you to know it. It attaches to things you must sit through: meetings, sermons, delays, queues, someone's story about their car.
⚠️ interminable ≠ indeterminable.
- interminable = has no end (endless)
- indeterminable = can't be determined (unknowable, unmeasurable)

An interminable wait is agony; a wait of indeterminable length is merely a mystery.
in-TERMIN-able — it will not terminate, and you desperately want it to.
The buried verb terminate gives you the meaning, and the fact that you're wishing for it gives you the tone of complaint.
1. The trial dragged through an interminable third week of expert testimony, each witness contradicting the last.
2. Her uncle told an interminable story about a fishing trip, and nobody could work out how to escape.
The Terminator is the thing that ends you — same root. An interminable meeting is the one nobody can terminate.
Latin terminus = "boundary, end", plus in- = "not." Literally unable to be ended.

That root is everywhere: terminate, terminal (the end of the line — airport, illness, or cable), terminus, exterminate, and determine (to set the limits of a question, i.e. settle it).

Stopping and starting again at irregular intervals.
Stopping and starting again, over and over, with gaps in between — never sustained for long.

The gaps are what the word is really about. Continuous rain falls all day; intermittent rain stops, teases you outside, then starts again. It also carries no promise of regularity: periodic means you can set your watch by it, intermittent just means it keeps coming back at its own convenience. Faintly exasperating in practice — intermittent power, intermittent signal, intermittent effort — because the thing is neither reliably there nor decently gone.
There's an intermission sitting inside it — same root, same idea: the show stops, then resumes.
An intermission is a gap with more to come, which is exactly what makes something intermittent rather than simply over.
1. The patient reported intermittent chest pain over several months, present for an hour or two and then absent for days.
2. The wifi's been intermittent all morning — two minutes of video call, then nothing.
Intermittent fasting — eat, stop, eat again. The whole diet is named after the gaps.
Latin intermittere = inter- ("between") + mittere ("to send, to let go") — literally to let go in between, i.e. to leave off for a while.

Mittere is one of the great GRE roots: transmit (send across), emit (send out), submit (send under), remit, omit, mission, missile, intermission.

Twisted together; so linked the two can't be separated.
Twisted or wound together — literally, like two vines or strands; figuratively, so closely linked that neither can be understood or dealt with alone.

The figurative sense is the one the GRE cares about. Connected is a line between two separate things; intertwined means the boundary is gone — fates, histories, economies, storylines that you can no longer pull apart cleanly. It's neutral in tone: an intertwined pair can be lovers or hostile neighbours. What it always implies is mutual, inseparable involvement, not mere proximity.
Hidden inside it: inter-TWIN-ed — two things twinned so tightly you can't say where one ends.
The buried twin gives you both halves of the meaning — twoness and inseparability — which is exactly what separates intertwined from plain connected.
1. The economic fortunes of the two nations became so intertwined that neither could impose sanctions without wounding itself.
2. Their friend groups are completely intertwined now — you can't invite one person without inviting eleven.
Every diagram of DNA is this word made literal: two strands of the double helix intertwined, and you can't read one without the other.
inter- (between) + twine, from Old English twīn = "double thread", straight from twā, "two."

That "two" root runs through more of English than you'd guess: twin, twist, twill (two-thread weave), between, and twilight (the "two lights" of dusk).

To hint at something subtly; or deeply private and close.
Verb (the GRE sense): to make something known indirectly — to hint, to suggest without stating.
Adjective: closely personal, private, deeply familiar; also detailed ("an intimate knowledge of the tax code").

The verb is genteel and deliberate. Imply is the neutral logical relation; insinuate is sly and usually nasty; hint is casual. To intimate something is to place it delicately in the air so the other person picks it up — and so that you can deny ever having said it. It belongs to diplomats, board meetings and polite letters: the chairman intimated that he might not seek another term.
State it and you're on record; intimate it and you can still deny it.
Same -ate ending, half the volume — the intimated message was delivered without ever being said.
1. In his resignation letter he intimated, without once naming the minister, that the decision had been taken above his head.
2. She never actually asked me to leave — she just intimated it, about six times, until I got the hint.
Department stores file lingerie under \"Intimates\" — the clothes worn innermost, closest to the skin. That is the root, literally.
Latin intimus = "innermost," the superlative of intus (within) — so an intimate friend is the one furthest inside the circle.

The verb comes from intimāre, "to put inside, to make known" — you get the thing inside the other person's head without putting it out loud.

Same within root: interior, internal, intrinsic, intestine.

Absolutely refusing to compromise or negotiate.
Refusing absolutely to compromise, negotiate, or shift position.

This is stubbornness at the bargaining table. Obstinate describes a temperament; intransigent describes a stance — someone who has been offered terms and will not move an inch. It carries a political, diplomatic weight (unions, parties, peace talks) and usually a note of exasperation from whoever is trying to reach a deal. Occasionally it flips admiring — an intransigent defender of principle — but the default is a complaint.
in- + trans-: he will not cross over — there is no transaction to be had.
The word hides transact, so it isn't general grumpiness — it's the specific refusal to do a deal.
1. Three weeks of mediation collapsed against an intransigent minority that would not concede a single clause.
2. He's intransigent about the seating plan — I've offered him four versions and he just says no.
It's newsroom boilerplate for stalled talks: \"both sides remained intransigent\" is the standard line in reporting on strikes, ceasefires, and budget standoffs.
Latin transigere = "to drive through to a settlement" (trans- across + agere to drive) — the same agere behind agent, agenda, act, exigent. Transaction is a deal driven through; in-transigent is the man who won't.

The modern word arrived via Spanish los intransigentes, the radical faction of 1873 who refused to enter any coalition — which is why it still smells of politics.

column2:
Fearless and steady in the face of danger or the unknown.
Fearless — but specifically unshaken by danger, hardship or the unknown, and staying that way over time.

Brave describes one act; intrepid describes a temperament. It belongs to people who go somewhere difficult and keep going: explorers, war correspondents, mountaineers, whistleblowers. Unlike foolhardy or reckless, it carries no hint of stupidity — the nerve is admired, not scolded. And it's often used with an affectionate half-smile ("our intrepid reporter braved the queue at the DMV"), which no other word in this family does.
Nobody is intrepid sitting on the sofa — the word demands a noun that's going somewhere: intrepid explorer, intrepid reporter, intrepid traveller.
Lock it to the journey and you get the nuance for free: sustained nerve heading into the unknown, not one flash of courage.
1. Shackleton's intrepid crew spent two winters on the ice and lost not a single man.
2. Ten minutes into the hike it started hailing, and our intrepid leader just pulled his hood up and kept walking.
The USS Intrepid, the WWII aircraft carrier now moored on the Hudson as New York's Intrepid Sea, Air & Space Museum — navies name ships for the quality they want in the crew.
Latin in- (not) + trepidus (alarmed, trembling). Literally "not trembling."

That gives you the pair free: trepidation = the trembling, intrepid = the absence of it. If you feel trepidation about the exam, the intrepid candidate next to you does not.

column2:
To fascinate; also, secret scheming or a covert plot.
Verb (1): to arouse someone's curiosity — the offer intrigued her.
Verb (2): to plot secretly — he intrigued against the king.
Noun: covert scheming; a secret plot (or, older, a secret love affair).

One word, two moods. Intrigued is warm, common and slightly flattering — you're leaning in, not merely interested. The noun is shady: intrigue is politics conducted in corridors, alliances made behind a hand. Both senses share one idea — something tangled enough that you can't see the whole of it, which is exactly what pulls you closer.

Note that the GRE prefers the sense you use least: the plotting one.
in-TRIG — a plot tricks you, and a mystery tricks you into leaning in.
The buried trick is literal — the Latin root is tricae, "tricks" — and it covers both halves: the scheming and the fascination.
1. The final years of the court were consumed by intrigue: whispered alliances, forged letters, and two poisonings no one investigated.
2. Okay, I'm intrigued — go on.
Political journalists live on the phrase "palace intrigue" — who's briefing against whom inside the White House. It's the noun in its natural habitat: not a scandal, just endless private manoeuvring.
Latin intricare = "to entangle", from in- + tricae = "tricks, complications, tangles."

That root pays out three ways: intricate (tangled together), extricate (untangle out of), intrigue (tangled up in). A plot and a puzzle are the same shape — a knot you can't yet see through.

Belonging to something by its own nature, not added from outside.
Belonging to a thing by its own nature — part of what it is, not something attached to it from outside.

The word is defined by its opposite. Intrinsic is always doing the work of separating the thing from its wrapping: the intrinsic value of gold vs. its market price, intrinsic motivation vs. a bonus cheque. Where innate is about being born with something and inherent just says "built in," intrinsic implies someone has stripped away the external stuff to see what survives. It's cool, analytical vocabulary — economists, philosophers and psychologists reach for it, and it carries no praise or blame on its own.
⚠️ intrinsic ≠ extrinsic. One prefix apart, exact opposites: intrinsic = from within the thing, extrinsic = from outside it. Money is an extrinsic reward; the joy of the work is intrinsic.
INtrinsic starts with IN — take everything off and what's still in there is intrinsic.
The word only matters when something external has been stripped away — the price tag, the prize, the packaging — leaving whatever the thing owns by itself.
1. The court held that the manuscript's intrinsic worth as a historical document far exceeded whatever it might fetch at auction.
2. Nobody's paying her to fix that code at midnight — she just finds it intrinsically satisfying.
Intrinsic motivation is the standard term in psychology and management for doing something because the thing itself is rewarding — as opposed to the extrinsic bonus, grade or promotion bolted onto it.
Latin intrinsecus = "inwardly, on the inside" (from intra, "within"), against extrinsecus, "outwardly." The whole pair comes over intact: intra- gives you intramural, intravenous, intranet; extra- gives you extraneous, extracurricular, extraterrestrial.

Grasped without conscious reasoning; or so simple it needs no explaining.
Two linked senses. Of a person or judgement: arrived at by immediate insight, without conscious reasoning — you knew before you could say why. Of a thing (an app, a tool, a layout): so well made that you understand it without being taught.

Applied to objects it is straightforward praise — the highest compliment a product review can pay. Applied to a person's reasoning it cuts both ways: it credits the speed of the insight while quietly noting the absence of proof. Compare the neighbours — instinctive is biological and involuntary (blinking, flinching), impulsive is a failure of self-control, while intuitive is genuine understanding that simply skipped the working-out.
Intuitive is what you need no tuition for.
The two words share a root, so let the contrast fix the meaning: if it has to be taught, it wasn't intuitive.
1. Her diagnosis was intuitive rather than deductive — she named the illness on sight, then spent an hour assembling the evidence for it.
2. The new remote is so intuitive my grandmother had it working before I'd found the manual.
It's the single most overused word in product reviews and app-store blurbs — "a clean, intuitive interface." Any time software is praised for needing no instructions, this is the word doing the work.
Latin intuērī = "to look upon, gaze at" — in- (upon) + tuērī (to watch, guard). Intuition is knowledge you get by looking straight at something, with no steps in between.

That root tuērī quietly runs a whole family of watching-over words: tutor (one who watches over you), tuition, tutelage, tutorial.

To flood — or swamp someone with more than they can handle.
To flood — literally, to cover land with water; figuratively, to swamp someone with far more of something than they can deal with.

The force of the word is sheer volume arriving from outside, not difficulty. A hundred routine emails inundate you; one brutal problem doesn't. It usually arrives passive and plural — inundated with calls, requests, applications, complaints — which quietly casts you as the shore and the stuff as the tide. Next to overwhelm (which can be emotional, or done by a single force) inundate is specifically about quantity pouring in.
Hidden in the middle: UND — the same wave as undulate — and you go under it.
Wave after wave is the point: inundation is measured in volume, not in weight.
1. After the levee failed, three thousand acres of farmland were inundated within the hour.
2. I asked one question in the group chat and got inundated with replies — forty messages before lunch.
It's the word flood reporting actually uses: BBC and local news say homes are "inundated" by floodwater, never just "wet" — the literal sense you hear every storm season is the same one behind "inundated with emails."
Latin inundare = "to overflow" — in- (onto) + unda (wave).

That wave washes through a useful family: undulate (move in waves), abundant (ab-undare, overflowing with), redundant (re-undare, overflowing again — surplus to need), and surround.

Spreading in where it isn't wanted; intrusive, encroaching.
Entering and spreading into territory that isn't yours — a plant overrunning a habitat, a tumour pushing past its original tissue, a surgical instrument going inside the body, a question reaching into private life.

The key is that it isn't a single act but a footprint. Intrusive describes a disruption you notice and resent in the moment; invasive implies something has got in and is now taking over. Medically and ecologically it's a technical term with no anger in it ("invasive procedure", "invasive species"); applied to people it's an accusation — invasive questions means you have crossed into ground you had no right to enter.
⚠️ invasive ≠ evasive.
- invasive = coming in where it's not wanted
- evasive = slipping away from what it doesn't want

An evasive witness dodges the invasive question.
Nothing invasive was ever invited — and it doesn't visit, it settles.
The near-rhyme invasive/invited fixes the "unwelcome" half, and "settles" fixes the other half — invasive things spread and stay rather than merely barge in once.
1. Introduced for erosion control, the vine proved catastrophically invasive, smothering forty thousand hectares of native forest within a decade.
2. Asking what I paid for the flat is a bit invasive, mate.
Every hospital brochure advertising "minimally invasive surgery" — keyhole instead of a full incision. The word is being measured there: how far in did they have to go.
Latin invadere = in- ("into") + vadere ("to go"). Literally to go in.

vadere is a quiet GRE workhorse: evade (go out of), pervade (go through — a pervasive smell), wade (go through water), and the whole -vasive family.

To coax someone into something by flattery or trickery.
To win someone over by flattery, charm, or sly deception — to sweet-talk them into doing something they wouldn't otherwise do.

The victim always says yes. Nobody is forced, bribed outright, or threatened; they are talked round, and only later work out they were handled. That makes it slyer than persuade, warmer than dupe, and less pathetic than wheedle — an inveigler is smooth, not whiny.

Watch the grammar, because the GRE does: you inveigle someone into doing something, or inveigle your way into a place you had no business being.
⚠️ inveigle ≠ inveigh.
- inveigle (into) = coax someone with charm
- inveigh (against) = attack something in furious words

He inveighed against the scheme; she inveigled him into joining it.
Inveigle rhymes with bagel — you don't shove anyone through the door, you hold out the bagel and let them follow you in.
The lure does the work, which is exactly why the target walks in willingly and blames themselves afterwards.
1. Having no invitation and no title, he simply inveigled his way past the doorman with a plausible smile and a borrowed name.
2. She somehow inveigled me into helping her move flats on a Sunday, and I still don't know how.
From Old French aveugler, "to blind" — itself from Latin ab oculis, "without eyes." To inveigle someone is literally to blind them, and the flattery is the blindfold.

That oculus (eye) shows up everywhere once you see it: ocular, oculist, binoculars, monocle, inoculate.

column2:
Fixed in a long-standing habit; ingrained by years of practice.
Fixed in a habit by long practice — doing something so persistently, for so long, that it has hardened into character. An inveterate gambler, liar, meddler, tea-drinker.

Two things set it apart from habitual. First, time: the habit has to be old, not just frequent. Second, tone: habitual is clinical, chronic belongs to disease, but inveterate is faintly amused — it's the word a profile writer uses for a charming vice. It can also attach to the habit itself rather than the person (inveterate hostility, an inveterate prejudice), and there it turns cold: too old to be argued away.
⚠️ inveterate ≠ invertebrate. One letter's difference in the eye, none in a hurried read — invertebrate is spineless (jellyfish, or a cowardly official). An inveterate coward has been one for decades; an invertebrate one simply has no backbone.
in-VETERAN-ate — an inveterate liar is a veteran liar: years of service, decorated in the field.
The word literally hides veteran, and both come from Latin vetus, "old" — the habit has seniority.
1. Forty years on the bench had not softened his inveterate distrust of expert witnesses.
2. He's an inveterate snoozer — nine alarms, and he still rolls in at ten past.
Latin vetus, veteris = "old" → inveterātus, "made old, grown chronic."

Same root gives you veteran (an old hand) and veterinary (originally the medicine of veterīnae, old working beasts). If you can see veteran inside it, you have the meaning: aged into the job.

Unfair in a way that stirs up resentment or envy.
Likely to provoke resentment, envy or ill will — and unfair in doing so. An invidious comparison is one that unjustly ranks people; an invidious distinction singles someone out for no defensible reason; an invidious position is one where whatever you choose, somebody ends up aggrieved.

The word points outward, at the effect on other people, not at the speaker's feelings. You are not invidious because you envy someone — you are invidious because your act breeds bad blood. It's a cool, formal word of criticism, favoured by judges, editorials and academics: it says unfair and needlessly divisive without ever raising its voice.
⚠️ invidious ≠ insidious.
- invidious = causing resentment; unfair (Latin videre, to see — the envious look)
- insidious = creeping, sneakily harmful (Latin sedere, to sit — an ambush lying in wait)

An invidious rule offends openly; an insidious disease works quietly.
Invidious doesn't feel envy — it causes it.
The envious person is the victim; the invidious act is what put the sour taste in their mouth.
1. Ranking colleagues by a single crude metric draws invidious distinctions between people doing quite different jobs.
2. Don't ask me to pick a favourite nephew — that's an invidious question and I'm not falling for it.
NVIDIA took its name from Latin invidia — the founders wanted a brand rivals would envy, and the logo came out green. Same root, and the green-with-envy joke is baked in.
Latin invidere = "to look against, to look at with the evil eye" → invidia, envy. From in- (against) + vidēre (to see) — the same vidēre behind video, evident, vision, provide, visa. And invidia, softened through French, is simply our word envy.

To fill with fresh energy; to enliven or revive.
To fill with fresh energy and life — to make someone (or something) feel strong, alert and awake again.

The energy comes from outside: a cold swim, a hard frost, a new manager, a cash injection. You rarely invigorate yourself; something does it to you. Compare encourage, which lifts your morale, and stimulate, which merely gets a reaction — invigorate is bodily and bracing, a physical jolt of vitality. It stretches easily to institutions and economies (reinvigorate the campaign), where it means the same thing: something limp has been given its pulse back.
in-VIG-orate — pour vigour in.
The in- is doing real work: vigour is being poured into you by something else, which is why the word suits cold water and new leadership rather than sheer willpower.
1. The mountain air, thin and freezing, invigorated the party more thoroughly than any breakfast could have.
2. Honestly, one strong coffee and I'm invigorated — ask me again at four o'clock.
The word lives on shower-gel and shampoo bottles — "invigorating mint and tea tree". Ad copy chose it because it promises a physical jolt, not a mood.
Latin vigēre = "to be lively, to thrive" → vigor. Straight to vigour, vigorous, and — same root family — vigil, vigilant (lively = wakeful).

The bonus: vegetable belongs here too, from vegetus, "full of life." Eat your vegetables, be invigorated.
