column2:
Untouched and unbroken, because breaking it was forbidden.
Free from injury, breach, or desecration — kept whole and untouched, usually because something sacred or solemn protects it.

This is not the same as intact, which is merely physical and neutral. An inviolate thing has survived untouched because touching it was forbidden: a vow, a sanctuary, a border, a secret, a right. The word carries reverence — the speaker approves of the thing being untouched. It's high-register and slightly ceremonial; you meet it in constitutions, treaties, and elegies far more than in speech.
inviolate vs. inviolable.
- inviolate = has not been violated (a fact about the present state)
- inviolable = cannot or must not be violated (a claim about its protection)

A treaty can be inviolable in principle and still not remain inviolate in practice.
-ate tells you the state it's in; -able tells you what it's able to withstand.
The suffix does all the work — inviolate reports that nothing has touched it, inviolable insists that nothing may.
1. For forty years the monastery library remained inviolate, its manuscripts unread by any hand outside the order.
2. We had one inviolate rule in that house: nobody talks about work at the dinner table.
Legal boilerplate you can find in a great many American state constitutions: "the right of trial by jury shall remain inviolate." Whenever a right is described as untouchable, this is the word the drafters reach for.
Latin violāre = "to treat with force, to dishonour," from vis = "force." Add the negative in- and you get "not forced open." Same root: violate, violence, violent, violation, inviolable.

🚫 Not violet. The flower is Latin viola, an unrelated word — pure spelling coincidence.

Quick-tempered by nature; permanently easy to set off.
Hot-tempered by disposition — quick to anger, easily provoked, permanently on a short fuse.

The word describes a standing character trait, not a current mood. Irate is what you are for ten minutes after someone dents your car; irascible is what you have been for forty years. It is also a notch more formal and more forgiving than bad-tempered — biographers, obituarists and critics use it for people whose temper is bound up with their talent, so it often arrives attached to admiration: the irascible old genius.
-ible means able to be: irascible = ire-able — always available for anger.
That suffix is the entire distinction: it names a permanent capacity for rage, not a fit of it.
1. Sub-editors learned to approach the irascible editor only after his second coffee, and never with a question.
2. Don't ask Grandad about the parking — he's irascible at the best of times.
It's the standard word in obituaries and profiles for the brilliant-but-difficult figure — the irascible chef, coach, or conductor. Gordon Ramsay in one adjective.
Latin ira = anger — giving ire, irate, irascible.

The buried -sc- is the Latin inchoative: "beginning to." So irascible = liable to start boiling. That same -sc- runs through adolescent (beginning to grow up), convalescent (beginning to get well), incandescent (beginning to glow).

Anger — especially anger you have provoked in someone else.
Anger — specifically anger provoked in someone by an offence.

Rage is loud and out of control; wrath is grand and punitive, the anger of gods and kings; ire is cooler and more formal, the word a newspaper uses. It is almost never anger you're currently feeling — it's anger someone else directs at the person who caused it. Notice it lives in a handful of set phrases: drew the ire of, raised the ire of, sparked the ire of. Short and headline-friendly, which is exactly why journalists reach for it.
You don't have ire — you draw it, the way a bad decision draws a crowd.
The verbs that cling to this word (drew, raised, sparked) tell you ire is always anger you provoked in somebody else, never a mood you're sitting in.
1. The decision to fell the old plane trees drew the ire of a parish that had otherwise agreed on nothing for a decade.
2. One badly worded email and he'd earned the ire of the entire group chat.
Dies Irae — "Day of Wrath", the medieval funeral chant. Its four-note melody is the standard shorthand for doom in film scores: the opening of The Shining, It's a Wonderful Life, Star Wars, The Lion King. If you've heard dread in a soundtrack, you've heard ire.
Latin ira = anger. Same root gives irate (angry right now) and irascible (quick to get angry, a permanent temperament) — a useful trio, since the GRE likes the distinction between a state and a disposition.

Annoying in a small, persistent, wearing way.
Annoying, tedious, wearing — something that grates by being petty and repeated.

Scale matters: infuriating is a fire, irksome is a drip. Irksome things are never dramatic — a form you must re-sign, a colleague who clears his throat, a rule that adds one pointless step. It's also a slightly bookish word, so it carries a note of restraint: the speaker is registering annoyance while making clear they are too civilised to shout about it.
irksome ≠ irascible. Irksome describes a thing that annoys you; irascible describes a person quick to anger. The irascible boss finds everything irksome.
Irk rhymes with quirk — irksome things are irritating quirks, not catastrophes.
The rhyme pins the word to the low end of the annoyance scale: small, recurring, wearing, never enraging.
1. The committee's habit of minuting every trivial decision was irksome, though no member was rude enough to say so.
2. Having to log in twice every single morning is just irksome.
Headline-ese lives on the verb: "Tariff plan irks allies." Newspapers reach for irks because it's four letters and means "annoyed, but not a crisis" — exactly the word's register.

Airtight; admitting no exception, gap, or loophole.
Adj.: so firm it cannot be broken, challenged, or wriggled out of — an ironclad alibi, contract, rule, guarantee.
Noun (historical): a 19th-century warship plated in iron.

The word promises invulnerability to attack, not mere strength. That's why it clings to things people are actively trying to poke holes in: a lawyer's case, a suspect's alibi, a company's warranty. Say a rule is strict and you describe how it's enforced; say it's ironclad and you're saying no exception exists to find. Applied to a person's rules or opinions it can tip cold — unyielding where a little give was wanted.
Iron has no holes — so an ironclad promise has no loophole.
Notice what the word attaches to — alibi, contract, guarantee, rule — always something an opponent is hunting for a gap in.
1. The prosecution's case rested on an ironclad chain of custody that the defence could not disturb.
2. Relax, I've got an ironclad excuse — I was on a flight with no wifi.
Every "ironclad money-back guarantee" in advertising — the phrase exists precisely to tell you there's no small print to hide in.

Unable to decide or stick to a decision; wavering.
Unable to decide, or unable to hold to a decision once made — hesitating, wavering, hanging back at the moment action is required.

Note what it is not: undecided is a temporary state about one question, and carries no blame — you're gathering facts. Irresolute describes the person, not the question. It's a character verdict, and a quietly damning one: the failure isn't lack of information, it's lack of spine. Formal and literary in register — a biographer calls a general irresolute; nobody says it across a dinner table.
⚠️ irresolute ≠ irresolvable.
- irresolute = the person can't decide
- irresolvable = the problem can't be settled
Buried in it is solute — the stuff that dissolves. The irresolute man's resolve dissolves the moment he has to act on it.
He may well have decided; what he cannot do is keep the decision solid under pressure.
1. Three days of irresolute silence from the cabinet cost the army the only crossing it could still defend.
2. He stood at the counter, irresolute, until the guy behind him just ordered for him.
Hamlet is the archetype — a man who spends five acts unable to act. His own diagnosis: "Thus conscience does make cowards of us all."
Latin solvere = "to loosen, release, dissolve"; re-solvere → to loosen a problem apart, and hence to settle it firmly in your mind. That one root pays out widely: solve, solvent, dissolve, absolve (loosen you from guilt), resolution, soluble.

So resolute = your purpose is settled; ir- = it isn't.

column2:
Cheekily disrespectful toward what others hold sacred.
Showing a lack of due respect for things other people treat as sacred — religion, authority, tradition, national heroes, the dead.

The tone is usually cheeky rather than hostile. Disrespectful is a complaint; blasphemous is a charge; irreverent is very often a compliment — the irreverent comedian, the irreverent obituary, the irreverent guide to Shakespeare. It implies wit and nerve, someone who knows exactly which altar they're refusing to kneel at and is enjoying it. Turn it negative only by context: irreverence at a funeral is a failure of manners, not a style.
⚠️ irreverent ≠ irrelevant. Near-identical on the page and a classic misread.
- irreverent = disrespectful, cheeky
- irrelevant = beside the point

An irreverent remark can be devastatingly relevant.
Irreverent won't kneel — but it's grinning, not snarling.
The word marks refusal of reverence, and that refusal is played for wit far more often than for insult.
1. His irreverent history of the monarchy treats four centuries of kings as a sequence of badly behaved houseguests.
2. Don't take her to the memorial — she gets irreverent the second things turn solemn.
Deadpool is the word's home turf — every review reached for irreverent, because the film mocks the sacred cows of superhero cinema while obviously loving them. That affectionate-mockery mix is the word exactly.
Latin verērī = "to stand in awe of, to fear." Add re- (intensive) and you get revere — and the whole family: reverence, reverent, reverend (literally "one who must be revered"), revered. Stick ir- on the front and you have the person who won't.

🚫 Not relevant. That's Latin relevāre, "to raise up, lighten" — same root as elevate, alleviate, lever, levity. Different word entirely.

Travelling from place to place, usually for work.
Adj.: travelling from place to place, especially to do a job. Noun: a person who does so.

The word is bound to work and a route. An itinerant preacher, judge, labourer or salesman moves because the job moves — there's a circuit, a season, a next town. That distinguishes it from nomadic (a whole way of life, often a culture) and from vagrant (no work, no home, and an insult). Itinerant is descriptive and faintly formal — an administrator's word — though it can carry a whiff of low status, since the people it describes usually don't own the place they're working in.
Itinerant is just itinerary with the end knocked off — someone whose life is the itinerary.
The overlap fixes both the spelling and the key nuance: not aimless drifting, but moving along a route, for work.
1. For thirty years he was an itinerant judge, holding court in one county town after another as the assizes required.
2. She's basically an itinerant hairdresser now — three salons, three cities, one very tired car.
American school districts advertise itinerant teachers and itinerant speech therapists — staff who serve four or five schools instead of one. If you ever see the word on a job posting, that's what it means.
Latin iter, itineris = "a journey, a route" — itself from ire, "to go."

That's a productive root: itinerary (the route written down), and from ire more broadly transit, exit, circuit, initial, ambition (originally going around canvassing for votes).

To put something valuable at risk of loss or harm.
To put at risk — to expose something to danger, loss, or failure.

The object is almost always a good you already hold: a career, a ceasefire, funding, a reputation, someone's safety. Endanger points at bodies and lives; jeopardize points at stakes and standing. It also implies your own action did it — you jeopardize a deal by mouthing off, not by bad luck. And the loss is only threatened, never certain: the thing is still salvageable, which is why the word so often arrives as a warning ("you're jeopardizing everything") rather than an obituary.
Hear the prize in jeopar-dize — you can only jeopardize something you've already won.
The word needs an asset in hand: your job, your visa, your lead, your marriage.
1. A single leaked memo jeopardized eighteen months of quiet diplomacy.
2. Don't jeopardize your whole scholarship over one stupid party.
The game show Jeopardy! is named for exactly this: every answer you give puts money you already have on the line.
Old French jeu parti = "a divided game" — a chess position or wager so evenly balanced that either side could win. An even-odds game became an uncertain outcome, and uncertainty became risk.

jeu comes from Latin iocus, "jest" — the same root as joke, jocular, jocose. parti from partire, "to divide" — part, partition, apartment.

Throw overboard; discard something valuable to lighten the load.
To throw cargo overboard to lighten a ship or aircraft in distress — and by extension, to discard something deliberately because carrying it has become too costly.

You don't jettison junk; you jettison things you'd have kept if you could. The word carries pressure behind it — a plan, a policy, a principle, a running mate — dumped because the vehicle won't stay up otherwise. Discard is neutral housekeeping, abandon suggests you walked away and left it lying there; jettison is a decision made under load, and it implies the thing had value and you're still moving afterwards.
Jettison = jet it out — you only jet it out when the ship must fly lighter.
The "jet" is literal (same root as the jet of a jet engine — stuff thrown out the back), and the "must fly lighter" is the nuance: it's a sacrifice, not a clear-out.
1. Facing a hostile committee, the minister quietly jettisoned the very clause he had spent two years defending.
2. Halfway through the move we just jettisoned the sofa — it was never getting up those stairs.
Watch any rocket launch stream: mission control calls out "booster jettison" and "fairing jettison" — expensive hardware thrown away on purpose, because the rest of the vehicle can't reach orbit dragging it.
Latin iactāre = "to throw" (frequentative of iacere). One root, a big family: eject, project, reject, inject, trajectory, conjecture.

The nautical branch is the fun one: jetsam (goods jettisoned, which sink or wash ashore — as opposed to flotsam, wreckage that floats off on its own), a jetty (thrown out into the water), and jet itself (a stream thrown forth).

Cheerful and light-hearted; a poet's word for bright spirits.
Cheerful, light-hearted, in bright and buoyant spirits — of a person, a mood, a morning, a crowd.

This is sunlit cheerfulness, not loud fun. Merry is warmer and more social, jolly is rounder and more physical, mirthful implies actual laughter — jocund is a lightness in the air, and it belongs to poets. Nobody describes a work chat as jocund without smirking; the word arrives already dressed for verse.
jocund ≠ jocular.
- jocund = cheerful — the mood
- jocular = joking — the behaviour

A jocular colleague makes the quips; a jocund morning just feels good.
Jocund = a joke's good mood, with the joke removed.
The word carries the cheer that jokes produce, not the jesting itself — which is exactly the line between jocund and jocular.
1. The company sat late over the wine, jocund and unhurried, as though the war were somebody else's news.
2. He came back from that holiday weirdly jocund — humming in the kitchen, saying good morning to people.
Wordsworth's daffodils, the poem everyone half-remembers: "A poet could not but be gay, / In such a jocund company." The flowers are the jocund company — cheerful, dancing, doing nothing funny at all.
Latin iucundus = "pleasant, delightful," from iuvare, "to please, to help" — the same root under adjuvant (a helping agent).

The twist worth keeping: the word got its spelling bent toward Latin iocus, "joke" — so jocund only looks like a cousin of joke, jocular, jocose, jest. It's a false family that stuck, and it's the reason the mnemonic works.

Showing sound judgment; wisely measured and restrained in choices.
Showing sound judgment — sensible, careful, well-considered in what you decide or do.

The praise is for restraint and proportion, not brainpower. A clever person can be reckless; a judicious one weighs the costs and stops at the right point. Notice how often it attaches to how much of something you use — a judicious edit, a judicious dose, a judicious silence. It's a calm, slightly formal compliment, the kind that shows up in reports and reviews rather than conversation.
⚠️ judicious ≠ judicial.
- judicious = wise, well-judged (anyone can be)
- judicial = to do with courts and judges (a judicial inquiry, judicial review)

A judge can hand down an injudicious judicial ruling.
Judicious almost always sits in front of "use of" — and use of always means not too much.
Judicious use of force, of salt, of quotation — the word is a compliment about knowing where to stop.
1. The trustees made judicious cuts, trimming travel and catering while leaving the research fellowships untouched.
2. I'd be judicious with that chilli oil — it's a lot hotter than it looks.
Every antibiotics leaflet and public-health campaign runs on the phrase "judicious use of antibiotics" — meaning use them sparingly and only when warranted, which is the word's whole personality in three words.
Latin judicium = "judgment," from ius (law) + dicere (to say) — literally to pronounce the law.

That root pays off across the exam: judge, judgment, judicial, judiciary, adjudicate, injudicious (rash), and prejudice — literally pre-judging, deciding before the evidence.

Sharp — in blade, senses, or appetite; also, to wail in grief.
Adj. 1 — sharp. Of a blade, an edge, a wind, a mind: cutting. A keen knife, a keen frost, a keen intellect.
Adj. 2 — acutely perceptive. A keen eye for forgeries, keen hearing — senses tuned finer than other people's.
Adj. 3 — eager, avid. Keen to help; a keen gardener. This sense is everyday British English and mildly informal.
Verb — to keen: to wail loudly in grief, especially over the dead. A completely different word wearing the same spelling.

The thread through the adjective is fineness of edge — metal, wit, senses, or appetite, all honed rather than blunt. Note the intensity gradient: interested is polite, keen is leaning forward, avid is close to hungry. And unlike shrewd or astute, keen carries no whiff of calculation — a keen observer simply sees more, without any implication that they're working an angle.
⚠️ keen ≠ ken. Keen = sharp/eager. Ken = the range of what you know — "quantum field theory is beyond my ken." Same ancient root (knowing), opposite exam answers.
Keen rhymes with clean — a keen edge cuts clean, whether it's a blade, an eye, or an appetite.
Every adjective sense is the same idea sharpened onto a different object: honed metal, honed senses, honed enthusiasm.
1. The critic brought a keen eye to the manuscript, catching an inconsistency three editors had walked past.
2. She's dead keen on the job — she's already emailed twice about the start date.
In Hamlet's play scene, Ophelia tells him "You are keen, my lord, you are keen" — meaning your wit is cutting — and Hamlet's reply, "It would cost you a groaning to take off mine edge," spells the metaphor out: keen = edged.
Old English cēne = "bold, brave, wise" — from the Germanic root for knowing (cunnan). That family gives you can, cunning, uncanny, and ken: all about knowledge, which is why keen drifted from "clever" to "sharp."

🚫 The verb is a different word. To keen over a corpse is Irish caoinim, "I weep" — borrowed into English in the 1800s. No connection to sharpness at all.

Using very few words; terse in a cool, deliberate way.
Using very few words — terse to the point of seeming cool, dry, or unbothered.

Brevity alone isn't the point. Concise praises efficiency; curt accuses you of rudeness. Laconic sits between them and adds temperature: the speaker could have said more and chose not to, and the silence around the words does the rest of the work. It's the one-word answer that lands harder than a paragraph — often admiring (the unflappable hero), occasionally chilly (the boss who replies "Noted.").
⚠️ laconic ≠ taciturn.
- laconic = says little when he speaks — style
- taciturn = rarely speaks at all — temperament

A taciturn man may go a whole dinner in silence; a laconic man answers every question, in four words.
Laconic = LACKing words — deliberately.
The lac- sound gives you "lack," and the deliberateness is what separates it from someone who simply has nothing to say.
1. His laconic dispatches from the front — "Held. Losses heavy." — told the ministry less than it wanted and more than it could bear.
2. I asked how the interview went and got a laconic "fine," so I assume it was a disaster.
Film critics reach for this word constantly for the strong-silent type — Clint Eastwood's Man with No Name, Ryan Gosling in Drive. "Laconic hero" is practically a stock phrase in reviews.
Greek Lakōnikos = "of Laconia," the region around Sparta — and the Spartans were famous for cutting speech to the bone.

The founding anecdote: Philip II of Macedon warned them, "If I enter Laconia, I will raze Sparta to the ground." The Spartans wrote back one word — "If." He didn't invade.

column2:
To attack someone with harsh, public, sustained criticism.
To attack someone with harsh, sustained criticism — and, in the older physical sense, to beat or thrash.

Volume and audience are what set it apart. You reprimand an employee behind a closed door; you lambaste a minister on the front page. It implies a pounding rather than a point — the critic keeps swinging past the moment anyone stopped disagreeing. Slightly journalistic in flavour, and it always makes the attacker sound forceful, never fair.
⚠️ lambaste ≠ bombast. Lambaste is what you do to someone (savage them); bombast is inflated, pompous speech you produce yourself. A bombastic speaker lambastes his rivals in a great deal of hot air.
Lamb + baste — the poor thing got publicly roasted.
The slang "roasted" is exactly the register: lambasting is loud, sustained, and served up for an audience, never a quiet word in private.
1. The editorial lambasted the committee for a decade of quiet inaction, naming every member in turn.
2. Mum lambasted me for twenty solid minutes over one unwashed pan.
This word lives almost entirely in news headlines — "Critics lambast sequel", "Senator lambasted over remarks." If you meet it anywhere else, someone is writing like a tabloid.
Probably lam ("to beat" — as in on the lam, running from a hiding) + baste ("to thrash"). Two words for hitting, welded together — the redundancy is the meaning: an excessive beating.

🚫 Nothing to do with basting a roast in the kitchen; that's a different baste entirely. The lamb is a pun, not a parent.

To mourn aloud; a song or outcry of grief.
Verb: to express grief or deep regret out loud. Noun: the expression itself — a song, poem, or outcry of mourning.

Mourn is the inward state; lament is the sound it makes. It is grief given shape and voice — which is why a lament can be composed, sung, and played at a graveside. It carries dignity, never hysteria.

The second, weaker sense is the one the GRE loves: to lament a decline, a lost standard, a vanished courtesy. That's regret spoken publicly with an elevated tone — a complaint that has put on a suit. Say you lament the state of modern journalism and you sound grave; say you whine about it and you sound small.
L-AMEN-T — amen is hiding inside it, and grief here is spoken aloud like a prayer at a graveside.
The buried amen fixes the key point: a lament is uttered, performed, heard — not silently endured.
1. In his final essay he lamented the disappearance of the unhurried sentence from public life.
2. Dad still laments selling that car, and he's been at it for thirty years.
The Bible has an entire book called Lamentations — five poems weeping over the ruins of Jerusalem. Same root, and it is nothing but grief said out loud.

To mock a named target publicly with ridiculing satire.
Verb: to publicly mock a person or institution with ridicule.
Noun: the piece of writing, cartoon, or sketch that does it.

Satire can be dry and impersonal; a lampoon has a target with a name. It's aimed, broad, and unmistakably rude — the goal is to make the audience laugh at someone until the dignity comes off. Parody imitates a style, satire exposes a vice, lampoon humiliates a person. Note also that it's almost always public and performed: you lampoon a president in a magazine, not a colleague over lunch.
Lampoon rhymes with harpoon — you don't gently tease the target, you spear it in public.
The rhyme carries the nuance: a lampoon is thrown at a named victim, and everyone watches it land.
1. The pamphlet lampooned the prime minister as a bloated toad in a powdered wig, and the print run sold out in a day.
2. Every year the students put on a show that lampoons the teachers, and every year one teacher takes it far too personally.
National Lampoon — the magazine that spun off Animal House and the Vacation films. The name is borrowed from The Harvard Lampoon, the college humour paper that has been mocking the powerful since 1876. The brand is the definition.
French lampon, thought to come from lampons! — "let's drink!" — the shouted refrain of 17th-century French drinking songs, which were where the rude verses about local bigwigs got sung.

That's the register in one word: a lampoon is tavern mockery, not drawing-room wit.

Slow and drooping with no energy — often attractively so.
Slow, drooping, without energy — either from real weakness (illness, heat, exhaustion) or from sheer unhurried ease.

The word is an aesthetic one. Lethargic is a symptom, sluggish is a complaint, lazy is an accusation — languid is the only one of the four that can be a compliment. A languid gesture, a languid summer afternoon, a languid gaze: slow enough to be stylish. Even in its weaker sense it stays poetic rather than clinical — you'd write "languid after the fever," not put it in a chart. The exception is business prose, where languid trading just means limp and disappointing.
Languid moves at the pace of a language spoken in a drawl — long, slow, and rather attractive.
The buried "lang" gives you the long, drawn-out pace, and the drawl gives you the tone: unhurried, not diseased.
1. The heat pressed down until the whole household turned languid, moving between shuttered rooms with the slowness of sleepwalkers.
2. Three days off and I've gone completely languid — I got up at noon and considered that an achievement.
Latin languēre = "to be faint, to droop." It hands you a tight family worth owning: languid (slow and drooping), languor (the pleasant heavy state itself), and languish (to droop over time — to waste away, or sit neglected: the bill languished in committee).

column2:
To weaken and fade while stuck somewhere, neglected.
Two linked senses:
1. To lose strength and vitality — to droop, weaken, fade.
2. To be left somewhere unpleasant, making no progress — languish in prison, languish in obscurity, languish at the bottom of the league.

The verb is passive and slow. Nobody languishes in a moment; you languish for years, quietly, while something withers. It also carries a whiff of blame pointed elsewhere — a manuscript languishes in a drawer, a bill languishes in committee, because whoever should have rescued it didn't. Compare suffer (active pain), deteriorate (clinical), rot (contemptuous): languish is the neglected-and-fading one, faintly sad rather than harsh.
⚠️ languish ≠ anguish.
- anguish = sharp, acute agony (a noun, mostly)
- languish = slow fading from neglect

Anguish is the scream; languishing is the long silence after.
Languish = long + wish — stuck a long time, wishing someone would come get you.
The two halves give you both halves of the meaning: the duration and the helpless waiting.
1. The reform bill languished in committee for three sessions before anyone thought to call a vote.
2. That guitar's been languishing in my parents' garage since 2011.
Stock newsroom phrasing you've read a hundred times: a painting languishes in an attic for decades before the auction, a club languishes at the bottom of the table, a hostage languishes in a cell. Learn the collocations and the word comes with them.
Latin languēre = "to be faint, weak," from the same root as laxus (loose, slack).

That gives you a cluster worth banking: languid (drooping, unhurried), languor (pleasant heavy tiredness), and the slackness family — lax, relax, release. Note the split: languid and languor can be sensual and rather nice; languish never is.

column2:
Lavish giving, usually from someone above to someone below.
Generous giving — money, gifts, favours — handed out on a grand scale; also the generous spirit behind it.

The word carries a height difference. Largesse flows downward: from the rich to the dependent, the state to the citizen, the patron to the artist. Plain generosity can pass between equals; largesse implies the giver could stop at any time and everyone knows it. That's why it turns sour so easily in print — "living on his father's largesse," "corporate largesse" — half compliment, half sneer at the person doing the receiving.
largesse rhymes with noblesse — and it's exactly what noblesse oblige obliges you to do.
The rhyme drags in the nobleman, which is the whole point: largesse is giving from above, not giving between equals.
1. The museum's new wing stands as a monument to one banker's largesse — and, engraved above the door, to his name.
2. We only got the good coffee machine because someone in Finance had a rare fit of largesse.
Political and business journalism runs on this word: "government largesse," "taxpayer largesse," "corporate largesse" — always with a raised eyebrow at who's footing the bill.
Latin largus = "abundant, plentiful" → French largesse. The same root gives you large, enlarge, and musical largo — literally "broad," hence slow and spacious.

Bone-deep weariness with no will to act.
A state of weariness and listlessness — no physical energy, and no will to summon any.

Tiredness with a flat battery is fatigue; lassitude is tiredness that has soaked into the mood. It's heavy, passive, faintly melancholy — the languor of a sickbed, a heatwave, a long convalescence, an empire in decline. Crucially it isn't laziness: laziness is a character flaw you're blamed for, lassitude is a condition that happens to you. The register is formal and literary; nobody says it about a Monday morning without irony.
⚠️ lassitude ≠ latitude. One letter apart in the middle: lassitude = exhausted listlessness; latitude = room to manoeuvre (or a line on a map). Being given latitude is freedom; being seized by lassitude is collapse.
-itude names a state you live in — solitude, serviitude, gratitude. Lassitude is tiredness you're living in, not tiredness you're feeling.
Fatigue passes after a nap; lassitude is the thing you wake up still inside.
1. The heat pressed down until a general lassitude settled over the whole household, and even conversation seemed like too much effort.
2. Fan's broken, it's thirty-five degrees, and nobody in this office has moved in an hour — total lassitude.
Read the side-effects leaflet folded inside almost any box of medication: "drowsiness, lassitude, nausea" is standard drug-labelling language — the pharmaceutical industry's word for this will flatten you.
Latin lassus = "weary, faint."

The sneaky payoff: alas is the same root — Old French ha las, literally "ah, weary!" So every time someone sighs alas, they're announcing their lassitude.

Freedom to act within limits; room to manoeuvre.
Freedom to act, choose, or interpret as you see fit — room to move within the rules.

Latitude is almost always given, not taken: a boss, a court, a coach, an editor grants it. That's what separates it from license, which suggests freedom already run to excess. Latitude still implies a boundary somewhere out there — you're being handed a wide field, not an open one. Common in formal and professional registers: considerable latitude, allowed wide latitude in sentencing.
⚠️ latitude ≠ lassitude.
- latitude = room to manoeuvre
- lassitude = weariness, listless lack of energy

One letter apart, opposite worlds — a manager grants latitude; a heatwave induces lassitude.
LAT is FLAT — latitude lines run flat and wide across the globe, and latitude is the wide flat space you're allowed to roam in.
Both senses come from the same idea of breadth, so the map lines you already know hand you the abstract meaning for free.
1. Appellate courts have historically granted trial judges wide latitude in matters of evidentiary procedure.
2. They gave me a lot of latitude on how to run the team, as long as the numbers landed.
The line every manager eventually says — "I'll give you some latitude on the deadline" — meaning: bend it, don't break it.
Latin lātus = "broad, wide" → latitudo, breadth. Same root gives dilate (spread wide) and latitudinarian (broad-minded, tolerant of doctrinal difference — a GRE word in its own right).

Deserving praise — usually the attempt, not the result.
Deserving praise; worthy of admiration.

The catch is what it usually praises: intentions, aims and efforts, not results. "A laudable goal," "a laudable attempt," "laudable restraint" — the word attaches to the trying. It is also cool and formal, the register of an editorial or a school report, so it praises from a distance: an examiner's word, not a friend's. Because of that, "laudable" often lands as polite consolation — you commend the effort precisely because you can't commend the outcome.
⚠️ laudable ≠ laudatory.
- laudable = deserves praise (the deed)
- laudatory = gives praise (the speech)

A laudatory review of a laudable effort.
-able means "able to be": laud-able = able to be praised, like lik*able*, read*able*. And "a laudable effort" is what you say when the effort failed.
The suffix splits it from laudatory (the praise being handed out), and the stock phrase reminds you the word tends to bless the attempt rather than the achievement.
1. The committee's aim of housing every applicant within a year was laudable, if wholly unfunded.
2. He tried to fix the boiler himself — laudable, but now we have no hot water and a flooded kitchen.
Cum laude on a graduation diploma — literally "with praise," and magna cum laude "with great praise." Same root, printed on millions of degrees.
Latin laudāre = "to praise" (noun laus, laudis = praise). It gives you laud (to praise, usually in print), laudatory, laudation, and cum laude.

The ending is the everyday -able = "fit to be" — so laudable is simply "fit to be praised."

Abundant to the point of excess; to pour out generously.
Adj.: given or existing in great, unstinting abundance — a lavish banquet, lavish praise, a lavish budget.
Verb (+ on): to bestow something in generous excess — she lavished attention on the new puppy.

The word measures scale, not virtue. Generous compliments the giver's heart; lavish comments on the sheer volume coming out — which is why it can be warm (a lavish welcome) or quietly damning (a lavish lifestyle on a civil servant's salary). Next to extravagant, which almost always means wasteful, lavish stays admiring more often than not; next to opulent, which is about the look of wealth sitting there, lavish is about wealth being poured out.
Lavish = LAVA-ish. It doesn't trickle — it pours, and it keeps coming.
The image of an overflow rather than a gift is exactly the nuance: what makes something lavish is the volume, not the kindness behind it.
1. The prosecution detailed a lavish lifestyle — three homes, a yacht, and a wine cellar no salary could explain.
2. Her grandmother lavishes food on anyone who walks through the door; you don't leave that house hungry.
Open any fraud or celebrity-downfall story and the phrase is waiting for you: "funded a lavish lifestyle." It's practically the word's home address in journalism — abundance with a raised eyebrow.
Latin lavāre = "to wash" → Old French lavasse, a downpour of rain. Lavish is rain, not a raindrop.

Same root, whole family: lavatory, lotion, launder, ablution — and lava, the stream that washes down the mountainside.

Slack where strictness was owed; negligently loose.
Not strict enough; slack where firmness was owed. Also, physically, loose or untensed — lax muscles, a lax rope.

The moral sense is an accusation. Relaxed is pleasant, easygoing is a temperament, but lax says a duty was there and someone let it go slack: lax security, lax enforcement, lax oversight, lax standards. It attaches to systems and the people responsible for them, and it is the word an inquiry report reaches for when nobody was quite negligent enough to blame outright. The physical sense carries none of this — a lax jaw is just a loose jaw.
Lax is relax with the re- — and the pleasure — stripped off.
Same looseness, but nobody chose it and nobody's enjoying it.
1. The audit attributed the breach to lax password protocols rather than to any deliberate act.
2. Their gym is so lax about memberships that half the people in there stopped paying months ago.
Latin laxus = "loose, slack." The family is worth having: relax (loosen again), release and lease (let go, let out), and — unforgettably — laxative, a pill whose entire job is loosening.

column2:
Drained of energy; sluggish and abnormally drowsy.
Drained of energy — abnormally drowsy, sluggish, slow to move or react.

The key is that it's a condition, not a character flaw. Lazy and indolent judge you: you could work, you choose not to. Lethargic is something that happens to you — heat, flu, jet lag, a heavy lunch, grief. It's usually temporary, and it carries a faint clinical edge; a doctor will ask if a patient has been lethargic, never if they've been lazy. Applied to a market, a crowd, or a plot, it means the same drained slowness — nothing is moving, and nothing seems able to.
le-THAR-gic — the stress lands on TAR, and that's what you're wading through.
Tar doesn't make you unwilling to move, it makes you unable to — which is exactly the involuntary sluggishness that separates lethargic from lazy.
1. By the fourth week of the heatwave the whole city had turned lethargic, its offices half-empty and its streets silent until dusk.
2. I had two slices of cake and now I'm too lethargic to even find the remote.
It's a live medical word, not just an exam word: paediatricians and vets treat "lethargic" as a red flag — "Is she feeding normally? Is she lethargic?" — meaning unusually limp and unresponsive, the symptom you call about.
Greek lēthargos = lēthē (forgetfulness) + argos (idle). Literally "drowsy forgetfulness" — the mind switched off along with the body.

Lēthē is the river in Hades whose water erased your memories; argos is a- (not) + ergon (work), the same ergon behind energy, ergonomic, and allergy. So lethargic is, precisely, not-working.

🚫 Nothing to do with lethal. That's Latin letum, "death" — pure sound coincidence.

Humour or lightness where seriousness was expected.
Lightness of manner — humour, joking, or a refusal to be solemn, especially at a moment that called for seriousness.

The word almost never stands alone: it exists in opposition to gravity. You only reach for levity when there is weight in the room — a funeral, a trial, a board meeting, a crisis — and someone punctures it. That makes it two-faced. From a disapproving speaker it means unseemly frivolity ("this is no occasion for levity"); from a grateful one it means welcome relief ("a moment of levity broke the tension"). The lightness is fixed; whether it's a sin or a mercy depends entirely on who's judging.
Levity levitates — it lifts the mood off a heavy moment.
Same lev- = light, and the image carries the nuance: something heavy was sitting there until the joke floated it away.
1. The chairman's attempt at levity during the layoff announcement was met with silence.
2. Ten hours into the drive, any levity helped — even Dad's terrible puns.
Harry Potter's Wingardium Levi*osa — the charm that makes a feather float. Same lev- root: light enough to rise*.
Latin levis = "light in weight" — the direct opposite of gravis, "heavy," which gives you gravity, grave, and grievous. Learn the pair and you get both halves of the seesaw.

lev- also pays out across the list: alleviate (lighten a burden), elevate, levitate, lever, relieve.

A legal debt, or a person who's a burden not an asset.
1. A legal or financial obligation — a debt, a claim someone can enforce against you. (Plural on a balance sheet: liabilities, the money you owe.)
2. A person or thing that costs you more than it gives — the opposite of an asset.

Sense 2 is the GRE one, and it's colder than burden or nuisance. A nuisance annoys you; a liability exposes you — it creates risk you'll have to pay for. Calling a teammate a liability isn't quite an insult about character; it's an accounting verdict: on net, they're in the debit column. That borrowed-from-the-ledger flavour is what gives the word its clinical sting.
liability ≠ libel. Libel (LYE-bul) is defamation in writing. You can, of course, incur liability for libel — which is exactly why the two get tangled.
li-a-BIL-ity — say it slowly and you say a bill.
A liability is whatever hands you a bill: a debt you owe, or a person whose mistakes you end up paying for.
1. The auditors found undisclosed liabilities buried in the subsidiary's accounts, wiping out the reported profit.
2. He's fast, sure, but he can't defend — at this level he's a liability.
Every Ltd. and LLC on a company name is short for limited liability — the whole point of the structure is that if the business goes under, creditors can take the company's money but not the founders' house.
From liable, most likely via Old French lier ← Latin ligāre = "to bind." A liability is what you are bound to — legally tied, unable to walk away.

Same root: ligament (binds bone to bone), oblige (bind toward), liaison (a binding-together), ally, league.

Someone morally unrestrained, especially sexually; a stylish debauchee.
Noun: someone who lives without moral restraint, especially in sex and drink — a debauchee.
Adjective: characterised by that unrestraint (libertine habits, a libertine court).

The word wears a costume. Pervert is clinical and disgusted, womaniser is small and modern, sleaze is grubby — but a libertine has style: wit, money, poetry, a philosophy of pleasure that he'd happily defend over wine. There's often a flicker of admiration in it, or at least amusement. Calling a man a libertine places him in a candlelit drawing room, not a courtroom.
⚠️ libertine ≠ libertarian. A libertarian wants the state off his back (politics). A libertine wants morality off his back (bedroom). Same root, very different dinner party.
A libertine takes liberties.
The word "liberty" is sitting right inside it, and the freedom he claims is always at somebody else's expense.
1. Rochester's verse scandalised the court precisely because a libertine wrote it with such elegance.
2. He talks like a philosopher, but he's just a libertine with a good vocabulary.
Johnny Depp played the Earl of Rochester in The Libertine (2004) — the Restoration poet who drank and whored his way to death at 33. The film opens with him saying "You will not like me."
Latin liber = "free." A Roman libertinus was a freedman — an ex-slave, free but never quite respectable. English first used libertine for a freethinker in religion, then the freedom slid from belief to behaviour.

That root is everywhere: liberty, liberal, liberate, libertarian, and — via French — deliver (de-liberare, to set free).

column2:
Perfectly clear — untroubled water, or effortlessly readable prose.
Perfectly clear and transparent — water, air, eyes you can see straight through. Extended to prose, music or reasoning: so clear it costs the reader no effort.

This is a compliment, and a slightly literary one. Transparent is a physical fact; lucid praises the mind behind the words; limpid praises the surface — it adds calm and beauty, the stillness of an untroubled pool. Water churning white over rocks is clear, but it isn't limpid. Nobody says it in conversation about a glass of water; it turns up in reviews, poetry, and obituaries of good writers.
⚠️ limpid ≠ limp. The first four letters are a decoy — limpid has nothing to do with floppiness or weakness. A limpid style is clean and strong, not feeble.
LIMP-ID — so clear you can see all the way down to the id.
The hidden id at the end reminds you that limpid clarity goes right to the bottom, nothing hiding in the depths — and that the limp at the front is a trap.
1. Her late essays are limpid — not a sentence you have to read twice.
2. The lake was so limpid you could count the stones eight feet down.
Latin limpidus = "clear", tied to lympha, "clear spring water" — the same root that gives English lymph and lymphatic, the clear fluid in your body. Lymph and limpid: both mean water you can see through.

column2:
Treat someone as a celebrity; publicly fête and parade them.
To treat someone as a celebrity — to fête, parade and make much of a person in public.

The key is that lionizing is done by a crowd: critics, salons, the press, a conference circuit. It describes the fuss around someone, not the merit inside them. And the word usually arrives with a raised eyebrow — a writer who says a figure was lionized is often hinting the adulation outran the achievement, or that fashion did the choosing. Compare praise (earned, about the work) and idolize (private, one person's devotion): lionize is public, social, and slightly theatrical.
The lion is in there: to lionize is to make someone the lion of the party — the exhibit everyone comes to gawk at.
Zoo-lion, not jungle-lion — the person is being displayed, which is why the word carries a whiff of spectacle rather than respect.
1. A poet lionized in his twenties, he spent the next forty years being politely forgotten.
2. They lionized her for one viral thread and now she can't get through a panel without a standing ovation.
This word lives in obituaries and book reviews — "lionized by critics", "lionized in life, reassessed in death" is close to a stock phrase in literary journalism.
In 1700s London, the caged lions at the Tower were the must-see attraction, so "showing someone the lions" meant showing them the sights — and by extension a famous person became a lion, a sight worth being brought round to see.

Latin leo, leonis also gives you leonine (lion-like) and, absurdly, dandelion — French dent-de-lion, "lion's tooth", for the jagged leaves.

To hate intensely, with a feeling of disgust.
To hate something intensely, with disgust — hatred that comes with a physical recoil.

Dislike is a preference; detest is a cold, considered verdict; loathe is visceral. It puts revulsion in the room: the thing is not just bad, it's repellent, and you want it away from you. Because it's so strong, it's also the standard verb for comic exaggeration — nobody says "I detest Mondays," but everybody loathes them.
⚠️ loathe ≠ loath.
- loathe (verb, voiced) = to hate with disgust
- loath (adjective, unvoiced) = reluctant, unwilling — "I am loath to interrupt."

She was loath to speak to the man she loathed.
breath → breathe, cloth → clothe, loath → loathe. The silent e stretches the vowel, voices the ending, and turns it into a verb.
If it ends in -the, it's an action you do — and loathing is very much something you do to a thing.
1. He came to loathe the ceremonial dinners — the toasts, the flattery, the practised warmth of men who despised one another.
2. I loathe coriander. It tastes like soap and I will die on this hill.
Wicked — Galinda and Elphaba's duet "What Is This Feeling?", whose chorus is nothing but the word: "Loathing — unadulterated loathing." Two roommates, instant mutual revulsion. That's the exact temperature of the word.
Old English lāð = "hateful, hostile" → the verb lāðian, to hate.

That one root splits into the pair that trips people up: loathsome (disgusting) and loathe kept the hatred, while the adjective loath kept only the milder old sense of being set against something — hence "reluctant."

Talking a great deal; chatty to excess.
Very talkative; inclined to talk a great deal.

The word is itself too fancy to be innocent — calling someone loquacious is a dry, faintly amused way of saying they don't stop. It sits between neutral and critical: talkative is a plain fact, garrulous is a complaint (rambling, tedious, usually about the elderly), voluble praises fluency and speed, verbose attacks wordiness on the page. Loquacious describes a person in flow — often charming, occasionally exhausting — and lets the speaker stay polite while noting the excess. It also does duty as an ironic understatement: "a loquacious witness" means one who told the court far more than anyone asked.
Lo-QUACK-ious — they quack on and on.
The buried "quack" catches both halves of the word: nonstop noise, and the mild comedy in how you'd describe it.
1. Ordinarily reserved, he became loquacious after the second glass of wine, holding the table for an hour on the subject of bridges.
2. Our cab driver was loquacious the entire way to the airport — I learned his whole divorce.
Latin loquī = "to speak." One of the highest-yield GRE roots going:

- eloquent — speaking out well
- colloquial — speech with others, i.e. casual
- soliloquy — speaking alone
- circumlocution — talking around the point
- ventriloquist — literally "belly-speaker"
- grandiloquent — speaking grandly, pompously

Spot loqu- or locu- and you're looking at a word about talking.

Clear and easy to follow; mentally sharp and rational.
1. Easy to understand; expressed with perfect clarity. 2. Mentally clear — able to think and speak rationally, especially in a break from confusion, fever, or dementia.

Praise for lucid writing is praise for the glass, not the view: the ideas arrive without the reader noticing the sentences. Clear describes any plain statement; lucid implies difficult material made transparent, so it's the word for a physicist's explanation, not a shopping list. Sense 2 carries a quiet sadness — a lucid interval only exists because the surrounding hours weren't.
⚠️ lucid ≠ lurid. One letter apart, opposite temperament: lucid = clear and rational; lurid = shockingly vivid, sensational, in glaring bad taste. A lucid account of the murder is what the coroner writes; a lurid one is what the tabloid prints.
Lucid prose is trans-LUC-ent — you see the thought, not the sentence.
Both words hide the same luc- (light), and lucid writing works exactly like glass: light gets through and the pane disappears.
1. Her lucid account of quantum entanglement left the room feeling, briefly, that they had understood it.
2. Grandad was lucid for about ten minutes this morning — he asked about the cricket score and everything.
Lucid dreaming — the state where you realise mid-dream that you're dreaming, and clarity switches on inside sleep. Juice WRLD's "Lucid Dreams" put the phrase on every playlist in 2018.
Latin lux, lucis = light, via lūcēre = to shine. It's a high-yield root: elucidate (shed light on), translucent (light passes through), pellucid (utterly clear), lucent, and Lucifer — literally light-bearer.

column2:
Producing a lot of money; very profitable.
Producing a lot of money; highly profitable.

It attaches to the activity, deal, or venture — never to the person. A contract, a sideline, a franchise, a career is lucrative; the man who owns it is wealthy. And unlike profitable (a flat accounting fact — even 2% is profitable), lucrative implies the money is notably good, better than you'd expect. Tone is admiring and slightly worldly: it says "the money is real" without moralising, which is exactly where its cousin lucre differs — that one drips with contempt.
Lucrative hides LUCRE — cold cash. But lucre is dirty and lucrative isn't: the deal is lucrative, the greed is lucre.
Same root, split tone — keep lucrative on the venture and neutral, and leave the sneer to lucre.
1. What began as a hobby restoring bicycles turned out to be startlingly lucrative, and within two years she had left the firm.
2. Teaching pays the rent, but the weekend wedding gigs are the lucrative bit.
Sports and business journalism runs on it — every transfer window brings a "lucrative endorsement deal" or a "lucrative five-year contract." The word is practically welded to the phrase.
Latin lucrum = "profit, gain." Straight into English as lucre, money — best known from the Bible's "filthy lucre" (1 Timothy), which is why lucre alone sounds greedy and grubby while lucrative stayed clean.

Mournful and gloomy, laid on almost comically thick.
Mournful, dismal, funereally sad — gloomy in a heavy, drawn-out, over-the-top way.

The word almost always carries a raised eyebrow. Sad is a feeling; lugubrious is a performance of sadness — the drooping face, the sighing voice, the funeral-organ delivery. Writers reach for it when the gloom is so thick it tips into comedy: a lugubrious waiter, a lugubrious ballad, a lugubrious basset hound. Call a genuinely grieving person lugubrious and you're mocking them, so it's a word applied from the outside, at a slight distance.
lugubrious ≠ salubrious. Same -ubrious ending, opposite worlds: salubrious = healthy, wholesome (a salubrious climate); lugubrious = dripping with gloom. A salubrious spa, a lugubrious funeral.
Loo-GOO — all that goo in the middle: gloom poured on thick and slow.
The word itself sags through four sluggish syllables, which is exactly the laid-on-too-thick sadness it describes.
1. The organ wheezed out a lugubrious hymn while the mourners shuffled past in the rain.
2. Stop being so lugubrious — you lost one tennis match, not the will to live.
Eeyore in Winnie-the-Pooh is the walking definition — the flat grey voice, the drooping ears, the "thanks for noticing me." Nobody has ever been more lugubrious.
Latin lugēre = "to mourn" — the verb for grieving at a funeral. Nothing in the word's shape tells you that, so it's worth the twenty seconds: lugubrious = mourning-grade gloom, not ordinary sadness.

column2:
A temporary calm; to soothe, often into false security.
Noun: a temporary pause in noise, activity, or violence — a quiet stretch inside something that hasn't actually stopped.
Verb: to soothe or quieten, especially into sleep or trust.

Both senses smuggle in the same idea: this won't last, and you shouldn't trust it. A lull isn't peace, it's an interval — the fighting resumes, the storm arrives, the shop gets busy again. And the verb is rarely innocent at GRE level: things get lulled into complacency, lulled into a false sense of security. Where calm and soothe are simply pleasant, lull lowers your guard — often to your cost.
⚠️ lull ≠ loll. Lull (LUL) = a quiet spell, or to soothe. Loll (LOL) = to lounge, droop, or hang slackly — he lolled on the sofa; the dog's tongue lolled out.
A lull is a lullaby — it works by putting you to sleep.
That's the catch built into the word: the quiet is doing something to you, and you wake up to find the noise never actually ended.
1. Three quiet weeks lulled the garrison into complacency, and the assault came on the fourth.
2. There's usually a lull around three o'clock — grab your coffee then.
Standard newsroom language: \"a lull in the fighting\" — reporters reach for it precisely because it means the shooting has paused, not stopped.

Gruesome and grim, dwelling theatrically on death.
Disturbing because it dwells on death, corpses, and bodily decay — grim, ghoulish, gruesome.

The word carries a whiff of theatre. Morbid describes a mind that broods on death; macabre describes the thing itself put on display — a skull-shaped candle, a hanging scene played for laughs, a museum of anatomical specimens. It's the register of Halloween, gothic fiction, and black comedy, so it can be said with relish: macabre humour is a compliment in a way morbid humour isn't quite.
macabre / cadavre — one sound apart, and both keep the corpse in the room.
French cadavre (corpse) rhymes it into place, and the shared shape reminds you that macabre isn't vaguely dark — it's specifically about death made visible.
1. The exhibition's macabre centrepiece was a chandelier assembled from the bones of the monastery's dead.
2. His jokes at the funeral were macabre, but honestly, the whole room needed the laugh.
Saint-Saëns' Danse Macabre — the skeletons-fiddling-at-midnight piece wheeled out every Halloween and in a hundred film scores. The word's whole flavour is in that music: death, but dancing.
English lifted it straight from the Old French phrase danse macabre, the medieval "Dance of Death" — a stock image of grinning skeletons leading pope, king, and peasant alike to the grave. That's why the word still implies death staged rather than merely feared.

Commanding total mastery; or loftily, unarguably authoritative.
Two related senses, and the GRE tests both.

1. Of a work or performance: showing complete mastery — comprehensive, commanding, the definitive treatment. A magisterial history of the Ottoman Empire.
2. Of a person or manner: speaking with the unquestionable authority of a master — lofty, imposing, brooking no argument.

This is far above authoritative. Authoritative means reliable; magisterial means so thoroughly in command that disagreement feels presumptuous. Sense 1 is high praise, usually reserved for decades-long scholarly work. Sense 2 tilts cool or faintly barbed: the magisterial speaker isn't arrogant exactly, but he addresses the room as a professor addresses freshmen.
magister = master. A magisterial book has mastered the subject; a magisterial manner acts like it has mastered you.
One root, two directions — praise when it points at the work, a raised eyebrow when it points at the person.
1. Gibbon's magisterial account of Rome's decline went unchallenged for a century.
2. He waved off the question with a magisterial little gesture, as if we'd all wandered in from the wrong meeting.
It lives on book jackets. Flip over any doorstop biography or history and the blurb almost certainly says "magisterial" — it's the reviewer's highest word for big, definitive, and never to be redone.
Latin magister = "master, teacher", from magis = "more, greater."

That root is everywhere: master, maestro, magistrate, mister, and — via magis — major, majesty, magnitude, magnify. All of them mean bigger, higher, in charge.

Generous and forgiving toward someone you could have crushed.
Generous, forgiving, and above pettiness — especially toward a rival, a loser, or someone who is at your mercy.

The word needs an occasion for spite. You are magnanimous only when resentment would have been fair and you decline it anyway: the winner who praises the beaten team, the wronged party who drops the charge. Plain kind costs nothing; magnanimous costs a grudge you were entitled to keep. It's high, slightly grand praise — and it quietly says the person had the power in the exchange.
⚠️ magnanimous ≠ munificent.
- magnanimous = big of spirit — forgives, refuses to gloat
- munificent = big of wallet — gives lavishly

A munificent donor writes the cheque; a magnanimous rival shakes your hand after beating you.
MAGNA = big. Too big to be petty.
Magna Carta is the great charter, and a magnanimous person is the one whose spirit is too large to squeeze the advantage they're holding.
1. In a magnanimous concession speech, she thanked the opponent who had spent six months calling her a fraud.
2. He was magnanimous about the dent in his car, which honestly made me feel worse.
Churchill's motto for his war memoirs: "In War: Resolution. In Defeat: Defiance. In Victory: Magnanimity. In Peace: Goodwill." — victory is exactly the moment the word belongs to.
Latin animus = "soul, spirit" — that half is the payload. It gives you unanimous (one spirit), animosity (spirit turned hostile), animated (given spirit), and the perfect GRE antonym: pusillanimous (pusillus, "tiny" + animus) — tiny-souled, cowardly, petty.

Big soul, small soul. Learn the pair together.

column2:
A crude temporary substitute made from whatever's at hand.
Serving as a temporary substitute, thrown together from whatever happened to be lying around: a makeshift raft, a makeshift office at the kitchen table.

Temporary says only "not for long." Makeshift adds two things: it was improvised, and it is slightly inadequate — it does the job, but visibly badly. There's a double edge to it. Calling a solution makeshift half-praises the resourcefulness and half-admits the thing is crude and will have to be replaced.
Nothing makeshift stays put — the second half of the word is shift.
A makeshift thing is built to be shifted out the moment the real one arrives.
1. Cut off by the flood, the villagers erected a makeshift bridge of scaffolding planks and rope.
2. We had no music stand, so he propped the sheet on a makeshift one made of two textbooks and a shoebox.
News reports run on this word: a makeshift memorial of flowers and candles on a pavement, makeshift hospitals in convention centres during Covid. Both are the same idea — real need, no proper facility, so people build one out of what's to hand.
From the old phrase "to make shift" = to contrive, to manage somehow. Shift here means an expedient, not movement.

That older sense unlocks a cousin: shiftless = not lazy in the sleepy sense but lacking resourcefulness, unable to contrive anything for yourself.

Wishing harm on others; full of deep ill will.
Wishing harm on others; full of ill will.

This is about disposition, not deed. A malevolent person may never lift a finger — the evil is in what they want for you. It's a cold, formal word, heavier than mean, nasty or spiteful, and it attaches to a whole character rather than one bad afternoon. It also works on things that have no hands: a malevolent presence, a malevolent silence, a malevolent stare. Malicious labels a specific act (malicious gossip, malicious code); malevolent labels a nature.
malevolent ≠ maleficent. Malevolent = wishing evil; maleficent = doing evil. Disney's Maleficent didn't just resent the baby — she cast the curse.
Male-VOL-ent hides vol, as in volition and volunteer — it's about what someone wills, not what they've done yet.
Lock onto that middle syllable and you'll always place the word in the mind rather than in the crime.
1. The report describes not incompetence but something malevolent: a system designed to make appeals fail.
2. He wasn't joking — that was a genuinely malevolent little smile.
Draco Malfoy — mal foi, "bad faith." Rowling loads her villains with the same mal- prefix (Malfoy, malediction, the Dark Mark's whole vocabulary of ill-wishing), and Malfoy is exactly the type: mostly sneering intent, rarely the one holding the wand.
Latin male (badly) + volens (wishing, from velle, "to will") — literally bad-wishing.

Flip the first half and you get its exact opposite: benevolent, well-wishing. Keep the second half and you get volition, voluntary, volunteer — all the will-words. Keep the first and you get malice, malign, malady, malfunction.

Illegal wrongdoing by an official abusing a position of trust.
Wrongdoing — specifically an illegal or dishonest act committed by someone holding public office or a position of trust: bribe-taking, embezzlement, rigging a contract.

This is courtroom-and-boardroom vocabulary, and it carries the weight of a breach of duty, not just bad behaviour. A private citizen who steals is a thief; a treasurer who steals is guilty of malfeasance. The word implies there was an office, a duty attached to it, and a deliberate betrayal of it — which is why it reads as heavier and colder than misconduct.
⚠️ malfeasance ≠ misfeasance.
- malfeasance = doing something wrongful in itself (the clerk took a bribe)
- misfeasance = doing a lawful act badly or improperly (the clerk filed the permit wrong)

Third of the set: nonfeasance = failing to act at all.
mal-FEE-zance — the official took a fee he shouldn't have.
The stressed syllable is literally fee, and the bribe-taking official is the archetypal malfeasant — someone paid to do a job who instead got paid to betray it.
1. The inquiry found no evidence of criminal malfeasance, but it did find a commissioner who had signed contracts he never read.
2. Losing the client wasn't malfeasance — he was sloppy, not crooked.
"Corporate malfeasance" is the stock phrase business journalism reaches for whenever an Enron- or FTX-style scandal breaks — executives looting the company they were trusted to run.
Latin male (badly) + facere (to do), through French faisance, "doing." Literally bad-doing.

Facere is one of the great GRE roots: feasible (do-able), factory, benefactor, malefactor. And male- runs through malevolent, malign, malady — anything that starts mal- is bad news.

To speak evil of someone, usually unfairly.
Verb: to speak evil of someone — to say damaging, hostile things about them, usually behind their back and usually unfairly.
Adjective: evil in nature or effect — a malign influence.

Criticism is aimed at the work; maligning is aimed at the person, and it's cumulative — a steady drip of ill-speaking rather than one bad review. Unlike slander, it carries no legal machinery; unlike vilify, it doesn't have to be loud. And it leans hard toward the undeserved: when someone is maligned, the sentence usually implies they didn't have it coming.
⚠️ malign ≠ malinger.
- malign = badmouth someone
- malinger = fake illness to dodge work

Both start mal- and both are GRE regulars; only one involves a fictitious backache.
MAL + ALIGN — you quietly align everyone against him.
The word literally hides align, which catches the slow, behind-the-back work of turning a room's opinion bad.
1. Historians have maligned the last emperor for two centuries, largely on the word of the men who deposed him.
2. Don't malign the guy — he actually covered your shift twice last month.
Sports and tech writing runs on one phrase: \"the much-maligned midfielder,\" \"the much-maligned Vista.\" Notice you never read rightly maligned — that \"much-\" is doing quiet defence work, hinting the pile-on was unfair.
Latin malignus = malus ("bad") + the root of gignere ("to be born") — literally "born bad." Its exact twin is benign, "born good."

Malus is a GRE goldmine: malice, malevolent, malady, malfeasance, dismal, even malaria (mal'aria, "bad air").

column2:
Easily shaped — by a hammer, or by influence.
Of metal: able to be hammered or pressed into new shapes without cracking. Of people, minds, or opinions: easily shaped by outside influence.

The shaping is always done to the thing by someone else. Flexible and adaptable credit the person with adjusting on their own; malleable hands the credit to whoever is holding the hammer. So it runs warm when the material is young and unformed (a child's malleable mind, a malleable early draft) and cold when the shaper has an agenda — a malleable board member, a malleable witness, is a person being used.
MALLEable = MALLET-able — soft enough that a mallet decides its shape.
The mallet is the point: something else swings, and the malleable thing takes whatever form it's given.
1. The new recruits were deliberately kept exhausted and isolated, the better to render them malleable.
2. He's a great first hire — smart, no bad habits yet, totally malleable.
Gold leaf on domes and picture frames exists because gold is the most malleable metal there is — a goldbeater can hammer a single gram out to a sheet you can see daylight through.
Latin malleus = "hammer." Same root gives you mallet, maul, and the malleus — the little hammer-shaped bone in your middle ear.

🚫 The mal- here is not "bad." Malevolent, malign, malice come from Latin malus (evil); malleable is pure hammer, no menace.

Wrist-iron; to shackle or bind, literally or figuratively.
Noun: an iron cuff for the wrists, usually one of a joined pair. Verb: to chain someone's hands — or, figuratively, to bind and hobble them.

Handcuffs are police procedure; manacles are dungeons, slave ships, chain gangs. The word carries weight, rust and cruelty, and it belongs to the wrists specifically — fetters go on the ankles. Used figuratively, it names a constraint imposed by an oppressor, never a mild self-inflicted inconvenience: you are manacled by debt or by law, not by a busy calendar.
Manacle = manual + shackle — the iron that owns your hands.
Manual work is hand work, so a manacle binds the hands — and whatever manacles you has taken away your power to act.
1. Prisoners were led from the hold still manacled, wrists raw where the iron had sat for weeks.
2. Three loans and a lease — he's completely manacled to that job.
Martin Luther King Jr., I Have a Dream: the Black American is "still sadly crippled by the manacles of segregation and the chains of discrimination."
Latin manus = "hand", via manicula, "little hand." One root, a large family: manual, manuscript (hand-written), manufacture (hand-made), manicure, manipulate.

Best pairing: manacle and emancipate are opposites from the same root — ex + manus + capere, "to take out of the hand" of an owner. One puts the iron on; the other takes it off.

Plain to see; or, to show something plainly.
Adj.: plain to see, needing no proof — evident to the senses, not inferred.
Verb: to show something plainly, to make it appear ("the illness manifested as a rash"; "manifest itself").
Noun: the official list of cargo or passengers on a ship or plane.

Obvious is casual and can be a bit dismissive; manifest is formal and carries weight — it's the word of judges, doctors and diplomats. It implies the thing is displayed so openly that arguing about it would be embarrassing: a manifest error, a manifest injustice, manifest incompetence. Note the direction of travel in the verb: something hidden — a disease, a talent, a grudge — comes out into view.
MAN + FIST — if you could close your fist around it, it isn't a matter of opinion.
The hidden word is also the real root, and it captures the strength of the adjective: manifest means so plainly there you could practically grab it.
1. The court found a manifest error of law and ordered a retrial.
2. He says he's fine, but his stress manifests as him reorganising the entire kitchen at 2 a.m.
The whole online "manifesting" trend — journalling your dream job into existence — is exactly this verb: making a thing come out into visible reality.
Latin manifestus = manus ("hand") + -festus ("struck, seized") — literally "caught by the hand," red-handed. What's caught in your hand can't be denied.

manus is a high-yield GRE root: manual, manipulate, manuscript, manacle, emancipate (e- out + manus + capere — released from the hand of a master).

column2:
Push a person or group to the edges, treating them as unimportant.
To push a person, group, or idea to the edge — of a society, a conversation, a decision — so that they remain present but powerless and unheard.

The violence here is quiet. To suppress or persecute is to act on someone directly; to marginalize is to leave them out — no ban, no confrontation, just a steady demotion to irrelevance. It often has no single villain: institutions, habits and defaults marginalize people without anyone deciding to. That's why the passive — marginalized — is the form you meet most.
Margin is sitting inside the word: still on the page, never in the text.
Marginalized people aren't erased — they're relegated to the blank strip at the edge, where nothing important gets printed.
1. The reforms, however well intentioned, marginalized the very tenants they claimed to protect.
2. They didn't fire him — they just marginalized him: no meetings, no email chains, a desk by the printer.
"Marginalized communities" is now standard vocabulary in news reports, policy documents and HR training — the phrase is so fixed that you'll rarely see the word doing anything else in the wild.

column2:
A rigid, petty enforcer of rules and discipline.
Someone who demands rigid, unbending obedience to rules and discipline — originally a military officer, now any boss, teacher or bureaucrat who drills people over the letter of the law.

The word is always an insult, and it lands on a specific target: not toughness, but pettiness dressed as rigour. A disciplinarian can be admired; a stickler is merely fussy about details. A martinet has power over subordinates and uses it on trivia — the untucked shirt, the form filed in the wrong colour of ink — while the point of the rule goes unnoticed.
Martinet is one letter off marionette — he wants everyone moving on his strings, in step, no slack.
The sound-echo carries the nuance: it's not discipline for its own sake but control over how other people move.
1. The new headmaster proved a martinet, measuring hemlines at the gate and logging each infraction in a leather ledger.
2. Our shift manager's a total martinet — clock in at 9:01 and you'll hear about it all week.
Gunnery Sergeant Hartman in Full Metal Jacket — the screaming, boot-polish-inspecting drill instructor is the word made flesh.
A real man: Jean Martinet, drillmaster to Louis XIV, who turned the French infantry into the best-drilled army in Europe through relentless parade-ground repetition. His name became the word for the type — and in French, martinet also came to mean a small whip used on schoolchildren.

Eponyms like this are worth collecting: boycott, chauvinist, maverick, quixotic — all people first, insults second.

Sentimental to the point of being sickening.
Sickly sentimental — emotional in a way that's laid on so thick it stops being moving and starts being nauseating.

Two things do the work here. It is always an insult, and the insult is about excess, not about feeling. A film can be sad, tender, even sappy and survive; call it mawkish and you're saying the emotion was manufactured, over-sugared, and it turned your stomach. It's a critic's word — cool, faintly superior, spoken by someone who is refusing to be moved.
Mawkish = a maw-ful of kiss — sweetness pushed down your gullet until you gag.
The word never means emotional; it means emotion so overdone that the body rejects it.
1. The eulogy slid from moving into mawkish the instant he began reciting song lyrics.
2. I wanted to like the ending, but it got so mawkish I had to look at my phone.
A house word of film and book reviewers: when a critic wants to say a tearjerker overplayed its hand, mawkish is the verdict — it carries a sneer that plain sentimental doesn't.
From Middle English mawke = "maggot" (via Old Norse mathkr). Mawkish first meant simply sickening, nauseating — maggot-ridden — and only later narrowed to one specific thing that makes you queasy: too much sugar in the feelings.

That buried disgust is the whole point of the word. It isn't "a bit soppy"; it's revolting.
