column2:
To step between two sides and broker an agreement.
To step between two opposed parties and help them reach agreement. Also, more abstractly, to be the middle thing through which something passes: screens mediate almost every conversation we have.

The key limit is power. A mediator has none — she shuttles, reframes, coaxes, and if the two sides refuse, nothing happens. An arbitrator hears both sides and rules, and the ruling binds. A judge does the same with the state behind her. So "the UN mediated a ceasefire" quietly tells you the parties agreed to it; nobody was made to.

The second sense is a favourite of academic prose — mediated by, meaning "transmitted through / brought about by way of" — and on the GRE it usually shows up in exactly that flat, technical register.
⚠️ mediate ≠ meditate. One letter apart. Mediate = go between two sides; meditate = sit alone with your own mind. A monk meditates; a diplomat mediates.
Media is sitting inside mediate — and the media carries messages, it doesn't hand down verdicts.
A mediator is a channel between two sides, which is exactly why she can broker a deal but never impose one.
1. Two neighbouring states, unwilling to speak directly, asked a retired ambassador to mediate the dispute over water rights.
2. Mum had to mediate between us for about an hour before either of us would admit anything.
Divorce and workplace mediation is the everyday version: you sit in separate rooms, the mediator walks between them, and if you won't agree, the whole thing collapses and you go to court instead — the powerlessness is the point.
Latin medius = "middle." The whole family is just positions relative to the middle: medium (the stuff in between), median (the middle value), intermediate, Mediterranean ("middle of the earth"), and mediocre — literally middling, which is why it's an insult.

Best of the lot: immediate = im- (not) + mediate — nothing in the middle. No go-between, no delay. That's why it means right now.

Habitual untruthfulness; lying as a character trait.
Untruthfulness — lying, especially as a habit or a condition rather than a single act.

A lie is a thing you told; mendacity is a thing you are, or a climate a whole household or institution breathes. That's why it lands so much harder than dishonesty: it is formal, faintly literary, and openly damning. Nobody calls their own fib mendacity. You use the word when you want to indict — to say the falsehood is systematic and the liar is corrupt through and through.
⚠️ mendacity ≠ mendicancy.
- mendacious = lying
- mendicant = begging (a mendicant friar lives on alms)

A beggar isn't a liar. Different Latin root entirely.
-acity names a standing quality: ten*acity*, ver*acity*, mend*acity*. It's the anti-veracity.
The suffix tells you this is a permanent trait, not one occasion — tenacity isn't one grip and mendacity isn't one lie.
1. The report exposed a culture of mendacity at the highest levels: falsified figures, doctored minutes, and three years of denials.
2. After the fourth version of his story, we stopped calling it a misunderstanding — the guy's mendacity was the whole problem.
Tennessee Williams's Cat on a Hot Tin Roof runs on this word — Brick keeps naming the family's rot as mendacity, "a system that we live in." It's the play's central accusation.
Latin mendum = "a fault, a blemish." A mendax is someone with a defect in his speech — a liar.

Same root, opposite direction: to a·mend or e·mend is to remove the fault, and plain mend is the worn-down English version. So mending fixes the flaw; mendacity is the flaw.

Motivated only by money; a soldier who fights for pay.
Noun: a soldier who fights for whoever pays him, not for a country or a cause.
Adjective: motivated purely by money.

The insult isn't plain greed. Greedy means wanting more; mercenary means money has taken the place of a motive that should have been there — loyalty, conviction, love of the work. A greedy doctor overcharges; a mercenary doctor only treats you because you can pay. That's why it stings when applied to artists, lawyers, athletes, friends: it says the cheque is doing all the work.
Mercenary hides commerce — he doesn't pick a side, he picks a buyer.
Same merc- as commerce and merchant: to him the war, the case, or the song is just stock to be sold.
1. Renaissance city-states defended themselves with mercenary companies, who decamped the instant a richer prince made an offer.
2. He's not disloyal exactly — just mercenary; wave a bigger salary at him and he's gone by Friday.
Deadpool, "the Merc with a Mouth" — merc is short for mercenary, and the whole joke is that he'll take any job from anyone for the right fee.
Latin mercēs, mercēdis = "wages, pay" → mercēnārius, "a hired hand." Same merc- root as commerce, merchant, market, mercantile — all the language of buying and selling.

The odd cousin: mercy. Wages → reward → the reward God grants → compassion. (And Mercedes is Spanish for "mercies," from the same word.)

Volatile in mood — brilliant, quick, impossible to predict.
Liable to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood or behaviour — volatile, quick-changing, hard to pin down.

Tone separates it from its neighbours. Fickle implies disloyalty; volatile implies danger; capricious implies whim exercised over other people. Mercurial carries a flicker of glamour — it's the word for the brilliant, quick-witted, temperamental one, so it often attaches to artists, strikers and star CEOs. The person is exhausting, but you're half-impressed.
⚠️ mercurial ≠ mercenary. Same merc- root, opposite charge: mercurial = moody and unpredictable; mercenary = coldly motivated by money. A mercurial manager throws chairs; a mercenary one sells you out.
Mercury in a thermometer — shoots up, drops back, and never sits still.
The only metal that won't hold a shape gives you both halves of the word: rapid swings, and a bright silvery shine that makes you watch anyway.
1. His mercurial temperament made him magnificent in rehearsal and impossible in negotiation.
2. She's brilliant, but she's mercurial — text her at ten and you'll get a different answer than at nine.
Football commentary runs on this word: the "mercurial" No. 10 — Gascoigne, Ronaldinho, Mbappé — dazzling one week, invisible the next. If you've heard a pundit say it, you've already got the meaning.
From Mercury, the Roman messenger god — winged heels, fastest of the gods, patron of merchants, travellers and thieves. Hence the metal mercury (quicksilver), which rolls away from your finger, and the planet, the quickest around the sun.

The root is Latin merx, mercis = goods, merchandise — which also gives commerce, merchant, market, mercenary. Speed and slipperiness came from the god; money came from the root.

column2:
Deserving of praise or official reward; creditable, commendable.
Deserving of praise, reward, or honour — worthy on the strength of what was actually done.

This is praise handed downward from an institution: the army, the court, the citation on a plaque. Admirable is what a friend says about you; meritorious is what the commendation letter says. It attaches to acts and service, rarely to a person directly — meritorious conduct, meritorious service, a meritorious career. It also carries a faint whiff of the dutiful: solid, creditable, worth a medal, but not dazzling.

Legal sense worth knowing: a meritorious claim is one with genuine legal substance — the opposite of frivolous.
⚠️ meritorious ≠ meretricious.
- meritorious = deserving of reward (Latin merēre, to earn)
- meretricious = gaudy, showily fake (Latin meretrix, prostitute)

Nearly the same letters, opposite verdicts: one earns the medal, the other is cheap glitter.
Merit + -orious, like glorious — the merit is the public, medal-pinning kind.
The word wears its root on its sleeve; the -orious ending tells you the praise is formal and announced, not a quiet pat on the back.
1. The tribunal restored his pension in recognition of forty years of meritorious service.
2. She got a meritorious mention for the science fair — solid work, but nobody's calling it genius.
The US military's Meritorious Service Medal — awarded for outstanding non-combat service. The word survives mainly on citations and plaques, which is exactly its register.
Latin merēre / meritum = "to earn, to deserve." The same root gives you merit, demerit, meritocracy (rule by the deserving), and emeritus — the professor who has earned his retirement and keeps the title.

Figurative, not literal — meaning carried across by comparison.
Not literal — meaning something by comparison rather than by fact. A metaphorical wall isn't made of brick; a metaphorical death is a career ending.

The word is almost always doing defensive work: it flags that a statement should not be taken at face value. That makes it the standing opposite of literal, and on the GRE it usually turns up as exactly that hinge ("a metaphorical, not a literal, reading of the text"). Register is neutral and slightly bookish — critics and essayists use it constantly; in speech it survives mainly as the hedge metaphorically speaking.
⚠️ metaphorical ≠ metaphysical.
- metaphorical = figurative, by comparison
- metaphysical = to do with ultimate reality — being, time, existence

A metaphorical journey is a career change. A metaphysical question is whether the journey is real at all.
If you can add "…so to speak" after it, it's metaphorical.
That little disclaimer is precisely the job the word does — warning you off the literal reading.
1. The poem's shipwreck is metaphorical: nothing sinks but the marriage.
2. "I said I'd kill for a coffee — that was metaphorical, put the knife down."
Greek meta- (across) + pherein (to carry) — a metaphor carries meaning across from one thing to another. Latin built the same word out of its own parts: trans + ferre = transfer. Metaphor and transfer are the same idea in two languages.

pherein keeps paying: phosphorus (light-carrier), semaphore (sign-carrier), amphora (carried by two handles), euphoria (carrying yourself well), Christopher (Christ-bearer).

Extremely careful with small details, almost anxiously so.
Showing extreme, exacting care with small details — nothing skipped, nothing approximate.

It's a compliment, but a slightly wincing one: meticulous people are admired and exhausting. Compare the neighbours — careful is ordinary diligence; fastidious is fussy and hard to please; punctilious is stiff about rules and etiquette; scrupulous is moral, about honesty rather than accuracy. Meticulous is purely about the detail work, and it carries a faint whiff of anxiety — the person who checks the figures a fourth time because a third wasn't enough.
me-TIC-ulous — the stressed syllable is a tick: every box on the checklist gets one.
The word's own accent lands on the tick-mark, which is exactly what a meticulous person does to every item, however small.
1. The restorer's meticulous work was invisible by design: four months of labour, and the canvas looked untouched.
2. He's meticulous about his coffee — scale, timer, thermometer, the whole ritual before eight in the morning.
"Meticulous attention to detail" is one of the most-used phrases in job ads and CVs — which tells you the register instantly: it's the professional world's highest-status form of fussiness.
Latin metus = "fear" → meticulosus = "full of fear, timid." In English it meant frightened right up to the 1800s, and only then slid into today's sense.

That slide is the whole word: meticulous care is care born of fear of getting it wrong. The anxious undertone isn't your imagination — it's the original meaning showing through.

column2:
Full of spirit and courage; gutsy, eager, hard to daunt.
Full of mettle — spirited, plucky, brave and eager, not easily daunted.

It's courage plus liveliness. A stoic is brave; a mettlesome person is brave and straining at the leash. The word is admiring but faintly amused — the classic subject is a mettlesome horse, all fire and hard to hold, and applied to a person it carries that same flavour of spirit that might be a little too much for the bridle. Slightly old-fashioned and literary; you'd meet it in a novel or a toast, rarely in an email.
⚠️ mettlesome ≠ meddlesome.
- mettlesome = full of fighting spirit (a compliment)
- meddlesome = always interfering in other people's business (an insult)

One letter apart, opposite verdicts.
Mettlesome is made of metal — steel in the spine; meddlesome just gets in the middle.
The tt spelling is literally the metal one, so hear "tempered steel" for spirit and "middle" for the busybody.
1. The regiment's mettlesome young lieutenants were forever volunteering for the reconnaissance no one else wanted.
2. She's a mettlesome kid — told the coach to his face she should be starting, and she wasn't wrong.
You already know the noun: "test your mettle", "prove his mettle" — sports commentary and job interviews run on it. Mettlesome is just the adjective for someone who has plenty to test.
Mettle is metal — the same word. English used metal figuratively for the stuff a person was made of (like tempered steel), and by around 1700 the two spellings split: metal for the substance, mettle for the temperament.

So "what is he made of?" is not a metaphor bolted on afterwards — it's the literal history of the word.

column2:
To copy someone's voice or manner closely, often mockingly.
Verb: to copy someone's speech, gestures or appearance closely — usually to amuse or mock. Noun: someone good at it. Adj.: imitative, fake (a mimic battle).

Mimicking is surface copying, and it points at its target. Imitate is neutral and can be sincere; emulate is admiring — you copy the excellence, not the mannerisms. A mimic copies the tics: the vowel, the walk, the throat-clearing. That's why it slides so easily into ridicule — reproducing someone exactly is one of the oldest ways of making a room laugh at them.

It also has a straight technical sense with no mockery at all: in biology, a harmless hoverfly mimics a wasp; in engineering, one system mimics another's output.
mi-mic — the word copies its own first two letters. So does the mimic.
The doubling is the definition: a mimic reproduces the surface of a thing, exactly and visibly.
1. Certain harmless snakes survive by mimicking the banded colouring of far deadlier species.
2. He mimicked the manager's little cough so well that everyone stopped laughing when the manager walked in.
The mockingbird's scientific name is Mimus polyglottos — literally "many-tongued mimic". Its entire act is stealing other birds' songs.
Greek mimos = "imitator, actor" — a performer who copied people on stage.

One root, a full family: mime, pantomime, mimicry, mimetic, and mimeograph (the old duplicating machine — literally a "copy-writer").

Extremely small; or so detailed it misses nothing.
1. Exceedingly small — small to the point of being hard to detect. 2. Of an examination or account: going into the tiniest particulars; painstakingly detailed.

Tiny is casual and minuscule just insists on smallness, but minute implies an observer straining to see — it's the word for cracks, traces, discrepancies, quantities under a microscope. That's why it slides so naturally into sense 2: if you're noticing things that small, you're being exhaustively thorough. "A minute inspection" isn't a short one — it's one that missed nothing.
my-NEWT — small as a newt, and you'd need a close look to spot one.
The correct pronunciation hands you the meaning: newt-sized, and only visible to someone actually looking hard.
1. Forensic analysis turned up minute traces of accelerant on the doorframe, invisible to the naked eye.
2. He gave me a minute account of his flight delay — every gate change, in order.
The minutes of a meeting are the same word: medieval Latin minuta scriptura, "small writing" — the record of the small details. Take the minutes (MIN-its) by writing down the minute (my-NOOT) points.
Latin minuere = "to lessen", past participle minutus = "made small." That root is a GRE goldmine: minus, minor, diminish, diminutive, minutiae, minimal, mince (to cut small).

The clock word comes from the same place — pars minuta prima, the "first small part" of an hour. The second is pars minuta secunda, the second small part.

Hating humanity in general, not any one person.
Hating, distrusting, or wanting nothing to do with humankind in general.

The scope is what defines it: this isn't a grudge against your neighbour, it's a low opinion of the whole species — people are selfish, stupid, and best avoided. It's a settled worldview rather than a mood, which is why it sounds almost philosophical, and why it's often used with a grin (a misanthropic old bachelor who feeds the cat and no one else). Compare hostile (aimed at someone), cynical (doubts motives, still shows up), antisocial (avoids people without necessarily despising them).
Philanthropic loves anthropos; misanthropic hates him — same humans, opposite prefix.
Both words point at humanity as a whole, so the misanthrope doesn't hate you — he hates humans, and you happen to be one.
1. His later essays grew steadily more misanthropic, treating civilisation as a mistake that had merely taken a long time to become obvious.
2. Two days of airport queues and I was feeling pretty misanthropic by the end of it.
The Grinch is the pop-culture misanthrope in full: he doesn't have a quarrel with any particular Who, he just can't stand Whos.
Greek misein (to hate) + anthrōpos (human being).

Both halves pay off elsewhere: misein gives misogyny (+ gynē, woman) and misandry (+ anēr, man); anthrōpos gives anthropology, anthropomorphic, and — with philein, to love — philanthropy, the exact mirror image.

A wrongdoer or troublemaker, named with dry, lofty contempt.
Noun: a wrongdoer, a villain, someone who behaves badly. Adjective: depraved, unprincipled.

Scale and tone are what you're buying. A criminal is a legal category; a miscreant is a moral judgement delivered from a height — the word is faintly archaic and very often dry or amused. Headmasters, magistrates and narrators use it. It fits the boys who egged the car far better than it fits a murderer, and when it is used of someone genuinely dangerous, the effect is deliberately arch, as though the speaker refuses to grant them the dignity of a bigger word.
miscre-ANT — a pest, not a predator.
The word literally ends in ant, which is the right size for it: miscreants are scurrying nuisances you sweep up, not monsters you flee.
1. The magistrate surveyed the row of miscreants with the weary contempt of a man who had seen this exact crime forty times before.
2. Some miscreant has been nicking my lunch from the office fridge.
Indian newspaper English keeps this word alive daily: \"unidentified miscreants set fire to two buses overnight.\" It's the standard police-blotter term for troublemakers nobody has managed to name yet.
Old French mescreant = "disbelieving" — mes- (wrongly) + creant, from Latin credere, "to believe." A miscreant was originally a heretic or infidel; since medieval Europe assumed the wrong faith meant the wrong morals, "unbeliever" slid into "scoundrel."

Credere is a workhorse root: credit, credible, creed, credential, credulous, incredulous — and recreant (one who re-believes, i.e. surrenders: a coward, a traitor).

Hoarding money meanly; stingy to a pitiful degree.
Extremely unwilling to spend or give — hoarding money out of greed, and living meanly in the process.

This is not thrift. Frugal is a compliment, thrifty is neutral, miserly is contempt: the person has more than enough and still won't part with it, denying others and themselves. The word carries a whiff of the pitiful — a miser sitting cold in a dark room to save on coal. It also travels beyond money: you can be miserly with praise, miserly with detail, which means grudging and withholding, never merely economical.
MISERLY has MISERY buried in it — stinginess that makes the hoarder wretched too.
The overlap is real, not a coincidence: both words come from Latin miser, "wretched," which is exactly the judgment the word passes on the hoarder.
1. He left a fortune of nine million pounds and a house with no heating — a miserly end to a miserly life.
2. Don't be miserly with the cheese, mate, it's a pizza not a rice cracker.
Ebenezer Scrooge in A Christmas Carol is the miser the word was made for — rich, freezing, refusing Bob Cratchit an extra lump of coal.
Latin miser = "wretched, pitiable." Note what that means: the root doesn't describe hoarding at all — it describes the state of the hoarder, which is the built-in verdict.

Same root: misery, miserable, commiserate (to be wretched together = to sympathise), and the Miserere psalm ("have mercy").

A name that's flatly wrong for the thing it names.
A name or term that is wrong or misleading for the thing it's attached to — "jellyfish" is a misnomer, since it's neither jelly nor fish.

The word polices labels, not facts. A misnomer says the name is inaccurate; it makes no claim that people are fooled or that anything important is at stake. Tone is dry and mildly pedantic — the voice of someone correcting a caption, not exposing a lie. It carries no accusation of dishonesty: most misnomers are historical accidents nobody bothered to fix.
⚠️ misnomer ≠ misconception.
- misnomer = the name is wrong ("peanut" is a misnomer — it's a legume)
- misconception = the belief is wrong (that peanuts are nuts is a misconception)

"It's a misnomer that goldfish have three-second memories" is the classic misuse — that's a misconception. No name is being challenged.
mis-NOM-er — a mis-nom. Nom is French for name, as in nom de plume.
Hear the nom buried in the middle and the word tells you it's the label that's wrong, not the idea.
1. "Civil war" is something of a misnomer for a conflict fought largely by foreign mercenaries.
2. Calling that a starter salad is a misnomer — it's three olives and a leaf.
Voltaire on the Holy Roman Empire: "neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire." Three misnomers in one name.
Old French mesnomer = mes- ("wrongly") + nommer ("to name"), from Latin nomen, name.

That root is everywhere on the GRE: nominate (put a name forward), nominal (in name only), nomenclature (a naming system), denomination, noun, and ignominy (ig- + nomen — literally namelessness, i.e. disgrace).

To make a bad thing less severe, not to remove it.
To make something bad less severe — to soften the force of a harm, penalty, or risk without removing it.

The damage still happens; you are only turning the dial down. That built-in limitation is the whole point: a seawall mitigates flooding, it doesn't prevent it. Compare alleviate, which relieves suffering (pain, hunger, a burden) and is warmer and more human — mitigate is cooler and more institutional, the verb of insurers, engineers, judges and climate reports: mitigate risk, mitigate damages, mitigate emissions. Applied to a person's conduct it means makes the offence look less bad rather than excuses it.
⚠️ mitigate ≠ militate.
- mitigate X = soften X
- militate against X = count as strong evidence against X (military root — the facts are fighting your case)

"Mitigate against" is the classic error: you mitigate a problem; evidence militates against a conclusion.
A mitten doesn't stop the punch — it just takes the sting out.
Mit-igate is padding, not armour: the blow still lands, only softer.
1. The court accepted that his youth and cooperation mitigated the offence, and reduced the sentence accordingly.
2. We can't stop the outage, but rolling back that one service should mitigate the damage.
Any courtroom drama's sentencing scene: the defence stands up to plead mitigating circumstances. Guilt is already settled — all that's left to argue is how hard the punishment lands.
Latin mitis = "mild, soft" + agere = "to make, drive" — literally to make mild.

That -igate ending is agere in disguise, and it recurs: fumigate (make smoke), navigate (drive a ship), litigate, castigate, instigate — plus agent, agenda, agile, act.

Unassuming about oneself; or moderate, small, unimpressive in size.
Three related senses, and the GRE leans on the second one:

1. Unassuming — not boastful about your abilities or achievements.
2. Moderate in size or amount — a modest raise, a modest apartment, modest gains.
3. Decorous — restrained in dress or behaviour.

All three share one idea: staying within measure, not overreaching. Sense 2 is where students get caught, because it's evaluative and slightly deflating — a "modest improvement" is real but underwhelming, and calling a house modest is a polite way of saying small. Sense 1 is warm praise, but only when the modesty looks genuine; falsely modest is a standing accusation. Compare humble, which can imply low status or self-abasement — modest implies you have something worth boasting about and decline to.
⚠️ modest ≠ modish. Modish (MOH-dish) means fashionable, in vogue — from mode as in style. One letter apart, near-opposite vibe: the modest dresser avoids attention, the modish dresser chases it.
Modest hides mode — you keep to the measure: modest ego, modest salary, modest hemline.
One idea covers all three senses — nothing exceeds its proper size, whether it's your self-regard, your paycheque, or your outfit.
1. Despite two decades at the frontier of the field, she remained modest about her contribution, crediting her collaborators at every turn.
2. It's a modest flat — one bedroom, no balcony — but the rent is half what I was paying.
Swift's "A Modest Proposal" (1729) — the essay that suggests the Irish poor sell their babies as food. The title is the whole joke: modest promises something small and reasonable, and the proposal is monstrous.
Latin modus = "measure, limit." A modest person keeps within the measure.

That root is worth banking: moderate, modify, modulate, mode, modicum (a small measure), commodious (well-measured, roomy), accommodate.

Fashionable right now — and faintly mocked for it.
Fashionable, stylish, in step with what's current.

But it almost never means elegant. Modish points at the calendar, not at taste: it's fashionable right now, which quietly implies it won't be next year. Call a jacket stylish and you've praised it; call it modish and you've suggested it's chasing something. Writers use it for ideas as much as clothes — a modish theory is one that's trendy in seminar rooms, and the speaker is not impressed.
modish = mode + -ish — in the current mode, with the -ish doing the sneering.
That -ish suffix hedges everywhere it appears (newish, youngish, girlish), and here it downgrades "fashionable" into "merely fashionable."
1. Critics dismissed the novel's fragmented structure as modish — a technique borrowed from whoever was being praised that season.
2. He turned up in some modish little collarless jacket that'll be embarrassing by Christmas.
Pie à la mode. French à la mode = "in the fashion" — ice cream on pie was simply the fashionable way to serve it, and the phrase stuck to the dessert. Same mode sitting inside modish.
French mode = "fashion, manner," from Latin modus = "measure, manner." One root, a big family: mode, model, modern, moderate, modify, à la mode, modus operandi — and outmoded, which is exactly what everything modish eventually becomes.

To soften someone's anger; to soothe and appease.
To soften someone's anger — to calm, appease, pacify a person who is upset.

The object is almost always a person or their feelings (mollify the critics, mollify her fears), never a physical thing. It implies a grievance already exists and you are making a gesture — an apology, a concession, a soothing word — to take the heat out of it. Unlike placate, which can hint at buying someone off, mollify is neutral about the tactic and focused on the result: temperature down. It also carries a whiff of partial success; things are written as "failed to mollify" about as often as they're written the other way.
⚠️ mollify ≠ mortify. Both are Latin -ify verbs about someone's feelings, and they pull opposite ways: mollify = soothe them; mortify = humiliate them.
Mollify = "mellow-fy" — you make the angry person mellow again.
The sound is nearly mellow, and that's exactly the job: not fixing the problem, just lowering the temperature of the person.
1. The chairman's carefully worded statement did little to mollify shareholders, who had come for a resignation, not a paragraph.
2. I brought her coffee to mollify her after showing up forty minutes late.
It's a newsroom staple: whenever a company apologises and the market shrugs, the report reads "the statement failed to mollify investors." Watch for it in any coverage of a corporate scandal.
Latin mollis = "soft" + -ficare (to make). To mollify is literally to make soft.

Same root: emollient — the moisturiser that softens skin — and mollusc, the soft-bodied creature in the hard shell.

Lasting only an instant; over almost as soon as it starts.
Lasting only a moment — a few seconds, gone almost as soon as it arrives.

It is the shortest word in its family: temporary can run for months, transient for a season, ephemeral carries a whiff of beauty and loss. Momentary is plain and clinical about duration — and it usually does quiet defensive work, framing something as too brief to count against you: a momentary lapse, a momentary hesitation, a momentary flash of anger. Say a failure was momentary and you are asking for it to be waved off.
⚠️ momentary ≠ momentous.
- momentary = lasting a moment (how long)
- momentous = weighty, historic (how much)

A momentary pause before signing; a momentous decision to sign.
-ary measures the clock; -ous measures the weight.
Momentary tells you a thing lasted one moment, momentous tells you it was full of moment — heavy, consequential.
1. The truce proved momentary; artillery resumed before the envoys had left the room.
2. There was a momentary panic when I couldn't find my passport, then I remembered it was in my jacket.
Pink Floyd's 1987 album A Momentary Lapse of Reason — and "momentary lapse" is the phrase the word lives in most naturally.
Latin momentum — originally the tiny weight that tips a balance scale (from movēre, "to move"). That one image split two ways: the instant it takes to tip → moment, momentary; the weight doing the tipping → momentous, momentum.

Unchanging to the point of dullness; tediously samey.
Unvarying to the point of tedium — the same note, the same task, the same view, on and on.

The word carries a verdict, not just a description. Repetitive can be neutral (repetitive strain, a repetitive motif); monotonous always means the sameness has worn you down. It's a complaint about the effect on the listener or worker: attention slides off, the mind goes numb. It works on sound (a droning voice), on work (data entry), and on landscape (a monotonous stretch of motorway) — anywhere sameness becomes a dull ache.
⚠️ monotonous ≠ monotone. Monotone is literal and narrow — one unchanging pitch, usually of a voice. Monotonous is the judgement — mind-numbingly samey, and applicable to work, scenery, food, anything.
Mono-tone-ous: one tone, no news — nothing changes, so the mind checks out.
The "no news" half is the nuance: the problem isn't repetition itself but the deadening lack of anything new.
1. The report's findings were significant, but delivered in so monotonous a voice that half the committee stopped listening by the second page.
2. Three weeks of packing boxes — the pay was fine, but God, it was monotonous.
Ben Stein's economics teacher in Ferris Bueller's Day Off — "Bueller… Bueller… Bueller…" — is the most famous monotone in film, and the shot of the glazed, half-dead classroom is what monotonous does to people.
Greek monos (one) + tonos (tone, pitch) — literally one-toned. The metaphor did the rest: a voice that never changes pitch became the model for anything that never changes at all.

tonos also gives you tone, intonation, atonal, baritone, and tonic.

Bitingly sarcastic; sharp, dark, clever criticism.
Adjective: biting and caustic in style — sharply, darkly critical.
Noun (technical): a chemical that bites into fabric so dye will fix to it.

The sting is intellectual. A cruel remark is just cruel; a mordant one is clever, dry, usually funny, and lands because it's true. The word half-praises the speaker even as it flays the target — critics, satirists and obituarists get called mordant, playground bullies never do.
⚠️ mordant ≠ moribund. Same mor- look, opposite Latin roots: mordēre (to bite) vs morī (to die). A mordant reviewer is very much alive; a moribund industry is on its way out.
A mordant line leaves more dents — teeth marks, not bruises.
Say it fast and "mordant" is "more dent": precise little bites of wit, not blunt-force insult.
1. Her memoir is mordant about the literary world that raised and then quietly discarded her.
2. He's got this mordant sense of humour — you laugh, then realise he just destroyed you.
Still a live technical word in dyeing: alum is the classic mordant, the thing that bites the colour into the cloth so it won't wash out — the same bite the adjective describes.
Latin mordēre = "to bite." Same root gives remorse (guilt that bites you back), morsel (a little bite), and the musical mordent (a quick nipped note).

Gloomy and sullen; sad in an unsociable, brooding way.
Gloomy, sullen, and ill-humoured with it — sunk in a bad mood and closed off to anyone trying to lift it.

Sad and morose are not interchangeable. Sad is pain you feel; morose is a mood other people have to put up with. It's sourness turned outward — the one-word answers, the refusal to be cheered, the black cloud parked at the end of the table. Calling someone morose carries a faint edge of blame: they're not just unhappy, they're being difficult about it.
morose ≠ morbid.
- morose = sullen, gloomy mood
- morbid = unhealthy fascination with death, disease, the gruesome

A morbid person can be perfectly cheerful about the autopsy photos.
There's a rose hidden inside morose — hand him one and he still won't smile.
The word isn't plain sadness but gloom that resists comfort, which is exactly why it grates on everyone nearby.
1. After the verdict he grew morose, taking his meals alone and answering letters in a single line.
2. Don't mind Dad — he goes morose for a week every time his team gets relegated.
Eeyore in Winnie-the-Pooh is the picture of morose — the flat monotone, the drooping tail, the way every attempt to cheer him up bounces straight off.
Latin mōrōsus = "peevish, set in one's ways," from mōs, mōris = "custom, habit, one's own will." The original sense was a person rigidly wedded to their own manner — hence prickly and hard to please.

That root also gives moral, morals, mores, morality.

🚫 Not from mors, "death." That's the mort- family — mortal, morbid, mortuary, moribund. Look-alike syllable, unrelated word.

Having many distinct sides or talents — and that's praise.
Having many distinct sides, aspects, or talents — a problem with several dimensions, a person good at several things.

The word flatters. Complicated and convoluted treat many-sidedness as a burden; multifaceted treats it as richness — depth, range, something rewarding to turn over. It's the word a citation or a profile piece uses ("a multifaceted career", "a multifaceted approach"), which also makes it faintly corporate when overused. Applied to an issue it means don't expect one cause; applied to a person it means don't put them in one box.
A facet is a little face — and a multifaceted thing has many, every one of them flattering.
The hidden word face gives you the meaning, and the gem-cutting sense reminds you the term is praise, not complaint.
1. The commission's report treats homelessness as a multifaceted crisis, resisting the temptation to name a single villain.
2. She's the most multifaceted person on the team — codes, negotiates, and somehow runs the offsite.
Job ads and performance reviews run on it: "a multifaceted role" is HR for you'll be doing five jobs, and "a multifaceted contributor" is the compliment you get instead of a raise.
From French facette, "little face" — the flat cut surfaces a jeweller grinds onto a gemstone, so a diamond literally has facets. Behind it, Latin facies = face, form.

Same root: facade (the face of a building), surface, efface and deface (rub out / spoil the face).

Ordinary and earthly — dull by routine, not by offence.
Ordinary, everyday, unremarkable — and by extension dull because it is routine. A second, older sense survives in formal writing: of this world, earthly rather than spiritual.

The dullness of mundane is the dullness of laundry, expense reports, and the school run. Compare its neighbours: banal sneers at something stale and unoriginal, tedious says it actively wears you out, prosaic says it lacks poetry. Mundane passes no such judgement — it simply places a thing at ground level, among the chores. Which is why it can be used with no contempt at all ("the mundane details of running a household") or with a quiet sigh, depending entirely on what it's set against.
MUNdane starts like Monday — the world's most routine, ground-level day.
Monday isn't offensive or exhausting, just relentlessly ordinary — exactly the flavour of dull that mundane carries.
1. After a decade of war reporting, he found the mundane rhythms of village life almost unbearable in their gentleness.
2. I had big plans for the weekend and spent it on mundane stuff — bins, laundry, a dentist form.
In fantasy fiction, ordinary non-magical humans get called mundanes — Cassandra Clare's The Mortal Instruments and the Shadowhunters series use it constantly. It's the word's original sense fossilised: people of this world, not the other one.
Latin mundus = "the world." So mundane first meant worldly — the earthly realm as opposed to the heavenly one. Once you're stuck down here with the taxes and the dishes, "worldly" slides naturally into "everyday," and "everyday" slides into "boring."

Same root in extramundane (beyond this world) and demimonde (French monde, "world" — the half-world of the socially disreputable).

Extremely generous, on a grand and public scale.
Extremely generous in giving — lavish, large-scale, open-handed.

Anyone can be generous; munificent carries the size of the gift and the standing of the giver. It's the word for a patron endowing a library wing, not a friend picking up the bill. The tone is formal and admiring — it's praise offered publicly, usually to someone with real means, and it always points at the scale of what was handed over.
munificent ≠ magnificent. Magnificent = splendid to look at; munificent = splendid in what it gives away. A munificent donor might fund a magnificent building.
Munificent = money-ficent — money made into a gift, and a big one.
The sound hook also carries the nuance: cash on a scale worth announcing, not small change.
1. The new research institute owes its existence to a munificent bequest from a former student.
2. He left a munificent tip — the waiter actually chased him down the street to check it wasn't a mistake.
Read the plaques in any university building: "Made possible by the munificent gift of…" — fundraising offices reach for this word precisely because it flatters the size of the cheque.
Latin munus = "gift, public duty" + facere = "to make" — literally gift-making.

That root pays out widely: remuneration (paying back), immune (exempt from public duty), community and commune (duties shared together), municipal (a town that takes on its own duties).

Revolt by subordinates against their own commanders.
Open revolt against lawful authority by the very people bound to obey it — classically sailors against their captain, soldiers against their officers. As a verb, to rise up in this way.

The word is institutional, not political. A population rebels; a crew mutinies. It presumes a chain of command, an oath, and a punishment — mutiny is a criminal charge under naval and military law, and historically a hanging offence. That's why it carries such force when borrowed for civilian life: calling the marketing team's revolt a mutiny casts the boss as a captain and the staff as insubordinate crew.
MY-tiny: a mutiny is always my own people — the ones sworn to take my orders.
Strangers can riot against you, but only your subordinates can mutiny.
1. Three officers were court-martialled for mutiny after they refused to weigh anchor.
2. One more mandatory Saturday and there'll be a full mutiny in the design team.
Mutiny on the Bounty — the real 1789 event and the films: Fletcher Christian and the crew seize the ship and set Captain Bligh adrift in an open boat. Textbook case, textbook word.
Latin movēre = "to move" → Old French mutin, "rebellious," from meute, "an uprising." A mutiny is literally a body of men set in motion against their commander.

That root is a GRE workhorse: motion, motive, momentum, emotion, promote, remove, mobile — all people or things being moved.

Short-sighted — literally, or blind to anything beyond the immediate.
Literally: nearsighted — able to focus on what's close, blurry on anything far off.
Figuratively (the GRE sense): unable to see past the immediate — planning, judging, or governing with no view of long-term consequences.

It's an accusation of narrow vision, not low intelligence. A myopic policy is usually a clever solution to this quarter's problem that wrecks the next decade. Compare ignorant (doesn't know) or foolish (can't reason): the myopic person sees perfectly well — just not far enough. It carries a faint condescension, the tone of an analyst or editorial writer, and almost always attaches to institutions, strategies, and outlooks rather than to people's characters.
MY-opic: all I can see is MY desk, MY quarter, MY problem — right now.
The word opens with my, which is exactly the radius of a myopic view: close, immediate, and no further.
1. The commission's report condemned a myopic energy strategy that secured cheap fuel for a decade and left the grid defenceless thereafter.
2. Cancelling training to hit the numbers this month is pretty myopic — who exactly is going to do the work in June?
It's on your glasses prescription: a minus number in the sphere column means myopia. Every optometrist uses the word literally, which is why the figurative insult lands so cleanly.
Greek myein (to shut, to close) + ōps (eye) — literally "shut-eye," from the squint nearsighted people make to sharpen a distant blur.

ōps / opt- is worth banking: optic, synopsis (a seeing-together), autopsy (seeing for oneself), biopsy, Cyclops.

The absolute lowest point of a decline or fortune.
The lowest point — of a career, a mood, a market, a nation's fortunes. In astronomy, the point on the celestial sphere directly beneath you, opposite the zenith.

It is a superlative, and usually a retrospective one: you survey a whole arc and name the single deepest trough in it. "A low point" is casual and can be one of several; the nadir is a verdict, and there is only one. The register is formal and faintly grand — which is why it stings: it dignifies the collapse even as it measures it.
Nay, dear — it does not get lower than this.
The sound gives you both halves of the word: the flat nay of rock bottom, and the finality — there's exactly one nadir, not a series of bad days.
1. The winter of 1943 marked the nadir of the regime's fortunes, and every general in the room knew it.
2. Eating cold beans over the sink at 2am was, I think, the nadir of my twenties.
Earth-observation satellites are described as looking "at nadir" — camera pointed straight down at the ground directly below. Every satellite image you've scrolled past on Google Maps is a nadir view.
Arabic naẓīr as-samt = "counterpart of the zenith" — the point diametrically opposite overhead. That same as-samt gave English azimuth, and a garbled copy of it gave zenith.

So one Arabic phrase hands you three words at once: zenith (top), nadir (bottom), azimuth (bearing). Medieval European astronomers took their star vocabulary wholesale from Arabic — as algebra, algorithm and alcohol also attest.

Too trusting and inexperienced to see how the world works.
Lacking the experience or judgement to see how things really work — trusting too easily, expecting the world to be simpler and kinder than it is.

It is not an accusation of stupidity. Calling someone naive faults their judgement while excusing their motives: they were unspoiled, not dishonest — which is why it can land as gentle indulgence ("sweetly naive") or as a put-down ("don't be naive"), depending entirely on who says it. Gullible is narrower — it means you actually got taken in. Ingenuous is the warm version — frank and unguarded, no fault implied.

There's also a flatly neutral technical use: naive art (untrained painters like Rousseau), and naive subjects in an experiment — people with no prior exposure to the thing being tested.
Naive rhymes with believe — the naive believe you.
The flaw isn't intelligence, it's that nothing has yet taught them to doubt.
1. The proposal rests on the naive assumption that goodwill alone will hold the ceasefire together.
2. Don't be naive — nobody upgrades your seat for free without wanting something.
The Kooks' 2006 hit "Naïve" — one of the most-played British indie singles of that decade, and a song addressed to exactly the kind of person the word describes.
French naïf / naïve, from Latin nativus = "inborn, natural" — from nasci, "to be born." A naive person is still in the state they were born in: untouched, untested, no experience layered on top.

That root is a GRE workhorse: native, natal, nascent, innate, nation, nature, renaissance (re-birth).

column2:
Excessive self-love that demands constant admiration from others.
Excessive self-love: an inflated sense of one's own importance, appearance, or talent, paired with a hunger for admiration and a thin skin about criticism. In psychology it names a personality disorder (NPD); in ordinary speech it's a charge you level at someone.

Vanity is about the mirror — how you look. Narcissism is about the audience — it needs other people to keep reflecting you back at yourself, and it goes cold when they stop. That's why it reads as a moral failing rather than a harmless foible: the narcissist doesn't just admire himself, he conscripts everyone else into admiring him too, and treats them as props when they won't. Note also the register split — clinicians use it diagnostically and neutrally; everyone else uses it as an insult.
Narcissus needed a mirror. The narcissist needs an audience.
The word has outgrown simple self-admiration — it now describes self-regard that runs on other people's attention.
1. The memoir slides from candour into narcissism by the second chapter, where every historical event exists chiefly to have happened near the author.
2. He calls it confidence; the rest of the team calls it narcissism and books the meeting room without him.
Narcissist has become the internet's favourite diagnosis — therapy-speak TikTok, r/relationships, "narcissistic abuse", the ex who was definitely one. That overuse is itself the lesson: the word now gets thrown at anyone selfish, which is exactly why the GRE will test the stricter sense.
From Narcissus, the beautiful youth of Greek myth who saw his reflection in a pool, fell in love with it, and wasted away staring — dying where he sat. The narcissus flower (the daffodil family) is named for him, said to have sprung up on that spot.

Freud borrowed the myth for the clinical term in 1914, which is how a Greek boy ended up in the DSM.

Just coming into being; newly formed, not yet developed.
Just coming into existence; newly born and still forming, not yet developed enough to judge.

The word points at a thing's earliest stage, with the future left open — a nascent industry, a nascent democracy, a nascent talent. It carries quiet promise and quiet fragility at once: something is genuinely there, but it could still die in the crib. Register is formal-journalistic — you meet it in essays, analyst reports and op-eds, almost never in speech. Note that it attaches to abstractions and movements far more than to people or objects; you'd say a nascent friendship, not a nascent baby.
Nascent = "nay-scent" — the first faint scent of something, before you can name the smell.
It's detectable but not yet defined — exactly the stage the word describes.
1. The treaty gave the nascent republic a border but not yet an economy.
2. She spotted the trend while it was still nascent — three shops in one city — and bought in early.
It's the default adjective of business and tech coverage: the nascent AI market, the nascent EV sector. If a journalist wants to say "this is real but too early to call," this is the word they reach for.
Latin nasci = "to be born" (present participle nascens). Learn this root once and you unlock a crowd: native, natal, prenatal, nativity, nation, innate (born in), cognate (born together), and Renaissance — literally a re-birth.

column2:
Carelessly failing a duty you owed — blameworthy, not merely sloppy.
Failing to give something the care it required — and being at fault for it.

Careless describes a temperament; negligent delivers a judgement. The word presupposes a duty owed — a parent, a driver, a surgeon, a landlord — and says you fell below the standard that duty demanded. That's why it lives so naturally in courtrooms and disciplinary hearings: calling someone careless is a complaint, calling them negligent is an accusation of blame. It also implies omission rather than action: the negligent party didn't do something wrong so much as fail to do the right thing.
⚠️ negligent ≠ negligible.
- negligent = culpably careless
- negligible = so small it can be ignored

A negligent engineer; a negligible difference. The shared root is real — both are things not picked up — but one blames a person, the other dismisses a quantity.
Careless is a habit; negligent is a verdict — you can only be negligent about something you were supposed to be doing.
Test it by asking "who was owed the care?" — if there's an answer, the word is negligent.
1. The inquiry found the shipping line negligent in its maintenance of the hull, and liability followed within the hour.
2. I was negligent with the houseplants for about ten days and now I own six sticks.
Every insurance policy, rental agreement and terms-of-service you've ever clicked through contains a gross negligence clause — the carve-out saying the company still pays if it was really their fault.
Latin neglegere = nec ("not") + legere ("to pick up, gather, read") — literally to not pick something up. What was lying there needing attention, you walked past.

legere is a workhorse root: legible, lecture, elect, select, collect, intelligent (picking between things).

Best of all, its exact opposite comes from the same place: diligent — the one who picks things up carefully.

A beginner, especially one newly admitted or converted.
A beginner — specifically someone newly admitted to a faith, field, craft or organisation.

The weight sits on newly arrived, not merely unskilled. A novice is the plain institutional term (a novice nun, a novice driver); an amateur is about not being paid; a neophyte has just crossed a threshold and been let in, and is being watched by the people already inside. It's a bookish word, and it usually carries a faint condescension from the initiated — you write that someone is a neophyte, you rarely say it to his face.
-phyte sounds like fight: the neophyte is new to the fight — just enlisted, not yet bloodied.
He's been signed up and admitted, which is exactly the point — the ignorance is inside the group, not outside it.
1. Among the veteran traders on the floor she was a neophyte, tolerated but not yet consulted.
2. Don't hand the new guy the Thanksgiving turkey — he's a total neophyte in the kitchen.
Neo in The Matrix — Greek neos, "new," and the entire film is his initiation: unplugged, taken in by people who already know, and told he understands nothing yet. That's a neophyte in one character.
Greek neos (new) + phyton (plant) — literally "newly planted." Early Christian writers used it for the fresh convert: a seedling just put in the ground, roots not yet taken.

Both halves pay off elsewhere: neo- gives neologism, neonatal, Neolithic; -phyte gives epiphyte, zoophyte, phytoplankton.

Irritating and nagging; a persistent, thorny little problem.
Irritating, vexing, causing persistent low-grade trouble.

Scale matters: a nettlesome problem is not a crisis, it's a nagging one — it keeps coming back, it stings, and it refuses to be solved cleanly. Infuriating is hot and loud; nettlesome is cool and bookish, the word a judge, an editorial writer, or a diplomat reaches for. It attaches most naturally to problems, questions, issues, details — the annoyances of the desk rather than of the heart — though a person who won't stop poking at you can be nettlesome too.
⚠️ nettlesome ≠ mettlesome. One letter apart, opposite feeling: mettlesome (from mettle, spirit) = spirited, plucky, full of courage — a compliment, often for a horse or a fighter. Nettlesome irritates you; mettlesome impresses you.
A nettle doesn't wound you — it stings, over and over, and the -some means you get a whole lot of that.
The word encodes its own intensity: repeated small stings, not a single deep cut.
1. The treaty foundered on the nettlesome question of who would police the border.
2. Setting up the printer was fine — it's the nettlesome little driver updates every other week that get me.
Pure courtroom-and-op-ed vocabulary: American judges and political columnists write "a nettlesome question" constantly, precisely because it flags a problem as thorny and unresolved without calling it a disaster.
Straight from the nettle, the weed that stings your ankles — to nettle someone has meant "to irritate" since the 1500s.

The payoff is the suffix: -some = "tending to produce." Lock it once and you get burdensome, troublesome, cumbersome, meddlesome, quarrelsome, loathsome, fulsome, noisome.

To cancel something out, making its force count for nothing.
To make something ineffective or harmless — to cancel out its force. In chemistry, to bring an acid or base to neutral; in politics or sport, to blunt an opponent's advantage; in military and intelligence-speak, to kill.

The word is cold and clinical. Destroy names the violence; neutralize hides it behind a chemistry-lab tone — the threat is simply balanced out of existence. That flatness is why bureaucracies love it: a general "neutralizes" a target, a defender "neutralizes" a striker, an antacid "neutralizes" acid, and the same calm verb covers all three. Note also that it often means cancelled, not removed — a neutralized force is still there, just made to count for nothing.
Put it in neutral — the engine still runs, the car goes nowhere.
Neutralizing doesn't smash the thing, it takes it out of gear so its power stops translating into effect.
1. A single defensive midfielder neutralized their playmaker for ninety minutes; he touched the ball often and changed nothing.
2. Take one of these before dinner — it'll neutralize the acid and you'll sleep fine.
Every antacid ad ever made: "neutralizes excess stomach acid." That's the literal chemistry sense doing all the metaphorical work — acid meets base, and the burn is cancelled.
Latin neuter = "neither" (ne + uter, "not one or the other"). A neutral party is on neither side; to neutralize is to force something into that position of counting for neither side. Same root: neuter, neutral, neutrality, neutron (the particle with neither charge).

Quick and light — in body or in mind.
Quick and light in movement — and, just as often, quick and light in thought.

The praise is for speed and deftness, never for power. A nimble boxer slips the punch instead of trading blows; a nimble mind sidesteps an objection instead of grinding through it. It's a warmer, older word than agile, which has been half-eaten by corporate jargon, and broader than deft, which stays in the hands. Faintly complimentary in every use — nobody is nimble by accident.
Nimble ≈ limber + nifty — light and quick, never strong.
The word always praises evasion and finesse rather than force, whether the thing moving is a body or a brain.
1. The pianist's nimble left hand carried the bass line while the right wandered off into ornament.
2. She's nimble enough in an argument — you never land a punch, she's already three feet to the left.
"Jack be nimble, Jack be quick, Jack jump over the candlestick" — the nursery rhyme is doing the definition for you: nimble sits right next to quick, and the proof is a light little jump.
Old English næmel = "quick to grasp," from niman, "to take" — nimble fingers are fingers quick to take. (The b was slipped in later for ease of saying it, exactly as in thimble and humble.)

Same root, opposite result: numb is literally "taken" — seized, and so robbed of feeling. Nimble hands take; numb hands can't.

column2:
High-born, or high-minded — honourable in a grand, self-sacrificing way.
Adj.: (1) of high birth or aristocratic rank; (2) of high moral character — honourable, generous, willing to lose something for a principle.
Noun: a member of the aristocracy.

Good and kind describe decency at ground level; noble describes decency at altitude. It implies elevation — someone rising above pettiness, self-interest, or revenge, usually at a personal cost. That grandeur is also its weakness in modern speech: because it sounds lofty and faintly antique, "how noble of you" is far more often sarcasm than praise. In science the same idea goes literal — noble gases and noble metals are the ones too aloof to react or corrode.
⚠️ noble ≠ Nobel. Noble (NOH-buhl) is the adjective; Nobel (noh-BEL) is the prize, named after Alfred Nobel, the Swedish inventor of dynamite. The surname has nothing to do with the word — spelling them alike is a standard slip.
The noble gases are too aloof to react; the noble person is too high to stoop.
Both senses turn on standing above the fray rather than merely being nice.
1. She refused the settlement on principle — a noble stand that cost her the contract and half her staff.
2. You cooked, you cleaned, and you let him take the credit? Very noble of you.
Mark Antony over Brutus's body in Julius Caesar: "This was the noblest Roman of them all" — praise for the one conspirator who acted from principle rather than envy. That's the moral sense in a single line.
Latin nōbilis = "knowable, well-known, famous," from noscere, "to know." The nobility were simply the families everybody had heard of — rank was fame first, virtue later.

That root pays out widely: notable, notorious (known, but badly), notice, recognize, cognition — and ignoble, literally "unknown," hence low-born, hence shabby.

column2:
In name only; token-small; or exactly as specified.
1. Existing in name only — the title is real, the power isn't. The nominal head of the family.
2. Of a price or sum: token, so small it's barely a real charge. A nominal fee of £1.
3. Technical (engineering, finance): as specified, on-spec — the stated or expected value, not the adjusted one. Nominal wages, nominal thrust.

Sense 1 is a quiet demotion. It doesn't accuse anyone of fraud — the label is genuine — it just drains it of substance, and it's usually said flatly by someone in a position to know. Sense 2 follows straight from it: a nominal fee is a price in name only, charged so the transaction exists on paper, not to make money.
⚠️ nominal ≠ minimal. Minimal just means very small. Nominal means small because it's only a token — the amount exists to name the thing, not to matter. A nominal charge is symbolic; a minimal charge is merely cheap.
NOM = name. A nominal king is a king in name; a nominal fee is a price in name.
Whatever follows the word is real on the label and hollow in fact.
1. The monarch remains the nominal commander of the armed forces, though no sovereign has issued an order in two centuries.
2. They charge a nominal two quid for the tour — basically just to stop people wandering in.
NASA flight controllers: "All systems are nominal." Not \"good\" — exactly as specified. It's the word Mission Control keeps saying in Apollo 13, right up until things stop being nominal.
Latin nomen, nominis = "name." One root, a lot of GRE words: nominate (put a name forward), nomenclature (naming system), misnomer (wrong name), denomination (a named unit — of money or of church), and ignominy (in- "without" + nomen — namelessness, hence disgrace).

column2:
Casually unconcerned; coolly unbothered in manner.
Coolly unbothered — showing no anxiety, excitement, or concern in a situation where most people would show plenty.

The word describes the surface, not the soul. Indifferent says you genuinely don't care; nonchalant says you don't look like you care — which is why it so often carries a whiff of performance. It's the shrug, the unhurried walk away from the explosion. Tone slides with context: admiring when the stakes are low (effortless cool), faintly critical when they're high (he was nonchalant about the missing money).
⚠️ nonchalant ≠ nonplussed. Nonplussed means bewildered, at a loss — the opposite of unbothered. The person who is nonplussed has no idea what to do; the nonchalant one just isn't showing it.
Nonchalant wears its French accent like sunglasses — cool, and meant to be seen.
The word points at the visible manner rather than the inner feeling, which is why nonchalance can be faked and indifference can't.
1. Asked whether the verdict troubled him, the defendant gave a nonchalant wave, as though the whole trial had been someone else's appointment.
2. She strolled in forty minutes late, nonchalant as anything, holding a coffee.
It's become a whole personality type online — the "nonchalant" boyfriend who replies "k" to everything. That's the word doing exactly what it means: calculated unbotheredness worn as a look.
French non + chaloir = "not to matter, not to concern," from Latin calēre, "to be warm." Literally: doesn't heat up.

That heat root is worth banking — it also gives calorie, scald, cauldron, chafe, and chauffeur (originally the man who stoked the engine).

column2:
So bewildered you don't know how to react.
So surprised, puzzled or bewildered that you have no idea how to react — speechless, blank, stalled.

It isn't ordinary confusion (not understanding something) and it isn't shock (an emotional blow). It's the specific stall: the situation is so unexpected that your response system produces nothing. Someone insults you at a funeral; someone answers a routine question with a personal confession — you stand there with nothing to say. Neutral about the person: being nonplussed says the world was strange, not that you were slow.
⚠️ nonplussed ≠ unfazed. The non- fools everyone into reading it as "not bothered, cool as ice" — the exact opposite. (American speech has drifted toward that misuse; the GRE tests the real sense.) Nonplussed = at a total loss.
Non plus — nothing more. Your brain has nothing further to add.
The word is literally no more — the point where you've run out of responses, which is blankness rather than calm.
1. Asked to justify the missing funds in front of the entire board, the treasurer was nonplussed, and the silence went on far too long.
2. She proposed on the second date — I was completely nonplussed, just standing there holding my coffee.
Latin non plus = "not more." It named the state where nothing further can be said or done — you've hit the wall of your own responses.

Same plus runs through ne plus ultra ("nothing beyond" — the absolute peak), plural, surplus.

Harmful, poisonous — physically or morally.
Harmful to health or life — poisonous, injurious. Most often of fumes, gases, chemicals, weeds; by extension of ideas and influences that corrupt (a noxious ideology).

The word claims real damage, not mere unpleasantness. A smell can be disgusting without being noxious; noxious fumes actually injure the lungs. Note the contrast with its own relative: an obnoxious guest is unbearable, a noxious gas is lethal — one offends, the other harms. When applied to ideas, the metaphor is deliberately medical: the belief is treated as a toxin seeping into people.
⚠️ noxious ≠ noisome.
- noxious = harmful (it damages you)
- noisome = foul-smelling (it offends your nose)

And noisome has nothing to do with noise — it's from annoy.
Strip the ob- off obnoxious and it stops being annoying and starts being deadly.
Same root, harder edge: obnoxious hurts your patience, noxious hurts your body.
1. The inquiry found that workers had been inhaling noxious vapours for years without protective equipment.
2. Don't run the generator in the garage — you'll fill the house with noxious fumes.
Governments publish official noxious weed lists — plants legally classed as harmful enough to be banned from sale. Not weeds that look untidy; weeds that damage crops, livestock or people. That's the whole word in one phrase.
Latin nocēre = "to harm." It runs through a useful family: innocuous (in- + nocuous = not harmful), innocent (doing no harm), nuisance (via French nuire), and obnoxious (originally exposed to harm).

🚫 Not Latin nox, "night." That gives nocturnal, equinox. Same-looking syllable, unrelated word.

To make void; to cancel out completely.
To make something legally void — to strip it of force so it counts as if it never held any. Also: to cancel out completely, so the net effect is zero.

Weaker words let something survive in reduced form: undermine leaves it standing but shaky, reduce leaves a remainder. Nullify leaves nothing. It carries the flavour of an authority striking a thing off the record — courts, referees, legislatures — or of two forces meeting and cancelling exactly. Note the arithmetic edge: a raise nullified by inflation isn't a smaller raise, it's no raise.
null + -ify — not weakened, zeroed.
The word wears its meaning on its face: whatever gets nullified is set back to null, the way a form field goes blank rather than merely small.
1. The Supreme Court nullified the statute, holding that the legislature had never possessed the power to pass it.
2. Two weeks of dieting, nullified by one wedding buffet.
Football commentary lives on this word: "the goal is nullified — the flag is up for offside." Not a goal that counted less; a goal wiped off the scoreboard entirely.
Latin nullus = "not any" (from ne + ullus, "not even one") + -ficāre, "to make" — literally make-it-none.

Same root gives you null, nullity, nil, and — hiding behind a prefix — annul (ad- + nullus), which is exactly what a court does to a marriage: not end it, but declare it never legally existed.

Charged with a felt divine presence; awe-inspiring and faintly terrifying.
Filled with, or suggesting, the presence of a divinity — spiritually charged, mysterious, awe-inspiring.

This is not the same as beautiful, serene, or even sacred. Sacred is a status something is granted; numinous is a sensation something inflicts on you. The word carries awe and a shiver of dread — the feeling of standing in a place where something vastly greater might be paying attention. Reserve it for cave paintings, empty cathedrals, the deep ocean, a total eclipse. Using it for a nice sunset is overclaiming.
numinous ≠ luminous. Luminous = giving off light. Numinous = giving off the presence of a god. A stained-glass window is luminous; the silence underneath it is numinous.
Numinous hides numen — a god's nod. Not light in the room: Someone in the room.
The one-letter gap from luminous is the whole distinction — one is illuminated, the other is inhabited.
1. The chapel's unlit interior had a numinous stillness that stopped conversation at the door.
2. I'm not religious, but standing under those redwoods was genuinely numinous — I couldn't talk for a minute.
C.S. Lewis used numinous as a technical term in The Problem of Pain, and then built a character out of it: Aslan, who is "good" but explicitly "not a tame lion." That mix of awe and fear is exactly what the word names.
Latin numen = "divine will, godhead" — literally a nod, from nuere, "to nod." A god signalled assent by inclining the head, so the nod itself became the name for divine power.

Same root, wildly different word: innuendo (from innuere, "to nod at") — meaning conveyed by a gesture rather than said outright.

The US dollar bill's "Annuit Coeptis" — "He nods at our undertakings" — is the same nuere staring at you from above the pyramid.

Stubbornly hard-hearted; unmoved by pleading, pity, or remorse.
Stubbornly refusing to change course — and, crucially, refusing to be softened: unmoved by pleading, pity, or remorse.

Stubborn and obstinate are about holding an opinion. Obdurate is about a hardened heart. You are obdurate when the widow begs and you say no, when the evidence of suffering is right there and you feel nothing. It carries a moral charge — the speaker is not describing you, they are condemning you — and it lives in formal, often near-biblical register: an obdurate sinner, an obdurate creditor, an obdurate refusal to apologise.
Ob-DUR-ate — too durable to break, no matter how hard you beg.
The dur is the same hard you hear in durable and endure, and the point of the word is that pleading bounces straight off.
1. The tribunal was obdurate: no appeal to hardship, however well documented, would reopen the case.
2. I said sorry about four times and he just sat there, arms folded, completely obdurate.
Milton's Satan, in Paradise Lost Book I, glares from the burning lake "with obdurate pride and steadfast hate" — the literal definition of a heart that will not soften.
Latin ob- (against) + durus (hard) — hardened against you.

Durus is a workhorse root: durable (lasting because hard), endure (stay hard through it), duress (hardship used as force), dour (a hard, grim face), indurate (to harden).

column2:
A deep bow; deference physically performed.
A bow, curtsy, or kneeling — a bodily gesture of respect to someone above you; by extension, deferential homage itself ("paying obeisance to tradition").

Where respect is an attitude and obedience is doing what you're told, obeisance is the performance — submission made visible, in front of witnesses. It belongs to courts, shrines and thrones, so in modern prose it carries either genuine ceremony or a dry sneer: when a columnist writes that tech CEOs paid obeisance to the new administration, the word is doing the mocking.
Obeisance has obey sitting right at the front — bend the "y" into a bow and you get the word.
Obedience is obeying; obeisance is the visible bending that shows it.
1. The courtiers made their obeisance as the queen passed, foreheads nearly touching the marble.
2. He hates the boss but still does that little obeisance — the nod, the laugh at the bad joke — every single morning.
Indian news copy runs on this word: "the Prime Minister paid obeisance at the temple" appears in headlines almost every week — always the bow, the offering, the cameras.
Old French obéissance ("obedience"), from Latin oboedīre = ob- (toward) + audīre (to hear) — to obey is literally to listen toward someone.

That gives you a free family: obey, obedient, audience, audible, audition, auditorium.

To deliberately muddy something so it can't be understood.
To make something deliberately unclear — to muddy a fact, a number, or an argument so nobody can see what's actually being said.

The key is method and motive. You don't obfuscate by hiding something; you obfuscate by piling stuff on top of it — jargon, qualifiers, footnotes, extra clauses. And it's never accidental: confuse can be clumsiness, obscure can be a passing cloud, but obfuscate is always someone's choice. It's the verb you reach for when a company's earnings report technically discloses everything and reveals nothing.
ob-FUSS-cate — bury the point under a fuss of words.
The fuss is the point: obfuscation adds noise rather than removing information, and the person doing it wants the noise there.
1. The report obfuscated the losses across nine appendices, each technically accurate and collectively unreadable.
2. Just answer the question — stop obfuscating.
Developers ship obfuscated JavaScript: the code still runs, but variables become `a`, `b`, `c` and the logic is scrambled so competitors can't read it. Same idea — nothing removed, everything made unreadable on purpose.
Latin ob- (over) + fuscāre (to darken), from fuscus, "dark, dusky." Literally to darken over — you throw shade across the meaning until nobody can make it out.

A harsh, thundering scolding delivered at length.
A harsh, vehement scolding — a tongue-lashing delivered at length and at volume.

Sitting at the top of the telling-off ladder: a reproach is quiet and wounded, a reprimand is official and dry, a rebuke is sharp and brief — an objurgation is sustained thunder, the kind that fills a room. The word is bookish and slightly grand, so writers often reach for it with a raised eyebrow: calling a parent's rant an objurgation makes the ranter sound self-important. Expect it in prose, almost never in speech.
objurgation ≠ abjuration. Objurgation = a furious scolding. Abjuration = a solemn renouncing under oath (to abjure violence is to swear it off). Same -jur-, opposite direction: one hurls words at you, the other swears words away.
Hidden jur, as in jury — an objurgation is a scolding handed down like a verdict.
That courtroom flavour is the nuance: it's not a mild word of correction but righteous judgement pronounced from on high.
1. The bishop's letter was less a correction than a sustained objurgation, five pages of thunder over a single missed service.
2. I was ten minutes late and got twenty minutes of objurgation for it.
Latin ob- (against) + jurgāre (to chide, quarrel), itself from jūs, jūris (law) + agere (to drive) — literally to drive law at someone.

That jūs root pays out everywhere: jury, justice, jurisdiction, perjury, abjure — and injury, which is in- + jūs, "not right."

Completely unaware of what's happening around you.
Completely unaware of something — it simply hasn't registered. Usually followed by to (or, in older/formal use, of).

The word is about a blank, not a choice. Someone indifferent has noticed and doesn't care; someone obtuse has been told and can't grasp it; someone oblivious never took it in at all. That's why it usually arrives with a faint sigh of reproach — you weren't malicious, you were just somewhere else while the room filled with smoke.

An older, more literary sense survives in formal prose: forgetful of, having let something slip out of mind entirely — "oblivious of past slights."
Oblivious lives in oblivion — the fact didn't get ignored, it never arrived.
Oblivion is the void where things are forgotten, and an oblivious person is standing in it while everyone else watches the thing happen.
1. Absorbed in the manuscript, she remained oblivious to the storm that had emptied the reading room around her.
2. He kept telling the joke, totally oblivious to the fact that the guy it was about was standing right there.
Harry Potter's memory-wiping charm — Obliviate! — is the same Latin root doing exactly what it says: the memory is erased, and the victim walks off oblivious.
Latin oblivisci = "to forget" — from ob- + the root of levis, "smooth": to wipe the wax tablet smooth so nothing is written on it any more.

That's the whole word in one image, and it also gives you oblivion — the state of being wiped clean, forgotten, gone.

Unclear, or little known; to hide or overshadow.
Adjective: (1) not clearly expressed — hard to make sense of; (2) not well known — small, forgotten, off the map.
Verb: to cover, dim, or overshadow something so it can't be seen or understood clearly.

Both senses are the same idea: something is in the way. The adjective is usually flat and descriptive rather than hostile — an obscure clause, an obscure Belgian poet — though the "little-known" sense carries a faint sniff of insignificance when someone says some obscure blog. Compare the neighbours: cryptic implies the vagueness was deliberate, arcane implies you'd need specialist initiation, while obscure just reports that the light isn't getting through. The verb is the GRE's favourite — it often means to hide by outshining: a charming manner obscures a ruthless one.
⚠️ obscure ≠ obtuse.
- obscure = the thing is unclear
- obtuse = the person is slow to grasp it

A badly drafted contract is obscure. The man who still can't follow it after four readings is obtuse.
Obscure = a screen pulled across — over the meaning (can't follow it) or over the name (never heard of it).
One word, one image, both senses: whatever's behind the screen is still there, you just can't get at it.
1. The treaty's final article is deliberately obscure, and every signatory reads it to suit itself.
2. He kept quoting some obscure 90s band nobody at the table had heard of.
Thomas Hardy's novel Jude the Obscure — Jude is a stonemason who dreams of Oxford and dies unknown. The title is the definition: a life nobody ever heard of.
Latin obscurus = "covered over, dark." That's why the verb still means to cover, and the adjective means what's left when the light can't reach.

Same root in chiaroscuro — the painter's technique of chiaro (light) against oscuro (dark).
