column2:
Fawning and servile — pleasing so hard it becomes contemptible.
Excessively eager to serve, please, or agree — fawning, servile, all deference and no spine.

The word is never a compliment. Deferential is respectful, attentive is good service; obsequious is what you call it when the pleasing has gone past dignity and started to look like a strategy. It carries a whiff of self-interest — the flatterer wants something — and it describes how the behaviour looks to a third party, not how it feels to the person being flattered. Classic targets: the yes-man, the courtier, the waiter who hovers, the junior who laughs a beat too long at the boss's joke.
obsequious ≠ obsequies. Obsequies (OB-si-kweez) are funeral rites — the ceremony, not the crawling. Same Latin root, opposite worlds: one follows a coffin, the other follows a boss.
ob-SEE-kwee-us — he'll do anything to seek to please us.
The buried "seek" is the whole nuance: this isn't natural politeness but pleasing that is aimed, effortful, and after something.
1. Every biographer notes the same failing: brilliant with his equals, obsequious the moment a duke entered the room.
2. He's not being nice, he's being obsequious — nobody compliments your parking that much for free.
Uriah Heep in Dickens's David Copperfield, forever wringing his hands and calling himself "ever so 'umble" — the textbook obsequious creep, and the humility is a con from the first page.
Latin ob- ("toward") + sequi ("to follow") — literally following close behind you, which is exactly what the word still describes.

sequi is a high-yield GRE root: sequel, sequence, consequence, subsequent, non sequitur ("it does not follow"), and — with a sound shift — pursue, persecute, prosecute.

Out of use because something better replaced it.
No longer in use or no longer useful, because something better has taken its place — fax machines, floppy disks, a skill the industry has moved past.

The word carries replacement, not just age. A vintage watch is old; a pager is obsolete — the world routed around it. That's why it stings when applied to people or jobs: outdated says you've fallen behind, obsolete says there's no longer a role for you at all. As a verb (to obsolete something) it's business-speak: a company obsoletes its own product line by launching the successor.
⚠️ obsolete ≠ obsolescent.
- obsolete = already dead, superseded
- obsolescent = on the way out, going obsolete but still in use

DVDs were obsolescent for years before becoming obsolete.
Obso-lete ends like delete — not merely old, but deleted from use.
The ending marks the difference between something dated and something whose function has been erased by a replacement.
1. The committee's procedural handbook, drafted in 1974, had been rendered obsolete by a single line of the new statute.
2. My charger's obsolete — they changed the port again.
Planned obsolescence — the reason your two-year-old phone suddenly can't take the update. Products designed to go obsolete on schedule.
Latin obsolescere, "to fall into disuse" — from solere, "to be accustomed." Something obsolete is what people are no longer accustomed to using.

Same root gives insolent: in- + solere, "not customary" — behaviour outside what's accustomed, hence rude.
column3: g04 register::neutral connotation::negative antonym::just-born-vs-outlived-its-era connotation::old-enough-to-be-discredited intensity::out-of-date-by-degree meaning::belonging-to-a-dead-era

column2:
Stubborn past the point of reason; immovably set.
Refusing to change your mind, your course, or your behaviour — and refusing past the point where anyone thinks it's reasonable.

The word carries a verdict. Determined, resolute and steadfast describe the same immovability with approval; obstinate is what the people you're blocking call it. It implies the resistance has stopped serving any purpose — you're holding out from sheer will, possibly against your own interests. It's also a notch more formal and colder than stubborn, which can be affectionate ("stubborn old mule"); obstinate rarely is.

It works on things too: an obstinate stain, an obstinate cough, an obstinate lid — anything that won't yield to repeated effort.
obstinate ≠ obstreperous. Both start obst-, both describe a difficult person — but obstinate is silently immovable, obstreperous (ub-STREP-er-uhs) is noisily unruly. The obstinate witness says nothing; the obstreperous one won't stop shouting.
There's an obstacle hiding in obstinate — and it's a person.
Same obst-, same idea: this isn't admirable firmness, it's something standing in the way that you've given up trying to move.
1. Despite three days of testimony and a mountain of documents, the minister remained obstinate in his denial.
2. He's so obstinate — the restaurant's been closed for a year and he still won't admit I was right about the reservation.
Lady Catherine de Bourgh's parting shot at Elizabeth Bennet in Pride and Prejudice: "Obstinate, headstrong girl!" — kept word-for-word in the 2005 film. Note who says it: the person being defied, furious that she can't win.
Latin ob- (against) + stāre (to stand) — literally to stand against. The obstinate man plants his feet.

stāre is one of the great GRE roots: stable, status, stationary, constant, circumstance, obstacle — everything that stands, stays, or gets in the way.

column2:
Noisily unruly; loud in a way that resists control.
Noisily and stubbornly resistant to control — loud, unruly, and hard to manage.

Two ingredients, both required: volume and defiance. Boisterous is just high spirits and nobody minds; obstreperous is the noise of someone refusing to be handled. It's also a word spoken from above — teachers about children, judges about witnesses, flight crews about passengers — so it carries a faint dryness, as if the speaker is too composed to say "screaming brat."
⚠️ obstreperous ≠ obsequious. Same ob- opening, opposite behaviour: obstreperous = loudly defying you; obsequious = fawning all over you.
Ob-STREP-erous: strep throat — a raw, roaring throat that will not shut up.
Ob- means against, so the noise is aimed at you: it's not cheerful loudness, it's loudness as resistance.
1. The chairman adjourned the meeting when the shareholders grew too obstreperous to be gavelled into silence.
2. One glass of wine and my uncle turns obstreperous — arguing with the TV, arguing with the waiter, arguing with me.
It's the standard airline-and-courtroom euphemism: passengers get removed for "obstreperous behaviour," witnesses get warned for it. Whenever an official body needs a polite word for making a scene and refusing to stop, this is the one.
Latin ob- (against) + strepere (to make a noise) — literally to roar back at. The ob- is the same "against" you already know from obstruct, oppose, obstinate: everything pushing the wrong way.

To make something unnecessary by preventing it in advance.
To make something unnecessary — to head off a difficulty so completely that it never has to be dealt with.

The key is pre-emption, not repair. You don't obviate a problem you're already in; a clever design obviates the need for a fix before anyone reaches for one. Prevent stops a thing from happening; obviate goes further and cancels the requirement itself — the meeting isn't rescheduled, it's called off. Dry, formal, and overwhelmingly used with an abstract object: the need, the requirement, the difficulty, the objection.
Obviate makes a need obsolete — same ob-, same result: no longer required.
It doesn't answer the question, it makes the question stop applying.
1. The new evidence obviated any need for a second trial; the charges were dropped outright.
2. If you just put the spare key under the mat, that obviates this whole conversation.
Live in engineering and patent prose as a fixed phrase: \"obviates the need for\" — a new sensor obviates the need for manual calibration. If you see obviate, the words the need for are almost certainly next.
Latin ob- (in the way of) + via (road) — to plant yourself across the road so the trouble never arrives.

via is a workhorse root: deviate (off the road), devious (off-road, hence sneaky), trivial (tri- + via, the three-way crossroads where anyone might be standing — hence commonplace), viaduct, previous, obvious.

obvious is the same ob + via — but there it means lying in the road where you can't miss it. Same root, opposite jobs: obvious is what's in your way; obviate is what gets in its way.

column2:
To block or seal off a passage, or hide from view.
To block or close off a passage or opening — or to cut off from view by getting in the way.

This is a physical, clinical word. Arteries occlude, sinuses occlude, a cloud occludes the sun, a pillar occludes your view of the stage. Where block is plain and obstruct suggests something lodged in the way, occlude is what a doctor, an engineer, or a computer-vision paper says — and it leans toward the passage being sealed shut rather than merely narrowed. You cannot occlude a plan or a proposal; only a channel or a line of sight.
⚠️ occlude ≠ preclude.
- occlude = physically shut a passage (a clot occludes the artery)
- preclude = rule out in advance (the clot precludes surgery)

One shuts a pipe; the other shuts a possibility.
Every -clude word is a door: exclude shuts you out, include shuts you in, occlude shuts the pipe.
The oc- is Latin ob-, "in the way," so occlude is the door slammed across a channel.
1. Fatty deposits had occluded the coronary artery almost entirely, leaving a channel barely wide enough for blood to pass.
2. Can you shift left? Your head's occluding half the whiteboard on the call.
Standard hospital phrasing you'll hear on any medical drama or in a real cardiology report: "a fully occluded artery." If you've ever had a dentist check your occlusion, that's the same word — how your teeth shut against each other.
Latin ob- ("in the way") + claudere ("to shut") — the same claudere that gives you close, exclude, include, seclude, preclude, recluse, and cloister. Learn the root once and you own the set: whatever the prefix does, -clude means a door is shutting.

column2:
Hateful and repulsive — it earns disgust, not mere dislike.
Extremely unpleasant — repulsive enough to deserve hatred, not merely dislike.

Weight is the whole difference. Unpleasant is mild, disagreeable is polite, odious is a denunciation: it carries moral disgust and asks the listener to share it. It attaches to regimes, laws, comparisons, duties and people — a tyrant is odious, a chore can be odious, but nobody calls a bad sandwich odious. Formal, faintly literary, and never neutral.
⚠️ odious ≠ invidious. Both love the noun comparison, so the GRE loves the pair.
- odious = hateful in itself; it disgusts.
- invidious = likely to breed ill-will; unfair singling-out that makes people resent you (or each other).

An odious remark revolts the room; an invidious distinction divides it.
Odious sounds like it stinks — and it does, but what it gives off is hate: odi- = hatred.
Reach for it only when something is repellent enough to deserve loathing, not just to be a nuisance.
1. The tribunal called the practice of collective punishment odious, and unjustifiable in any legal tradition.
2. Cleaning out the office fridge is the most odious job on the rota, and somehow it's always mine.
The old proverb "comparisons are odious" — Shakespeare hands it to the idiot constable Dogberry in Much Ado About Nothing, who mangles it into "comparisons are odorous." The joke only lands because the two words sound alike and don't mean alike.
Latin odium = hatred → odiosus, "hateful." Odium survives untouched in English (public odium).

The root then goes underground in a way worth knowing: Latin inodiare, "to make hateful," softened through French into annoy, noisome (from the clipped form noy) and ennui — three GRE words that all began life as hatred and cooled into irritation and boredom.

🚫 Not related to odour. That's Latin odor, "smell" — deodorant, malodorous. Same sound, different family.

Pushily helpful or bossy without the authority to be.
Pushily eager to help, advise, or enforce rules when nobody asked — meddling dressed up as service.

The sting is the mismatch between how small the person's authority is and how large they act. A helpful colleague is helpful; an officious one plants himself between you and the photocopier to explain the form you already filled in. It's not cruelty, it's self-importance — the busybody, the clipboard, the jobsworth. Always an insult, never a compliment, and it usually says the person enjoys the power more than the task.
⚠️ officious ≠ official. Official = actually holding the authority. Officious = acting as if you do. The security guard is official; the neighbour who tells you where to park is officious.
An officious man keeps his office in his head, not on the door.
The word literally contains office, and that's the joke — he behaves like a functionary without ever having been given the job.
1. The undersecretary was officious to the point of obstruction, demanding stamped copies of documents no statute required.
2. Some officious guy at the gym kept correcting my form — mate, you don't work here.
Dwight Schrute in The Office — "Assistant to the Regional Manager," volunteer sheriff's deputy, self-appointed enforcer of rules nobody voted on. Same root, exact meaning.
Latin officium = "duty, service" → officiosus, originally "obliging, dutiful" — a compliment. English soured it: too much duty, offered too freely, becomes interference.

Same root gives office, official, officiate, officer — the whole vocabulary of people with jobs, and one word for the man who only thinks he has one.

Signalling that something bad is coming.
Giving the sense that something bad is about to happen; menacing in the way a sign is menacing.

The key is that ominous describes a forecast, not an attack. A growling dog is threatening; the sudden silence just before it growls is ominous. Nothing has happened yet — the word lives in the gap between the warning and the harm, which is why it attaches so naturally to weather, silence, a doctor's pause, a phone call at 3am. Faintly literary in flavour, but perfectly at home in speech.
⚠️ ominous ≠ onerous.
- ominous = boding evil, threatening
- onerous = burdensome, heavy going (Latin onus, "load")

An onerous contract exhausts you. An ominous one means you're about to be ruined.
There's an omen sitting inside ominous — and an omen never hits you, it only warns you.
That hidden word carries the nuance: the danger is still ahead, and the word points at the sign rather than the strike.
1. The dispatches from the frontier grew shorter and more ominous with each passing week.
2. My boss said "let's talk Monday" and walked out — which felt pretty ominous.
Stock music libraries have a category literally tagged "ominous" — the low string drone under a trailer as the screen goes dark. You've heard the word's exact meaning scored a hundred times.
Latin omen, ominis = a sign, a foretelling — straight into English as omen and ominous.

The same root gives you abominable, from ab-ominari, "to shrink away from as a bad omen." The Abominable Snowman is, etymologically, a walking bad sign.

To leave out, or fail to do, something expected.
To leave something out — to not include it — or to fail to do something you were supposed to do.

Delete removes what was there; omit means it never made it in. That's why an omission is so often a fault of absence: nobody sees the gap unless they know what should have filled it. And something can only be omitted if it had a claim to be there — you can't omit an irrelevance. The word carries a faint whiff of accountability (an accountant who omits an asset, a witness who omits a detail) without ever quite accusing anyone of lying.
⚠️ omit ≠ emit. One letter apart, same Latin root, opposite directions: omit = leave out; emit = send out (a chimney emits smoke).
oh-MIT = "oh, missed it" — the thing that should have been there isn't.
The pronunciation is literally the reaction to an omission: you notice the gap only afterwards.
1. The report was accurate in every particular but omitted the one figure that would have embarrassed the board.
2. I omitted the part where I cried in the car, obviously.
Strunk & White's most quoted rule of writing: "Omit needless words."
Latin ob- (away) + mittere (to send) — "to send away, let go."

mittere is one of the highest-yield GRE roots: mission, missile, transmit, emit, remit, submit, admit, permit, commit, intermittent, remiss. Once you hear "send" inside a word, the rest falls out.

Present everywhere at once; impossible to escape.
Present everywhere at once — or, loosely, present so constantly that you can't get away from it.

The word starts in theology: omnipresence is a property of God, alongside omnipotence and omniscience. That grandeur never fully washes off, which is why everyday use is usually half-joking or half-annoyed — an omnipresent advert, an omnipresent boss, an omnipresent summer song. Ubiquitous means found in many places; omnipresent means there the whole time, inescapably, watching. One is a distribution; the other is a presence.
God is omnipresent. So are the ads.
The word only has two homes — the divine and the exasperated — and nobody has ever been pleased that something was omnipresent.
1. In the medieval imagination, an omnipresent deity made privacy theologically impossible: there was no room without a witness.
2. That chorus was omnipresent last summer — supermarket, taxi, gym, my own head at 3 a.m.
Latin omnis = "all" + praesens = "present, at hand."

Omnis is one of the best-value roots on the GRE: omniscient (all-knowing), omnipotent (all-powerful), omnivore (eats all), omnibus ("for all" — a bill bundling everything, and the horse-drawn vehicle for everyone, which we shortened to bus).

All-knowing; aware of everything at once.
Knowing everything — every fact, every motive, every hidden thing, all at once.

It's a word built for gods and narrators. Applied to an actual person it almost always tilts: either awe ("the omniscient Ms. Patel, who knew about the party before we planned it") or a sneer at someone who behaves as if nothing can be told to them. Knowledgeable is a compliment about effort; omniscient is an absolute, so a human can only ever approximate it — which is why it lands as either worship or mockery, rarely plain description.
⚠️ omniscient ≠ prescient.
- omniscient = knows everything, across all time
- prescient = knows what's coming beforehand — foresight only

A prescient investor called the crash. An omniscient one wouldn't have needed to call it.
Omni + sci — all + science. Nobody in the room qualifies, so if you're calling a colleague omniscient, you're being sarcastic.
The word is an absolute, and absolutes applied to humans read as irony.
1. The novel is told by an omniscient narrator who moves freely between the minds of all seven passengers.
2. Ask Dev — he's omniscient about the office gossip, somehow knows things before they happen.
Straight out of English class: third-person omniscient — the narrator who can see inside every character's head, as opposed to limited, who's stuck with one. If you've ever labelled a point of view, you've used this word.
Latin omnis (all) + scīre (to know).

Both halves pay rent across the GRE: omnis gives omnipotent (all-powerful), omnipresent, omnivore, omnibus; scīre gives science, conscience (knowing-with-yourself), prescient (knowing beforehand), and nescient (not knowing — ignorant).

Burdensome; heavy with obligation, often unfairly so.
Burdensome — imposing a heavy, troublesome load of work, duty or expense, usually more than is fair.

The weight is obligation, not difficulty. Arduous describes effort (an arduous climb); onerous describes being bound to something you can't put down — paperwork, upkeep, a clause in a contract. A crossword can be hard but never onerous; filing quarterly returns is onerous even though a child could do it. The word also carries a quiet complaint: calling terms onerous is one step from calling them unjust.
Onerous ≈ owner-ous — what you own, owns you: the mortgage, the upkeep, the duty you can't hand back.
That's why onerous attaches to terms, duties and contracts rather than to puzzles — it's heavy because you're bound to it, not because it's clever.
1. The bank's revised terms were so onerous that the smaller borrowers walked away rather than sign.
2. Watering his neighbour's plants sounded easy until he saw the list — twelve pots, twice a day, an unexpectedly onerous favour.
Standard contract-desk vocabulary: negotiators strike out "onerous terms," and accounting has a formal category for the onerous contract — one where the cost of honouring it now exceeds anything you'll get back. The word survives precisely where obligations are priced.
Latin onus, oneris = "burden, load" — the same onus English borrowed whole: the onus is on you.

Best payoff is the opposite: ex- (off) + onerare (to load) = exonerate, literally to take the burden off someone — which is exactly what clearing a person of blame does.

Former — held the role once, not now.
Former, ex-, previous — someone or something that once held a role and no longer does: a onetime rival, her onetime employer.

Where ex- is blunt and personal and erstwhile is arch and literary, onetime is the tidy, journalistic option — it states the fact of a finished role without any feeling about it. It usually carries an implied then vs. now contrast: the onetime ally is mentioned precisely because he's now an enemy. Note the grammar, which is half the word: it only sits in front of a noun. You can say his onetime partner, never "his partner is onetime."
⚠️ onetime ≠ one-time. Solid, onetime = former. Hyphenated, one-time usually = happening only once (a one-time payment). A onetime donor used to give; a one-time donor gave exactly once.
Onetime goes before the noun, because the person's time is already behind them.
If the word can't follow "is," you're dealing with the "former" sense, not the "only once" sense.
1. The committee was chaired by a onetime finance minister, long since retired from public life.
2. That's my onetime flatmate — we haven't spoken since the lease ended.
Justin Bieber's debut single "One Time" (2009) — and it means once, not former, which is exactly the split to remember: two words for the counting sense, one word for the has-been sense.

Blocking light; or impossible to see into or understand.
Literally: not letting light through — frosted glass, thick paint, milk.

On the GRE, almost always figurative: impossible to see into or understand. Opaque prose, an opaque ruling, an opaque procurement process.

The word implies a total barrier, not a dim one. Obscure means hard to make out — you squint and eventually get there. Opaque means the surface gives you nothing back. And because transparency is the civic virtue, calling an institution opaque is close to an accusation: the blockage looks chosen, not accidental.
⚠️ opaque ≠ obtuse. Opaque is the thing that can't be seen into; obtuse is the person who can't see. An opaque explanation defeats everyone; an obtuse listener misses a clear one.
op-aque = op-packed — packed so solid that no light, and no meaning, gets through.
The "packed" sound carries the key nuance: the block is complete, so nothing leaks out to help you.
1. The committee's funding criteria remained opaque, and applicants were left to infer the rules from who had been rejected.
2. Sorry, I read your text four times and it's still completely opaque to me — what time are we meeting?
The opacity slider in Instagram, Photoshop or Figma: drag it to 100% and the layer is opaque — you can't see a thing behind it.

column2:
Exploiting any chance that appears, usually without principle.
Seizing whatever chance presents itself — and, in most human contexts, doing so without regard for principle, loyalty, or long-term plan.

The word rarely describes a strategy; it describes the absence of one. Call a politician's reversal opportunistic and you're saying the position was chosen by circumstance, not conviction. Note the split, though: in sport, tactics, and biology the word loses its sting and becomes pure praise or plain description — an opportunistic striker is a compliment, an opportunistic feeder is just a fact about the animal. Damning of people, neutral of organisms.
opportunistic ≠ opportune.
- opportune = well-timed, a favourable moment (an opportune arrival) — praise for the timing
- opportunistic = exploiting the moment — usually a judgement on the person
opportun-ist, like pur-ist or career-ist — an -ist is someone with one commitment, and his is to the opening itself.
The purist believes in purity and the careerist in his career; the opportunist believes in nothing but the gap in front of him.
1. Critics dismissed the ceasefire proposal as opportunistic — a bid for legitimacy timed to the week the sanctions took effect.
2. He's not loyal to the team, he's just opportunistic — the second a better offer landed he was gone.
In medicine, an opportunistic infection is one a healthy body shrugs off — thrush, pneumocystis — that turns lethal the moment the immune system is weakened. The pathogen isn't strong; it's just waiting for the opening.
Latin ob portum = "toward the harbour" — said of a wind that happens to be blowing your ship home. So an opportunity was originally just favourable weather you didn't arrange.

That gives you the whole word's judgement for free: the opportunistic man has no course of his own, he simply sails wherever the wind is already going. Same portus root as port, portal, import, export.

Harsh public scorn — and the disgrace it leaves behind.
Harsh public criticism and scorn directed at someone — and, in its second sense, the disgrace that results from it.

Scale and audience are what set it apart. Criticism can be one editor's note; opprobrium is a crowd. It carries a moral charge — the target hasn't merely been wrong, they've done something the public finds shameful — and the word is heavy, formal, the register of leaders, editorials and sentencing remarks. Note the double life: you can heap opprobrium on a man, and he can live under it afterwards.
⚠️ opprobrium ≠ approbation. One letter apart, near-opposites: approbation = approval, praise; opprobrium = condemnation, disgrace. Approbation applauds.
Opprobrium is always heaped — never a pinch of it, always a pile, and always in public.
The collocation gives you the two things the definition alone won't: the sheer quantity, and the fact that a crowd is doing the pouring.
1. The verdict drew such public opprobrium that the judge's name was known in every household within a week.
2. He deleted the tweet in ten minutes, but by then the opprobrium was already unstoppable.
Latin ob-/op- = "against" + probrum = "a shameful act, a reproach." Literally: the shame thrown at you.

That op- is the prefix of hostility across English — oppose, opponent, obstruct, object. Whenever you see it fused onto a root, something is being aimed against something else.

Elaborately decorated — usually more decoration than the thing needed.
Elaborately decorated — covered in carving, gilding, curls, flourishes.

The word tilts. Applied to a Baroque altarpiece it can be admiring; applied to anything modern, and to writing above all, it's a polite complaint — ornate prose is prose smothered in adjectives and subclauses, where a plain sentence would have done the job. Compare elaborate (complex, no verdict) and opulent (expensive, not necessarily fussy): ornate is specifically about surface decoration, and it always hints that someone couldn't stop adding.
Ornate = ornament + -ate: it's been ornament-ed — and one curl past enough.
The -ate ending marks something done to the object, so an ornate thing is never plain-born — it was decorated, and the word quietly asks whether it needed to be.
1. The chapel's ornate ceiling — every inch gilded, every rib carved — took four decades and three bankrupt patrons to finish.
2. His emails are so ornate that by the end of paragraph two you still don't know what he actually wants.
It's the default adjective of property listings and auction catalogues: \"ornate cast-iron fireplace,\" \"ornate Victorian mirror.\" Nobody ever writes ornate about a thing built after 1930.
Latin ornāre = "to equip, to adorn" → ornātus, "adorned." Straight to ornament, adorn, ornamental.

The useful bonus: suborn is the same root (sub- "secretly" + ornāre "equip") — to secretly fit someone out to lie for you, i.e. bribe a witness. A GRE word hiding inside a decorating verb.

column2:
To harden into bone; to become rigid and unchangeable.
Literally: to turn into bone — cartilage hardening into skeleton.
Figuratively (the GRE sense): to become rigid, fixed, and incapable of change.

The word only bites because of what it implies about the past: something that ossifies was once soft, living, adaptable — a reform movement, a ritual, a bureaucracy — and has now set hard. Rigid describes a state; ossify narrates a decline. It's a diagnosis delivered from the outside, almost never about oneself, and it carries a faint contempt: the thing still has its shape, but nothing moves in it anymore.
An ossified committee is a fossil — you can still read the shape, but nothing's alive in it.
Foss- and oss- rhyme, and the image carries the nuance exactly: not destroyed, just hardened past the point of change.
1. What began as a radical experiment in governance had, within two generations, ossified into ceremony.
2. Their whole hiring process has ossified — nobody can tell you why the third interview exists, just that it's always been there.
Radiologists date a teenager's age from X-rays by checking how far the growth plates have ossified — soft cartilage turning to bone on a predictable schedule. That's the literal sense doing daily work.
Latin os, ossis = "bone", plus -ify ("make into"). The root is quietly productive: osseous (bony), ossuary (a bone-house for stacked remains), ossicle (the three tiny bones of the middle ear).

🚫 Not related to osteo- words (osteoporosis, osteopath) — those are Greek osteon, also "bone." Two languages, same idea, unconnected spellings.

column2:
Showy in a way meant to be noticed and admired.
Showy and extravagant in a way designed to be noticed — wealth, taste, learning or piety put on display for an audience.

The judgement is on the motive, not the price tag. Lavish describes scale; opulent describes richness; ostentatious says the point of the thing was to be seen. A quietly expensive watch is opulent; the same watch worn sleeve-up all evening is ostentatious. It also works outside money — ostentatious grief, ostentatious humility, an ostentatious display of concern — anywhere sincerity is being performed.
ostentatious ≠ ostensible. Same Latin root, opposite jobs: ostentatious = showing off loudly; ostensible = the reason shown on the surface, hinting the real one is hidden ("his ostensible motive was charity").
-tatious like flirtatious — both are performances aimed at somebody watching.
You can't flirt alone and you can't be ostentatious alone; the word always implies an audience the display is aimed at.
1. The new headquarters, all marble atrium and no meeting rooms, struck the board as ostentatious at a moment when staff were being let go.
2. He didn't need a gold phone case — that's just ostentatious.
Gatsby's parties in The Great Gatsby — the shirts, the orchestra, the fireworks. All of it staged so one person across the bay would look. That's ostentation with a purpose.
Latin ostendere = "to stretch out in front of, to show" (ob- "before" + tendere "to stretch"). Ostentation is holding something out for people to look at.

tendere is a workhorse root: extend, tension, contend, portend, tendency — all stretching in some direction.

To force someone out of a position of power or possession.
To force someone out of a position — an office, a throne, a job, a board seat — or out of possession of property.

What gets ousted is usually a role, not a room. The removal is involuntary and final, but the method is left open: a palace coup, a shareholder vote, and a quiet 3am memo all count. Compare the neighbours — evict is about property and paperwork, expel is about being thrown out of an institution, depose is reserved for rulers. Oust is the newsroom's all-purpose verb, and it lives in the passive: nobody ousts themselves, they are ousted. The noun is ouster (the act of removal, not the person doing it).
OUST = OUT + S(eat) — you're out of your seat, and someone else is in it.
Ousting is always about a seat — of power, of office, of the board — so the person doesn't just leave, they are replaced.
1. The junta ousted the elected president before dawn, and the state broadcaster was reading the new decrees by breakfast.
2. Two bad quarters and the founder was ousted by his own board.
November 2023: every headline on the planet ran the same verb when OpenAI's board ousted Sam Altman — and then un-ousted him five days later.
Anglo-French oster ("to remove"), from Latin obstāre = ob- ("against") + stāre ("to stand"). To oust is to remove someone from where they stand — same stāre behind obstacle, obstruct, station, and status.

Bizarre and extravagant, as if from another world.
So strange or extravagant that it seems to belong to no normal world — bizarre, wildly unconventional, faintly absurd.

The word judges from a comfortable distance. Grotesque recoils, outrageous is offended, but outlandish mostly raises an eyebrow: it says this is too much, and not quite serious. It attaches to things that overreach — outlandish claims, outlandish prices, an outlandish hat — and it carries a whiff of amused disbelief rather than moral alarm. Calling a theory outlandish dismisses it as too weird to bother refuting.
Out-land-ish — it looks like it wandered in from out of the land, some other land entirely.
The three chunks sit right there on the surface, and they tell you the exact flavour of strange: not evil, just unmistakably not from around here.
1. The witness offered an outlandish account of the evening that no other testimony supported.
2. He turned up in an outlandish neon suit and acted like nobody would notice.
Outlander — the Gabaldon novels and the Starz series — is the same out-land root: the title means foreigner, the woman who does not belong to this place or century.
Old English ūtlendisc = "of a foreign land" (ūt out + land + -ish). It first meant simply foreign, and then drifted the way suspicion drifts: what comes from elsewhere looks odd, and odd swallowed foreign entirely.

Compare barbarian (Greek: someone whose speech sounds like bar-bar) — languages keep building "weird" out of "not from here."

To surpass, especially by pulling ahead in speed or growth.
To go faster than, or grow beyond, something else — to surpass it, usually by pulling ahead of it.

Exceed is arithmetic and static: a number is bigger than a limit. Surpass usually praises an achievement. Outstrip implies a race already in motion — both things were moving, and one drew away. That's why it lands so naturally on rates and quantities: demand outstrips supply, costs outstrip revenue, growth outstrips forecasts. The loser isn't standing still; it's simply being left behind. Neutral in tone, slightly formal, and the native language of newspapers and economists.
A drag strip is where cars race — to outstrip someone is to beat them down it.
That keeps the racing sense in front: outstripping isn't quiet excess, it's pulling away from something that was moving too.
1. Throughout the decade wage growth failed to outstrip inflation, and households grew quietly poorer.
2. Our shipping costs have outstripped the budget three months running — something's got to give.
Newsroom shorthand you've read a hundred times: "demand outstrips supply" — the standard line in every story about house prices, GPUs, or concert tickets.

Done openly, undisguised — the opposite of covert.
Done or shown openly, in plain view, with no attempt to disguise it.

The word is almost never wasted on things nobody would hide. You call something overt precisely because concealment was the expected option — overt hostility, overt racism, overt surveillance, an overt act of war. So it carries a faint charge: either the person has stopped bothering to pretend, or the openness is itself the point (a show of force meant to be seen). Neutral cousins like open or obvious have none of that undertone.
⚠️ overt vs. covert — one letter, opposite meanings.
- overt = out in the open
- covert = hidden, concealed

They are not a prefix pair. Covert comes from cover; overt comes from open. Unrelated roots that happened to collide.
Overt = open. Covert = covered.
The first letter of each word is the first letter of its meaning, and overt is the one where the cover has been deliberately dropped.
1. The tribunal held that stockpiling weapons on the border constituted an overt act of aggression, not a defensive precaution.
2. He didn't even try to hide it — that was overt favouritism and everyone in the room saw it.
Every spy film — Bourne, Bond, Mission: Impossible — runs on covert ops. Overt is the same job done where everyone can watch: the aircraft carrier parked off your coast rather than the man in your hotel.
Old French overt, past participle of ovrir "to open" (modern French ouvert), from Latin aperīre = to open.

Same root: aperture (an opening), overture (the piece that opens the opera; to make overtures is to open negotiations), aperitif (the drink that opens the meal).

To calm someone's anger, or force a region into quiet.
To calm someone's anger or agitation; also, of a country or region, to force into quiet submission.

Both senses share a faint whiff of condescension. You pacify a screaming toddler, a furious customer, a restless crowd — the word treats the other side's feeling as noise to be switched off rather than a grievance to be answered, so a pacified person is quiet, not satisfied. In the political sense it's a euphemism doing heavy lifting: armies "pacify" territory the way a nurse quiets a ward, which is exactly why the word turns up in official reports and rarely in honest ones.
A pacifier doesn't feed the baby — it just stops the noise.
To pacify is to quiet the complaint without addressing what caused it.
1. The governor's speech did little to pacify a city that had spent the night in the streets.
2. I bought him a coffee to pacify him, but he was still sulking an hour later.
Melanie Martinez's "Pacify Her" — off Cry Baby, the album built entirely around dummies, tantrums and being soothed rather than heard. Title match and meaning match at once.
Latin pax, pacis = "peace" + -ficāre = "to make." Literally peace-make.

That root pays out across the list: pact (a peace agreed), appease, pacifist, and the Pacific Ocean — named by Magellan because he crossed it in unnervingly calm weather.

Extremely careful and thorough; done with patient, laborious attention.
Done with extreme care and thoroughness, attending to every small detail; of a person, willing to put in that grinding, unglamorous effort.

This is a compliment, and a slightly awed one — it credits patience and stamina, not talent. Meticulous describes the standard of the result; painstaking describes the labour behind it, the hours nobody saw. It attaches naturally to slow, fiddly work: a painstaking translation, a painstaking reconstruction, painstaking research. Call a five-minute job painstaking and it sounds sarcastic.
⚠️ painstaking ≠ painful. Painstaking work is hard on the worker's patience but praised; painful work simply hurts. The pain in painstaking is taken voluntarily.
You take pains — you don't feel them. The pains are the price of the care.
Split the word at the right seam — pains-taking — and it stops meaning "agonising" and starts meaning "willing to go to trouble."
1. The catalogue is the product of forty years of painstaking archival work, each attribution traced to a surviving receipt.
2. She spent the whole weekend painstakingly peeling the old labels off, one corner at a time.
The phrase film studios and museums live by: "painstakingly restored" — the label on every 4K remaster and every cleaned-up old painting, doing the work of telling you how many quiet hours went into it.
From the old idiom to take pains = to go to trouble, where pains means effort, not hurt — the same sense in "he was at pains to explain."

Behind it is Latin poena = penalty, price paid, which also gives penalty, penal, penitent, subpoena, punish — and pine (to pine away). Effort as the price you pay is the thread.

So intense it seems physically touchable.
Literally: able to be touched or felt with the hands. Almost always used figuratively: a feeling or atmosphere so intense it seems to have physical presence — palpable tension, palpable relief, palpable dread. A third sense survives in phrases like a palpable lie: so obvious it might as well be solid.

The word marks intensity, not just visibility. Something obvious is merely easy to see; something palpable presses on the room. That is why it attaches to collective moods — a crowd, a courtroom, a silence — rather than to one person's private mood.
⚠️ palpable ≠ palatable. Palatable (PAL-uh-tuh-buhl) is from palate — tasty, or acceptable enough to swallow: a palatable compromise. One is felt, the other is tasted.
PALPable — you could lay your palm on it.
The word insists the thing is dense enough to touch, which is exactly why it outranks "obvious."
1. As the verdict was read, the tension in the courtroom was palpable.
2. He said he was fine, but the sulk coming off him was palpable from across the kitchen.
Live sports and news commentary run on it — "you can feel it, the tension in this stadium is palpable" is the reflex line every commentator reaches for before a penalty shootout.
Latin palpāre = "to touch, to stroke." Same root gives you palpate — what a doctor does pressing your abdomen — and palpitate, a heart beating hard enough to feel.

Contemptibly small — too little to deserve respect.
Ridiculously small in amount or worth — so small it's insulting. Most often attached to money, wages, offers, turnout, percentages.

The word does two jobs at once: it measures and it sneers. Meagre is pitiable, trifling is merely unimportant, modest is polite — but calling a sum paltry says the giver should be ashamed. There's an implied comparison behind it: paltry next to what was owed, promised, or expected. That's why "a paltry £5" works and "a paltry mountain" doesn't.
Paltry sounds like poultry — a paltry sum is chicken feed.
"Chicken feed" is already English's phrase for an amount too small to be worth accepting, and that dismissive shrug is exactly what paltry adds on top of "small".
1. After eighteen months of litigation the family was awarded a paltry sum, barely covering their legal costs.
2. They want a full rewrite by Friday and they're offering a paltry two hundred quid for it.
Business journalism runs on it: "shares rose a paltry 0.3%", "a paltry 12% turnout". The number alone is neutral — paltry is the reporter telling you it's an embarrassment.

column2:
A supposed cure-all for every problem.
A single remedy that cures all diseases, fixes all problems — a universal solution.

The catch is how it's actually used: nine times out of ten the word arrives with a negative attached. Writers reach for panacea precisely to deny one exists — "microfinance is no panacea," "AI is not a panacea for education." Calling something a panacea straight-faced is almost always a setup for deflating it. So it carries a faint whiff of overclaiming: a remedy is modest and real, a panacea is the thing credulous people believe in.
The word almost always comes wearing the word "no" in front of it: no panacea.
Learn the collocation, not just the definition — if you can hear "it's no panacea," you've got both the meaning (cure-all) and the sceptical tone in one move.
1. Land reform was presented to the villagers as a panacea, though it addressed neither drought nor debt.
2. Sure, a standing desk helps your back — but it's not some panacea for sitting on your laptop all day.
The Hippocratic Oath opens by swearing "by Apollo Physician, by Asclepius, by Hygieia, by Panacea" — two Greek healing goddesses whose names became English words: hygiene and panacea.
Greek pan (all) + akos (cure) — literally "all-cure."

pan- is a workhorse prefix worth owning: pandemic (all the people), panorama (all the view), pantheon (all the gods), panoply (a full suit of armour → a complete array).

Flamboyant, stylish confidence — flair in how something is done.
Flamboyant confidence of style — doing something difficult with visible flair, dash, and apparent ease.

The word almost always approves. Flamboyance and ostentation accuse you of showing off; panache grants that the showing-off was earned and enjoyable. It also attaches to the manner, not the person's character — you win with panache, dress with panache, resign with panache. And it implies an audience: panache is style performed, gracefully, usually under some pressure.
⚠️ panache ≠ panacea. Panache (puh-NASH) is stylish flair; a panacea (pan-uh-SEE-uh) is a cure-all remedy. Same first four letters, no relation.
Panache ends like flash and dash — and that's exactly what it is: flash, with dash.
The rhyme carries the nuance too, because flash alone is vulgar and dash alone is mere nerve — panache is the pair together, style plus daring.
1. He conducted the final movement with such panache that the orchestra rose before the audience did.
2. She parallel-parked the van in one go, on a hill, in the rain — absolute panache.
In Rostand's Cyrano de Bergerac, the dying Cyrano says the one thing he keeps is "mon panache" — literally his hat plume, and the play's whole idea of style that survives defeat. It's the most famous last word in French theatre.
French panache = the plume of feathers on a helmet, from Latin pinna (feather, wing). The swagger meaning is the plume itself: a bright flourish worn where everyone can see it, on a man riding into a fight.

Same feather root gives you pinnacle, pinnate, pinion, and pen (a quill).

Serving as the defining model or textbook case of something.
Serving as the model or defining case of something — the example that sets the pattern everything else is compared against.

It sounds like praise but usually isn't. Exemplary commends; paradigmatic merely classifies — it says this is the standard instance of the type, and the type can be a disaster. A paradigmatic bureaucratic failure is still a failure. Register is academic: historians, critics and scientists reach for it when they want "textbook case" without sounding casual.
Exemplary = the best example. Paradigmatic = the example.
One word hands out praise, the other just points at the case the whole pattern is built on.
1. The Dreyfus affair remains the paradigmatic instance of a state closing ranks against inconvenient evidence.
2. That three-hour meeting with no decision was paradigmatic of this whole company.
"Paradigm shift" — Thomas Kuhn's phrase from The Structure of Scientific Revolutions, now thoroughly colonised by corporate slide decks. The paradigmatic case is whatever the current paradigm treats as normal.
Greek para- ("beside") + deiknynai ("to show") → paradeigma, a thing shown alongside as the pattern to copy — exactly what a model does.

That para- runs through parallel, paraphrase, parody, paramedic; deiknynai is cousin to Latin dicere/index, the pointing-and-showing family behind indicate and digit.

Self-contradictory on its face, yet somehow true.
Self-contradictory on the face of it — and yet true, or at least standing up to scrutiny.

The word does real work only when both halves survive. Something merely contradictory is broken: one side must be wrong. Something ironic is a wink at a mismatched outcome. Paradoxical keeps both sides alive at once — the drug that causes the symptom it treats, the rule that makes obeying it impossible. Tone is analytical rather than critical: calling a finding paradoxical says this is worth thinking about, not this is nonsense.
Contradictory means it's wrong. Paradoxical means it's wrong and true anyway.
Save the word for contradictions that survive inspection — the safety feature that causes accidents, the crowd that leaves you lonelier.
1. The study reached the paradoxical conclusion that the most heavily policed districts reported the least confidence in the police.
2. It's a bit paradoxical, but the more sleep-tracking apps I install, the worse I sleep.
Catch-22 is the purest paradoxical rule in fiction: you can be grounded for insanity, but asking to be grounded proves you're sane. The book gave English a phrase for exactly this shape of trap.
Greek para- (beside, contrary to) + doxa (opinion, belief) → paradoxos, "contrary to received opinion."

That dox unlocks a set: orthodox (straight opinion), heterodox (other opinion), doxology (doxa also = glory, so: words of praise). And para- runs through parody (a song sung alongside), parallel, paranormal.

A perfect example; the standard others are measured against.
A model of excellence — a person or thing so perfect in some quality that everyone else gets measured against it.

Not merely "very good." A paragon is the benchmark: the phrasing is almost always a paragon of + a virtue (patience, integrity, restraint, efficiency). Because the praise is absolute, it tips easily into sarcasm — "he's a paragon of punctuality" said about a man forty minutes late does real damage.
⚠️ paragon ≠ paradigm.
- paragon = the best example (of a virtue) — praise
- paradigm = the typical example, the pattern or framework — neutral

You're a paragon of virtue; you work within a paradigm.
Paragon — a paragon doesn't meet par, it sets par.
Golf's par is the score everything else is judged against, which is exactly what a paragon is for a virtue.
1. Her predecessor was held up as a paragon of judicial restraint, a standard no successor was expected to reach.
2. Look, I'm no paragon of healthy eating, but even I don't have cake for breakfast.
Hamlet on mankind: "how noble in reason... the beauty of the world, the paragon of animals" — the top specimen, the one the rest are compared to.
Italian paragone = a touchstone: the dark stone jewellers rubbed gold against, reading the streak to judge its purity. A paragon is still that — the thing you test others against.

Narrow in outlook; concerned only with your own small patch.
1. Narrow in outlook — concerned only with your own small circle, unable to see beyond it. 2. Literally: belonging to a parish (parochial school).

The insult isn't about intelligence, it's about horizon. Calling a view parochial says the person is competent inside their little patch and has never thought past its edge. It's cooler and more condescending than narrow-minded, which implies stubbornness or bigotry; parochial implies you simply never had the range. It attaches easily to institutions and debates — parochial concerns, a parochial dispute — meaning small-stakes squabbles that matter to no one outside the village.
Parochial has parish in it — a mind that never leaves its own parish.
The village church marks the edge of the world for someone parochial: everything inside it is known, everything outside it is invisible.
1. Her critics dismissed the report as parochial, framing a global crisis entirely in terms of one county's tax base.
2. Once you've lived abroad for a year, the arguments back home start to sound pretty parochial.
In the US, a parochial school is a church-run school — the everyday survival of sense 2, and a free reminder that the whole word is built on parish.
Greek oikos = "house, dwelling" → paroikia, "a neighbouring dwelling," which became Church Latin for a parish.

That oikos root pays off widely: economy (managing the house), ecology (study of the house), ecumenical (the whole inhabited house — the opposite of parochial), diocese.

Stingy to a fault; sparing with money, praise, or assumptions.
Extremely unwilling to spend or give — stingy, tight-fisted, sparing to the point of meanness.

A frugal person spends carefully and you admire them; a parsimonious one hoards and you judge them. It's a cold, formal word — the kind used in an obituary or an audit, not a shout across a table. And it stretches past money: you can be parsimonious with praise, with detail, with sympathy.

One flip side worth knowing, because the GRE loves it: applied to a theory or explanation, parsimonious is praise — it means economical, using the fewest assumptions necessary.
Parsimonious ≈ "parses my money" — he parses every penny before he parts with it.
The word isn't about spending little, it's about the obsessive counting that precedes it.
1. The estate revealed a man parsimonious in life and lavish only in death, having left a fortune he never once enjoyed.
2. My landlord is so parsimonious he times the hallway lights.
Occam's razor is formally called the law of parsimony — of two explanations, take the one that spends fewer assumptions. That's the same word doing its complimentary job, and it's how scientists and statisticians actually use it ("the more parsimonious model").
Latin parcere = "to spare, to refrain from using" → parsimonia, thrift. The whole word is just "sparingness," which is why it fits both the miser and the lean theory.

🚫 Not from parse (Latin pars, "part") — handy as a sound hook, unrelated by blood.

column2:
Biased toward one side; or, fond of something.
Everyone knows sense 1: incomplete, only a part (a partial refund). The GRE wants senses 2 and 3.

2. Biased — favouring one side. A partial judge, referee, or examiner has quietly taken a side. This is the fault that impartial denies. It's milder and cooler than prejudiced or partisan: partiality is a soft tilt, often unconscious, often affection-driven — the teacher who marks her favourite generously. It accuses you of leaning, not of hating.

3. partial to = fond of. Only in that fixed phrase, and it's warm, mild, faintly understated: I'm partial to a strong cup of tea. Never "I'm partial to my wife" — it's for tastes, not loves.
Partial hides PART — a partial judge takes your part.
To take someone's part is to side with them, which is exactly what the biased sense means — and the same lean, softened, gives you partial to.
1. The defence argued that a juror who had lunched with the prosecutor could hardly be anything but partial.
2. Don't ask me to pick the winner — I'm shamelessly partial to the underdog.
You meet the negative daily: news outlets and jurors swear they are impartial, and referees are accused of partiality every weekend. That's the word doing real work — always as the thing being denied.
Latin pars, partis = "part, side." A part of something, and a side in a quarrel, are the same word — which is why partial means both "incomplete" and "taking sides."

That root is everywhere: party (a side), partisan (a side-taker), participate, impart, portion, apart, counterpart.

Just good enough; or able to be crossed.
Two senses, one logic.

1. Good enough — and no better. Adequate, acceptable, satisfies the minimum. A passable imitation. Passable French.
2. Able to be crossed or travelled. The road is passable again after the flood.

Sense 1 is faint praise, and deliberately so. Fine is neutral; decent is mildly warm; passable actively signals the ceiling — it clears the bar and stops there. Calling a meal passable tells you the cook will not be asked again. It's the word of examiners, critics and polite disappointment: the thing survived judgement rather than won it.
It doesn't pass with honours — it just passes.
The word wears its own limit: a bare pass mark, never a distinction.
1. His grasp of the treaty's clauses was passable, though the committee had hoped for mastery.
2. The wine was passable — nobody had a second glass.
Straight from pass. Both senses are the same picture: a road you can get through, and a performance that gets through — scraping past the checkpoint either way.

Accepting what happens without acting; acted upon rather than acting.
Not acting; accepting or absorbing what happens without resistance, initiative, or protest. In grammar, the voice in which the subject is acted upon rather than acting ("the ball was thrown").

Applied to a person it carries a quiet reproach, because it measures you against something you could have done and didn't. A calm person is at peace, a docile one obeys, a passive one simply stands there. It's milder than supine or servile — but rarely a compliment, except in technical pairings like passive income, passive smoking, passive solar heating, where it means nothing more than "without active effort."
⚠️ passive ≠ impassive.
- passive = takes no action
- impassive = shows no emotion

A negotiator can be impassive — stone-faced — while working the phones hard. That's the opposite of passive.
Passive: your turn comes and you pass — the game goes on without you.
The "pass" hook catches the crucial part: a turn was available to you, which is why passivity gets blamed and mere calmness doesn't.
1. Faced with mounting evidence of fraud, the board remained passive, minuting its concerns and doing nothing further.
2. Don't be so passive — if you want Friday off, just go and ask for it.
"Mistakes were made." The classic political non-apology is also the textbook specimen of the passive voice: something happened, and no one did it. Every style guide holds it up as the sentence that hides its own actor.
Latin patī, passus = "to suffer, to undergo" — to be on the receiving end.

That root pays off widely: patient (one who undergoes), compassion (suffering with), passion — which originally meant suffering, which is why the Crucifixion is called the Passion of Christ, not a romance. Passive is the plain adjective of the family: you don't do, you're done to.

An open imitation or medley of another's style.
A work that openly imitates the style of another artist, period, or genre — or a piece assembled out of bits of several sources, a medley.

The key is that a pastiche hides nothing. Plagiarism steals and denies it; parody imitates in order to mock; a pastiche imitates without either — usually in homage, sometimes just as a stylistic exercise. Which is why the word cuts both ways: call a novel "a loving pastiche of Chandler" and it's praise, call it "mere pastiche" and you've said it has borrowed style and no soul of its own.
Pastiche = "paste-ish" — other people's styles pasted together, openly, with the seams showing.
Paste implies assembly rather than theft or ridicule, which is exactly the space pastiche occupies between plagiarism and parody.
1. His late symphonies are an elegant pastiche of Mahler, faithful in every gesture and original in none.
2. The whole bar is a pastiche of a 1950s diner — chrome stools, jukebox, the lot.
Stranger Things is the cleanest example going: a pastiche of Spielberg, Stephen King and John Carpenter — every source lovingly copied, none of it mocked, none of it hidden.
French pastiche ← Italian pasticcio = a pie — a crust stuffed with whatever ingredients were to hand. From Latin pasta, "dough."

So the root family is literally food: pasta, paste, pastry, pâté. A pastiche is a pie of other people's styles.

column2:
Obvious, plain to see — usually said of a lie.
Adj.: obvious, plain for anyone to see — needing no proof or argument. (The familiar noun — an exclusive right to an invention — is the same word, explained below.)

Register is formal-to-legal, and the company it keeps is telling: a patent lie, patent nonsense, a patent absurdity, patently unfair. Almost nobody calls a pleasant fact patent. Where obvious is neutral and evident suggests something you inferred from evidence, patent means the thing is lying wide open — and the speaker is usually exasperated that anyone pretended otherwise.
⚠️ patent vs. latent — exact opposites, one letter apart.
- patent = lying open, in plain sight
- latent = lying hidden, not yet showing

A latent flaw becomes patent the day the bridge falls.
You never hear a patent truth — only a patent lie.
The word attaches almost exclusively to falsehood and absurdity, so learn it as the adjective you use when something false is insultingly easy to see through.
1. The defence rested on a claim of ignorance that the documents rendered patently false.
2. Come on — that excuse is patent nonsense and you know it.
Newsrooms and courtrooms run on the adverb: "patently false," "patently absurd," "patently unfair" turn up constantly in reporting and judgments — you have almost certainly read it this month without registering it.
Latin patēre = "to lie open." A medieval king's grant came as litterae patentes, "letters patent" — an open document, unsealed so anyone could read it. That single image runs both senses: what is patent lies open to view, and a patent is your claim published openly for all to see.

Its mirror is latēre, "to lie hidden" → latent. Open vs. hidden, one letter apart.

column2:
To talk down to someone; also, to be a customer of.
Two senses, and the GRE tests both.

1. To treat someone as an inferior while appearing kind — to talk down. The sting is that it comes wrapped as help: the explanation you didn't need, the praise pitched at a child, the slow careful voice. Plain rudeness insults you openly; patronizing insults you while doing you a favour, which is why it's harder to object to without looking ungracious.

2. To be a customer of a shop, or to sponsor an artist or cause. Fully neutral, even complimentary — "she patronized the same tailor for forty years." Same word, no condescension at all.

Both senses run through the noun patron: the rich backer. Sense 2 is what a patron does; sense 1 is what it feels like to be on the receiving end.
A patron funds you and thinks he owns you — so to patronize is to treat someone like your charity case.
The hidden word patron gives you both meanings at once: the sponsor's money (sense 2) and the sponsor's superior smile (sense 1).
1. The report patronizes its readers, defining "inflation" twice and pausing to reassure them that economics is not so very difficult.
2. Don't patronize me — I've been doing this job longer than you've been alive.
"Thank you for patronizing our business" on a shop receipt or door sign — the sense that has nothing to do with condescension, printed by people trying to be polite.
Latin pater, patris = "father." A patron was a father-figure protector; to patronize is to play the father to a grown adult — funding them, or lecturing them.

The root is worth a lot of GRE words: paternal, paternalistic (governing people "for their own good"), patriarch, patrimony, patriot, expatriate.

A small, easily forgiven sin or minor fault.
A small sin — a minor offence, a trifling fault, the kind of wrongdoing nobody is going to prosecute.

The word does two things at once: it admits the fault and waves it away. You cannot call something a peccadillo without also excusing it, which is why it turns up in indulgent, faintly amused, worldly-wise sentences — often about appetites (drinking, gambling, flirting) rather than blunders. Note the difference from its neighbours: a transgression is grave, a foible is a harmless quirk of temperament and not an offence at all, and a peccadillo sits between them — a real wrong, deliberately shrunk.
Peccadillo starts like peck — and it ends in the Spanish "little" suffix -illo. A peck of a sin, not a bite.
The sound tells you the scale: a peck is the smallest thing a bird can do to you, and -illo shrinks whatever it's attached to.
1. His biographers treat the affair as a peccadillo, tucked into a footnote between two chapters of genuine achievement.
2. Leaving the milk out isn't a crime, it's a peccadillo — stop apologising.
Standard political-scandal vocabulary: reporters reach for "youthful peccadilloes" precisely when a party wants the story filed under minor and forgotten.
Spanish pecadillo, little sin — diminutive of pecado, from Latin peccāre, "to sin, to stumble."

Same root gives you the high-value GRE word impeccable: literally un-sin-able, incapable of fault — hence flawless taste, an impeccable record. Also peccant (offending, faulty).

column2:
Mildly odd; or belonging exclusively to one person or group.
Two senses, and the GRE almost always wants the second.

1. Strange, odd — but mildly so. Peculiar is the gentlest word in its family: bizarre startles you, weird unsettles you, peculiar just makes you tilt your head. It's the polite British word for "there's something off here and I'd rather not say what" — a peculiar smell, a peculiar man, a peculiar silence at dinner.

2. Belonging exclusively to one person, group, or place. This sense carries no oddness at all: a dialect peculiar to the islands, a talent peculiar to her. Watch for the preposition — "peculiar to X" is nearly always sense 2, and the test rewards you for spotting it.
Peculiar and pecuniary share a root: your own cattle. What belongs to you alone eventually starts to look odd to everyone else.
The exclusive-property sense came first, and the "strange" sense is just what exclusivity looks like from the outside.
1. The nesting behaviour is peculiar to this one subspecies; no related bird does anything like it.
2. He's got a peculiar way of answering the phone — three rings, then a whisper.
The King James Bible calls the faithful "a peculiar people" (1 Peter 2:9) — not a weird people, but God's own people. That line is the exclusive-possession sense preserved in amber.
Latin pecū = "cattle" → pecūlium, the private herd a Roman slave or son was allowed to own → pecūliāris, "one's own."

Cattle were the first money, so that root runs straight into your wallet: pecuniary (relating to money), impecunious (broke), peculate (to embezzle — to treat public funds as your own).

Fussing over trivial details or showing off learning.
Excessively concerned with minor rules, technicalities, or the parading of one's learning — correcting the comma while the building burns.

It is always an insult. The behaviour it describes is identical to meticulous or scrupulous; the difference is entirely in whether the fuss was worth it. Praise the same person and you get "rigorous"; resent them and you get pedantic. Built into the word is a charge of misplaced priorities — the pedant is right about the small thing and wrong about what mattered, and rather enjoys the correction.
⚠️ pedantic ≠ pedestrian. Both are sneers, but different ones: pedantic = fussing over trivial details; pedestrian = dull, unimaginative, ordinary. A pedantic essay nitpicks; a pedestrian essay bores.
Ped-ANT-ic — he's picking over ants while you're pointing at the elephant.
The hidden ant is the size of the detail he's chosen to die on.
1. His commentary on the poem was pedantic to the point of uselessness — six pages on the manuscript's punctuation, not a word on what the thing meant.
2. Sorry to be pedantic, but it's fewer people, not less people.
The internet's "well, actually…" reply — the guy who ignores your entire point to correct one detail in it. That is pedantry with a keyboard.
From Italian pedante, "schoolmaster" — most likely tied to Greek paid-, paidos = "child." The pedant is the schoolmaster who never left the classroom, still drilling rules at grown adults.

That root pays out widely: pedagogy (leading children), pediatrician, encyclopedia (a circle of child-rearing, i.e. general education).

🚫 Not the ped- of pedal, pedestrian, pedestal — that's Latin pes, pedis, "foot." Same-looking prefix, unrelated family.

column2:
Dull and unimaginative; ordinary to the point of boring.
Noun: a person travelling on foot.
Adjective (the GRE sense): dull, unimaginative, uninspired — ordinary in a way that bores.

The adjective is a critic's dismissal, and its sting is that it doesn't call the work bad. It calls it competent and earthbound: nothing wrong, nothing lifting off. Banal accuses you of recycling other people's ideas; pedestrian accuses you of plodding along with your own. It's most at home reviewing prose, music, cooking, argument — anything that could have soared and instead walked.
⚠️ pedestrian ≠ pedantic.
- pedestrian = dull, plodding, unremarkable
- pedantic = fussily obsessed with tiny rules and details

A pedestrian lecture sends you to sleep; a pedantic one corrects your pronunciation of "espresso."
Pedestrian prose walks — it never flies.
The word literally means "on foot," and the insult is exactly that: stuck at ground level, moving but never taking off.
1. The reviewer conceded that the novel was flawlessly constructed, then killed it in one word: pedestrian.
2. Dinner was fine — just a bit pedestrian, honestly. I could've made that at home.
Every "PEDESTRIANS ONLY" sign you walk past is the literal sense doing the work for you — people on foot, at foot speed. The insult is the same picture applied to someone's writing.
Latin pes, pedis = "foot" → pedester, "on foot," which the Romans already used to mean plain, prosaic writing.

That root pays off across the exam: pedal, pedestal, pedicure, biped, centipede, plus two you'll meet on the GRE — impede (feet shackled = to hinder) and expedite (feet freed = to speed up).

Belittling; a word chosen to express contempt.
Adjective: expressing contempt or disapproval; belittling.
Noun: a word that does the belittling.

This is a label you put on a word, not on a person — you say "'bureaucrat' is a pejorative", not "he was pejorative to me." That gives it a cool, almost clinical register: the person saying "pejorative" is calm; the word being described is not. It's also wider and weaker than slur — a pejorative can be a mere sneer buried in a suffix (poetaster, starlet) rather than an outright attack.
⚠️ pejorative ≠ prerogative. A prerogative is an exclusive right you hold ("that's the boss's prerogative"). Similar rhythm, opposite worlds — one insults, one entitles.
Deliberately mis-say it — pe-JEER-ative. A pejorative jeers.
The jeer is baked into the word itself, which is why you label the term pejorative rather than the speaker.
1. Once neutral, the word drifted into pejorative use and now appears in the style guide's list of terms to avoid.
2. He called my playlist "eclectic," but the tone was pure pejorative — he meant it was a mess.
Wikipedia boilerplate: scroll to almost any article on a nickname or slang term and you'll hit the sentence "the term is often used as a pejorative." It's the internet's standard way of saying this word carries a sneer.
Latin peior = "worse" → pejorare, "to make worse." A pejorative word makes its target worse than it is.

Same root, disguised: impair (via Latin impejorare) literally means to make worse — which is exactly what impairing something does.

Crystal-clear — see-through water, or luminously clear prose.
Transparently clear — either physically (water, glass, air you can see straight through) or mentally (prose, an explanation, a mind that admits no murk).

Clear is a plain report; pellucid is a compliment. It carries light with it — the sense that the thing isn't merely see-through but luminous, unclouded, almost beautiful in its clarity. You'd call a mountain stream or a great teacher's explanation pellucid; you wouldn't say it of a windowpane unless you were feeling lyrical. It's a literary word, and it always praises.
pel-LUC-id — the stress lands squarely on the LUC, the light.
Say it aloud and you hear lucid sitting inside the word with per- ("through") in front — clarity that light passes all the way through, not just clarity you can tolerate.
1. The lake was so pellucid that the boat seemed suspended above its own shadow.
2. His notes are pellucid — I understood the whole topic in one read, which never happens.
Latin per- (through) + lucēre (to shine) — light shining all the way through.

That luc- root is a GRE goldmine: lucid (clear-minded), elucidate (to shed light on), translucent (light passes, images don't), lucent, lux/lumen — and Lucifer, literally "light-bearer."

column2:
A habitual, slightly indulgent liking for something.
A strong and habitual liking or inclination for something — a taste you keep coming back to.

A penchant is a known fondness, the thing people would list about you: a penchant for loud jackets, for gossip, for arriving late. It's lighter and more indulgent than its neighbours — a propensity sounds clinical (a propensity for violence), a proclivity hints at vice, but a penchant is usually charming or wryly noted, and often attaches to something a bit frivolous. Nobody has a penchant for breathing; you have a penchant for good champagne.
p-ENCHANT — a penchant is a small enchantment.
The word you're charmed by sits inside it, and that's the right strength: a penchant delights you, it doesn't compel you.
1. The ambassador was tolerated despite a penchant for saying, at dinner, precisely what everyone else had agreed not to.
2. He's a decent flatmate, but he's got this penchant for reorganising my kitchen when I'm out.
Sports commentary runs on it — \"he has a penchant for the dramatic\" is what they say about the player who always scores in the 90th minute.
French pencher = "to lean" (← Latin pendere, to hang/weigh). A penchant is literally which way you tilt.

That unlocks the whole cluster, because they're all leaning words: inclination (clinare, to lean), proclivity (clivus, a slope), propensity (pendere again — hanging forward). Four GRE words, one gesture.
