column2:
Piercing past the surface — of insight, gaze, sound, or cold.
Of a mind, question, or gaze: sharp enough to see past the surface — to what someone is hiding or hasn't admitted. Of a sound, smell, or cold: piercing, forcing its way in, impossible to shut out.

Both senses share one idea: it gets through the barrier. That's what separates it from sharp or shrewd, which describe the quality of a mind in general — penetrating is about what it does to the thing it's aimed at. A shrewd analyst reads the market well; a penetrating question leaves the witness with nowhere to stand. Aimed at people, it's flattering about the observer and uncomfortable for the observed — a penetrating stare is admiring of no one.
Sharp stops at the surface; penetrating gets in.
Whether it's a question, a stare, a siren or a stink, the word always means the barrier failed to hold it out.
1. Her penetrating analysis of the budget exposed assumptions the committee had never thought to state aloud.
2. He gave me this penetrating look and I knew he'd worked out I hadn't read the email.
Interviewers get praised for penetrating questions — the ones that get past the media training to an actual answer. If you can hear the collocation penetrating question, you have the word.

Quietly, dreamily thoughtful, with a shade of sadness.
Deep in quiet, dreamy thought — and usually a little sad with it.

Thoughtful is about consideration for others; contemplative and reflective are about mental effort or depth. Pensive is about mood, and it carries a faint grey weather-front of melancholy: someone staring out of a train window, not someone solving a problem. It's also mostly an observed state — it describes how a person looks from the outside, which is why it attaches so easily to faces, silences and portraits.
Nobody says "I feel pensive" — they say "you look pensive."
It's a mood read off someone's face from across the room, which is exactly why it means quietly, sadly lost in thought rather than thinking hard.
1. Between the two movements the conductor stood pensive, the baton lowered, as if reluctant to disturb what the orchestra had just done.
2. He got pensive after the third drink and started talking about his dad.
Dumbledore's Pensieve — the stone basin you pour memories into and brood over. Rowling built the name straight out of pensive (+ sieve), and the object does exactly what the word means.
Latin pendere = "to hang, to weigh" → pensāre, "weigh carefully" → French penser, "to think." Thinking as weighing.

That root hangs a lot of GRE words off it: ponder (weigh in the mind), compensate (counter-weigh), suspend, pendant, pending, poise.

Dirt-poor — or mean enough with money to look it.
Two linked senses: (1) extremely poor, destitute — a penurious old age; (2) stingy, unwilling to part with money — a penurious tip.

Context decides which, and the overlap is the point: the word describes someone who lives as though there is nothing, whether or not there actually is. Sense (2) is where the GRE lives, and it is an insult — frugal and thrifty praise you for spending carefully, penurious says your meanness is a defect. It's also a bookish word: you'd write it in a novel or an essay, not hiss it across a restaurant table.
⚠️ penurious ≠ pernicious. Similar shape, unrelated: pernicious = quietly destructive, doing harm by degrees (a pernicious rumour). Penury is about money; pernicious is about damage.
Penurious = down to the last penny — either you have one, or you act like it.
The false penny-echo carries both senses at once, which is exactly how the word behaves.
1. Widowed at thirty, she passed the remaining decades in penurious retirement, heating one room of the house.
2. He's not broke — he's just penurious; the man split a birthday dinner bill by the item.
Latin penuria = "want, scarcity" — straight into English as penury, meaning grinding poverty.

🚫 Nothing to do with poena (punishment) — that root gives penal, penalty, penance, penitent, repent. Two different "pen-" families; don't let penitentiary pull penurious toward guilt.

Recurring year after year; enduring by coming back.
Adj.: lasting through the years, or — more precisely — coming back again and again. Noun: a plant that lives on and reflowers each year (as opposed to an annual).

The word carries recurrence, not just duration: something that fades and returns on schedule, so reliably you stop being surprised. That's the difference from perpetual (never stops) and eternal (never ends). Tone flips with the object: a perennial favourite is affectionate — it keeps coming back because people love it; a perennial problem or perennial complaint is weary — it keeps coming back because nobody ever fixed it.
A perennial comes back. A perpetual never left.
Perennial things go away and return on a cycle, which is why it fits favourites, candidates and unfixed problems rather than things that simply never stop.
1. Funding for the arts is a perennial casualty of the budget: cut, restored, and cut again.
2. Dad's perennial joke about the sat-nav gets wheeled out every single road trip.
The plant tags at any garden centre: annuals die off and you rebuy them next spring; perennials cost more because they come back on their own, year after year.
Latin per (through) + annus (year) = "through the year."

annus is a workhorse root: annual, anniversary, annuity, biennial (every two years), millennium (mille + annus), superannuated (over-yeared, i.e. obsolete or pensioned off).

Calculated betrayal by someone who was trusted.
Deliberate breach of faith — treachery by someone who was trusted, and who traded on that trust.

You cannot be perfidious to a stranger. The word requires a bond first — an ally, a spouse, a treaty, an oath — and it condemns the violation of the bond, not merely the lie. Next to it, dishonesty is petty and deceit is technique; perfidy is a moral verdict, delivered in a raised register. It belongs to statesmen, historians and courtroom rhetoric, and it carries real contempt: a lawyer says perfidy when betrayal isn't damning enough. In the laws of war it's a defined crime — feigning surrender in order to shoot.
Perfidy is fidelity with a per- bolted on — the faith has to exist before it can be broken.
Spot the fid buried in the middle and you get both the meaning and the condition: no prior trust, no perfidy.
1. The treaty was signed in the morning and the border crossed by night — an act of perfidy the smaller nation never forgave.
2. He smiled, took the credit for her slides, and called it teamwork; the perfidy was breathtaking.
"Perfidious Albion" — the centuries-old French sneer at England, meaning the island that signs treaties and breaks them. Still trotted out in European newspapers whenever Britain reneges on something.
Latin per- (through, to destruction) + fidēs (faith, trust) — literally faith wrecked.

That root is a goldmine: fidelity, infidel, confide, bona fide, affidavit, fiancé (one pledged), and the Marines' Semper Fi. Even the classic dog's name Fido is Latin for "I trust."

column2:
Done as a duty, with minimum effort and zero interest.
Done merely as a duty — mechanically, with the minimum effort, and no real interest.

The key is that the thing does get done. A perfunctory inspection happens; a perfunctory apology is offered. What's missing is care. That makes it a quiet insult: you're not accusing someone of failing, you're accusing them of not bothering. Careless implies sloppiness; perfunctory implies indifference wearing the costume of compliance.
perfunctory ≠ peremptory. Perfunctory is a limp handshake — going through the motions. Peremptory (puh-REMP-tuh-ree) is a slammed door — commanding, allowing no refusal. Low energy vs. overbearing energy.
There's no funk in per-FUNK-tory — the motions happen, the soul doesn't.
The stressed syllable is literally funk, so hear it as a performance with all the groove drained out — technically played, emotionally absent.
1. The board gave the whistleblower's report a perfunctory review and voted, as everyone had expected, to do nothing.
2. He gave the fridge a perfunctory wipe, decided that counted as cleaning, and sat back down.
The cashier's "How are you today?" — asked, answered, and heard by nobody. That's the most perfunctory sentence in daily life.
Latin perfungī = "to get through with, discharge a duty" — per- (through) + fungī (to perform). Baked into the word is the idea of getting something over with.

That root fungī also gives you function (a thing's performance), defunct (no longer performing at all), and fungible (one unit performs the same job as another).

column2:
Full of grave danger; risky in a serious, weighty way.
Full of danger; likely to get you hurt, ruined, or killed.

Dangerous is the flat, everyday word — a dangerous road, a dangerous chemical. Perilous is its elevated cousin: it carries weight and a whiff of narrative, and it attaches to journeys, crossings, voyages, missions, and times. It also stretches beyond physical harm to precarious situations — a company in a perilous financial position isn't about to explode, it's about to collapse. Reach for it when the danger is grave and the moment feels consequential; use it for a wobbly stepladder and you sound like you're narrating a trailer.
Peril is sitting right inside it — and peril is what heroes face, not what you find in the kitchen.
The hidden word gives you the meaning free; the company peril keeps (quests, voyages, crossings) gives you the grand register.
1. The expedition's final ascent was the most perilous stage, undertaken in darkness and thinning air.
2. Lending him the car with no insurance? Mate, that's a perilous move.
The US national anthem: "through the perilous fight, o'er the ramparts we watched..." — a battle at night, exactly the grand-danger register the word lives in.
Latin perīculum = "a trial, a risk" — from a root meaning to try, to attempt.

That root pays out elsewhere: experīrī ("to try out") gives you experience, experiment, and expert — all of them people or things that have been tested. Peril is simply the test that can kill you.

At the outer edge — secondary, not the main thing.
Literally: lying at the outer edge or boundary. Figuratively: secondary, marginal — off to one side of the main business. As a noun: a device attached around a computer (mouse, printer).

Calling something peripheral is a soft demotion. It doesn't claim the thing is wrong or worthless — only that it isn't the point. That is exactly what makes it a debating move: "a peripheral concern" concedes your issue exists while quietly sliding it off the table. Trivial is openly contemptuous, irrelevant flatly denies any connection; peripheral is the polite one, and usually the one worth pushing back on.
Peripheral vision — you can still see it. You're just not looking at it.
Peripheral things are present and real, merely outside the centre of attention — which is why the word demotes without quite dismissing.
1. Questions of consent were treated as peripheral to the study's design, and the ethics board later said so in writing.
2. Don't argue about the font — that's peripheral. Get the numbers right first.
Your mouse, keyboard and headset are sold as peripherals — the kit arranged around the computer, not one piece of which is the computer.
Greek peri- = "around" + pherein = "to carry." The periphery is the line carried around a shape — its outer boundary.

peri- unlocks a run of GRE words: perimeter (measure around), periscope (look around), peripatetic (walking around), periodontal (around the tooth).

pherein gives metaphor (carry across), euphoria (bearing up well), paraphernalia (the stuff carried alongside).

column2:
Quietly, gradually destructive — harm that hides itself until too late.
Causing serious harm — but gradually, quietly, and often invisibly until the damage is done.

The word is almost never used for a punch, a bomb, or a car crash. It's reserved for the slow poison: a pernicious influence, a pernicious doctrine, a pernicious habit, a pernicious myth. Harmful states the fact; destructive is loud and visible; pernicious adds the creep — it works on you while you're not looking, and it's usually said with moral disapproval by someone educated and alarmed.
⚠️ pernicious ≠ perfidious.
- pernicious = quietly destructive (a harmful effect)
- perfidious = treacherous, faithless (a betrayer)

A perfidious ally stabs you in the back; a pernicious rumour rots you from the inside.
It has "nice" sitting right in the middle — per-NICI-ous — and that's the whole point: it looks nice while it kills you.
Pernicious harm is the kind that doesn't announce itself, so the friendly-looking spelling matches the word's disguise.
1. The report identified social media's pernicious effect on adolescent attention spans, accumulating year by year until it was mistaken for normal.
2. Skipping breakfast started as a time-saver, but it turned into a pernicious little habit that wrecked my afternoons.
Pernicious anaemia is still the standard medical name for B12-deficiency anaemia — christened before the cause was known, when it was a disease that quietly wasted you away and then killed you. The label survives as a fossil of exactly this meaning: slow, hidden, fatal.
Latin per- (thoroughly) + nex, necis (violent death) → perniciosus, "thoroughly deadly."

That death-root reappears in internecine (mutually destructive — inter + necāre, to kill) and, via its Greek cousin nekros, in necrosis and necromancy.

To commit — a crime, fraud, hoax, or outrage.
To carry out or commit something — a crime, a fraud, a hoax, an atrocity.

The object is never innocent. You commit a crime or commit to a plan, but you only perpetrate things the speaker disapproves of: no one perpetrates a kindness. It also carries a whiff of officialdom — police reports, court transcripts, journalism — which is why it turns funny when aimed at something trivial: who perpetrated this haircut?
⚠️ perpetrate ≠ perpetuate.
- perpetrate (PUR-puh-trayt) = do the bad thing
- perpetuate (per-PECH-oo-ayt) = keep it going forever

You perpetrate a fraud; you perpetuate a stereotype.
Only a perp can perpetrate.
The cop-show word perp is hiding in the first syllable, and it tells you the object is always a wrongdoing — never a favour, never a plan.
1. The commission concluded that the massacre had been perpetrated by units acting under direct orders.
2. Someone perpetrated a group chat at 2am and now I have 400 unread messages.
"Perp walk" — the parade of a handcuffed suspect past the cameras. Perp is just a clipped perpetrator, and every police procedural you've ever half-watched runs on it.
Latin per- (thoroughly) + patrare (to bring about) — to see a deed all the way through.

The confusable twin comes from somewhere else entirely: perpetuate ← perpetuus, "continuous," which also gives perpetual and perpetuity. Different root, different job.

To keep something — usually something bad — going indefinitely.
To cause something to continue indefinitely — to keep it alive, going, in force.

Technically neutral, but look at what people actually perpetuate: myths, stereotypes, cycles of poverty, an unjust system, a feud. The word carries a quiet accusation — you didn't start it, but you're keeping it running, and it should have died. Preserve protects something worth having; prolong stretches something that was going to end anyway; perpetuate hands the bad thing to the next generation. The rare positive use is deliberately grand: to perpetuate her memory.
perpetuate ≠ perpetrate.
- perpetrate = commit an act (a crime, a fraud, a hoax) — one deed, one doer
- perpetuate = keep it going — no single deed, just continuation
You perpe*trate* a crime once; you perpe*tuate* a stereotype forever.
The -trate word is a single act with a culprit; the -tuate word is the endless continuation of something that ought to have stopped.
1. Far from correcting the record, the textbook perpetuated a version of the war that historians had abandoned decades earlier.
2. Paying him off just perpetuates the whole mess — he'll be back next month asking for more.
Legal and financial paperwork keeps its cousin alive: a trust that runs in perpetuity never ends — same root, same idea of something that refuses to stop.
Latin perpetuus = "continuous, unbroken" — per- (through) + petere (to go toward). It runs straight through without a break: perpetual, perpetuity, perpetual motion.

🚫 Not perpetrate. That's Latin patrare, "to bring about, accomplish" — a completed deed, not an unending one.

Steady effort kept up despite difficulty or discouragement.
Steady, continued effort at something difficult, kept up despite failure, delay, or discouragement.

Persistence is neutral and can grate — a persistent cough, a persistent salesman. Perseverance is praise: it presumes real obstacles and a person who deserves credit for outlasting them. It's the virtue on the good side of a line whose bad side is obstinacy — same refusal to stop, but pointed at something worth finishing. Note also that it's slow-burn, not intense: perseverance is measured in months of grinding, not one heroic push.
Persevere hides severe — you stay severe with yourself all the way through (per-).
The hidden word gives you both halves of the meaning: strictness with yourself, sustained for the whole distance.
1. Her perseverance through eleven years of rejected manuscripts is the only reason the novel exists at all.
2. He's not the smartest guy on the team, but sheer perseverance got him through the exam on the fourth try.
NASA's Mars rover Perseverance — named by a middle-schooler in a national contest, then flown 300 million miles to grind away at Martian rock for years. The name is the job description.
Latin per- (through, thoroughly) + sevērus (strict, serious) → persevērāre, "to keep at it strictly."

That second root is the useful one: it also gives severe, severity, and the GRE word asseverate (to declare earnestly, in dead seriousness).

Keen-sighted in judgement; sees through people and situations.
Having sharp insight — able to notice and understand what others miss, especially about people and motives.

This is praise, and formal praise at that. Shrewd hints that you're working an angle; astute is practical, the eye for a good deal; perceptive is the everyday word. Perspicacious is the cerebral top of that scale: penetrating judgement, seeing through a situation rather than merely noticing it. Noun: perspicacity.
perspicacious ≠ perspicuous.
- perspicacious = the reader sees clearly (keen-minded)
- perspicuous = the writing is clear (lucid, easy to follow)

A perspicacious critic praises a perspicuous argument.
per-SPY-cacious — hear the spy: not just clever, but seeing straight through you.
A spy's whole job is reading people and detecting what's being hidden, which is exactly the kind of intelligence this word names.
1. A perspicacious reader of the market, she sold three months before the crash and never once explained how she knew.
2. One perspicacious question from a junior analyst and the whole business case fell apart.
Latin perspicere = "to see through" (per- through + specere to look).

That spec- root is a GRE workhorse: inspect (look into), conspicuous (visible from all sides), circumspect (looking around before acting), specious (looks good, isn't), prospect, spectacle, specimen.

column2:
Stubbornly persistent — holding on past the point of reason.
Holding stubbornly and unyieldingly to a purpose, opinion, or course of action; refusing to let go.

Tenacious is a compliment — grit, endurance, admirable grip. Pertinacious is the same grip held about an hour too long: the persistence has curdled into obstinacy and the speaker is tired of it. It's a formal, slightly bookish word, and it usually carries a sigh — a pertinacious creditor, a pertinacious cough, a pertinacious rumour that will not die. Applied to people, it says they will not drop this, and not admiringly.
pertinacious ≠ pertinent. Same Latin family, opposite jobs: pertinent = relevant, to the point; pertinacious = doggedly won't let go. A pertinent question is worth asking; a pertinacious questioner won't stop asking it.
Per-tenacious — tenacious per-severed past the point anyone wanted.
Hear tenacious sitting inside the word, then let the per- ("thoroughly, all the way through") push the admirable version into the annoying one.
1. Her pertinacious pursuit of the buried invoices exhausted three lawyers before the firm finally settled.
2. He's pertinacious about that parking fine — four appeals now, over eighteen quid.
Jack Black's band Tenacious D — the name is the same ten- root worn as a badge: "the D" that never lets go. Pertinacious is that, minus the charm.
Latin per- (thoroughly) + tenax / tenēre (to hold) — literally holding on all the way through.

That root is a GRE goldmine: tenacious (gripping), tenet (a belief you hold), tenure (holding a post), retain, contain, sustain, abstain — all holding something, or holding back from it.
column3: g06 register::formal connotation::negative antonym::refusing-to-budge-vs-caving-in connotation::refusal-to-bend-condemned lookalike::impertinent-impudent-pernicious-perspica meaning::persistent-to-the-end root::root:-ten-re-to-hold-holding-back-holdin

column2:
Directly relevant — and worth the room's attention.
Relevant to the matter at hand — and relevant in a way that actually bears on the decision, not just adjacent to the topic.

Relevant is the neutral, everyday word: it merely states a connection. Pertinent is a judgement, usually made by someone with standing — a chair, a judge, an examiner — that this fact deserves the room's attention. It lives in formal registers: legal filings, application forms, meeting minutes. Its negative, "not pertinent," is a polite way of saying stop talking about that.
⚠️ pertinent ≠ impertinent. The im- doesn't cancel relevance — impertinent means rude, cheeky, out of line ("an impertinent question"). Something irrelevant is not pertinent; someone insolent is impertinent.
Relevant is a fact about the topic; pertinent is a verdict about your time.
Anything can be relevant, but a thing is pertinent only once someone has ruled that it's worth hearing.
1. The tribunal declined to admit the letters, holding that nothing in them was pertinent to the charge.
2. "That's a fair point, but is it pertinent right now? We've got ten minutes left."
Every job application and insurance form that asks you to "include any other pertinent information" — the bureaucratic house word for stuff that actually matters here.
Latin pertinēre = "to reach through to, to belong to" — per- (through) + tenēre (to hold). A pertinent fact holds on through to the point.

That tenēre root is a GRE goldmine: pertain, tenacious, tenure, tenant, retain, sustain, abstain, tenet — all of them about holding.

Spread through every part of something; saturating.
Spread throughout every part of something; present everywhere in a place, a system, or a mood.

Widespread is about coverage — how much of the map it reaches. Pervasive is about saturation — it has soaked into the thing, seeped into corners you wouldn't check. Damp, smoke, propaganda, anxiety: things that get into the material rather than sitting on top of it. It also carries a hint of the unnoticed — pervasive things are so evenly distributed that people stop registering them, which is why writers reach for it when describing corruption, bias, or dread.
⚠️ pervasive ≠ persuasive. One letter apart, and both turn up in GRE sentences about influence. Pervasive = everywhere (it spread). Persuasive = convincing (it argued). An ad campaign can be pervasive without being remotely persuasive.
Widespread covers the map; pervasive soaks the sponge.
Reach for pervasive when the thing has got into everything rather than merely spread across a lot of it.
1. A pervasive distrust of the courts had settled over the province long before the first protest.
2. There's a pervasive smell of burnt coffee in this office and nobody will admit whose fault it is.
Pervasive computing — the industry name for the idea that chips end up in the thermostat, the doorbell, the watch, the car, until computing is in everything rather than parked on a desk. The term was chosen for exactly the saturation sense.
Latin per- (through) + vādere (to go) → pervade, "to go through." The same vādere builds a tidy GRE set: invade (go in), evade (go out of), and their adjectives invasive and evasive — so pervasive is simply the "goes right through it" member of the family.

Childishly sulky and irritable over trivial things.
Sulky and bad-tempered in a childish way — snapping, pouting, or huffing over something small.

The word is a put-down of the scale of the anger, not just its heat. Irascible or truculent grant the anger some force; petulant denies it any dignity — it says a grown adult is behaving like a thwarted six-year-old, and the offence they're nursing wasn't worth it. You can be petulant about a cold coffee; you cannot be petulant about an injustice.
PETulant — sulking over pet peeves, not real wrongs.
The hidden pet keeps the key limit in view: the grievance is small and personal, which is exactly why the sulking looks childish.
1. The minister's petulant refusal to answer the question told the chamber more than any answer would have.
2. He went all petulant because we started the film without him.
Football commentary owns this word: a needless retaliatory kick at an opponent is always "a petulant kick" — the standard verdict on Beckham's red card against Argentina in 1998.
Latin petere = "to seek, to make for, to attack." A petulans was someone forever lunging at things — impudent, unable to sit still under a slight.

The root is everywhere on the GRE: petition (seek a favour), appetite (seek food), impetus and impetuous (rushing at), compete (seek alongside), repeat (seek again), centripetal (seeking the centre).

column2:
Someone smugly indifferent or hostile to art and ideas.
Someone smugly indifferent or actively hostile to art, culture and ideas, who values only what is practical, profitable or comfortable. As an adjective: crass, uncultured, materialistic.

It is a snob's word, and it cuts both ways. Calling someone a philistine says they can't see the value of a poem or a painting — but it also announces that you can, and that you're looking down from a height. Ignorant is a lack; a philistine isn't merely ignorant, he's contentedly ignorant, even proud of it — the man who says "I could have painted that" and thinks he's scored a point.
Starts with phil-, but loves nothing it can't put a price on.
The spelling promises a lover of something — like philosophy or philanthropy — and delivers a man who looks at a Rothko and asks what it sold for.
1. The gallery's new director dismissed the trustees as philistines who measured every acquisition by its insurance value.
2. Sorry to be a philistine, but I fell asleep about ten minutes into the opera.
Goliath was a Philistine — 1 Samuel, the giant brute jeering at the Israelite line until a shepherd boy drops him with a stone. Same people, same reputation: all bulk and swagger, no finesse.
Hebrew P'lishtim, the Philistines — the Israelites' coastal enemies in the Old Testament, cast throughout as crude warlike outsiders.

The modern sense is student slang. German university men called the non-academic townsfolk Philister — outsiders, the enemy across the wall — and Matthew Arnold hauled it into English in Culture and Anarchy (1869) to mock the middle class that cared about money and not beauty. That sneer is still audible in the word.

🚫 Nothing to do with Greek phil-, "love." Philosophy, philanthropy, philology, bibliophile — all that family, and the philistine belongs to none of it.

Calm and unexcitable — by nature, not by effort.
Calm, unexcitable, hard to stir — sluggishly even-tempered by nature.

This is temperament, not achievement. Stoic means you endure pain without flinching; serene means an inner peace worth having. Phlegmatic means the alarm simply never went off — the person is constitutionally slow to feel anything much. That gives it a double edge: British writers use it admiringly ("a phlegmatic captain") for the man who doesn't panic, but it can just as easily mean torpid, unresponsive, a bit cold-blooded. Whether it's praise depends entirely on whether the situation deserved a reaction.
Phlegm is thick, slow, sluggish stuff — and so is a phlegmatic person.
The word you already know for the goo gives you the tempo: nothing moves it quickly.
1. Shelling resumed at dawn, and the sergeant received the news with the same phlegmatic shrug he gave the weather.
2. I told him the flight was cancelled and he just kept eating — he's the most phlegmatic person I've ever met.
Greek phlegma = "inflammation, clammy humour." Medieval medicine held that your personality came from whichever of the four bodily humours you had most of — and each one is still an English word:

- blood → sanguine (cheerful, optimistic)
- yellow bile → choleric (hot-tempered)
- black bile → melancholic (gloomy)
- phlegm → phlegmatic (cool, sluggish, unmoved)

Learn the set once and you get four GRE words from one theory.

Fake — and said with contempt, by someone who feels fooled.
Adjective: not genuine — fake, counterfeit, put on.
Noun: the person doing the faking.

Counterfeit and fraudulent describe the object coolly; phony is a judgement thrown at it. It's colloquial and hostile, and it carries a sneer the neutral words don't: the speaker feels taken in. It also stretches past objects to people and manner — a phony accent, a phony smile, a phony friend — where it means insincere posturing rather than literal forgery. Nobody calls something phony from a neutral distance; they call it phony because they've seen through it.
Phony starts with "fo" — so does fool. You only say it once you've felt fooled.
The sound hook carries the nuance: phony isn't a cool description of fakery, it's the accusation you make after the fake stops working on you.
1. The gallery's prize Vermeer proved phony, a competent forgery sold twice before anyone thought to test the pigment.
2. He gave me that phony smile again, the one he uses on customers.
Holden Caulfield in The Catcher in the Rye uses phony as his whole worldview — adults, schools, movies, everyone is a phony. The word's contempt is basically the book's voice.
🚫 Nothing to do with phone. That's Greek phōnē, "sound" — telephone, phonetics, symphony, cacophony, euphony. Identical opening, unrelated word.

Charming as a painting; quaint, weathered, postcard-pretty.
Charming to look at in the way a painting is — quaint, striking, worth framing. Also used of language: a picturesque description is vivid and colourful.

The word is sized small. Sweeping mountains are sublime or majestic; a fishing village with crooked roofs, a ruined mill, a cobbled lane — that's picturesque. It carries age and irregularity, never sleek modernity: nobody calls an airport picturesque.

It can also turn quietly barbed. Call someone's hardship "picturesque" and you've admitted you're admiring it from the outside, as scenery.
⚠️ picturesque ≠ picaresque.
- picturesque = pretty as a picture
- picaresque (pik-uh-RESK) = of a novel following a likeable rogue through episodic adventures — Don Quixote, Huckleberry Finn

One letter apart, and the GRE knows it.
Picturesque = you'd stop the car for a photo. A postcard, not a palace.
The test isn't grandeur or importance — it's whether the small, weathered, charming thing makes you reach for the camera.
1. The valley's picturesque hamlets — stone, moss, and smoke — have been photographed so often that the residents no longer look up.
2. It's a picturesque little café, but the coffee's terrible and there's nowhere to sit.
Property listings and travel brochures run on this word — "picturesque cottage", "picturesque coastal village" — which is exactly the register: small, old, charming, photographed from its best angle.
Italian pittoresco = "in the manner of a painter" (pittore, painter), through French pittoresque, then bent by English speakers to match picture.

The -esque suffix means "in the style of" and is worth owning outright: statuesque (like a statue), grotesque, arabesque, burlesque, Kafkaesque, Romanesque.

🚫 Not picaresque. That's Spanish pícaro, "rogue" — a different word with a different ancestor.

Devoutly religious — or showily virtuous at no real cost.
Devoutly religious; faithful in observance and duty — and, by extension, high-mindedly virtuous.

Two settings, and they pull opposite ways. Said of a believer or a ritual, it's straight description: a pious woman, a pious custom. But drop it next to an abstract noun and it turns acid — a pious hope is one nobody expects to come true, a pious platitude is virtue on display costing the speaker nothing. Devout stays warm; sanctimonious is openly hostile; pious sits in between and lets context decide, which is exactly why writers reach for it when they want to sneer without being caught sneering.
There's an IOU hiding in p-IOU-s: piety is a debt of duty — to God, to parents, to country.
That's the Roman sense precisely, and it explains the modern sneer: a pious hope is someone making a show of paying a debt that costs them nothing.
1. The abbey's founder was a pious man who gave away two-thirds of his estate and kept a stone cell for himself.
2. Everyone nodded along to his pious little speech about teamwork, then went straight back to hoarding their own data.
Twelve popes have taken the name Pius — the Latin adjective itself, chosen precisely because it advertises dutiful devotion.
Latin pius = "dutiful, devoted", noun pietās. That noun split into two English words with very different jobs: piety (duty owed upward, to God) and pity (compassion owed downward, to the wretched) — same root, opposite directions.

Also from it: expiate (pay off a wrong), impious, and pittance — originally a small charitable donation left in a will, which is why it now means a miserably small amount.

Sharp in a pleasing way — tangy, or intriguingly provocative.
Sharp in a way you enjoy. Of food: agreeably pungent, tangy, zesty — a bite that wakes the tongue up. Of a remark, a face, a detail, a scandal: pleasantly stimulating, intriguing, a little provocative.

The word carries a built-in verdict: praise. Pungent and acrid describe a sharpness that may well be unpleasant; piquant insists the sharpness is a pleasure. It also implies the sharpness is small and well-judged — a piquant sauce is not a mouthful of chilli, and a piquant remark is not a savaging. Register is a touch refined: food writers, critics and novelists use it, and it flatters both the thing described and the speaker's palate.
⚠️ piquant ≠ poignant.
- piquant (PEE-kuhnt) = sharp and delightful
- poignant (POYN-yuhnt) = sharp and sad — it hurts in a moving way

A piquant detail makes you lean in; a poignant one makes your throat tighten.
Piquant = "peek" + "want" — a sharpness that makes you peek, then want more.
The sound spells out the nuance: this kind of sharpness attracts rather than repels.
1. Her memoir is at its best in the piquant margins — the small, faintly scandalous details she clearly enjoyed committing to print.
2. Add a squeeze of lime at the end; it makes the whole thing piquant instead of just heavy.
It lives on menus and in food writing — Creole sauce piquante is a standard dish name, and any restaurant review praising a "piquant" dressing means sharp-and-lively, never harsh.
French piquer = "to prick, to sting."

Same prick gives you pique: piqued my curiosity (something pricked your interest) and a fit of pique (your pride got pricked). Hold the image of a small, sharp jab — pleasant on the tongue, provoking to the mind.

Brief and full of substance — brevity that actually lands.
Short and loaded — few words carrying real substance.

Its neighbours are all colder. Concise only promises nothing is wasted; terse hints at bluntness bordering on rude; curt has crossed that line; laconic describes a person who habitually says little. Pithy is the one that promises the line was good — you cannot be pithy and dull. It's the word for a great one-liner, a proverb, an epigram, a summary that beats the report it replaced. Almost always praise, and usually praise for the writing or speaking, not the person.
Pith is the core running down a plant stem — pithy means all core, no padding.
Strip a sentence of everything that isn't load-bearing and what's left is the pith — which is why "pithy" compliments the content, not just the length.
1. Her dissent ran to a single pithy paragraph that was quoted more often than the ninety-page majority opinion.
2. Keep the toast pithy — two lines, one joke, sit down.
Hamlet, mid-"To be or not to be": "enterprises of great pith and moment" — pith there meaning weight, substance, the stuff that matters.

column2:
To soothe someone's anger, usually with a concession.
To calm someone's anger or hostility, usually by giving them something — a concession, an apology, a gesture.

The word assumes real anger already exists: you don't placate a happy person. And it quietly implies the fix is transactional and often token — "a few tweaks to placate the shareholders" says the tweaks were cheap and the shareholders were a nuisance. Appease carries the stink of surrendering to a bully; mollify is gentler and softer, about feelings; placate sits in between, faintly weary, faintly cynical about the person being soothed.
Plac-ate = hand them a plaque and hope they ate it up.
You're buying off someone's anger with a token offering — which is exactly the slightly hollow flavour of placate.
1. The minister released a token draft of the report, hoping to placate a press corps that had scented a cover-up.
2. I bought him a coffee to placate him after I lost his charger.'
Latin placāre = "to soothe" — the causative of placēre, "to please." One root, a lot of GRE words: placid (calm), complacent (pleased with yourself), placebo (Latin for "I shall please" — a pill that soothes and nothing more), and the useful opposite implacable (not able to be soothed — a rage or an enemy that no concession will touch).

column2:
Calm and unruffled, sometimes to the point of dullness.
Calm, still, undisturbed — a placid lake, a placid temperament, a placid afternoon.

The key is absence of disturbance rather than active peace of mind. Serene is elevated, almost spiritual; tranquil describes a setting; placid describes a surface that nothing ruffles — water, a face, a disposition. Which is why it tips so easily into faint insult: a placid person is unflappable, but also possibly unexcitable, incurious, a bit bovine. Cows are called placid. Say it of a colleague and half the room hears a compliment, the other half hears "no inner life."
⚠️ placid ≠ pallid. Placid = calm; pallid = pale, drained of colour (or, figuratively, feeble — a pallid imitation). One letter's difference, opposite territory.
Placid rhymes with flaccid — no tension in it, and maybe no spirit either.
The rhyme carries the whole nuance: nothing is taut, nothing is rippling, which is restful on a lake and slightly damning in a person.
1. The river ran placid and glassy for a mile, giving no hint of the falls below.
2. He stayed weirdly placid through the whole argument, which honestly made it worse.
Lake Placid, New York — the Winter Olympics town, named for exactly the mirror-flat water the word describes. The 1999 crocodile film borrowed the name as a joke: placid lake, very unplacid contents.
Latin placidus = "pleasing, gentle," from placēre, "to please" — the same root behind please, pleasant, placate (make someone pleased again), complacent (pleased with yourself), implacable (not able to be pleased or appeased), and placebo (Latin "I shall please" — a pill that pleases rather than cures).

column2:
Sounding sad and appealing for sympathy; mournful.
Sounding sad in a way that begs for sympathy — mournful, wistful, slightly wounded.

It is almost always about a sound or an expression, not a situation: a plaintive cry, a plaintive melody, a plaintive look. Mournful is grief with weight behind it; plaintive is thinner and higher — it appeals rather than laments. And it carries a hint of quiet complaint, of asking to be pitied, which is why a child's "but why?" is plaintive while a widow's silence is not.
⚠️ plaintive ≠ plaintiff.
- plaintive = sounding sad (adjective)
- plaintiff = the person who brings a lawsuit (noun)

Same root, same sound — one whimpers, the other sues.
Plaintive has plaint in it — a complaint, but sung, not shouted.
The word is a grievance turned into a sound, which is why it always applies to a tone rather than to a person's circumstances.
1. A plaintive oboe carried the melody, thin above the strings, as though it were asking the orchestra a question no one would answer.
2. He gave a plaintive little "you never text me anymore" and went back to his phone.
It's a staple of music writing: reviewers reach for plaintive for a lone harmonica, a minor-key falsetto, or a Coldplay piano line — the sound that's sad and pleading rather than merely slow.
Latin plangere = "to beat the breast, to lament loudly." Via French plainte, a lament, it gives a tight family: complaint, plaintiff (the one who brings the grievance), and plangent (a loud, resounding, mournful sound).

Note the split: plangent kept the loudness of the root; plaintive kept only the sorrow.

Easily moulded — and so, easily influenced.
Adj.: capable of being shaped or moulded — and, of a person or mind, easily influenced, impressionable.

Forget the noun. On the GRE, plastic almost never means the material in your kitchen drawer; it means the property that material was named for. A plastic substance takes a new shape and keeps it. A plastic young mind absorbs whatever it's given.

Tone shifts with the subject: applied to brains, childhood, or an art form, it's neutral or admiring (a plastic medium). Applied to someone's convictions, it turns faintly contemptuous — plastic implies someone else's hands did the moulding. A separate colloquial sense is purely derogatory: fake, mass-produced, insincere — a plastic smile.
⚠️ plastic ≠ elastic. An elastic thing springs back; a plastic thing stays bent. Bend a ruler and let go — elastic. Bend a spoon — plastic.
Plasticine — the modelling clay. Plastic is the clay stage, not the finished toy.
The word names the moment when something can still be pressed into any shape at all.
1. The infant brain is remarkably plastic; pathways severed by injury are often rerouted within months.
2. He's got no politics of his own — he's plastic, he just agrees with whoever spoke last.
Plastic surgery has nothing to do with plastic — the name predates the material. It's moulding surgery: reshaping flesh.
Greek plassein = "to mould, to form." The material got the name because it's mouldable — the adjective came first.

Same root: plasma (formed substance), protoplasm, plaster, plastique (mouldable explosive), and -plasty in rhinoplasty.

A stale moral remark delivered as if it were wisdom.
A flat, stale remark offered as though it were profound — "everything happens for a reason," "at the end of the day, we're all human."

The sting isn't staleness alone; it's the pretence of depth. A cliché is just worn out and can be harmless. A platitude wears the face of wisdom, usually with a moral tint, and asks you to nod along. Calling something a platitude is an accusation: you had nothing to say, so you said something that sounded wise. It's the standard charge against politicians' condolences and corporate mission statements.
⚠️ platitude ≠ plenitude. Plenitude is abundance, fullness (plenty) — a compliment. A platitude is empty; a plenitude is full.
PLAT- is flat. It sounds deep, but it lands flat.
The word literally carries flat inside it, which is exactly the gap it names — profound in delivery, flat in content.
1. The eulogy dissolved into platitudes about journeys and better places, saying nothing the man had actually been.
2. Spare me the platitudes — just tell me whether I still have a job.
Every corporate values slide — "We put people first," "We embrace change" — is the natural habitat of the platitude; that's the word critics reach for the moment a leader says a lot and means nothing.
French plat = "flat" (as in a flattering nothing), built to rhyme with attitude. Same root runs through plate, platter, plateau, platform, plaza — and platypus, Greek for "flat-foot." Spot plat- and think flat.

column2:
Believable on the surface — convincing, but not thereby true.
Seeming reasonable, believable, likely to be true — on the face of it.

That last phrase is the whole word. Plausible rates how something sounds, not whether it's true: an alibi, an excuse, a theory. Calling an argument plausible is faint praise — you're saying it survives first contact, nothing more. And in the mouth of a skeptic it tips negative: a plausible enough story means you don't believe a word of it. Compare credible (you actually lean toward believing it) and specious (it looks good and is definitely false); plausible sits between them, deliberately uncommitted.
plausible ≠ feasible. Plausible = believable (a claim, a story). Feasible = doable (a plan, a schedule). A plausible explanation of the delay; a feasible way to fix it.
Plausible gets the applause, not the verdict.
It's the story the room claps for on hearing — approval, not proof.
1. The defence offered a plausible account of the missing hour, though the jury noticed it rested entirely on the accused's own word.
2. Nice try — that's a plausible excuse, but I saw your car outside the pub at six.
"Plausible deniability" — the Cold War spy-and-politics phrase for arranging things so the boss can be believed when he says he knew nothing. Every thriller and every corporate scandal runs on it, and it captures the word exactly: believable, not true.
Latin plaudere = "to clap, applaud" → plausibilis, "deserving applause." It meant approval-worthy long before it meant believable — the audience claps, that's all.

Same root: applaud, applause, plaudits — and explode, from explodere, "to clap a bad actor off the stage."

column2:
Bends easily — physically flexible, or too easily influenced.
Literally: bending easily without breaking — willow branches, leather, young wood.
Of people: easily influenced, yielding to whoever is pushing.

Two very different temperatures depending on the object. Applied to a material it's pure praise (pliant leather is good leather). Applied to a person it's rarely a compliment: flexible says you adapt well, pliant says you have no resistance in you — you take the shape of whoever's hands you're in. Softer and more passive than docile (which implies obedience to authority) and nowhere near as grovelling as obsequious; a pliant person isn't fawning, just shapeable. It's the word a manipulator would use about a mark.
Pliant = plywood — thin layers that bend instead of snapping, because there's nothing solid inside.
The material sense and the human sense are the same fact: it gives way under pressure rather than holding its shape.
1. The old bookbinder chose a pliant calfskin that would fold around the spine without cracking.
2. They wanted a pliant deputy, not someone who'd argue back in meetings.
Latin plicāre = "to fold." That one root folds out into a huge family: ply, pliers, pliable, apply, comply, imply, reply, complicated (folded together), duplicate (folded twice), and ballet's plié — a bend at the knee.

Note comply especially: comply and pliant are the same fold, which is exactly why the human sense drifts toward "does what he's told."

Slow, heavy and dull — steady, but with no spark.
Moving, working, or written in a slow, heavy, laborious way — trudging rather than striding.

Two things travel with it: weight and dullness. A plodding walker is tired-footed; a plodding lecture, novel, or investigation grinds forward with no lightness and no spark. Note that it attacks pace and life, not competence — the plodding worker generally does finish, and is often perfectly reliable, which is why it can carry grudging respect (a plodding but thorough detective). Aimed at someone's mind, it bites harder: dogged, unimaginative, incapable of a leap.
Plod rhymes with clod — a heavy lump of earth, and an old word for a slow, dull man.
Plodding work has that clod-like weight: it does arrive, but heavily and without a flicker of life.
1. The biography is meticulous but plodding — six hundred pages that advance the argument an inch at a time.
2. Two hours in and the film was still plodding along, so I checked my phone twice.
Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, one of the most quoted lines in English: "The ploughman homeward plods his weary way" — the whole tired, heavy-footed image in five words.
column3: g05 register::neutral connotation::negative antonym::brisk-vs-dragging antonym::gripping-vs-sleep-inducing connotation::dull-in-a-reviewer-s-register meaning::dull-by-sameness-by-length-by-pace meaning::moving-far-too-slowly

column2:
A small cunning tactic used to gain an advantage.
A cunning little manoeuvre designed to get an advantage — a tactic with a hidden motive behind it.

Scale is what marks it out. A plot is grand and sinister, a scheme is elaborate, a stratagem is military; a ploy is small, tactical and slightly cheap — one move, not a campaign. It's also the word people reach for once they've seen through the thing: "that's just a ploy to get you to stay on the call." Naming something a ploy is halfway to dismissing it.
Ploy rhymes with toy — a toy-sized trick, and it toys with you.
Both halves of the rhyme carry the nuance: a ploy is small-time rather than grand, and its purpose is to play someone.
1. The delegation's sudden concern for procedure was a transparent ploy to stall the vote until morning.
2. He forgot his wallet again — I'm starting to think it's a ploy.
Its natural habitat is the phrase "just a marketing ploy" — the limited-time-only countdown, the "only 2 left in stock!" banner. You meet the word every time you don't fall for one.
Ploy is employ with the front bitten off — an 18th-century Scots clipping meaning "an employment, a bit of business." A ploy is simply what you employ to get your way.

Underneath sits Latin implicāre, "to fold in, entangle" — which also gives you imply, implicate, complicate, pliable.

Brave and spirited despite being small or outmatched.
Brave and spirited in the face of long odds — determined when you have every excuse to quit.

Two things narrow it. First, size: plucky is almost always used of someone small, young, poor, injured, or outgunned — you can't call a superpower plucky. Second, tone: it's warm but faintly patronising, the word a commentator uses for the team that fought hard and lost 4–1. Brave respects you; plucky pats you on the head while it admires you.
Plucky is one letter off lucky — and you only get called plucky when luck was never on your side.
The word only attaches to the underdog: no favourite is ever plucky.
1. Outnumbered and out of ammunition, the plucky garrison held the pass for three more days.
2. She's tiny, but she's plucky — she'll argue with a bouncer twice her size.
British sports and news commentary runs on it — the plucky underdog, the plucky minnows knocked out in the quarter-finals. The phrase that fixed it in the language was WWI propaganda's "plucky little Belgium": small, overrun, admired.
A pluck was a butcher's word for the heart, liver and lungs — the organs plucked out of a slaughtered animal. Nineteenth-century boxing slang borrowed it for courage, so a fighter with pluck literally had guts. Same logic that gives us heart, spine, stomach for a fight.

column2:
Sharply, tenderly moving — sadness that pierces rather than smothers.
Emotionally piercing — moving in a way that hurts a little, usually because something tender is mixed with loss, distance, or time running out.

Sad is the temperature; poignant is the sharpness. A funeral is sad. The dead man's dog still waiting at the door is poignant. The word almost always carries a bittersweet double note — sweetness that stings precisely because it's gone or going — and it's a term of praise when applied to art: a poignant film has earned its ache rather than manufactured it. Reserve it for the small, precise detail that pricks, not for general gloom.
⚠️ poignant ≠ piquant. Same Latin root, opposite department.
- poignant (POYN-yuhnt) = sharp to the heart — bittersweet, moving
- piquant (PEE-kunt) = sharp to the tongue — tangy, zesty, pleasantly stimulating

A piquant sauce; a poignant goodbye.
Poignant is point with a silent g — it doesn't sadden you broadly, it pricks you at one exact spot.
The pinpoint is the whole nuance: poignancy comes from one piercing detail, not from a general fog of sadness.
1. The most poignant exhibit was not the wreckage itself but a child's shoe, catalogued and labelled beside it.
2. I was fine until the last five minutes, and then it got so poignant I had to pretend something was in my eye.
It's the film critic's default word for a bittersweet drama — scan any Rotten Tomatoes blurb wall and you'll hit "a poignant meditation on…" within three reviews. That's exactly its native habitat: praise for art that aches.
Latin pungere = "to prick, to pierce" — through French poindre. High-yield root: puncture, punctual (hitting the exact point in time), punctuate, pungent, expunge, compunction (a prick of conscience), and point itself.

So poignancy is literally a piercing — the emotion goes in.

Composure that shows — balanced, unrattled self-possession.
Noun: composed, dignified self-assurance — especially under pressure. Also physical balance: a body held steady, nothing wobbling.
Verb: to hold balanced or suspended — she poised the pen above the form; the cat was poised to spring.

Both senses are one idea: weight held in perfect balance. Calm describes an inner state nobody can see; poise is composure that shows — steady voice, unhurried hands, no fidgeting. It also carries a whiff of grace and breeding, so it's what you praise in a diplomat, a dancer, or a fifteen-year-old handling a hostile question well. And poised to adds a second flavour entirely: not relaxed at all, but coiled and ready, weight already shifted toward the leap.
Poise rhymes with noise — and poise is what makes none.
The rattled person clatters, stammers, and fusses; the poised one produces silence and stillness under exactly the same pressure.
1. Cross-examined for six hours, the witness answered every question with the same unhurried poise.
2. I'd have burst into tears — she just said "thanks for the feedback" and sat back down. Total poise.
Beauty pageants literally score it — Miss Universe judges contestants on poise alongside the interview, which tells you the word means bearing you can watch, not a feeling you have.
Old French pois = "weight," from Latin pendere, "to weigh, to hang." Poise is weight hanging in balance — which is why a cat can be poised to pounce and a person poised under fire: both are holding a load without tipping.

That root is everywhere on the GRE: pendulum, suspend, pending, pensive (weighing thoughts), ponder, compensate (weigh out payment), and equipoise (equal weight — perfect balance).

column2:
To split a group into two hostile extremes, erasing the middle.
To split a group into two sharply opposed camps, with nothing left in between. (Technical sense: to give something poles — as with light, magnets, or charge.)

The key isn't that people disagree; it's that the middle ground vanishes. A polarizing figure or issue drags everyone toward one extreme or the other — you can't stay lukewarm about it. That's why polarizing is the standard word for a celebrity or policy people either adore or loathe, never merely quite like.
Poles are as far apart as two points can get — and nobody lives at the equator anymore.
To polarize is to push every last person to the North or South pole of an argument, emptying out the temperate middle.
1. The referendum polarized a country that had, until then, treated the question as a matter of mild indifference.
2. That show polarizes everyone I know — half my friends call it a masterpiece, the other half won't finish episode one.
Polarized sunglasses — the lens filters light down to a single plane and kills the glare. Same idea, physical version: everything gets forced into one orientation.

Aggressively argumentative; written to attack, not to weigh.
Aggressively argumentative — written or spoken to attack a position and demolish it, not to weigh it.

A polemical piece is one-sided by design. That's the key: it isn't failed analysis, it's deliberate combat, and everyone involved knows it. Calling an essay critical means it examines; calling it polemical means it swings. The word is often faintly dismissive — "that's less a study than a polemic" says the author had already decided before starting — but in a debate, a philosophy seminar, or an op-ed page it can be plain description, even praise.
pole-MIC-al — someone grabs the mic and goes to war with it.
A polemic is public and aimed at an opponent, never a quiet private disagreement.
1. His pamphlet on the reforms was frankly polemical, conceding nothing to the other side and pausing only to sharpen the insult.
2. Don't read the comments — that thread stopped being a discussion and went full polemical about an hour ago.
Christopher Hitchens' God Is Not Great is described everywhere — by admirers and critics alike — as a polemic: a book-length attack, not a survey.
Greek pólemos = "war." A polemic is literally warfare conducted in words, which is why the tone is always adversarial rather than exploratory.

column2:
A person with deep expertise in many different fields.
A person of wide-ranging expertise — someone who has genuine command of many unrelated fields (physics and poetry and medicine), not just an interest in them.

The word is close to reverent. You don't call yourself one; other people award it to you, usually in a profile or an obituary. The depth is the whole point: a dilettante samples many subjects and masters none, a polymath masters them. Reach for it only when the breadth is real, or the praise curdles into flattery.
poly (many) + math — but not many maths: many learnings.
The -math is the Greek word for learning, so a polymath has learned much across many subjects — mathematics just happens to be another child of the same root.
1. A restless polymath, she published on protein folding, medieval finance, and the acoustics of cathedrals — and was taken seriously in all three.
2. He's read one book on architecture and now he's calling himself a polymath.
Leonardo da Vinci is the word's default illustration — painter, anatomist, military engineer — and \"the ultimate polymath\" is close to a fixed phrase whenever he comes up.
Greek polumathēs = "having learned much" — poly- (many) + manthanein (to learn).

That second half is the useful one: mathēma meant "a thing learned", which is why mathematics is literally "the learned subject." And poly- pays out everywhere on the GRE: polyglot (many tongues), polygamy (many marriages), polymer (many parts), polygon (many angles).

Inflated self-importance, especially in grand, ceremonious manner and speech.
Inflated self-importance — especially the grand, ceremonious manner of someone who treats their own opinions like state announcements.

Arrogance is about claiming superiority; pomposity is about the style: the orotund voice, the long Latinate words, the pause before the obvious. It attaches to the delivery more than the belief. And it's a comic charge, not a fearsome one — the pompous man is ridiculous, someone to be punctured at a dinner party, not feared. Nobody has ever described their own manner as pomposity.
Pomposity = pomp with no occasion — a one-man parade.
Ceremony is fine at a coronation; pomposity is bringing that same fanfare to a status meeting.
1. The committee's report collapsed under its own pomposity, taking four hundred words to recommend a slightly larger bin.
2. He can't just say "I disagree" — there's always this pomposity where he clears his throat and says "if I may offer a perspective."
Elgar's "Pomp and Circumstance" — the march every graduation processes to. Same pomp: grand ceremonial display. Pomposity is that music playing in someone's head while they answer an email.
Latin pompa = "solemn procession," from Greek pompē (a sending, a parade). The word started as pure spectacle — the parade itself — and only later curdled into the sneer at people who march through ordinary life as if a crowd were watching.

Family: pomp, pompous, pageant.

column2:
So heavy it moves slowly; so laboured it bores.
1. So heavy or bulky that it moves slowly and without grace. 2. (of speech, writing, style) laboured and dull — weighed down by its own seriousness.

Both senses are complaints. A ponderous thing has mass but no lightness of touch: the freight train, the man in armour, the 600-page novel where nothing happens. Applied to prose or a speaker, it says the effort shows — every sentence arrives like furniture being dragged across a floor. Weight is the literal core; tedium is what the GRE usually wants.
ponderous ≠ pondering. Same root, opposite compliment: to ponder is to think deeply; ponderous describes something that merely feels heavy — often with no thought in it at all. A ponderous lecture is boring, not profound.
Ponder weighs the idea; ponderous just weighs a ton.
Both come from "weight," but only one of them earns it — ponderous is the heaviness without the thinking.
1. The ponderous machinery of the appeals court took four years to produce a ruling of two pages.
2. Two hours in and the documentary was still ponderous — I gave up and made toast.
It's a stock word in film reviews: a self-important three-hour epic gets called "ponderous" almost every time. If a critic uses it, they mean slow and full of itself — not deep.
Latin pondus, ponderis = weight. That one root carries a useful family: ponder (weigh an idea in the mind), preponderance (the side that outweighs), imponderable (something that can't be weighed up at all), and even pound — the lb. is from Latin libra pondo, "a pound by weight."

To be an omen of — usually of something bad.
To be a sign or warning that something is going to happen — to foreshadow, to be an omen of.

The subject is almost never a person: clouds, silence, a drop in sales, a cough portend. Things portend; people predict. And what's portended is nearly always bad — you can portend civil war, collapse, or ruin, but "portends a lovely afternoon" reads as a joke. Weightier and more solemn than suggest or indicate, which are flatly neutral; broader than foreshadow, which belongs to plots and novels. It's the word news anchors reach for when they want dread without saying "doom."
⚠️ portend ≠ portentous. Portend is the clean verb ("this portends trouble"). But portentous, its own adjective, has drifted: it usually now means pompously self-important, not ominous. A portentous speaker is a windbag, not a prophet.
port-END — whatever it points to is an ending, not a beginning.
The hidden end is your reminder that the word tilts negative: things portend collapse, famine, and war far more often than they portend anything good.
1. The sudden withdrawal of foreign capital portended a crisis that the finance ministry spent a decade denying was coming.
2. That noise the engine's making? Nothing good, mate — it portends a very expensive Tuesday.
Standard market-commentary furniture: every recession cycle brings the headline "Does the inverted yield curve portend a recession?" — an impersonal signal, an unwelcome outcome, exactly the word's natural habitat.
Latin portendere = por- (a form of pro-, "forward") + tendere, "to stretch" — the omen stretches forward into the future.

Tendere is a GRE workhorse: extend, contend, distend, tendon, tendency, intend — and pretend, literally "stretch out in front" as a screen. Same stretch, different direction.

Striking an attitude for effect, with no intention behind it.
Behaviour or speech adopted for effect — striking an attitude to impress, intimidate, or signal a position you don't actually intend to act on.

The word is an accusation of hollowness. Calling a threat posturing says the speaker is performing toughness with no intention of following through; calling a principled stand posturing says the principle is a costume. It's cooler and more dismissive than grandstanding (loud, attention-hungry) and more strategic than pretending — a posturer usually wants something out of the pose, typically leverage.
Posture is a position you hold on purpose — posturing is holding a moral position the same way: consciously, for the room, and only until you can relax.
Nobody's straight back at a dinner table is natural, and neither is the outrage of a politician who knows the cameras are on.
1. The ultimatum was dismissed by every analyst as posturing, calculated to extract concessions before the deadline rather than to precipitate a war.
2. Ignore him — all that gym-bro chest-thumping is just posturing, he'd run a mile from an actual fight.
\"Political posturing\" is one of the most-used phrases in news writing — any time a correspondent says a bill, a walkout, or a threat was \"mere posturing,\" they mean it was theatre staged for voters, not governing.
Latin pōnere / positus = "to place, to put." A posture is literally how you've placed your body; posturing is placing yourself in a stance for an audience.

Same root, whole GRE family: position, posit, deposit, compose, impose, juxtapose, repository.

column2:
Powerful in effect; a little goes a long way.
Powerful — but specifically able to produce a strong effect. A potent drug, a potent argument, a potent symbol.

Where strong describes the thing itself and forceful describes how it's delivered, potent describes what it does to you: concentrated capacity, effect out of proportion to size. A small dose, a single sentence, a two-word slogan can all be potent. It's why the noun is potency — a measurable strength-per-unit, printed on pill bottles. Slightly formal, and quietly admiring of the power even when the thing wielding it is poison.
⚠️ potent ≠ portent. One letter apart, no relation.
- potent = powerful, effective
- portent (n.) = an omen, a sign of what's coming — adj. portentous
Impotent means it can't do a thing — strip the im- and potent is the thing that does.
The negative is the more familiar word, and it pins the meaning exactly: potency is not size or noise but whether the thing actually works.
1. The prosecution's most potent evidence was a single timestamp neither witness could explain away.
2. Careful with that punch — it's way more potent than it tastes.
Every medicine box you own is rated for potency: 200 mg vs 500 mg, "extra strength," "high-potency" vitamins. Same word, doing its literal job — how much effect per dose.
Latin posse / potens = "to be able, being able." Enormously productive: potential (able to become), omnipotent (able to do all), potentate (a ruler), possible, and — via French — power itself.

So the core sense is always ability, not bulk. Something potent can do something.

Unstable; liable to collapse at any moment.
Dangerously unstable — liable to fall, collapse, or be taken away at any moment. Also: dependent on chance or on someone else's goodwill.

The danger isn't in the harm, it's in the balance. A dangerous road hurts you; a precarious ledge is perfectly fine right up until it isn't. The thing is holding — but nothing guarantees it keeps holding, and you don't control what does. That's why it fits both a boulder on a cliff edge and a job, a truce, or a bank balance: the common thread is a position you occupy only on sufferance.
You're not holding it up — you're praying it holds.
The word is literally built on Latin precari, "to pray," so a precarious position is one kept by prayer and permission rather than by any grip of your own.
1. The ceasefire was precarious, sustained less by trust than by the exhaustion of both armies.
2. He balanced the last mug on a precarious tower of dishes and backed away very slowly.
Labour economists talk about precarious work — gig shifts, zero-hours contracts, rolling three-month renewals — and have coined the precariat for the class living on it. Same idea: you have the job only until someone else decides you don't.
Latin precārius = "obtained by begging", from precārī, "to pray, entreat" (root prex, precis = prayer). In Roman law a precarium was property you held purely at the owner's pleasure — revocable the instant he changed his mind. That legal sense (held by another's favour) drifted into the physical one (liable to fall).

Same root: pray, deprecate (pray away → belittle), imprecation (a curse prayed down on someone).

To trigger something suddenly and early; or rashly hasty.
Verb: to bring something on suddenly and ahead of its time — precipitated a crisis, precipitated his resignation. In chemistry, to make a solid drop out of a solution.
Adj.: headlong, rash — acting before thinking. Noun: the solid that dropped out.

What you precipitate is nearly always bad, and usually not what you intended: the tension was already loaded, and your act merely tipped it over the edge. The word doesn't say you created the disaster — it says you dropped it early. As an adjective it's a quiet rebuke; precipitate action isn't decisive, it's undercooked.
⚠️ precipitate ≠ precipitous.
- precipitate = hasty, rushed (of an act or a person)
- precipitous = steep, sharply falling (of a cliff or a graph)

A precipitous decline in sales; a precipitate decision to shut the factory.
Precipitation falls out of the sky unasked — to precipitate is to make something fall out early.
Same word you hear in every weather forecast: something comes down suddenly, and nobody chose the timing.
1. The assassination did not cause the war so much as precipitate it, collapsing a decade of alliances into six weeks.
2. Don't do anything precipitate — sleep on it, then send the email.
Every forecast's "40% chance of precipitation" is this exact word — stuff dropping out of the sky on its own schedule, not yours.
Latin prae- (forth) + caput, capitis (head) = thrown head-first off a height. That's the whole image: the precipice is the cliff you go over.

The caput family is worth owning: capital, captain, decapitate, per capita, chapter (little head, a section heading).
