column2:
Dangerously steep; or sudden and sharp, of a fall.
1. Dangerously steep — a cliff, a staircase, a mountain road.
2. Of a fall or decline: sudden, sharp and alarming — a precipitous drop in sales.

The word always carries a whiff of danger. A hill can be steep and pleasant; call it precipitous and you've said it could kill you. Applied to numbers, it's the graph line falling off a cliff — not a dip, not a slide, a plunge. Journalists and analysts reach for it precisely because it sounds alarming, so it does editorial work that "sharp" doesn't.
⚠️ precipitous ≠ precipitate (adj., pri-SIP-uh-tuht).
- precipitous = steep — describes a drop or a thing
- precipitate = rash, headlong, done too soon — describes an act or a decision

A precipitous cliff; a precipitate withdrawal.
Precipit-ous hides precipice — the edge you fall off.
If you can see the precipice in the word, you'll always land on steep drop rather than hasty.
1. The path narrowed and turned precipitous, falling away on the left into three hundred feet of nothing.
2. One bad quarter and the stock took a precipitous dive — down forty percent before lunch.
It's the default word of financial news: every "shares fell precipitously" headline is the same picture — the chart going over the edge.
Latin praeceps, praecipit- = "headlong," literally prae (forward) + caput (head) — going head-first off something.

That gives you precipice (the drop), precipitate (to hurl headlong → to rush), and precipitation (water falling headlong out of the sky).

And caput = head is a GRE workhorse: capital, captain, decapitate, per capita.

To rule something out in advance; make it impossible.
To make something impossible in advance — to rule it out before it can happen.

The force is structural, not personal. A person forbids; a fact, rule, clause, or condition precludes. Nobody has to refuse you — the possibility simply never exists. That's why it lives in formal registers: contracts, medicine, policy. Two shapes to know: X precludes Y ("the injury precluded a comeback") and X precludes someone from doing Y. The stock GRE collocation is preclude the possibility of.
⚠️ preclude ≠ exclude.
- exclude = shut out something that exists (you're excluded from the party)
- preclude = shut out the option before it arises (the schedule precluded a party at all)
pre- + -clude = closed beforehand — the door was locked before you ever walked up to it.
Because the closing happened in advance, no one ever had to turn you away — which is why preclude sounds impersonal rather than hostile.
1. Her prior work for the regulator precluded her from advising the firm on the merger.
2. Sorry — the 6 a.m. flight kind of precludes any chance of me coming out tonight.
Contract and policy boilerplate runs on it: "Nothing in this Agreement shall preclude either party from…" Once you notice it, you'll see it in every terms-of-service page and insurance clause you skim past.
Latin prae- (before) + claudere (to shut) — literally "to shut in advance."

Claudere is a workhorse root: include (shut in), exclude (shut out), seclude (shut apart), conclude (shut off the argument), recluse (one shut away), closure, cloister.
column3: g11 register::formal connotation::neutral antonym::heading-it-off-vs-bringing-it-on intensity::getting-in-the-way:-friction-drag-and-fl meaning::head-it-off-in-advance root::root:-claudere-to-shut-close

column2:
Showing adult ability or maturity strikingly early, usually a child.
Showing an ability or maturity far earlier than the usual age — a five-year-old playing Chopin, a nine-year-old who argues like a barrister.

The word is nearly always aimed at children, and it carries a small barb. Gifted is pure praise; precocious admires the speed while hinting that something has arrived out of order — the child is charming, a little too knowing, possibly insufferable at dinner. Applied to an adult it's almost a joke. Used of talent (a precocious striker, a precocious debut novel) the barb softens into "astonishingly young."
PRE-COCIOUS = PRE-COOKED — done long before the rest of the batch is even warm.
Being finished early is impressive, but something rushed to the table ahead of schedule always feels faintly unnatural — which is exactly the word's undertone.
1. Mozart's precocious command of counterpoint had emptied the courts of Europe of rivals before he turned fifteen.
2. She's seven and she just corrected my grammar — precocious is one word for it.
Sports commentary runs on this word: every 17-year-old who scores on debut is a "precocious talent." Same in book reviews — a "precociously assured first novel" means she's twenty-three and it's not fair.
Latin praecox = "ripening early" — prae- (before) + coquere (to cook, to ripen). Fruit that came in ahead of season was praecox; so is the child.

coquere pays out elsewhere: concoct (cook together), decoction, cuisine, kitchen — and, best of all, apricot, the early-ripening fruit, literally the same root.

An awkward, difficult situation you're stuck inside.
A difficult, awkward or unpleasant situation — especially one you're stuck in, where every way out costs you something.

Scale matters: a problem is something to solve, a crisis is an emergency, a predicament is a bind. It's mid-sized trouble with a whiff of the wry — you can be in a predicament and still be embarrassed rather than terrified. It also carries a faint hint that you walked into it yourself, which is why "he's got himself into a right predicament" sounds natural and "he's got himself into a right catastrophe" doesn't.
pre-DIC-a-ment ≈ "predict a mess" — you can see the mess coming and still can't step out of it.
The sound hook also fixes the size of the trouble: a mess, not a disaster.
1. Caught between a contract he could not honour and a client he could not afford to lose, the young architect described his predicament with careful understatement.
2. I'd told both of them I was free on Saturday — so yeah, bit of a predicament.
Latin praedicāre = "to proclaim, declare publicly" (prae- "before" + dicāre "to make known"). Same root gives you preach and predicate — all about asserting something about someone.

It began as dry logic jargon: a praedicamentum was one of Aristotle's categories, a state or condition you could assert of a thing. Neutral. Then English speakers started using "what a predicament!" about unfortunate conditions, and the sourness stuck to the word permanently.

🚫 Not from predict. That's prae- + dīcere ("to say beforehand") — a cousin, not a parent. A predicament isn't a forecast; it's a fix you're already in.

A long-standing, mild preference for one kind of thing.
A standing preference — a liking for one kind of thing that you bring with you, already formed, before the particular choice comes up.

Weight matters: a predilection is mild and habitual, not a passion. You don't have a predilection for your spouse; you have one for corner tables, Belgian beer, or nineteenth-century novels. It's the most formal member of its family, and it often arrives with a raised eyebrow — writers use it for tastes that are slightly telling ("a predilection for lost causes", "a predilection for younger men"), so it can quietly editorialise while sounding perfectly polite. Being pre-formed is the point: it colours your judgement before the evidence is in.
Pre-di-LECT-ion — you elected it before the vote was held.
The -lect- is the same "choose" as in elect and select, and the pre- tells you the choosing was already done — the leaning exists before the options are on the table.
1. The judge's predilection for precedent over principle was well known to everyone who argued before her.
2. He'll order the spiciest thing on any menu — a lifelong predilection for punishing his own tongue.
Doctors use it flatly, with no glamour at all: a disease "has a predilection for" a certain site — melanoma for the back, TB for the lungs. It just means that's where it tends to turn up — which is exactly the everyday sense, stripped of taste.
Latin prae- ("before") + dīligere ("to choose out, to prize"), itself dis- + legere, "to pick, to gather, to read."

That legere is a workhorse: select, elect, eligible, collect, lecture, legible. And dīligere — "to pick out lovingly" — is where diligent comes from; a diligent worker was originally a caring one.
column3: g11 register::formal connotation::neutral antonym::craving-vs-recoiling intensity::strength-of-inclination lookalike::predilection-proclivity-propensity meaning::a-settled-leaning-toward root::root:-legere-to-pick-out-read-attention-

column2:
To foreshadow by resembling — an early version of what follows.
To show the shape of something before it exists — to be an early version, model, or hint of what later comes to pass.

Foreshadow lives inside stories and leans ominous: a stray remark that hints at the murder. Prefigure is cooler and more structural — the earlier thing simply has the form of the later one, and typically has no idea it's doing so. There's no prophet and no omen; the resemblance is spotted afterwards, by an observer, which is why the word belongs to critics, historians and theologians rather than fortune-tellers.
Pre-FIGURE — the figure, the shape, was already drawn; nobody predicted it, we just recognise the outline later.
The hidden word figure keeps you on "form, not forecast" — prefiguring is resemblance noticed in hindsight, not prediction made in advance.
1. The 1919 general strike prefigured the labour upheavals that would convulse Europe a decade later.
2. Burnt toast, dead battery, lost keys — Tuesday morning pretty much prefigured the whole week.
Music criticism runs on this word: some obscure 1977 record is forever said to have prefigured punk, or grunge, or synthpop, by a decade — meaning nobody involved was predicting anything, the sound was just already there.
Latin prae- (before) + figura (shape, form), from fingere (to shape, to mould).

That root is worth banking: figure, configure, disfigure, effigy (a moulded likeness), figment and fiction (things shaped out of nothing), feign (to shape a false front).

To plan an act — usually a wrongful one — in advance.
To think out or plan an act in advance, before carrying it out.

Technically the word is neutral — you could premeditate a proposal. In practice almost nobody does. Premeditate has been colonised by the courtroom: it turns up attached to murders, attacks, frauds, and betrayals, and its whole function there is to make the act worse. A crime of passion is impulsive; a premeditated one was rehearsed in the mind first, and that forethought is exactly what raises the sentence. So when you use it of something innocent ("a premeditated compliment"), it reads as arch or faintly sinister — the word drags its criminal baggage along.
Pre + meditate — he meditated on it beforehand. Nobody asks whether you meditated first unless the deed was ugly.
The word is literally "thinking ahead," but the only time anyone bothers to point that out is when the thinking ahead is evidence against you.
1. The prosecution argued that the purchase of the rope a week earlier proved the killing was premeditated, not a sudden loss of control.
2. That wasn't a slip of the tongue — she'd premeditated every word of that toast.
Every courtroom drama hinges on it: premeditated murder is what makes a killing first-degree rather than manslaughter. The whole plot is usually one question — did he think about it beforehand?
Latin prae- (before) + meditārī (to ponder, turn over in the mind) — so, literally, to meditate in advance.

Meditārī traces to a root meaning "to take appropriate measures," which also gives you medicine, remedy, moderate, modest — the family of weighing things carefully before acting.

To be a sign of something coming, usually bad.
Verb: to be a sign or warning of something that is coming. Noun: the omen itself, or the feeling of foreboding it gives you.

The subject is usually a thing, not a person — falling share prices, a cough, a red sky. A forecaster predicts; the storm clouds presage. And the thing coming is nearly always bad: you can presage disaster, collapse, or war, but "presaged a lovely afternoon" reads as a joke. Weightier and gloomier than foreshadow, which is what a novelist does on purpose; presage is what the world does to you.
Pre-sage — the sage knew before it happened, and he looked worried.
The word literally has sage sitting inside it, and the worried face is the reminder that what's foreseen is bad news.
1. The tremors of that spring presaged the collapse of the whole banking order.
2. That weird grinding noise from the engine presaged a very expensive Tuesday.
Latin prae- (before) + sagīre (to perceive keenly, to sense). A Roman praesāgium was a foreboding — a thing sensed before it arrived.

That second root is the payoff: sagīre also gives you sagacious (keen-scented, shrewd) and sage (one who perceives keenly). Learn one, get three.

Knowing what's coming before it comes.
Knowing — or appearing to know — what is going to happen before it happens; showing unusual foresight.

The praise here is for analysis, not magic. Prophetic and clairvoyant carry a whiff of visions and the supernatural; prescient credits someone who read the evidence early and read it right. It attaches to memos, essays, warnings, films, investments — sober things.

It is also almost always retrospective. You don't call a forecast prescient while it's still a forecast; you call it prescient once reality has caught up and vindicated it.
Pre-sci-ent = pre-science: you had the knowledge early — but the compliment only arrives late.
The sci is the same sci as in science and omniscient, and nobody is ever called prescient until events have proved them right.
1. His 1998 memo warning that the bank's models understated correlated risk now reads as unnervingly prescient.
2. Mum was prescient about that guy — she called it in week one and we all laughed.
This is the word film critics reach for when a story turns out to have predicted real life — Network, The Truman Show, half the Black Mirror episodes. If a review says a film "feels prescient," it means the world went and proved it right.
Latin prae- (before) + scīre (to know) — literally "knowing beforehand."

Scīre is a workhorse root: science, conscience (knowing-with yourself), omniscient (all-knowing), conscious, and the GRE-friendly nescient (not knowing — ignorant).

To lay down as a rule, or order a treatment.
To lay something down as a rule or order — with the authority to make it binding. Medically: to order a specific treatment for a patient.

The word assumes standing. You recommend if you're a friend, you prescribe if you're a doctor, a statute, a style manual. It's not aggressive the way dictate is — it's calm, official, and not up for discussion. Watch for the GRE's favourite non-medical use: prescriptive rules tell you how you ought to write or speak, as opposed to descriptive ones, which just report how people actually do.
prescribe ≠ proscribe. Near-identical on the page, near-opposite in force:
- prescribe = order it done ("the doctor prescribed rest")
- proscribe = forbid it outright ("the regime proscribed the party")

One letter flips a command into a ban.
PREscribe writes it in; PROscribe writes it off.
The pre- word puts an instruction on the page for you to follow; the pro- word puts a name on a list to be got rid of.
1. The charter prescribes the precise order in which the successors must be consulted.
2. She prescribed me two weeks off and said she'd know if I was still checking email.
The entire legal category of prescription drugs vs over-the-counter rests on this word: someone with authority has to write the order down before the pharmacy is allowed to hand it over.
Latin prae (before) + scrībere (to write) — literally "written down in advance." That root pays for itself: describe, inscribe, subscribe, transcribe, script, scripture, conscription.

And it explains the trap. Proscribe is pro- (publicly, out front) + scrībere: in Rome, a proscription was a list of names posted in the Forum — men declared outlaws, to be hunted and killed. Written up in public = condemned.

Overstepping — taking a liberty or standing you haven't been granted.
Overstepping: taking a liberty, a right, or a familiarity that hasn't been granted to you.

The charge isn't that you were wrong — it's that you assumed standing you don't have. Correcting your professor's Latin, calling the CEO "Dave" on day one, ordering for someone else at dinner: presumptuous. Arrogant describes a permanent inflation of the self; presumptuous describes a single act of reaching past your place, and can be levelled at an otherwise modest person. It also has a curious polite use — English speakers pre-emptively accuse themselves of it ("it would be presumptuous of me to advise you") precisely to prove they aren't.
⚠️ presumptuous ≠ presumptive.
- presumptuous = rudely overstepping
- presumptive = presumed, assumed-for-now — the heir presumptive, the presumptive nominee

Calling someone the presumptive winner is neutral reporting. Calling them presumptuous is an insult.
Pre-SUMP-tuous = pre (before) + sume (take) — he took it before it was offered.
The whole offence lives in that pre-: not the taking, but the not-waiting.
1. It would be presumptuous of the committee to declare a verdict before the evidence has been heard.
2. Bit presumptuous of him to bring a girlfriend to my wedding when he RSVP'd for one.
Its natural habitat is the hedging work email: "Apologies if this is presumptuous, but I've gone ahead and drafted it." You use the word to apologise for the very thing you're doing anyway.
Latin sumere = "to take" — a root that pays out everywhere: assume (take on), consume (take up entirely), resume (take up again), subsume (take under), presume (take beforehand). Even sumptuous belongs — Latin sumptus, "expense," what's been taken out of your purse.

Straining to seem cleverer or classier than you are.
Claiming — through manner, vocabulary, or taste — an importance, refinement, or depth you don't actually possess.

The word attacks the performance, not the person's actual status. A genuinely learned professor can't be pretentious for using long words; the undergraduate imitating him can. Compare the neighbours: pompous is inflated self-importance (a manner), ostentatious is vulgar display of money (a yacht), pretentious is a bid for cultural credit — the unread Proust on the shelf, the wine notes, the film that thinks it's saying something. It is never a compliment and never neutral; calling something pretentious is a verdict that the substance doesn't back the show.
pretentious ≠ portentous. Portentous primarily means ominous, foreboding — a portent of disaster. (It has a secondary "pompously solemn" sense, which is exactly why the pair is a trap.) Ominous sky = portentous. Affected art student = pretentious.
Pretentious = pretending, with an extra syllable for show.
The word literally contains pretend, and the padding on the end is the word doing the very thing it describes.
1. The novel's ambitions collapse into pretentious obscurity — three hundred pages of portent about nothing in particular.
2. Twelve quid for a coffee and they call the guy a "barista artisan"? Bit pretentious.
It's the standard one-word kill in reviews — of films, restaurants, and wine lists. A critic who writes pretentious has said the thing is trying to be profound and isn't, and no further argument is offered.
Latin prae- (before) + tendere (to stretch) — to stretch something out in front of you as a claim. Hence pretend, pretext, pretension.

Tendere is a workhorse root: extend (stretch out), distend (stretch apart), contend (stretch against), intend (stretch toward), portend (stretch forward as a sign), tendon (the stretchy bit).

column2:
To win out through strength; to be widespread or dominant.
Three linked senses:

1. To win out — to prove stronger and come out on top after a struggle (justice prevailed).
2. To be widespread or currently dominant — usually as prevailing (the prevailing wind, the prevailing view).
3. prevail upon/on someone — to persuade them, by pressing until they give way.

Nothing prevails quickly. You win a race in ten seconds; you prevail in a war, a lawsuit, an argument that has gone on too long — the word carries the weight of resistance overcome, not just a result. Sense 2 falls straight out of sense 1: whatever won out is now the thing in force everywhere. And note it's intransitive with over or against, never "prevail someone."
⚠️ prevail ≠ prevaricate. Prevail = win out. Prevaricate (pri-VAR-i-kayt) = dodge the question, speak evasively. Identical first four letters, opposite postures — one stands firm, one squirms.
You win a race; you prevail in a war — and whatever prevailed becomes the prevailing wind.
Prevailing always implies a contest of strength or endurance, which is exactly why the participle came to mean "dominant, in force everywhere."
1. After four years of litigation the smaller firm prevailed, and the patent was struck down.
2. Everyone wanted to keep arguing, but common sense prevailed and we went home.
Faulkner's 1950 Nobel Prize speech, one of the most quoted lines in American letters: "I believe that man will not merely endure: he will prevail." The contrast is the definition — enduring is surviving; prevailing is coming out on top.
Latin prae- (before, ahead) + valēre (to be strong, be worth) — literally to be stronger than.

Valēre is a workhorse root: valid (strong enough to hold), value, valour, invalid, equivalent, convalesce (to grow strong again), and prevalent — prevail's own adjective.

Dodge the truth with shifty, evasive half-answers.
To speak evasively — to dodge, hedge, and shift ground so as to mislead without ever committing to a flat lie.

The whole force of the word sits in that gap. A liar says the false thing; a prevaricator says technically-true things in an order designed to leave you wrong. It's a formal, faintly lawyerly accusation — the word an editorial or a judge reaches for when "lied" would be too blunt, too actionable, or simply unprovable. Note also that it describes a manner of answering, not a single utterance: one dodge is a dodge, but a witness who keeps sliding is prevaricating.
⚠️ prevaricate ≠ procrastinate.
- prevaricate = dodge the truth
- procrastinate = dodge the work

They sound alike and both mean "avoid," which is exactly why the GRE likes the pair. A witness prevaricates; a student procrastinates.
Pre-VARY-cate — the story varies every time you ask it.
No single falsehood you can point to, just an answer that never twice comes out the same shape.
1. Pressed on what he knew and when, the minister prevaricated for forty minutes and conceded nothing.
2. Stop prevaricating — did you eat the last slice or not?
Standard newsroom vocabulary. When a politician won't answer, the write-up says he prevaricated — a way of alleging dishonesty in print without saying "lied" and inviting a libel suit.
Latin praevaricari = "to walk crookedly, to straddle" — from varus, "bent, knock-kneed." The literal image is a ploughman whose furrow wanders instead of running straight.

In Roman law it hardened into something sharper: a praevaricator was a prosecutor secretly in league with the defendant — straddling both sides of the case. Crooked line, crooked answer.

Same root gives you varicose veins — bent, twisted ones.

First — in rank, in quality, or in preparing something beforehand.
Adj.: first in rank or quality — prime suspect, prime location, prime minister.
Noun: the peak stretch of something's life — an athlete past his prime.
Verb (the one the GRE tests): to prepare something in advance so that it will work when the moment comes — prime a pump with water, prime a wall before painting, prime a jury with an opening statement.

As an adjective it's the language of the butcher and the estate agent: top-of-the-line, plainly stated, no poetry in it. The verb is where the interest lives — priming is always preliminary, a step whose whole value is that it comes before. Applied to people it slides toward coaching and manipulation: a witness who has been primed has been told what to say, and someone primed for disappointment has been quietly set up to fall.
⚠️ prime ≠ prim. Prim (PRIM) means stiffly proper, fussily correct — a prim schoolmistress in a buttoned collar. One letter apart, nothing in common.
Everything prime is first: first in rank (prime minister), first in quality (prime cut), first in time (prime the pump).
If a sentence uses prime as a verb, it's the third one — the action that has to happen first for the real thing to work.
1. Counsel had plainly primed the witness: every answer arrived a half-second too smoothly.
2. Three coffees and a pep talk and he was primed for the interview.
Optimus Prime — the Transformers leader is literally "best-first," and he is the foremost of them all.
Latin primus = "first." The root pays out across the whole exam: primary, primitive, primeval, premier, prince, principal, prima donna (first lady of the opera), primate (first-ranked bishop, then first-ranked animal).

Untouched and unspoiled — in perfect original condition.
In its original, unspoiled condition — untouched, undamaged, as good as the day it was made; hence also spotlessly clean.

The key is history, not appearance. Immaculate means no stain on it; pristine means nothing ever happened to it. A jacket scrubbed for three hours is immaculate; a jacket still in the box is pristine. That's why the word attaches so naturally to wilderness, coastlines, snowfall, and second-hand goods — things whose value lies in never having been used, walked on, or touched.
pris-TEEN rhymes with clean and unseen — pristine is clean because it's been unseen.
Nobody has handled it, so there was never anything to clean off — that's the difference between pristine and merely tidy.
1. The expedition mapped a pristine stretch of reef, untouched by trawlers and unvisited by divers.
2. He kept the record sleeve pristine — never even slid it out of the plastic.
Every used-car ad and eBay listing that says "pristine condition, one owner" — the seller is claiming the thing has no history, not that they gave it a good wash.
Latin prīstinus = "former, earliest, original", built on pri- "before". English borrowed it in the 1500s meaning simply original, and only later drifted to clean — which is why "pristine" still carries "as it was at the start."

Same pri- family: prior, prime, primal, primitive, primary.

Unimpeachable honesty, especially with money and public trust.
Complete honesty and moral uprightness — especially incorruptibility in handling money, office, or public trust.

Integrity is warm and broad; you can have integrity as an artist or a friend. Probity is cold and official. It's the word for a treasurer who never touched the fund, a judge who couldn't be bought — honesty of the kind that survives an audit, not honesty of the heart. It lives in obituaries, judicial citations and procurement rules, and almost never in conversation.
probity ≠ propriety. Probity = you are genuinely honest. Propriety = you observe the accepted forms of decent behaviour. A charming embezzler can have flawless propriety and zero probity.
Nobody praises your probity until money has passed through your hands.
The word surfaces only where funds, contracts or public office are involved, which pins it to incorruptibility rather than general niceness.
1. The bench was chosen for probity as much as for learning; a single questionable payment would have ended any of their careers.
2. Twelve years as club treasurer and not a penny out of place — the man's probity was boring, and that was the point.
In UK and Australian government tendering, big contracts require an appointed probity adviser or probity auditor — a real job title whose whole function is to certify that nobody was bought.
Latin probus = "good, upright", via probāre = "to test, to prove." Probity is honesty that has been tested and passed.

That root spreads wide: prove, approve, probe, probation (a testing period), probable (what tests out as likely), and reprobate — literally re-tested and rejected, hence a scoundrel.

A natural leaning toward something, usually something bad.
A natural, habitual leaning toward some behaviour — an inclination you were born with or fell into, not one you chose.

The word carries a faint smell of vice. A penchant is for good coffee; a proclivity is for gambling, brawling, or lying, and it's the word prosecutors and psychiatrists reach for. It also implies the tendency is settled and characteristic — not a mood but a disposition. Used of something innocent ("a proclivity for crosswords"), it sounds either arch or faintly like an accusation.
Proclivity hides cliv- = slope — and slopes run downhill.
You're already tilted that way and gravity does the rest, which is why proclivities tend toward the vices rather than the virtues.
1. The biography is candid about the composer's proclivity for ruinous debt.
2. He's got a real proclivity for picking fights he can't win.
Listen to any true-crime documentary or courtroom scene: nobody has a liking for anything — they have \"violent proclivities.\" The word almost never leaves that neighbourhood.
Latin pro- (forward) + clivus (slope) — literally "a slope forward," a tilt.

Same slope gives you declivity (a downward slope) and acclivity (an upward one), both GRE-worthy; the related root clinare ("to lean") gives incline, decline, recline, proclivity's whole leaning family.

Recklessly wasteful with money — squandering, not returning.
Adj.: spending money or resources with reckless, wasteful abandon. Noun: the person who does it.

This is a moral verdict, not a neutral description. Extravagant can be admiring; prodigal says the money was squandered — poured out until there was none left, usually by someone who should have known better. It carries the smell of an inheritance blown, a fortune wasted.

One twist the GRE loves: prodigal has nothing to do with coming back. Because of the parable, people use it to mean "the returning one." The prodigal son was prodigal before he came home — that's why he had nothing left.

A second, milder sense survives with of: prodigal of praise, prodigal of detail — lavishly generous, no insult intended.
⚠️ prodigal ≠ prodigy.
- prodigal = wasteful spender
- prodigy = astonishingly gifted young person

Mozart was a prodigy. His patron's heir was probably prodigal.
Prodigal = "prod-it-all" — he prods it all out the door until the vault is empty.
The word is about the money going out, not the man coming back.
1. Two generations of prodigal heirs reduced the estate to a mortgaged shell.
2. He got the bonus on Friday and by Sunday it was gone — absolutely prodigal with it.
The Parable of the Prodigal Son — the boy who demands his inheritance early, blows it all abroad, and crawls home broke. The story is so famous that the word got dragged toward "returning"; remember that the title describes how he spent, not how he came back.
Latin prodigere = "to drive forth, squander" — pro- ("forth") + agere ("to drive"). You're driving your money out the door.

agere is a workhorse root: agent, agenda, agile, act, exact, navigate.

🚫 Not the source of prodigy. That's Latin prodigium, "an omen, a portent" — a marvel, not a waster.

column2:
Enormously large or great — astonishingly so.
Enormous in size, amount, or degree — and enormous in a way that causes amazement.

Big is a measurement; prodigious is a reaction. It carries the stare. A prodigious appetite isn't just large, it's large enough that people comment on it; a prodigious output means a body of work whose sheer volume seems barely human. It leans admiring even when the thing itself is unwelcome (a prodigious hangover), and it sits high in register — you'll meet it in essays, obituaries and match reports, rarely in casual speech.
prodigious ≠ prodigal.
- prodigious = astonishingly large
- prodigal = recklessly wasteful with money (the Prodigal Son blew his inheritance)

Spend prodigious sums and you're impressive; spend prodigally and you're broke.
Prodigy is hiding inside prodigious — a prodigy is a child so far past normal that people gawk, and that's the size a prodigious thing is.
Both words demand an audience reaction, so if nobody would raise an eyebrow, it isn't prodigious.
1. Balzac's prodigious output — some ninety novels fuelled by fifty cups of coffee a day — killed him before he turned fifty.
2. He put away a prodigious amount of biryani for someone who claimed he wasn't hungry.
Sports commentary lives on this word: a batsman with prodigious power, a bowler getting prodigious turn, a golfer with a prodigious drive. Whenever the ball goes further than it has any right to, the commentator reaches for prodigious.
Latin prodigium = an omen, a portent, an unnatural sign — something that made Romans stop and look up. That's why the word still means "huge enough to astonish" rather than plain "huge", and it links straight to prodigy.

🚫 Not the root of prodigal. That's prodigere, "to drive forth, squander" — same first four letters, opposite idea.

Competently skilled through practice — solidly good, not brilliant.
Competent at something through training and practice — you can do the thing reliably and well.

Note where it sits on the scale: above adequate, well below masterful. Proficient is earned, unglamorous praise — it implies drilled skill rather than talent, and it quietly stops short of brilliance. Call a surgeon proficient and you've said she won't kill you; call her virtuosic and you've said something else entirely. It also wants an object — you're proficient in French, at soldering — where skilled or able can stand alone.
Pro-fic-ient rhymes with suf-fic-ient — and that's exactly the level: sufficient skill, not stunning skill.
The rhyme pins the ceiling of the word — solidly good enough, never dazzling.
1. Two years in Lisbon left him proficient in Portuguese, though he still lost every argument in it.
2. She's proficient enough with Excel to fake her way through the interview.
LinkedIn and CV language levels: Elementary → Limited working → Professional working proficiency → Full professional → Native. School test rubrics do the same — Below Basic, Basic, Proficient, Advanced — where "Proficient" is literally the band just under the top one.
Latin proficere = "to make progress, get ahead" (pro- forward + facere to make/do) — so a proficient person is one who has advanced, not one born able.

The -ficient / -fect family from facere is GRE gold: efficient (working well), sufficient (enough made), deficient (falling short), munificent, perfect, profit (also from proficere — what advances you).

column2:
Recklessly extravagant; wasteful on a shameful, ruinous scale.
Adj.: recklessly extravagant, squandering money or resources on a grand scale. Secondary (older, still live): shamelessly immoral, dissolute.

Plain wasteful is a household complaint; profligate is a judgement. It implies scale, momentum, and a whiff of moral rot — not a person who left the tap running, but one burning through an inheritance, a treasury, or a reputation. That's why it's the standard word in budget fights: profligate spending accuses the spender, not just the spending. The two senses share one idea — a person letting something valuable run to ruin, whether it's a fortune or their own character.
⚠️ profligate ≠ prolific. Near-twins by sound, opposite economics: profligate pours resources out (wasteful); prolific pours output in (abundantly productive). A prolific author writes twelve novels; a profligate one spends the advances on all twelve before writing any.
Profligate = the profit gate left wide open — money floods out and nobody moves to shut it.
The open gate captures the nuance the word adds to wasteful: the scale of the loss and the absence of shame about it.
1. A decade of profligate borrowing left the province unable to service the interest, let alone the debt.
2. He's got four streaming subscriptions he never opens — pretty profligate, for a man who moans about the price of milk.
"Profligate spending" is boilerplate in every budget row and election debate — once you notice the collocation, you'll hear it on the news within a week.
Latin prōflīgāre = "to strike down, ruin" — pro- (forward) + flīgere (to strike). The original sense is wrecked: first morally wrecked (dissolute), then financially wrecking (squandering).

flīgere is a quiet workhorse root: conflict (strike together), afflict (strike at), inflict (strike upon). A profligate has been struck down — usually by his own hand.

column2:
Reaching the bottom — deeply insightful, or utterly complete.
Two senses, one idea. (1) Showing or requiring great depth of thought or feeling — a profound remark. (2) Complete, thoroughgoing, reaching all the way down — profound silence, profound ignorance, profound change.

Depth is the whole point, and it is what separates profound from its neighbours. Intense is about force, extreme is about distance from the middle, profound is about how far down something goes. So praise that calls an idea profound says it reached bedrock, not that it was clever or loud — which is why the word turns sour so easily in the sceptic's mouth (pseudo-profound, profound-sounding). And in sense (2) it carries no admiration at all: profound ignorance is ignorance that goes all the way down.
pro-FOUND — it goes down as far as the foundation.
Same buried root as foundation: profound things sit at the bottom, whether that's a bottomless insight or bottomless silence.
1. Her final essay makes a profound claim about grief: that it is not an emotion we pass through but a room we move into.
2. He nodded like it was profound, but honestly it was just a fortune cookie.
Medicine uses it as a grading term, not a compliment: hearing loss runs mild → moderate → severe → profound, where profound means the bottom of the scale — essentially total.
Latin pro- (forward, toward) + fundus (bottom) — literally "toward the bottom."

fundus pays off elsewhere: foundation and fundamental (what sits at the bottom), fund (the bottom stock of money), and founder — when a ship founders, it goes to the bottom. Keep that separate from flounder, to thrash about clumsily.

Great depth of thought, insight, or feeling.
Great depth — of thought, insight, or feeling. Also, countably, a profundity = a remark of that depth ("he offered a few profundities and left").

Depth, not difficulty. A dense paragraph can be merely obscure; profundity means the thought actually reaches something at the bottom. That's why the word is so often used with a raised eyebrow — pseudo-profundity, mistaking obscurity for profundity, drunken profundities at 2am. Straight, it is high praise and slightly grand; in the plural, it usually means someone thinks they're being deep.
Pro-FOUND-ity: it has found the bottom. A platitude never left the surface.
The "found" you hear in the middle is really Latin fundus, "bottom" — profundity is thought that got all the way down there.
1. Critics praised the novel's profundity, though a few suspected the author of dressing simple ideas in difficult sentences.
2. Three beers in, he started dispensing profundities about the meaning of work.
Latin profundus = pro- ("forth, toward") + fundus ("bottom") — literally going toward the bottom, first of water, then of thought.

Fundus is a workhorse root: fund (the bottom store of money), foundation, fundamental, and founder (a ship that goes to the bottom — not the same word as flounder).

Pouring out in great quantity; abundant to the point of excess.
Given out or flowing in very large amounts — abundant to the point of overflow, even extravagance.

The word carries the sense of something pouring out, unstoppable and slightly beyond measure. Plentiful is a calm fact about quantity; profuse is liquid and uncontrolled. That's why the things it attaches to are things that stream: sweat, blood, tears, apologies, thanks, praise. Applied to a person's manner, it tips towards too much — profuse thanks are the kind that make the room uncomfortable.
Profuse things POUR — sweat, blood, tears, apologies. Nobody has profuse chairs.
The word only fits what can stream out of something, so if it can't flow, it can't be profuse.
1. The manuscript's margins were covered in profuse annotations, each hand more cramped than the last.
2. He turned up an hour late with a bunch of flowers and profuse apologies, none of which explained anything.
You've met the adverb far more than the adjective: in every hospital drama and first-aid manual, someone is bleeding profusely, and in every awkward email, someone apologises profusely.
Latin profundere = "to pour forth" — pro- (forth) + fundere (to pour). The past participle profusus is literally poured out.

Fundere is a workhorse root: fuse, infuse, transfusion, diffuse, effusive (gushing with feeling), refund (pour money back), confuse (poured together into a mess).

🚫 Not related to profound. That one is pro- + fundus, "bottom" — depth, not flow.

column2:
To multiply rapidly, each copy spawning more.
To multiply rapidly — to increase in number by producing more copies of itself. Also transitive: to cause something to spread that way (to proliferate weapons).

Things don't proliferate by being added one at a time; they proliferate the way cells and rumours do — each one spawning the next, faster than anyone is tracking. That's why the word so often arrives with a faint note of alarm: conspiracy theories proliferated, nuclear weapons proliferated, bubble-tea shops proliferated on one street. It can be perfectly neutral in biology, but in ordinary use the implication is usually out of hand. Increase is a measurement; proliferate is a warning.
PRO-LIFE-rate — the rate at which life makes more life.
The word literally hides life multiplying at a rate, which is exactly the runaway, self-copying growth it describes.
1. Unregulated by the state, private militias proliferated across the border provinces within a single decade.
2. Ever since he got the label printer, little stickers have proliferated on every drawer in the kitchen.
The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty — the whole international project of stopping nuclear weapons from spreading to more and more countries. If you know the treaty, you already know the word.
Latin prōlēs = "offspring" + ferre = "to bear." To proliferate is literally to bear offspring — hence the sense of self-copying rather than mere adding.

prōlēs also gives prolific (producing lots) and proletariat (in Rome, the class so poor their only contribution to the state was children). ferre is everywhere: transfer, confer, refer, fertile.

column2:
Tediously long-winded; far more words than the point needs.
Using far too many words — long-winded to the point of tedium.

The complaint is length, not content: a prolix argument may be perfectly sound, just drowned. It belongs to prose and formal speech rather than chatter — garrulous is the neighbour who won't stop talking, prolix is the memo that takes four pages to say no. It's a critic's word, cool and bookish, and it always disapproves.
⚠️ prolix ≠ prolific.
- prolix = too many words (an insult)
- prolific = produces a lot of work (a compliment)

A prolific novelist writes twenty books; a prolix one writes a thousand pages of the first.
Prolix ≈ prolongs — it prolongs the sentence, the speech, the meeting; never the point.
The fault named by prolix is purely duration: the idea arrives eventually, but only after everyone has stopped listening.
1. The judgment was learned but hopelessly prolix, burying a simple finding under ninety pages of citation.
2. His toast was so prolix that the starters went cold before anyone got to drink.
Polonius in Hamlet is prolixity itself — he rambles his way to "brevity is the soul of wit," and Gertrude cuts him off with "More matter, with less art."
Latin prolixus = "poured forth, stretched out" — pro- (forth) + liquere (to flow), the root of liquid, liquor, liquefy. A prolix writer's words simply keep flowing out.

To multiply and pass onward — plants, waves, or ideas.
To multiply and pass onward — to breed new plants from cuttings, to transmit a wave or signal through a medium, or to spread a belief, rumour, or error so that it keeps reproducing.

The difference from spread or disseminate is the chain. Disseminate scatters from one source outward, one-to-many, and stops. Propagate means each copy becomes a new source: the plant makes plants, the error in row 3 corrupts every row after it. In botany, physics and computing it's coldly technical. Aimed at ideas, it turns faintly hostile — you hold a view, but you propagate a myth, and the verb implies you know better and are multiplying it anyway.
Propaganda is hiding inside propagate — and propaganda isn't news, it's news manufactured to breed.
The buried word gives you both halves at once: relentless multiplication, plus the whiff of blame when the thing being multiplied is a belief.
1. Sound propagates roughly four times faster through water than through air.
2. One bad cell reference propagated through the whole spreadsheet and blew up the quarterly numbers.
Anyone who has changed a domain name has sat waiting for DNS to propagate — the new address copying itself server to server across the internet until every corner of the network has it. Same idea in hardware as propagation delay: how long a signal takes to work its way through a circuit.
Latin propagare = "to set slips" — gardening, literally: pin a cutting into the soil and let it become a whole new plant. From pro- (forward) + the root pag-/pac- (to fasten, fix), which also gives pact and compact — things fastened down.

That's the whole word. You don't broadcast a cutting; you plant it, and it grows into something that can be cut from in turn.

An ingrained tendency, usually toward a fault.
A built-in leaning toward a particular behaviour — an inclination you keep acting on, usually without choosing to.

A tendency is a plain observation; a penchant is a taste you enjoy indulging (a penchant for red wine). A propensity is diagnostic — it sounds like a trait someone has been assessed and found to have, which is why lawyers, psychologists and statisticians reach for it. And because it's the word used for things people can't help, it tilts toward faults: propensities are for violence, for exaggeration, for spending, far more often than for kindness.
⚠️ propensity ≠ propinquity.
- propensity = a leaning toward a behaviour
- propinquity = nearness in space or kinship (the propinquity effect: you befriend whoever sits closest)
Listen for what follows it: a propensity for violence, for lying, for overspending — the word walks in ahead of a flaw.
The collocation carries the connotation: if you can't imagine the phrase as a compliment, you've got the register right.
1. The report noted the firm's propensity to under-price risk in precisely the quarters when regulators were not looking.
2. He's got a propensity for texting his ex at 2am, and no amount of advice has ever fixed it.
Courts fight constantly over propensity evidence — proof that a defendant has done this sort of thing before. It's generally inadmissible, precisely because a jury hearing "he has a propensity for theft" will convict on the character rather than the facts. That's the word's whole flavour in one rule.
Latin pro- (forward) + pendere (to hang, to weigh) → propendere, "to lean toward." You are already hanging in that direction before the situation arises.

pendere is a workhorse root: pendulum, pending, suspend, append, pensive (weighing things in your mind), and ponder.

column2:
Correctly foretelling the future — a label given in hindsight.
Accurately foretelling what later happens; or having the solemn, oracular manner of a prophet.

In practice the word is a verdict handed down afterwards. A forecast is prophetic only once reality has confirmed it — you don't call a prediction prophetic while it's still pending. That's what separates it from prescient (clear-sighted about the future, judged on the thinking) and ominous (foreboding, judged on the mood): prophetic is scored on the outcome. It also carries a faint chill of the supernatural — the speaker knew more than they had any right to know.
⚠️ prophecy ≠ prophesy.
- prophecy (PROF-uh-see) = the noun, the prediction itself
- prophesy (PROF-uh-sye) = the verb, the act of predicting

He prophesies; what he utters is a prophecy.
Nobody calls a prediction prophetic about tomorrow — only about yesterday's warning that came true.
The word is awarded in hindsight, which is why it almost always shows up with turned out to be or eerily.
1. His 1998 essay on the fragility of global credit markets now reads as grimly prophetic.
2. Remember when you said that group project would collapse? Bit prophetic, mate.
"The Simpsons predicted it" — the running internet joke about old episodes matching later news. The headlines write themselves: eerily prophetic. Nobody said it in 1995; everybody says it now.
Greek prophētēs = "one who speaks forth" — pro- (forth, before) + phēnai (to speak). The prophet's job was speaking on behalf of a god, and only secondarily speaking ahead of time.

That phē-/phe- root for speech runs everywhere: euphemism (speaking well of), blasphemy (speaking harm), aphasia (loss of speech).

🚫 Not profit. Identical in speech, no relation — that's Latin proficere, "to make progress."

To appease an angry power by offering something.
To win back the favour of someone offended — to appease a power that is angry with you, usually by giving something up.

Where placate and mollify just soothe a mood, propitiate assumes a hierarchy: gods, kings, inspectors, your furious head of department. You are the smaller party, and you pay — an offering, a concession, a sacrifice. It also carries a faint ritual smell, so using it of an ordinary person quietly mocks them as a petty deity demanding tribute.
⚠️ propitiate ≠ expiate.
- propitiate = appease the offended party
- expiate = atone for the offending act

You expiate your sin; you propitiate the god who saw it.
Pro-pity — you work for the pity of someone who outranks you.
The hidden "pity" carries the whole nuance: you're the one begging upward, and it costs you something.
1. The villagers propitiated the mountain with an offering of grain before any climb began.
2. He brought her coffee and a muffin, trying to propitiate her after forgetting the meeting entirely.
Propitiation is a load-bearing word in Christian theology — the blood sacrifice that turns away divine wrath (Romans 3:25). That's where the word's built-in sense of paying to calm an angry power comes from.
Latin propitius = "favourable, gracious" — originally an augur's word for birds flying the right way. To propitiate is literally to make favourable.

Same root gives you propitious = favourable, well-omened ("a propitious moment to ask"). Learn the pair together: you propitiate the god so the omens turn propitious.

Favourable — conditions promising success, judged before the attempt.
Favourable; offering good conditions for success. Applied to moments, times, circumstances, weather, signs.

It describes the setup, not the score. Lucky is a verdict on what already happened; propitious is a forecast — the conditions have tilted your way and nothing has been attempted yet. The word is formal and carries a faint residue of omens and gods: you don't say a sandwich is propitious, you say the moment is. Its natural companions are moment, time, circumstances, omen.
⚠️ propitious ≠ propitiate.
- propitious (adj.) = the gods are already favourable
- propitiate (v.) = to make them favourable — appease, buy off

You propitiate an angry client; you wait for a propitious moment to send the invoice.
Propitious — the odds are pro you. It's a weather report, not a result.
The pro- tells you something is leaning in your favour, and "weather report" fixes the tense: propitious always points forward, at conditions, before the attempt.
1. The generals waited for a more propitious moment to advance, when the fog had lifted and the ground had dried.
2. Empty flight, upgrade at the gate, sun in Delhi — pretty propitious start to the trip.
Indian weddings run on this word: before a venue is booked or a card is printed, someone is hunting the calendar for a propitious date — the muhurat. Same instinct as the Latin: find the moment the heavens are leaning your way.
Latin propitius = "favourable, gracious" — said of gods inclined toward you: pro- (forward, toward) + petere (to seek, to go at).

petere pays off across the exam: petition (formally seek), appetite (seeking toward), compete (seek alongside), impetuous (rushing at), centripetal (seeking the centre), and propitiate (make the god lean your way).

Correct behaviour by accepted social standards; decorum.
Behaviour that conforms to accepted standards of manners, taste, and correctness — decorum. In the plural, the proprieties are the specific rules you're expected to observe.

This is about fittingness, not goodness. A person can breach propriety without doing anything wrong — showing up in jeans to a funeral, asking a colleague's salary, hugging a head of state. It's a formal, slightly starchy word, and the speaker who uses it is invoking a shared code: we all know how this is done. Which is why it cuts both ways — upholding propriety sounds dignified, obsessing over it sounds stuffy.
⚠️ propriety ≠ property. One letter apart, both from the same root, but propriety = correct conduct, property = the stuff you own. Read the extra -i- before you answer.
Propriety = proper + -ty — the quality of being proper, not of being good.
Proper is about fitting the occasion, so propriety polices what's appropriate rather than what's moral.
1. The committee dissolved not over any crime but over a lapse of propriety: the chair had voted on her own brother's contract.
2. You can wear what you like, but there's a certain propriety to not filming the eulogy on your phone.
Jane Austen runs on this word — and so does Bridgerton, where a single unchaperoned walk is a scandal. Nothing illegal happens; propriety is simply breached, and that's enough to end a season.
Latin proprius = "one's own, particular to oneself." What is proper to a situation is what belongs to it.

Same root, one family: proper, property, appropriate (to make one's own), proprietary, expropriate, misappropriate.

Dull and unimaginative; flat as prose, not poetry.
Dull, flat, unimaginative — lacking poetry, colour, or wonder. Literally: written in prose rather than verse.

The charge is against imagination, not competence. A prosaic report can be accurate, well-organised and entirely correct, and still be lifeless. Where banal means worn out by repetition and mundane means of the everyday world, prosaic points at the flatness itself — of the writing, or of the explanation. Its most common move is deflation: the thrilling theory collapses and the prosaic truth stands there, which is that someone forgot to plug it in.
PROSE is sitting right inside it — and prose is exactly what poetry is not.
Prosaic writing reads like a shipping manifest: nothing wrong with it, all the poetry drained out.
1. His verse never rises above the prosaic: correct metre, sound grammar, and not one line you would carry home.
2. Everyone assumed sabotage, but the reason was prosaic — the cleaner had unplugged the server to charge her phone.
A newsroom staple: "the truth is rather more prosaic." Whenever a headline promises a mystery and the article ends by explaining it away, that's the sentence doing the work.
Latin prosa ōrātiō = "straightforward speech", from prorsus, "straight ahead" (pro- + versus, "turned forward").

The contrast is physical: verse turns at the end of every line — like a plough turning at the end of a furrow — while prose just runs straight on. That versus root also gives you verse, version, reverse, diverse, converse, versatile.

Luckily timed, as if arranged by a benevolent higher power.
Happening at exactly the right moment, as though arranged by a benevolent higher power; luckily timed, opportune.

Lucky is blind chance. Providential implies the good fortune looks designed — the rain stops the fire, the letter arrives the morning before the deadline. Even in fully secular use the word keeps a faint theological glow: someone or something was looking after you. It's warm, formal, and always positive, and it attaches to timing above all — a providential delay, a providential encounter.
⚠️ providential ≠ provident.
- providential = fortunately timed, as if by divine arrangement (about luck)
- provident = prudent, saving for the future (about foresight — a provident aunt who bought insurance)

A provident man plans for the storm; a providential wind blows it away.
Providential = something provided it — and provided it just in time.
The hidden word provide is the whole meaning: the help was supplied, not stumbled upon, and the point is the timing.
1. The fog that settled over the harbour that night proved providential, screening the retreat from the guns on the far shore.
2. My phone died right before I could send that text — honestly, providential.
Providence, Rhode Island — Roger Williams, banished into the winter wilderness in 1636, named the place he survived at for God's providence. A whole city named after lucky-looking-like-design.
Latin providēre = "to see ahead" (pro- "before" + vidēre "to see"). Divine providence is God's foresight arranging events; what falls out of that arrangement is providential.

The root pays rent across the exam: provide, provision, purvey, prudent (a squashed form of providens), and on the vidēre side evident, vision, video, visage.

Narrow-minded and unsophisticated; from outside the capital.
Literally: belonging to a province rather than the capital — provincial government, provincial newspapers.
On the GRE: narrow in outlook, unsophisticated, limited to the concerns of one small place.

The insult is aimed at the mind, not the postcode. A provincial person may be perfectly clever and well-off; the charge is that their frame of reference stops at the town line, so they mistake local custom for universal truth. Note who is speaking: provincial is a word the centre uses about the edge, and it always carries a whiff of the metropolitan sneer — which is why it can make the speaker sound as snobbish as the target sounds narrow. Compare parochial (same idea, colder and more institutional) and rustic (about manner and setting, not mental horizon).
⚠️ provincial ≠ provisional.
- provincial = narrow-minded, from the sticks
- provisional = temporary, pending confirmation (a provisional government, a provisional offer)

Four letters apart, nothing in common.
A provincial has seen one province — and thinks it's the world.
The word hides its own limit: one province is the whole map to them.
1. Her novels were dismissed as provincial by critics who had never troubled to leave the capital.
2. He's not stupid, he's just provincial — anything past the county line may as well be the moon.
In France, everything outside Paris is la province — and when a Parisian calls something provincial, it is never a compliment. Same word, same sneer, in English.
Latin provincia = a territory conquered by Rome and run by a governor — i.e. everywhere that wasn't Rome. The condescension is baked in from the start: Rome was where things happened, the provinces were where you got posted.

That single root gives province, provincial, provincialism — all of them measuring distance from the centre.

Deliberately calculated to provoke a strong reaction.
Deliberately designed to cause a strong reaction — argument, anger, or desire.

The word always implies intent. A provocative statement isn't accidentally offensive; it was aimed. Which reaction it aims for decides the tone: in a review or a seminar, provocative is praise — the book unsettles you productively, it starts the argument. Applied to clothing or a look, it means sexually suggestive. Applied to a remark at a family dinner, it means you were asking for a fight. Same intent, three different targets, so the connotation swings entirely on context.
provocative ≠ evocative.
- provocative = calls out a reaction (you argue back)
- evocative = calls up a memory or mood (you drift off)

A provocative essay picks a fight; an evocative one smells like your grandmother's kitchen.
pro-VOKE ≈ poke — and nobody pokes you by accident.
The sound hook carries the crucial part: provocative isn't merely offensive, it's aimed, a jab meant to make you jump.
1. His provocative thesis — that the famine was engineered, not endured — drew furious rebuttals from three continents.
2. She only said it to be provocative, and it worked; the whole table stopped eating.
Book jackets and film reviews lean on it constantly — "a provocative new work" is critic-speak for this will start arguments, and that's the point. Note it's a compliment there.
Latin pro- (forth) + vocāre (to call) — literally to call forth a reaction out of you.

That vocāre root is a GRE goldmine: evoke (call up), revoke (call back), invoke (call upon), convoke (call together), advocate (one who's called to your side), vocation (a calling).

Outstanding skill in a field; originally, bravery in battle.
Exceptional skill or ability in some field — and, in older or heroic use, bravery in battle.

Unlike skill or competence, this word admires. You don't have prowess at loading the dishwasher; prowess is displayed, and someone is impressed. It also almost never stands alone — it arrives bolted to a domain: military prowess, athletic prowess, technical prowess, prowess in the courtroom. And it's faintly grand, so claiming it about yourself sounds like boasting; it's a word other people use about you.
Pro-wess — what a pro possesses, and never without a field to be pro at.
The hidden "pro" gives you both halves of the word: expert-level ability, always in a named domain.
1. The chronicle dwells less on the king's statecraft than on his prowess in the field, where he is said to have unhorsed three men in a single charge.
2. Everyone found out about his prowess at the barbecue when he produced ribs that shut the entire party up.
Live sports commentary keeps this word alive: "his prowess in front of goal," "her prowess from the baseline." If a pundit is praising someone's specialist ability, this is the noun they reach for.
Old French proesce = "bravery, valour," from prou = "brave, worthy."

Same root gives you proud — and, oddly, prude, from prudefemme, "a fine, upstanding woman," which soured over the centuries into "prim." Bravery → self-regard → primness, all from one stem.

🚫 Not the prow of a ship. That's Latin prora, "front end." Pure spelling coincidence.

An authorised stand-in — a person, vote, or substitute measure.
1. A person authorised to act for another — to vote, sign, or attend in their place; also the authority itself ("she holds my proxy").
2. A stand-in measure: something used to represent a thing you can't observe directly. "Tree rings are a proxy for past rainfall."

Nothing shady about it — a proxy is an appointed substitute, openly delegated, whereas an impostor or front substitutes without permission. What it does carry is a hint of second-hand-ness: a proxy is not the real thing, only the thing standing where the real thing should be. Hence proxy war (the superpowers fight through other people's armies) and by proxy (it happened, but you weren't there for it).
A proxy acts pro you — with your say-so. An impostor acts as you — without it.
The pro- ("on behalf of") is the whole word: authorised substitution, not impersonation.
1. Unable to attend the shareholders' meeting, the trustee voted by proxy.
2. Test scores are a lousy proxy for how much a kid actually understands.
A proxy server does exactly what the word says: it fetches the page on your behalf, so the site sees the middleman's address instead of yours.
A squashed-down procuracy — from Latin procurare = "to manage on behalf of" (pro- "for" + cura "care"). Same cura runs through procure, curator, curate, cure, secure, accurate, and sinecure (a job without care — i.e. no actual work).

🚫 Nothing to do with proximity. That's proximus, "nearest" — the resemblance is pure accident.

Wisely cautious; showing foresight about consequences.
Showing good judgement about the future — acting with foresight, caution, and an eye on the consequences.

Not the same as merely cautious. A cautious person avoids risk out of nerves; a prudent one has weighed the odds and chosen the safer path deliberately. It's praise, but sober, adult praise — the word belongs to money, policy and risk, and it carries a faint chill of the unexciting. Call someone's decision prudent and you're saying it was sensible, not that it was brave.
⚠️ prudent ≠ prudish. Prudent = wisely cautious about consequences. Prudish = squeamishly proper about sex and propriety. A prudent banker; a prudish aunt.
It's always a prudent investment, a prudent reserve, prudent to wait — never a prudent adventure.
The company prudent keeps tells you its meaning: it's the vocabulary of counting the cost before you spend.
1. The committee judged it prudent to hold reserves against a downturn no one had yet forecast.
2. Might be prudent to check the weather before you book that hike.
Prudential, the insurance giant — the whole business is charging you today for a risk that arrives tomorrow, which is prudence in one word.
Latin prūdēns, a squashed form of prōvidēns = "foreseeing" (pro- ahead + vidēre to see). Prudence is literally seeing ahead.

Unsqueeze it and the family opens up: provident (saving for the future), improvident (reckless with it), providence, provide, vision, evident.

Dirty-minded; greedy for sexual detail as a spectator.
Having or catering to an excessive, unwholesome interest in sex — the leer, the appetite for dirty detail.

The word judges the watcher, not the act. Nobody is prurient for having sex; you're prurient for wanting to hear about it. So it attaches to the onlooker, the tabloid reader, the "just curious" questioner — and it's an accusation every time, delivered in a cold, formal register (courts, critics, editorials) rather than shouted. Lewd and obscene describe the material; prurient describes the itch the material is designed to scratch.
⚠️ prurient ≠ puerile. Both are sneers at bad taste, but puerile (PYOO-uh-ryl) = childish, silly; prurient = dirty-minded. A fart joke is puerile. Reading someone's divorce filings for fun is prurient.
Prurient is pure with the r shoved in — hands clean, mind filthy.
The word never accuses you of doing anything, only of wanting to look.
1. The biographer dwells on the marriage with a prurient attention that tells us more about him than about his subject.
2. Don't pretend it's research — you're scrolling her photos out of prurient nosiness.
It's a load-bearing legal term in the US: material counts as obscene only if it "appeals to the prurient interest" — the Miller test. Every ratings fight and banned-book case runs through that one word.
Latin prurire = "to itch, to crave." A prurient interest is literally an itch — which is why the medical word for itching is pruritus. Keep the itch and the whole nuance follows: the itch is in the observer, and it wants scratching.

Childishly silly, in a way that invites contempt.
Childishly silly — immature in a way that embarrasses adults: snickering, name-calling, toilet jokes, sulking.

The word is a verdict, not a description. Childlike is warm (wonder, innocence); childish is a plain complaint; puerile is the same complaint delivered from a height — it says the behaviour is beneath the speaker and beneath the occasion. It attaches especially to humour and to public conduct: a puerile stunt in parliament, a puerile joke in a eulogy. Note the sting works only against someone old enough to know better; a child cannot be puerile.
Puerile — poo jokes, said by someone too grand to laugh at them.
The spelling hands you the schoolboy humour the word describes, and the sniffy tone of the person using it.
1. The committee dismissed his objection as puerile point-scoring unworthy of the office he held.
2. Grow up — arguing about who called shotgun is so puerile.
It's the film critic's standard sneer for gross-out comedy: a review calling a film "puerile" isn't saying it's for kids, it's saying grown men made it.
Latin puer = "boy." Puerile is literally boyish — which tells you why it's never a compliment about an adult. Same root in puerperal (puer + parere, "to bear") — puerperal fever, the infection of childbirth.

🚫 Not related to pure, despite the sound. That's Latin purus — purify, puritan, purge.

Eager to fight; combative by temperament.
Eager to fight; combative, quarrelsome, always up for a scrap.

This is a standing disposition, not a mood. Someone angry has been provoked; someone pugnacious goes looking. Compare the neighbours: belligerent belongs to armies and drunks and implies real violence; truculent is sullen and menacing; pugnacious is usually verbal and often faintly admiring — the columnist, the trial lawyer, the small striker who won't be bullied. It carries energy and relish, so a pugnacious person is a nuisance you might also enjoy watching.
PUGnacious — a pug is a squashed-faced little dog and old boxing slang for a fighter. Small, scrappy, spoiling for it.
The "pug" sitting at the front is no accident — boxers were called pugs from the same fist-root, and it pins the word's flavour of eager scrappiness rather than genuine menace.
1. His pugnacious style of cross-examination unsettled witnesses long before it ever produced a confession.
2. Three minutes into the meeting he was already picking fights — pugnacious little man, isn't he?
Latin pugnus = "fist" → pugnāre, "to fight."

One root, a useful cluster: pugilist (a boxer — a fist-fighter), impugn (to attack a claim at it, with words), repugnant (literally fighting back against you — hence repellent).

column2:
Exact to the last small point of correct form
Exact about the small points of correct form — etiquette, protocol, procedure, ceremony. A punctilious host seats the guests in the right order; a punctilious officer salutes the right way every time.

Meticulous is about the accuracy of the work; punctilious is about the propriety of the conduct. That's why the word lives in diplomacy, the military, and old-fashioned manners. Tone swings on context: it praises someone reliable to the last detail, but tilts toward fussy when the details being guarded are pointless ones.
punctilious ≠ punctual. Same Latin root, different point: punctual = arrives on time; punctilious = observes every rule of proper form. A punctilious man may still be late.
Punctual + tedious = punctilious — on the dot about every tiny point, sometimes to the edge of tedium.
The blend holds both halves of the word: exactness about small points, plus the faint sigh it can provoke.
1. The ambassador was punctilious in matters of precedence, and would not begin the dinner until every delegation was seated in its correct rank.
2. He's punctilious about the group chat — full sentences, proper punctuation, and a reply to every single message.
Latin punctum = "a point" → Italian puntiglio = "a fine point, a small scruple, a point of honour." Punctilious is literally full of fine points.

The root pays out across the exam: punctual (on the dot), punctuate (put in the points), puncture (make a point-hole), compunction (a pricking of conscience), pungent (sharp enough to prick the nose).

A small twinge of conscience or doubt before acting.
A twinge of doubt or unease about whether what you're doing is right — a flicker of conscience that makes you hesitate.

Size and direction are what define it. A qualm is small and internal: not guilt (which comes after), not remorse (heavier, longer), not an objection (which you'd say out loud). It's the private wobble before you act. And it lives mostly in the negative — "no qualms about" is the phrase you'll meet nine times out of ten, meaning someone did the thing without so much as a flinch.

A second, older sense survives: a sudden wave of faintness or nausea.
qualm rhymes with calm — and a qualm is the little ripple that breaks it.
The rhyme fixes the silent L and the scale: a qualm disturbs your calm, it doesn't destroy it.
1. The committee approved the merger without a qualm, untroubled by the four hundred jobs it would quietly erase.
2. I had no qualms about eating the last slice — nobody had labelled it.
Boardroom and news English runs on the negative: a lawyer, a hiring manager or a pundit will say a company "had no qualms about" doing something ruthless. Hear the phrase and you know the speaker disapproves.
Old English cwealm = plague, torment, death — and the word's first modern use was a sudden fit of physical sickness. The moral sense grew straight out of that: a qualm is nausea of the conscience.

column2:
A stuck-between state where every available choice has a cost.
A state of uncertainty over what to do, especially when you must choose and every option costs you something.

The word describes the person, not the problem — you are in a quandary, paralysed, turning it over. A conundrum is a puzzle that has an answer waiting to be found; a quandary has answers, and you dislike all of them. Milder and more everyday than predicament (which implies you're already in trouble), it carries a faint air of hand-wringing — the speaker is stuck, and slightly embarrassed to be stuck.
Qu-AND-ary: on one hand… and on the other.
The and sitting in the middle of the word is the two competing options you're wedged between.
1. Faced with a dying patient and a family divided over treatment, the surgeon found herself in a genuine quandary.
2. I'm in a bit of a quandary — both parties are the same night and I've said yes to both.

Enforced isolation of the possibly infected, to stop contagion.
Noun: a period of enforced isolation for people, animals, or things that may carry disease. Verb: to place under such isolation.

The key is suspicion, not confirmation. You isolate the sick; you quarantine the exposed — the ones who might be carrying something and are held apart until the doubt clears. It's precautionary and time-bounded, and it's imposed by an authority (port, hospital, government), not chosen. The metaphorical uses keep that flavour: a quarantined file, a quarantined dataset, a politician quarantined by his own party — set aside as a possible contaminant, pending judgement.
Quarantine is a waiting room, not a ward.
You're held there because you might be infectious, whereas isolation is for those already known to be.
1. Livestock imported from the mainland were quarantined for six weeks before being admitted to the herd.
2. They quarantined the new laptop off the network until IT could confirm it was clean.
Your antivirus doesn't delete a suspicious file — it drops it in Quarantine, sealed off but not condemned, exactly the sense of the word: guilty until cleared.
Italian quarantina giorni = "about forty days." Plague-era Venice made arriving ships sit at anchor for forty days before anyone could land. The number is baked into the word: Italian quaranta ← Latin quadrāgintā, "forty," from quattuor, "four" — the same four that gives you quart, quarter, quadrant, quartet.
