column2:
To settle firmly, or firmness itself; also, to separate into parts.
Verb: to settle something unsettled — a dispute, a doubt, a plot — or to decide firmly to do a thing. Technically: to break something down into its parts (resolve a force into vectors, resolve two stars through a telescope).
Noun: hard, settled determination.

The verb's quiet claim is finality: you don't resolve an argument you merely paused, and a story that resolves has no loose ends left. The noun is stronger and more dignified than determination — it names the firmness that survives after doubt has been faced, which is why it collocates with strain: steely resolve, her resolve wavered, test his resolve. You can be determined about lunch; resolve is reserved for things that cost something.
Re-solve = un-loosen the knot. Untangle the mess (settle it, split it into strands) and what's left standing is your resolve.
The root means loosen, so every sense is a knot coming apart — a dispute, an image, a doubt — and the noun is what remains once the doubt is gone.
1. Sanctions were intended to break the government's resolve; eighteen months on, they had only hardened it.
2. We finally resolved the seating chart at 1 a.m., and honestly nobody won.
Your monitor's resolution — 1080p, 4K — is exactly this word's technical sense: how finely the screen can separate the image into distinguishable dots. High resolution = more loosened apart into detail.
Latin re- + solvere = "to loosen, untie." The knot-loosening idea runs through the whole family: solve (untie the problem), dissolve (loosen apart in liquid), absolve (untie you from blame), soluble, solution.

Note the shape: a solution of salt and a solution to a puzzle are the same word, because both are things coming undone.

Clever at solving problems with whatever's available.
Clever at finding ways to solve problems — especially with whatever is to hand, under pressure, when the obvious means aren't available.

This is praise for improvisation, not for intellect. Ingenious rates the idea; resourceful rates the person, and it quietly implies the conditions were bad — no budget, no manual, no backup. Calling someone resourceful says less about how much they know than about how badly they refuse to be stuck.
Resource + full — and the joke is that the resourceful one is the person whose resources ran out.
The word looks like "well-supplied," but it's earned in exactly the opposite conditions — you only get to prove it when you're short.
1. Cut off from resupply for six weeks, the garrison proved remarkably resourceful, distilling drinking water over cooking fires.
2. She's the most resourceful person I know — the car died in the middle of nowhere and she had it running on a shoelace.
MacGyver became so synonymous with this that English absorbed the name as a verb — to MacGyver something is to fix it with tape, a paperclip and no proper tools. That's resourcefulness in one word.
Re- + Latin surgere = "to rise." A resource is literally what lets you rise again after a fall — so the resourceful person is the one who keeps getting back up.

Same root, quietly everywhere: surge, resurgent, insurgent (rising against), resurrection, and source (where water rises from the ground).

Impatient and hard to control; restless under authority.
Impatient, fidgety, and hard to keep under control — said of people or animals who are being made to wait, obey, or hold still.

Restless is private: you toss in bed, you can't settle, nobody else is involved. Restive almost always has an authority in the picture — troops, a crowd, a class, a province, a horse under a rider — and it means the grip is starting to slip. It's the state just short of mutiny, which is why journalists reach for it: a restive electorate, restive backbenchers, the restive north. Never a compliment, and never about sleep.
⚠️ restive ≠ restful. They look like cousins and mean opposites: restful = calm and soothing; restive = agitated and refusing to be handled. Nothing restive is restful.
Restive is restless with a rider on top.
The agitation isn't free-floating — someone is trying to control you, and you're about to stop cooperating.
1. By the third hour of delay the passengers had grown restive, and the gate agent stopped making announcements altogether.
2. Twenty minutes into the lecture the back row got restive — phones out, chairs scraping.
A newsroom workhorse: any foreign-desk report will hand you a restive province, restive troops, a restive population — always meaning "not in open revolt yet, but close."
Latin restāre = "to stay back, remain." A restive horse originally refused to move — it stood there, balking at the spur. The sense drifted from stubborn stillness to the twitching, barely-contained impatience of something that won't obey. Same root as arrest (make it stay put) and the rest in "the rest of them" (what remains).

🚫 Not the rest you get in bed. That's Old English ræstan, an unrelated word that just happens to sound identical — which is exactly what makes restive/restful such a reliable trap.

To strike back at whoever harmed you first.
To strike back at someone who has harmed you — returning injury for injury, usually in the same coin.

The word is structurally second: it needs a prior blow to exist, so it quietly assigns blame to whoever moved first. Compare its neighbours — avenge is moral and elevated (you avenge a murdered brother), revenge is personal and hot, but retaliate is cool, transactional, almost procedural. It's the verb of tariffs, sanctions, air strikes, and office politics: a measured counter-move, not a passion. Note too that it doesn't need to be just — only responsive.
Nobody can retaliate first.
The word carries its own backstory — a retaliation is always the second blow, which is why it lets the retaliator claim the moral high ground.
1. When the tribunal upheld the sanctions, Beijing retaliated within the week, matching the tariff line for line.
2. Push him in a meeting and he won't argue — he'll retaliate three months later in your performance review.
Trade-war headlines run on this word: every round of tariffs is met by retaliatory tariffs, and HR policies everywhere ban retaliation against whistleblowers — the legal term for punishing someone for complaining.
Latin talis = "of such kind" → retaliare, "to return the like." That's the whole nuance sitting in the root: the response is supposed to match the offence.

Same root gives lex talionis, the ancient law of "an eye for an eye" — measured, equal payback, not unlimited revenge.

🚫 Not related to tally (Latin talea, a notched stick), even though "settling the score" makes them feel like cousins.

Holding back what you could say, especially about yourself.
Unwilling to speak freely — holding back what you could say, especially about your own feelings, plans, or affairs. (Noun: reticence.)

Shyness is temperament; reticence is a decision. A shy person can't get the words out; a reticent one has them and keeps them. It's also narrower than taciturn, which means habitually short on words in general — reticence usually attaches to a subject: reticent about his finances, about her first marriage. Which way it reads depends on the scene: on a diplomat it's discretion, on a witness it's evasion.
reticent ≠ reluctant. Reticent is about speech (won't say); reluctant is about action (won't do). "Reticent to sign the contract" is the mistake — that's reluctant. If nobody's talking, it's reticent.
retiCENT — he won't give you his two cents.
He has the opinion; he just isn't handing it over — which is holding back, not being tongue-tied.
1. Ordinarily expansive about his research, he grew notably reticent whenever the funding source came up.
2. Mum's weirdly reticent about how she met Dad — thirty years and we've never got the story.
Latin reticēre = "to keep silent" — re- (back) + tacēre (to be silent). That root pays off across the exam: tacit (understood without being said), taciturn (habitually silent), tacitly.
column3: g14 register::formal connotation::depends antonym::letting-it-out-vs-keeping-it-in antonym::talks-too-much-vs-says-little intensity::sparing-with-words meaning::saying-little root::root:-tac-re-to-be-silent

column2:
Shy and reserved; inclined to withdraw from attention.
Shy, reserved, unassuming — inclined to keep out of the spotlight and out of company.

On the GRE this is almost never about leaving a job. It's a settled disposition, not a mood: a retiring person isn't anxious or awkward, they simply decline attention. That makes it gentler and mildly approving where timid is weak and antisocial is hostile — a retiring colleague does excellent work and lets someone else present it.
retiring ≠ reticent.
- retiring = holds back your presence — you leave the room
- reticent = holds back your words — you stay, and say nothing

A reticent guest sits silent at the party. A retiring one never came.
Retiring = always retiring early — from the party, the stage, the conversation.
The whole word is just retire doing its ordinary job, applied to attention rather than to work.
1. A retiring scholar, he published prolifically and lectured almost never, declining every honour that required a speech.
2. He's not exactly retiring — he'd been at the mic for twenty minutes before anyone could stop him.
The stock phrase "shy and retiring" is now used almost entirely sarcastically — "our new boss isn't the shy and retiring type." If you've heard the phrase, it was probably an insult about someone loud.
French retirer = re- ("back") + tirer ("to pull, draw"). To retire is literally to draw yourself back — from an army, from a job, or from the room.

That one image covers both senses, so you never have to store them separately.
column3: g28 register::neutral connotation::neutral antonym::at-home-among-people-vs-shut-away-from-t antonym::brass-nerve-vs-shrinking-back antonym::playing-it-down-vs-puffing-it-up intensity::pulling-away-from-people meaning::keeping-apart-from-people

column2:
To cut back sharply — spending, operations, or staff.
To cut back — to reduce spending, shrink operations, or (in British, Indian and Australian usage) lay off staff.

This isn't trimming for elegance; it's contraction under pressure. A company retrenches when revenue falls, a government retrenches when the deficit bites, a household retrenches after a job loss. The word carries a defensive posture — pulling back to what you can still hold — and in corporate mouths it's mildly euphemistic: retrenched sounds tidier than sacked.
⚠️ retrench ≠ entrench. Same trench, opposite move: entrench = dig in and become immovable (entrenched interests); retrench = pull the line back and cut. One fortifies, one shrinks.
Re-trench: draw the trench in tighter — everything left outside it gets cut.
The word wears its meaning on the outside — trench is a cut, and retrenching means cutting your perimeter back to what you can still defend.
1. Faced with a third straight quarter of losses, the board voted to retrench, closing two plants and freezing all hiring.
2. We're going to have to retrench a bit this year — no holiday, and the car can wait.
Standard business-page vocabulary: headlines like "Airline retrenches 3,000 staff" — and in Indian labour law, retrenchment is the formal term for layoffs under the Industrial Disputes Act.
French retrancher = "to cut off, cut away" (re- + trancher, to slice). Same slice gives you trench (a cut in the ground), trenchant (cuttingly sharp — a trenchant critique), and entrench.

A gushing, unstructured outpouring of enthusiasm.
An outpouring of extravagant, ecstatic enthusiasm — in speech or writing. Also, in music, a free-form piece that wanders where it likes instead of obeying a set structure.

Both senses share one idea: form has been abandoned. A eulogy is organised praise; a rhapsody is praise that has run off its leash — the speaker is carried away, gushing, no longer building an argument. That's why the verb rhapsodize (the form the GRE actually tests) usually comes with a faint raised eyebrow: he rhapsodized about his new grill for forty minutes. Sincere, yes — but excessive, and slightly funny to watch.
Rhap = rap: a rhapsody is freestyle — stitched together on the fly, no chorus to come back to.
The sound hook carries the nuance: it's not the content that marks a rhapsody but the unstructured, run-on delivery.
1. The review dissolved into rhapsody — three paragraphs on the light in a single shot, and not one word on the plot.
2. Don't ask him about his espresso machine unless you've got twenty minutes for the full rhapsody.
Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" is the definition in action: ballad, then opera, then hard rock, no repeating chorus — a song deliberately stitched from mismatched pieces, exactly what the word names.
Greek rhaptein (to stitch) + ōidē (song) — a "stitched-together song." A rhapsode was the travelling reciter who sewed episodes of Homer into one performance.

That ōidē is worth banking: ode, melody, parody, comedy, prosody all carry it.

The art of persuasion; or persuasive talk with no substance.
1. The art of persuasive speaking and writing — its techniques, structures, and figures. 2. Language crafted to persuade or impress but thin on substance or sincerity.

The word runs hot or cold depending on who's holding it. In a classroom it's a neutral discipline: Aristotle wrote a treatise on it, and rhetorical devices are just tools. In politics and journalism it's nearly always a slur — "empty rhetoric", "inflammatory rhetoric" — talk offered instead of action or truth. What stays constant across both senses: rhetoric is about how something is said, never whether it's true. That's why the GRE likes it — passages use the neutral sense while everyday instinct expects the insult.
Empty rhetoric. Heated rhetoric. Campaign rhetoric. — judge it by the company it keeps.
Alone the word names a neutral craft, but the adjectives that habitually attach to it all mean "all talk, no substance," which is exactly the split you need to hold.
1. Cicero's mastery of rhetoric could turn a losing case into an acquittal before the jury had stopped listening.
2. Cut the rhetoric and just tell me what the rent's going to be next year.
You already use the adjective without thinking: a rhetorical question is asked purely for effect, with no answer wanted — proof that the root is about effect on the listener, not information.
Greek rhētōr = "public speaker, one who addresses the assembly." The word is built on the speaker, not the subject — which is exactly why it always describes delivery rather than truth.

Strict exactness of method; severity; harsh conditions.
1. Strict, unbending exactness — especially of method, proof, or reasoning. 2. Severity; harsh enforcement. 3. (usually plural, rigors) punishing conditions: the rigors of the Arctic winter.

One word, two opposite emotional charges, decided entirely by what is being rigorous. Applied to a method, it's the highest compliment in academic English — methodological rigor means nothing was hand-waved. Applied to a person or a regime, it's cold and unforgiving. Applied to circumstances, it's plain suffering. Note the register: this is a word for journals, courts, and training manuals, not for casual complaint.
rigor ≠ vigor. One letter apart, opposite feel: rigor is stiffness and strictness, vigor is energy and vitality. A rigorous argument is airtight; a vigorous argument is energetic — and possibly sloppy.
Rigor is rigid — rigid method earns praise, rigid conditions inflict pain.
Same stiffness either way, and which sense you're in depends only on whether the stiffness is in an argument or in the weather.
1. The referees rejected the paper not for its conclusions but for its lack of statistical rigor.
2. Two weeks into boot camp the rigor of it had him asleep by nine every night.
Rigor mortis — the stiffening of a body after death, the phrase every crime drama uses to time a murder. Same word, literal sense: stiffness.
Latin rigor = "stiffness, numbness," from rigēre, "to be stiff." Everything follows from stiffness: rigid (won't bend), rigidity, rigorous (won't bend the standards), rigor mortis (won't bend at all).

Strong enough to withstand stress without breaking.
Strong and sturdy — but specifically strong enough to keep working under stress: a robust body, a robust economy, a robust argument, a robust system.

The word is about withstanding, not about size or force. A weightlifter is powerful; a system that survives bad input is robust. Nor is it rigid — a robust thing bends and keeps going where a brittle thing snaps. On the GRE it usually turns up in technical or economic prose (robust growth, robust findings, a robust defence of a theory), where it's a quiet compliment: this thing has been tested and held.

Two spillover senses worth knowing: of flavour, full-bodied and strong (robust coffee, a robust red wine); of debate or exercise, vigorous, hearty, no-holds-barred.
Robust = won't bust.
The word literally ends in bust, and that's exactly the test — pile pressure on a robust thing and it refuses to break.
1. The committee demanded a robust methodology — results that would survive being run again with different data.
2. He's eighty and still chopping wood; the man's absurdly robust.
Coffee packaging. Every bag promising a "rich, robust flavour" is selling you the full-bodied sense — strong, dark, no thinness to it.
Latin rōbur = "oak", and by extension "strength, hardness". Rōbustus meant literally "oaken" — built of oak, hence tough.

Same root gives you corroborate: con- (together) + rōborāre (to strengthen) — to strengthen a claim by putting more evidence beside it.

Basic, undeveloped — only the roughest first stage.
Basic and undeveloped — limited to the first rough beginnings of a thing. In biology, of an organ: only partly formed, never grown into full function (a whale's hind limbs).

Note what it does not say: not wrong, not broken — just barely begun. Basic is flat description; rudimentary is a measurement against what should have been there, so it usually lands as a quiet downgrade. "Rudimentary French" means you can order coffee and nothing more; "rudimentary sanitation" means a hole in the ground. Applied to a person's skill it is polite and damning at once.
RUDE is hiding at the front — and rude first meant rough, unfinished, not impolite.
Rudimentary things are rough-hewn and stopped early, not offensive.
1. The excavation revealed a rudimentary drainage system: two stone channels and no more.
2. He's got a rudimentary grasp of the spreadsheet — he can open it and that's about it.
Standard in software release notes: "rudimentary support for dark mode" is the polite way of saying it technically exists and you won't enjoy it.
Latin rudis = "raw, rough, unworked" — of stone before the chisel. A rudiment is the first rough stage of anything.

Same root, two GRE payoffs: rude (originally unpolished, only later ill-mannered) and erudite — e- "out of" + rudis, literally worked out of the rough, i.e. polished by learning. Erudite is the exact opposite end of the same block of stone.

To turn a thought over slowly, repeatedly, often broodingly.
To turn something over in the mind — to think it through slowly, repeatedly, at length.

The word carries duration and repetition. You consider a job offer in an afternoon; you ruminate on it for a fortnight. And unlike ponder or reflect, which point forward toward a conclusion, ruminating often goes nowhere — the same thought chewed again and again. Psychologists use it flatly negatively: rumination is the depressive habit of replaying a grievance or humiliation on a loop. So the word tilts inward and slightly stuck, even when the tone is mild.
Ruminate ≈ "ruin it" — chew a thought long enough and you ruin it.
The sound hook catches the word's real flavour: not brisk thinking but the slow, circling kind that spoils your evening.
1. Having lost the election, he retreated to the countryside to ruminate on where the campaign had gone wrong.
2. Stop ruminating over one bad text — she probably just fell asleep.
Therapists use it as a technical term: rumination is the clinical name for the thought-loop you can't get out of at 2 a.m., and \"you're ruminating\" is a standard thing to hear in a CBT session.
Latin rūmināre = "to chew the cud," from rūmen, the first stomach of a cow. A ruminant brings food back up and grinds it a second time — which is exactly what your brain does with an embarrassing memory.

Too sacred or important to be touched, changed, or criticised.
So sacred, or treated as so important, that it must not be touched, changed, cut, or criticised.

The literal religious sense (an oath, a relic, a shrine) is now the rarer one. In modern prose it's almost always secular and faintly sardonic: a budget line, a Sunday lunch, a founder's original vision. Calling something sacrosanct usually says less about the thing than about the people defending it — they've put it beyond argument, and the writer is raising an eyebrow at that. Compare sacred, which is sincere, and inviolable, which is legal and cold; sacrosanct carries a whiff of protected privilege.
You almost never meet this word standing up — you meet it being knocked down: "nothing is sacrosanct."
The word's natural habitat is the negative, which tells you it means fenced off from change — and that someone is about to climb the fence.
1. The committee insisted that the charter's first article was sacrosanct and would not be reopened for debate.
2. Cut whatever you like from the script — but the last scene is sacrosanct, don't touch it.
Standard boardroom and Westminster boilerplate before bad news: "In this review, no department is sacrosanct." Whenever you hear it, cuts are coming.
Latin sacrōsanctus = sacer ("sacred") + sanctus ("consecrated") — holy said twice, belt and braces, because it originally described something protected by a binding religious oath.

Both halves are GRE workhorses: sacer → sacred, sacrifice, sacrament, consecrate; sanctus → saint, sanctuary, sanctity, sanction, sanctimonious.

Cruel in a way that enjoys the victim's suffering.
Cruel in a particular way: taking pleasure in someone else's pain, humiliation or fear.

Plain cruelty can be careless, cold, or a means to an end — the bully wants your lunch money. Sadistic cruelty is the end: the suffering is the reward, and the person is savouring it. That makes it the heaviest word in the family, at home in courtrooms and criminal profiles. Colloquially it also runs as hyperbole — a sadistic exam schedule, a sadistic spin instructor — where the joke is precisely that they seem to be enjoying your misery.
SAD is hiding inside sadistic — but it's your sadness, and he's delighted by it.
The word isn't cruelty alone; it's cruelty plus pleasure, so if nobody's enjoying it, it isn't sadistic.
1. The tribunal found the guards' treatment of prisoners not merely negligent but sadistic, calculated to prolong distress for its own sake.
2. He scheduled the meeting for 7 a.m. on a Monday and I swear he had a sadistic little smile about it.
In true-crime documentaries, "sadistic" is never loose language — profilers and prosecutors use it as a technical classification, meaning the offender was motivated by the victim's suffering itself.
From the Marquis de Sade, the 18th-century French aristocrat and novelist who was jailed for decades and wrote at length about cruelty as pleasure. His name became the condition: sadism, sadist, sadistic.

Its mirror is an eponym too — masochistic, from the Austrian writer Leopold von Sacher-Masoch, who wrote about taking pleasure in receiving pain. Two men, two novels, one compound: sadomasochism.

🚫 Not from sad. Pure coincidence — English sad is Old English sæd, "full, sated." Useful hook, false relative.

wise in a shrewd, far-seeing, practical way
Having keen judgment and foresight — able to read a situation, or a person, and see where it is heading.

This is wisdom with a practical edge. Wise suggests depth and moral weight; shrewd suggests self-interest and a sharp eye for advantage; sagacious sits between them — respectable, admiring, and always about judgment applied to the future. You call a decision sagacious when it looked unremarkable at the time and turned out to be exactly right. The word is formal and slightly grand, so it flatters: it's the adjective for elder statesmen, canny investors, and — a long literary tradition — unusually clever dogs.
sagacious ≠ salacious. Salacious (suh-LAY-shuhs) means lewd, indecently sexual — salacious gossip. One letter and one vowel apart, opposite worlds: praise a colleague's salacious judgment and you have said something very different.
SAGAcious — he sees the whole saga before it's played out.
The hidden word carries the key nuance: this isn't just knowing things, it's seeing how the story ends.
1. The treaty was the work of a sagacious diplomat who had anticipated the alliance's collapse a decade before it came.
2. Gran's sagacious enough to know that when the two of them go quiet, something's been broken.
Latin sagax = "keen-scented," from sagīre, to perceive sharply — originally the nose of a hunting hound picking up a trail nobody else can detect. That's the image inside the word: sensing what's there before there's evidence.

Same root gives presage (prae- "before" + sagire) — to sniff out what's coming. Note that sage is not a relative: that's Latin sapere, "to taste, to be wise" (sapient, insipid, savour).

Health-giving — especially of air, climate, or surroundings.
Health-giving — good for the body, said above all of places: air, climate, sea breezes, a mountain village, a spa town.

It's a word about environments, not habits. A diet is healthy; a coastline is salubrious. The register is genteel and slightly old-fashioned, which is why it survives most vigorously in the negative: "a less than salubrious part of town", "an insalubrious hotel" — and there it has quietly slid from unhealthy to seedy, disreputable. So the positive sense praises the air, and the negative sense insults the neighbourhood.
⚠️ salubrious ≠ salutary.
- salubrious = physically wholesome — air, climate, surroundings
- salutary = producing a good effect, usually a corrective one — a salutary lesson, a salutary shock

Salubrious feels pleasant. Salutary often doesn't — it's the unpleasant thing that does you good.
Salubrious shares its front end with salute — and a salute is a wish for your health.
A salute only wishes you well; salubrious surroundings actually do the work.
1. Victorian doctors sent consumptive patients to Davos for its cold, dry, salubrious air.
2. The rent was cheap, but let's just say the area wasn't the most salubrious.
Estate agents and travel writing keep it alive: a listing boasts of a salubrious neighbourhood, and a reviewer damns a bar as "less than salubrious" — the same word doing praise and sneer.
Latin salūs, salūtis = "health, safety, well-being." One root, a useful family: salute and salutation (originally wishing someone health), salutary (health-producing), and the toast in Italian — salute!

Beneficial in effect — especially something unpleasant that does you good.
Producing a good effect, especially a corrective one; beneficial. (Older, narrower sense: health-giving.)

The thing that is salutary is usually unwelcome at the time. Look at what the word actually attaches to: a salutary lesson, a salutary warning, a salutary shock, a salutary reminder. It's the sharp experience that improved you — the failed exam, the near-miss, the bill that finally forced a budget. Beneficial is neutral about how it felt; salutary implies it stung and worked anyway. It's a formal, slightly stern word: the register of leader columns and school reports, not casual praise.
⚠️ salutary ≠ salubrious. Same root, different jobs: salubrious = physically healthy or wholesome as a place or condition (a salubrious climate, a less-than-salubrious hotel); salutary = beneficial in its effect, usually through a hard lesson.
A salutary lesson is a slap you end up saluting.
The word hides salut- (as in salute), and that's the whole nuance: it hurt, and afterwards you acknowledge it did you good.
1. The collapse of the fund had at least one salutary consequence: no regulator could any longer pretend the risk was hypothetical.
2. Getting outplayed by a fourteen-year-old was a salutary experience — I've actually been practising since.
Every time someone raises a glass and says "Salut!" (or Spanish "¡Salud!" after a sneeze), they're using this exact root — wishing you health. That's the buried sense in salutary.
Latin salūs, salūtis = "health, safety, well-being." To salute someone was originally to wish health on them; a salutation is that wish in words; salubrious is the air that supplies it. Salutary keeps the payoff rather than the greeting: whatever leaves you better off.

Showily, smugly moral — parading a virtue you may lack.
Making a showy display of moral superiority — preaching virtue in a tone that says and you fall short.

The word is a verdict on the performance, not the piety. A person can be genuinely devout without being sanctimonious; what earns the label is the parade — the sighing, the lecture, the visible halo. It also carries a strong hint of hypocrisy: the sanctimonious usually moralise about a sin they quietly commit. Note who uses it — nobody ever calls themselves sanctimonious. It is always an accusation, thrown at someone whose righteousness has become unbearable.
⚠️ Don't hear parsimonious. Same -monious ending, unrelated word: parsimonious = stingy with money; sanctimonious = preachy about morals. Miserly wallet vs. superior tone.
Sanct (saint) + -monious (like ceremonious) = sainthood performed as ceremony.
The saintliness is staged for an audience, which is exactly why the word stings.
1. The editorial struck a sanctimonious tone, condemning a corruption its own proprietor had profited from for a decade.
2. Spare me the sanctimonious speech about recycling — you flew to Ibiza three times last year.
Latin sanctus = "holy, consecrated." One root, a whole GRE cluster: sanctify (make holy), sanctuary (holy place, hence refuge), sacrosanct (untouchable), sanctum, saint.

Sanctimonious once simply meant holy — it soured into sarcasm, and the sneer is now permanent.

To officially approve — or, as a noun, to punish.
Verb: to officially approve or authorise. Noun (1): that official approval. Noun (2): a penalty imposed to force compliance — usually plural: sanctions.

It is its own opposite, and the GRE loves that. Both senses come from the same idea: an authority laying down a binding rule, and either blessing what fits it or punishing what doesn't.

Register matters more than you'd think. Sanction is never casual approval — a friend doesn't sanction your haircut. It implies a body with the standing to permit: a government, a church, a governing council, a licensing board. And when it bites, it's coercive rather than merely punitive — sanctions are meant to change behaviour, not just express displeasure.
Singular verb = permission; plural noun = punishment. He sanctioned the raid / They imposed sanctions.
Grammar disambiguates the contronym far more reliably than context does — if you see "sanctions" sitting there as a plural noun, it's the penalty sense almost every time.
1. The committee declined to sanction the expedition, judging the route too hazardous to bear the institution's name.
2. Trade sanctions kicked in overnight and suddenly nobody could ship anything.
Any news bulletin about Russia, Iran or North Korea — "fresh sanctions" is one of the most-spoken phrases in international news, and it's always the punishment sense.
Latin sanctus = "holy, made binding" (from sancīre, to consecrate). A sanction was originally a decree made sacred — untouchable, enforceable.

That root pays for itself: saint, sacred, sanctuary, sanctify, sacrosanct, and the GRE favourite sanctimonious (holier-than-thou).

Cheerfully confident, especially when things look bad.
Cheerfully confident that things will turn out well — especially when there's good reason to think they won't.

Optimism is the general word; sanguine is optimism with the volume down. It describes a settled temperament rather than a mood, and it almost always shows up against a backdrop of trouble: you are sanguine about the deficit, the diagnosis, the deadline. That's what gives it its edge — depending on the writer, it's either admirable composure or a polite way of saying someone hasn't grasped the danger. Formal, and common in finance and journalism ("investors remain sanguine").

An older, near-dead sense means blood-red or ruddy-complexioned, which is the bridge back to the root.
⚠️ sanguine ≠ sanguinary. Same blood root, opposite temperature: sanguine = cheerful and unworried; sanguinary = bloodthirsty, gory. A sanguine general expects to win; a sanguinary one enjoys the killing.
Sanguine starts with sang — while everyone else panics, he sang.
The calm cheerfulness is the whole point: sanguine isn't excitement, it's humming through a crisis.
1. Despite two failed harvests, the old man remained sanguine about the estate's prospects, as though ruin were merely a rumour.
2. Markets have gone haywire and he's still sanguine about his pension — I wish I had his nerves.
It's the standard word of market commentary: any week you can find a headline saying investors are "sanguine about inflation" — always meaning calm so far, possibly foolishly.
Latin sanguis, sanguinis = blood. Medieval medicine held that four bodily humours set your personality; the man with blood dominant was ruddy, warm and cheerful — the sanguine type. The temperament outlived the theory.

Same root: sanguinary (bloodthirsty), consanguineous (related by blood), and the red wine punch sangria.

Mocking something to expose its folly, with a point to make.
Using irony, exaggeration or ridicule to expose folly, vice or stupidity — usually in politics, institutions, or fashionable opinion.

Satire aims at a target, and it wants that target fixed or shamed: there's a moral engine under the joke. Sarcasm, by contrast, is personal and spoken — a jab at you, in the room, right now. A sarcastic remark makes the speaker sound sour; a satirical piece makes the speaker sound clever and a little dangerous. Note too that satirical describes the work far more than the person — an essay, a cartoon, a sketch show, a novel.
Sat-IRICAL hides IRONICAL — but irony with a target and a grudge.
Plain irony just says the opposite of what it means; satire points that irony at somebody who deserves it.
1. Swift's satirical proposal that the Irish poor sell their children as food was read, by a few humourless readers, as sincere policy advice.
2. The whole sketch was a satirical take on wellness influencers, and half the audience didn't realise they were the joke.
The Onion — headlines written straight-faced as real news precisely so the target is the thing being reported on. Every time someone shares an Onion piece and a relative believes it, that's satire working exactly as designed.
Latin satura — from lanx satura, "a full plate," a mixed dish of assorted food. Roman satire was a medley: a bit of everything, all of it skewering someone. Gives you satire, satirist, satirize.

🚫 Not from satyr. The Greek goat-man got attached to the word later by mistaken association; the two are unrelated, which is why the spelling is sati-r-e, not saty-r-e.

Barely enough; noticeably short of what was needed.
Barely enough — and pointedly less than what was needed, expected, or deserved.

Scarce describes supply: the thing is hard to come by. Scant describes a shortfall against a standard — there is some, just not enough to do the job. That's why it almost always sits directly in front of a noun and carries a note of reproach: scant evidence, scant regard, scant attention, scant comfort. Saying a report gave the objections scant attention is a criticism of the report, not a statement about how much attention exists in the world.

It also does quiet duty as a precise measure: a scant cup means fill it and then take a little back.
Scant rhymes with can't — there's scant flour, so you can't finish the cake.
Scant isn't "none" and it isn't "little" — it's the amount that leaves you unable to do the thing.
1. The commission devoted three hundred pages to procedure and scant attention to the victims.
2. We had a scant ten minutes to make the connection, so we ran.
Baking recipes use it as a technical measure: "a scant cup of sugar" means fill the cup, then tip a little out — deliberately just under.

column2:
Harshly critical in a way that genuinely wounds.
Of criticism: severe enough to wound — bitter, contemptuous, and aimed to leave a mark.

Harsh is blunt; scathing is skilful. It carries a note of scorn and usually a note of style — the scathing reviewer is enjoying himself, and the audience is enjoying it with him. It attaches to the attack, not the attacker: a scathing review, report, rebuke, dismissal. And it implies the target actually got hurt — you don't call a criticism scathing if it bounced off.
⚠️ scathing ≠ seething.
- scathing = lashing out — words that flay someone
- seething = boiling inside — silent, contained rage

A seething man says nothing. A scathing man says far too much.
You already know unscathed — untouched, unharmed. Strip the un- and you get the thing doing the harm.
Scathe means to injure, and it survives in modern English almost only in its negative, so let unscathed hand you the meaning for free.
1. The committee's report was scathing, describing the ministry's oversight as "negligent to the point of complicity."
2. She sent one scathing text about his playlist and he hasn't recovered since.
Newsroom boilerplate: watchdogs and auditors release "a scathing report," critics file "a scathing review." If you've read a headline this week, you've met the word in its natural habitat.
Old Norse skaða = "to injure, to damage" — the Vikings left it behind in English as scathe.

Same root as German Schaden (harm), which you already know from Schadenfreude — joy at someone else's damage. Fitting: that's roughly what a scathing review runs on.

A formal split of a group into rival factions.
A formal split of a group into opposing factions — especially a church, party, or institution — usually over doctrine or principle. Also the resulting division itself.

A rift is emotional and may heal; a dispute is an event. A schism is structural and permanent: one body becomes two, each claiming to be the true one. The word carries an ecclesiastical shadow even in secular use, so calling a party split a schism implies a war over orthodoxy, not tactics — heretics on one side, the faithful on the other.
sch-ISM — a split over an -ism.
The word hides ism precisely because a schism is never about personalities — it's a rupture over doctrine, and it ends with two organisations where there was one.
1. The reform vote produced a lasting schism, and within a year the dissenting bishops had consecrated a rival hierarchy.
2. There's a proper schism in the group chat now — half of them won't book the same flight as the other half.
The Great Schism of 1054, when Christianity split into Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox — the textbook case, and the reason the word still smells of churches.
Greek skhizein = "to split, to cleave" → skhisma, "a cleft."

Same root gives schizophrenia (literally "split mind") and schist, the rock that flakes apart in sheets. Hear schizo- inside schism and the meaning is free.

Sparkling with wit; brilliantly lively — usually of talk.
Literally throwing off sparks or flashes of light; figuratively, brilliantly clever and lively — of conversation, wit, prose, a performance.

It is praise for output, not for a person's looks or character: you have a scintillating hour of talk, a scintillating essay, a scintillating first half. It also implies flash rather than depth — quick, bright, entertaining, not necessarily profound. And it carries the heaviest sarcasm load of any compliment in English: "scintillating" said flatly means the opposite.
⚠️ scintillating ≠ titillating. Scintillating = sparkling with wit. Titillating = teasingly arousing. A dinner guest can be one without being the other.
Scintillating wants one partner: conversation — and half the time it's said with an eye-roll.
Lock in the collocation and you get both the meaning (sparkling talk) and the tone (mock praise for talk that sparkles not at all).
1. Her scintillating account of the Congress of Vienna kept a lecture hall awake at nine in the morning.
2. Two hours of him explaining his fantasy football team. Scintillating.
Astronomers call the twinkling of stars scintillation — the atmosphere making a steady point of light flicker. Same word, doing its literal job.
Latin scintilla = "a spark." English kept the noun whole: a scintilla of evidence is one spark of it — the standard courtroom phrase is "not a scintilla."

The same spark reached us twice through French: tinsel (estincelle, sparkle) and stencil (originally, to spangle with bright colour).

Open contempt — and the flat rejection that comes with it.
Noun: open contempt — the feeling that something or someone is beneath consideration, and the show of it.
Verb: to treat with that contempt; also, to reject something flatly as unworthy ("she scorned the offer").

Contempt can sit silently behind a polite face, and disdain is cool and aloof — a raised eyebrow, a turned shoulder. Scorn is the loud one: it curls the lip, it speaks. You pour scorn, heap scorn, laugh someone to scorn. And its second sense adds a refusal — to scorn help isn't merely to despise it, it's to push it away.
Scorn scorches — disdain is cold, scorn burns.
The near-rhyme fixes the temperature: this is contempt that comes out hot and audible, not the chilly silence of disdain.
1. The pamphlet was met with scorn by the very clergymen it hoped to persuade.
2. He scorned the umbrella, walked out, and came back looking like a drowned cat.
"Hell hath no fury like a woman scorned" — the most-quoted line in English about being rejected with contempt (Congreve's original: "nor hell a fury like a woman scorned").

Painstakingly careful to do what is morally right.
Taking great care to do what is right — honest, principled, refusing the shortcut even when nobody would notice. By extension, painstakingly exact in carrying something out.

The moral sense is the core one. Meticulous and thorough describe a standard of workmanship; scrupulous describes a conscience. A meticulous accountant gets the columns to balance; a scrupulous accountant won't fudge them. When it does mean "exact" — scrupulous attention to detail — it still carries a whiff of duty, of care owed rather than care taken.
⚠️ scrupulous ≠ scurrilous.
- scrupulous = morally careful (high praise)
- scurrilous = grossly abusive, slanderous (a scurrilous rumour)

Near-identical shape, opposite moral verdict.
You meet unscrupulous far more often than scrupulous — and never about a tidy desk.
The common negative is always an accusation of dishonesty, which fixes the positive as moral care rather than mere neatness.
1. The committee's report was scrupulous in acknowledging every dissenting voice, even those it went on to reject.
2. He's annoyingly scrupulous about splitting the bill — he'll work out who had the extra coffee.
Consumer-protection boilerplate runs on the negative: warnings about unscrupulous lenders, landlords, and brokers — the word regulators reach for when they mean "will cheat you and sleep fine."
Latin scrūpulus = a small sharp pebble — the kind in your shoe. From there it became the nagging little thing you can't ignore: a scruple, a prick of conscience.

So a scrupulous person is one who feels the pebble — who can't walk on past the small wrong. That also gives scruple, unscrupulous, scrupulosity.

column2:
Diligent and painstaking; steadily persistent at a task.
Diligent in a steady, painstaking, keep-at-it way — persistent care applied over time.

The word praises stamina and attention to detail, not brilliance or speed. A sedulous researcher checks every footnote; a sedulous student grinds through the list nightly. It's bookish and slightly old-fashioned, so it carries a whiff of the patient plodder — nearly a synonym for assiduous, but where industrious suggests energy and output, sedulous suggests unhurried thoroughness.
⚠️ sedulous ≠ sedentary. They look like relatives and mean near-opposites: sedentary = sitting around, barely moving; sedulous = working away without letting up. Unrelated roots.
SEJ-uu-luhs — the same sound that sits inside schedule (SKEJ-uul): the sedulous one just works the schedule, day after day.
It's not flair, it's turning up and doing the hours.
1. Decades of sedulous cataloguing by a single curator turned a shed of loose papers into a national archive.
2. She's not the smartest in the class, but she's sedulous — three hours a night, every night, no exceptions.
Robert Louis Stevenson said he learned to write by "playing the sedulous ape" — patiently copying Hazlitt, Lamb and the rest until the style stuck. The phrase survives as the standard tag for painstaking imitation.
Latin sēdulus = "sincere, diligent," from sē dolō — "without guile." Honest work, no shortcuts: the sense travelled from not cheating to taking real pains.

🚫 Not from sedēre, "to sit" — that root gives sedentary, sediment, session, reside. Sedulous only looks like it belongs to that family.

Giving in freely to your own comforts and whims.
Giving free rein to your own appetites, comforts and whims — food, spending, moods, time — without restraint.

Note the direction the word points. An indulgent parent is soft on someone else; self-indulgent turns that leniency inward, and the moment it does, it becomes a criticism. It's a mild one, though: it accuses you of weakness, not wickedness. A self-indulgent person is undisciplined, not evil.

Its sharpest use on the GRE is about art. A self-indulgent novel, film or solo is one made to please its maker rather than its audience — the director who wouldn't cut his own footage, the guitarist who won't stop soloing. Read it there as unedited, unrestrained, uninterested in you.
"Indulge me" is asking someone else for the favour — self-indulgent is granting it to yourself and never asking.
The prefix marks exactly what's missing: an outside party whose patience or judgement had to be consulted first.
1. Critics dismissed the three-hour director's cut as self-indulgent — every darling that should have been killed was lovingly preserved.
2. I spent the whole Sunday in bed with cake and old films, which was self-indulgent and I'd do it again.
Dessert advertising runs on this root: "indulgent" chocolate, ice cream sold as pure indulgence — the word is a selling point right up until you attach self- to it, and then it's an insult.

Hyped to shock or thrill, often at truth's expense.
Two senses, and the GRE only cares about one of them.

Everyday: outstandingly good — "a sensational performance."

Exam sense: designed to produce a shock, a thrill, a gasp — usually at the cost of accuracy or proportion. A sensational account of a crime plays up the gore; sensationalism is the charge levelled at coverage that inflames rather than informs.

The word points at the effect on the audience, not the truth of the thing. That's why it can flip from compliment to insult with no change of form: call a singer sensational and you're praising her; call a newspaper sensational and you're saying it manufactures excitement it hasn't earned. On the GRE, assume the disapproving reading — it almost always sits near words like lurid, tabloid, overwrought.
Sensational aims at the senses, not the brain — built to make you gasp, not to make you think.
The word hides sensation — a jolt you feel — which is exactly the complaint: it works on your nerves instead of your judgement.
1. The inquiry criticised the paper's sensational treatment of the disappearance, which had converted a family's grief into three weeks of front pages.
2. Don't get your facts from that channel — it's sensational rubbish dressed up as news.
Any headline built as "You won't BELIEVE what happened next" — clickbait is sensationalism with a share button.
Latin sentīre = "to feel, to perceive." One root, a large family: sense, sensory, sentient, sentiment, consent (feel together), dissent (feel apart), resent (feel it back), even scent.

So sensational literally means "of the feelings" — content aimed at the nerve endings.

Awash in tender feeling, often more than the thing deserves.
Governed by tender feeling — nostalgia, affection, pity — rather than by reason; or indulging that feeling beyond what the occasion warrants.

Two temperatures. Said of a person keeping their grandmother's chipped teacup, it's warm and harmless. Said of a novel, a film, or an argument, it's a put-down: the emotion has been laid on thicker than the subject can bear, and the writer is enjoying the feeling rather than earning it. That critical edge is why the GRE likes it — sentimental prose is cheap prose. Note also that a sentimental person is not simply an emotional one: rage and terror are emotions, but nobody calls them sentimental. The word covers only the soft, sweet, backward-looking end of the range.
⚠️ sentimental ≠ sententious.
- sentimental = soppy, awash in feeling
- sententious = preachy, dishing out pompous moral maxims

A sentimental eulogy makes you cry; a sententious one lectures you.
Hidden inside it: senti-MENTAL. Sentimental value is value that exists only in your mental picture of the thing — never in the thing.
That gap between the object and the feeling piled onto it is exactly what makes the word a criticism when it's aimed at writing.
1. Critics dismissed the memoir as sentimental — every death arrived on cue, scored for strings.
2. I know it's a cracked mug, but I'm too sentimental to bin it.
The everyday phrase "it has sentimental value" — the standard excuse for keeping something objectively worthless. That's the whole word in three syllables: the worth is in you, not in the object.
Latin sentīre = "to feel." One of the highest-yield roots on the test: sentient (able to feel), sentiment, consent (feel with), dissent (feel apart), resent (feel back at), sensitive, sense.

column2:
Lucky by accident — you found what you weren't looking for.
Happening by a lucky accident — especially when the accident hands you something good that you weren't looking for.

Plain luck isn't enough. A serendipitous event needs a find: a discovery, a meeting, a solution. And it must be unsought — if you were hunting for it, finding it is just success. Penicillin (a contaminated dish) is serendipitous; a lottery win is merely lucky. Tonally the word is warm, a little whimsical, faintly self-congratulatory — it's the word people reach for in wedding speeches and startup origin stories to make a coincidence sound like fate.
⚠️ serendipitous ≠ fortuitous.
- serendipitous = by chance and happily
- fortuitous = by chance, full stop — the outcome can be terrible

A fortuitous collision is still a collision.
Buried in the middle is DIP — you dipped in blind and came up holding treasure.
The dip is unaimed, which is the whole point: the good thing found you, not the other way round.
1. The discovery was entirely serendipitous: a mislabelled sample, left out over a long weekend, yielded the enzyme three years of directed research had missed.
2. We only met because my train was cancelled — pretty serendipitous, honestly.
The 2001 John Cusack film Serendipity — two strangers collide over the same pair of gloves in a department store and spend the movie letting chance decide. The title is the plot.
Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754, from the Persian tale The Three Princes of Serendip — Serendip being the old name for Sri Lanka. Walpole's princes, he wrote, "were always making discoveries, by accidents and sagacity, of things they were not in quest of."

That last clause is the definition: accident plus the wit to notice.

Calm and untroubled — visibly, cloudlessly so.
Calm, clear and untroubled — of a sky, a sea, a face, a temperament.

Other calm-words describe an inner state; serene describes calm that shows. It's the visible, unclouded surface: no ripple, no cloud, nothing agitating the picture. Where placid can hint at dullness and calm is merely the absence of storm, serene is elevated, almost luminous — the word you reach for describing a monk, a lake at dawn, or someone smiling politely while everything around them burns. It's also faintly grand: European princes are still styled Your Serene Highness.
⚠️ serene ≠ sere. Sere (SEER) means dried up, withered — sere grass in August. Same first four letters, opposite mood, and both turn up on the GRE.
Serene rhymes with clean — a sky wiped clean of cloud, a face wiped clean of worry.
The rhyme carries the nuance: serenity is about a surface with nothing on it, which is why the word works equally for weather and for people.
1. Hours after the verdict she remained serene, as though the sentence had been passed on someone else entirely.
2. Everyone else was panicking about the deadline and he just sat there, serene, eating a sandwich.
The Serenity Prayer — \"grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot change\" — recited at every AA meeting and printed on a million fridge magnets.
Latin serēnus = "clear, cloudless" — originally a weather word, only later applied to people. That's why serene still feels like describing a sky.

Same root: serenity, and serenade — music for a clear, calm evening.

🚫 Not serendipity. That comes from Serendip, an old name for Sri Lanka, via a Persian fairy tale. Similar opening, unrelated word.

column2:
To cut off completely; break a connection for good.
To cut off or cut through — a limb, a cable, a rope — and, figuratively, to break a connection completely: ties, relations, links, contact.

The force of the word is finality. You can weaken, strain, or loosen a relationship; when you sever it, there is nothing left joining the two halves. It's also the formal, almost diplomatic verb for the act — countries sever diplomatic relations, a firm severs ties with a client. In the physical sense it carries a wince: a severed artery, a severed cable, clean through.
⚠️ sever ≠ severe. Sever (SEV-er) = to cut off. Severe (suh-VEER) = harsh, extreme. Near-twins on the page, unrelated in root and meaning.
sever ends in ever — what you sever is cut off for ever.
That's the whole nuance: not loosened, not strained — separated permanently.
1. After the memo leaked, the ministry severed all contact with its former ally.
2. He severed the cable with one snip and the whole street went dark.
The Apple TV+ series Severance — employees have their work memories surgically severed from their personal ones. The show is the definition acted out. (Same word behind severance pay: the money that goes with cutting you loose.)
Latin separare = "to separate," worn down through Old French sevrer. The same root gives separate, severance, and — surprisingly — several, which originally meant "separate, distinct" before it drifted into meaning "a few."

A hollow fake with all the trappings of the real thing.
Noun: something passed off as genuine that is hollow inside — a fraud, an imitation.
Adjective: fake but dressed in the trappings of the real thing — a sham trial, a sham marriage.
Verb: to feign — he shammed a limp to get out of drill.

Where fake describes an object and scam describes an operation, sham attacks the legitimacy of a form: it fastens onto ceremonies, institutions, and procedures that go through every correct motion while meaning nothing. A sham election has ballots, observers, a result — and no choice. The word is always a verdict, never a description; calling something a sham is a small act of contempt, and the speaker is claiming to have seen through it.
Sham rhymes with scam — the scam is the con being run, the sham is the hollow thing it hands you.
One letter apart, one step apart: the scam is the act, the sham is the empty object or ritual it produces.
1. The tribunal was a sham: the verdict had been drafted a week before the first witness was called.
2. He shammed a stomach bug all Monday, then posted a photo from the beach by two.
Newsrooms have a fixed phrase for it — "sham election" is the standard wire-copy label for a vote with one plausible candidate and a pre-known result. That collocation alone will carry the word for you.

To dodge a duty you were supposed to carry out.
To avoid or neglect a duty, task, or responsibility — to slide out of something you were obliged to do.

The object is always an obligation. You can dodge a party or duck a phone call, but you can only shirk a duty — so the word carries the accusation with it. Avoid is neutral, evade suggests cunning, but shirk suggests laziness or cowardice: the work still exists, and someone else is now carrying it. It's the standard verb when the failure is moral rather than tactical — "shirk his responsibilities," "never shirked a hard job."
Shirk rhymes with work and hides irk — the work irks you, so you shirk it.
The rhyme fixes the one thing shirking always applies to (work, duty, obligation — never pleasure), and irk supplies the motive.
1. The inquiry found that the board had shirked its duty of oversight for the better part of a decade.
2. He's not ill — he's shirking, and everyone on the late shift knows it.
"Shirking" is the actual technical term in economics and management for employees not pulling their weight — whole models of pay and monitoring are built on stopping workers from shirking.

Sharp practical judgment, especially about people, money, and advantage.
Having sharp practical judgment — quick to size up a person, a deal, or a situation and see where the advantage lies.

It's a compliment with a cold edge. Wise implies moral depth; intelligent implies brainpower; shrewd implies you can't be fooled and you know what things are really worth. It's the intelligence of the marketplace, not the library — which is why shrewd survives being applied to someone you don't especially like. Push it one step further and you get cunning or crafty, where the self-interest stops being tasteful.
shrewd ≠ shrewish. Same root, opposite compliment: shrewd = astute; shrewish = nagging and ill-tempered.
You can be a shrewd investor, negotiator, or judge of character — never a shrewd saint.
The word lives wherever money and motive are, and it praises your eye for advantage rather than your goodness.
1. Her decision to buy the land before the rail line was announced proved shrewd: its value tripled within two years.
2. He's not the smartest guy in the room, but he's shrewd — he always knows who's bluffing.
Football pundits reach for it constantly: a low-fee signing who turns out brilliant is always called "a shrewd piece of business." Same instinct in the business press, where Warren Buffett is a shrewd investor rather than a wise one.
From Middle English shrewe = "a wicked, malicious person" (and the small sharp-nosed animal, believed venomous and spiteful). Shrewd first meant "dangerous, wicked," then drifted through "cunning" to today's "astute."

That history is exactly why the word still has a faint chill in it — the praise was originally an insult, and never fully lost the edge.

Piercingly high-pitched; or grating and over-insistent in tone.
Literally: high-pitched and piercing to the point of pain — a whistle, a smoke alarm, a scream.

Figuratively (the GRE sense): of a voice, a critic, or a campaign — loud, insistent and grating, harping on one note until people stop listening.

No one is ever shrill in a good way. And the figurative use is a rhetorical weapon: to call an argument shrill is to refuse to engage with it, attacking the pitch of the complaint rather than its substance. The word says more about the listener's irritation than the speaker's logic — which is why it's so often aimed at women and at activists.
Shr-ILL — the noise makes you ill.
The word ends in ill because the complaint is never that the sound is loud, but that it hurts to hear.
1. The debate degenerated as the panel's objections grew shrill, each speaker pitching louder rather than better.
2. Her alarm went off with a shrill beep that could wake the dead.
Lindy West titled her memoir Shrill (later a Hulu series with Aidy Bryant) precisely because it's the insult thrown at women who won't quieten down — she took the slur and put it on the cover.

A job that pays well and requires almost no work.
A position that carries pay, title or status but almost no actual duties.

The scorn falls on the post, not the person — a sinecure is a job that has been hollowed out, usually because someone was rewarding a friend, a donor, or a retiring grandee. You can hold one and still be industrious; there is simply nothing to do. That's what separates it from idleness or a soft job: the emptiness is built into the office. The word is dry and faintly damning, the vocabulary of political journalism and board minutes rather than complaint.
⚠️ sinecure ≠ cynosure. A sinecure is a cushy no-work job; a cynosure (SY-nuh-shoor) is the centre of attention, the thing all eyes turn to. Both are obscure, both start with a sy- sound — the GRE knows it.
Sign here, collect the cheque, cure nothing.
The holder isn't accused of shirking — the post itself was created with no work attached to it.
1. The ambassadorship to a friendly island nation had long served as a sinecure for donors who had given generously and expected something framed on the wall.
2. Head of "Strategic Vision"? That's a sinecure — he shows up for the Christmas party and that's it.
Latin sine cura = "without care." It began as a church term: a benefice sine cura animarum — a paid living without the cure (care) of souls, i.e. a parish priest's salary with no parish to look after.

Cura is a workhorse root: curate and curator (one who takes care of), manicure (care of the hands), accurate (done with care), procure, and secure — se- "free from" + cura, literally without care too. And sine returns in sine qua non, "without which, not."

Winding, curving, snake-like — and usually gracefully so.
Full of curves; winding, undulating, snake-like in motion or shape.

Two flavours, both curved. Of things: a river, a road, a coastline that bends repeatedly. Of movement: a dancer, a cat, a melody line that flows without a break. Either way the word admires — sinuous curves are elegant, supple, unhurried. Compare tortuous, which is the same twisting seen as an ordeal (a tortuous mountain pass, a tortuous argument). A sinuous path is a pleasure to follow; a tortuous one is a trial. There is a faint serpent under the word too, so it can shade into sly or seductive depending on what's doing the curving.
⚠️ sinuous ≠ sinewy.
- sinuous = curving, winding
- sinewy = lean and stringy with muscle; tough (from sinew, tendon)

A sinuous dancer flows. A sinewy farmhand could lift your car.
Sinuous is an S. Tortuous is a knot.
Both twist, but the S is a graceful line you'd trace with a finger, while the knot is the twisting you curse at.
1. The road climbed in sinuous loops, each bend opening onto the same valley from a slightly higher angle.
2. She had this sinuous way of moving through a crowded bar without ever touching anyone.
Latin sinus = "a curve, a fold, a bay."

That one root pays out repeatedly: your sinuses (curved hollows in the skull), insinuate (literally to worm your way in along a curve — which is why insinuating is never straightforward), and the sine curve in maths, which got its name through a chain of mistranslations but keeps the shape.

To go around the edge of; to evade by never confronting
Verb: to lie along the edge of something (the road skirts the lake), to pass around it rather than through it, or — the GRE sense — to avoid a subject or a rule by going around it: skirt the issue, skirt the law.

Skirting is evasion that never looks like refusal. You don't deny the question, you don't break the rule — you stay adjacent to it and keep moving. That's the difference from flout (open defiance) and from lie (direct falsehood): someone who skirts the law obeys every letter of it while defeating its point, and a politician who skirts a question answers at length without ever touching it. There's also a live sense of dangerous proximity — skirting bankruptcy, skirting the edge of legality — where the word means "close enough to be worrying."
⚠️ skirt ≠ shirk.
- skirt = go around it (an issue, a rule)
- shirk = dodge the work you owe (a duty, a shift)

You skirt the question; you shirk your responsibilities.
A skirt hangs round the outside and never touches the middle.
That's exactly what the verb does — circle the edge of the thing, never make contact with the centre.
1. The treaty's drafters skirted the question of sovereignty entirely, burying it under two hundred pages of trade schedules.
2. Stop skirting it — did you tell her or not?
Skirting board — the strip of wood running along the bottom edge of a wall, and the outskirts of a town, its outer rim. Both are the same idea in plain sight: skirt = the border of a thing.
Old Norse skyrta, "shirt" — skirt and shirt are the same word, split in two. The garment sense narrowed to the lower, hanging part, i.e. the hem, and from "hem" came the general meaning border, edge — which is where the verb lives.

Nervously jumpy; liable to shy or bolt at nothing.
Easily startled; nervously excitable and liable to shy away or bolt. Said first of horses, then of people, then of markets.

Timid describes a settled disposition; skittish describes a hair trigger — the animal was fine a second ago, then a plastic bag moved. The word carries the sense that the reaction was out of proportion to the threat, so calling someone skittish quietly implies they're being unreasonable: an investor skittish about a stock isn't reasoning, he's flinching. It also shades into unwilling to commit — skittish about marriage, about signing, about going back in the water. Mildly belittling, never dignified.
Skittish = skitter-ish. A skittish creature doesn't run — it skitters, sideways, away from nothing.
The skitter is the tell: motion that's jumpy and unnecessary rather than a considered escape.
1. The mare grew skittish as the storm gathered, refusing the gate she had walked through a hundred times.
2. He's been skittish about dating ever since the last one ended — one text and he's out.
Financial news runs on this word: "markets were skittish ahead of the Fed decision." It's the standard way of saying investors are selling on nerves rather than news.
