column2:
Sneaky underhanded scheming — shady, but faintly comic
Underhanded, sneaky behaviour — trickery, scheming, dishonest dealing done out of sight.

Tone does the work here. Fraud and malfeasance belong in an indictment; skullduggery belongs in a newspaper column, and it half-winks while it accuses. It suggests backroom deals, rigged committees and quiet double-crossing rather than violence or grand evil — serious enough to condemn, small and colourful enough to enjoy. Because it sounds faintly comic, it's also the word people reach for when they suspect wrongdoing but can't prove it.
Skull-DUG-gery: somebody's been digging where they shouldn't — under the table, behind your back.
The buried "dug" gives you the secrecy, and the clownish bounce of the word gives you the register — shady scheming, not atrocity.
1. The inquiry uncovered a decade of quiet skullduggery in the awarding of state contracts.
2. There's no way he won that raffle three years running — that's skullduggery if I ever saw it.
Derek Landy's bestselling Skulduggery Pleasant series — a wisecracking skeleton detective. The title is a pun on skull, not the real origin, but it does lock the spelling in.
🚫 Nothing to do with skulls. No graverobbing, no bones. It's an altered form of Scots sculduddery, meaning obscenity or lewdness — origin otherwise unknown. English mangled the spelling toward skull, and the false image has stuck ever since.

A spoken lie that damages someone's reputation.
Noun: a false spoken statement that damages someone's reputation. Verb: to make such a statement about someone.

Three things have to be true for slander, and the GRE tests all three: the claim is spoken (not written), false (not just unkind), and presented as fact (not opinion). Calling your boss an idiot is an insult; saying he embezzled money is slander. That factual pretence is what gives the word its legal teeth — badmouth and trash-talk are social, slander is actionable, the kind of thing a lawyer's letter follows.
⚠️ slander ≠ libel. Same crime, different medium: slander is spoken, libel is written or published. A rumour whispered at a party is slander; the same rumour tweeted is libel.
Slander is Spoken; Libel is Letters.
The initial letter tells you the medium, which is the only thing separating the two words.
1. The former minister sued for slander, alleging that the remarks made on air had cost him his seat on the board.
2. Don't go slandering him at the pub — you don't actually know he took the money.
Online, "that's slander" has become a stock joke reply to any unflattering claim about you — mock-legal outrage over something trivially small.
Latin scandalum = "a stumbling block, a trap" (from Greek skandalon). It came into English through Old French esclandre, where the -nd- wobbled into an l.

So slander and scandal are literally the same word, split in two: the scandal is the disgrace, the slander is the lie that manufactures it.

Small in degree; or to snub by treating as unimportant.
Adj.: small in amount or importance — a slight delay, a slight fever; also slender of build.
Verb: to snub someone by treating them as unimportant. Noun: the snub itself.

The GRE cares about the verb. A slight is an insult delivered by underrating, not by attacking — you slight someone by leaving them off the list, skipping their name in the credits, greeting everyone in the room but them. Nobody raises their voice; the wound is that you weren't worth the effort. And because the offence is by definition small, the word quietly puts the injured party on trial too: he never forgot the slight tells you as much about him as about the man who snubbed him.
⚠️ slight ≠ sleight. Sleight means cunning dexterity and survives in exactly one phrase — sleight of hand. Same sound, different word: the magician has sleight, the snubbed guest nurses a slight.
Slight hides light — to slight someone is to make light of them.
Both senses fall out of that: light in weight (a slight fever) and lightly regarded (a slight to your host).
1. The ambassador read the omission of his title as a deliberate slight, and left the reception before dinner was served.
2. Don't take it personally — she wasn't slighting you, she genuinely didn't see you standing there.
All of Pride and Prejudice is set in motion by a slight: Darcy declines to dance with Elizabeth at the Meryton ball, and she spends the next three hundred pages not forgiving him for it.

Untidy and careless — in dress, habits, or work.
Untidy and careless — in dress, in habits, or in work. A slovenly room, a slovenly clerk, slovenly reasoning.

Messy describes a state; slovenly delivers a verdict. It says the disorder is habitual and the person can't be bothered — grubby collar, unwashed dishes, corners cut. The word also carries the speaker's disdain, which is why it lands as an insult and almost never as self-description. Note the reach beyond appearance: careless thinking and slapdash prose get called slovenly too.
sl- is English's disgust cluster: slime, slop, sludge, slouch, slob — slovenly is the person.
If a word starts with sl- it's usually something you'd rather not touch, and slovenly is that judgment aimed at someone's habits.
1. The inspector's report condemned the ward's slovenly record-keeping: undated charts, missing signatures, notes scrawled in three different hands.
2. He turned up to the interview in a slovenly state — creased shirt, yesterday's stubble — and wondered why he didn't get the job.
Orwell, Politics and the English Language: "our thoughts are foolish, but the slovenliness of our language makes it easier for us to have foolish thoughts." Proof the word attacks sloppy thinking, not just sloppy shirts.

Slow and low on energy, in a way that signals trouble.
Moving, working, or reacting more slowly than it should — and lacking energy while it does.

Slowness on its own is neutral; sluggish is slowness read as a symptom. A sluggish engine needs servicing, a sluggish market worries investors, a sluggish student worries a teacher. Nobody chooses to be sluggish, and nothing desirable is ever described that way — the word quietly diagnoses a fault, whether that's fatigue, congestion, or underperformance. It's mild, everyday criticism rather than contempt: closer to underpowered than to lazy.
A slow Sunday sounds lovely. A sluggish Sunday sounds like you're coming down with something.
Swap the words in any sentence and sluggish always adds the sense that something is wrong.
1. Trade across the region remained sluggish for a third consecutive quarter, defying every forecast of recovery.
2. My laptop's been so sluggish since the update that I've started making tea while it boots.
Business news runs on this word — "sluggish growth," "sluggish demand," "a sluggish start to the quarter." It's the standard polite way to say bad, but not yet a crisis.
From slug, which in Middle English (slugge) meant a lazy person — the slimy garden mollusc was named after the insult, not the other way round. Same root gives you sluggard, an old word for a habitual idler.

Not drunk; clear-eyed, serious, restrained, free of excess.
1. Not drunk. 2. Serious, restrained, and clear-headed — free of excitement, exaggeration, or excess. 3. Of colours or clothes: plain, quiet, undecorated. Verb: sober (up) — to make or become serious or clear-headed.

On the GRE it's almost always sense 2, and it's usually approving: a sober assessment is one you can trust because nobody is hyping it. Sober isn't sad and it isn't dull — it's unintoxicated in the broad sense, judgment unclouded by drink, hope, or panic. When something is described as sobering, it has jolted you out of comfortable optimism.
⚠️ sober ≠ somber. Sober = serious and clear-eyed; somber (sombre) = gloomy, dark, funereal. A sober analysis is useful; a somber mood is miserable.
Sober strips something away — the drink, the decoration, or the drama.
A sober man has lost the drink, a sober grey suit has lost the decoration, and a sober forecast has lost the drama.
1. After a decade of triumphalist forecasts, the committee delivered a sober account of what the project would actually cost.
2. Give it a night — you'll feel differently about quitting once you're sober and it's Monday.
News writing runs on the figurative sense: "a sobering reminder," "sobering new figures" — the standard way a headline says stop feeling optimistic.
Latin sōbrius = sē- ("without") + ēbrius ("drunk"). That second half is the payoff: ēbrius gives you inebriated — so sober is literally un-inebriated, and sobriety is the state of it.

A speech spoken alone on stage, thoughts voiced to no one.
A speech in which a character, alone, speaks their thoughts aloud — to themselves and to the audience, not to anyone in the scene. By extension, any extended bout of talking to oneself.

The defining condition is no listener. A monologue is aimed at people: a stand-up set, a villain's gloat, a rant at a dinner table. A soliloquy is private thought that happens to be audible — which is why it reads as sincere; there's no one to perform for, so no reason to lie. Almost always a theatre or literary word; calling your flatmate's kitchen mutterings a soliloquy is a deliberate joke.
Solo is hiding in the front of it — a soliloquy is a solo, and a solo has nobody else on stage.
The moment another character is being addressed, it stops being a soliloquy and becomes a monologue.
1. Iago's soliloquies are the only place in the play where he tells the truth, because they are the only place he has no one to deceive.
2. He wandered off into a ten-minute soliloquy about his fantasy team while the rest of us ate in silence.
"To be, or not to be" — Hamlet, alone on stage, arguing with himself about whether to go on living. The most famous soliloquy in English, and a perfect specimen: nobody is listening, so nothing is being sold.
Latin sōlus (alone) + loquī (to speak).

loquī is a GRE goldmine: loquacious (talkative), eloquent (well-spoken), colloquial (conversational), grandiloquent (pompously grand), circumlocution (talking around a point), ventriloquist (one who "speaks from the belly"), obloquy (speech against someone — public disgrace).

Drowsy, or making you drowsy.
Drowsy, half-asleep — or making you that way. It runs both directions: a somnolent student and the somnolent lecture that produced him.

Register is literary and atmospheric rather than clinical. Sleepy is a plain fact; somnolent is a mood laid over a whole scene — a hot afternoon, a dozing village, a courtroom after lunch. It also goes figurative for things that ought to be active but aren't: a somnolent market, a somnolent regulator. Milder and more pleasant than torpid or lethargic, which carry a whiff of failure; somnolent just carries heavy eyelids.
SOM-nuh-luhnt — the word yawns: one stressed syllable, then two that mumble off into sleep.
Say it aloud and the trailing "-nuh-luhnt" does the drowsiness for you, which is exactly the slow, heavy-lidded mood the word describes.
1. By three o'clock the courtroom had turned somnolent, the clerk's pen slowing to a crawl as counsel read the schedules aloud.
2. That documentary was so somnolent I was out cold before the opening credits finished.
Latin somnus = "sleep" — the Roman god Somnus himself. The root is everywhere once you see it: insomnia (in- = not, so: no sleep), somnambulist (sleep + ambulare, "to walk" — a sleepwalker), somniferous (sleep-bearing).

So somnolent is simply "full of sleep" — and if you know insomnia, you already knew the root.

Worldly and refined, or elaborately complex — never simple.
Two live senses. Of people and taste: worldly, cultivated, alert to fine distinctions — someone who has been around enough to stop being impressed easily. Of things: highly complex and advanced — a sophisticated algorithm, a sophisticated attack, sophisticated instrumentation.

The link between the two is loss of simplicity. Sophistication is never innate; it's acquired, layered on, worked up. That's why the word carries a faint chill — a sophisticated friend is more knowing than a charming one, and sophisticated machinery is admired for its intricacy, not its elegance. Praise the naturalness of something and you'd never reach for this word.
⚠️ sophisticated ≠ sophistic (also sophistical). Sophistic reasoning is subtle in the bad way — clever, plausible, and fallacious. A sophisticated argument is impressive; a sophistic one is a trick.
The opposite of sophisticated isn't cheap — it's naive.
Fix that antonym and both senses follow: a sophisticated person has lost their innocence, and a sophisticated system has lost its simplicity.
1. Her prose is sophisticated to the point of coldness — every effect calculated, nothing left to accident.
2. It wasn't some kid guessing passwords; this was a sophisticated attack, months in the planning.
Every security breach report you've ever skimmed calls the hack "sophisticated" — which tells you the word means elaborate and advanced, not classy. Nobody thinks the malware had good taste.
Greek sophos = "wise" → sophistēs, the sophist: a paid teacher of rhetoric whom Plato painted as a peddler of clever nonsense. Latin sophisticatus then meant "adulterated" — wine sophisticated with water was wine tampered with, not wine improved. That tampering sense is the ancestor of today's "not simple, not natural."

The root pays out widely: philosophy (philo- love + sophos wise), sophist, sophistry (plausible false reasoning), and sophomore — literally sophos + mōros (fool), the wise fool, which is exactly why sophomoric means juvenile pseudo-cleverness.

Clever-sounding argument built to deceive.
Reasoning that looks valid and isn't — clever, plausible, elegantly constructed argument used to mislead rather than to find the truth.

A fallacy can be an honest mistake; sophistry is a charge of bad faith. It accuses you of knowing better and arguing anyway, and of enjoying your own cleverness while you do it. That's why it stings: it says the polish is the trick. Reserve it for arguments that are too well-made to be innocent — the tobacco lawyer, the ideologue, the politician who never once misspeaks.
Sophistry wears sophisticated clothes — a lie in a good suit.
Both come from Greek sophos, "wise," and the whole point of sophistry is that it sounds far too smart to be dishonest.
1. The defence rested on pure sophistry: a chain of impeccable inferences from a premise no one had agreed to.
2. Don't give me that sophistry — you said you'd be home by eight and it's midnight.
Greek sophos = "wise." The Sophists were paid teachers in 5th-century Athens who trained ambitious young men to win any argument, either side, for a fee. Plato loathed them, and his contempt stuck to the word for 2,400 years — which is why sophistry still means "rhetoric for hire" rather than "wisdom."

Same root, and the shifts are worth knowing: philosophy (love of wisdom), sophomore (sophos + moros, fool — a "wise fool"), and sophisticated, which originally meant adulterated, tampered with.

Sleep-inducing; a genteel word for crushingly dull.
Adj.: sleep-inducing, drowsy-making. Noun: a drug that puts you to sleep.

Two lives in one word. In medicine it's flat and technical — a soporific is a sedative, no judgement attached. Everywhere else it's a polite weapon: calling a lecture, a novel, or a minister's speech soporific is a dry, faintly amused way of saying it was unbearably dull, without ever stooping to the word "boring." Register is bookish and a little arch, which is exactly why it stings.
So poor a speech, it's terrific at knocking you out.
The sound of the word hands you both halves — so-por-ific — and the sarcasm of "terrific" matches the word's genteel-insult tone.
1. The court's judgment, some four hundred pages of procedural history, had a soporific effect on all but the most dutiful reader.
2. Two chapters of that thing and I was gone — genuinely soporific, better than melatonin.
Beatrix Potter, The Tale of the Flopsy Bunnies: "It is said that the effect of eating too much lettuce is soporific." The rabbits promptly fall asleep in the grass — the word's most famous outing, and in a children's book.
Latin sopor = "deep sleep" + -ficus (facere, "to make") — literally sleep-making.

The -fic half is the reusable part: terrific (fear-making), horrific, prolific, beneficent, soporific. Spot -fic and you're looking at a word that makes something.

Dirty and morally grubby — sleazy, squalid, driven by low motives.
Two linked senses: physically filthy and squalid (a sordid basement flat), and — far more common on the GRE — morally grubby: sleazy, ignoble, driven by low motives.

The word's real charge is cheapness. A sordid act isn't grand or dramatic evil; it's small, self-serving and a bit embarrassing — money, lust, spite, a petty betrayal. Calling a scandal sordid says the people in it were shabby, not terrifying. It also carries a whiff of exposure: details become "sordid" the moment they're dragged into daylight. Where squalid leans on physical filth, sordid leads with the moral kind and only sometimes means actual dirt.
sor-DID — the sordid part is never the crime, it's what he did it for.
The word hides did, and it's the motive behind the deed — money, lust, spite — that earns the label.
1. The biography declines to linger on the poet's finances, treating that sordid business as beneath its subject.
2. Spare me the sordid details of your breakup, I'm eating.
Court and tabloid reporting runs on two fixed phrases: "a sordid affair" and "all the sordid details." If you've read a scandal write-up, you've read this word.
Latin sordēs = "filth, dirt" → sordidus, which meant both dirty and stingy, mean, shabby. That second Latin sense is the one English kept underneath the surface — why sordid implies a cheap motive, not just a dirty one.

column2:
Free from flaw — solid and valid rather than brilliant.
Adj.: free from defect, damage or error — whole, healthy, structurally solid. A sound building, a sound argument, a sound night's sleep, of sound mind.

Verb (the GRE's other trick): to measure the depth of water — and by extension to probe cautiously. You sound out a colleague before proposing something; you sound the depths of a problem.

The praise in sound is deliberately unglamorous. Calling a plan sound is not calling it brilliant, imaginative or bold — it's saying you have looked for the crack and there isn't one. It's the verdict of an engineer or an auditor, not an admirer: reliability, not flair. Hence the sting hidden in "a sound, if unexciting, choice." The negative, unsound, is much harsher than it looks — unsound reasoning means broken at the foundation, and of unsound mind is a legal finding of incapacity.
Sound sleep, sound mind, sound argument — the word never means good, it means nothing in it is broken.
Run the collocations and you can hear that sound is always certifying an absence of flaws rather than a presence of merit.
1. The auditors found the firm's accounting sound, though its strategy struck them as timid.
2. That's sound advice — boring, but he's never once been wrong about this stuff.
Taylor Swift's "Safe & Sound" (from The Hunger Games) — sound there isn't noise, it's the old meaning: unharmed, whole, nothing broken.
Old English gesund = "healthy, uninjured" — the same word as German gesund, which is why you say Gesundheit! when someone sneezes: health to you. Nothing to do with noise.

🚫 Three unrelated "sounds." Sound (noise) is Latin sonus (sonic, sonorous, resonate). Sound (to measure depth) is Latin sub + unda, "under the wave" (sounding, sound out). Sound (a channel of water, Puget Sound) is Norse sund. Only the healthy one is gesund.

Thinly scattered; few, with gaps between.
Thinly scattered over an area; few and far between — sparse hair, a sparse crowd, sparse vegetation, sparse notes.

The key idea is distribution, not absence. Sparse things are there; they're just spread thin, with gaps between them. That's why it pairs so naturally with space and surfaces (sparsely populated, sparse coverage) and why it's the neutral, almost measuring word — a scientist calls data sparse without complaining about it, whereas meagre or paltry would be a judgement.
⚠️ sparse ≠ scarce.
- sparse = thinly spread out (a sparse audience — plenty of empty seats between people)
- scarce = in short supply (tickets were scarce — hard to get any at all)

Water can be scarce in a region; the villages there are sparse.
SPARSE = SPARE + S — what's there is spare, spaced out, with room to spare between.
Hearing spare inside it keeps you on the right idea: not gone, just stretched thin across the gaps.
1. The plateau supports only sparse scrub, its shrubs standing metres apart on bare rock.
2. His notes for the meeting were pretty sparse — three bullet points and a question mark.
In tech it's everywhere: a sparse matrix is one that's mostly zeros, with the few real values scattered thinly through it — same word, same picture, just in numbers.
Latin spargere = "to scatter, sprinkle." Sparse things have been sprinkled, not poured.

Same root: disperse (scatter apart), intersperse (scatter among), and aspersion — to cast aspersions is literally to sprinkle dirt on someone's name.

column2:
Bare and comfortless — austerity by discipline, not by accident.
Bare, plain, without comfort or ornament — and, of a person or regime, marked by hardiness and strict self-denial.

The key is chosen deprivation. Meagre and destitute mean you had no choice; spartan implies discipline behind the bareness — a soldier's bunk, a training camp, a monk's cell, a designer's stripped-back room. It can be quiet praise (tough, unfussy) or a dry complaint (there was nothing to eat and one thin blanket), and the same sentence often carries both.
Spartan = spare — spare by choice, not by poverty.
The first syllable hands you spare, and the Spartan soldier behind the word supplies the missing half: the bareness is a discipline, not a misfortune.
1. The retreat's accommodation was deliberately spartan: a cot, a washbasin, and a single high window.
2. Her fridge is spartan — mustard, half a lemon, and a very old soy sauce.
The film 300 — the Spartans who fight in nothing but a cloak and a shield are the literal source of the adjective. Same idea sells the Spartan Race: mud, no comfort, on purpose.
From Sparta, the Greek city-state that raised its boys in barracks on stolen food and black broth. The word is an eponym doing exactly what it says.

Bonus GRE word from the same place: Sparta sat in the region of Laconia, and the Spartans' famously clipped speech gives us laconic — using very few words. (Asked to surrender, they reportedly replied: "If.")

column2:
Looks like sound reasoning; isn't.
Superficially convincing but actually false — an argument, claim, or excuse that passes a quick look and collapses under a second one.

The word is aimed almost always at reasoning, not at objects or people. And it carries a specific insult: the thing is dressed up. A liar is crude; a specious argument is well-tailored — plausible structure, respectable vocabulary, rotten logic. Calling something specious says you inspected it and found the shine was the whole product.
specious ≠ spurious.
- specious = sounds right, reasoning is bad
- spurious = isn't genuine, origin is fake

A specious argument is really an argument, just a bad one. A spurious quotation was never said at all.
Specious is one letter off spacious — a spacious argument: impressive room, nothing in it.
Both words promise something grand on first look, and the specious one turns out to be empty inside.
1. The defence rested on a specious distinction between advising a crime and ordering one — the jury saw through it in an hour.
2. He gave me some specious line about the traffic, which would've worked if I hadn't watched him leave the pub.
Latin speciōsus = "good-looking, showy," from species (appearance) ← specere, "to look at." The word originally meant handsome — and then slid, as flattering words do, into only handsome.

That root is a GRE goldmine: species, specimen, spectacle, inspect, conspicuous, perspective, suspicion — all about looking. Specious is the one where looking is all you get.

Theorize without hard evidence; also, bet money on risk.
1. To form a theory or opinion without firm evidence — to reason toward a conclusion you can't prove.
2. To buy something risky (stock, land, crypto) hoping the price moves your way.

Both senses share one thing: you're acting on a view, not on facts. Speculate sits above guess — it implies actual reasoning, which is why analysts and historians do it respectably — but below infer or deduce, which claim real evidence behind them. It also carries a built-in disclaimer, which is why "I won't speculate" is the standard press-conference dodge: saying it out loud admits you don't know.

In money, the contrast is sharp: an investor analyses a business and holds; a speculator bets on the price and flips. Calling someone a speculator is rarely a compliment.
Built on spec = built with no buyer lined up. Speculate = act on the spec, not the fact.
Whether the spec is a hunch about a murder or a hunch about a stock, you're committing to a view you can't yet verify.
1. Historians still speculate about why the settlement was abandoned; the excavation has yielded no answer.
2. Don't ask me — I'm not going to speculate on why they broke up.
The Big Short is two hours of speculation in the money sense — a handful of outsiders betting against the housing market on a view nobody else held.
Latin specula = "watchtower," from specere = "to look." To speculate is to scan the horizon from a height — you can see something out there, but you can't go down and check it.

That root is a GRE goldmine: spectacle, inspect, prospect, conspicuous, specimen, suspect, spectrum — and circumspect, literally "looking around," hence cautious.

Someone who spends money wastefully and extravagantly.
A person who spends money extravagantly and wastefully — and, as an adjective, the habit itself (spendthrift ways, spendthrift heir).

The disapproval is about squandering, not about amount. A billionaire buying a jet isn't a spendthrift; an heir burning through an inheritance he can never rebuild is. The word carries the sense of a finite pot being drained — which is why it clings to inheritances, trust funds, and lottery winners. Tone is faintly old-fashioned and more exasperated than damning: a raised eyebrow, not a moral charge.
A spendthrift spends the thrift — the savings are the thing being burned.
The word looks like it should mean "frugal", but thrift here is the object of the spending, not the manner of it — so it means the exact opposite of thrifty.
1. The estate passed to a spendthrift nephew who had sold off the last of the paintings before the year was out.
2. One bonus and he turns into a total spendthrift — new speakers, new bike, rent still unpaid.
Spendthrift trust is a live term in estate law: money left to someone whose relatives assume they can't be trusted with a lump sum, so the trust pays it out in a controlled drip and creditors can't touch it. If a lawyer says it about you, it isn't a compliment.
Thrift originally meant "thriving, prosperity, accumulated savings" — it's the noun of thrive. So a spendthrift is literally one who spends his thriving.

Only later did thrift narrow into "frugality" (the habit that produces the savings), which is what makes the word look self-contradictory today. Same root: thrive, thrifty, thrift shop.

Occurring irregularly and unpredictably, in scattered bursts.
Happening at irregular, scattered intervals — now and then, here and there, with no pattern you could predict from.

The key isn't rarity, it's irregularity. Periodic rain comes on a rhythm; sporadic rain comes whenever. And the word usually carries a faint disappointment: it attaches to things that ought to be steady but aren't — sporadic attendance, sporadic effort, sporadic funding. Something is limping along rather than running.
Sporadic gunfire, sporadic applause, sporadic attendance — always something that should be continuous and isn't.
Learn the word by its company: sporadic marks a broken, patchy version of something you expected to be sustained.
1. Sporadic outbreaks of cholera continued along the river for a decade, flaring in one village while the next went untouched.
2. He goes to the gym sporadically — twice in January, then nothing until June.
The stock phrase of every news bulletin from a conflict zone: "sporadic fighting continued overnight" — meaning nobody can say when or where the next burst comes.
Greek sporas / sporad- = "scattered", from speirein, "to sow" — seed flung by hand lands wherever it lands.

Same sowing root gives you spore and diaspora (dia- "across" + speirein = a people scattered abroad).

Not genuine; resting on no legitimate basis at all.
Not genuine; lacking any legitimate basis or origin. A spurious document is a forgery, a spurious claim rests on nothing, a spurious correlation is a pattern that isn't really there.

It's the vocabulary of dismissal. Calling an argument false engages with it; calling it spurious refuses to — you're saying it never had standing in the first place. And unlike fraudulent or phony, it doesn't require a liar: statistics throw up spurious results with nobody deceiving anyone. Cool, formal, faintly contemptuous — the word of judges, editors and scientists.
⚠️ spurious ≠ specious.
- spurious = not genuine — no real basis, whether or not it looks convincing
- specious = deceptively convincing — it does look good, and that's the problem

A specious argument seduces you. A spurious one just doesn't hold up.
Spurious claims deserve to be spurned.
Same opening four letters, and it captures the tone — you don't rebut something spurious, you brush it aside.
1. The court dismissed the petition as spurious, finding no evidence that the signatory had ever existed.
2. He gave some spurious excuse about traffic, but we'd all seen his car in the lot since nine.
Spurious correlation is the standard term in stats and data science — and Tyler Vigen's Spurious Correlations charts (US cheese consumption vs. deaths by bedsheet entanglement) made it a running internet joke.
Latin spurius = "illegitimate, of unknown father." A spurious child had no acknowledged parentage — and that's still exactly the accusation: a spurious quote, gospel or manuscript is one whose claimed origin is a lie.

column2:
Reject with contempt, especially something offered.
To reject something with contempt — to turn down an offer, a gift, a person, or advice in a way that insults whoever made it.

You can only spurn what was offered. Decline is polite, refuse is firm, reject is neutral — spurn adds scorn, and the sting lands on the person doing the offering, not the thing offered. It's why the standard collocations are all about wounded pride: a spurned lover, spurned advances, spurned his outstretched hand.
⚠️ spur ≠ spurn.
- spur = drive someone onward
- spurn = kick someone away

One letter, opposite directions.
spurn = spur + turn — you turn your back and give it the heel.
The word literally hides the boot in it, which is why spurning is always insulting rather than merely negative.
1. Having spurned every offer of mediation, the union found itself bargaining alone.
2. He asked her out three times and got spurned three times — you'd think he'd take the hint.
Hamlet's "To be or not to be" lists what makes life unbearable: "the pangs of despised love, the law's delay, the insolence of office, and the spurns that patient merit of the unworthy takes" — the snubs a decent person swallows from lesser people.
Old English spurnan = "to kick, to strike with the foot" — the same family as spur, the thing on a rider's heel.

The physical sense never really left: to spurn is to shove something away with your foot. That's the whole nuance in one root — a refusal delivered as a kick.

To waste something valuable through carelessness or folly.
To waste something valuable — money, time, talent, a lead, a chance — through carelessness or folly.

Waste is broad and can be blameless (wasted water, wasted effort). Squander always points a finger, and it needs a good hand to begin with: you squander an inheritance, a two-goal lead, a first-class mind. The word carries the ghost of what could have been — the resource was real, it was yours, and you dribbled it away. It's the verb of choice for a blown opportunity you'll never get back.
Squander = your fortune goes on a wander — it strolls off and never comes home.
Nothing is stolen and nothing is bought; the value just drifts away because nobody was watching it.
1. An heir to three estates, he squandered the lot within a decade and died in rented rooms.
2. We had two hours to finish and squandered the first ninety minutes arguing about the font.
Standard commentary-box English: a team that goes 2–0 up and draws 2–2 has squandered the lead — you'll hear it every match weekend.

Sedate and conventional to the point of dullness.
Settled, sober, conventional — respectable in a way that has stopped being interesting.

The word rarely praises. Calling a man dignified admires him; calling him staid says he owns three grey suits and has never surprised anyone. It's a gentle, well-mannered put-down, and it attaches especially well to institutions — old banks, country clubs, provincial towns — where the dullness is a matter of policy rather than personality.
staid ≠ stolid. Staid = sedate and conventional (about habits and manner). Stolid = impassive, unmoved (about feeling). A staid banker follows the rules; a stolid one doesn't flinch when the market crashes.
Staid is just stayed — it stayed home, stayed put, stayed the same.
The homophone is the whole word: staid people never went anywhere, literally or otherwise.
1. The firm's staid oak-panelled offices had not admitted a new idea since 1954.
2. His parents are pretty staid — don't expect anyone to be doing shots at the wedding.
Business journalism runs on this word: every fintech story opens with a startup shaking up "the staid world of banking." If you've read a tech-versus-incumbent article, you've met it.
Staid is an old past participle of stay — the way laid comes from lay. Something staid has been stayed: held in place, fixed, unmoving.

Stay itself traces to Latin stāre, "to stand," which hands you stable, static, status, constant, stance — a whole family built on not moving.

column2:
Loyal, sturdy, long-serving — dependable and immovable, admiringly so.
Adj.: loyal, dependable and hard to shift — steadfast in support, and (older sense) physically sturdy and robust.
Noun: the long-serving reliable one: a stalwart of the party / of the club.

This is a word of praise for endurance. Stubborn says you won't move and that's a flaw; stalwart says you won't move and thank God for it. It carries a hint of physical solidity and of time served — a stalwart has been there for years, through the bad seasons, doing the unglamorous work. You don't call a brilliant newcomer a stalwart.
STAL- as in stall: a stalwart holds his stall and is worth keeping in it.
The word literally packages "standing-place" + "worth", which is exactly its flavour — not just immovable, but admirably so.
1. Two stalwarts of the movement, both past eighty, were still handing out leaflets in the rain.
2. He's not flashy, but he's been a stalwart — twelve years and he's never once let the team down.
Sports commentary lives on this word: the "club stalwart" is the defender with 400 appearances, no glory, and no intention of leaving.
Old English stælwierþe, generally traced to staþol ("foundation, standing place") + weorþ ("worth") — literally "worth its place." Same sta- family as stall, stand, and steadfast: all of them about not moving.

column2:
To stop a flow — blood, money, losses.
To stop or check the flow of something — classically blood from a wound, by extension money, losses, or people leaving.

The word presupposes a leak already in progress: you can stop anything, but you only stanch what is escaping. It carries triage, not repair — pressure on the wound, a hand over the hole. Something stanched is contained, not cured, which is exactly why finance and politics reach for it: stanch the outflow of deposits, stanch the loss of members.
⚠️ stanch ≠ staunch (adj.). Stanch stops a flow; staunch means loyal, unwavering — a staunch ally, a staunch defender. The spellings overlap in the verb, but the adjective never means "to stop."
Stanch makes it STAND still — blood, cash, or customers.
The buried sta- is Latin stare, "to stand": you're not fixing the wound, just making the flow stand still.
1. Field medics were trained to stanch arterial bleeding with a tourniquet before any thought of evacuation.
2. Cutting the free snacks isn't going to stanch the bleeding — we're losing a million a month.
"Stanch the bleeding" is boardroom and business-news boilerplate — every quarterly-loss story about a company trying to stop the cash pouring out.
Old French estanchier, "to stop the flow," from Latin stāre = "to stand." Make the blood stand still.

That root is a GRE goldmine: stagnant (standing water), static, stance, constant, stable, stanza (a "standing place" in a poem), substance.

Unwavering in loyalty or resolve, especially under pressure.
Firm and unwavering — in loyalty, belief, or resolve — especially when there is pressure to give way.

This is a word of praise, and it praises constancy under strain. Resolute describes a decision; persistent describes effort; stubborn describes an obstruction. Steadfast is about staying — the friend who doesn't drift when your reputation goes bad, the refusal to abandon a position when abandoning it would be easier. It leans slightly noble and old-fashioned, so it attaches naturally to people, allies, faith and support rather than to trivial things: a steadfast ally, not a steadfast preference for oat milk.
Stead + fast — and fast here means stuck fast, not speedy. Think "hold fast," "stuck fast," colourfast.
The old sense of fast is fixed in place, so a steadfast person is fixed in their place — they don't move when moved against.
1. Through two decades of exile and ridicule, she remained steadfast in the belief that the verdict would eventually be overturned.
2. He's not clever, he's not quick, but he's steadfast — he'll be there at 6 a.m. every single time you ask.
The Psalms' refrain "his steadfast love endures forever" — the standard English rendering, and the reason steadfast love still sounds like the word's natural home: loyalty that outlasts everything.
Old English stede (place) + fæst (firm, fixed) = "fixed in place."

stede survives all over English once you spot it: instead (in the place of), homestead, bedstead, "in his stead", and steady.

column2:
to originate in; arise as a result of
To originate in; to arise as a result of some earlier cause.

What it points at is almost always abstract — problems, beliefs, conflicts, resentments, policies — not physical objects. A river doesn't stem from a lake; a dispute stems from a misunderstanding. And it looks backwards: "stems from" is the move you make when you've got an effect in hand and are naming its source. Compare results in, which runs the other way, and derives from, which is drier and more technical. Neutral in tone, but it drifts toward diagnosing trouble — you far more often read that a failure stemmed from something than that a triumph did. The from is obligatory; the verb never stands alone in this sense.
⚠️ stem from ≠ stem.
- stem from = come out of a source
- stem (alone) = stop the flow — stem the tide, stem the bleeding

Two unrelated verbs. One traces a flow back; the other dams it.
A stem always runs back to a root — so stem from names the root, never the branch.
The phrase is a backwards-pointing verb: you say it about the cause, not the consequence.
1. The commission concluded that the outage stemmed from a single misconfigured server, not from sabotage.
2. Half his stress stems from the fact that he refuses to say no to anyone.
Stem cells — the same metaphor, made literal: the cell every other cell type grows out of.

Severe and unsmiling; strict with a face to match.
Adj.: severe, unsmiling, unwilling to bend — of a person, a face, a rule, or a warning.
Noun: the back end of a ship (an unrelated word that happens to be spelled the same).

Strictness plus a grim expression: strict describes the rules you enforce, stern describes the face you enforce them with. It sits below harsh and cruel on the scale, and usually carries authority rather than malice — a stern parent, a stern judge, a stern rebuke — so it can even be faint praise, implying someone who holds a line others would let slide. Say a face is stern and you mean it gives nothing away and forgives nothing.
Stern rhymes with learn — a stern look isn't cruelty, it's a lesson.
The rhyme keeps the disciplinary edge attached: sternness is severity aimed at correcting you, not at hurting you.
1. The committee issued a stern rebuke to the minister, stopping just short of demanding his resignation.
2. Mum gave me one stern look across the table and I put the phone away.
The most-replayed shot in Titanic: the stern rearing straight up out of the water before the ship goes down — that's the noun, the rear end of the hull.
Two different words wearing the same coat.

Adjective: Old English styrne = "rigid, severe" — from the same root family as stare, the fixed, unblinking look. Stern people don't move their faces.

Noun: Old Norse stjórn = "steering" — the rear is where the steering gear lived. Same root gives steer and starboard (steer-board, the side the oar hung on).

To brand as shameful; to attach lasting social disgrace.
To mark someone or something out as shameful — to attach social disgrace to a person, group, condition or behaviour.

The disgrace comes from the crowd, not a court. You condemn an act; you stigmatize a whole identity, and the mark outlasts whatever prompted it. Note also which way the sympathy runs: a speaker who says a group is stigmatized is almost always saying the shame is undeserved. That's why it sits so naturally in the passive — addicts are stigmatized, poverty is stigmatized — with the branding hand left conveniently offstage.
Stig- sounds like stick: a stigma is a mark that sticks to the person, not the deed.
Criticism is aimed at what you did and expires; a stigma is stuck onto who you are and doesn't.
1. Nineteenth-century asylums stigmatized the very patients they claimed to be treating, so that release from the ward was never release from the label.
2. Don't stigmatize the guy for taking a mental health day — half the office needs one.
Every mental-health campaign you've scrolled past — "end the stigma," "fight the stigma" — is built on this word, and on exactly its sympathetic slant.
Greek stigma = "a mark made by a pointed instrument" — specifically the brand or tattoo pricked into slaves and criminals so everyone could see what they were. From stizein, "to prick."

The root pays off elsewhere: astigmatism = a- (without) + stigma (point) — an eye that can't bring light to a single point.

Sparing, grudging — giving less than is due.
Giving sparingly, holding back, rationing out less than is wanted or deserved. To stint on something is to skimp on it; to stint someone is to keep them short.

This isn't thrift you admire — it's withholding something that ought to have flowed freely: praise, effort, food, money, time. A budget airline is economical; a host who serves one sandwich to twelve guests is stinting. Note where you'll actually meet it: nine times out of ten in the negative — without stinting, never stinted, unstinting support. So when the bare positive form shows up on the exam, read it as grudging rationing.
Stint and stunt are the same word wearing different vowels — both cut something short before it reaches full size.
A stunted tree never got its full growth; a stinting host never gave you your full share.
1. The committee was unstinting in its praise, devoting three full pages to her contribution.
2. Don't stint on the garlic — nobody's ever complained about too much.
You already use the noun: "I did a two-year stint at Deloitte." A stint is a rationed, measured-out spell of time — the same idea of a portion cut to size.
Old English styntan = "to blunt, to make dull, to cut short." Blunt it → shorten it → give less of it. The same root surfaces as stunt (to check something's growth), which is why the two feel related — they are.

Enduring hardship calmly, without complaint or visible emotion.
Adj.: enduring pain, hardship or loss without complaint and without visible emotion. Noun: a person who does that.

The key is that the feeling is there. A stoic person isn't numb or indifferent — they mind very much, and simply refuse to make a scene about it. That's why the word carries quiet admiration: it implies self-command, not coldness. Impassive describes a blank face; apathetic means you don't care; stoic means you care and hold the line anyway.
⚠️ stoic ≠ stolid.
- stoic = bears suffering without complaint — admiring
- stolid = dull, unresponsive, showing no emotion because there's little going on — insulting

Same "unmoved face", opposite compliment.
Stoic = "stow it" — the feelings get stowed away, not thrown away.
Stowed cargo is still on board, which is exactly the difference between a stoic and someone who simply feels nothing.
1. Through three years of failed treatments she remained stoic, answering every enquiry about her health with the same steady politeness.
2. He took the rejection email like a stoic — shrugged, made a coffee, and went back to work.
Marcus Aurelius's Meditations — the emperor's private notes on enduring what you can't control — is the bestseller behind the whole modern "Stoicism" wave on podcasts and self-help shelves. Same word, capital S.
Greek stoa = "porch." Zeno of Citium taught in Athens under the Stoa Poikilē, the Painted Porch — so his followers were "the porch people," Stoics. A philosophy of enduring hardship calmly got named after the address where it was taught.

column2:
Impassive to the point of seeming dull.
Showing no emotion or reaction; heavy, impassive, unexcitable.

The word carries a faint insult. Describing someone as stolid is not praising their composure — it hints that nothing much is going on behind the face. A stolid clerk stamps your form while you weep at the counter; a stolid ox stands in the rain. It suggests dullness and slow blood, not discipline. Used of faces, expressions, crowds, and peasants in nineteenth-century novels.
⚠️ stolid ≠ stoic.
- stoic = feels the pain, refuses to show it — admirable
- stolid = doesn't seem to feel much at all — unflattering

The stoic soldier is brave; the stolid soldier is thick.
Stolid is solid with a T — a solid lump of a person, and the T is for thick.
Solid is a compliment, stolid is the same immovability turned into a criticism.
1. The jury remained stolid throughout the testimony, not a flicker of feeling crossing a single face.
2. He just gave me this stolid stare, like I'd told him the weather instead of that I was quitting.
Latin stolidus = "dull, stupid, unmovable" — a sibling of stultus ("foolish"), which gives you stultify (to make something look stupid or futile). The Latin meant stupid outright; English softened it to unexpressive, but the sneer never fully washed out.

column2:
Bitter, ongoing conflict between people or groups.
Bitter, angry conflict — sustained discord between people, factions, or classes.

A fight is an event and a dispute has a topic; strife is a condition. It hangs over a household, a union, a country for years, and it rarely names a winner. The word is elevated, faintly biblical, and it clings to collective nouns: civil strife, sectarian strife, industrial strife, marital strife. Nobody says "me and Dave had strife" — it's too big a word for two people and one argument.
Strife is what you get when two sides both strive — against each other, for years.
The buried strive gives you both halves of the nuance: effort on both sides, and no end in sight.
1. Decades of sectarian strife left the city partitioned by walls that no map acknowledged.
2. There's been nothing but strife in that office since the merger — half of them won't even share a lift.
Cloud Strife, the hero of Final Fantasy VII — a surname picked to advertise a life of conflict, inner and outer.
Old French estrif (quarrel), from estriver, "to strive." Same root, split in two: strive kept the effort, strife kept the fighting.

Strict and exacting; demanding tight compliance with rules or standards.
Strict, exacting, allowing no slack — of rules, standards, conditions, or requirements that must be met precisely.

Compare the neighbours: harsh and draconian describe punishment and imply cruelty; stringent describes the tightness of the bar, not the pain of failing it. That makes it the rare strictness-word that can be a compliment — stringent safety testing, stringent peer review — because the tightness is the point. It attaches to systems, not personalities: standards, criteria, controls, budgets are stringent; a strict grandmother is not.
⚠️ stringent ≠ strident.
- stringent = tight standards — a rule that admits no slack
- strident = loud and grating — a voice or tone that grates

A stringent policy is quietly unbending; a strident critic is impossible to ignore.
Stringent starts with string — pulled taut, zero slack.
The word measures how tightly the rule is strung, not how badly it hurts to break it.
1. Admission to the programme is governed by stringent criteria: two published papers, a research proposal, and a reading knowledge of German.
2. They've got stringent rules about laptops in the exam hall — even the case has to stay outside.
Standard news vocabulary you've already absorbed: stringent emissions standards, stringent lockdown restrictions, GDPR routinely called the world's most stringent privacy law. Note that in every one of those, stringent is doing regulatory work, not moral scolding.
Latin stringere = "to draw tight, bind." The whole family is about tightening: strict (bound), restrict and constrain (bound back), stricture (a narrowing), astringent (a lotion that tightens the skin).

Learn the root once and four GRE words come with it.

column2:
Quieter and less lively than usual; softened, toned down.
Of a person: quiet, low-spirited, noticeably less lively than usual. Of light, colour, or sound: softened, muted, toned down.

The word only works against a former higher level — it names a drop. A naturally shy person isn't subdued; a loud friend who has gone quiet after bad news is. Something pressed them down, and the word leaves that cause unnamed but implied, which is why "the mood was subdued" hangs so heavy in a news report. Applied to light or colour it loses the sadness entirely and becomes tasteful: subdued décor is deliberately restrained, never drab.
Sub-dued = turned down, not turned off — the dimmer switch, not the off switch.
Whatever is subdued is still running, just held below its normal level — that residue of the original energy is the whole word.
1. The delegation returned in a subdued mood, having conceded far more than its mandate allowed.
2. He's usually the loudest one in the pub, so his subdued hello told me something had happened.
"Subdued lighting" is estate-agent and restaurant-menu boilerplate — the dimmed, flattering half-light you sit in on a nice evening. Same word, no sadness at all.
Latin sub- (under) + dūcere (to lead) — literally led under, brought beneath someone's control. To subdue an enemy is to conquer them; to be subdued is to have that pressure applied to your mood.

dūcere is a GRE workhorse: induce, deduce, conduct, produce, seduce, ductile, aqueduct — all leading something somewhere.

Based on personal feeling or viewpoint, not external fact.
Belonging to the observer rather than the observed — shaped by personal feeling, taste, or point of view. Also, in a stricter philosophical sense: existing in the mind, not out in the world.

Note that it is not a polite word for biased. Bias is a distortion you could in principle correct; subjectivity is simply the fact that the judgment lives inside a particular head — pain, beauty, and "too spicy" are subjective without anyone being at fault. The negative charge only appears when someone deploys it as a verdict ("that's purely subjective"), meaning: unverifiable, so it doesn't count as evidence.
Ob-ject = thrown in front of you, out there. Sub-ject = thrown underneath — the self doing the looking.
Objective facts sit outside where anyone can check them; subjective ones sit under your own skull where nobody else can get at them.
1. Aesthetic judgment, Kant argued, is subjective and yet somehow demands the agreement of others.
2. Scoring interviews out of ten is hopelessly subjective — one panellist's "confident" is another's "arrogant".
Doctors' notes are literally built on the split: the SOAP note opens with S — Subjective (what the patient reports: "it burns at night") before O — Objective (what the thermometer and the blood panel say).
Latin sub- (under) + jacere (to throw) — the subject is what's "thrown under": a king's subjects live under his power, and the subject of a sentence sits under the action.

jacere is a top-tier GRE root — project (throw forward), eject, inject, reject (throw back), dejected (thrown down), conjecture (throw ideas together), trajectory (the path of a throw), abject (thrown away).

Lower in rank; to rank one thing beneath another.
Adj./noun: lower in rank; a person who works under someone else's authority.
Verb: to place or treat something as less important than something else.

The word is neutral and structural — it describes a position on an org chart, not a character flaw. A subordinate simply reports to someone; a subservient person grovels. Keep those apart: rank vs. temperament.

The verb is where the GRE lives, and it almost always takes to: you subordinate X to Y, meaning you deliberately let X lose so Y can win. There's a cost implied — something real gets sacrificed to the thing ranked above it.
-AYT does it; -uht is it. Same split as sepa-RAYT / SEP-ruht, dele-GAYT / DEL-uh-guht, moder-AYT / MOD-uh-ruht.
The full -AYT ending is always the action you perform, while the mumbled -uht is the person or the state that results.
1. The treaty subordinated every commercial interest to the single goal of preventing another war.
2. She's technically my subordinate, but she's been here twenty years and everyone asks her first.
Every grammar lesson you've ever sat through: a subordinate clause (because it was raining) can't stand on its own — it has to hang off a main clause. The name tells you its rank.
Latin sub- (under) + ordinare (to arrange in rank), from ordo, ordinis = order, row, rank. Literally: put in the row beneath.

That root pays out across the test: ordain, ordinary, coordinate (co- = arranged at equal rank), insubordinate (refusing to sit below), and best of all inordinate — outside the order, hence excessive.

Excessively obedient; serving another's will at the cost of your own
1. Excessively willing to obey — submitting to someone else's will past the point of self-respect. 2. (of a thing) subordinate, serving a larger purpose: form subservient to function.

Obedience is what the word describes; contempt is what it adds. A soldier who follows orders is obedient; a soldier who has stopped having opinions is subservient. Deferential respects authority and keeps its own judgment — subservient hands the judgment over. It's almost always an outsider's verdict: nobody calls themselves subservient, and the word quietly indicts the person above as much as the person below.
⚠️ subservient ≠ subversive.
- subservient = props the power up (sub- + serve)
- subversive = tears the power down (sub- + vertere, "to turn")

Four shared letters, opposite politics.
SERVE is sitting in the middle, and sub- puts you under while you do it.
Not just serving — serving from beneath, which is why the word stings rather than compliments.
1. The court chronicler's history is worthless: every page is subservient to the king who paid for it.
2. He wasn't being polite, he was being subservient — he agreed with her twice before she'd finished the sentence.
Burger King's 2004 viral ad Subservient Chicken — a man in a chicken suit who did whatever you typed into the box. The whole joke was the word: it obeys anything, and there's something faintly degrading about watching it.
Latin sub- (under) + servīre (to serve), from servus = slave. That root runs through servant, service, servile, servitude, deserve — and serf.

Pair it with the vertere (to turn) family — subvert, invert, divert, avert — and the two sub- words stop blurring for good.

To sink back down, or gradually die away on its own.
To sink back down to a lower or normal level — floodwaters, a swelling, ground under a building — and, by extension, for anything intense to gradually die away: pain, noise, panic, applause, a fever, a scandal.

Two things define it. First, it needs a prior rise: something swelled, surged, or flared, and now it's settling back. Second, it happens of its own accord. Suppress and quell need someone doing the work; subside is what a thing does when left alone, on its own timetable. It's also gradual, never abrupt — a riot subsides into muttering; it doesn't subside in a snap.
Tide → subside: it goes down on its own, and nobody drains it.
The rhyme fixes the two essentials — something that had risen is now falling, slowly and without help.
1. As the applause subsided, the conductor turned back to face the orchestra.
2. Give it two days — the swelling should subside on its own.
Straight out of any doctor's or pharmacist's mouth: "Take these and the pain should subside within a few hours." Nobody says "the pain should cease" — because subside is exactly the promise of a slow, unattended fade.
Latin sub- (down, under) + sīdere (to settle, sink down), a cousin of sedēre, "to sit."

That sitting root is a GRE goldmine: sediment (what settles at the bottom), reside (sit back), preside (sit in front), sedentary (sitting), assiduous (sitting at it doggedly), insidious (sitting in ambush), dissident (sitting apart).
column3: g24 register::neutral connotation::neutral antonym::swelling-vs-dying-down meaning::dying-down-gradually root::root:-sub--under-from-below

column2:
To back a claim with evidence so it holds up.
To support a claim with evidence — to show that an assertion, charge, or rumour actually holds up.

It presupposes a claim already floating in the air and under suspicion: you substantiate allegations, rumours, charges, a story. Compare its neighbours — verify is a neutral fact-check, corroborate means a second independent source agrees with the first, while substantiate is the burden falling on the person who spoke: put something solid under what you said, or it collapses. Courtroom, newsroom and HR-investigation register; a boss saying "can you substantiate that?" is not curious, they are challenging you.
You mostly meet it as unsubstantiated rumour — so substantiate is simply giving the rumour the substance it was missing.
Learn the negative collocation first and the positive verb defines itself: evidence is the substance, and a claim without it has none.
1. The tribunal dismissed the complaint, finding that the witness could not substantiate a single one of her allegations.
2. He keeps saying the place is haunted, but he's never substantiated it with anything better than a creaky door.
In HR and police case files, the closing verdict is literally one word: the complaint is recorded as substantiated or unsubstantiated — evidence found, or not.
Latin substantia = "substance", from sub- (under) + stare (to stand) — what stands under a thing and holds it up. To substantiate is to put a foundation under a claim so it stands.

Stare is a GRE workhorse: circumstance, constant, stable, status, stationary, obstacle — all things standing.

To absorb into a larger category as a sub-case.
To absorb something into a larger category or body, so that it is treated as a part or instance of that larger thing.

It's a filing verb, not a destroying verb. Absorb and swallow up suggest the smaller thing dissolves; subsume says it still exists — it has simply lost its separate standing and now counts as a sub-case of something bigger. A department gets subsumed into a ministry, a claim gets subsumed under a general principle, three tribes get subsumed under one label. Cool, formal, faintly bureaucratic: the tone of reorganisation charts and philosophy papers, rarely of anger.
Sub + sum — your line item gets tucked under someone else's sum.
Nothing is deleted; it just stops being counted on its own and gets folded into a bigger total.
1. Later theorists subsumed these scattered observations under a single law of diminishing returns.
2. Our team got subsumed into Platform last quarter — same people, new org chart, no more standalone budget.
The word every acquisition announcement reaches for: the startup isn't shut down, it's subsumed into the parent company — brand retired, staff still there, now a line under someone else's P&L.
Latin sub- (under) + sumere (to take) — literally "to take under."

sumere is a GRE workhorse: assume (take on), presume (take beforehand), consume (take up entirely), resume (take back up), presumptuous (taking too much).

So fine or understated it's easy to miss entirely.
So fine, delicate or understated that it's easy to miss — a subtle shade of blue, a subtle difference in wording, a subtle hint. Applied to people and minds it means the opposite of blunt: able to perceive or produce fine distinctions.

Praise, mostly — it credits precision and restraint, the skill of doing a lot with very little. But the same fineness can be sinister: a subtle poison, a subtle manipulator, a subtle argument that quietly cheats. When the object is a person's method rather than a thing's texture, listen for that second, craftier sense.
Even the b in subtle is too subtle to hear.
The word performs itself — something is genuinely there, doing its work, without ever announcing itself.
1. The novel's power lies in its subtle shifts of tone; nothing is ever stated, and everything is understood.
2. He winked, nudged me, and mouthed the plan across the table — real subtle, mate.
The flat, sarcastic one-word verdict — "Subtle." — dropped after someone does something spectacularly unsubtle. You've heard it used almost exclusively as an insult.
Latin subtilis = "finely woven" — from sub (under) + tela (the warp threads on a loom). A subtle fabric is one whose threads are too fine to pick out individually; a subtle idea is the same thing in thought.

That tela comes from texere, "to weave" — which also gives you textile, texture, text, and context. Weaving is hiding in more words than you'd think.

To undermine and overturn something quietly, from within.
To undermine and overturn something established — a government, an authority, a rule, a convention — usually by working from inside or underneath it rather than attacking it head-on.

The method is what marks the word: an army overthrows a regime, but a mole subverts it. Subversion is quiet, internal, corrosive — it hollows the thing out until it collapses. Applied to power it's an accusation (subversive elements, subverting democracy); applied to art, genre, or stereotype it flips positive — a film that subverts expectations is being praised for cleverness, not condemned.
A submarine attacks from below the surface — and vert is a turn. Subvert = turn it over from underneath, unseen.
The whole point of the word is that the damage comes from below and out of sight, not from a frontal assault.
1. The pamphlets were banned on the grounds that they sought to subvert lawful authority.
2. She kept smiling and agreeing in meetings while quietly subverting every decision he made.
"Subverting expectations" is now standard film-criticism vocabulary — the phrase the internet argued about for years over Star Wars: The Last Jedi, where a twist that overturns what the audience assumed is either brilliant or infuriating depending on who's talking.
Latin sub- (under) + vertere (to turn) = "to turn from below, overturn."

Vertere is a GRE workhorse: invert (turn in), avert (turn away), divert (turn aside), revert (turn back), convert (turn with), versatile (easily turned), vertigo (the spinning), controversy (turned against each other).

column2:
Only surface-deep; not going into the substance.
Existing at or affecting only the surface — and by extension, going no deeper than appearances: shallow in thought, feeling, or attention.

Two lives, one idea. Literally it is neutral and even reassuring: a superficial wound is the good kind, a superficial crack won't bring the wall down. Figuratively it is a quiet insult — a superficial reading, a superficial charm, a superficial person. The sting isn't that they're wrong, it's that they stopped at the surface when there was more underneath. Milder and more clinical than shallow, which attacks the person; superficial usually attacks the effort.
⚠️ superficial ≠ superfluous.
- superficial = only skin-deep
- superfluous = more than needed, unnecessary

A superficial edit skims the page; a superfluous edit shouldn't have been made at all.
super + FICIAL — it never gets past the face.
Whatever it touches, it stays above the face of the thing and never goes in.
1. His knowledge of the treaty proved superficial: fluent on the preamble, silent on every clause that mattered.
2. We had a superficial chat about the weather and then both pretended we had somewhere to be.
In hospitals it's a compliment, not a jab — triage notes grade burns as superficial (first-degree, top layer only) before partial-thickness and full-thickness. Same word, zero insult: it just means the damage stayed on the surface.
Latin super (above) + facies (face, surface) — literally "on the face of it."

facies is a workhorse root: face, surface, facade (a front with nothing behind it), facet, deface, prima facie (at first face — how it looks before you look harder).
column3: g13 register::neutral connotation::depends antonym::deep-vs-skin-deep intensity::effort-withheld meaning::for-show-only meaning::four-ways-of-not-really-doing-it

column2:
More than is needed; surplus to requirements.
Beyond what is needed or wanted; surplus to requirements.

The word doesn't say a thing is bad or useless — it says there is too much of it. A fourth adjective in a sentence, a second apology, an extra assistant on a two-person job: each might be perfectly good on its own and still be superfluous. Redundant points at duplication (this repeats what we already have); superfluous points at quantity (we simply didn't need this much). It's a formal, faintly fastidious word — the register of an editor with a red pen, and there's usually a hint of disdain in it.
Super-FLU-ous = a super flow — the cup doesn't fail, it just overflows.
Overflow is the exact idea: what spills over is the same good stuff, there's just more of it than the cup required.
1. The committee's report was thorough to the point of exhaustion; three of its five appendices were superfluous.
2. Mate, you've packed six pairs of shoes for a weekend — that's a bit superfluous.
Shakespeare hands the word to King Lear, raging at his daughters for stripping away his retinue: \"Our basest beggars / Are in the poorest thing superfluous\" — even the poorest man owns something more than he strictly needs, and that surplus is what makes him human.
Latin super (over) + fluere (to flow) — literally overflowing.

Fluere is a workhorse root: fluent (words flow), fluid, influence (originally an astrological "in-flowing"), affluent (wealth flowing toward you), confluence (rivers flowing together), influx, flux.

Replace something older, cancelling its authority.
To take the place of something older, weaker, or out of date — and in doing so, to cancel its authority. The superseded thing isn't just less popular now; it no longer counts.

Tone is procedural and bureaucratic: rules, editions, models, treaties, software versions. Compare supplant, which carries scheming or force — you supplant a rival, you oust him. Nobody is elbowed aside in a supersede; the new thing simply arrives with better standing, and the old one quietly becomes waste paper.
Super + sede = sit above — the new rule takes the old one's seat.
Once something sits in that seat, the previous occupant isn't merely demoted — it's void.
1. The 1958 constitution superseded every ordinance passed under the provisional government.
2. Don't print that form — it's been superseded, there's a new one on the intranet.
Office and engineering life runs on it: the red SUPERSEDED stamp across an obsolete drawing, and the standard opening line of any policy memo — "This document supersedes all previous versions."
Latin super (above) + sedēre (to sit) — literally to sit on top of. That sedēre root is a GRE workhorse: sedentary (sitting), sediment (settling), preside, reside, session, subsidy, assiduous (sitting doggedly at it), dissident (sitting apart).

🚫 Note the spelling: -sede, not -cede. Precede, concede, recede come from cedere, "to go, to yield" — different root. Supersede is the only English word ending in -sede; "supercede" is simply wrong.

To take the place of by displacing or ousting.
To take the place of something or someone else — by pushing them out.

Replace is neutral bookkeeping: the old thing left, the new thing moved in. Supplant has a loser in it. The thing supplanted was in possession, and is now dispossessed — by a rival, a newer technology, a younger favourite. Often there's a whiff of scheming (the courtier who supplants the king's advisor), but it's just as at home in cool analytical prose about markets and ideas. The one constant: displacement, not mere succession.
⚠️ supplant ≠ supplement. Supplant replaces the original; supplement adds to it. One letter apart, near-opposite in meaning — the GRE knows this.
sup-PLANT — you plant your foot under his and trip him out of his spot.
The hidden plant is literal — Latin planta is the sole of the foot, and supplanting is tripping someone up to stand where they stood.
1. Within a decade, the vernacular had supplanted Latin as the language of serious scholarship.
2. The intern learned the new system in a week and quietly supplanted half the team.
Business writing runs on this verb: Netflix supplanted Blockbuster, streaming supplanted radio. Notice it's never used for a friendly handover — always for the one that got wiped out.
Latin supplantāre = "to trip up" — from sub- (under) + planta (the sole of the foot). To supplant someone was to hook your foot under theirs and bring them down.

That planta also gives you plantar (as in plantar fasciitis — the sole of your foot) and plant itself (something pressed into the ground by foot).

Bending easily without breaking; flexible and strong at once.
Bending and moving easily without breaking or resisting — of a body, a material, or by extension a mind or a prose style.

Praise, almost always. Limp, floppy and flabby describe things that bend because they have no strength; supple describes things that bend and spring back — the gymnast, the well-worn leather, the fencer's wrist. It also escapes the faint contempt in pliable and malleable, which hint at a person too easily bent by others: a supple negotiator is quick and adaptive, not a pushover.
⚠️ supple ≠ supine. Both open with sup- and both describe bodies, but they are near-opposites in spirit: supple = flexible and strong; supine = lying face-up, and figuratively passively inert, refusing to resist.
Sup-ple ends in the same fold you hear in pleat — but a pleat folds and stays folded; supple folds and springs back.
The -ple is literally a fold (Latin plicāre), and the word's whole value is that the fold is temporary — bend, return, no damage.
1. Decades at the loom had left her hands scarred but still supple, capable of the finest work in the room.
2. These boots are stiff now, but give them some oil and a month of wear and they'll go lovely and supple.
It's the standard sales word for good leather — every jacket, handbag and car-seat listing promises "soft, supple leather," meaning it bends with you instead of cracking.
Latin supplex = "bending under, kneeling" — from sub ("under") + plicāre ("to fold, to bend").

plicāre is a workhorse root: pliable, pliant, ply, comply, apply, imply, complicated, explicate, duplicate, replicate — all folding.

Supplicate ("to beg") is a true cousin, not a false friend: same supplex, the same kneeling body. One branch kept the bending, the other kept the begging.

To beg humbly, from below, as if kneeling.
To beg humbly and earnestly for something — to entreat someone who has power over you.

The word carries posture. To request is horizontal, between equals; to plead is urgent; to supplicate is to ask from below, kneeling, hands out, all dignity deliberately surrendered. It belongs to prayer, to petitioning kings, to the defeated asking mercy. Used of ordinary life it is faintly withering — "he supplicated for a raise" says the man abased himself.
⚠️ supplicate ≠ supplant. Supplicate = beg on your knees. Supplant = oust someone and take their place. The supplicant is under you; the supplanter replaces you.
SUPPLE is sitting right inside supplicate — you make yourself supple, and bend.
Not a coincidence either: both words are the knee folding under you, which is why supplicating always sounds like self-abasement rather than a plain request.
1. The envoys came not to negotiate but to supplicate, kneeling on the marble until the emperor deigned to look up.
2. I'm not going to supplicate to some ticket bot for concert seats — if it sells out, it sells out.
In Islam, du'a — the personal prayer made with open, upturned palms — is standardly rendered in English as "supplication." The gesture is the definition.
Latin sub- ("under") + plicāre ("to fold, bend") — to bend down under someone.

That plicāre is a workhorse root: complicate (fold together), replicate (fold back), implicate (fold in), application, pliable, and — through French — deploy and employ.

column2:
To forcibly hold something down, hidden, or unexpressed.
To put down by force (a revolt, a protest), or to keep something from surfacing — evidence, a report, a laugh, a cough, a memory, an immune response.

The force comes from above and stays applied. What's suppressed isn't destroyed; it's held down, and the pressure implies it would come back the moment the hand lifted. That's what separates it from abolish or eradicate (the thing is gone) and from conceal (hidden, but nobody had to lean on it). It also carries a whiff of illegitimacy when the object is information — a government that suppresses a report is understood to be hiding something.
⚠️ suppress ≠ repress. You suppress deliberately — you know the impulse is there and you sit on it. You repress unknowingly — the mind buries it below awareness. A witness suppresses testimony; a patient represses a trauma.
sup-PRESS = press the lid down on a boiling pot — the steam is still in there.
Suppression is ongoing pressure, not removal, which is why suppressed dissent, suppressed laughter, and suppressed memories all come back the second the lid comes off.
1. The regime suppressed the findings for a decade, and the archive surfaced only after its collapse.
2. She suppressed a grin as her boss confidently mispronounced the client's name for the third time.
A gun suppressor — what films loosely call a silencer. It doesn't remove the noise, it presses it down. The word does exactly what it says.
Latin sub- (under) + premere (to press) — literally press down under.

Premere is a workhorse root: press, oppress (press against), repress (press back), compress (press together), express (press out), depress (press down), imprint. Learn one, get seven.

An excess so large it sickens instead of satisfying.
Noun: an excessive amount of something — classically food or drink — and the sick, cloyed feeling that follows.
Verb: to feed or supply to the point of disgust.

A surplus is neutral bookkeeping; abundance is a blessing. Surfeit always tips past the point where more stops being good: it carries the queasiness of the tenth pastry. Use it and you imply the recipient is full, sated, faintly nauseated — a surfeit of information isn't just a lot, it's more than a mind can digest.
⚠️ surfeit ≠ forfeit. A surfeit is having far too much; to forfeit is to lose what you had as a penalty. Same -feit ending, opposite direction of traffic.
A surplus that no longer fits.
The word literally holds sur- ("over") and sounds like fit — it's the amount that has stopped fitting, in the stomach or in the head.
1. A surfeit of choice, the study argued, leaves shoppers less satisfied than a shelf with three options.
2. I had a surfeit of cake at that wedding and I'm still recovering.
Twelfth Night opens on it: "If music be the food of love, play on... that surfeiting, / The appetite may sicken, and so die." Orsino wants so much music that his craving overdoses itself — the word's exact flavour.
Old French surfait = sur- ("over," from Latin super) + faire ("to do, make," from Latin facere). Literally overdone.

That sur- is a workhorse: surpass, surplus, surcharge, surmount, surreal — all "over/beyond."

column2:
To overcome an obstacle — to climb over and rise above it.
To overcome a difficulty, obstacle, or limitation. (Literally, in architecture: to sit on top of something — a dome surmounted by a golden cross.)

What you surmount is an obstacle, never an opponent — barriers, odds, prejudice, poverty, a language gap. You beat a rival; you surmount the thing standing in your way. The image is vertical: the difficulty stays where it is and you get above it.

It's formal and quietly heroic — it concedes the obstacle was real, but claims no gloating. And you'll meet it most often wearing its negative coat: insurmountable.
Sur- (over) + mount (climb) — you don't smash the wall, you end up standing on it.
The word is literally "climb over," which is why it takes obstacles rather than enemies as its object.
1. Having surmounted every procedural objection, the defence finally put its case to the jury.
2. She surmounted a fear of flying by booking twelve short-haul flights in a row.
Sports commentary lives on the negative form: a team goes three goals down and the lead becomes "insurmountable." Same word, same wall — just too high to climb.
Old French sur- (over, above, from Latin super) + monter (to climb, from mons/montis, "mountain").

That sur- prefix is a GRE workhorse — once you hear it as "over," you get surpass (go over), surplus (over the amount), surfeit (over-supply, to excess), surcharge, surreal (above the real), even surname (the name written over yours).
