column2:
Secret and sneaky, because open doing would be stopped.
Done in secret and by stealth, specifically because open doing would be forbidden, punished, or embarrassing.

Scale is what separates it from its neighbours. Covert and clandestine are big secrecy — operations, cells, affairs, things planned to stay hidden. Surreptitious is small and quick: the glance at your phone under the table, the extra file copied to a USB stick, the bite taken from someone else's plate. It also carries a whiff of guilt that discreet doesn't — being discreet is tactful, being surreptitious means you'd have been stopped if anyone had looked up.
⚠️ surreptitious ≠ serendipitous. Similar length, similar -itous ending, opposite spirit: surreptitious is deliberately sneaky, serendipitous is a lucky accident.
Sur-REPT-itious hides a reptile — it moves without a sound, and you only notice afterwards.
The word is about the small silent slither, not the grand conspiracy — the thing that gets away with it while you're looking elsewhere.
1. The clerk had for years made surreptitious alterations to the ledger, each too small to notice and too regular to be accident.
2. He took a surreptitious look at the answers while the invigilator was turned around.
"Surreptitious recording" is the fixed legal phrase for taping a conversation without telling the other person — the exact thing wiretap and one-party-consent laws are written about.
Latin sub- ("under") + rapere ("to seize, snatch") → surripere, "to snatch from underneath."

rapere is a workhorse root: rapid (snatched away fast), rapture (seized by emotion), rapacious (grabbing greedily), ravish, and usurp (usu + rapere — to seize by use).

column2:
A stand-in who fills a role belonging to someone else.
A substitute — a person or thing put in someone else's place to carry out their role.

The word is fussier than replacement or substitute. A surrogate takes over a role that properly belongs to another: a surrogate mother, a surrogate father figure, a surrogate decision-maker for an unconscious patient, a surrogate war fought by proxies for the great powers. There's usually a faint second-best flavour — the surrogate does the job, but everyone knows who was supposed to be there. In US political coverage it's a standard term of art: a campaign surrogate is the deputy sent out to speak in the candidate's voice.
A surrogate doesn't replace a thing — it replaces a relationship: surrogate mother, surrogate family, surrogate war.
You'd never call a spare tyre a surrogate, because the word wants a role someone else was meant to fill.
1. The court appointed a surrogate to consent to treatment on the patient's behalf.
2. Her flatmate's dog has become a full surrogate child — she talks to it more than to actual people.
Surrogate mother is the phrase that keeps the word alive in ordinary speech — a woman who carries a pregnancy in another's place. Note it's exactly the role, not the person's body parts, that the word is naming.
Latin subrogāre = "to ask in place of another" — sub- here meaning "in place of," plus rogāre, "to ask, to propose." Originally the Roman act of proposing a substitute official.

rogāre is a high-yield GRE root: interrogate (ask between/thoroughly), arrogant (claiming for oneself), prerogative (asked for first — a privilege), abrogate (ask away — repeal), derogatory (asking down — belittling).

Arousing doubt; questionable, dodgy, not to be relied on.
Adj.: open to doubt — dodgy, questionable, not to be relied on. Not "feeling suspicion," but attracting it.

Direction is the whole point: the adjective is always passive. A suspect claim is one we doubt; it says nothing about what the claim thinks. Compare suspicious, which swings both ways — a suspicious neighbour may be watching you, or being watched.

Tone is dry understatement. Calling data "suspect" is a quiet, professional way of saying it may be garbage: cooler than fraudulent, more damning than unproven. It's the word an auditor or a referee uses when they don't yet want to say fake.
SUS-pect starts with sus — and "sus" means exactly that: dodgy, not to be trusted.
The slang is literally clipped from this word, so the stress that lands on SUS is also the meaning of the adjective.
1. The committee dismissed the survey, noting that its sampling method was suspect and its margins of error implausibly narrow.
2. Three sources, all quoting each other? That timeline looks pretty suspect to me.
Sports commentary lives on this adjective — "their defence is suspect", "the knee is suspect". It's the pundit's polite way of saying this will fall apart under pressure.
Latin sub- ("under") + specere ("to look") — to look at someone from underneath, sideways, askance. That sidelong glance is still in the word.

specere is a GRE workhorse: inspect, spectacle, conspicuous, circumspect (looking around you = cautious), perspicacious, prospect, retrospect.

To cheat someone out of money through elaborate deception.
Verb: to cheat someone out of money or property by deception. Noun: the scheme itself.

The mechanism is trust, not force — a swindler talks you into handing it over. A mugger robs you; a swindler is invited in. The word also implies scale and a story: a plausible investment, a fake charity, a sure thing. Compared with defraud (legal, clinical) or con (street-level, small), swindle is the tabloid word — vivid, contemptuous, and always with a gullible victim somewhere in the sentence.
Swindle rhymes with dwindle — your savings dwindle while he's still talking.
Nothing is grabbed; the money quietly drains away under the cover of a good story.
1. The prospectus was elegant, the returns imaginary; he had swindled two hundred pensioners before anyone thought to check the registry.
2. Forty quid for a "guided tour" that lasted ten minutes — we got swindled.
The Sex Pistols' 1980 film The Great Rock 'n' Roll Swindle, in which manager Malcolm McLaren gleefully claims he invented the band to fleece the record industry — the word used exactly right: money extracted by performance.
From German schwindeln = "to be dizzy" — and, by extension, to tell tall tales. A Schwindler was a giddy schemer; London slang borrowed it in the 1760s. The swindler makes your head spin, and you sign.

Giving a broad overview of the whole at once.
Giving a broad general view of a whole subject at once — everything laid out together, seen from above.

A synoptic account isn't merely a short one. Summary means shortened; synoptic means wide — all the parts visible in relation to each other. The word is formal and faintly technical (meteorologists, theologians, planners, strategists use it straight), and it's quietly approving: breadth achieved, altitude gained. Nobody calls a rambling overview synoptic.
⚠️ synoptic ≠ synaptic. Synaptic belongs to the synapse — the gap between nerve cells. One is a wide view; the other is a tiny junction in your brain.
Syn-OPTIC hides OPTIC — it's the wide-angle lens, not the zoom.
You get the whole scene in a single frame, which is exactly why a synoptic view buys breadth and gives up fine detail.
1. The commission's report opens with a synoptic chapter placing three decades of policy failure on a single page.
2. Skip the deep dive for now — just give me the synoptic version before the meeting starts.
Matthew, Mark and Luke are called the Synoptic Gospels — they can be set side by side in parallel columns and read together, because they share one broad view of events. John, which doesn't line up, is excluded.
Greek syn- (together) + opsis (sight, view) — "seeing it all together."

Opsis is a workhorse root: synopsis (the view-together), optic (of sight), autopsy (auto- + opsis = seeing for oneself), myopia (short sight), biopsy (viewing living tissue).

Understood and agreed without ever being said aloud.
Understood, accepted or agreed without being put into words.

The key is that something was communicated — just never spoken. Silence here isn't emptiness, it's a signal: you stayed quiet, and that counted as a yes. So tacit carries a faint whiff of complicity, which is why it pairs so naturally with things people would rather not say aloud — tacit approval of a shady deal, a tacit admission of guilt. Compare implicit, which is colder and more logical (implied by the content itself, no audience required); tacit needs two parties and an understanding between them.
tacit ≠ taciturn. Same root, different target: tacit describes a thing (an agreement, consent) that went unspoken; taciturn describes a person who habitually says little. A taciturn man can give you tacit consent by saying nothing at all.
Tacit never travels alone — it's always tacit approval, tacit consent, tacit agreement, tacit understanding.
Every one of its partner-nouns is a form of saying yes, which tells you tacit means agreement-by-silence, not just silence.
1. The committee's failure to object was taken as tacit endorsement of the new policy.
2. Nobody ever agreed out loud that I'd do the dishes — it was just a tacit thing once he started cooking.
Tacit knowledge is standard business and academic vocabulary for the stuff a veteran employee knows but can't write down — how to ride a bike, how to read a room. It walks out the door when they quit, precisely because nobody ever said it aloud.
Latin tacēre = "to be silent." It quietly hands you three GRE words: tacit (unspoken but agreed), taciturn (a person of few words), and reticent (re- + tacēre — holding back what you could say).

column2:
Habitually silent; saying little by nature.
Habitually silent; saying little by temperament, not by mood.

This is a standing character trait, not a one-off silence. A quiet person happens not to be talking; a taciturn person is built that way — you could know him for ten years and still get three-word answers. It carries a faint chill: not shy, not sad, just closed. Applied to a friend it's affectionate-gruff; applied to a witness or a colleague it hints at something withheld.
⚠️ taciturn ≠ reticent.
- taciturn = silent by nature, about everything
- reticent = holding back on one particular subject

A taciturn man rarely speaks; a chatty man can still be reticent about his divorce.
TACITurn — tacit means unspoken, and the -urn ending makes it permanent, like nocturnal and saturnine.
The word literally has "tacit" sitting inside it, and the tacked-on ending turns a single unspoken thing into a lifelong disposition.
1. The new ambassador was taciturn to the point of discourtesy, offering nothing beyond the sentence his brief required.
2. My grandad's taciturn — you get "fine" for how was your day and that's the whole conversation.
Calvin Coolidge was nicknamed "Silent Cal" for exactly this. The famous story: a dinner guest told him she'd bet she could get more than two words out of him. His reply — "You lose."
Latin tacēre = "to be silent" — which also gives you tacit (understood without being said), tacitly, and reticent (re- + tacēre, to keep silent about). The Roman historian Tacitus carried the same name.

column2:
Instinct for saying the delicate thing without causing offence.
A sure instinct for what to say — and what to leave unsaid — in a delicate situation, so that the truth lands without wounding.

Tact is not politeness and not kindness. Politeness is a set of rules anyone can follow; tact is judgement, applied live, under pressure: the right words, the right moment, the right amount. Diplomacy is its public, professional cousin — nations and negotiators have diplomacy; a friend telling you your marriage is over has tact. It's a compliment you rarely hear paid directly; the word almost always shows up as an accusation of its absence — tactless, "he has no tact."
tact ≠ tacit. Tact is a delicate touch; tacit (TAS-it) means unspoken, understood without being said — a tacit agreement. Similar sound, unrelated roots: tangere (touch) vs tacēre (be silent).
Tact is tactile — it's knowing how hard to press.
Same root, same idea: the tactful person handles a raw subject the way you'd handle a bruise, by touch rather than by force.
1. The ambassador broke the news of the refusal with such tact that both delegations left believing they had won something.
2. Maybe don't let Dave give the eulogy — the man has zero tact.
The famous line — usually pinned on Churchill, though nobody can prove he said it — defines it better than any dictionary: "Tact is the ability to tell someone to go to hell in such a way that they look forward to the trip."
Latin tangere / tactus = "to touch." Tact is literally a light touch in handling people.

That root is a GRE goldmine: tactile (touchable), tangible (graspable), tangent (a line just touching a curve), intact (untouched), contact, contagion (spread by touch).

🚫 Not tactics. That's Greek taktikos, "to arrange in order" — an unrelated word that just happens to collide.

Only glancingly related — touches the main point, then veers off.
Only glancingly related to the matter at hand — touching it at one point and then heading off elsewhere. (Literal geometry sense: a tangent line touches a curve at exactly one point.)

It's a soft dismissal. Irrelevant denies any connection; tangential concedes a real one and then rules it out as beside the point — which is why academics and lawyers reach for it. Calling someone's remark tangential is politer than calling it irrelevant, and just as fatal. It also describes a manner of thinking: someone who is tangential wanders off the thread mid-conversation.
A tangent touches the circle once and keeps going — tangential facts touch your point once, then leave.
The single point of contact is the whole idea: real contact, immediately abandoned.
1. The committee ruled the testimony tangential to the charge and struck it from the record.
2. Sorry, this is a bit tangential, but did anyone actually book the venue?
The everyday phrase "going off on a tangent" is this word doing its job — the speaker touched the topic once and shot off in a straight line away from it.
Latin tangere = "to touch." One root, a long list: tangible (touchable), tactile, contact, contagion (touching-together disease), intact (not touched), contingent (touching on circumstances).

column2:
Real enough to touch, measure, or point at.
Literally: able to be touched — having physical substance. In practice, far more often: real enough to be shown, measured, or pointed at rather than merely claimed.

The word does its real work as the opposite of vague. When someone demands tangible results, they aren't asking for something touchable — they're saying that promises, intentions and good feelings don't count as evidence. So tangible carries a faint edge of scepticism about whatever preceded it: a manager asking for tangible progress has already decided the last report was fluff.
Tangible starts with tang — a tang is a taste you can actually detect, not one you're told about.
Both words demand that something register on the senses before you'll believe it exists.
1. The treaty produced no tangible reduction in troop numbers, only a shared vocabulary of restraint.
2. Six months of meetings and not one tangible thing to show for it.
Every company balance sheet splits tangible assets (buildings, machines, stock) from intangible ones (brand, goodwill, patents) — the accountant's line between what you could trip over and what you can only argue for.
Latin tangere = "to touch." One root, a whole GRE cluster: tangent (a line just touching a curve), tangential (barely touching the topic), contact, contagious (caught by touch), tactile, and intact — literally un-touched.

Temptingly attractive but kept just out of reach.
Temptingly attractive — but held just out of reach, so the desire is never satisfied.

The withholding is the word. Anything delicious can be tempting; only something you can almost-but-not-quite have is tantalizing. It carries a built-in gap: the smell through a closed kitchen door, a clue that stops one step short of the answer, a result that's "tantalizingly close." Take away the frustration and you've just got alluring.
Tantalizing = a taunt with a prize attached.
Hear the taunt in tant- — the thing dangles the reward and then pulls it back.
1. The dig yielded a tantalizing fragment of the inscription, breaking off precisely where the king's name would have appeared.
2. We were tantalizingly close to the playoffs — one point, one game, and it slipped away.
Food advertising runs on it: "tantalize your taste buds" is a decades-old ad cliché — the smell reaching you before the meal does.
From Tantalus, the Greek king punished in Hades by being stood in water up to his chin beneath a fruit tree: the water drained away whenever he stooped to drink, the branches lifted whenever he reached to eat. Eternal near-miss.

That myth also named a metal — tantalum, so called because it sits in acid and refuses to absorb any of it, like Tantalus in his pool.

Equal in effect to something graver, though not literally it.
Equivalent in effect or seriousness to something else — even if it isn't that thing literally. Always followed by to: tantamount to treason, tantamount to a confession.

It isn't a maths word. Nobody says two halves are tantamount to a whole; you say it when an act technically isn't the grave thing but counts as it. That gap is the whole point — the speaker is stripping away the technicality and naming what the act really amounts to. So it tends to arrive attached to something damning, in the voice of a prosecutor, an editorial, or a diplomat: refusing to answer was tantamount to admitting it.
⚠️ tantamount ≠ paramount. Same -amount ending, unrelated jobs: tantamount to X = equal in effect to X; paramount = supreme, above all others (safety is paramount). Paramount needs no "to."
Tant-amount — it amounts to the same thing, and what it amounts to is usually bad.
The word amount is sitting inside it, and "amounts to" is exactly how you'd say it in plain speech — walking out now amounts to quitting.
1. The court held that the company's silence, given its duty to disclose, was tantamount to fraud.
2. Asking him to babysit your cat is tantamount to giving the cat away — you're never seeing it again.
A newsroom and courtroom staple — "tantamount to a declaration of war," "tantamount to an admission of guilt." Notice it never introduces good news; hearing the collocation teaches you the tone.
Anglo-French tant amunter = "to amount to as much" — tant (so much) + amounter, from Latin ad montem, "to the mountain," i.e. to go up to a total.

That mount root pays out widely: amount, surmount, insurmountable, paramount, mountain, mount.

To dull the shine of; to blemish a reputation.
Verb: to lose (or cause to lose) shine — metal going dull and discoloured; by extension, to damage a reputation.
Noun: the dull film itself.

The damage is surface-level and gradual. A scandal doesn't tarnish a career the way it ruins one — tarnish means the gleam is gone, not the thing. It also implies there was a shine: you can only tarnish something that was admired. And unlike sully or besmirch, which sound morally outraged, tarnish is cool and factual — the word a newspaper uses.
⚠️ tarnish ≠ burnish. Same ending, opposite jobs: burnish = rub to a shine (and figuratively, to boost a reputation); tarnish = lose the shine. A PR firm burnishes an image; a leak tarnishes it.
Varnish goes on and adds gloss; tarnish creeps in and takes it away.
One letter apart, exact opposites — and both are about a thin surface layer, never the substance underneath.
1. The verdict was overturned, but the accusation had already tarnished a reputation forty years in the making.
2. Don't put the good spoons in the damp cupboard — they'll tarnish in a week.
In Elden Ring, you play as the Tarnished — an exile stripped of the golden grace they once had. Fallen from shine, not destroyed: exactly the word.

Tiresomely long, slow and repetitive.
Tiresome because it is too long, too slow, and too samey — dull in a way that wears down your patience.

The complaint is about duration, not difficulty. Hard work can be gripping; tedious work is easy and endless — form-filling, a meeting that will not end, a speaker circling the same point. Boring describes a thing that fails to interest you; tedious describes a thing that keeps going after it stopped interesting you. It's a mild, civilised word — you can call a report tedious in writing without sounding rude, which is exactly why people reach for it.
tedious vs. odious — they rhyme perfectly and that's the trap. Tedious = boring you to death. Odious = deserving hatred. A tedious colleague wastes your afternoon; an odious one deserves your contempt.
Dull takes one syllable. Te‑di‑ous takes three — the word drags on longer than it needs to, exactly like the thing it describes.
The extra syllables are the meaning: tedium is what happens when something outstays its welcome.
1. The transcript ran to four hundred pages of tedious procedural wrangling before a single witness was called.
2. Sorting the receipts took all evening — mind-numbingly tedious, but somebody had to do it.
It's the standard word in every software pitch: "automate the tedious parts of your workflow." Nobody says difficult there — the promise is to delete the slow, repetitive bits, not the hard ones.

Reckless nerve; presumptuous boldness the speaker resents
Reckless boldness — nerve, gall, audacity in the face of someone or something you should have deferred to.

Courage is admired, audacity can be admired, temerity never is. The word is a verdict, and it's always the offended party's verdict: whoever says it thinks you overstepped, overreached, and didn't know your place. A private who questions the general has temerity; the general who charges the hill has courage. Same nerve, different standing.
⚠️ temerity ≠ timidity. They look like cousins and mean opposites: temerity = too much nerve, timidity = too little. If a sentence rewards you for pairing it with shy or meek, you've picked the wrong word.
Nobody ever simply has temerity — they always "had the temerity to," and somebody is always furious about it.
The word arrives welded to that phrase and to an affronted speaker, so if you can hear the indignation, you've got the nuance.
1. Having lost the case, counsel then had the temerity to bill the estate for his travel.
2. He forgot my birthday and then had the temerity to ask why I was quiet.
Latin temere = "blindly, at random, without thinking" — temerity is boldness with the eyes shut.

🚫 Not related to timid. That's timēre, "to fear" — timid, timorous, intimidate. One letter apart, opposite ideas.

column2:
Moderate by mixing in the opposite; also, toughen by heat.
Verb (the GRE sense): to moderate something strong by mixing in its opposite — justice tempered with mercy, ambition tempered by caution.
Verb (technical): to toughen metal or glass by controlled heating and cooling.
Noun: your habitual state of mind (an even temper), or the loss of it (lost his temper).

To temper is not to cancel. Nothing is deleted — a counterweight is added until the thing sits in proportion, so the result is balanced, not diluted. That's why the metal sense isn't a contradiction: tempered steel isn't softer steel, it's steel brought into balance and made harder to shatter. And note the pull of the verb's usual objects — you temper enthusiasm, expectations, criticism, zeal: always something running hot.
⚠️ temper ≠ tamper.
- temper = moderate it, bring it into balance
- tamper (with) = meddle with it, interfere improperly

A jury's verdict can be tempered by mercy; a juror can be tampered with.
Temper hides temperature — you don't kill the heat, you regulate it.
Both senses run through that one idea: the smith tempers the blade by controlling the heat rather than removing it, and you temper a claim by dialling it down, not dropping it.
1. The judge tempered the severity of the sentence with an acknowledgment of the defendant's youth.
2. Great news, but let's temper expectations — one good quarter isn't a turnaround.
The tempered glass screen protector on your phone — same word, and it shows the sense the definition hides: tempering made that glass tougher, not weaker.
Latin temperāre = "to mix in due proportion." That proportion-mixing idea fans out into a family worth owning: temperature (the degree of heat), temperate (a mild climate, a moderate person), temperance (restraint in drink), temperament (your personal mix), distemper (a bad mix — disorder, disease).

Stormy and violently emotional — usually a relationship, not weather.
Stormy — literally of the weather, but in practice almost always figurative: violently turbulent, driven by high emotion.

The word carries heat, not just trouble. A turbulent decade is unstable; a tempestuous marriage has shouting, slammed doors and passionate reconciliations. It implies people with big feelings, and it borrows the glamour of a storm — which is why journalists reach for it about affairs, divas and volatile geniuses. Applied to a person or relationship it's disapproving, but never dull.
⚠️ tempestuous ≠ temperamental.
- tempestuous = stormy, violently passionate (the storm has broken)
- temperamental = moody, unpredictable (it might, at any moment)

A temperamental soprano sulks; a tempestuous one throws the score at the conductor. Unrelated roots, too.
There's a tempest sitting inside it — and the storm is never the weather, it's the marriage.
Nine times out of ten the thing being called tempestuous is a relationship, a temper or a career, so hear "tempest" and then move it indoors.
1. Their correspondence records a tempestuous decade: three separations, two reconciliations, and one duel.
2. They had a tempestuous thing going for about six months — screaming matches, then flowers, then screaming matches.
Shakespeare's The Tempest — the storm in Act I is conjured by Prospero out of pure rage and grievance, which is exactly the word's figurative sense: weather made of feeling.
Latin tempus = "time" → tempestas = "season, weather" → then, because bad weather is the weather people talk about, "storm."

That single root pays out widely: tempo, temporal, temporary, contemporary, extempore (out of the moment, unrehearsed).

🚫 Not from temper / temperature. Those are Latin temperāre, "to mix in proportion" — hence temperate, temperament, distemper. Similar sound, different family.

Of time; or worldly rather than spiritual.
1. Relating to time — temporal sequence, temporal distortion.
2. Relating to this world rather than the spiritual one — earthly, secular.

Sense 2 is the one the GRE actually wants, and it follows straight from sense 1: what exists in time is perishable, so temporal came to mean everything that isn't eternal. A bishop has spiritual authority; a king has temporal power. Used of ambition or pleasure, it quietly implies smallness — mere worldly stuff, set against something lasting.

(A third, purely anatomical sense: the temporal lobe, behind your temple.)
⚠️ temporal ≠ temporary.
- temporal = of time (or of this world)
- temporary = lasting only a short time

A temporal record spans centuries; a temporary one gets deleted Friday.
Temporal is the exact opposite of eternal — in time, therefore of this world.
Anything caught inside time is earthly and perishable, which is how a word about clocks became a word about kings, money, and everything the soul is supposed to outlast.
1. The papacy's temporal holdings shrank to a few acres, though its spiritual reach was undiminished.
2. He talks about enlightenment a lot for a guy whose goals are all pretty temporal — car, corner office, bigger flat.
Every sci-fi temporal anomaly / temporal paradox — Doctor Who, Star Trek, Loki — is the time sense doing its day job.
Latin tempus, temporis = "time." One root, a lot of GRE mileage: tempo (speed in time), contemporary (sharing a time), extemporaneous (out of the moment, unrehearsed), temporize (stall for time), temporary, and even tempest (via tempestas, "season, weather").

Able to be defended or maintained under attack.
Able to be defended, held, or maintained — of a position, theory, claim, or job.

It began as a military word (a fort you can hold against attack) and now lives mostly in argument: a tenable theory is one that survives cross-examination. Note how modest it is — tenable doesn't mean true or convincing, only that it hasn't yet been demolished. "Her reading of the poem is tenable" is a long way from praise; it means you can't quite disprove it. Applied to a job or a situation, it shifts to survivable: a position that can still be occupied without collapse.
⚠️ tenable ≠ tenuous.
- tenable = holds up
- tenuous = thin, flimsy, barely holding on

They look like cousins and are near-opposites: a tenuous argument is exactly the one that isn't tenable.
You'll almost always meet it wearing the un-: his position became untenable, so he resigned.
Define it backwards from the far commoner untenable — whatever can't be held is untenable, so tenable is the fort still standing.
1. No tenable account of the manuscript's provenance has yet been offered, though three have been attempted.
2. Blaming the intern for a decision he made himself wasn't a tenable line and he knew it.
Political journalism runs on the negative: when a minister's "position becomes untenable", that's the standard press signal that a resignation lands within the week.
Latin tenēre = "to hold" — one of the great GRE root-mines: tenacious (holding on), tenant (one who holds property), tenure (the holding of a post), tenet (a belief you hold), plus retain, contain, sustain, detain, abstain.

Slanted to push a cause while posing as fair.
Written or argued with a deliberate slant — designed to promote a particular cause or conclusion rather than to inform fairly.

The word attaches to things, not temperaments: a tendentious history, a tendentious footnote, a tendentious survey question. And it carries a specific accusation — the piece poses as neutral analysis while quietly steering you. Calling something biased points at the author's blind spot; calling it tendentious says the slant was engineered. It's the standard weapon of the academic book review: polite in sound, lethal in effect.
tendentious ≠ contentious.
- tendentious = slanted toward a cause
- contentious = causing arguments, or itself quarrelsome

A tendentious report is one-sided; a contentious one starts a fight. A dull, careful paper can be tendentious, and a scrupulously fair one can be contentious.
Tendentious has a tendency built into it — the argument is leaning before the evidence arrives.
Same root, same meaning: it tends one way on purpose.
1. Reviewers dismissed the biography as tendentious — every ambiguity in the archive resolved, implausibly, in the subject's favour.
2. "Do you still think the manager is doing a bad job?" is a tendentious question and you know it.
Wikipedia has an actual conduct policy called "Tendentious editing" — for editors who technically follow the rules while bending every article toward one side.
Latin tendere = "to stretch, to aim." A tendentious text is aimed — pointed at a conclusion in advance.

That root is a GRE goldmine: tendency, tension, extend, intend, contend, portend, pretend, and tent (stretched cloth).

Provisional, not final; or hesitant, testing the ground.
Two linked senses:

1. Provisional — arranged but not settled, and everyone knows it may change: a tentative agreement, a tentative date, tentative conclusions.
2. Hesitant — done without confidence, as if testing whether the ground holds: a tentative step, a tentative knock, a tentative smile.

Sense 1 is neutral and businesslike — a placeholder, pencil rather than pen, and no criticism is implied. Sense 2 is about manner, and there the word quietly reports timidity: someone who sounds tentative in a meeting has lost the room. Note the difference from reluctant: a tentative person isn't unwilling, just unsure — they're going ahead, only lightly.
⚠️ tentative ≠ tenuous.
- tentative = not final — it may still change
- tenuous = not strong — thin, flimsy, barely holding (a tenuous grip, a tenuous connection)

A tentative alliance may be rock solid once signed; a tenuous one is already fraying.
A tent isn't a house. You pitch it, and you can un-pitch it tomorrow.
Tentative opens with tent — anything tentative is pitched rather than built, standing only until someone decides otherwise.
1. The two governments announced a tentative settlement, subject to ratification by both parliaments.
2. He gave the door a tentative knock, half hoping nobody was in.
Every Outlook or Google Calendar invite gives you three buttons: Accept, Decline, and Tentative — the "probably, don't hold me to it" answer.
Latin temptāre / tentāre = "to try, to test, to feel out."

Same root gives attempt (to try) and temptation (something testing you) — and tentacle, literally a feeler. Picture how an octopus arm moves and you have sense 2 exactly: reaching out to test before committing.

So thin or slight it could snap at any moment.
Thin, slight, insubstantial — and so weak that it may not hold. Used of connections, arguments, evidence, claims, and grips: a tenuous link, a tenuous grasp on power.

A tenuous claim isn't a lie — it's a claim resting on almost nothing. That's the sting: you're not accused of fabricating, you're told your reasoning is a thread. Compare flimsy, which is blunter and more dismissive, and dubious, which questions honesty rather than strength. Tenuous is the polite, academic word for "this barely holds together," which is exactly why reviewers and judges reach for it.
⚠️ tenuous ≠ tenacious. They look like siblings and are opposites in spirit: tenuous = thin, barely holding (Latin tenuis, thin); tenacious = gripping hard, refusing to let go (Latin tenēre, to hold). A tenacious lawyer can still have a tenuous case.
Tenuous almost never travels alone — it comes with a link, a grasp, a hold, a connection.
Every one of those nouns is something that can snap, which tells you the word is about the strength of an attachment, not the truth of a fact.
1. The prosecution's case rested on a tenuous chain of inference, each link plausible and none of them proven.
2. He's got a pretty tenuous grasp of how the code works — he just restarts it when it breaks.
Newsroom staple: a tenuous ceasefire, a tenuous connection to the suspect — it's the word editors use when something is technically holding but nobody expects it to.
Latin tenuis = "thin". The payoff is the family: attenuate = thin something down, weaken it (attenuated virus, attenuated signal), and extenuating circumstances — facts that literally thin out your guilt.

Lukewarm — in temperature, or in enthusiasm.
Literally: lukewarm — neither hot nor cold. Figuratively: showing little enthusiasm, warmth, or conviction.

The figurative sense is the one the GRE wants, and its sting is that it isn't hostility. A tepid response doesn't attack you; it just fails to care. Cold means rejection, hot means passion — tepid is the flat middle where nobody could be bothered either way. That's why "tepid applause" and "a tepid endorsement" land harder than outright criticism: praise with the heat taken out reads as polite dismissal.
⚠️ tepid ≠ torpid.
- tepid = lukewarm, unenthusiastic
- torpid = sluggish, dormant, barely moving (a hibernating bear is torpid)

A tepid audience claps limply; a torpid audience is asleep.
Tepid rhymes with insipid — and both mean meh.
Insipid food has no flavour and tepid feeling has no heat, so the shared "-pid" ending files them together as the vocabulary of underwhelm.
1. The proposal met with a tepid reception from the board — no objections raised, and no hands offered either.
2. He said he "liked" my haircut in this tepid little voice, which honestly was worse than saying nothing.
"Tepid reviews" is standard critic-speak — the word that surfaces when a film isn't a disaster, just a shrug, and the Rotten Tomatoes score parks somewhere around 45%.

Brief to the point of coldness; few words, no warmth.
Using very few words — brief, clipped, stripped of anything decorative.

But brevity alone isn't the point. Concise is a compliment; laconic is dry and stylish; terse usually comes with a chill. A terse reply is grammatically fine and emotionally shut — the shortness is doing the talking, signalling irritation, reserve, or "this conversation is over." Applied to prose it can be praise (Hemingway is terse), but applied to a person it means they gave you the minimum and nothing more.
⚠️ terse ≠ tense. One letter apart, and both fit "a ___ exchange."
- terse = short on words
- tense = short on ease — strained, anxious

A terse exchange has few words; a tense one may have plenty.
Terse rhymes with curse and worse — the words get cut short, and the mood gets worse.
The rhyme carries the coldness that plain "brief" doesn't have.
1. The minister's terse two-line denial only sharpened the reporters' suspicions.
2. I asked if he was okay and got a terse "fine" — so, obviously, not fine.
Standard newsroom shorthand: when a company or celebrity is caught out, the coverage says they "issued a terse statement" — three sentences, no apology, no questions taken.
Latin tersus = "wiped clean, polished" (from tergēre, to wipe). Terse first meant polished in style — language buffed until nothing surplus remained — and slid from "nothing wasted" to "nothing offered."

Same root scrubs your dishes: detergent = de- (away) + tergēre (wipe).

column2:
Complete in every detail — nothing skipped, nothing left unchecked.
Complete in every respect; done with attention to every part, leaving no gap.

Thorough praises the process, not the talent. A thorough investigator isn't necessarily clever — they simply went everywhere and checked everything. Set against neighbours: meticulous perfects each inch and can shade into fussiness; exhaustive stresses that nothing remains; thorough is the honest, workmanlike middle — full coverage, no shortcuts.

It also works as a flat intensifier before a noun, and there it usually turns nasty: a thorough nuisance, a thorough scoundrel — meaning "completely, in every respect."
⚠️ thorough ≠ through. One extra o changes everything: through = from end to end (preposition), thorough = leaving nothing out (adjective). She went through the files is movement; she was thorough with the files is quality.
thorough = through + an extra O — it goes all the way through, and then some.
The spare letter is the spare effort: a thorough job doesn't just pass through the material, it covers every corner of it.
1. The audit was thorough to the point of cruelty: eleven years of receipts, every one matched to a bank line.
2. Give the pan a thorough scrub — not that thirty-second rinse you did last time.
A thoroughbred racehorse at the Derby is one bred through and through — pedigree verified all the way back, no gaps in the line. Same word, hiding in plain sight.
thorough is through — both from Old English þurh, which split into a short preposition and a long adjective. That history is the definition: to be thorough is to have gone right through the thing.

The family keeps the sense literal: a thoroughfare is a road that runs all the way through (hence the "No Thoroughfare" sign), and thoroughgoing doubles down on the same idea.
column3: g16 register::neutral connotation::positive antonym::meticulous-vs-slapdash connotation::careful-in-every-detail-coverage-precisi intensity::degrees-of-coverage meaning::careful-to-the-last-detail meaning::leaving-nothing-out

column2:
Fearful and hesitant; too nervous to act.
Fearful and nervously hesitant; lacking the nerve to act.

Timid is plain and can be affectionate — a timid child, a timid smile. Timorous is bookish and faintly withering: it paints someone shrinking, hedging, trembling at a decision they ought to make. You'd call a shy toddler timid; you'd call a committee that won't commit to anything timorous. It describes a settled disposition, not a passing flutter of nerves.
timorous ≠ temerity. They look like cousins and mean opposites: timorous = shrinking with fear; temerity (and temerarious) = reckless nerve. The timorous clerk lacked the temerity to speak up.
TIM-er-uhs — say it fast and it's tremulous: the trembling kind of scared.
The near-homophone carries the nuance — not merely quiet, but visibly quivering at the thought of acting.
1. The ambassador's timorous reply satisfied no one: it conceded nothing and defended nothing.
2. Don't be so timorous — just ask her for the raise.
Robert Burns, To a Mouse: "Wee, sleekit, cow'rin, tim'rous beastie" — the small creature bolting from the plough is the picture of the word.
Latin timēre = "to fear." It gives you timid, timorous, and intimidate (literally "to put fear into").

column2:
A long, angry, abusive rant.
A long, angry, abusive speech — a sustained verbal attack, usually delivered at volume and at length.

The word passes judgement on the speaker, not the target. Calling something a tirade says the person lost control, went on far too long, and stopped persuading anyone several minutes ago. Nobody describes their own outburst as a tirade; it is what other people call it afterwards. Length is essential — a single cutting remark can never be one.
Tirade begins with tire — it rants on until everyone in the room is tired of it.
The hidden word carries the key nuance: a tirade is defined by exhausting length, not just anger.
1. His resignation letter degenerated into a three-page tirade against colleagues who had, by then, stopped reading.
2. She launched into a tirade about the parking situation and we just stood there holding our coffees.
Newsroom boilerplate: "launched into a foul-mouthed tirade" is the standard phrase for a footballer at a referee or a politician caught on a hot mic — you've read the sentence a hundred times.
French tirade, from Italian tirata = "a pull, a long drawn-out stretch," from tirare, "to pull." A tirade is speech drawn out — the same tirer gives English retire (to draw back).

Done merely for show; a minimal, symbolic stand-in.
Adj.: done as a minimal gesture — just enough to look like compliance, never enough to matter.
Noun: a sign, mark, or keepsake that stands for something bigger (a token of gratitude; a subway token).

Both senses share one idea — a stand-in for the real thing — but the tone splits hard. The noun is warm or plain: a token of affection is a genuine emblem. The adjective is dismissive, almost an accusation: a token raise, a token apology, a token seat on the board. It concedes that the thing happened while denying it any weight. Watch the collocations — token gesture, token effort, token resistance, token amount — the word almost always sits in front of a noun that should have been substantial and wasn't. Related tokenism is flatly pejorative: including someone as a symbol so you can point at the symbol.
A token is a coin that isn't money — a token effort is work that isn't work.
It's shaped like the real thing, it passes at a glance, and it's worth nothing outside the machine it was minted for.
1. The ministry's inquiry proved a token exercise: three afternoons of testimony, no findings, no consequences.
2. They gave us a token pay rise and expected us to shut up about the extra hours.
The arcade token — you hand over real money and get back a brass disc that looks like a coin, spends like a coin, and buys nothing anywhere else. That gap between looks like currency and is currency is the adjective in one object.
Old English tācen = "sign, mark, portent" — still visible in betoken (to be a sign of). It traces to a root meaning to show, the same one behind Latin dīcere and English indicate, index, digit, dictate.

So the oldest sense is simply a sign — and the modern insult follows straight from it: a token effort is a sign of effort, offered instead of the effort.

column2:
Sluggish inactivity; a near-total loss of energy or motion.
A state of sluggish inactivity — physical, mental, or both: no energy, no motion, no appetite for either. Also the biological sense: the dormant, slowed-metabolism state an animal drops into to survive the cold.

Laziness is a choice and sloth is a sin; torpor is a condition. It carries no moral scolding — the person (or economy, or bureaucracy) isn't refusing to act, they've gone inert. It's a heavy, clinical, slightly literary word, and it stretches easily from a body to an institution: the torpor of a provincial town, decades of administrative torpor.
⚠️ torpor ≠ stupor. They rhyme, so the GRE will happily swap them.
- torpor = sluggish, energyless inactivity (a hibernating animal)
- stupor = dazed near-unconsciousness (a drunk man on the floor)

Torpor is slow. Stupor is senseless.
Torpor = torque-poor. The engine is intact; there's just no force left to turn it.
Torpor isn't refusal to move but the absence of power to move, which is why it fits a hibernating animal and a stalled economy equally well.
1. Reform proposals arrived every spring and died in the same committee, victims of a torpor no minister cared to disturb.
2. Two helpings of biryani and the whole table sank into afternoon torpor.
Nature documentaries use it in its exact technical sense: a hummingbird burns so much fuel that it drops into torpor every night — heart rate crashing, body cooling — just to survive until morning.
Latin torpēre = "to be numb, stiff, motionless." Gives torpid (sluggish) and — the one that sticks — torpedo, originally the electric ray, a fish that numbs what it touches. The weapon was named after the fish.
column3: g14 register::formal connotation::negative antonym::full-of-life-vs-drained-of-it antonym::lying-dormant-vs-breaking-out connotation::energy-gone-pity-attached intensity::boredom-to-total-inertia meaning::sleep-inducing-vs-sleepy-vs-shut-down

column2:
Full of twists — winding, or too convoluted to follow.
Literally: full of bends and turns — a tortuous road, a tortuous mountain river.
Figuratively: so twisting that it's hard to follow — tortuous reasoning, a tortuous negotiation, tortuous prose.

The complaint is about the path, not the pain. A tortuous explanation isn't painful, it's serpentine: it goes there eventually, by way of everywhere else. Circuitous is neutrally roundabout and convoluted stresses tangle, but tortuous carries a faint whiff of evasion — call someone's logic tortuous and you're hinting they twisted it that way on purpose.
tortuous ≠ torturous.
- tortuous = full of twists (a road, an argument)
- torturous = causing agony (a torturous three-hour wait)

The extra r is the one on the rack.
Tor-tu-ous = a tour with too many turns.
You get there in the end, but by a route nobody would design on purpose.
1. The treaty emerged only after eighteen months of tortuous negotiation, each clause bought with a concession elsewhere.
2. His excuse was so tortuous that by the end I'd forgotten what he was apologising for.
Latin torquēre = "to twist." It powers a huge GRE family: torque (twisting force), contort, distort, extort (twist money out of someone), retort (a reply twisted back at you), torsion — and tortilla, the little twisted-and-rolled flatbread.

Torture comes from the same root — the rack twisted the body. So both words twist; the question is only what's being twisted. Road → tortuous. Victim → torturous.

To promote loudly, usually with something to gain.
Verb: to promote something loudly and persistently — to talk it up, usually because you stand to gain. Noun (chiefly British): a street hustler who solicits business; a ticket tout buys up seats and resells them at a markup.

Praise is admiration offered freely; touting is salesmanship with an angle. The word quietly implicates the promoter: whoever is touting has skin in the game, and the claim is probably inflated. That's why the passive form is a journalist's favourite weapon — "touted as the next big thing" almost always sets up the sentence where it wasn't.
⚠️ tout ≠ taut. Same letters, swapped: taut (TAWT) means pulled tight — a taut rope, a taut thriller. A tout is a hustler; taut is tension.
Tout rhymes with shout — and he's shouting about it because he's selling it.
The rhyme gets you the volume, and "selling it" gets you the self-interest that separates touting from honest praise.
1. The ministry touted the reforms as the most sweeping in a generation; independent auditors found the budget unchanged.
2. He's been touting that juicer to everyone in the office since he got it half-price.
When the Oasis reunion tickets sold out in 2024, the outrage was all about touts — resellers who grabbed seats and flipped them for thousands. British headlines used the word straight, no explanation needed.
Old English tōtian = "to peer out, stick out, crane your neck." A tout was originally a lookout — the man scanning the crowd for a mark. That's still exactly where you find him: outside the gate, spotting buyers before anyone else does.

Easily led, managed, or solved.
Easy to manage, control, or deal with. Of a person or animal: obedient, easily led. Of a problem: solvable, workable with the tools you have.

Applied to people it is faintly condescending — praise from the person holding the reins. A tractable employee isn't enthusiastic, just compliant; docile stresses gentleness, pliable stresses being reshaped, but tractable stresses being steerable by someone else. Applied to problems it loses all that and turns purely technical: a tractable equation is one that yields to method rather than defeating it. Its negative twin intractable — a stubborn person, an unsolvable problem, a chronic pain that won't respond to treatment — shows up on the GRE more often than the positive form.
Tractable = tract*or*-able — you can tow it wherever you want.
The credit belongs to the driver, not the thing being pulled, which is exactly why calling a person tractable is a backhanded compliment.
1. The new recruits proved unusually tractable, absorbing the drill without a murmur of complaint.
2. Break the whole thing into small chunks and suddenly it's a tractable problem.
Standard shop-talk in tech and research: a problem is "computationally tractable" if it can actually be solved in reasonable time — and "intractable" if the compute blows up. If you've sat in an engineering review, you've heard it.
Latin trahere, tractus = "to pull, to drag." Tractable = pullable.

That root drags a whole GRE family behind it: tractor (pulls), traction (grip that pulls), attract (pull toward), retract (pull back), extract (pull out), subtract (pull away), protract (drag out), contract (pull together), even treaty and trace.

column2:
Calm and still, as if never disturbed at all.
Free from disturbance — calm, still, quietly peaceful.

Calm is often calm after something: the sea settles, the crowd quiets, you talk someone down. Tranquil implies nothing ever disturbed it in the first place — a settled, undisturbed stillness. It attaches most naturally to places and scenes (a tranquil lake, a tranquil village at dusk), and when applied to a person it describes an untroubled inner state rather than composure under pressure. Warm, faintly literary, always approving.
A tranquilizer has to make you calm; something tranquil already was.
Same root, opposite route — the drug imposes stillness, while tranquil describes stillness that was never broken.
1. The monastery sat above the treeline, so tranquil that the ringing of a single bell carried for miles.
2. We found this tranquil little café behind the station — no music, no queue, nobody in a hurry.
The Moon's Sea of Tranquility — where Apollo 11 landed, giving the most famous radio line in history: "Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed." A place chosen and named for being flat, still and undisturbed.

column2:
To rise beyond a limit or category entirely.
To rise above and beyond a limit, a category, or ordinary experience — to go past something so completely that its rules no longer apply to you.

Compare the neighbours: surpass and exceed are competitive and measurable — you beat a number, a rival, a record, and you stay on the same scale. Transcend leaves the scale behind. A film that surpasses other action films is still an action film; a film that transcends the genre is no longer judged as one. It carries a lift of admiration and often a whiff of the spiritual or philosophical — the self, death, language, the physical world are the things people say get transcended.
⚠️ transcend ≠ transgress. Both start trans- ("across"), but transcend = climb beyond (rise above a limit); transgress = step across (violate a rule). One elevates you, one gets you in trouble.
Ascend gets you to the top of the ladder; transcend means you no longer need the ladder.
Both words are the same -scend ("climb"), but trans- takes you clean out of the system rather than to the top of it.
1. Her late work transcends portraiture altogether; the sitter is almost incidental to what the paint is doing.
2. It started as a school project, but honestly it kind of transcended that — people are using it for real now.
Transcendental Meditation — the practice the Beatles flew to Rishikesh in 1968 to study with the Maharishi, and the reason half the White Album exists. The whole promise in the name: get beyond ordinary thought.
Latin trans (beyond) + scandere (to climb) — literally "to climb beyond."

That -scend is a workhorse: ascend (climb up), descend (climb down), condescend (climb down to someone's level — which is exactly why it's an insult), ascendancy (having climbed to dominance).

An act breaking a moral or legal line; a violation.
A breach of a law, rule, or moral code — an act of crossing a line you were meant to stay behind.

Weight and register are what set it apart. A violation is administrative, a crime is legal, an offence is procedural — a transgression is moral. It belongs to conscience, scripture and sermon, and it implies there was a boundary with authority behind it, not just a regulation. That gravity is also why it flips so easily into dry humour: "forgive my transgressions" over the last slice of cake works precisely because the word is far too grand for the crime.
You confess a transgression; you report a violation.
The verbs it keeps company with tell you the line crossed was a moral one, not a clause in a rulebook.
1. The committee judged his falsification of the data a transgression grave enough to end a thirty-year career.
2. She snuck out at 2am, which in that house counted as a serious transgression.
Isaiah 53:5 — "But he was wounded for our transgressions" — a line most people have heard sung, since Handel set it in Messiah. That biblical home is exactly why the word still smells of sin rather than paperwork.
Latin trans (across) + gradī, gressus (to step, to walk) — literally to step across. The line is right there in the word.

-gress = step unlocks a whole GRE shelf: progress (step forward), regress (step back), digress (step aside, off topic), egress (step out, an exit), congress (step together), aggression (step toward — i.e. at you). Same root gives gradual, grade, degree — steps by another name.

Lasting only briefly; passing through rather than staying.
Adj.: lasting only a short time; passing through rather than staying.
Noun: a person who stays somewhere briefly — a short-stay guest, or (in American news and police usage) a drifter with no fixed address.

Of all the "short-lived" words, this is the cold one. Ephemeral and evanescent are for sunsets and beauty; fleeting has a sigh in it. Transient is the word an engineer, a doctor, or a hotel manager uses — a transient voltage spike, a transient population, a transient fever. It reports impermanence as a fact, with no wistfulness attached, which is exactly what makes the noun sense sound so clinical when it's applied to a human being.
⚠️ transient ≠ intransigent. Transient = passing through. Intransigent = refusing to budge an inch. They share a look, not a root — and they're near-opposites in spirit.
Trans-i-ent = in transit. Anyone in transit is on the way somewhere else.
Same root, same idea — the thing is only passing through, which is a statement of logistics, not a lament.
1. The town's population is largely transient: oil crews arrive in March and the streets are empty again by autumn.
2. Don't panic about the error message — it's transient, it clears itself after a reboot.
A TIA — transient ischaemic attack, the "mini-stroke" — is named for exactly this word: the blockage passes, the symptoms clear within minutes, and that's precisely why people ignore it.
Latin trans (across) + īre (to go) → transīre, "to pass through." The present participle transiēns is literally "going across."

īre is a workhorse root worth banking: transit, transition, exit (ex-it — "he goes out"), itinerant, circuit, perish (per-īre, "to go through to the end").

column2:
Lasting only briefly; a passing phase, not a fixture.
Lasting only a short while; not permanent by its very nature.

Where fleeting is about speed and ephemeral is about sheer brevity, transitory is about impermanence as a property: the thing is a phase, and phases end. It suits abstractions — power, fame, pain, pleasure, an economic condition — and carries a faint moral or philosophical hum, the voice of someone telling you not to get attached. Compare transient, which more often describes things or people literally passing through (a transient population, a transient guest); transitory is what you say about the state of the world, not the man at the door.
⚠️ transitory ≠ transitive.
- transitory = short-lived
- transitive = carrying over to an object — a transitive verb takes one; a transitive relation passes along (if a=b and b=c…).

Same root, opposite usefulness on the exam.
Transitory — whatever it describes is only in transit, never resident.
The word wears transit on its face: it isn't stopping here, it's passing through on its way out.
1. Marcus Aurelius returns again and again to the same consolation: honour, grief and empire alike are transitory.
2. Don't panic about the bad reviews — this stuff is transitory, nobody will remember by Friday.
In 2021 the Federal Reserve insisted that surging prices were "transitory" inflation — a phase that would pass on its own. It didn't, and the word got retired from Fed press conferences in disgrace.
Latin transīre = "to go across" — trans (across) + īre (to go).

That little verb īre is a GRE workhorse: exit (ex- out), transit, circuit (circum- around), initial (in- going in), perish (per-īre, to go through and be gone), ambition (amb-īre, going around canvassing for votes), itinerary.

column2:
A long, systematic book exhaustively covering one subject.
A long, formal, systematic written work that covers one subject thoroughly and methodically.

Size and rigour are the whole point. An essay explores, an article reports, a tract preaches a short partisan message — a treatise sets out to be the definitive handling of its topic, chapter by chapter, from first principles. It implies authority and exhaustiveness, and it implies weight on the shelf.

Because of that heft, it's also the standard word for gentle mockery: any document far longer than the occasion deserved gets called a treatise.
⚠️ treatise ≠ treaty. Same root, different worlds: a treatise is a book that handles a subject; a treaty is a signed agreement between states. Nations sign treaties; scholars write treatises.
A treatise treats one subject — and treats it to death.
To "treat of" a topic is to handle it, and a treatise handles it so completely that nothing is left to say.
1. Hume was twenty-eight when he published his treatise on human nature, three volumes of it, and it fell, in his words, dead-born from the press.
2. He replied to a one-line email with a four-page treatise on why the meeting should be moved.
Hume's A Treatise of Human Nature — the go-to example of the form: a young philosopher trying to settle an entire field in one enormous book.
Latin tractāre = "to handle, to drag about" (from trahere, to pull). To treat a subject is literally to get your hands on it.

That root is a GRE goldmine: tract (a pulled-out stretch of land, or a pamphlet), extract, contract, retract, tractor, traction, protracted.

Sharp and penetrating — criticism that cuts to the heart of it.
Of speech, writing, or analysis: sharp, vigorous and penetrating — it cuts straight to the essential point.

The word praises the mind behind the remark, not the damage it does. Scathing is about hostility, acerbic about sourness of tone; trenchant is about accuracy — the criticism lands because it's right, and you admire the person who made it even if you're the one bleeding. Hence its natural home: reviews, essays, courtroom argument, political commentary. Almost never used for praise or for small talk — a trenchant compliment sounds wrong; a trenchant critique sounds inevitable.
⚠️ trenchant ≠ truculent. Both sound aggressive and start the same way, but truculent means belligerent and scowling — a bad temper, not a good argument. A trenchant critic is worth reading; a truculent one is just spoiling for a fight.
Trenchant has trench in it — it doesn't bruise the argument, it cuts a channel clean through it.
A trench is a deep, deliberate cut, which is exactly the difference between a merely angry remark and a trenchant one.
1. Her dissent was the most trenchant paragraph in the entire judgment: four sentences that dismantled the majority's reasoning.
2. He doesn't say much in meetings, but when he does it's usually pretty trenchant — one question and the whole plan falls apart.
Read the back of almost any serious non-fiction paperback and you'll find it: "a trenchant analysis of…" is standard blurb-speak for a book that cuts deep, and reviewers reach for it constantly.
French trancher = "to cut" (ultimately Latin truncare). Same root gives you trench (a cut in the ground), retrench (cut back spending), truncate (cut short), and trenchant — literally cutting.

column2:
Too small or slight to be worth bothering about.
So small, slight or unimportant that it isn't worth attention — a trifling sum, a trifling error, a trifling delay.

The word doesn't just measure size, it passes judgement. Small is a fact; trifling is a shrug — the speaker has already decided the thing is beneath discussion, and often sounds a little grand doing it. It's the register of lawyers, memoirs and polite contempt.

Turned on a person, it flips from "tiny" to "frivolous, unserious, not worth relying on" — a trifling young man. (In Southern US and Black American English, triflin' sharpens this further: lazy, useless, no-account.)
Tri-FLING — small enough to fling away, and calling it that is always a put-down.
The buried fling gives you both halves at once: negligible in size, and dismissed with a flick of the wrist.
1. The defence dismissed the discrepancy as a trifling clerical error, unworthy of the court's time.
2. He got this worked up over a trifling ten quid?
The dessert trifle — sponge, jam and whipped cream, gloriously mostly air — is named for exactly this: a light nothing. Rachel's beef-and-custard disaster in Friends is the version everyone remembers.

So small or ordinary it isn't worth your attention.
So small, ordinary or inconsequential that it isn't worth attention or effort.

Minor concedes that a thing is small but real; trivial denies it any weight at all. It's a verdict rather than a measurement — call someone's objection trivial and you've dismissed it, not sized it. That sting is why "this isn't trivial" is a standard way of insisting something matters.

One neutral exception worth knowing: in maths, logic and programming, a trivial case or trivial solution just means the degenerate, obvious one (x = 0) — no insult, pure jargon.
TRIVIAL = TRIVIA + al — pub-quiz facts: perfectly true, and nobody's life depends on them.
The hidden word carries the exact nuance — trivial things aren't false or tiny, they're simply not worth anyone's attention.
1. The court held the breach trivial, awarding damages of a single pound.
2. Stop sweating the font — that's trivial, we ship tomorrow.
Trivial Pursuit — the board game built entirely out of facts that are fun to know and useless to have. Same root as trivia, and the name is the definition.
Latin trivium = tri- ("three") + via ("road") — a fork where three roads met. That's the public street corner, so trivialis meant "the sort of thing you hear at a crossroads": common, vulgar, everyday chatter.

The via half is a workhorse: deviate (off the road), devious, viaduct, convey, and obvious — literally ob viam, "lying in the road" right in front of you.

column2:
Aggressively sullen; scowling and spoiling for a fight.
Aggressively defiant and hostile — scowling, bristling, obviously spoiling for a fight. Of speech or writing: savagely harsh, out to wound.

Anger alone isn't enough. Truculent describes a settled disposition, not a flare-up: the person is sullen and combative at once, radiating a dare. It also carries a whiff of the subordinate resisting authority — the truculent teenager, the truculent witness, the truculent shop steward. Where belligerent means actively attacking you, truculent means glowering at you, waiting for an excuse.
TRUCK-ulent — he comes at you like a truck, and he's already revving.
The hidden truck gives you the aggression and the sheer bulk of the mood — heavy, oncoming, daring you not to move.
1. The witness grew steadily more truculent, answering each question with a question of his own.
2. One coffee before nine and he's fine; without it he's truculent all morning.
Latin trux, trucis = "fierce, savage, grim" — used of wild beasts and of faces.

🚫 Nothing to do with truce. That's Old English trēow, "pledge, good faith" — the exact opposite mood. The lookalike is pure coincidence.

column2:
Cloudy with stirred-up sediment; by extension, muddled.
Cloudy, thick, opaque — water (or any liquid) you can't see through because sediment is churned up in it. Figuratively: muddled, confused — turbid prose, turbid emotions.

The murk is suspended, not dyed: something stirred the bottom and it hasn't settled. That's the difference from murky, which is the everyday word and drifts into moral vagueness (murky dealings); turbid stays physical and precise, which is why lab reports and river surveys use it. Applied to writing or thought, it accuses you of clouding a thing that could have been clear.
⚠️ turbid ≠ turgid.
- turbid = cloudy, full of stirred-up silt
- turgid = swollen — and of prose, bloated and pompous

Turgid writing is overblown; turbid writing is unclear. Both are insults, different ones.
Turbid water has been dis-TURB-ed — the mud is up off the bottom.
The word hides disturb, which pins the exact nuance: the cloudiness comes from stuff stirred into suspension, not from dirt staining the water.
1. After the storm the river ran turbid and brown, carrying half the hillside toward the sea.
2. His explanation got more turbid the longer he talked, until nobody knew what he was actually asking for.
Turbidity is a number people actually measure — your city's water-quality report, a pool test kit, an aquarium filter spec, all rated in NTU (nephelometric turbidity units). Low turbidity = you can see through it.
Latin turba = "crowd, uproar" → turbidus, "stirred up." A milling crowd and clouded water are the same idea: everything churning at once.

Same root: disturb, perturb, turbulent, trouble, turbine — all things that stir.

column2:
Violently unsettled and unstable — churning air, water, or times.
Violently disturbed and unstable — churning, unpredictable motion. Used literally of air, water and weather (turbulent seas), and figuratively of periods, crowds, emotions and relationships (a turbulent decade, a turbulent marriage).

The force here is disorder, not malice. A turbulent situation isn't attacking anyone — it's heaving and unsettled, refusing to hold still, and nobody can predict what it does next. That's what separates it from violent (deliberate force) and chaotic (no pattern at all): turbulence has plenty of energy, just no stability. Applied to a person, it shades into "unruly, troublemaking."
⚠️ turbulent ≠ truculent.
- turbulent = churning, unstable — a state of disorder
- truculent = aggressively defiant, spoiling for a fight — an attitude

Turbulent seas; a truculent teenager.
Turbulent has disTURB buried in it — it doesn't hit you, it just won't sit still.
Same turb- as disturb and perturb: the word is about being unsettled and churned up, not about deliberate aggression.
1. The republic emerged from a turbulent decade of coups, currency collapse and street violence with its institutions barely intact.
2. Their first year of marriage was pretty turbulent — three house moves and a lot of shouting.
Henry II's outburst about Thomas Becket — "Who will rid me of this turbulent priest?" — four knights took it literally and murdered the archbishop. Note the sense: Becket wasn't violent, he was unruly and impossible to settle.
Latin turba = "a crowd, an uproar" — picture a mob, and you have the whole word. Gives you disturb (stir the crowd up), perturb (thoroughly unsettle), turbid (water clouded by churned-up sediment), and via turbo (a spinning top) even turbine.

Swollen; or writing swollen with pompous, tedious grandeur.
Literally: swollen, distended, bloated with fluid — a turgid river, turgid tissue.

On the GRE, almost always figurative: writing or speech that is inflated, ponderous, and exhausting to get through.

Where bombastic is loud and grandiloquent is showy, turgid is heavy. A bombastic speaker at least entertains you; turgid prose puffs itself up and puts you to sleep at the same time. The word passes judgement on the effect — you sank in it. That double charge, pompous and tedious, is why it's the reviewer's favourite insult for a bad novel or a bad report.
⚠️ turgid ≠ turbid.
- turgid = swollen (prose, rivers, egos)
- turbid = cloudy, muddy, murky (water, thinking)

Turbid water is unclear; turgid writing is unbearable.
Turgid prose is gorged — stuffed with words, not ideas.
The g in turgid pulls in gorged: fat, full, and slow-moving, which is exactly what the word accuses a piece of writing of being.
1. The commission's turgid report buried its one useful recommendation under forty pages of throat-clearing.
2. I quit his novel by page thirty — "turgid" doesn't begin to cover it.
British football commentary lives on this word — a dire goalless match is "a turgid 0-0" in every match report on the Monday. Same idea as the prose sense: bloated, slow, nothing happening.
Latin turgēre = "to swell." Biology kept it straight: turgor pressure is the water pressure that keeps a plant cell swollen and a leaf standing up — let it drop and the plant wilts.

🚫 Not turbid. That's Latin turba, "crowd, uproar" — which also gives you disturb, turbulent, perturb. Stirred-up, hence murky. Different root, different word.
