column2:
Depravity; base, shameful wickedness — usually "moral turpitude".
Depravity — wickedness of a base, shameful, disgraceful kind.

This isn't a word for ordinary bad behaviour. Where wickedness is moral and misconduct is procedural, turpitude is the vocabulary of tribunals: conduct so foul it disqualifies you — from the job, the office, the country. It survives almost entirely inside the fixed legal phrase moral turpitude, so it carries a whiff of the statute book. Used of everyday failings, it's deliberately grandiose, and usually a joke.
⚠️ turpitude ≠ torpitude. There's no such word — you're reaching for torpor (Latin torpēre, "to be numb"): sluggishness, inertia, the family of torpid and torpedo (the ray that numbs you). Turpitude is Latin turpis, "vile" — filth, not laziness. A sinner has turpitude; a sloth has torpor.
Turp- ≈ turd: turpitude is moral filth — and it almost never appears without moral bolted in front of it.
The gross-out sound gives you the meaning and the collocation gives you the register: this is the word of disciplinary boards and visa forms, not of everyday scolding.
1. The bar association struck him off not for incompetence but for moral turpitude — four years of quietly forged client signatures.
2. Mate, you were twenty minutes late, it's not exactly turpitude — nobody's revoking your badge.
Every US visa application asks whether you have ever been arrested for "a crime involving moral turpitude." That form is where most people meet this word for the first and only time — and it tells you everything about its register.

Everywhere at once; impossible to get away from.
Present everywhere at once; found in every place you look.

Stronger than common or widespread. Common is a statement of frequency; ubiquitous is a statement of inescapability — the thing has saturated the environment so completely you stop noticing it. It also carries a faint weariness when applied to fads, logos, or slogans: ubiquitous often means "and frankly, enough." Applied to infrastructure (wifi, sensors), it's purely neutral and slightly admiring.
ubiquitous ≠ iniquitous.
- ubiquitous = everywhere
- iniquitous = grossly unjust, wicked (iniquity = sin)

An iniquitous regime; a ubiquitous advert.
You can't quit it — it's already everywhere. (ubi-QUIT-ous)
The hidden quit holds the nuance: a ubiquitous thing isn't merely frequent, it's something you can't get away from.
1. By the late 1990s the mobile phone had become ubiquitous, altering the texture of public life before anyone thought to object.
2. That song was ubiquitous last summer — supermarket, taxi, gym, wedding, my own head at 3am.
Ubiquitous computing is a real, named field — Mark Weiser's 1988 term at Xerox PARC for computers dissolving into everyday objects. That's the world you now live in, and it's why the word turns up constantly in tech writing.
Latin ubīque = "everywhere," from ubi = "where."

Same root gives ubiquity, and ubiquitin — the protein was literally named for being found in every cell they looked in.

Hidden beyond what's stated — especially a concealed motive.
Lying beyond what is openly stated — kept back, undisclosed. Chiefly of motives: the real reason, hiding behind the reason you were given.

It does not mean evil, only concealed — and the charge lands on the hiding, not the aim. A man with an ulterior motive for buying you dinner may only want a job reference. The word is also almost welded to one noun: nine times out of ten you'll meet it as ulterior motive(s), delivered as a raised eyebrow rather than an outright denunciation — polite suspicion, the sort you can voice at a dinner table.
Interior, exterior, ulterior — the -erior that sits further out than the reason you were shown.
All three are Latin comparatives of position, and ulter means "beyond," so an ulterior motive is simply the one parked further back than the visible one.
1. The committee's sudden concern for procedure was widely read as ulterior — a way to bury the report without appearing to.
2. He's been weirdly nice all week, so obviously there's an ulterior motive.
Latin ulter = "beyond" — ulterior is its comparative ("farther"), ultimus its superlative ("farthest"). That gives you ultimate (the farthest point), ultimatum (the final demand), ultra- (beyond the limit: ultraviolet, ultrasonic), and, via French outre, outrage — going beyond all bounds.

Offence or resentment, especially taken a shade too readily.
Offence, resentment, or wounded pride — the feeling of having been slighted.

It survives almost entirely in one phrase: to take umbrage at something. That phrasing carries a faint eyebrow-raise. Where offended is neutral about whether the offence was warranted, umbrage quietly suggests the person is a touch thin-skinned and rather enjoys the grievance — it's the word for a colonel bristling at a junior officer's tone, not for someone hurt by real cruelty. Formal, slightly arch, and often used at the expense of the person taking it.
You never feel umbrage — you take it, the way you take a stand.
The verb gives the game away: this offence is picked up and held on purpose, which is why the word always hints at self-importance.
1. The ambassador took umbrage at being seated below the trade delegation and left before the toast.
2. Don't take umbrage, but that shirt is doing you no favours.
Dolores Umbridge in Harry Potter — Rowling built the name on umbrage, and the character is one long fit of bristling, punitive offence-taking.
Latin umbra = "shadow." Umbrage first meant literal shade, then "a shadow cast over someone" — a slight — and finally the resentment itself.

The root is everywhere: umbrella (a little shade), penumbra (half-shadow), adumbrate (to sketch in shadow, to foreshadow), sombre (sub umbra, under shadow).

Plain; without decoration or embellishment.
Plain — carrying no decoration, ornament, or embellishment. Used of rooms, dress, prose, and facts.

The word is descriptive, and often quietly approving: drab and bare say something is lacking, but unadorned says nothing unnecessary was added. A cathedral is ornate; a Quaker meeting house is unadorned — and the second is a choice, not a failure. Applied to speech or writing it means stripped of flourish, which on the GRE usually pairs with honesty: the unadorned truth is the truth with no flattering trim on it.
un-AD-ORN-ed — nothing has been ORNamented onto it.
The orn sitting in the middle of the word is the same orn as in ornament, so unadorned = ornaments removed, not beauty removed.
1. The chapel was unadorned — whitewashed walls, wooden benches, and a single window above the altar.
2. She gave me the unadorned version: the deal was dead, and it had been dead for a week.
Journalists and lawyers live on the collocation "the plain, unadorned facts" — facts with no spin, no adjectives, no narrative bolted on.
adorn ← Latin ad- (to) + ornāre (to equip, to embellish). Same root gives ornament, ornate, and suborn (literally to equip secretly — i.e. to bribe a witness).

So ornate and unadorned are exact opposites built from the same Latin block.

Pure and complete, with nothing lesser mixed in.
Pure, unmixed, complete — with nothing lesser stirred in to dilute it.

It lives almost entirely with positive abstractions: unalloyed joy, unalloyed delight, unalloyed admiration, an unalloyed success. You don't get unalloyed misery. And note how often it arrives negated — "the deal was not an unalloyed good" is the reviewer's civilised way of saying there's a catch. Compared with pure (plain, wide-ranging) or utter (blunt, loud), unalloyed is formal and faintly wry: it concedes that a bit of alloy is the normal state of things.
The word is just un- + alloy: gold with no cheap metal stirred in.
An alloy dilutes precious metal with base metal, so unalloyed joy is joy with no cheaper feeling mixed into it.
1. Her return to the stage after twelve years was met with unalloyed delight.
2. Free pizza and no meeting? Mate, that's unalloyed good news.
Op-ed and boardroom boilerplate: "not an unalloyed good." Whenever a columnist says that about AI, globalisation, or a merger, they mean good, but there's a catch — which is exactly why the word is worth owning.
From alloy ← Old French aloier ← Latin alligare = "to bind to" (ad- + ligare, "to tie"). An alloy is a metal bound to another, usually a cheaper one — so unalloyed is metal bound to nothing.

The lig- root ties a lot together: ally, alliance, ligament, oblige, liable.

To weaken something by removing the support beneath it.
Verb: to weaken something by taking away what holds it up — undercut an argument, a policy, your own authority. Also commercial: to sell cheaper than a rival, taking their customers out from beneath them.

Nothing is attacked head-on. What's undercut is still standing, just hollow: the claim remains on the page, but the support under it is gone. Set it against undermine — undermining is patient, usually deliberate, a slow tunnelling under someone's position over months. Undercutting takes one gesture, and it is very often self-inflicted: the trembling voice that undercuts the confident speech, the single exception that undercuts the whole rule.
You undermine a rival over months; you undercut him in a sentence.
Undermining is slow deliberate sabotage, while undercutting is a single stroke that pulls the floor away — and it's usually the speaker's own slip that does it.
1. The witness's cheerful contradiction on cross-examination undercut the entire theory of the prosecution's case.
2. They undercut us by two quid a unit, and just like that we lost the contract.
The haircut called an undercut — shaved underneath, long on top — is the word doing its literal job: the whole mass is left in place, the support beneath it is cut away.
Plain under + cut, and the source is mining and logging: you undercut a coal seam or a tree by chopping a notch out of its base, so the mass above comes down under its own weight. That's the figurative sense exactly — you never touch the top, you remove what it rests on.

column2:
To weaken gradually and covertly, from underneath.
To weaken something gradually and from below — to erode its support until it can no longer hold: someone's authority, a rival's credibility, public confidence, the premise of an argument.

The damage is slow, indirect, and usually deniable. Sabotage is a single destructive act; attack and denounce happen in the open, on the record. Undermining is the opposite posture — smiles in the meeting, doubts dropped in the corridor. Note also what it takes as an object: things that stand on a foundation. You undermine authority, trust, a case, a regime — not a person's arm or a rock.
Nobody ever undermines you to your face — the digging happens underground.
The word carries its own method: covert, beneath notice, and visible only when the thing above finally falls.
1. Each leaked memo further undermined the minister's claim that she had known nothing.
2. He kept undermining me in front of the team — never disagreeing outright, just "clarifying" everything I said.
The Incredibles ends with The Underminer drilling up through the street — a villain who literally attacks from below, named for exactly this word.
The mine here isn't a coal mine — it's the siege tactic. Attackers dug a tunnel (a mine) under the castle wall, propped the roof with timber, then burned the props: the tunnel collapses, and the wall comes down with it. No breach, no battering ram — the wall simply loses what it was standing on.

Same root gives you landmine and minefield: the buried threat you don't see until it goes off.

column2:
To emphasize; to make something impossible to overlook.
Verb: to emphasize; to make a point impossible to miss.
Noun: the line drawn under text — and the `_` key.

On the GRE it's almost always the verb, and the giveaway is who does the underscoring: usually not a person but an event, a fact, a statistic. A crash underscores the need for regulation. The word carries a quiet implication — the importance was already there; the event merely made it visible. That's what separates it from stress or insist (a speaker pushing) and from exaggerate (inflating). Underscoring adds no volume, just a pointing finger. Neutral, slightly formal, at home in editorials and reports.
A score is a scratch — you scratch a line under the sentence you don't want skipped.
The mark itself does nothing to the sentence; it just makes the reader's eye stop there, which is exactly what the verb means.
1. The committee's own data underscored the fragility of the system it had been defending for a decade.
2. Losing my keys twice in one week really underscores the fact that I need one place to put them.
It's the house verb of serious journalism — every news report ends with some version of \"the incident underscores growing concerns about…\". Spot that sentence once and the word is yours.
Score comes from Old Norse skor = "a notch, a cut." Debts and points were once tallied by cutting notches into a stick — hence keep score, settle a score, and scoreline. Under + score = cut a line underneath.

Deliberately restrained; effective precisely because it doesn't announce itself.
Deliberately restrained — presented with less emphasis, volume, or decoration than the thing could easily carry.

Almost always a compliment, and a quietly class-coded one: it credits someone with enough confidence not to shout. A black dress with no jewellery is understated; an actor who lets a silence do the work is understated. That separates it from plain or modest, which describe what's simply absent — understated implies real substance held back on purpose. Aim it at a number instead of a style, though, and it sours: an understated death toll means someone pitched the figure too low.
⚠️ understated ≠ underrated.
- understated = restraint chosen by the thing itself
- underrated = a verdict handed down by everyone else, who don't value it enough

An understated watch can be world-famous. An underrated one, by definition, isn't.
The word wears its meaning: under-stated, said below full strength — on purpose.
That "on purpose" is the whole compliment, since nobody praises an accidental whisper.
1. The memorial's power lies in its understated design: one long slab of names, and nothing else.
2. Calling that meeting "a bit tense" is the most understated thing I've heard all week.
"Understated elegance" is boilerplate in watch and car reviews and luxury ad copy — and it always means the same thing: expensive, and refusing to say so.

column2:
Applying to every case or person, with no exceptions.
Applying to every member of a group without a single exception — and, by extension, found everywhere.

Strength is what separates it from its neighbours. Widespread tolerates holdouts, general quietly admits exceptions, common just means frequent — but universal claims totality, so one counterexample destroys it. That absoluteness is exactly why GRE argument passages love the word: when an author calls something universal, the question usually turns on the case that isn't covered.
Universal has the universe inside it — and nothing sits outside the universe.
If even one case escapes the rule, it was never universal, only common.
1. The declaration asserts rights held to be universal, binding on every state regardless of custom or creed.
2. Pizza is basically the universal food — I've never met anyone who says no to it.
A universal remote — the one that works with any brand of TV. That's the meaning in a plastic shell: no exceptions, everything covered.
Latin unus (one) + vertere / versus (to turn) — "turned into one," rolled into a single whole.

Both halves pay off elsewhere: unus gives unify, unison, unanimous; vertere gives convert, divert, avert, invert, adverse, versatile.

Never done before; no earlier case exists on record.
Never done, known, or seen before — there is no earlier case of it on record.

Strictly, it's a claim about the historical record, not about size or drama: a thing can be tiny and still unprecedented. News and marketing have worn it down into a vague intensifier meaning "huge," but the GRE will use it literally — no prior instance. Note also that it says nothing about likelihood: an event can be fully predicted and still unprecedented, because prediction looks forward and precedent looks back.
⚠️ unprecedented ≠ unpredicted. Unprecedented = it has never happened before. Unpredicted = nobody saw it coming. Epidemiologists predicted a pandemic for years; when it came, it was still unprecedented in living memory.
Un-PRECEDENT-ed — a judge with no precedent has no case to cite.
The whole word is just precedent wrapped in negatives, so it points at the empty archive, not at how big or shocking the thing is.
1. The court's ruling was unprecedented: no bench had ever extended the doctrine to private contracts.
2. Three sick days in one week? For him that's unprecedented — the man came in with a broken wrist once.
2020 made it a punchline: every brand email on earth opened with "in these unprecedented times," until the phrase became a joke about corporate filler.
Latin prae- (before) + cedere (to go) — a precedent is literally the thing that "went before."

That root is a GRE goldmine: precede, recede, secede, concede, accede, antecedent, cede, procedure.

To untangle and solve — or to progressively fall apart.
Literally, to undo something woven or knitted by pulling its threads apart. Figuratively it runs in two opposite directions, and the GRE tests both:

- Transitive — you unravel it: to untangle and solve. Unravel the mystery, the plot, the accounting fraud. Patient, thread-by-thread work; the answer was always in there, knotted up.
- Intransitive — it unravels: to fall apart progressively. The ceasefire unravelled. His marriage unravelled. Not a sudden break but a slow, self-accelerating disintegration — one thing gives, then everything attached to it.

What links them is the sweater: the same pull that reveals the pattern also destroys the garment. Note the tone difference — the first is a compliment to someone's intelligence, the second is an obituary for something that used to hold together.
⚠️ ravel is not the opposite of unravel. Ravel means to fray or tangle — and, confusingly, also to unravel. The `un-` here doesn't reverse anything, so if a passage uses ravel, do not read it as "weave back together."
Same loose thread, two endings: the detective unravels the case, the suspect unravels on the stand.
Pulled deliberately it yields the truth; pulled by circumstance it just comes apart — one verb, both outcomes.
1. Three years of forensic accounting were needed to unravel the shell companies the money had been threaded through.
2. She held it together through the funeral and then unravelled completely in the car park.
"Unravel" — the Tokyo Ghoul opening theme, a song entirely about a mind coming apart at the seams. The intransitive sense, four minutes long.

Willing to cheat or exploit, with no conscience getting in the way.
Having no moral restraint — willing to lie, cheat, or exploit people to get what you want.

The word points at a missing brake rather than a wicked heart. A scrupulous person hesitates; the unscrupulous one simply doesn't feel the tug. So it usually describes method, not personality, and lands on people operating in a system: unscrupulous lenders, landlords, developers, campaign managers. It also quietly implies competence — the unscrupulous tend to win, which is exactly why they're worth warning about. Milder and more clinical than evil or depraved; sharper and more deliberate than dishonest, which can be a one-off lapse.
un-SCREW-pulous — he'll screw you over and not lose a minute's sleep.
The sound hook carries the whole nuance: not just that he does you harm, but that nothing inside him objects.
1. The inquiry found that unscrupulous brokers had sold complex derivatives to pensioners who could not possibly have understood them.
2. Don't buy a used car from that guy — he's completely unscrupulous, he'll wind the odometer back and smile at you while he does it.
It's the standard word in consumer-protection warnings — trading-standards notices and scam alerts perpetually warn about "unscrupulous traders" and "unscrupulous contractors" preying on the elderly.
Latin scrupulus = a small sharp stone — the pebble in your sandal you can't ignore. It came to mean a tiny nagging doubt, and then a scruple: the moral pang that makes you stop.

So unscrupulous is literally nothing in the shoe. Nothing pricks; he keeps walking.

Same root: scruple, scrupulous (careful to the point of conscience), scrupulosity.

Improper; offending against good taste or dignity.
Not proper, not fitting, offending against good taste or dignity — especially given the occasion, the setting, or the person's position.

The offence is against decorum, not morality. An unseemly act doesn't harm anyone; it looks bad — grabbing at an inheritance before the funeral, a judge shouting in court, two ministers bickering on camera. That's why the word is a favourite of polite disapproval: it's genteel, slightly old-fashioned, and used by someone who is embarrassed for you rather than angry at you. Compare disgraceful (moral condemnation) and rude (blunt, personal): unseemly is cooler and more institutional — a raised eyebrow, not a raised voice.
unseemly ≠ unsightly. Unsightly = ugly to look at (a scar, a heap of rubbish). Unseemly = improper to be seen doing. An unsightly building; an unseemly argument.
Un-SEEM-ly — it doesn't seem right. Not wrong in the soul, wrong in the room.
The hidden seem is the whole point: the word judges how a thing appears to onlookers, so it condemns bad taste rather than sin.
1. The heirs began dividing the estate with an unseemly haste that the family solicitor found difficult to watch.
2. Maybe don't text your ex at your brother's wedding — it's a bit unseemly.
Political and legal reporting runs on two set phrases: "unseemly haste" and "an unseemly row" — the press's polite way of saying this looked awful without alleging anything actionable.
From Old Norse sœmiligr, "becoming, fitting," from sœma = to befit. That's the same root as seem, which originally meant "to be fitting" — the modern sense "appear to be" came later.

So the spelling isn't a coincidence you have to memorise: seemly = as it should appear, unseemly = not as it should appear.

to scold sharply, naming the fault to someone's face
To scold someone severely, reproaching them face-to-face for a specific fault.

You always upbraid someone for something — the offence gets named. That's what separates it from berate (sheer volume), reprimand (official, on the record), and chide (mild, almost fond). Upbraiding is reproach: moral disappointment with an edge, delivered by someone who assumes they hold the high ground. It's also bookish — people don't upbraid each other in a kitchen argument, they write about it afterwards.
Up + braid — your faults get dragged up and braided together into one long rope.
Upbraiding isn't one sharp bark, it's a sustained recital of everything you did wrong, woven strand by strand.
1. The abbot upbraided the young monk for his idleness, item by item, until the boy stared at the flagstones.
2. She upbraided him for forgetting her birthday — again — and he had absolutely no defence.
The King James Bible, James 1:5: God "giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not" — i.e. gives without throwing it back in your face later. That line is why the word still sounds pulpit-formal.
Old English upbrēdan = up + bregdan ("to pull, snatch, weave" — the ancestor of braid). The original sense was to throw something up against a person as a reproach. The fault is lifted up and flung in their face.

column2:
Smoothly polished and socially at ease, especially in conversation.
Smooth, polished and socially at ease — the poise of someone who has been everywhere, met everyone, and can keep a difficult dinner table talking.

The word is about surface, and that's a compliment — an urbane person is unruffled, lightly witty, never earnest or awkward. It's more than polite: politeness is following rules, urbaneness is making the rules look unnecessary. It skews male, older, and worldly, and it carries a faint suggestion that the charm may be all there is — call a man urbane and you praise his manner while saying nothing at all about his depth.
⚠️ urban ≠ urbane.
- urban = of the city (urban planning, urban decay)
- urbane = of the city's manners (an urbane host)

Same root, one letter apart, completely different exam answer.
Urban is where you're from; urbane is what the city did to your manners.
The extra -e adds the polish and pulls the stress to the fancy end — er-BAYN — turning a place into a personality.
1. The ambassador was urbane to the last, deflecting a hostile question with a joke about his own tailoring.
2. He's the most urbane guy in the office — somehow he can tell you your work is rubbish and you leave feeling flattered.
Urbane is the standing epithet film critics reach for with Cary Grant — dinner jacket, raised eyebrow, never once flustered. If you can picture Grant, you have the definition.
Latin urbs = "city" → urbānus, "of the city," hence refined. Rome's insult pair was urbānus vs rūsticus — city-smooth against country-clumsy — which is why rustic still means rough-edged today.

The same urbs gives you urban, suburb (sub- = under/near the city) and urbanise.

Built for use, not beauty; plainly functional.
Adj.: made for use, not for looks — strictly functional, plain, no ornament. Also: relating to utilitarianism, the ethics of "greatest good for the greatest number." Noun: a person who holds that view.

Applied to objects and buildings, it's faint praise with a shrug inside it: the thing works, and that is genuinely all you can say for it. Not ugly — ugliness takes effort — just indifferent to beauty. Compare spartan (bare by discipline, almost proud of it) and austere (severe, morally weighted); utilitarian carries no principle at all, only usefulness. In the philosophical sense the word goes fully neutral and technical, so let the sentence tell you which one you're looking at.
Utilitarian wears utility on its sleeve — and nobody has ever decorated a utility room.
The utility room holds the boiler and the mop: it exists to work, and no one asked it to be nice.
1. The post-war housing estates were relentlessly utilitarian — concrete, right angles, and not one gesture toward grace.
2. The kitchen's pretty utilitarian, but honestly? Everything's within reach and nothing's ever broken.
Utilitarianism — Bentham and Mill's "the greatest happiness of the greatest number" — is the same word doing philosophy: judge an action purely by how useful the outcome is, never by how noble it looks.
Latin utilis = "useful," from uti = "to use." Same root gives utility, utensil, utilise, and utilitarian — all of them about a thing earning its keep by doing a job.

Completely — usually of something extreme and bad.
Completely, absolutely, to the very limit — with nothing left over.

It is not interchangeable with completely. Completely measures ("completely full", "completely covered"); utterly judges. It attaches to states and qualities, usually extreme and usually bad — utterly ruined, utterly useless, utterly exhausted, utterly appalled. You can be completely full, but never utterly full.

Register is a notch above totally, which is casual teenage emphasis. Utterly is the intensifier of someone genuinely at the end of their patience — a critic, a disappointed parent, a narrator.
Utterly = outerly — pushed all the way out to the edge, and the edge is usually a cliff.
The word literally means "to the outermost degree," and what sits out at that extreme is nearly always something dire — ruin, uselessness, exhaustion.
1. The expedition's plan, drawn up in comfort a continent away, proved utterly unsuited to the terrain.
2. I'm utterly knackered — don't ask me to look at another spreadsheet tonight.
The pull-quote on any film poster or book jacket: "Utterly compelling." "Utterly devastating." Critics reach for utterly precisely because very sounds weak and totally sounds unserious.
From Old English ūtera = "outer" — the comparative of ūt, "out." To do something utterly is to take it as far out as it goes.

That root gives you out, outer, utmost (= outmost), and the adjective utter in utter nonsense, utter chaos.

🚫 Don't fuse it with the other utter — to utter a word — which came in separately from Middle Dutch ūteren, "to make known." Same spelling, different job.

To waver back and forth, unable to settle on a decision.
To swing back and forth between opinions or courses of action, never settling on one.

It describes a pattern, not a moment. Waver once and you're human; vacillate and you've been dithering for weeks. The word also judges: people rarely describe their own careful deliberation as vacillating. Waver is sympathetic, equivocate means you're being slippery on purpose — vacillate says you genuinely cannot hold a position, and the speaker's patience has run out.
⚠️ vacillate ≠ oscillate.
- oscillate = swing back and forth regularly, usually physical or mechanical (a pendulum, a fan, a voltage)
- vacillate = swing back and forth mentally, out of indecision

A fan oscillates. A coward vacillates.
VAS-illate — a vase teetering on the shelf edge: tips one way, tips back, never commits.
The word is about the wobbling rather than the choosing, which is why it lands as an accusation of weak nerves and not of careful thought.
1. The board vacillated for three months over the merger, and by the time it committed, the offer had been withdrawn.
2. Stop vacillating and pick a restaurant, or I'm ordering pizza.
Latin vacillāre = "to sway, to totter." It was said of drunks and wobbly furniture long before it was said of minds — the physical unsteadiness is the original picture.

🚫 Not from vacuus ("empty"). Vacant, vacuum, vacation, evacuate are a separate family; the shared vac- here is a coincidence.

column2:
Empty of thought or content; mindlessly blank.
Empty — literally void of contents, but almost always used of a remark, expression, or mind that contains no thought at all.

The word is a sneer, and it lands hardest when something should have had substance: a vacuous speech had a podium, an audience and twenty minutes, and delivered nothing. Vague means you can't tell what was meant; vacuous means nothing was meant. Reach for it about the smile that registers no one home, or the comment that sounds like an idea until you try to hold it.
⚠️ vacuous ≠ fatuous. They rhyme and both insult, but vacuous = empty (no content), fatuous = smugly silly (plenty of content, all of it foolish). A blank stare is vacuous; a pleased-with-itself joke is fatuous.
Vacuous = vacuum + -ous. A vacuum is empty space; a vacuous remark is empty where the meaning should be.
The vacuum cleaner in the word tells you the contents have been sucked out of something built to hold them.
1. The minister's statement was a masterpiece of vacuous reassurance: three hundred words, not one commitment.
2. He just gave me this vacuous grin, like the question had gone straight through him.
In logic and CS, a statement like "every file in this empty folder is corrupted" is vacuously true — true only because there's nothing there to check. The technical sense preserves the ordinary one exactly: true, but empty.
Latin vacuus = "empty," from vacāre, "to be empty, to be free." That root is everywhere: vacuum, vacant, vacate, vacation, evacuate, vacancy — and vacation is literally the time your desk stands empty.

Serving as a farewell; a formal parting address.
Adj.: serving as or relating to a farewell. Noun (chiefly US): the farewell address itself.

This is goodbye with a podium under it. A final email is just the last one; a valedictory email knows it's the last one, looks back over the whole run, and hands something on. The word carries ceremony, deliberateness, and a low hum of elegy — it attaches to address, speech, tour, interview, lecture, almost never to anything casual. Note the implication: someone has chosen to mark the ending rather than simply reach it.
Every valedictorian gives the goodbye speech — and gives it from a stage, in a gown, having rehearsed.
The word you already know supplies both halves: valedictory means farewell, and it means farewell done formally.
1. In his valedictory address to the court, the retiring justice warned that habits of courtesy, once lost, are not easily rebuilt.
2. She fired off one valedictory message to the group chat and left it for good.
The valedictorian at graduation — literally the student chosen to deliver the valedictory. The salutatorian speaks second and says hello (salutare); the valedictorian closes and says goodbye.
Latin vale ("farewell" — literally "be well," from valēre, to be strong) + dīcere ("to say"). Two of the most productive roots on the GRE: valēre gives valid, valour, prevail, convalesce; dīcere gives verdict, edict, dictate, benediction, malediction.

Courage in the face of danger — the medal-worthy kind.
Great personal courage in the face of danger — above all, courage in battle.

Where bravery is the everyday word and nerve is cheeky, valor is ceremonial. It belongs to citations, eulogies and medals, and it almost always implies combat or a heroic rescue: you show valor storming a position, not asking your boss for a raise. It also carries a whiff of the old-fashioned — used of ordinary modern life, it sounds either grand or mock-grand, which is exactly why it works as a joke.
Nobody hands out a Medal of Bravery — the medal says valor.
Valor is the officially decorated, battlefield grade of courage, not the everyday kind.
1. The citation praised his valor under fire: he crossed forty metres of open ground to drag two wounded men back to the line.
2. She opened the fridge, sniffed the leftovers, and ate them anyway — valor, of a sort.
Shakespeare's Falstaff, dodging a fight in Henry IV: "The better part of valour is discretion." The joke only lands because valour means battlefield courage — he's redefining bravery as running away.
Latin valēre = "to be strong, to be worth." Strength and worth are the same idea in this root, which is why it splits two ways: valiant, valor, prevail, convalesce (strength) and value, valid, invalid, evaluate, avail (worth).

Note the pair invalid — in-VAL-id (not strong: a sick person) and IN-vuh-lid (not valid: a bad argument). One root, two stresses.

column2:
To defeat utterly and finally; the heroic word for conquest.
To defeat someone completely and finally — in battle, in competition, or in the case of a fear or a habit, to crush it for good.

Defeat is the neutral scoreboard word; vanquish is the heroic one. It comes with trumpets — knights, dragons, armies, demons — and it implies the loser is not merely behind but finished, with no rematch implied. Because the register is that elevated, using it for small stuff is a deliberate joke: you vanquish an enemy nation, and you "vanquish" your inbox only with a smirk. It also takes abstract objects gracefully — vanquish doubt, grief, temptation — where beat would sound flat.
Van-QUISH — squish them so hard they vanish.
The squish-and-vanish pair carries the totality: not edged out, but flattened out of existence.
1. The young king vanquished the rebel lords in a single autumn and never faced a challenge again.
2. She finally vanquished her fear of flying — twelve hours to Tokyo, no white knuckles.
The Aston Martin Vanquish — the brand's flagship supercar, named to say it doesn't merely beat the competition, it ends it.
Latin vincere = "to conquer" (past participle victum), reaching English through Old French vainquir.

That one root is a GRE goldmine: victor, victory, invincible ("not conquerable"), convince (conquer someone's doubts), evince, convict, evict.

🚫 Not related to vanish, despite the sound — that's Latin evanescere, "to fade away."

Flat and empty; offering nothing to interest anyone.
Offering nothing — no flavour, no substance, no spark. Flat, empty, lifeless.

What makes it sting is that vapid things are usually not unpleasant. A vapid smile, a vapid pop song, a vapid conversation about the weather — all perfectly agreeable on the surface, and completely hollow underneath. Boring says you were bored; vapid says there was nothing there to be interested in. It's a critic's word, faintly snobbish, and it always looks down on what it describes.
Vapid rhymes with insipid — and means the same thing.
Both describe something with all the flavour drained out, whether it's a soup or a screenplay.
1. The novel's dialogue is vapid — three hundred pages of pleasant people saying nothing to one another.
2. He gave me this vapid smile and asked if I'd had a nice weekend, for the fourth time.
It's the stock verdict in music and film reviews — the word a critic reaches for when a song is catchy, glossy, and utterly empty.
Latin vapidus = "flat, stale" — said of wine that had lost its kick. Same root as vapor: the good stuff has evaporated, and what's left in the glass is flavourless liquid.

That image is the definition. Vapid = the wine's gone flat.

Bribable; corruptly available for purchase.
Open to bribery; capable of being bought. Used of officials, judges, police, journalists — and of the systems they rot.

Narrower and nastier than corrupt. Corrupt covers any kind of rottenness — cronyism, cover-ups, abuse of power. Venal names one specific mechanism: there is a price, and you can pay it. And unlike mercenary, which merely means money-motivated (a mercenary lawyer is legal, just cold), venal means the person's duty itself is on sale. It is a contemptuous word — you accuse someone of venality, you don't confess to it.
⚠️ venal ≠ venial.
- venal = bribable, for sale
- venial (VEE-nee-uhl) = a minor, forgivable sin — the opposite of mortal

A venial fault gets you a shrug. A venal one gets you indicted.
Venal like a vending machine — insert money, the official dispenses the verdict you want.
Same root as vend: the venal man isn't merely dishonest, he's stocked and priced.
1. The republic did not fall to invaders; it was hollowed out by a venal senate that auctioned its provinces to the highest bidder.
2. Every permit took three months unless you knew which venal clerk to slip an envelope to.
Latin vēnum = "thing for sale" → vēnālis, "on sale." Same source as vend, vendor, vending machine — literally the goods-for-money family.

🚫 Not venial. That's Latin venia, "forgiveness, indulgence" — a venial sin is one the Church will pardon. Different root, opposite moral weight.

to revere deeply, just short of worship
To regard with deep, reverential respect — the kind owed to saints, elders, sacred texts, and the honoured dead.

Admire is about qualities; respect is about standing; venerate is one notch below worship. It carries incense on it: age, holiness, tradition, a figure placed above ordinary criticism. That's also why it turns sour so easily — say a nation venerates its founders and you're hinting the reverence has stopped being examined.
Ven-ERATE — you don't just rate them highly, you rate them as divine.
The hidden rate fixes it as an act of ranking someone, and "divine" marks how far above the scale veneration puts them.
1. The village still venerates the hermit's grave, leaving bread and coins on the stone each spring.
2. My grandad venerates that car — you're not allowed to eat in it, sit in it, or breathe near it.
The Catholic Church draws a formal line between veneration of saints and relics and worship, which is reserved for God alone — the distinction that gives the word its exact altitude: as high as you can go without crossing into worship.
Latin venerārī = "to revere," from Venus, veneris — the goddess, and before that "love, desire, charm."

🚫 The false friend that isn't: venereal comes from the same root. Venus split into the sacred branch (venerate, venerable, veneration) and the carnal one (venereal). Same goddess, opposite ends of her portfolio.

column2:
Truthfulness; the accuracy of a claim or a person.
Truthfulness — either the habit of a person who doesn't lie, or the accuracy of a particular statement, document, or account.

Two things mark it out. It's formal, almost forensic — journalists, lawyers and historians use it; you'd never say a friend's excuse lacked veracity out loud. And it lives overwhelmingly in the negative or interrogative: questioned the veracity, disputed the veracity, doubts about its veracity. Compare honesty, which is warm and personal, and accuracy, which is cold and about facts alone — veracity sits between them, covering both the truth of the claim and the reliability of the one making it.
⚠️ veracity ≠ voracity.
- veracity = truthfulness (verus, true)
- voracity = ravenous appetite, greed (vorare, to devour)

A witness has veracity; a wolf has voracity. Same for veracious vs voracious.
Nobody ever praises someone's veracity — they question it.
The word almost always arrives attached to doubt, so if you can hear "questioned the ___ of his account," the blank is veracity.
1. The committee spent three days probing the veracity of the minister's expense claims.
2. Look, I'm not doubting your veracity — I just think you misremembered the date.
Veritaserum, the truth potion in Harry Potter — veritas (truth) + serum. Three drops and you cannot lie: veracity in liquid form.
Latin vērus = "true" → vēritās, truth. It pays out across the whole exam: verify (make true), verdict (vere dictum, truly said), veritable (genuinely so), aver (assert as true), verisimilitude (the look of truth), and plain very — which once meant "truly," as in the very man I wanted.

🚫 Not vorare, "to devour" — that's voracious, devour, carnivore, omnivore.

column2:
Using far more words than the point requires.
Using far more words than the job needs; wordy, padded, bloated.

The complaint is about the prose, not the person. Call someone garrulous or loquacious and you're describing a chatterbox; call their report verbose and you're describing a style problem — the ideas may be fine, but they arrive buried under three clauses of throat-clearing. It's the standard verdict on legal contracts, academic papers and consultants' slide decks, and it's cool and clinical rather than heated: an editor's word, not an insult shouted across a room.

One exception to the sting: in software, verbose mode is a neutral setting — you want the extra output.
Verb + -ose — and -ose means "full of": grandiose (full of grandeur), bellicose (full of war), verbose (full of words).
Lock the suffix once and you get a free read on a whole family of GRE adjectives that all mean "overloaded with the thing named."
1. The judgment ran to four hundred verbose pages, of which perhaps twenty carried the reasoning.
2. Just tell me what broke — your emails are so verbose I never get to the point.
Any command line: `curl -v`, `npm install --verbose`. The `-v` flag literally means "print every last detail" — the one place being verbose is a feature.
Latin verbum = "word." The family is huge and all of it is about words: verb, verbal, verbatim (word for word), proverb, adverb.

The convincing appearance of truth — not truth itself.
The quality of seeming true — of being lifelike, plausible, convincingly real.

It is a word about appearance, not fact. A novel, a film set, an alibi, a forged passport can all have verisimilitude; none of them is thereby true. Critics reach for it as praise for craft — the dialogue sounds like people actually talk, the 1840s kitchen has the right grease on it — and it stays cool and technical rather than admiring. Notice too that it's almost always used of something made: you praise the verisimilitude of a performance, not of a mountain.
⚠️ verisimilitude ≠ veracity.
- verisimilitude = looks true
- veracity = is true, habitually truthful

A con man's story can have great verisimilitude and zero veracity.
Veri-similitude — read it as "very similar": similar to the truth, which is exactly not the same as being it.
The word's own halves confess the limit — resemblance is all it ever claims.
1. The jury was swayed less by evidence than by the verisimilitude of the witness's account — the small, useless details no liar would bother to invent.
2. The costumes are gorgeous, but there's no verisimilitude — nobody in 1912 had teeth like that.
This is a film-and-TV critic's workhorse word — the standard praise for something like The Wire or a meticulous period drama. It always means "it feels real," never "it happened."
Latin vērus (true) + similis (like) — "truth-like."

Both halves pay off across the exam. vērus gives verify, verdict (vere dictum, "truly said"), veritable, aver — and very itself, which once meant "true" (the very man). similis gives similar, simulate, assimilate, resemble, simultaneous.

Used to stress that a metaphor or exaggeration is fully deserved.
Used before a noun to insist that a strong description — usually a metaphor or an exaggeration — is fully deserved: a veritable army of lawyers, a veritable goldmine.

It is almost never a plain synonym for true or real. Its job is licensing: the speaker reaches for an over-the-top comparison and then plants veritable in front of it to say "and I stand by that." Drop it and the sentence still works — an army of lawyers — so what it adds is stance, not information. Tone is formal-genteel and faintly theatrical; it's the voice of the restaurant review and the auction catalogue, which is why overuse reads as purple prose.
⚠️ veritable ≠ venerable.
- veritable = genuinely deserving the name (a veritable institution = really is one)
- venerable = old and revered (a venerable institution = ancient and respected)

One letter apart in the middle, and both love the word institution.
Veritable = very-table — it doesn't say true, it says take my exaggeration as true.
The "veri" is the truth root, but in practice the word works as an intensifier bolted onto a metaphor.
1. The archive proved a veritable goldmine: three unpublished letters surfaced in the first afternoon.
2. By eight o'clock her desk was a veritable graveyard of coffee cups.
It's the house style of food and travel writing — "a veritable feast," "a veritable paradise." If you've read a menu blurb or a Sunday supplement, you've met it.
Latin vērus = "true", via vēritās = "truth." That one root pays out across the exam: verify, verity, veracious (truthful), aver (to assert as true), verdict (vērē dictum, "truly said"), and verisimilitude (the look of truth).

Harvard's crest reads VERITAS — same root, same three letters at the front.

Skilled at many different things; useful in many ways.
Able to turn your hand to many different things — and be good at all of them. Also used of objects: a tool or material with many uses.

The praise is about range plus competence, which is what separates it from its neighbours. Adaptable means you cope when conditions change; flexible means you bend to others' demands; versatile means you already have several skills sitting ready. It's a compliment nobody objects to — an actor who does comedy and Chekhov, a fabric that works in summer and winter.
⚠️ versatile ≠ volatile. Same rhythm, opposite temperament: versatile = usefully many-sided; volatile = liable to explode or swing wildly.
Hiding in it is versa — as in vice versa: it turns the other way, and any other way you need.
The versatile one keeps turning to face a new task and lands each one well.
1. A versatile performer, she moved from stand-up to Shakespeare without any visible change of gear.
2. Get the black one — it's the most versatile jacket you own; it goes with everything.
Sports commentary lives on this word: the cricketing all-rounder who bats, bowls and keeps, or the footballer who can fill in at three positions, is always called "the most versatile player in the squad."
Latin vertere = "to turn" → versatilis, "capable of turning." The same root turns up everywhere on the GRE: convert, invert, divert, avert, revert, adverse, vertigo, and anniversary (the year turning round again).

Energy with style — flair in performance or expression.
Energy, spirit and enthusiasm — especially the stylish kind shown in performance or expression.

Vigour is force; verve is force with flair. You praise a pianist, a writer, a winger, a lawyer's closing argument for verve — never a person merely working hard. It implies dash, confidence and a bit of swagger in the execution, so it's almost always admiring, and it sits slightly above everyday speech: reviewers, critics and match reports use it far more than friends do.
Verve rhymes with swerve — not just speed, but a stylish swerve.
Anyone can run straight at full effort; verve is the flourish you put on it.
1. She played the Rachmaninoff with a verve that made the older, tidier recordings sound embalmed.
2. He can't cook much, but he chops onions with such verve you'd think he trained in Paris.
The Verve — the Britpop band behind Bittersweet Symphony. Bands don't name themselves "Diligence"; they pick a word that means swagger and style.
Straight from French verve, "enthusiasm," which from the beginning meant artistic inspiration — the fire in a writer or performer. That's why English verve still attaches to prose, playing and performance rather than to plain hard graft.

Surviving only as a useless remnant of something once functional.
Surviving only as a remnant of something that was once larger, whole, or useful — and no longer doing the job it was built for.

Two things have to be true at once: it's a leftover, and it's functionless. A small thing isn't vestigial; a thing that used to matter and no longer does is. Biologists own the word (the appendix, the tailbone, a flightless bird's wings), and when it travels outside biology it carries that clinical detachment with it: calling a committee's veto power vestigial isn't an insult, it's a diagnosis — the power is still on the books, but evolution has moved past it.
Vestigial = a vestige with a suffix — the footprint stays, the foot has walked off.
What's left is only evidence that something was there, not the thing itself still working.
1. The monarchy retains a vestigial power to dissolve parliament, exercised now only on the government's own instruction.
2. Those tiny buttons on your jacket cuff are totally vestigial — nobody's unbuttoning a sleeve.
The little fifth pocket sewn inside the right front pocket of your jeans — it held a pocket watch in the 1890s. Pure vestigial structure, still on every pair made today.
Latin vestīgium = "footprint, track." A vestige is the mark a thing leaves behind after it's gone.

Same root pays off elsewhere: to investigate is literally to follow the footprints in — track the traces back to what made them.

🚫 Not vestibular. That's the inner-ear balance system, from vestibule (entrance hall) — similar sound, unrelated word.

column2:
Irritated frustration, or the thing that causes it.
Irritation and frustrated annoyance — or the thing causing it ("the leak was a constant vexation").

Scale matters: fury is hot and outward, vexation is low-grade and inward — the teeth-grinding of someone stuck with a petty, repeated obstacle they can't fix. It carries a whiff of helplessness that anger doesn't, and it's the more bookish word: you write of a character's vexation, you shout in rage. Law keeps the harsher old sense alive in vexatious litigation — lawsuits filed purely to harass.
Vex rhymes with hex — a small curse that nags at you, not a lightning bolt.
Vexation is the persistent low-level torment of a minor jinx, not the explosion of real rage.
1. Her letters betray a quiet vexation at being praised for her husband's work.
2. Three trips to the DMV in one week — you can imagine my vexation.
The King James Bible, Ecclesiastes: "all is vanity and vexation of spirit." Everything is pointless, and it's irritating.
Latin vexāre = "to shake, jolt, harass" — literally to be rattled about. Gives vex, vexatious, and the vexed question (one shaken back and forth without resolution).

Able to survive or work — good enough to proceed.
Capable of surviving on its own — a viable seed sprouts, a viable newborn lives outside the womb. By extension: workable enough to go ahead with — a viable plan, a viable business, a viable candidate.

Notice how low the bar is. Viable promises survival, not success: it says the thing won't collapse, nothing more. That makes it quietly damning as praise — call a proposal "a viable option" and you've said it's alive, not that it's good. Feasible asks whether you can do it at all; viable asks whether it can keep going once you have.
Viable = vital, sur-vive, vivid — the vi is life. A viable plan has a pulse; that's the whole claim.
If you remember that viable only certifies a heartbeat, you'll never mistake it for a compliment.
1. Below twenty-four weeks the foetus was not considered viable, and the surgeons planned accordingly.
2. Look, moving in with your parents is a viable plan — it's just not a fun one.
Every startup's MVP — Minimum Viable Product: deliberately the least you can ship that still survives contact with a customer. The whole term hangs on viable meaning "barely alive, but alive."
French vie = "life", from Latin vīta. Same root: vital, vitamin, survive, revive, vivid, vivacious — anything with that vi- is about living.

column2:
Keeping steady, alert watch for danger or wrongdoing.
Keeping steady, alert watch for danger, error, or wrongdoing.

The word carries duty and endurance, not nerves. Anxious watching is jumpy and self-protective; vigilant watching is a post you hold — the night nurse, the sentry, the auditor. It's sustained over time and almost always approving: to call someone vigilant is to praise them. Compare wary (suspicious of a specific thing) and observant (notices detail, danger or not) — vigilant is watchfulness aimed at threat, kept up indefinitely.
⚠️ vigilant ≠ vigilante.
- vigilant (adj.) = watchful, and it's a compliment
- vigilante (n., vij-uh-LAN-tee) = a private citizen who punishes crime without legal authority — usually a criticism

A vigilant neighbourhood calls the police; a vigilante skips that step.
Vigilant has vigil sitting inside it — and nobody keeps a vigil for five minutes.
A vigil is an all-night watch, which is exactly the endurance the word implies: not a startled glance but a shift you don't abandon.
1. Border officials were instructed to remain vigilant for forged documentation during the busiest weeks of the season.
2. Be vigilant at that crossing — half the drivers there treat the red light as a suggestion.
Every transit system in the world runs the same line: "Please stay vigilant and report any unattended baggage." You've heard it on a platform this year.
Latin vigil = "awake, watchful" → vigilāre, "to keep watch."

One root, a useful family: vigil (the all-night watch), vigilante, reveille (the wake-up bugle, via French réveiller), surveillance (sur- "over" + veiller "watch"), and — fittingly — invigilate, which is what the person pacing the aisles at your GRE centre is doing.

To attack someone's reputation as wicked or worthless.
To attack someone's reputation in public — to write or speak about them as wicked, worthless, contemptible.

Scale and intent are what mark it out. You criticise an argument, you insult a person to their face, but you vilify someone over weeks, in print, to a crowd — it's sustained character assassination aimed at turning opinion against them. And it leans heavily toward the unjust: the word arrives most often as "unfairly vilified," with the writer signalling that the target didn't deserve it. Use it about your own side and you're claiming victimhood, not describing debate.
Vile + -ify — you don't just call someone vile, you manufacture their vileness.
The -ify suffix means make into (purify, falsify), so vilifying is a production process, not a single insult.
1. For a decade the pamphleteers vilified her as a traitor, until the archives were opened and the charge collapsed.
2. Don't vilify the guy in the group chat — he missed one deadline, he didn't burn the office down.
"Vilify" is a single by Device (David Draiman's band, 2013) — a Mainstream Rock hit built entirely on the idea of being torn down in public.
Latin vīlis = "cheap, of low value" + -ficāre (to make). To vilify is literally to cheapen a person — to mark them down in the public estimate.

Same root: vile, revile, vilification.

🚫 Not from villain. That's Latin villa — a farmhand, a peasant, someone tied to the estate. Everyone assumes vilify = "make into a villain"; the real image is a price tag being slashed.

column2:
Poisonously severe; bitterly, spreadingly hostile.
1. Of a disease, toxin or organism: extremely poisonous, fast-acting and hard to fight off — not just present, but aggressively destructive.
2. Of feelings or language: bitterly hostile, venomous, spreading.

Two words sit close by and both fall short. Vehement is force without malice — you can be vehement in defence of someone. Virulent is never neutral: it carries the poison metaphor intact, so virulent racism or virulent criticism implies something toxic that also spreads and infects. It's the strongest of the three, and it always condemns.
⚠️ virulent ≠ virile.
- virulent = poisonous, deadly (Latin virus, poison)
- virile = manly, vigorous, potent (Latin vir, man)

One syllable apart, opposite connotations — virile is a compliment.
VIRUS + VIOLENT = virulent.
The word is those two crammed together, which is exactly the meaning — harm that spreads like an infection and hits like an assault.
1. The pamphlet's virulent attacks on the clergy were considered too inflammatory to reprint for a century.
2. He's not just annoyed at the ref — that's virulent, he's been ranting for three days.
Every pandemic news bulletin: "a more virulent strain." Note it never means "more common" — it means the thing does more damage once it's in you.
Latin virus originally meant "poison, slimy venom" — the germ sense is modern. Virulentus = "full of poison."

So virulent hatred isn't a metaphor stretched thin; it's the literal, original word — hatred with venom in it.

Boldly future-seeing — or an impractical dreamer, depending on tone.
Adj.: having unusually bold, original foresight about what the future could be. Noun: the person who has it.

The word cuts both ways, and the GRE loves that. Applied to a founder, an architect, a reformer, it's high praise — they saw what nobody else could. But visionary schemes, visionary plans, a visionary with no head for numbers means the opposite: the vision exists only in his head. The judgment sits in the context, not the word — the same trait is genius if it lands and delusion if it doesn't.

A third, older sense survives in religious and literary texts: someone who literally sees visions — mystical, prophetic, possibly hallucinating.
A vision is either the future you can see — or a thing that isn't actually there.
Both meanings of vision live inside visionary, which is exactly why the word can praise a genius or dismiss a dreamer.
1. The cathedral was the work of a visionary builder who designed for a skyline that would not exist for two hundred years.
2. Great pitch, but his business plan is pure visionary nonsense — no costs, no timeline, just vibes.
Every Steve Jobs obituary and keynote retrospective reaches for the same word — "a visionary" — used in the fully admiring sense, for someone who described products years before they could be built.
Latin vidēre = "to see" (past participle vīsus). It's one of the great GRE roots: vision, visible, evident, envision, revise (look again), survey (look over), provide and prudent (both from pro-vidēre, "to see ahead" — the prudent person saw it coming).

Visible aliveness; the power to endure and keep going.
The state of being strongly, visibly alive — energy, animation, glow — and, more abstractly, the capacity to survive and keep going.

Two settings, one idea. Of a person, it's health you can see: colour in the face, spring in the step. Of a thing — a language, a party, a neighbourhood, a business — it's the sign that it hasn't ossified and won't die out. Energy is a quantity you spend today; vitality is the underlying life that keeps producing it. That's why you can be exhausted and still have vitality, and why an economy can be "busy" without it.

Always approving, and slightly formal — an obituary or a review says a writer "retained her vitality into her eighties"; nobody says it about a caffeinated Tuesday.
Vitamins give you vitality — same first four letters, same job: keeping the life in you.
Vitamins aren't a stimulant that spikes you, they're what sustains life over time — exactly the difference between mere energy and vitality.
1. Despite three decades in exile, the movement retained a vitality that its state-funded rivals had long since lost.
2. He's seventy-four and still swims every morning — the man's got more vitality than my flatmate.
In RPGs — Dark Souls, Elden Ring, countless others — Vitality is the stat that governs how much health you have. Level it up, and you take more punishment before dying. That's the word, literally: the size of your reserve of life.
Latin vita = "life." That one root pays out across the exam: vital (life-sustaining, hence essential), vitamin, revitalise, viable (able to live), and curriculum vitae — "the course of a life."

🚫 Not vitiate (VISH-ee-ayt, "to spoil, corrupt"). That's Latin vitium, "fault" — same first three letters, opposite family. Vitality fills a thing with life; vitiate ruins it.

To spoil or corrupt something, destroying its validity.
To spoil, impair, or corrupt something — and, in legal use, to render it invalid or void.

The damage comes from within and from one flaw: a single bad ingredient, a single false premise, a single act of fraud, and the whole thing is no longer sound. You don't vitiate a wall by knocking it down; you vitiate an argument by smuggling one bad assumption into it. Compare ruin (total, physical) and taint (contaminated but still standing): vitiate sits between them — the thing survives in form but no longer works, or no longer counts. Formal and slightly bookish; it lives in law, philosophy, and criticism.
Vitiate has a vice buried in it — one vice, and the whole thing is void.
Vice and vitiate are the same Latin root, and the sense is the same: one hidden fault is enough to cancel the whole.
1. The study's conclusions were vitiated by a sampling error nobody caught until publication.
2. One dodgy signature and the whole deal's vitiated — we're back to square one.
The old legal maxim "fraud vitiates everything" (fraus omnia vitiat) — still quoted in contract cases: prove fraud anywhere in the agreement and the entire agreement collapses.
Latin vitium = "fault, defect, blemish." Same root as vice (a moral defect), vicious, and vituperate (to abuse someone verbally — literally "to bring up their faults").

column2:
Lively and sparkling in an attractive, sociable way.
Lively and high-spirited in an attractive, sparkling way — full of animation in company.

The energy here is social, not physical: a vivacious person talks, laughs, lights up a room. An athlete is energetic; a hostess is vivacious. It's warmer than lively and less exhausting than exuberant, and it carries a whiff of charm — you enjoy being near a vivacious person. Note the usage skew: it's applied to women far more often than men, which is why it can read as slightly dated or faintly patronising depending on who says it.
⚠️ vivacious ≠ voracious.
- vivacious = bubbling with life (viv- = live)
- voracious = ravenously hungry — for food, or for books

A vivacious reader is fun at parties; a voracious reader gets through four books a week.
Viva-cious — she is the "viva!" in the room.
The word literally opens with a cheer, which is the right register: it's sparkle and charm, not stamina.
1. Her letters are as vivacious as her conversation — every page seems to be talking over the last one.
2. He's fine one-on-one, but put him next to his vivacious sister and he vanishes.
Coldplay's "Viva la Vida" — "long live life." Same viv- root; a vivacious person is that title in human form.
Latin vīvere = "to live" → vīvax, "lively, long-lived."

One of the best-value GRE roots: vivid (life-like), revive, survive, vital, convivial (living together = good company), vivisection (cutting the living).

Loudly and insistently outspoken, usually in protest.
Loud, insistent, and impossible to ignore — crying out, usually in complaint or demand.

Volume alone isn't the point. A loud person is just audible; a vociferous one is loud about something — objecting, demanding, refusing to drop it. It attaches almost automatically to protest: vociferous opposition, vociferous critics, vociferous denials. There's a faint eye-roll in it — the speaker registers the noise as much as the argument — though a crowd can be vociferous in support too.
⚠️ vociferous ≠ voracious.
- vociferous = loud, clamouring (vox, voice)
- voracious = ravenously hungry, insatiable (vorare, to devour)

A vociferous reader complains about books; a voracious reader devours them.
Voci = voice, and it sounds like ferocious — a voice turned ferocious.
That pairing gets you both halves at once: it's about the voice, and it's the voice raised in attack rather than merely turned up.
1. The proposal met vociferous opposition from residents, who packed the council chamber and shouted down every attempt to move to a vote.
2. Dad's the most vociferous fan in the stand — you can hear him over the whole crowd.
News writing runs on one phrase: "a vociferous critic of" — it's the standard label for whoever is loudest against a policy, a boss, or a government. Learn the word inside that collocation and it comes back instantly.
Latin vōx, vōcis (voice) + ferre (to carry) — literally voice-carrying.

Both halves pay off elsewhere. From vōx: vocal, vocation (a calling), evoke, provoke, advocate. From ferre: transfer, refer, conifer (cone-carrying), pestiferous (plague-carrying).

Liable to change suddenly and dangerously; quick to evaporate
Liable to change suddenly, sharply, and without warning — of a substance, evaporating at low temperature; of a person, market, or situation, apt to erupt.

The word carries latent danger, not mere inconstancy. A fickle friend changes her mind; a mercurial boss swings between charm and gloom; a volatile situation is one you back away from, because the change it threatens is violent. Even in its neutral technical senses — a volatile solvent, a volatile stock, volatile memory — the shared idea is that the thing will not stay put and cannot be relied on to be there in a moment.
⚠️ volatile ≠ voluble. Voluble means fluent, talkative, speech flowing easily — a voluble host, not a dangerous one. Same first three letters, unrelated roots (volare = fly; volvere = roll).
Vola-tile: it's about to fly off — the handle, the beaker, the charts.
"Fly off" catches both halves at once: the literal escaping vapour and the figurative sense that something is a moment away from blowing.
1. The ceasefire held, but the border remained volatile, and both governments kept their embassies half-staffed.
2. Don't bring up the divorce — he's been pretty volatile all week.
Your RAM is volatile memory: cut the power and everything in it is simply gone. That's the word doing its literal job — the data flies away.
Latin volāre = "to fly." Volatilis meant flying, fleeting — first used in English of birds and insects, then of liquids that "fly off" as vapour, and only later of tempers and markets.

Same root: volley (a flight of arrows), volant (flying, in heraldry), vol-au-vent (pastry so light it "flies in the wind").

column2:
Talking freely and fluently; words pour out with ease.
Talking a great deal, and doing it easily — fluent, rapid, unstoppable speech.

The key is flow, not volume. Talkative counts words; loquacious is the neutral bookish label; garrulous is a complaint about rambling on. Voluble points at the fluency itself — the speaker never gropes for a word, never stalls. That makes it tilt admiring when the person is charming or persuasive (a voluble host, a voluble advocate), and faintly wary when the flow feels practised or hard to interrupt.
⚠️ voluble ≠ voluminous. Voluble = pouring out speech; voluminous = huge in bulk (voluminous robes, voluminous case files). A voluble witness talks endlessly; voluminous testimony fills a filing cabinet.
Voluble rhymes with soluble — the words dissolve out, no lumps, no stalling.
It names the smoothness of the delivery, not merely the quantity of it.
1. Normally reserved in committee, the minister turned voluble the moment the subject touched his own department.
2. Two coffees in and she was suddenly voluble, running through every piece of office gossip without pausing for breath.
Political reporting leans on one collocation constantly: "a voluble critic of" — the person who is never short of something to say against the policy.
Latin volvere = "to roll" — speech that rolls out of you.

That root is a GRE goldmine: revolve (roll back), evolve (roll out), involve (roll in), convoluted (rolled together, hence tangled), and volume (originally a rolled scroll).

column2:
To decline gradually, especially after reaching a peak.
Verb: to decrease gradually in size, strength, intensity, or influence.
Noun: used almost only in the phrase on the wane — in decline.

The decline is slow, natural, and measured from a height. Things that wane were once full: a moon, an empire, a reputation, someone's patience. Nothing crashes or snaps — it thins out. That built-in "after the peak" is what separates wane from dwindle (shrinking toward nothing, no peak implied) and from plummet (fast and alarming). Wane is calm about it; the speaker is observing a curve, not sounding an alarm.
⚠️ wane ≠ wan. Wan (WON) is an adjective meaning pale, sickly, feeble — a wan smile, a wan face. One letter apart, unrelated words.
Nothing can wane that wasn't full first.
The word smuggles in a former peak, which is why waning influence implies the person once had plenty of it.
1. By the third century the empire's authority over its western provinces had visibly waned.
2. My enthusiasm for the group project waned somewhere around the fourth unanswered message.
The moon on your weather app: waxing (growing toward full) and waning (shrinking after it). That pairing is where nearly everyone first meets the word, and it fixes the "decline from fullness" sense for free.
Old English wanian = "to lessen, dwindle." Same family as want — which originally meant lack, not desire, and still does in the phrase found wanting (= found deficient). Worth banking: on the GRE, wanting often means missing something, not wishing.

Lacking, deficient — falling short when actually measured.
Lacking; absent altogether, or present but falling short of the required standard. The evidence was wanting. / His technique was found wanting.

The everyday sense — wanting a coffee — is desire. The GRE sense flips the direction: the deficiency is in the thing, not a craving in the person. Two shades sit inside it: total absence (rainfall was wanting that year) and, more commonly, failure to measure up when something is tested against a standard. That second shade is quietly damning — "found wanting" is the verdict of an examiner, an auditor, a judge, and it stings more than inadequate because it implies the thing was actually weighed and came up short. Formal, faintly biblical, and almost always negative.
⚠️ wanting ≠ wanton. Wanting = lacking, deficient. Wanton (WON-tuhn) = unrestrained, malicious, or lewd — wanton cruelty. One is short of something; the other has no limits at all.
A wanting dish isn't hungry — it's missing the salt.
The want belongs to the object, which is short of something, not to a person who desires it.
1. The committee reviewed the safety protocols and found them wanting in every respect that mattered.
2. I tried his so-called famous lasagne and, honestly, it was a bit wanting.
The phrase's home is the writing on the wall in Daniel 5 — Belshazzar is told "Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting." That single line is why "found wanting" still carries the sound of a final verdict.
Want entered English from Old Norse vanta, "to lack" — and lacking was the original meaning. The desire sense came later and second-hand: "I want bread" began life as bread is lacking to me. So the GRE meaning isn't a strange outlier; it's the older, straighter sense, still visible in wanting and in for want of a nail.

column2:
Justified by the circumstances; deserved, not excessive.
Justified by the circumstances — deserved, called for, proportionate. (Second sense, from commerce: guaranteed, as in goods warranted free of defects.)

The word carries a whiff of the courtroom and the audit report: it doesn't say an action was good, it says there were sufficient grounds for it. Something is warranted when the evidence licenses it, not when you merely feel like doing it — which is why it lives so naturally in the cool, impersonal voice of officials ("no further action is warranted"). Its negative twin does most of the heavy lifting on the GRE: an unwarranted assumption, an unwarranted intrusion, unwarranted optimism — the charge each time is disproportion, a response bigger than its grounds.
No warrant, no warranted — you need the paper, not just the feeling.
A judge signs a warrant only when the evidence justifies the search, so warranted always means backed by grounds rather than by mere impulse.
1. The committee concluded that the outrage, however loud, was not warranted by the facts.
2. Two hours late and no text — honestly, a bit of shouting was warranted.
The sticker on your laptop or phone: warranted against defects for two years. Same word, older sense — the manufacturer is standing behind the claim.
Old North French warant = "protector, guarantee." Northern French kept the w-; Parisian French turned the same sound into gu- — so English, greedily, borrowed both forms of several words:

warranty / guarantee, warden / guardian, ward / guard, wile / guile.

A warrant is the paper that guarantees an act is lawful — hence warranted = backed, licensed, justified.

Watchful and distrustful of a specific danger.
On guard; watchful because you suspect danger or a trick.

Cautious is a general policy — you're careful crossing any road. Wary is aimed at something in particular: a person, an offer, a promise that doesn't quite add up. It carries distrust, and it keeps its eyes open rather than backing away — you can be wary of someone and still shake their hand, watching the whole time. Slightly milder and more everyday than leery, more suspicious than prudent.
wary ≠ weary. Wary (WAIR-ee) = watchful, suspicious. Weary (WEER-ee) = exhausted. A wary traveller checks the locks; a weary traveller falls asleep on top of them.
beware → be wary. Same word, one letter lighter.
Beware is the warning shouted at you; wary is the state you're in once you've heard it.
1. Investors remained wary of the company's projections, which had been revised upward three times in a single quarter.
2. He gave me a wary look, like he was still deciding whether I'd actually pay him back.
Old English wær = "watchful, on one's guard." The same root gives aware (watching outward), beware (be on guard), and the -ward/guard family — ward, warden, guard, regard all come from the sense of keeping watch over something.
