column2:
Drifting off the proper path; wilfully hard to control.
Hard to control or predict; drifting off the proper course — morally, or just physically.

A rebellious teenager is fighting you; a wayward one has simply wandered somewhere you can't follow. The word carries a faint pastoral disapproval, the tone of a parent or a preacher, and often a little pity or fondness mixed in — you don't call someone wayward unless you'd rather they came back. It also stretches to things with a mind of their own: a wayward strand of hair, a wayward pass, a wayward missile.
-ward always names a direction: homeward heads home, wayward heads away.
That's literal history — wayward is awayward with the a worn off, so the word means "turned away," not "fighting back."
1. The report described a wayward institution: funds unaccounted for, minutes unrecorded, trustees who had not met in two years.
2. He was a wayward kid — never nasty, just never once where he said he'd be.
Kansas, "Carry On Wayward Son" — the wandering son told to carry on, rest coming when he's done. The whole song is the word.
Middle English awayward = "turned away" — the initial a- simply fell off. So the "way" you see is really away, and -ward is the same direction-suffix as in toward, backward, homeward, wind­ward.

Worn down by long effort — or fed up with something.
Adj.: worn out — drained by long effort, strain, or endurance.
Verb: to tire someone out, or (as weary of) to grow sick of something.

Not the same as sleepy or tired. Weary is the tiredness that comes after a long haul, and it carries a note of the spirit going out of you as well as the body: a weary soldier, a weary smile, a weary sigh. It's slightly literary, and it always implies something wore you down.

Weary of shifts the meaning to fed up: weary of his excuses = out of patience, not out of energy.
⚠️ weary ≠ wary. Weary (WEER-ee) = worn out. Wary (WAIR-ee) = cautious, on guard. One letter, opposite states: the weary sentry has stopped being wary.
WEARy — you've been worn down, not sent to bed.
The hidden wear fixes the nuance: weariness is erosion by long use, which is why a night's sleep doesn't quite fix it.
1. After three years of litigation the family were weary of the whole business, and settled for a fraction of the claim.
2. He gave me this weary look, like if I asked him one more question he'd walk into the sea.
Simon & Garfunkel open Bridge Over Troubled Water with "When you're weary, feeling small" — and the pairing with feeling small is the whole nuance: worn down in spirit, not just short on sleep.

To coax someone by flattery and persistent sweet talk.
To get something out of someone by soft, flattering, persistent charm — sweet-talking them into it.

Coax can be kind and even tender; cajole is insistent; wheedle is the sly one. It always implies the flatterer is working an angle, and that the flattery is a tool rather than a feeling. Faintly comic too — the classic wheedlers are children after sweets and salesmen after signatures, not villains.

Watch the two grammars: you wheedle someone into doing something, and you wheedle something out of someone.
Wheedle rhymes with needle — both work on you steadily, but the needle jabs and the wheedle flatters.
Same nagging persistence, opposite method: needling is pressure by irritation, wheedling is pressure by honey.
1. Over three dinners he wheedled the old woman into changing her will, praising her judgement at every course.
2. She wheedled an extra day off out of her manager by telling him he was the only reasonable person in the building.

Playfully fanciful; driven by passing whims, not reason.
Playfully odd and fanciful; acting on passing fancies rather than reason.

Two settings, two flavours. Applied to art, design, or manner, it's warm praise: quaint, imaginative, gently silly — whimsical hats, whimsical little illustrations. Applied to decisions, rules, or power, it turns critical: choices made on a passing impulse, with nothing solid behind them. Capricious is that same unpredictability with the charm stripped out and menace added; whimsical stays light, unless the person indulging their whims controls your fate.
The word wears its own root on its sleeve: whim-sical — ruled by a whim.
A whim is small, harmless and short-lived, which is why the word stays charming — right up until the whim belongs to your boss.
1. The architect gave the sober granite façade one whimsical touch: a stone owl peering from the cornice.
2. He's a great cook but a whimsical one — you never know if dinner's at seven or eleven.
"Whimsical" is the adjective every critic reaches for with a Wes Anderson film — the symmetrical pastel dollhouse worlds of The Grand Budapest Hotel. Same for Tim Burton and Willy Wonka: charming, fanciful, running on its own private logic.

Headstrong; or done deliberately, with blame attached.
Two senses, both unflattering.

1. Headstrong — set on having your own way, deaf to advice or authority. Said of children, mules, and adults behaving like both.

2. Deliberate — done knowingly, on purpose, when you should have known better: willful negligence, willful blindness, willful destruction of evidence.

The link between the two is blame. Intentional and voluntary are neutral descriptions of a state of mind; willful is a charge. Sense 2 is the harsher one precisely because it rules out the excuse — you didn't slip, you chose, and choosing is worse. Even sense 1 is never praise: a determined person has resolve, a willful person has a problem with being told.
⚠️ willful ≠ willing. Same root, opposite temperament: willing bends to your wishes, willful insists on its own.
Will + full — so full of his own will there's no room for yours.
It isn't a lack of will but a surplus, aimed only at itself — which is why the word always sounds like a complaint.
1. The court found the breach willful rather than inadvertent, and trebled the damages accordingly.
2. She's a willful kid — tell her not to touch it and that's the only thing she wants to touch.
Read almost any contract or insurance policy and you'll hit the carve-out "except in cases of gross negligence or willful misconduct" — the clause that says a company can cap its liability for mistakes, but never for things it did on purpose.

Crafty; wins by tricks and cleverness, not force.
Crafty; skilled at getting what you want by tricks, feints and clever manoeuvring rather than by force or honesty.

Tone separates it from its neighbours: devious and duplicitous are accusations, but wily carries a grudging half-smile — the wily negotiator, the wily old fox who outmanoeuvred everyone in the room. It implies experience and quick wits, and it's usually applied to someone playing a weaker hand well. Calling a villain wily is almost a compliment to his brain.
wily ≠ wiry. Wily = full of tricks (mind). Wiry = lean, thin and tough (body). One letter apart, and both love the word old: the wily old lawyer, the wiry old climber.
Wily is just wile + y — someone made of wiles.
A wile is a single trick, so a wily person is one whose whole method is tricks — which is why he wins by outsmarting rather than overpowering.
1. The wily ambassador conceded the small point loudly, having already secured the large one in private.
2. Don't play cards with my grandmother — she's wily, and she'll have your money in twenty minutes.
Wile E. Coyote — the name is the word. Nothing but schemes, traps and mail-order contraptions, never brute force.

column2:
Quietly, fondly sad about something gone.
Quietly sad with longing — usually for something past, distant, or out of reach.

The sadness is soft and half-pleasant. Mournful is grief, melancholy is a settled gloom, bitter is a grudge; wistful is the gentle ache of remembering something fondly and knowing it's not coming back. It carries resignation — the wistful person isn't reaching for the thing, only looking at it. Often used of faces, voices, and glances rather than arguments: a wistful smile, a wistful sigh, gazing wistfully out of a window.
⚠️ wistful ≠ wishful. Wishful thinking means believing something because you want it to be true — it's self-deception, and slightly foolish. Wistful is sad longing with no illusion attached. She was wistful about her twenties; he was wishful about his chances.
Wistful is a whisper of a wish — too quiet to act on, too sweet to let go.
The whisper captures the register: not a cry of grief, just a soft private ache you never say out loud.
1. He grew wistful at the mention of the old house, as though some part of his life were still standing in its rooms.
2. She got all wistful scrolling through photos from that summer, then closed the app and went back to work.
The Beatles' "In My Life" is wistfulness in three minutes — \"There are places I'll remember all my life, though some have changed\" — fond, backward-looking, and completely free of bitterness.

To hold out against force or pressure without giving way.
To hold out against a force, attack, or pressure — and not give way.

The word is about structural survival, not suffering. Endure and bear look inward at pain patiently absorbed; withstand looks outward at the thing pushing on you and reports that it failed. It takes a force as its object — a siege, a storm, 200 mph winds, scrutiny, temptation — and it quietly implies you were built well enough for the job.
Withstand has stand sitting inside it — the test isn't whether it hurt, it's whether you're still standing.
Something hit you and the structure held, which is why the word implies strength rather than patience.
1. The garrison withstood three months of bombardment before the walls finally gave.
2. My phone case is fine, but I don't think it can withstand another drop like that.
It's the standard verb on spec sheets: a watch rated to withstand 100 m, a roof built to withstand hurricane-force winds. Whenever a product boasts about toughness, this is the word it reaches for.
Old English wiþ = "against" (not "alongside") + standan = "to stand." To withstand is literally to stand against.

That old adversarial with- unlocks a set: withhold (hold back), withdraw (draw back), and best of all notwithstanding = "not standing against it" → despite. The fossil survives in ordinary speech too: to fight with someone is to fight against them.

column2:
Full of grief — or so badly done it's pitiable.
Two senses, and the GRE will use either.

1. Full of sorrow; expressing grief — a woeful sigh, a woeful expression.
2. Pitifully bad; lamentably inadequate — a woeful performance, a woeful lack of preparation.

Sense 2 is the one that trips people, and it is a judgement, not a description: calling a defence woeful says it was so incompetent that watching it was painful. Compare bad (flat), dismal (bleak, joyless), abysmal (bottomlessly bad, pure scale) — woeful alone carries the sting of grief, as though the failure were a small tragedy. It also runs faintly theatrical: a woeful face is a face wearing its sadness for an audience, which is why woeful pairs so naturally with sarcasm.
Woeful defending doesn't feel woe — it causes it.
That flip is the whole second sense: the thing isn't sad, it's so bad that it makes you despair.
1. The report described a woeful neglect of the archive: damp ledgers, unlabelled boxes, whole decades unaccounted for.
2. Three hours of revision and I still bombed it — woeful, honestly.
Football commentary and match reports live on this word — "a woeful clearance", "woeful finishing" — always meaning bad enough to be sad, never merely sad.
Woe is Old English wā — not a noun originally but a cry, the sound you make when struck. That's why the word still sounds like a wail.

Same root gives woebegone, literally "beset by woe" — surrounded by it, hence that hangdog, defeated look.

Hostile or fearful toward foreigners and foreign things.
Hostile to or fearful of foreigners, immigrants, and anything foreign.

Despite the -phobic ending, this is not a clinical fear — it's a charge. Nobody describes themselves as xenophobic; it is what an opponent calls your immigration policy, your tabloid headline, your remark about "these people coming over here." It's also broader than racist: xenophobia targets the outsider — nationality, accent, origin, foreign food, foreign customs — so a country can be xenophobic toward people of its own race. The "fear" half is largely a polite fiction; what the word actually names is exclusion and contempt.
Ends in -phobic, but it isn't a phobia. Arachnophobia is a diagnosis; xenophobia is an accusation.
The suffix promises a private fear, but the word is always used as a public verdict on someone's politics.
1. The election was fought on xenophobic rhetoric: closed borders, foreign hands, a nation supposedly under siege.
2. He insists he's "just being realistic" about immigration, but half the pub can hear how xenophobic it sounds.
The alien in Alien is a Xenomorph — literally "strange form," the outsider whose foreignness is the whole horror.
Greek xenos = "stranger, foreigner" + phobos = "fear."

Xenos is worth banking: xenon (the noble gas, named "the strange one" because it wouldn't react with anything), xenophile (a lover of the foreign — the exact opposite), xenograft (tissue transplanted from another species).

And phobos gives you every -phobia you'll ever meet — plus Phobos, the moon of Mars named for the god of Fear.

To produce as a return; or to give way under pressure.
Verb, sense 1: to produce or give forth as a return — a crop, a profit, a result. Sense 2: to give way — to surrender ground, position, or the right of way under pressure. Noun: the amount produced (a harvest's yield, a bond's yield).

Yielding is softer than surrendering. Capitulate and submit imply defeat; yield implies give — the thing bends rather than breaks, and often does so gracefully, reasonably, or tactically ("I yield to my colleague"). It can even be a courtesy rather than a loss. Note the two adjectives the GRE loves: yielding = pliant, soft, easily pressed; unyielding = rigid, inflexible, refusing an inch.
Hidden inside yield is field: a field gives up its crop, a driver gives up the road.
Every sense is the same act of giving over — producing, conceding, bending — which is exactly why unyielding means "won't give an inch."
1. The negotiators, unyielding for three days, finally yielded on the question of tariffs.
2. Push the door hard — the latch sticks, but it'll yield eventually.
The red-and-white triangular YIELD sign at a junction: not "stop," not "go" — give way to whoever's already there. That's the whole nuance of the word in one road sign.
Old English gieldan = "to pay, repay" (cognate with German Geld, "money"). Payment is the thread through all three senses: a field pays you a crop, a bond pays you a yield, and a driver pays over the right of way.

Same root gives you guild — originally a group bound by the dues its members paid in.

Fervently, tirelessly devoted to a cause — sometimes excessively.
Burning with energetic devotion to a cause, belief, or duty — and acting on it tirelessly.

Where eager and enthusiastic describe a mood, zealous describes a mission: there is always something being served. It sits one notch below fanatical and knows it — praise a zealous reformer and you concede the intensity might be too much. The word admires the commitment while raising an eyebrow at the person.
Zealous always takes a cause: a zealous convert, a zealous prosecutor, a zealous defender of tradition. Nobody is just zealous.
Eagerness lives in you; zeal is aimed at something outside you, which is exactly why it can tip over into zealotry.
1. The new inspector was zealous to a fault, citing kitchens for infractions his predecessor had waved through for twenty years.
2. He's gone zealous about the gym — six a.m., every day, and he will tell you about it.
Every lawyer swears by it: the professional standard is "zealous advocacy" — the duty to push your client's case as hard as the rules allow. It's the one context where being too committed is the job description.
Greek zēlos = "ardour, fervent rivalry." It splits into two English branches: zeal / zealous / zealot (burning for a cause) and — through Old French jalous — jealous, the same fire turned possessive. Zeal wants the cause; jealousy wants to keep it.

The highest point — of the sky, or of a career.
The highest point — literally, the point of the sky directly overhead; figuratively, the peak of someone's power, fame, or fortune.

Where peak is flat and everyday and pinnacle suggests a hard-won summit, zenith borrows its grandeur from the sky — it's the word for empires, careers, and reputations, not for stock prices this week. It also carries an arc: something rose to get here, and the phrasing "at the zenith of his power" almost always means the narrator knows what came afterwards. Used of the present it flatters; used of the past it quietly announces the decline.
Z is where the alphabet tops out and stops — the zenith is where the climb tops out and stops.
The word marks a summit already reached, so whatever comes next is descent rather than more rise.
1. At the zenith of its influence the company set prices that three continents simply paid.
2. He hit his zenith at twenty-four and has been dining out on it ever since.
Weather and astronomy use it literally every day: the sun is at its zenith at local noon — straight overhead, as high as it will get, and sinking from that moment on.
Arabic samt al-ra's = "the path over the head." Medieval scribes copying the Latin misread samt as senit — and the typo became the English word.

That same samt gives you azimuth (a compass direction), and its opposite point in the sky, nadir, is Arabic too (naẓīr, "counterpart"). Three GRE-friendly words straight out of Arabic astronomy: zenith overhead, nadir underfoot, azimuth around the horizon.
